In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
The introduction


All praise is due to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, and peace and blessings be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and all his companions, and upon those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.
And I bear witness that there is no deity except Allah alone, with no partner for Him, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. He conveyed the message and fulfilled the trust, and he bore witness to the nation and called Allah as a witness to that. He said: "O Allah, have I conveyed [the message]?" They said: Yes. He said: "O Allah, bear witness," three times they said: Yes, they bear witness for themselves, and he (peace and blessings be upon him) bears witness for them, then Allah, Exalted is He, bears witness to that. Then he (peace and blessings be upon him) joined the highest companion, and the companions after him carried the trust and fulfilled it in the best manner, and they conveyed it to those after them, and the truth appeared and falsehood perished, Islam prevailed and darkness was dispelled.
Then after them came a generation that neglected the trust and thus they were lost; they exchanged fire for light, so they were burned and did not find illumination. They forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves; they became deaf while they could hear, their eyes see but they are blind and do not perceive. They have hearts with which they desire, but they do not understand, and they are constricted in their chests. Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the true guidance, and whoever Allah guides is the rightly guided, and whoever He leads astray, you will not find for him a guiding ally." As for what follows,


[Page 2]

Indeed, Allah - Exalted is He - has revealed the best of speech, a Book that guides to that which is most upright, guiding thereby those who follow His pleasure to the paths of peace. He has clarified and defined the path of truth and faith, as well as the paths of misguidance and the devil, and He commanded to follow His chosen one and intimate friend, saying: { Say, "This is my path; I invite to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me." } (1). He prohibited following the devil and warned, saying: { And do not follow the footsteps of the devil. } (2). He commanded to oppose and fight him, saying: { Indeed, the devil is to you a foe, so take him as a foe. } (3). He commanded that He alone be worshipped and that none other be worshipped, for what He has deemed good is good, and what He has deemed evil is evil, and there is no one to overturn His decree. { The judgment is only for Allah. He has commanded that you not worship except Him. } (4), { And it is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should have any choice in their matter. } (5). The trust that Allah and His Messenger have testified we must carry is to worship Allah alone, to make people worship Him, and to bear witness to this among the people, conveying it to them and subjecting them to it, { And thus We have made you a just nation that you will be witnesses over the people and the Messenger will be a witness over you. } (6).
However, Allah - Glorified and Exalted - has willed that the situation remains as it is, and He is more eloquent than any speech, for those who understand the meaning of the message, the meaning of the trust, the meaning of the testimony, and the meaning of Allah's commands and prohibitions, and what Allah has said. Exalted is He.
__________
(1) Surah Yusuf, 108.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 168.
(3) Surah Fatir, 6.
(4) Surah Yusuf, 40.
(5) Surah Al-Ahzab, 36.
(6) Surah Al-Baqarah, 143.


[Page 3]

And indeed, it is among the things that deepen the decline, the confusion of misguidance, and the distance of error, that the eyes become dazzled by the light of fire, and the hearts that are in the chests become blind, so that the disease is imagined to be a cure, and poison is thought to be an antidote, and the liar is believed, while the truthful is denied, and the trustworthy is betrayed, while the treacherous is entrusted, and that the ignorant is listened to, and the knowledgeable are blinded to the light, and they hasten to follow the one who says: "This fire is light and that light is fire."
This is because after the rule of Islam was removed from life, and the rule of tyranny was substituted for it, a group emerged that alters and distorts, attributing to the rulings of disbelief the quality of legitimacy, the legitimacy of Islam, emptying Islam of its substance and filling it with something else, new, and they invoke renewal, interpreting and changing to reconcile between the rulings of Islam and the rulings of disbelief, and they justify it as development, or under the pretext of keeping up with the times or preserving what remains.
And one of them says: "Let not your eyelids flutter, O Muslims! For Islam is flexible and suitable for every time and place," and with these and other claims, Islam, in the name of Islam, is stripped of its truth and essence, and becomes something else.
The distorters, in the name of renewal and development, have found the idea of interests (masalih) and objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), so they leaned on it, claiming that the Sharia came for the interests of the servants, thus reversing the truth, and instead of it being: "the interest is where the Sharia is," they claimed that "the Sharia is where the interest is." The objectives of the Sharia became a substitute for the Sharia itself. And if it is said: "O people, the Sharia, the Sharia!"


[Page 4]

Those whose efforts have gone astray in this worldly life while they think they are doing good – in the best of cases – said: "Leave these people alone, for they are stagnant, they do not evolve, nor do they innovate, and they do not understand reality. Indeed, there are secrets in the Sharia (law) and priorities and balances in the religion. When these texts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah confront them, they become confused and evasive, they search and dig, then they take snippets and say." Among the things they said were: "The interests (masalih) and the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), al-Shatibi and the Muwafaqat of al-Shatibi, the Muwafaqat: the masterpiece of al-Shatibi, the Sheikh of the objectives." They took snippets and then had the audacity to say: "Those who confront us with the texts are still governed by the complex of the text, and they delude themselves that they are people of jurisprudence (fiqh) while others are merely literalists." What audacity is this! And what kind of jurisprudence is this! And among whom do they rush!
The researcher examined these statements and opinions.
The interests (masalih), and the unregulated interests (masalih mursala)! That's fine, let it be, but what you have brought forth is neither interests nor unregulated interests; it is, in the terminology of usul al-fiqh, nullified interests, contradicted by the texts, so they are, therefore, corruptions (mafasid).
The objectives, the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia)! Yes, let it be, but what you have brought forth is not the objectives of the Sharia; it is your objectives, or the objectives of the sick-hearted. So where in the objectives of the Sharia does the preservation of religion become the freedom of belief and the right to change one's religion? And where in the objectives of the Sharia is the abrogation of the Sharia, so that apostasy becomes a human right, and the killing of an apostate becomes a crime? And is it in the objectives of the Sharia that the text states: { and He has forbidden usury } (1) and the objective is: usury is permissible, with time and place being sufficient for that!
And where in the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) does the preservation of wealth mean the freedom of ownership, and the preservation of the intellect mean the freedom of opinion? Is this in our religion, we Muslims?
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 275.


[Page 5]

They said: Al-Shatibi and the new al-Shatibi, the Muwafaqat, and how much we need what is in it!
Is al-Shatibi to sacrifice the religion on the thresholds of its objectives, and to dissect the belly of the Sharia at the doorsteps of public interest (maslaha)?
The researcher looked into the Muwafaqat and studied it from beginning to end, and from end to beginning. It contains depth, and its author is one with intention, and it requires reflection and re-reflection; so let it be, the researcher immersed himself in it and contemplated it well. The result was that al-Shatibi is slandered by one group and misunderstood by another.
In summary, al-Shatibi is innocent of what is attributed to him regarding public interests and objectives. The researcher continued studying al-Shatibi through al-I'tisam, and found that those who take him as a veil behind which they hide are, in his view, innovators.
The Muwafaqat does not agree with these people, and al-Shatibi warns against them and their methodology. From here arose the motivations for researching this topic, which can be summarized as follows:
1 - Religion is a duty and a trust upon everyone who comprehends it. The researcher saw it as his duty to clarify that the objectives of the Sharia do not negate the Sharia, nor do they invalidate its rulings. If the objectives are the objectives of the Sharia, they are a branch of it, and the Sharia is the root; it is not correct for the branch to invalidate the root. There must be a confrontation with any thought or proposal that calls for disregarding the Sharia or transgressing its limits, especially if it is done in the name of Islam.
2 - Since some have clung to al-Shatibi and his Muwafaqat, attributing to him what he does not say, and what he has consistently warned against, it was necessary to clarify the reality of this matter, and that there is no basis in al-Shatibi or in the Muwafaqat for anyone who wishes to alter or change the rulings of the Sharia under the pretext of its objectives, whether with good or bad intentions.
3 - As the discussions about al-Shatibi and his ideas regarding the objectives or his theory in them increased, and about his new approach to understanding the Sharia, research was presented on this and around it, in books, on the pages of magazines and newspapers, and on television screens, and the researcher found that all of it was far from al-Shatibi and from his ideas, methodology, or innovations; he felt that he had to clarify what he sees as correct in this regard.


[Page 6]

And the researcher sees that this work is among the works of carrying the call, and among the works of dialogue or intellectual struggle. He asks Allah, Exalted is He, to grant this work acceptance with Him, and to bestow upon it great reward and recompense.
I intended for this book to be a study of the true concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi. Therefore, its subject is an analytical study of al-Shatibi's ideas, particularly what he has written in the book al-Muwafaqat. This book is an analytical study of the texts of al-Muwafaqat.
In this study, I relied on the edition that was prepared by the two scholars Muhammad al-Khidr Hussein from Tunisia and Muhammad Hasanein Makhlouf. It consists of four volumes in two volumes, where the first scholar prepared the first and second volumes, and the second scholar prepared the third and fourth volumes. Thus, whenever I refer to or cite al-Muwafaqat, I have referred to this edition, and if I refer to another, I will note that.
I have not provided biographical information about the figures in this book except briefly and where I found it necessary, such as the figures who are frequently cited.
I have extracted all the verses that appeared in the book. I have also extracted all the hadiths mentioned in it in a concise manner, relying on the CD of the Noble Hadith Encyclopedia program, produced by Sakhr Company, second edition, which contains the nine books of hadith (mentioned in the list of sources and references), and it relies on global numbering. Whenever I did not find sufficient information in this program, I indicated the book or books from which I derived it, mentioning the name of the book, its edition, the hadith number, the volume, and the page.
I have not included any statement or opinion of al-Shatibi without substantiating it with a text or texts from him, even if this opinion had been clarified in a previous chapter, in order to maintain the completeness of the chapter's unity and its independence as much as possible. Often, I have provided more than one text to indicate al-Shatibi's position or opinion, in order to prevent misinterpretation of his statements.


[Page 7]

I have structured this book or this study with an introduction, followed by a definition of al-Shatibi and his era, then ten chapters and a brief conclusion, followed by indexes of the noble verses and the honorable hadiths, sources and references, and then the contents of the book.
Chapter One: The Introduction to the Emergence of the Idea of the Objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia). It contains an introduction to the emergence of the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) and its development, along with three sections: the first on qiyas (analogy), the second on the pathways of the cause and its conditions, and the third on the pathway of the relationship and suitability, which are necessary for entering the discussions of usul al-fiqh, qiyas, and ta'leel (causal reasoning). In particular, the pathway of the relationship and suitability serves as a prelude to the idea of the objectives of the Sharia.
Chapter Two: The Emergence of the Idea of the Objectives of the Sharia. It contains a brief presentation of the emergence of the idea, followed by three sections on how it originated and developed among the scholars of usul before al-Shatibi, which forms a prelude to the idea of the objectives according to al-Shatibi.
Chapter Three: The Criteria for the Objectives According to al-Shatibi. It contains three sections, the first and second on the preliminaries and criteria, then the references and foundations that al-Shatibi deemed necessary for understanding his book (al-Muwafaqat), and the third section on the results and the concept of benefit (maslaha) and harm (mafsada) according to al-Shatibi.
Chapter Four: The Intention of the Legislator in Establishing the Sharia Initially and in Establishing it for Understanding. It discusses the types of the legislator's objectives, which are four, and the statements of al-Shatibi and his methodology in understanding the two types: the first being the establishment of the Sharia initially, and the second being its establishment for understanding.
Chapter Five: The Intention of the Legislator in Establishing the Sharia for Obligatory Acts and in the Subjection of the Obligated to Its Rulings. It discusses the statements of al-Shatibi and his methodology in understanding the two types: the third being the establishment of the Sharia for obligatory acts, and the fourth being the subjection of the obligated to the rulings of the Sharia.
Chapter Six: The Objectives of the Obligated. It contains a prelude and three sections explaining the impact of intention or objective in the actions of the obligated, the impact of agreement or disagreement between the intention of the legislator and the intention of the obligated in action, and an explanation of legal tricks (hiyal) and al-Shatibi's stance on them.


[Page 8]

Chapter Seven: Al-Shatibi's Methodology in Understanding the Sharia. It contains three sections explaining al-Shatibi's methodology in establishing the rules and principles solely through induction. His methodology in understanding the Sharia and deriving rulings in general, as well as his methodology and views on understanding the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is one of the most important applications of his ideas in the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia).

Chapter Eight: Ijtihad and Taqlid. This chapter discusses al-Shatibi's views on ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), taqlid (following a legal school), and fatwa (legal opinion) and the criteria for each, as well as the qualified mujtahid (jurist) and its conditions. It is similar to the previous chapter in terms of its importance as it is a result of his ideas on the objectives of the Sharia, and it includes a section on the principle of the consequences of actions according to him.

Chapter Nine: Applying the Idea: Three General Principles. This chapter explains the application of his idea of induction and establishing principles through the study of three general principles in three sections. The first: on the principle of public interest (maslaha) that is not explicitly stated, the second on the principle of istihsan (juridical preference), and the third on the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i), which includes a discussion on the principle of harm.

Chapter Ten: The Idea of Maqasid According to Al-Shatibi: Presentation and Discussion. It contains three sections, the first presenting his idea and highlighting its foundation and pillars briefly. The second and third sections discuss al-Shatibi's idea and methodology through examining its foundation and pillars.

Introduction to Al-Shatibi and His Era

Introduction to Al-Shatibi:
He is Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Musa ibn Muhammad al-Lakhmi al-Gharnati, known as al-Shatibi(1), one of the scholars of the Maliki school in al-Andalus.
He became known as al-Shatibi due to his ancestry from Shatiba, and his family sought refuge in Granada after the fall of Shatiba to the Christians.
Al-Shatibi lived his entire life in Granada during the eighth century of the Hijra. There is some disagreement regarding his birth and death, but it is generally accepted that he died in the year 790 AH - 1388 CE. This is based on one of his students, Abu Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Asim, who composed the book Al-Muwafaqat in six thousand verses, mentioning the date of his death, saying (in verse):

__________
(1) Ahmad Baba al-Tanbukti, Nail al-Ibtihaj bi-Tatwir al-Dibaj, p. 46, in the margin of Al-Dibaj by Ibn Farhun, 1st ed., Dar al-Saada, Egypt, 1329 AH.


[Page 9]

Until his life came to an end ... in the year ninety to seven hundred(1)


Ahmad Baba al-Tanbukti said: "He passed away on Tuesday in the month of Sha'ban in the year 790, and I have not come across his date of birth, may Allah have mercy on him."(2)
As for his birth, there is no verified statement regarding it. The Tanbukti, whose book is considered one of the most precise references for his biography, states that he did not come across the date of his birth.
Dr. Hamadi al-Abidi has favored the view that his birth was around 730 AH based on the fact that he was a close friend and peer of the minister Ibn Zamrak, who was born in 733 AH, and based on his understanding that al-Shatibi was young in 756(3).
As for Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, he preferred in his introduction to the book Fatwas of al-Shatibi(4) that al-Shatibi was born before the year 720 AH, based on the fact that the death of his earlier teacher Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn al-Zayyat was in the year 728 AH. Therefore, at the very least, al-Shatibi must have been young at that time, and he referred to this matter in his introduction to the book al-Ifadat wa al-Inshadat(5).
__________
(1) Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, verification and commentary on the book of al-Ifadat wa al-Inshadat by al-Shatibi, p. 32, 2nd ed., 1406 AH, 1986 CE, Al-Risalah Foundation, Beirut.
(2) al-Tanbukti, Nail al-Ibtihaj, p. 46.
(3) Hamadi al-Abidi, al-Shatibi and the Objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), p. 12, 1st ed., 1412 AH - 1992 CE, Dar al-Qutayba, Beirut and Damascus.
(4) This book is not by al-Shatibi, but was published by Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, and it contains the fatwas of al-Shatibi from his two books: al-Muwafaqat and al-I'tisam.
(5) See: Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, his commentary on the "Al-Irfadat wa al-Inshadat" by al-Shatibi, p. 17, footnote number 2.


[Page 10]

The more likely view is that of Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, and his argument in this regard is sound. As for Dr. al-Ubaidi's statement, it holds no weight. The friendship between Ibn Zamrak and al-Shatibi does not prevent one from being twenty years older than the other or more. Furthermore, there is no evidence that al-Shatibi was young in the year 756 AH. This statement is a confusion between his two reports, number 66 and number 67, where he mentioned in one of them the date of the death of his earlier teachers, and in the other that he was young, but the two reports are different and unrelated to each other(1).
His Era:
Al-Shatibi lived in the city of Granada(2) during the time of the Nasrid kings, in the state of Banu Nasr, which at that time did not enjoy stability, primarily due to the Christians' attempts to eradicate Islam in Andalusia. To illustrate the conditions of the era in which al-Shatibi lived and to shed light on the features of this period, it is useful to refer to historical milestones in the lives of Muslims in Andalusia.
The Islamic state in Andalusia was founded by Abd al-Rahman ibn Muawiya ibn Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, nicknamed the Falcon of Quraish. He was known as Abd al-Rahman al-Dakhil because he was the first of the Umayyad princes to enter Andalusia after fleeing and escaping from the Abbasids(3). He entered Cordoba in the year 139 AH, as a conqueror, and then he established the foundations of the state, independent from the caliphate, but he did not call himself caliph.
The Abbasids attempted to reclaim Andalusia in the year 149 AH but failed.
__________
(1) See: al-Shatibi, al-Ifadāt wa al-Inshādāt, report number 66, and report number 67, p. 143, which is the source mentioned earlier, edited by Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan.
(2) Al-Fayruzabadi said in al-Qamus al-Muhit: Granada: "And the correct form is: Aghranata. Its meaning is: the pomegranate, in the Andalusian dialect," p. 877, Dar al-Ma'rifah and Dar al-Mu'ayyid, supervised by Muhammad Na'im al-Arqousi, 1415 AH - 1994 CE.
(3) Ibrahim al-Sharifi, Islamic History, p. 149, 2nd ed., Nofal Foundation - Beirut, 1391 AH - 1971 CE.


[Page 11]

Charlemagne, the king of the Franks, attempted, in collaboration with the rulers of the Spanish cities, to eliminate the emirate of Abd al-Rahman, but he failed.
Abdul Rahman revitalized and developed his emirate, encouraging the sciences and arts, agriculture, and industry, so that Cordoba became the capital of Al-Andalus. The civil and architectural manifestations were evident through its mosques, institutes, palaces, and gardens. Development continued after him, and the civilization of Al-Andalus was reflected in the active intellectual and cultural movement. Cordoba received special attention in terms of urban development, beauty, the construction of hospitals, houses of knowledge, and places of worship. Sciences and knowledge spread, seminars and intellectual and philosophical discussions were held, translation flourished, and Al-Andalus thrived, enjoying security and stability. Many Spaniards embraced Islam, and among them emerged writers who contributed to the spread of the Arabic language(1).
Then weak princes succeeded to the rule, and weakness spread within the body of the state for sixty-two years, until Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir took power in the year 300 AH. During his reign, al-Andalus reached its golden age, prosperity prevailed, and urban, agricultural, and industrial projects were realized, in addition to the mosques, schools, and hospitals that were established. Palaces were built, streets were illuminated with lanterns, lush gardens spread, and students from all over al-Andalus came to study in its institutes and universities. The wealth of the country increased, and the state's resources multiplied. A great deal was spent, and much was saved. Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir's rule lasted fifty years, from 300 to 350 AH, and he called himself caliph(2).
Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir was succeeded by his son al-Hakam, who ruled for 16 years, during which he focused on the development of the country. He was then succeeded by weak rulers who handed over the governance to others, leading to its loss, and the ambitious seized power from them, resulting in the fall of the caliphate in the year 417 AH. Small states emerged in the cities, and their rulers were known as the kings of the factions.
__________
(1) Ibrahim al-Sharifi, Islamic History, p. 153.
(2) See: the same reference: p. 154 - 155.


[Page 12]

These conditions of division, weakness, conflict, and ambitions encouraged the Christian states in the north to pounce on the Muslims.
And when the danger intensified in Andalusia and the kings of the taifa (small kingdoms) were unable to repel the attack of the Christian kingdoms that united in northern Spain, al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad, the king of Seville, sought help from the Almoravids, the rulers of Morocco. Their forces crossed into Andalusia and inflicted a crushing defeat on the armies of the Christian kingdoms at the Battle of Zallaqa in the year 479 AH - 1086 CE. The assistance of the Almoravids and their overwhelming victory played a crucial role in saving Andalusia and maintaining the Islamic presence there.
Once the danger subsided, the Muslim princes returned to infighting and disputes over power, and the contagion spread to the rulers of Morocco, leading to discord among them and weakening their authority. The Christian rulers in northern Spain seized the opportunity and prepared armies to invade the southern states, resulting in the fall of all of them except for Granada, which remained steadfast like a towering mountain. The fall of Córdoba occurred in the year 634 AH - 1236 CE, and Seville in the year 646 AH - 1248 CE (1).
__________
(1) See, Ibrahim al-Sharifi, p. 157.


[Page 13]

During this time, one of the kings of the taifa states emerged, namely Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Hud, who was titled Amir al-Muslimin Sif al-Dawla, the one who relies on Allah. He controlled a number of important Andalusian cities, including Cordoba and Granada. In the year 635 AH - 1238 CE, Ibn Hud passed away, and Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr, known as Ibn al-Ahmar (1), appeared, the founder of the Nasrid dynasty, and he declared himself the Amir of southern Andalusia, making Granada the capital of his state. This was in the year 635 AH - 1238 CE (2).
The era of Muhammad ibn al-Ahmar was characterized by the strengthening of his state and the growth of its wealth. The Nasrids stood against the armies of the northern Christians, repelling them with determination and faith. Granada became the center of the Muslims and their major stronghold in Andalusia after the kingdoms and states fell before the attacks of the Christian kings who united to eradicate Islam. The Muslims were expelled from their lands and paid tribute to the infidels, yet the Islamic presence in Andalusia continued for more than two and a half centuries after Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Nasr (Muhammad ibn al-Ahmar), nicknamed al-Shaykh al-Ghalib bi-Allah, managed to establish and strengthen his state in southern Andalusia (3).
__________
(1) Ibn al-Ahmar's lineage goes back to Sa'd ibn Ubadah, the Ansari Khazraj companion. See: History of Morocco and Andalusia, previously referenced with a citation to Subh al-A'sha in the Art of Composition by al-Qalqashandi, 5/260.
(2) See: History of Morocco and Andalusia from the 6th century AH to the 10th century AH, authored by Dr. Ahmad Audat, Dr. Shahada al-Natour, Dr. Jamil Baydoun, and Mr. Muhammad Muhasina. Dar al-Amal for Publishing and Distribution, Irbid, 1st edition, 1410 AH - 1990 CE.
(3) See: Ibrahim al-Sharifi, Islamic History, p. 157. And History of Morocco and Andalusia, p. 2.


[Page 14]

However, this state was unable to protect the Muslims in Andalusia, so cities and fortresses fell, which aroused the ambitions of the Christians who tried to eliminate Granada, but they could not, and Granada grew stronger(1). Granada became a refuge for Muslims fleeing from the advance of the Christians since the establishment of the Nasrid state. Al-Maqri says: "When the Franks seized most of the lands of Andalusia, its people migrated there, and it became the desired city"(2).
During the era of Granada, there were three powerful Christian kingdoms: Portugal, Aragon, and Castile, with the latter being the strongest of these kingdoms. Each of these kingdoms was individually stronger than Granada. They united their forces and sought assistance from others, launching crusades against Granada, and were able to achieve some victories, yet they did not accomplish their objectives.
Then the Crusader forces gathered and attacked Granada, and the Muslims sought assistance from Morocco, and events and wars took place in which the Muslims achieved a tremendous victory in the year 674 AH.
The conflict continued, and in the year 718 AH, the Castilians attacked Granada and advanced upon it with the help of the English. The Muslims sought assistance from the Marinids in Morocco, and they responded. The Muslims were able to achieve victory and defeat the Franks in a battle near Granada(3).
The confrontations between the Muslims and the Spaniards continued, and the Muslims were defeated in a naval battle in the year 740 AH - 1339 CE, in which forces from Aragon, Castile, and Portugal participated. A battle occurred in the year 741 AH, which was the Battle of Tarifa, in which the Muslims used cannons that fired flames for the first time, but they lost the battle. The Crusaders, when victorious in a battle, committed the most heinous atrocities against the Muslims(4).

(2) Abu al-Abbas Ahmad al-Maqri, Nafh al-Tayyib fi Ghusn al-Andalus al-Ratib, 1/148, 7 volumes, edited by Ihsan Abbas, 1st edition, Dar Sader - Beirut.
(3) See: History of Morocco and Andalusia, p. 165.
(4) See: The History of Morocco and Al-Andalus, p. 169.


[Page 15]

And the Spaniards began to wreak havoc and destruction in the lands of Andalusia. Despite all this, Granada remained strong, and peace treaties were concluded between the Muslims and the Spaniards, including a peace treaty with Pedro IV in the year 736 - 789 AH, 1336 - 1387 CE. Security and peace prevailed in the realms of the Kingdom of Granada, and it flourished. Despite the Spaniards' attempts to divide the properties of Granada, they failed(1).
In the year 867 AH, Gibraltar fell into the hands of the Castilians, which was a severe blow to the Muslims, and the arrival of supplies from Morocco to Al-Andalus came to a halt(2).
And the rule of Granada was taken over in the year 887 AH - 1482 CE by Muhammad ibn Ali, nicknamed Abu Abdullah al-Saghir, who agreed to surrender Granada in the year 897 AH - 1492 CE to the monarchs of Castile and Aragon, and he departed to Morocco. Thus, the Islamic state in Andalusia came to an end, and it was said about this Abu Abdullah al-Saghir (the light):


Weep like women for a kingdom that was lost... You did not preserve it like men.


The political situation:
This was a reference to historical milestones and events that the Muslims of Andalusia went through. These events explain the migration of the al-Shatibi family to Granada. They also clarify the political situation of the time of al-Shatibi, but there are events that shed greater light on the political situation of the time of al-Shatibi, that is, the eighth century of the Hijra.
__________
(1) See: the same reference, p. 172.
(2) See: the same reference, pp. 172 - 174.


[Page 16]

Lisan al-Din ibn al-Khatib (1) said: "After al-Ghalib, by the command of Allah, the founder of the state, his son and namesake Sultan Abu Abdullah took over, and his reign lasted until he died in 701 AH. After him, his son and namesake Abu Abdullah Muhammad took over, but he was deposed on the day of Eid al-Fitr in 708 AH, and he died in Shawwal of 711. After him, his brother Nasr Abu al-Juyush took over, but his situation became chaotic, and he sought power from his uncle's son Sultan Abu al-Walid Ismail, who seized the governor's house on the second of Dhul-Qi'dah in 713 AH. Nasr was deposed and moved to the city of Wadi Ash, where he died in 722 AH. The reign of Sultan Abu al-Walid continued until the 23rd of Rajab in 725, when he was attacked by his cousin along with a group of his relatives, and they killed him at his door. Their efforts were in vain, and they were all killed that day. His son Muhammad took over and continued until Dhul-Hijjah of 734, when he was killed at the foot of Jabal al-Fath by his troops from the Maghreb. After him, his brother Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf took over, and his reign lasted until the day of Eid al-Fitr in 755" (2), and he was killed during his prayer (3).

(1) He was a minister in the Nasrid state.

[Page 17]

"Then Sultan Muhammad V, known as al-Ghani Billah, assumed the emirate and continued from 755 AH to 793 AH. His rule faced bloody events during this period. He was subjected to a coup in the year 760, after which he fled to Morocco and returned in 763. Granada experienced three successive coups during these three years: the first in the month of Ramadan in the year 760, which ended with the flight of Sultan al-Ghani Billah to Morocco and the ascension of his brother Ismail II in his place. The second coup occurred in Sha'ban in the year 761, in which Ismail II was killed and the murderer, Abu Said al-Barmikh, who was his sister's husband, took the throne. The third coup in Jumada al-Thani in the year 763 resulted in the return of al-Ghani Billah to his throne, and al-Barmikh was killed by the King of Castile."(1)
Some sources indicate that al-Barmikh was addicted to hashish, and this vice spread among the people openly, and poems were composed about it.(2)

[Page 18]

The tongue of Lisan al-Din Ibn al-Khatib speaks of the tyranny of the Bermejo and his consumption of the people's wealth, saying: "He was a tyrant (1), devouring the fodder and pasture, and by eliminating the crops, he deprived the means of prosperity, opened the doors of calamity, and permitted some taxes (2), giving a little and then withholding (3). Days did not pass before he returned to his tyranny (4) and oppressed the subjects with his evil, burdening them with the need to tether their horses after drowning their provisions for his soldiers" (5).
Economic Condition:
From what has been mentioned, it is evident that there was a rise followed by a decline in the state of Al-Andalus, which is reflected in the emergence and growth of the state, then its decline and fall. This is also evident in the growth of wealth and the increase in spending and saving, followed by a worsening of need, which was witnessed during the era of al-Shatibi.
Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan states: "We learn from a text directed to al-Shatibi that Muslims needed some essential resources, and some questioned: Does this need permit them to sell to the disbelievers what they had been prohibited from selling to them because it strengthens them? The text of the question is: Is it permissible for the people of Al-Andalus to sell items that the scholars prohibited selling to the people of war, such as weapons and others, due to their necessity for essentials in other matters like food and clothing, or is there no difference between the people of Al-Andalus and others in the lands of Islam?" (6).

[Page 19]

He points to the food shortage, saying: "As indicated by another inquiry, the food shortage drove them to exploit the maritime resource, but the charter of the ships was made without the wage being known at the time of the contract. They wondered: how could this be when the situation in the Andalusian region is not hidden, or its need for food, and most of its food now comes from the sea, and many of the people of the region seek to cause the establishment of a ship or to buy one, yet they are prevented from that by the chartering in the aforementioned manner, while the situation in the homeland is not concealed and the necessity is evident" (1).
Among the indicators of economic weakness is the state's inability to meet the needs of the people and its need to impose taxes. This is evident in the differing opinions of the scholars, as due to the political conditions and external wars, a financial crisis befell the state. The government of Granada consulted the jurists regarding the permissibility of imposing additional taxes on the people of the kingdom to meet the mobilization for combat, but they refrained from that. However, al-Shatibi deviated from their consensus and issued a fatwa permitting it, saying: "If we appoint an obeyed Imam, in need of increasing the soldiers to defend the borders and protect the kingdom that spans vast territories, and the treasury is empty while the needs of the soldiers rise to what is insufficient for them, then it is permissible for the Imam, if he is just, to impose on the wealthy what he deems sufficient for them in wealth until the treasury's funds become apparent. Then he has the discretion to impose that on the crops, fruits, and other things so that the specification of people does not lead to estrangement of hearts, and this occurs rarely in many cases such that it does not harm anyone and achieves the intended goal" (2).

(1) Same reference, p. 14.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 2/380. Edited by Abdul Razzaq al-Mahdi, Dar al-Kitab al-Arabi, 2nd ed., 1418 AH - 1998 CE.


[Page 20]

The reports indicating the loss of wealth and savings in Andalusia are numerous, and this situation that the economic condition has reached indicates a decline and deterioration, but does not indicate famine. Therefore, these conditions do not prevent the existence of wealth and luxury in society. Professor Abu al-Ajfan says: "Despite this tumultuous situation, a kind of extravagance spreads, along with a penchant for jewelry among the wealthy elite, and an artistry in adornment and extravagance in the forms of ornaments among women, as well as a passion for music that becomes widespread even in the shops frequented by the youth"(1).
Scientific Condition:
The level of scholarship and the prevailing cultural climate in Granada during the life of al-Shatibi was good and flourishing, and it did not decline significantly and suddenly except with the fall of Granada and its submission to its enemy. However, it is noted that this level gradually declined in accordance with the political situation. Whenever the rulers had a vision of expansion and the spread of Islam, this was followed by the dissemination and expansion of Islamic sciences, along with a cultural movement. Wherever the rulers exerted effort to maintain stability or the existing situation within their borders, and to maintain a steady level of influence and interaction, this condition was followed by stagnation. This means that the movement of scientific production and the cultural movement in society would stabilize. This was the case in Granada, had it not become a destination and gathering place for scholars coming from all parts of Andalusia, which led to an interaction that affected scientific, intellectual, cultural, industrial, and artistic activity.
__________
(1) Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, commentary and annotation on the "Irfadat wa al-Inshadat" of al-Shatibi, pp. 14, 15, referencing the "Lamhah al-Badriyah" of Ibn al-Khatib, pp. 28, 29.


[Page 21]

Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan said: "As for the cultural climate that Granada experienced during the life of al-Shatibi, it was relatively flourishing, as the tradition of scientific interest continued, and scholars engaged in enriching the reservoir of knowledge with their writings and research, while the chain of hadith and the narration of books of knowledge and the documentation of the programs (1) of the scholars persisted" (2).
Education and authorship were active, and two large scientific institutions were established in Granada: the Great Mosque and the Nasrid School. Authorship covered various branches of empirical, legal, and philosophical sciences. Professor Abu al-Ajfan states: "Thus, the scientific movement was flourishing until the late eighth century, indicating a strength that was able to resist the period of decline that was seeping into Andalusia and pushing it toward its inevitable fate. The thinkers and scholars of Andalusia during this turbulent time made attempts at reform and healing divisions, called for jihad, instilled a spirit of determination in souls, and raised awareness of the looming danger" (3).
__________
(1) Programs: "A type of record that includes the scholars of its authors and what they took from them in narrations, and what they read to them from books, or it includes the scholars of a particular scholar whom another person undertook to gather and mention what was taken from them." See: Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, his edition of the Book of Programs of al-Majari, p. 59, and the book is by Abu Abdullah Muhammad al-Majari al-Andalusi, who died in 862 AH, 1st ed., 1984, Dar al-Gharb al-Islami, Beirut - Lebanon.
(2) See: Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, his edition of the Al-Irfadat wa al-Inshadat of al-Shatibi, p. 15.
(3) The same reference, p. 17.


[Page 22]

He also said: "Industries flourished in this kingdom that the inhabitants mastered and inherited from their ancestors who built the most magnificent civilization in the Andalusian peninsula. Among these were the manufacturing of weapons, silk and woolen fabrics, ceramic vessels, various types of paper and leather. The export of these industries provided income and stimulated commercial activity. The southerners and other nations with close economic ties to Andalusia had commercial establishments in Granada, and Granada entered into trade treaties with the Republic of Genoa and the Kingdom of Aragon" (1).
This atmosphere witnessed a surge in the pursuit of knowledge and in scientific and jurisprudential dialogue and discussion, and its results appeared in the enthusiasm for authorship and research, with the names of scholars shining brightly and their works becoming well-known. At the forefront of each field were prominent figures such as Ibn al-Fakhar al-Biri in the sciences of language, Ibn al-Saigh and Abu Hayyan in the science of grammar in particular, Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence), Ibn Jazi and Ibn Asim in fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Zamrak in literature and politics, Ibn Hudhayl the Wise in philosophy, and many others besides them (2).
__________
(1) Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan, in his work on the sewer program, p. 15, referring to the end of Andalusia, Muhammad Abdullah Anan, 1st ed., Egypt, 1949.
(2) Hamadi al-Abidi, al-Shatibi and the Objectives of the Sharia, pp. 47-50, referring to: Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, Isn't the dawn near?, p. 79, 1st ed., Tunisian Distribution Company.


[Page 23]

However, there is a matter that should be pointed out, which is that this flourishing in terms of science and culture does not necessarily indicate health and the continuation of progress. Indeed, Andalusia has gone through periods of scientific and cultural, civilizational and societal flourishing, and this situation in the eighth century is a remnant of that prosperity; it is a continuation of past progress. This is evidenced by the fact that Granada fell before the end of the ninth century, and that Muslims in Andalusia were gradually losing their authority and power. Therefore, it is noted that this advanced scientific and cultural state is limited to the explanation and preservation of existing knowledge, as evidenced by stagnation and lack of interaction with what is beyond the borders. New writings were nothing more than commentaries and summaries, and the high scientific level is a relative level, resulting from comparisons with the level of surrounding countries, whether in Europe or the Maghreb. However, in comparison to the situation in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Hijra, it indicates stability and stagnation in the legislative aspect. What confirms these conditions is the absence of any school of thought in Granada other than the Maliki school. Al-Shatibi said: "For the writings of the Hanafi school are as if they do not exist in the Maghreb, as are the writings of the Shafi'i school and others from the people of the schools."(1)
Cultural community climate:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/273.


[Page 24]

Thus, the society of Granada witnessed a proliferation of sciences and knowledge, along with a multitude of scholars, which is a relatively advanced state. However, the important difference lies in the direction of the society in its cultural and scientific movement, which was one of regression and decline. This situation led to what al-Shatibi indicated regarding the spread of innovations (bid'ah) and closure, such that opposing or non-dominant opinions were not accepted even if supported by legal evidence, and to issuing fatwas based on blind imitation, applying the statements of jurists or the established rules of the school without delving into their foundations. Therefore, al-Shatibi depicts the state of affairs through the hadith: "Islam began as something strange and will return as something strange as it began, so blessed are the strangers" (1), and he speaks of the masters of ignorance, sectarian fanaticism, and the exaggeration in glorifying others besides Allah. He holds the scholars accountable for this ignorance, as they issue fatwas for the ruler according to his desires, or for their relatives or followers, and who alter rulings under the pretext of facilitation or necessity. Below are a number of statements that depict some of these conditions:

(1) Narrated by Muslim in the Book of Faith, no. (370). See: Sharh Muslim by al-Nawawi, 2/354, edited by Sheikh Khalil Mamoun Shihah, 1st ed., 1414 AH - 1994 CE, Dar al-Ma'rifah - Beirut, and narrated by Ibn Majah in the Book of Trials: (3986), and by al-Tirmidhi: (2630).

Al-Shatibi says: "When I wanted to adhere to the straight path, I found myself a stranger among the majority of the people of my time"(1). He also says: "I hesitated between following the Sunnah on the condition of opposing what people were accustomed to... I saw that destruction in following the Sunnah is salvation, and that people will not avail me anything from Allah... The Day of Judgment arose upon me, and blame poured upon me, and the arrows(2) of reproach were directed at me, and I was attributed to innovation and misguidance, and placed in the ranks of the ignorant and the foolish... At times, I was accused of opposing the allies of Allah... and at times, I was accused of opposing the Sunnah and the community"(3).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 1/18.

He says: "Indeed, some people have strayed due to neglecting the evidence and relying on men, thus departing from the path of the Companions and the Followers, and they followed their desires without knowledge, leading them away from the straight path" (1). He mentioned examples of this, including: "The opinion of the blind followers of an Imam who claim that their Imam is the Sharia, to the extent that they are averse to attributing any virtue to any scholar other than their Imam. So when someone reaches the level of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and speaks on issues without being linked to their Imam, they criticize him and direct arrows of criticism at him, considering him among those who have deviated from the path (2), and those who have separated from the community without any evidence from them, but merely based on popular habit. Imam Baqi ibn Makhlad encountered this type of people when he entered Andalusia coming from the East, to the extent that they made him an outcast in the courtyard and marginalized him... Among them is the opinion of the Nabat (a sect) in these times who turned away from studying the knowledge they intended to discuss and act upon, then returned to following some of the shaykhs from whom they learned in their youth, a time when one is likely to lack scrutiny of the one from whom they take knowledge or to be negligent of the one from whom they received it. They then elevated those shaykhs to the highest degrees of perfection and attributed to them what they have been attributed in error, or they understood from them without verification or inquiry into the authenticity of the reported issue, and they rejected all that was transmitted from the earlier generations that is true and correct... So reflect, O people of understanding, on the state of relying on a man for fatwa (legal opinion) without seeking the legal evidence, but merely for immediate interest. May Allah protect us from that by His grace" (3).

(1) The same source, 1/537.

[Page 27]

He said in al-Muwafaqat: "Many of the followers of the jurists give fatwas to their relatives or friends that they do not give to others, following their own interests and desires or the interests of that relative or friend" (1). He also said: "Some of them might justify this in situations where they claim necessity and urgent need, based on the principle that necessities permit the prohibited, thus taking what aligns with their interests" (2).

Al-Shatibi established this position regarding these circumstances as a point of contention between him and the scholars of his time, to the extent that he was accused of the aforementioned charges and others. He expressed this, as has been shown, and among his expressions is also his saying (al-Basit):

"I have been afflicted, O people, with a variety of trials ... from whom I have to manage until it nearly destroys me.
To avert harm, not to seek a benefit ... so sufficient for me is Allah in my intellect and in my religion" (3).

Dr. Hamadi al-Abidi says: "There were violent confrontations between al-Shatibi and those jurists to whom he directed his criticism and warned people against. Whenever he issued a fatwa permitting something, they issued a fatwa prohibiting it, and whenever he issued a fatwa prohibiting something, they issued a fatwa permitting it" (4).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/73.
(2) The same source, 4/81.
(3) See: al-Tanbakti, Nail al-Ibtihaj, p. 49.

[Page 28]

Al-Shatibi's dispute was led by one of his teachers, Abu Said ibn Lub (1), who was known for his leniency in issuing fatwas. Al-Shatibi referred to this in one of his statements, noting that leniency was something students learned from their teachers. He said: "And he said (2): I wanted to alert you to a principle in fatwa that is very beneficial and well-known among the traditions of scholars, which is that they did not impose strictness on the questioner when he came seeking a fatwa" (3). He then said: "Before this session, various issues regarding the statements of Malik and his companions were overwhelming me, but after that session, Allah illuminated my heart with the light of those words, and the darkness of those issues was lifted all at once; all praise is due to Allah for that" (4). However, he later changed his position on leniency and the fatwas of his teacher, leading to disputes and a fierce attack against him, along with numerous accusations directed at him. For example, this statement from al-Muwaq (5): "Look at the belittlement of this al-Shatibi and his denial of the chief of scholars, Ibn Lub, whose fatwas we follow in matters of belief, permissible and forbidden, and his school of thought regarding necessary oaths and other rulings on blood, marriages, and divorce" (6).
This atmosphere had a significant impact on al-Shatibi's thought and his call, leading to his book al-I'tisam being a clarification of these ideas and similar ones, as well as a response to them. The Muwafaqat established principles for regulating the methodology of thinking and deduction.

[Page 29]

And indeed, this picture reflects the era of al-Shatibi: political turmoil and coups within, military attacks and Crusader threats from abroad, ongoing wars and the fall of Islamic cities, and the Muslims' flight to Granada after being expelled from their lands, constantly seeking assistance from the Muslims in Morocco while maintaining fragmentation and division into small states, all of which foreshadow a bleak fate for the Muslims in those lands. This fate is confirmed by the absence or weakness of political thought and the lack of interest among scholars in politics. For example, there is nothing in al-Shatibi's extensive and important works that indicates his concern for political conditions except in terms of issuing fatwas to the people not to sell to the disbeliever what he could use against them, or regarding the permissibility of imposing taxes on the people out of necessity. Therefore, when the Christians were unable to control Granada due to the latter's reliance on the Marinid state in Morocco, they plotted and took control of Gibraltar, the only outlet for supplying the Muslims, and this occurred in the year 867 AH - 1462 CE(1). This made it easier for them to eliminate the Muslims in Granada, and then to completely eradicate the Muslims in Andalusia in the year 897 AH - 1492 CE. This indicates a lack of political thinking, which is a sign of decline and degradation, regardless of the scientific and economic level of the state.
__________
(1) The Muslims should have exerted every effort to regain Gibraltar, as its loss was a precursor to their complete expulsion from Andalusia. They originally entered it only through Gibraltar. But to which rulers do we refer? How similar today is to yesterday!


[Page 30]

The lack of political thought is a harbinger of the end of any state and the destruction of any nation, no matter how powerful it may be (1). It goes without saying that political thought cannot exist without the existence of political theory, system, and legislation upon which this thought and thinking are based. However, even if laws, systems, and legislations exist—as is the case—if there is no thought regarding responsibility for the nation and its issues and the management of its affairs based on these laws and legislations—this is political thought—then their existence is equivalent to their non-existence.
The Sheikhs of al-Shatibi:
Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi benefited from scholars who were among the finest scientific centers in the Maghreb during his time. Among these scholars were those who settled in Granada, being from its people, and some who came from the land of Morocco to settle there or to carry out certain tasks (2).

Their land is fertile, rich, and beautiful. Likewise, the wealthy states in the Gulf quickly lost their wealth to their enemy and became feeble states that cannot move without permission from their enemy. And here is the Islamic nation, with all its peoples, in a lamentable state of backwardness despite the enormous wealth beneath the earth and on its surface, despite the vast numbers of degree holders in various fields of knowledge, and despite its large population and the tremendous sacrifices it makes.

[Page 33]

Among his most important students are three prominent figures: Abu Yahya Muhammad ibn Asim, his brother Abu Bakr the judge, and Abu Abdullah Muhammad al-Bayani. The aforementioned brothers come from a well-known scholarly family in Granada. Abu Yahya was a scholar, an eloquent speaker, a literary writer, and the inheritor of his teacher al-Shatibi's position. He was also a hero of jihad and was martyred in the noble battlefields in the year 813 AH.
Judge Abu Bakr was a jurist (faqih), a scholar of legal theory (usuli), and a hadith narrator (muhaddith) to whom people turned for fatwas. Among his writings is the "Tuhfat al-Hukam," which has received attention in terms of explanation, commentary, and study. He also composed verses on the principles of jurisprudence, grammar, inheritance, and recitations. He summarized his teacher al-Shatibi's book "al-Muwafaqat" and named his summary "Nail al-Muna in Summarizing al-Muwafaqat" (1). He passed away in the year 829 AH (2).
Another of his students was Abu Ja'far Ahmad al-Qassar, the Andalusian from Granada. Al-Shatibi would review some issues with this student while composing his book "al-Muwafaqat," discussing them with him and then recording them (3).
Among his students was also Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Abdul Wahid al-Majari, who passed away in the year 862 AH, the author of the program. He mentioned in his program that al-Shatibi was one of his teachers, stating: "I recited the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik from memory to him, and he narrated it to me from his teacher, the eminent scholar Abu Abdullah al-Biri." He noted that he learned from him the book of Sibawayh, the summary of Ibn al-Hajib, and the Muwatta of Imam Malik, along with the chains of narration to their authors (4), and he heard some of the "al-Muwafaqat" from him (5).
His scholarly status:

[Page 34]

Al-Shatibi was one of the distinguished scholars of his time, known for his rejection of fanaticism, rigidity, and blind imitation. He was also steadfast in his opinions, intelligent, pious, and knowledgeable, which indicates the independence of his character and the depth of his thought. This earned him the animosity of the rigid and provoked the traditionalists of his era.
The reputation of al-Shatibi spread during his lifetime and transcended the borders of Andalusia. His books indicate the breadth of his knowledge in every branch of the sciences, whether in philosophy and the principles of religion, or in logic and the principles of jurisprudence, or in the sciences of language and the various branches of Islamic law. He himself pointed to this when he said: "Since the time my mind was opened to understanding, and I directed my pursuit towards knowledge, I have examined its intellectual and legal aspects, its principles and branches. I did not limit myself to one type of knowledge over another, nor did I single out one category from among its types... Rather, I plunged into its depths like a skilled swimmer, and I advanced in its fields with the boldness of the courageous... Being oblivious to the words of the speaker and the reproach of the reproacher, and turning away from the rejection of the rejecter and the blame of the blamer until the Most Generous, Most Compassionate Lord bestowed upon me an understanding of the meanings of the Sharia that I had not anticipated... From there, my soul was strengthened to walk in His path as much as Allah made easy for me, so I began with the principles of religion in action and belief, then with its branches built upon those principles" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 1/17.


[Page 35]

His student al-Majari said about him: "The Sheikh, the Imam, the renowned scholar, a unique fabric and the only one of his era" (1). Imam Ibn Marzouk al-Hafid said about him: "The Sheikh, the professor, the jurist, the accomplished Imam, the righteous scholar" (2). Ahmad Baba al-Tanbukti translated him in Nيل الابتهاج, describing him as: "The Imam, the accomplished scholar, the exemplary, the great memorizer, the diligent mujtahid" (3). He said: "He was a foundational scholar (usuli), a commentator (mufassir), a jurist (faqih), a hadith scholar (muhaddith), a linguist (lugawi), an eloquent speaker (bayani), a steadfast debater (nazar), pious, righteous, ascetic, and a Sunni. He was an absolute Imam, a meticulous researcher, an adept dialectician in the sciences, one of the distinguished and verified scholars, and one of the great Imams who were proficient and trustworthy. He had a firm foundation and supreme leadership in the sciences of jurisprudence, principles, exegesis, hadith, Arabic, and others, with thoroughness and verification... on a solid foundation of righteousness, jurisprudence, thoroughness, and piety" (4).
His Works:
Al-Shatibi has significant works, the most important of which are two: al-Muwafaqat and al-I'tisam, both of which are published. Some of his works have not reached us, and his writings indicate a vast knowledge and comprehensive understanding, as well as precision and insight, self-confidence and independence, the ability to investigate and verify, the pursuit of rare and overlooked matters, and integrity in seeking truth and correctness, while avoiding fanaticism and rigidity. He attempted to renew and revive Islamic thought, discarding impurities that had attached to it and correcting deviations that had occurred. Al-Shatibi's works are:

(2) Al-Tanbukti, Nيل الابتهاج, p. 47.
(3) The same source, p. 47.
(4) The same location.


[Page 36]

1 - The Muwafaqat. It is the most famous of his books and the deepest in content. He titled it: "The Title of Defining the Secrets of Obligation," and then he proceeded to refer to it as "the Muwafaqat." Through it, he attempted to establish a methodology for articulating the principles and deriving the branches. Therefore, it is a book on the principles (usul). If we consider al-Shatibi's (may Allah be pleased with him) intended meaning of the term principle or principles, it is more accurate to say that the book is about the principles of the principles, and this will become clear - if Allah wills - in the explanation of his idea regarding the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), which is the subject of this book.
Much has been said about the Muwafaqat, but only a little of this is correct, and it contains ambiguities that cannot be resolved or understood in terms of the true intended meaning except through extensive review and connecting the texts in various places.
The book is available in several editions and has been edited by several scholars, the most prominent of whom is Dr. Abdullah Daraz. It is published in four volumes. Al-Shatibi (may Allah be pleased with him) divided it into five sections: the first is on the scientific introductions needed as a prelude to the other sections; the second is on rulings and what relates to them, whether from the address of obligation or the address of status; the third is on the objectives; the objectives of the Legislator and the objectives of the obligated; the fourth is on the legal evidences, which are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas); and the fifth is on the rulings of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), taqlid (following a jurist), and fatwa (legal opinion), and on the conditions of the mufti (the one giving the fatwa) and the mustafti (the one seeking the fatwa).


[Page 37]

There has not been sufficient attention given to the book or its content that matches some of the praise and commendation it has received since the time of al-Shatibi until now. As for the time of al-Shatibi and his students, the main point is that some of his students heard parts of it from him or in his presence. One of his students, namely the judge Abu Bakr ibn Asim, summarized the book and named his summary: "Nail al-Muna in the Summary of the Muwafaqat" (1). His brother Abu Yahya ibn Asim composed it in six thousand verses and named his composition: "Nail al-Muna from the Muwafaqat" (2). As for the summary, I have not found any mention of its existence today. As for the composition, there exists a manuscript of it in the Escorial Monastery under number 1164. He began his composition with the following lines (the rajas):

Praise be to Allah, who by His grace ... has spread in the prescribed matters the secret of His wisdom
And has prepared minds for guidance ... in accordance with the address and the obligations

Then he said:

Knowledge is the most worthy of what time requires ... and its books are the trusted companion
And the source that is sweet and abundant ... and among the most important of them is the Muwafaqat
By our master, the distinguished scholar ... that is Abu Ishaq, the son of al-Shatibi
For it is a book of good objectives ... beyond which there is no goal for the seeker
And he had named it with the title ... and chose, from a vision, that second name
And I have heard some of it from him ... and from him in my visits to him
But my disagreement with it was ... only a small amount that is not sufficient

Until he said:

And making for it among the attributes ... (Nail al-Muna from the Muwafaqat)
Its count does not exceed in writing ... six thousand of the composed
And here I am with what I intended to bring ... presenting the ruling of the preliminaries

The first is: "Al-Marafiq 'ala al-Muwafiq" by Mustafa bin Muhammad Fadl bin Mamin, who passed away in 1328 AH - 1910 CE. It is a poem with a brief explanation, and this poem was printed along with its explanation in 1324 AH in Tunis(3).

Another aspect of the attention given to the book is its printing and commentary. Abu Ubaida, mentioned earlier, referred to five editions (1). The first was in 1302 AH - 1884 CE at the Tunisian State Press. The second was in 1327 AH - 1909 CE, where the first part was printed in Kazan, the capital of the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia. The third was in 1341 AH - 1922 CE in Egypt, with commentary by the two scholars Muhammad Khidr Hussein and Muhammad Hassanein Makhlouf, where the first commented on the first and second parts, and the second commented on the third and fourth parts. The fourth was in Egypt with commentary and verification by Sheikh Abdullah Daraz. The fifth was in Egypt with verification by Muhammad Muhyi al-Din Abdul Hamid. Thus, the edition verified by Abu Ubaida himself is the sixth edition.
In addition to this, there have been books and articles discussing the book al-Muwafaqat, the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and al-Shatibi (2). Most of them appear in this book through references to or discussions of them.
2 - Al-I'tisam. Al-Shatibi authored it after al-Muwafaqat, but did not complete it; it consists of two parts and its subject is innovations (bid'ah). No one has written anything like it in this regard - and Allah knows best - and people have relied on it in this subject to this day. The importance of this book comes from several aspects, including its comprehensiveness regarding types of innovations, and the immense ability of al-Shatibi to penetrate into the depths of the soul and understand its motivations, as well as the depth and precision that allows for distinguishing between similar or intertwined matters, such as distinguishing between public interest (maslaha) and preference (istihsan), and distinguishing each from innovations.

[Page 40]

The seriousness of al-Shatibi is evident in the two mentioned books through his precision and his clarification of the intended meaning of any term he uses, as well as his thoroughness and elaboration on this meaning. This includes the intended meaning of innovation (bid'a) and his examination of the sects, the meaning of what is permissible (mubah), and his establishment of criteria and boundaries for what is necessary, what is needed, what is commendable, or what is supplementary, along with his extensive explanation of what constitutes a concession (rukhsah) and what does not.
In the book al-I'tisam, he frequently applies the principles he previously established in al-Muwafaqat.
3 - The Book of Majalis. This is a commentary on the book of sales from Sahih al-Bukhari. Al-Tanbukti states that it contains benefits and investigations that only Allah, Exalted is He, knows (1).
4 - Sharh al-Khalasah. This is a book on grammar, in which he explains Ibn Malik's Alfiyyah in four large volumes. Al-Tanbukti said about it: "I do not know of any work that has been composed on it that matches it in research and investigation" (2).
5 - The Title of Agreement in the Science of Derivation. Dr. Hamadi al-Abidi said: "It is a book, as its title indicates, in the science of morphology and the jurisprudence of language, and it is likely similar to the book al-Khasais by Ibn Jinni. He has taken it from his references in his commentary on Ibn Malik's Alfiyyah, and some references mention that this book was lost while the author was still alive" (3).
6 - Usul al-Nahw. Dr. al-Abidi said: "It is a book on the rules of language, including grammar and morphology, which is limited to the essential rules that are indispensable, and he has made it for students of this science. It is said that it was also lost" (4).
7 - Al-Ifadat wa al-Inshadat. This is a book in which the author mentions some news and events that occurred with him or that he is aware of, which may be beneficial to mention. He also mentions some events in which poetry is recited. This book is printed with the investigation of Professor Muhammad Abu al-Ajfan.
