Chapter One
An Introduction to the Emergence of the Idea of
Objectives of the Sharia

It contains an introduction and three sections:

Section One: Qiyas (analogy).
Section Two: The Paths of Reason and Their Conditions.
Section Three: The Path of Analogy and Correspondence.

Chapter One
An Introduction to the Emergence of the Idea of the Objectives of the Sharia

Introduction to the Emergence and Development of the Science of Usul al-Fiqh (principles of jurisprudence):
Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) is considered the first to define the principles of deduction and organize them into general and comprehensive rules. Al-Zarkashi said: "Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) was the first to compile a work on the principles of jurisprudence. He authored the book al-Risala, the book of the Rules of the Qur'an, the book of the Differences of Hadith, the book of the Invalidity of Istihsan (preference), the book of the Gathering of Knowledge, and the book of Qiyas" (2).
Sheikh Muhammad Abu Zahra said: "Indeed, al-Shafi'i was worthy of being the first to document the rules of deduction" (3).
Before al-Shafi'i, the jurists would exercise ijtihad (independent reasoning) without having clear boundaries for deduction before them; rather, they relied on their understanding of the meanings of the legal texts, their reasons, and what their texts and objectives implied.
__________
(1) See: the same reference, pp. 99-100.
(2) See: Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit fi Usul al-Fiqh, 1/7.
(3) Muhammad Abu Zahra, Usul al-Fiqh, pp. 13-16.


[Page 42]

Then, after Imam al-Shafi'i, works in this science continued to emerge, and some disagreed with him on the principles, while others disagreed with him on the branches and related matters without disagreement on the principles themselves. Some agreed with him and followed him in his principles and branches and what relates to them. The principles referred to here are the sources of legislation or its general proofs, which are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas). Sheikh Muhammad Abu Zahra states: "In truth, the jurists of the four schools did not disagree with al-Shafi'i regarding the proofs he established, which are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy. These principles are agreed upon, and any additions to them are a matter of disagreement between him and most of them" (1).
As for those who opposed him, they are the Zahirites and the Shi'a. The Zahirites reject all forms of analogy (2) and rely only on the apparent meanings of texts, while the Shi'a have a significant disagreement as they consider the sayings of the Imams to be a legal proof akin to the Book and the Sunnah. The words of the Imams, in their view, specify the legal texts.
As for the Hanafis, Malikis, and Hanbalis, their principles align with those of al-Shafi'i, albeit with differences in details (4). Those who followed al-Shafi'i in his principles and details, and embraced his opinions, are his followers who were active in the science of usul al-fiqh and produced numerous works in it.
__________
(1) The same source, p. 17.
(2) See: Ibn Hazm, al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam, 8/515, authored by Abu Muhammad Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Hazm al-Zahiri. 384 AH - 456 AH. Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyyah. Beirut. 1st ed.
(4) The same reference, p. 367 - 368, and Muhammad Abu Zahra, Usul al-Fiqh. p. 16.


[Page 43]

Books have been authored on the methodology of al-Shafi'i in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that were and still are the foundation and support of this science. The most significant works known from the ancients are three books: the "Al-Mu'tamad" by Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Tayyib al-Basri al-Mu'tazili, who passed away in 436 AH. The second is the book "Al-Burhan" by Abdul Malik ibn Abdullah al-Juwayni, who passed away in 478 AH. The third is the book "Al-Mustasfa" by Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, who passed away in 505 AH. Then came Abu al-Husayn Ali, known as al-Amidi, who passed away in 631 AH. He compiled these books and added to them in his book "Al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam." A similar endeavor was undertaken by Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, who passed away in 606 AH. He compiled these books and added to them in his book "Al-Mahsool." After these scholars came al-Zarkashi, who passed away in 784 AH. He gathered the aforementioned books and others from the writings of the ancients, amounting to over two hundred (1), and compiled them in his book "Al-Bahr al-Muhit fi Usul al-Fiqh."
Among the most significant books of usul for the Hanafis is "Usul al-Bazdawi" by Fakhr al-Islam Ali ibn Muhammad al-Bazdawi, who passed away in 482 AH, and "Usul al-Sarakhsi" by Imam Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Sahl al-Sarakhsi, who passed away in 490 AH.
With the development of the science of usul from al-Shafi'i to these scholars, two matters are observed:
First: The growth and diversification of this science, and the emergence of branches, details, restrictions, and exceptions to the principles and rules.
Second: The influence of theology (kalam) and logic on these branches, and the emergence of logical reasoning in establishing arguments, examples, and proofs. Thus, a theoretical approach emerged that seeks to establish the rules and to detail and explain the principles of the school in order to support it, even if this did not have an effect on independent reasoning (ijtihad) and deduction (istinbat) (2).
__________
(1) See: al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr al-Muhit fi Usul al-Fiqh. 1/40.
(2) See: Introduction by Dr. Muhammad Hasan Hayto to his edition of the book: "Al-Mankhul min Ta'liqat al-Usul" by the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali, pp. 1-12. Dar al-Fikr, Damascus, 2nd ed., 1400 AH - 1980 CE.


[Page 44]

The scholars of usul (usul al-fiqh) among the Hanafis distinguished themselves by not advocating for a particular school in the principles, but rather supporting a school in the branches. Hence, it was said that the paths of usul branched into two ways:
The first: the method of the jurists, which refers to the method of the Hanafis.
The second: the method of the theologians, which refers to the method of the Shafi'is, Malikis, and Hanbalis.
Then after that arose what is called the method of the later scholars, which refers to the approach of the scholars who combined both methods in their books. Dr. Muhammad Hassan Hayto says: "This 'Epistle' was the first book compiled in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), and thus the imams and scholars continued to explain it and draw light from it"(1). He then says: "Many works were authored on it, and compilations were refined, and the paths of researchers in it branched into two methods:
The first method is that which is known as the method of the theologians, and they are the Shafi'is and the majority.
The second method is that which is known as the method of the jurists, specifically the Hanafis(2).
Then he said: "The method of the theologians: this was concerned with clarifying issues and establishing principles, and it tends towards rational argumentation as much as possible, abstracting the foundational issues from the jurisprudential branches, similar to the scholars of theology"(3). Then he said: "The method of the jurists: this is more relevant to jurisprudence and more suitable for the jurisprudential branches, establishing the foundational principles based on what has been transmitted from the branches by their imams, claiming that these are the principles that those imams observed when they derived those branches.."(4). After that, Dr. Hito mentions some of the most important books that combine the two methods, such as (The Collection of Collections) by Imam Taj al-Din al-Subki, and (The Certainty of Authenticity) by the scholar Muhibb al-Din ibn Abd al-Shakur(5).
__________
(1) The same reference, p. 6.
(2) The same place.
(3) The same place.
(4) The same reference, p. 7.
(5) See: the same reference, p. 12.


[Page 45]

And the method of the later scholars, in my view, was nothing but an influence from the followers of the jurists' method through the approach of the theologians, by relying on the principles of logic and theology in the foundational discussions. It was not a third method as much as it was a drift towards logical and theological means in debates and responses, and as much as it was attempts to encompass the various opinions that were in agreement, similar, or contradictory in comprehensive books, in eras when the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) knew no creativity except in compilation, explanation, abbreviation, annotation, arrangement, and classification. The situation remained stagnant until al-Shatibi came and examined this great legacy and made his reformist attempt to reconcile between the two methods, the method of the jurists and the method of the theologians.
The most notable difference between the two approaches appears in the discussions of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), particularly in the topics of analogy (qiyas), reasoning (ta'leel), and the pathways of reasoning.
This difference will be clearly manifested in the first and second chapters of this book. It will also show how the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) emerged as a result of this difference through the efforts of Imam al-Juwayni (may Allah have mercy on him), and how it subsequently became a part of the discussions in the science of Usul al-fiqh.
The idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) is based on the premise that the Sharia was established for the benefit of the servants in both realms, this world and the Hereafter. The benefits of the Hereafter are attaining the pleasure of the Merciful (Ar-Rahman), achieving bliss and gardens, and being saved from punishment and the Fire.
As for the interests of this world, they are what a person strives to attain or preserve, or to avert and protect oneself from, for the sake of their livelihood, and this is according to what Allah has created in them and determined from their characteristics and needs.
Most scholars have agreed that the interests of this world are based on five matters that serve as the foundations or necessities to which all interests return, namely the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and wealth. The rulings of the Sharia (Islamic law) lead to the preservation of these interests.


[Page 46]

And since these interests (masalih) are the results of the Sharia (Islamic law) or are intended by it, some scholars have argued that these interests are the causes (illal) of the Sharia. Others have maintained that they are objectives (maqasid) and not causes. This difference has had its impact on the foundational studies (usul al-fiqh) among the imams of jurisprudence, as well as on the concept of the objectives of the Sharia in the thought of Imam Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi.
Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) held that the objectives of the Sharia are its causes, but the establishment of a purpose as a legal objective requires legal evidence. Al-Shatibi had a methodology in this matter that distinguished him from his predecessors, through which he sought to reconcile between the differing opinions, and hence the name of his book: al-Muwafaqat.
In order to understand the reality of this disagreement regarding the reasoning based on interests, and the difference in how an interest is considered a legal interest, or how an objective is deemed a legal objective, it is necessary to clarify the meaning of a cause in the Sharia and how it is established, along with its conditions and pathways.
The reasoning of a legal ruling based on an interest that the jurist sees as intended by the ruling is reasoning in a sense or description that he deems appropriate or suitable to be intended by the Legislator. From here, the disagreement among the imams emerged regarding the issue of reasoning based on the appropriate description. Is the appropriateness of the description evidence of it being a cause, that is, is appropriateness a pathway among the pathways of the cause? The answer to this question is the root of the differing opinions among the imams.
Therefore, it is also necessary to understand the meaning of appropriateness, and whether it is evidence of the cause, or a condition for it, or neither? And what is the difference between the two?


[Page 47]

The appropriateness of a description to serve as a cause for a ruling or an objective intended by the legislator varies according to the perspectives of the scholars and jurists. What one jurist claims to be appropriate may be opposed by another who argues that it is not appropriate. This is based on the differing understandings, perceptions, and intellects of people. Therefore, there must be a legal criterion to indicate whether the description is appropriate or not.
Claiming the appropriateness of a description without a legal proof of its appropriateness is merely an imagination. Thus, the appropriateness is referred to as "ikhala." Some have described it as an inner imagination, meaning it is a personal internal feeling of the individual, and this is not a legal proof. This will become clear in its appropriate context later.
If it is established after legal consideration that the description is appropriate in reason or imagination but is legally rejected, then it is dismissed and is termed as "nullified." If it is established that it is legally accepted, then it is termed as "considered," meaning it is confirmed to be legally valid.
However, the manner in which the consideration of the description or meaning is established to be appropriate and valid for reasoning, or in other words, to be a legally recognized interest (maslaha) for justifying the ruling, has remained a point of contention among scholars. The disagreement regarding appropriateness as a method of reasoning is, in essence, a disagreement regarding how to consider the description. If the meaning of consideration is that the legal evidence indicates a certain matter, then it is legal based on that, and there is no dispute about this. However, the contested consideration, which is the crux of the disagreement, means that the ruling aligns with a certain interest or an appropriate description, and thus a cause is claimed. Therefore, to understand the idea of reasoning based on interest and the concept of objectives (maqasid) according to al-Shatibi, it is necessary to clarify the meaning of consideration or the meaning of the ruling's alignment with the appropriate description in legal terminology. Especially since al-Shatibi came to mediate between the two parties, affirming the idea of reasoning based on the considered appropriateness after setting conditions that may make it acceptable to those who oppose reasoning based on it. This will be detailed when discussing his methodology.


[Page 48]

Indeed, those who reject reasoning based on the appropriate description rely on the fact that reasoning requires evidence; a description does not establish a cause unless it appears in one of the legal pathways for causation, and this is not a matter of dispute. However, they believe that the appropriateness is not a pathway for causation, meaning it is not evidence for it but rather a condition for it. If the appropriate description does not have a legal evidence indicating its validity or nullification, then it is considered unsubstantiated and has no proof.
As for those who reason based on the appropriate description, they rely on the idea that appropriateness in itself is a pathway for causation. The fact that a description is appropriate is evidence of its causative nature, provided that there is no evidence indicating that it is nullified. Since this claim requires evidence, its proponents have sought to establish that the default in rulings is reasoning, and to make this claim a foundational principle (qawa'id) of jurisprudence. If a legal evidence indicates the causative nature of a certain description, then it is the cause. If we do not find evidence for that, then reasoning must be based on some description even if it does not appear in a pathway, based on that principle. Thus, the absence of reasoning contradicts the default. From here, the legitimacy of reasoning based on the appropriate description arises, and appropriateness becomes a pathway for causation.
Here, the disagreement has shifted to a dispute over this principle, where those who accept it have built upon it, and those who reject it have dismissed the consideration that the reasoners have proposed.
From here, al-Shatibi came to establish the principle of reasoning with absolute certainty, and to lay down a new methodology for how to consider the description, and consequently for how to regard the description as an objective and a cause. This is the methodology of beneficial induction - in his view - which will be clarified and detailed in its appropriate context.


[Page 49]

Add to this another issue, which is that considering a certain description as a public interest (maslaha) and thus a legal objective (maqsad) and a reason for legislation is only for the purpose of building the legislation upon that. The reason is one of the pillars of analogy (qiyas), and analogy has other pillars, including the origin, which is the legal ruling that is being reasoned. The existence of the ruling and the existence of its reason leads to giving the same ruling to another incident that does not have a text, based on that reason or interest. However, in the matter of reasoning based on public interest, those who advocate for public interest may see benefits or harms in certain incidents that require a ruling, but without finding an origin or ruling to base it on. So, giving the ruling here based on the existing interest or harm in the incident without finding an origin to base it on—does this fall under analogy or is it something else? The existence of the origin is a pillar of analogy, and its absence invalidates the process of analogy. This is another issue that has posed a barrier for those who advocate reasoning based on public interests. Here, a disagreement arose among those who reason based on public interests; some called this matter analogy based on the premise that if a specific interest does not have an origin to be based on, there are origins for the category of interest. Others did not consider this a form of analogy but rather termed it: reasoning (istidlal). This matter will also be clarified in detail in its appropriate place.
It is generally held among the usul scholars that this is not analogy but rather reasoning, and more specifically, it is public interest (istislah) or unregulated public interest (maslaha mursala). The term reasoning is broader than unregulated public interests as it is also applied to preference (istihsan), presumption (istishab), and others that do not have a specific or direct evidence regarding the matter, but rather rely on a principle that is not specific to the issue, just as those who reason based on appropriate measures rely on the principle of the origin in the reasoning of rulings, and just as it is also relied upon in some jurisprudential matters based on the principle of presumption.


[Page 50]

This introduction does not aim to explain and clarify these foundational terms, which will be addressed in full in this chapter and the next. Rather, its purpose is to indicate that in order to fully grasp the concept of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi, one must understand the emergence of the concept of objectives among the usuliyyin (foundational scholars) who preceded him, and one must also be familiar with the meanings of some terms and foundational concepts related to analogy (qiyas) and its discussions. While some of these terms may require only a basic understanding, others necessitate deeper exploration and insight.

For this reason, this chapter serves as an introduction to the concept of objectives in general, and subsequently to the concept of objectives according to al-Shatibi in particular. Therefore, the discussions in this chapter will introduce analogy, its cause, its pillars, its conditions, and its pathways. It will elaborate on the pathway of suitability, and on the meaning of the alignment of the ruling with public interest (maslaha) or description, which is consideration (i'tibar) and its categories. It will also clarify the meaning of inference (istidlal) and the meaning of unregulated public interest (maslaha mursala). Throughout and after this, the differences among the usuliyyin on these issues will be presented, which will reinforce what has been mentioned earlier and illustrate how the concept of objectives emerged, how al-Shatibi's idea of objectives was new and different from those that preceded it.

The first section
Analogy

The concept of analogy and its discussions:
Analogy in language means estimation. It is said that one measures something by another if he estimates it by it, such as estimating distance in meters when measuring it, or weight in pounds when measuring it. It is stated in Lisan al-Arab: "To measure something by something means to estimate it by its example" (1), and it is said: "And to measure something means to estimate it; it is a linguistic variation of measuring" (2), and it is said: "You compared between two things if you measured between them" (3).
__________
(1) Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab 6/187, Dar Sader, Beirut
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.


[Page 51]

In the legal terminology, many phrases have been mentioned in the definition of qiyas (analogy), the most famous of which is the statement of Abu al-Husayn al-Basri: "Qiyas is the attainment of the ruling of the original in the branch due to their similarity in the reason for the ruling according to the mujtahid (jurist)"(1).
Al-Amidi mentioned the definition of Judge Abu Bakr al-Baqillani: "Qiyas is the carrying of a known upon another known in establishing a ruling for both or denying it from both by a common factor between them"(2).
These definitions and others have not escaped criticism and the arrows of critique. Some of the imams of usul (principles of jurisprudence) from the Shafi'i school have stated that the most solid of them is the definition of the aforementioned judge. Al-Zarkashi said(3): "The scholars among us have chosen it"(4).
However, al-Amidi mentioned a definition of qiyas as: "It is the equality between the branch and the original in the reason inferred from the ruling of the original"(5), and he commented, saying: "This phrase is comprehensive and sufficient for the purpose of others"(6).

(2) Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam 3/167. Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya, Beirut, edited by Sheikh Ibrahim al-Ajuz.

See in his biography: Introduction to the editing of his mentioned book, vol. 1.

[Page 52]

The discussions on qiyas (analogy) branch out in the foundational books of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) to establish it as a principle and source of legislation, then to respond to its deniers and refute their arguments and doubts, followed by defining it, categorizing it, and clarifying its pillars, with detailed research on each pillar regarding its conditions and the validity of its consideration. Among its most important discussions are the cause (illah), its conditions, its pathways, its proof, and the objections raised against it. Al-Juwayni (1) says: "Qiyas is the basis of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and the origin of opinion, from which jurisprudence and the methods of Sharia branch out... Whoever understands its sources, categories, valid and invalid forms, what objections are acceptable and what invalidates them, and comprehends their ranks in clarity and obscurity, and knows their pathways and locations has encompassed the essentials of jurisprudence" (2).
Qiyas is categorized based on its clarity or obscurity, or based on the type of its cause in terms of its evidence or pathway, whether it is a text, a hint, or an inference.
Its authority:
Qiyas is considered one of the agreed-upon sources of legislation, although some have denied it. Al-Zarkashi said: "The author of al-Qawati' stated: All the imams from the Companions and the Followers, as well as the majority of jurists and theologians, have agreed that legal qiyas is a fundamental principle of Sharia, used to derive rulings for which there is no textual evidence" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni: He is Imam Abdul Malik ibn Abdullah ibn Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Hayawayh al-Juwayni al-Naysaburi, known as Abu al-Maali, and he was titled Imam al-Haramayn. He was a Shafi'i scholar, lived from 417 to 478 AH, and his biography is found in numerous sources. See: The introduction of the editor to the book Al-Burhan, pp. 23-35, referring to: Wafayat al-A'yan 2/341, and Tabaqat al-Shafi'iyya 5/165.
(2) See: Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan fi Usul al-Fiqh 2/485, paragraph: 676-677, edited by Abdul Azim Mahmoud al-Dib, Dar al-Wafa for Printing, Publishing, and Distribution, Mansoura, 3rd edition, 1412 AH - 1992 CE.
(3) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr al-Muhit fi Usul al-Fiqh 4/14.


[Page 53]

The deniers of it have acknowledged some of its types, but they have not gone beyond them as a form of analogy. Al-Zarkashi said: "And Abu Bakr al-Sirafi stated in his principles: 'The deniers of analogy are as if they have denied the naming, otherwise they acknowledge it'" (1).
And al-Shawkani said: "Then know that the deniers of analogy did not claim to disregard everything that is called analogy, even if its cause is explicitly stated or it is definitively established with the absence of a distinguishing factor; rather, they made this type of analogy indicated by the evidence of the original, included under it" (2).
And al-Amidi said: "This is also the view of the predecessors among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), the Followers, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and most of the speaking jurists. The Shi'a, al-Nizam, and a group of the Mu'tazila of Baghdad, such as Yahya al-Iskafi, Ja'far ibn Mubashshir, and Ja'far ibn Harb, argued against the rational acceptance of it" (3). The Zahiri (literalist) school also rejected it, and Ibn Hazm expressed this trend clearly in his book: Al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam in its eighth volume (4).

(4) "As for the Zahiris, they reject all analogy and rely only on the apparent texts. Even what is called clear analogy is not considered by them to be analogy; rather, they consider it a text. Their consideration of the text is merely a consideration of the apparent text. The leader of this school is Abu Sulayman Dawud ibn Khalaf al-Isfahani, who died in the year 270 AH. He was originally a Shafi'i and learned his sciences from the companions of al-Shafi'i, then he abandoned the Shafi'i school and chose for himself a specific school that relies only on the text, and it is called the Zahiri school. Among them is Imam Ibn Hazm, who was promoted by some people and presented in a favorable light, leading to an interest in his books, even though they are inferior to the books of other jurisprudence and usul in terms of legal research and reasoning."


[Page 54]

The proponents of qiyas (analogy) have cited evidence from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, as well as the consensus of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) on the authority of qiyas and its status as a source of legislation. These evidences are discussed in the foundational books of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), and it is not our topic to address them here(1).
The pillars of analogy (qiyas):
It has pillars that are not valid without them, which are the original case that is being compared, the ruling of the original case indicated by the Sharia, and the branch that is compared to the original. The reason for the ruling of the original case, which is a description present in the original, and by its presence in the branch, the ruling can be extended from the original to the branch.
Al-Amidi said: "When the meaning of analogy (qiyas) is known, it consists of four pillars: the original case (asl), the branch case (far'), the ruling of the original case, and the common characteristic (wasf al-jami')"(2). It is essential for all four pillars to be present for the analogy to be valid. Al-Zarkashi said: "The original case, the branch case, the reason (illah), and the ruling of the original case must all be mentioned in the analogy"(3).
His conditions:
It has conditions that must be met for it to be valid, and its conditions are the conditions of its pillars. The aim here is not to elaborate on the discussions of analogy (qiyas), but rather to mention some of these conditions as examples of these discussions, and to provide further detail on the rationale (illah) and its conditions, which are necessary in the research.
One of the conditions of the original (asl) - for example - is that it should not be derived from another, meaning that it should not be a branch in another analogy. If it is a branch, then it is not more deserving of being analogized to than its original(4).
One of the conditions for the branch (far') is that the reason ('illah) present in it must share in the reason of the origin (asl); otherwise, it is not possible to extend the ruling of the origin to the branch(5).
One of its conditions is that its ruling is not explicitly stated, for there is no analogy (qiyas) in a ruling when there is a text regarding it(6).
__________
(1) For example, see: Al-Burhan by al-Juwayni, vol. 2; Al-Ihkam by al-Amidi, vol. 3; Al-Bahr al-Muhit by al-Zarkashi, vol. 4; Al-Mahsul by al-Razi, vol. 5; and others.
(2) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/171.
(3) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit 4/67.
(4) Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam 3/174. Al-Amidi mentioned this condition among the conditions for the ruling of the origin.
(5) The same source, p. 219.
(6) The same source, p. 221.


[Page 55]

One of the conditions for the ruling of the original (asl) is that it must be a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), because the purpose of analogical reasoning (qiyas) on the original is to ascertain the legal ruling(1), and because the subject matter is legal analogy, not logical or rational analogy. The latter is one of the means of knowledge in rational matters, and it is not a pathway to know the ruling of the Sharia, neither through certainty nor conjecture. What is being sought is the ruling of Allah, Exalted is He, and there is no way to it except through textual evidence.
Another condition is that the evidence for the establishment of the ruling of the original must be a legal evidence.(2)
It is also a condition that there should be no deviation from the norms of analogy, such as the number of units of prayer (rak'ahs), the estimation of the amounts of zakat, and the limits and expiations, as they are not rationally understood. An example of this is the acceptance of the testimony of al-Hakim alone, which is an exception to the rule(3), as well as the allowances for travel and wiping over the socks.(4)
Another condition is that the cause (illah) must be established through one of the evidences that indicate it, which are referred to as the pathways of the cause.(5)
As for the conditions of the cause, we will address them in the second section of this chapter.
The cause:

People would come to Zaid ibn Thabit, and he would not write a verse except with the testimony of two just witnesses. (4) See Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/175 - 176, and for more details on these conditions, see: Al-Ihkam by Al-Amidi, vol. 3, Al-Mahsool by Al-Razi, vol. 5, Al-Mustasfa by Al-Ghazali, vol. 2, Irshad al-Fuhul by Al-Shawkani, and Al-Bahr al-Muhit by Al-Zarkashi, vol. 4.
(5) See: the previous footnote.


[Page 56]

The cause (illah) is a pillar of analogy (qiyas) and is not valid without it. It is the common description between the original case (asl) and the branch case (far') that allows for the transfer of the ruling from the original to the branch. Al-Zarkashi said: "The cause: it is a condition for the validity of analogy, as it brings together the original and the branch" (1), and he said: "The majority of the scholars of analogy among the jurists and theologians hold that the cause is necessary in analogy, and it is a pillar of analogy that cannot stand without it" (2). This is the legal cause. The term "cause" is a shared term between the rational cause (illah 'aqliyya) and the legal cause (illah shar'iyya), and it has linguistic and technical connotations.
In terms of language, it is mentioned in Lisan al-Arab: "The cause (al-'ilal) and the ailments (al-'alal): the second drink, and it is said: drinking after drinking successively; it is said: he drank (alal) after he quenched his thirst (nahal)" (3), and it is also mentioned: "The man suffers (ya'il) from illness, and he suffers (ya'lu) from the ailments of drinking" (4).
Al-Zarkashi said: "The cause in language is said to be a name for what changes the ruling of a thing upon its occurrence, derived from the ailment which is the disease, because its effect on the ruling is like the effect of the cause on the essence of the sick person" (5), and he said: "It is said that it is a transfer of the ruling from the original to the branch, like the transition of the cause from health to illness" (6). He also said: "It is said that it is derived from the ailments after quenching, which is the repeated drinking of water again and again, because the jurist in extracting it revisits the matter after consideration, and because the ruling is repeated with the repetition of its existence" (7).
As for the technical definition in legal terminology, that is, the cause of legal analogy, there are five opinions:
"The first is that it is the identifier of the ruling, meaning that it has become a sign of the ruling; if the meaning is found, the ruling is found" (8).
"The second is that it is the cause of the ruling in the sense that the legislator has made it obligatory in itself" (9).

(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit 4/101.
(3) Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab 11/467.
(4) The same source.
(5) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit 4/101.
(6) The same source.

(9) The same source, 4/102.


[Page 57]

"The third: it is that which necessitates the ruling by itself and not by the decree of Allah, which is the view of the Mu'tazila based on their principle of rational good and evil." (1)
"The fourth: it is that which necessitates by custom, and this was chosen by Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi." (2)
As for the fifth view, it is: "the motivator for legislation in the sense that the description must encompass a valid interest that is intended by the legislator in establishing the ruling." (3)
As for the first view: that it is the identifier, meaning a sign of the ruling, there is no doubt that the cause is an identifier of the ruling and a sign of it, as it is a description that exists in the original. However, this is not sufficient for identification or application, and it will become clear when mentioning the conditions of the cause that the cause, which is a pillar in analogy (qiyas), is not sufficient for it to be merely a sign or indicator. There must be in this sign or indicator or description something that makes it suitable for reasoning or indicative of it. For example, the smell of wine is a sign of it, but it is not suitable for reasoning with it, unlike intoxication, as it has an additional element that makes it suitable for reasoning, provided that all other conditions of the cause are met.
Al-Amidi, for example, uses the term indicator in relation to the cause, but he does not mean a mere indicator. He says: "The rational cause necessitates the ruling by itself and not by designation, whereas the legal cause is in the sense of an indicator or sign or in the sense of a motivator." (4) He also says: "They disagreed on the permissibility of the cause in its original meaning being that of a mere indicator, and the preferred view is that the cause in its original meaning must be that of a motivator, meaning it must encompass a valid wisdom that is intended by the legislator in establishing the ruling; otherwise, if it were merely a descriptive characteristic without wisdom, but a mere indicator, then reasoning with it in its original sense would be impossible." (5)

(1) The same place.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/102.
(3) The same place, and the meaning of valid interest is that the description is appropriate and indicative of reasoning.
(4) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 4/283 - 284.
(5) The same place, 3/180.


[Page 58]

As for the second opinion: that it is self-evident in itself, meaning that the legislator has made it self-evident, I do not see it differing from the meaning of the motivator. The statement that the legislator has made it self-evident means that it has come within a legal framework or is indicated by a legal proof, and the statement that it is self-evident means that it includes what makes it suitable for reasoning. This is the same meaning as the motivator itself as it has been defined. Wherever it is mentioned in the words of the imams that it is in this sense, it is an indicator, the intended meaning is that it is an indicator in the usage of the theologians and not the jurists, as it is known that the legal proofs from the texts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah are, for the theologians and the usulists, indicators of the rulings, while for the jurists, they are proofs of them. In this sense, al-Amidi said: "The rational cause necessitates the ruling by itself and not by designation, whereas the legal cause is in the sense of an indicator or a sign or in the sense of a motivator" (1). Al-Zarkashi said: "It is divided into rational: which does not become a cause by the designation of a designator but by itself, and it is self-evident and does not change with time like the movement of the mover, and legal: which has become a cause by the designation of a designator" (2). He then said: "The legal causes are only called causes metaphorically or broadly; otherwise, in reality, the cause is what necessitates the ruling by itself, which is the rational cause, while that which necessitates it by another is not a cause in the view of the theologians but is an indicator of the ruling" (3).
As for the third opinion: that it is self-evident for the ruling by itself and not by the designation of Allah, this is the opinion of the Mu'tazila and aligns with their doctrine of rational good and evil, and that Allah must act in accordance with what is best and legislate what is best. Al-Zarkashi said: "The Mu'tazila and those who agreed with them among the jurists have greatly restricted this, claiming that His actions are constrained by wisdom and limited by the aspect of what is beneficial" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, 4/283 - 284.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/103.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 4/112.


[Page 59]

As for the fourth opinion: it is that which is necessitated by custom, and it is the view of Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in (al-Mahsool). Its essence is that the actions and rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are not to be rationalized. This is based on theological premises and on the notion that rationalization implies that Allah is complete in purpose, which is certainly refuted. Accordingly, for him, the cause does not hold in the sense of being necessitated by itself nor in the sense of being a motivator. The meaning of necessitated by custom is that Allah has established things in such a way that whenever this occurs, that occurs, as if we say, whenever eating occurs, satiety occurs, or whenever retribution occurs, preservation occurs. Thus, it is necessary to presume the occurrence of satiety with eating or the occurrence of preservation with retribution. This presumption is not a matter of rationalization but rather a matter of the custom running in this way. This will be documented in the third discussion of the third chapter.
This statement is refuted because rationalization in analogy (qiyas) does not mean rationalizing the actions of Allah concerning His essence, but rather it is rationalization of the legal ruling based on what the legislator has established as a cause. Al-Zarkashi said: "Know that the doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah is that His rulings, Exalted is He, are not rationalized, in the sense that He does not do anything for a purpose, nor is He motivated by anything to do something. Rather, He, Exalted is He, is capable of bringing about benefits without their causes and eliminating harms without their motivators" (1).
He also said: "Some of the later scholars stated: It has become well-known among the theologians that the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are not rationalized, and it has become well-known among the jurists that rationalization exists and that the cause is in the sense of a motivator. Many people mistakenly think that it is the motivator for the legislation, leading to a contradiction between the statements of the jurists and those of the theologians. This is not the case, and there is no contradiction; rather, the intended meaning is that the cause motivates the action of the obligated person. An example is the preservation of lives, which motivates retribution, which is the action of the obligated person ruled by the law. Thus, the ruling of the law has no cause or motivator" (2). He then said: "And Allah has established the custom that retribution is a cause for preservation" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit 4/112.
(2) The same source, 4/113.
(3) The same location.


[Page 60]

As for the fifth opinion: it is that it is the motive for legislation. Its meaning is that the described attribute, in addition to being an indicator or sign of the ruling, is not merely a sign devoid of any meaning; it encompasses a benefit (maslaha) that is suitable for which the legislator may have enacted the ruling. The assertion that it is a benefit suitable for justification does not mean that it has become an independent cause by itself, but rather that it is valid to be a cause if its other conditions are met. The first of these conditions is that it must come in one of the paths of causation (1).
This is the concept of causation in legal terminology. The term causation is used in the terminology of grammarians to refer to what is called a cause in language, which is not a cause in analogy. An example of this is the "lam" of purpose in language, as the cause that follows it is not a cause in the original analogy.
Al-Razi said: "Indeed, He, Exalted is He, said: { And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind } (2), and by consensus, that cannot be an objective... like the poet's saying: 'Prepare for death and build for destruction,' and the 'lam' here is not for purpose... I say: The people of language have stated that the 'lam' is for justification, and their statement is a proof. If that is established, it must be said that it is a metaphor in these instances" (3).
The term causation is sometimes used for certain meanings in the sense of metaphor, which are not causes in analogy, such as the reason, the basis, and others. Al-Shawkani said: "And causation has names that differ according to different terminologies, such as reason, indicator, motivator, necessitator, impulse, carrier, basis, evidence, necessitating factor, obligatory factor, and influencer. The scholars have agreed that there must be evidence for the cause" (4).
__________
(1) Paths of justification: This will be discussed in the next section.
(2) Surah Al-A'raf, 179.
(3) Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, Al-Mahsool fi Usul al-Fiqh 5/140, edited by Taha Jaber Al-Alwani, Dar Al-Resalah, 2nd ed., 1412 AH - 1992 CE.
(4) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 207.


[Page 61]

Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the meaning of the cause (illah), which is a cornerstone in analogy (qiyas), by defining the terms that are frequently used in the books of usul (principles of jurisprudence) in the sense of cause or with the term cause metaphorically, which are not actually causes, leading to the misconception that they are the cause of analogy, such as the term reason (sabab) and the term criterion (manat).
Reason (sabab):
It is said in Lisan al-Arab: "A reason is anything that one uses to reach something else, and in another version, anything that one uses to intercede for something else, and it has been caused to it, and the plural is reasons. Anything that one uses to reach something is a reason, and I made so-and-so a reason to so-and-so in my need, and a means and a conduit" (1). This is the linguistic meaning.
As for the legal terminology, it is a sign or indicator that defines the existence of the legal ruling. Al-Zarkashi said: "In Sharia, most scholars say it is the apparent, defined description that the evidence of the hearing indicates to be a defining factor for the legal ruling" (2), and he added: "Like making the decline of the sun a defining factor for the obligation of prayer... like the decline for prayer and the sighting of the crescent in Ramadan for the obligation of fasting, and like the minimum threshold (nisab) for zakat" (3).
The fact that the reason is a defining factor for the legal ruling means that the ruling exists with its presence but not by its existence. The presence of the sun in the sky is a sign that indicates the entry of the time for the noon prayer and the existence of the ruling of the noon prayer, which is obligation. Similarly, the crescent of Ramadan is a sign that indicates the entry of the month of Ramadan and the existence of the legal ruling, which is the obligation of fasting. Likewise, the crescent of Shawwal indicates the existence of the holiday and the obligation to break the fast, and the existence of the minimum threshold for zakat is a sign of the existence of the ruling, which is the obligation of zakat.
All of these are mere signs or indicators and do not contain a rational meaning that can be used for reasoning. The sun in the sky is suitable for indicating the existence of the ruling but is not suitable for reasoning the ruling of prayer, and the same applies to other examples.
__________
(1) Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab 1/458.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit 1/264.
(3) Same source.


[Page 62]

The description being a defining characteristic of the existence of the ruling, meaning that the cause is indeed a cause, is a legal matter that requires evidence from the Sharia. Therefore, it has been defined as: "The evidence of the text indicates that it is a defining characteristic of the legal ruling."
The rationale (illa) has what the cause has; it is also a sign or indication that identifies the existence of the ruling. However, it is more than that, as it encompasses a rational meaning. Thus, the rationale is a cause, but not every cause is a rationale. An example of this is theft, which is an identifying sign of the existence of the ruling that mandates cutting off the hand, and adultery is an identifying sign of the existence of the ruling that mandates flogging or stoning. So, theft was a cause, and adultery was a cause, but the arrangement of the punishment for the act includes a wisdom that is suitable for reasoning with it. The description was not merely an abstract sign devoid of a rational meaning; it was not just a cause but rather a rationale(1).
__________
(1) It should be noted here that theft, adultery, and other prescribed punishments, although they are rationales, cannot be used for analogy (qiyas) because the rationale here is not a description in the place to which the ruling was given, meaning it is not part of the place, but rather the whole place itself. If we want to extend the ruling of theft or adultery to another place (i.e., to a branch), it can only extend to theft or adultery. The ruling is then taken from the generality of the text and not by analogy. The incident that receives the same ruling is considered a root and not a branch. These rationales are called limited rationales because they do not extend to a branch. They are called rationales because they contain the meaning of a rationale.


[Page 63]

Therefore, the reason can sometimes be a cause, but it should be noted that there is a difference between them in legal terminology. The reason exists for the ruling to be present at it, not by it, whereas the cause exists for the ruling to be present at it and by it. Both can be so (i.e., a reason or a cause) by the designation of the legislator. If the term "cause" is used for the reason without it being a cause, meaning the element of analogy, this is a case of linguistic metaphor and not that it is a cause that justifies the rulings. Al-Amidi said: "The preferred view is that the cause must be, in essence, a motivator, meaning it must include a valid wisdom that is intended by the legislator in establishing the ruling. Otherwise, if it were a description without wisdom, merely an indication, then justifying rulings by it in essence is impossible" (1). He also said: "What they mentioned regarding the impossibility of justifying by the descriptive characteristic is only valid if it is said that justifying by the descriptive characteristic means the motivator" (2). The connection between Al-Amidi's statements above indicates that he permits the use of the term "cause" for mere indications even if they are not the element of analogy.
Moreover, it should be noted after distinguishing between the cause and the reason in legal terminology that the cause in legal terminology is a reason in the linguistic sense. The fact that the cause is the motivator for the ruling or the reason for the ruling means that it leads to the ruling, which is the meaning of the ruling encompassing a rational meaning, or a meaning valid to be intended by the legislator in establishing the ruling (3).
Maqsad:
Maqsad in the language is the name of the place of connection, and connection means hanging. It is said in Lisan al-Arab: "To connect something means to hang it. The connection is what is hung" (4). It is also said: "It is said: something was connected to it, meaning it was hung on it." Quraq bin Qays al-Asadi said (the long):

(3) And see what Al-Zarkashi mentioned regarding the distinction between the cause and the reason in Al-Bahr al-Muhit 4/104 - 105.
(4) Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab 7/418.


[Page 64]

"A land where my amulets were tied upon me, and the first land that touched my skin is its dust."(1)
The term "manat" has been used in the discussions of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) in the same linguistic sense.
Sheikh Jamal al-Din al-Asnawi(2) said: "The 'manat' is the name of the place of attachment, and 'attachment' means hanging and sticking. Habib al-Ta'i said:
A land where my amulets were tied to me, and the first earth that touched my skin was its dust.
Any amulet that is tied to me. When the ruling is linked to the cause and is dependent on it, it is called a point of reference (manat) (3).
The reason that is the cornerstone of analogy (qiyas) is not the legal basis (manat), nor is the legal basis the reason, but when the ruling that is based on reasoning is linked to its reason and dependent upon it, it is called a legal basis. This is a figurative term. Al-Zarkashi said: "The legal basis is the reason." Ibn Daqiq al-Eid said: "Their expression of the legal basis for the reason is a matter of linguistic metaphor, because when the ruling is dependent upon it, it is like a tangible thing that is attached to something else; thus, it is a metaphor in the sense of likening the abstract to the tangible. This has become established in the terminology of jurists to the extent that nothing else is understood when it is mentioned in general."(4)

[Page 65]

The basis of the ruling, based on what has been mentioned, is the subject of the ruling, that is, the place or reality to which the ruling pertains. For example: buying is permissible and usury is forbidden. The fact that the action is a sale is the subject of permissibility or the basis of permissibility in this action, and the fact that the action is usury is the subject of prohibition or its basis. Similarly, sheep are lawful and pigs are forbidden; thus, the fact that something is sheep is the basis of permissibility, while the fact that it is a pig is the basis of prohibition.
And the basis in the aforementioned examples is not the cause, and the mentioned rulings are not based on a cause at all.
In rulings that are based on a cause, since the ruling is linked to its cause, the term "basis" (manat) is used to refer to the cause metaphorically, which may mislead one into thinking that the cause is truly the basis; hence, this clarification is necessary. The usul scholars (usuliyyun) have differed regarding the reasoning behind rulings. Some have held that the original principle in rulings is reasoning, and that reasoning applies to all rulings, although in some rulings reasoning is suspended due to the inability of the jurist to grasp the cause, such as the number of units of prayer, the estimation of shares, obligations, expiations, and others. Others have rejected this reasoning, stating that a ruling is not to be reasoned unless its cause is established by legal evidence (1).
Those who adhere to the principle of reasoning in rulings are those who have used the term "basis" to mean "cause." An example of this is the text mentioned about al-Zarkashi earlier. Since all rulings have causes according to this group, the basis of the ruling is its cause for them. This means that one must search in the basis of the ruling for a description that is suitable for reasoning, to link the ruling to it. This description becomes the cause of the ruling and its basis, and from here arose expressions among this group such as "refining the basis" (tanqih al-manat) and "deriving the basis" (takhrij al-manat), in addition to the expression "establishing the basis" (tahqiq al-manat).
Establishing the basis:
__________
(1) This disagreement and the debate surrounding it will be addressed later in detail and with documentation.


[Page 66]

Al-Amidi said: "Since the cause (illah) is the subject of the ruling and its basis, the examination and ijtihad (juridical reasoning) in it is either in establishing the basis, refining it, or deriving it. As for establishing the cause, it is the examination of the existence of the cause in individual cases after knowing it in itself... as in the direction of the qibla, for it is the basis for the obligation to face it... and the determination of this direction as the qibla in cases of ambiguity is presumed through ijtihad and examination of the indicators" (1). He also said: "Like justice (adalah), for it is the basis for the acceptance of testimony... as for whether this witness is just, it is presumed through ijtihad" (2). He stated: "Like the intoxicating strength (shidda al-mutriba), for it is the basis for the prohibition of drinking wine; thus, the examination of its presence in the beverage is the establishment of the basis" (3).
Accordingly, establishing the basis is the process of verifying whether the reality corresponds to the reality for which the ruling was given or not. The ruling is the obligation to face the qibla, and the subject of the obligation is facing the qibla. Verifying the direction of the qibla is the establishment of the basis, and it is known that the direction of the qibla is not the cause of the ruling, that is, of the obligation. Likewise, the description of justice in a witness; the legislator has stipulated that the witness must be just, and verifying his justice for the acceptance or rejection of his testimony is the establishment of the basis. Similarly, the intoxicating strength, if it is intoxication, for intoxication is the basis for prohibition, and verifying whether something is intoxicating or not is the establishment of the basis.
Refining the basis:
Al-Amidi said: "As for refining the basis, it is the examination and ijtihad in determining what the text indicates as a cause without specification, by eliminating what has no relevance in consideration from the accompanying descriptions" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam 3/264 - 265.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source.


[Page 67]

Since the basis of the ruling is the reality or the subject to which the ruling pertains, and since the rulings are reasoned—according to those who say that reasoning is the original basis for rulings—there must be a description in the subject that is suitable for reasoning, and for this reason the ruling was established. The other descriptions in the subject have no effect on the ruling. An example of this is the prohibition of alcohol. The fact that something is alcohol is the basis for its prohibition. Considering that reasoning is the original basis for rulings, there must be a reason for the ruling that is one of the descriptions of alcohol, meaning it is a description in the basis. If we look at descriptions such as liquidity, color, or smell, we find that they are not suitable for prohibition. However, if we consider the description of intoxication, we find it suitable for prohibition, making it a valid reason—according to them—.
The process of establishing that other attributes have no effect on the ruling is called the refinement of the legal basis (tanqih al-manat). This is the meaning of what al-Amidi stated above. Al-Asnawi said: "The refinement of the legal basis means clarifying what the legislator has linked the ruling to, that is, what he has associated it with and made it contingent upon, which is the cause."(1)
The extraction of the legal ruling:
Al-Amidi said: "As for the extraction of the legal ruling (takhrij al-manat), it is the consideration and ijtihad in establishing the reason for the ruling indicated by the text or consensus without its cause. This is similar to the ijtihad in establishing that the intoxicating severity is the reason for the prohibition of alcoholic beverages."(2)
Al-Zarkashi said: "As for the extraction of the legal ruling (takhrij al-manat), it is the juristic effort (ijtihad) in deriving the reason (illah) for the ruling indicated by the text or consensus without addressing its reason at all"(3). It is a process of establishing or identifying the description present in the legal ruling's basis, which is the reason for the ruling. This is unlike refinement (tanqih), which is the establishment of the unsuitability of descriptions for reasoning, so that only one description remains, thus becoming the reason without establishing it, but based on the premise that the original reasoning is through a description, and there is none other than it, so it becomes the reason.


The second section
The paths of reasoning and their conditions


Introduction:
__________
(1) Al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul 4/138. And see: al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit 4/227.
(2) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/265.
(3) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit 4/227.


[Page 68]

The cause (illah) is a comprehensive description that connects the original (asl) and the branch (far'). There are many comprehensive descriptions, but not every comprehensive description is suitable for reasoning (ta'lil). Therefore, there must be a legal evidence (dalil shar'i) to consider the description in reasoning. Likewise, the intended meaning of the cause is the legal cause. Nothing can be considered legal unless it is established through a legal means, that is, indicated by the Sharia. Accordingly, the intended meaning of the paths of the cause (masalik al-'illah) is its evidences, that is, the legal evidences indicating that the description is a cause. Al-Zarkashi said: "The paths of the cause: that is, the ways indicating the cause" (1). He also said: "Know that it is not sufficient in analogy (qiyas) to merely find the comprehensive description in the original and the branch. Rather, there must be evidence that supports it in consideration. The evidences are of three types: consensus (ijma'), text (nass), and inference (istinbat)" (2). Al-Shawkani said: "The scholars have agreed that there must be evidence for the cause" (3). Abu al-Husayn al-Basri said: "The path of the legal cause is only the Sharia; we say this because the path of the legal cause is how its ruling is established and its effect in it. For example, its ruling is established with it in the original and is negated with its absence, and it is known that this depends on the Sharia because its ruling and the way it is established according to the cause are only obtained through the Sharia" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/165.
(2) The same source.
(3) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 207.
(4) Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, al-Mu'tamad fi Usul al-Fiqh, 3/249.


[Page 69]

Similarly, the description may come in one of the paths of reasoning (ta'lil), but it is not suitable for extending the ruling based on it, because the description must have conditions for it to be considered a reason (illah) or for the ruling to be extended based on it (1). For example, Allah, Exalted is He, says: { Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun } (2), and He says: { That they may witness benefits for themselves } (3). The "lam" in both texts is for reasoning, and the path of reasoning here is the text. However, the descriptions that come after the "lam" are not suitable as reasons for analogy, as the decline of the sun in the first verse is merely an indication; it is a cause but not a reason for the obligation of prayer. The testimony of benefits in pilgrimage is a result that may or may not occur, and it is not a suitable reason for the obligation of pilgrimage. Thus, the descriptions in the two verses do not mean the motivator. For a description to be a motivator, it must include a wisdom that is intended by the legislator in enacting the ruling, which is one of the conditions of the reason. Therefore, even if the reason appears in one of the paths of reasoning, it is not considered so until its conditions are met. Al-Shawkani said: "It has twenty-four conditions" (4). Al-Amidi mentioned under the title "On the Conditions of the Original Reason" twenty issues (5). The books of usul (principles) are filled with mentioning and discussing them.
Below are some paths of reasoning and their conditions to the extent necessary to understand the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi, based on what has been clarified in the introduction to this chapter that the objectives of the Sharia for him are its reasons.
Paths of reasoning:
The first path: consensus (ijma). This is like the consensus of the Companions on the fact that childhood is a reason for establishing guardianship over a minor in establishing the guardianship of marriage by analogy to the guardianship of property. (6)
__________
(1) See: Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam. 3/179.
(2) Surah Al-Isra, 78.
(3) Surah Al-Hajj, 28.
(4) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 207. Al-Zarkashi elaborated on these twenty-four conditions in his book Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/119 - 140.
(5) See: Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam, 3/179.
(6) See: the same reference, 3/222.


[Page 70]

The second approach: the explicit text (1). This is when a proof from the Book and the Sunnah is mentioned for the reasoning with a term that is designated for it in the language, without needing any further consideration or inference. It is of two types:
The first type: what is explicitly stated as the description being a reason for the ruling, such as stating explicitly that the reason for the ruling is such and such, or that the cause of its legislation is such and such (2), or stating explicitly what implies that according to the linguistic usage, like his saying - peace and blessings be upon him -: "I had prohibited you from storing the meat of the sacrificial animals for the sake of the drafters." (3) And like his saying - peace and blessings be upon him -: "The permission to enter is made for the sake of sight." (4) And like His saying, Exalted is He: { For that reason, We decreed upon the Children of Israel } (5). Thus, the phrase (for the sake of such and such) or (for the reason of such and such) is explicit in mentioning the reason.

(2) See: al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, 3/222.
(3) Narrated by Muslim from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) in the Book of Sacrifices, Chapter on the prohibition of eating the meat of sacrificial animals, (3643), and Abu Dawood (2429), and al-Nasa'i (4355), and Malik in al-Muwatta (918), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (23115).
(4) Narrated by al-Bukhari (5772), and al-Tirmidhi (2633), and Ahmad (21737).
(5) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 32.


[Page 71]

The second section: What has been mentioned with a letter from the letters of reasoning, such as "lam" (ل), "ki" (كي), "in" (إن), and "ba" (ب). As for "lam," it is like His saying, Exalted is He: { so that there will be no argument for the people against Allah after the messengers } (1). This indicates reasoning by the description that the "lam" has entered upon, as the scholars of language have stated that it is for reasoning. As for "ki," it is like His saying, Exalted is He: { so that it will not be a state of wealth among the rich from you } (2). And as for "in," it is like the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding the martyrs of Uhud: "Wrap them in their blood, for they will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection with their veins gushing blood, their color like blood and their scent like musk" (3). And as for "ba," it is like His saying, Exalted is He: { a reward for what they used to do } (4).
Al-Amidi said: "These are the explicit forms of reasoning, and when they occur, it is necessary to believe in the reasoning unless evidence indicates that reasoning was not intended, in which case it would be a metaphor for what was intended by it. This is the case with 'lam,' as if one were to say: 'Why did you do such and such?' and he replies: 'Because I intended to do so.' And as in the saying of someone: 'I pray for Allah' and the poet's saying: 'Prepare for death and build for destruction.' The intention of the action does not suffice to be a reason for the action or its purpose. Likewise, the essence of Allah, Exalted is He, cannot be a reason for prayer, nor can death be a reason for birth, nor can destruction be a reason for building. Rather, the reason for the action is what motivates the action, which are the things that can serve as motivators" (5). This means that reasoning with what has a letter of reasoning requires that it be a suitable description.

(1) Surah An-Nisa, 165.
(2) Surah Al-Hashr, 7.
(3) Narrated by al-Nasa'i (1975).
(4) Surah As-Sajda, 17. And Surah Al-Ahqaf, 14. And Surah Al-Waqi'a, 24.
(5) Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam fi Usul Al-Ahkam, 3/224. As for his statement in the text: "It is necessary to believe in reasoning," I do not find it precise; it is more accurate to omit the word "belief," so that the text reads: "Reasoning is necessary" or "The ruling must be reasoned," as the matter pertains to speculative legal rulings and juristic preference.


[Page 72]

"The third approach: what indicates causation through indication and allusion" (1). This is what the evidence indicates in a suggestive manner rather than explicitly. That is, the text indicates the cause by its implied meaning rather than its literal wording. It is divided into two categories:
The first: that the implied meaning indicates causation, whether it is a concept of agreement or a concept of disagreement. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: {Indeed, the alms are for the poor and the needy and those employed to collect them and for bringing hearts together} (2). The implication is that those who are not among these mentioned have no right to the zakat, and these descriptions are suitable for causation; therefore, they serve as causes. The bringing together of hearts is a reason for giving zakat, and if this quality is removed, the right to zakat is also removed. The same can be said for their being poor, needy, or workers collecting it.
This category corresponds to the first category of the explicit text indicating causation, but that is from the literal meaning while this is from the implied meaning.
The second: "that the causation is necessary from the meaning of the term by its placement, not that the term indicates causation by its placement" (3).
In this case, the text may not have a concept of agreement or disagreement, and it may have a concept but does not indicate causation. However, the presence of a certain term or condition makes causation necessary from this placement, that is, from the association with this term or condition. It has several cases:
__________
(1) The same location.
(2) Surah At-Tawbah, 60.
(3) Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam, 3/224.


[Page 73]

Among them: the arrangement of the ruling based on the description with the conjunction "fa" (ف) indicating consequence and causation in the words of Allah or His Messenger or the narrator from the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him): As for the words of Allah, it is as in His saying: {And as for the thief, the male and the female, amputate their hands} (1). And as for the words of His Messenger, it is like his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever revives dead land, it is his" (2). And his saying: "You have control over yourself, so choose" (3). And as for the words of the narrator, it is as in the saying: "The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) forgot in the prayer, so he prostrated" (4). Al-Amidi said: "In all these instances, it indicates that what the ruling is arranged upon with 'fa' is a reason for the ruling, because 'fa' in the language is indicative of consequence" (5). Thus, 'fa' does not imply causation linguistically. However, its presence indicates that the ruling occurs following the description, and the arrangement of the ruling following the description serves as a reminder that the description was a cause for the ruling, meaning a reason for its legislation, thus it becomes a cause. Causation is necessary for this arrangement, that is, for the arrangement of the ruling based on the description with 'fa', which provides a concept suitable for causation.

[Page 74]

And among them is that the legislator differentiates between two matters in ruling by mentioning a characteristic; this indicates that this characteristic is the reason for the differentiation. If it had not been mentioned, the differentiation would not have existed, and the ruling would have included both matters. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: { And do not approach them until they are pure } (1). The legislator's differentiation between the two matters, purity and menstruation, in the permissibility of approaching them indicates the reason for the prohibition, which is menstruation. This differentiation is based on the term of limitation (until). And like the saying of the Prophet - peace and blessings be upon him -: "Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt, equal for equal, hand to hand; if these types differ, then sell as you wish, provided it is hand to hand" (2). The legislator's differentiation between the two matters, which are the same kind and their difference, in the permissibility or prohibition of selling these types indicates the reason for the prohibition, which is the sameness of the kind.

As for al-Bukhari, he mentioned four types in the Book of Sales, Chapter on What is Mentioned in Selling Food and the Like, and the Chapter on Selling Barley for Barley, but he did not mention silver or salt (1190) and (2028). There is a narration from Muslim by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "... whoever adds or seeks to add has engaged in usury, the giver and the taker are the same in this" (2971).


[Page 75]

One example of this approach is when the legislator mentions a description that is appropriate alongside the ruling, such as his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "The judge should not rule while he is angry"(1). This indicates that anger is a reason that prevents judgment due to the confusion of thought and disturbance of state it causes(2). The judge's role is to render judgment, and his sitting is for the purpose of judgment; thus, if he is prevented from judging in a certain state, this indicates that this state is the reason for the prohibition.
This section corresponds to the second section of the two divisions of the explicit text's indication of reasoning, but that is from the stated meaning (manṭūq) and this is from the implied meaning (mafhūm).
These three paths: consensus (ijma), textual evidence (nass), and indication and hint (tanbih wa imā') are agreed upon among the jurists. As for the subsequent paths, they are subject to disagreement; the proponents of the method of the theologians among the usuliyyin, specifically the Imams of the Shafi'i school, accept and defend them. Conversely, the proponents of the method of the jurists among the usuliyyin, namely the Hanafis, reject them.
The Shafi'i scholars refer to the reasons that come with these three pathways as the stated reasons (al-‘ilal al-mansusah), while the reasons that come with the other pathways that will follow are referred to as the inferred reasons (al-‘ilal al-mustanbatah). As for the Hanafi scholars, they mean by the inferred reasons (al-‘ilal al-mustanbatah) the reasons that come specifically with the pathways of indication and hinting, while the stated reasons (al-‘ilal al-mansusah) for them are those that come with the pathways of consensus (ijma) and text (nass).
The fourth approach: exploration and division. Some usul scholars have advocated for it. It is based on the premise that the foundation of rulings is reasoning. Its meaning is that the observer must thoroughly investigate all the attributes that could potentially be the reason for the ruling—based on the assumption that every ruling must have a reason. This is the exploration, then he examines these potential attributes one by one and establishes that they are not the reason for the ruling except for one of them, which is the division. Thus, the attribute that remains is the reason.
__________
(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari, in the chapter "Can a judge rule or give fatwa while angry" (6625), and by Muslim in the chapter "The dislike of a judge ruling while angry" (3241), and by al-Tirmidhi (1254) who said it is good and authentic, and by al-Nasa'i (5326).
(2) See: al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/230.


[Page 76]

This approach establishes the cause by negating what is besides it, rather than by examining it.
Al-Zarkashi said: "It is linguistically the act of testing, and from it is the probe that is used to test the wound, which is called the 'mismar'. It is named this way because the observer of the ailment divides the attributes and tests each one of them to see whether it is suitable for the cause or not?"(1).
Those who assert that the basis of rulings is the reasoning behind them differ on the validity of this approach. As for those who reject this view, they do not adopt this method. Al-Sarakhsi said: "The evidence that the existence of a proof of invalidity in other attributes does not establish the validity of the attribute claimed by the reasoner in legal matters is that there are some rulings in the Sharia that are not based on reasoning at all. Thus, the existence of evidence for the invalidity of other attributes does not negate the possibility of evidence for the invalidity of this attribute"(2).
Al-Zarkashi said: "Ibn al-Hajib transmitted in his discussion on the division and classification the consensus of the jurists that a ruling must have a reason."(3)
The fifth approach: analogy and consideration. This is also based on the principle that the original basis for rulings is reasoning. This approach and its details, especially the meaning of consideration (i'tibar) and its types, have a fundamental relationship with the concept of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi. Therefore, it will have - if Allah wills - a separate discussion.

(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/200. And see also: al-Ihkam by al-Amidi. 3/233. And al-Mahsul by al-Razi. 5/217. And Irshad al-Fuhul by al-Shawkani, p. 213.
(2) al-Sarakhsi, Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Sahl, Usul al-Sarakhsi. 2/232, Dar al-Ma'rifah, Beirut, edited by Abu al-Wafa al-Afghani.
(3) al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/111.


[Page 77]

The sixth approach: the approach of analogy (shabah). Its definitions have varied, and much has been said about it. Al-Shawkani said: "Analogy (shabah), which some jurists call inference (istidlal)..." Ibn al-Anbari said: "I do not see a more obscure issue in the matters of usul (principles) than this." They have disagreed on its definition; al-Juwayni said: "It cannot be defined." Others said: "It can be defined"(1). Al-Ghazali said: "The meaning of analogy is the association of the original and the branch by a description, while acknowledging that this description is not a cause (illa) for the ruling, unlike the analogy of the cause, which is an association based on what is the cause of the ruling. If the usuliyun (principles scholars) did not intend to include this type of analogy in their discussions, I do not know what they meant, and how they distinguished it from pure analogy (tard) and from similarity"(2). Al-Juwayni said: "Analogy does not correspond to the ruling in the manner of kinship; it is distinct from pure analogy, as pure analogy is a mere ruling that is not supported by meaning or similarity"(3). He then elaborated, stating in summary: "The analogy of similarity is the resemblance of the branch to the original in a way that strongly suggests the inclusion of the branch with the original, without the emergence of a cause that necessitates the inclusion. An example of this is the inclusion of ablution (wudu) with dry ablution (tayammum) in the requirement of intention (niyyah), for there is no suitable meaning in either ablution or dry ablution that necessitates the inclusion of one with the other. Nevertheless, the observer finds within himself a strong feeling of the correctness of the inclusion and an inclination towards it, even if he cannot articulate the cause of the analogy. Thus, the analogy of similarity is not a mere ruling but rather a following of conjecture. Al-Juwayni cited al-Shafi'i's expression regarding the issue of including ablution with dry ablution, intending thereby to indicate that al-Shafi'i relied on similarity without being able to articulate the cause, saying: 'Two purifications; how can they be separated?'(4). The statement of the one who said: 'Whoever's divorce is executed, his repudiation is executed' is considered an analogy of similarity(5).
