(1) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul. p. 220. And see: Al-Mahsool by al-Razi, vol. 5.
(2) Pure analogy (tard): meaning that whenever the description is found, the ruling is found.
(3) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa. 2/311.
(4) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/527. Paragraph: 725.
(5) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/527. Paragraph: 725.


[Page 78]

Al-Amidi cited an opinion from Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, who said: "Qadi Abu Bakr went to interpret it by analogy of indication, which is the combination of the original and the branch in a way that does not suit the ruling but necessitates what suits the ruling" (1). He then chose another meaning, which is what is below the suitable and above the rejected, and said: "Perhaps the basis for calling it a resemblance (shabah) is this meaning" (2). He said: "An example of this is al-Shafi'i's statement regarding the issue of removing impurity: 'Purification intended for prayer is not valid without water, for the commonality is purification, and its suitability for specifying water after investigation is not apparent'" (3). He stated that this is what most of the scholars have concluded (4).
The seventh method: rejection and opposition. It is based on the principle of reasoning. Rejection (tard) is the existence of the ruling in all cases where the description exists, provided that the description is neither suitable nor resembling (shabah) (5). For if it were suitable, it would return to the method of analogy and suitability. And if it were resembling, it would return to the method of resemblance.
Opposition (aks) is the negation of the ruling with the negation of the description, and both rejection and opposition are referred to as circularity, meaning that the ruling revolves with the description in existence and non-existence (6). Al-Amidi said: "There has been disagreement about this; a group of usul scholars have gone to the view that it indicates that the description is a cause... and what the scholars among us and others hold is that it does not imply causation, neither definitively nor probabilistically, and this is the preferred view" (7). Al-Juwayni considered it a method and regarded opposition as a condition in the rejected description (8).

The eighth method: the principle of correlation (al-tard) and some usul scholars have argued that correlation without the condition of contrariety is a cause. Thus, correlation becomes a method for them. Al-Razi stated this in al-Mahsool. He said: "What is meant by it (i.e., correlation) (1) is the description that is not known to be suitable or necessitating the suitable if it is present with the description in all cases differing from the place of dispute, and this is what is meant by correlation and continuity"(2). Al-Juwayni rejected it.

Those who rejected the method of correlation and contrariety also rejected the method of correlation as it is more deserving of that. Al-Amidi said: "And if it is known that correlation and contrariety do not serve as evidence for causation, then correlation by itself is more deserving of not being evidence"(3). Al-Zarkashi said: "Correlation: and it is not meant by it that the cause does not get negated, for that is the claim of contrariety, but it is meant that its cause is neither suitable nor effective"(4)... And those who say that correlation and contrariety are not evidence, in the case of correlation not being evidence, it is more so from the first perspective... and those considered by the scholars to hold that reliance on it is invalid because it is a form of nonsense, Imam al-Haramayn said: And the judge went to extremes in condemning those who believe in linking God's judgment to it"(5). He said: "Ibn al-Sam'ani said: And Abu Zayd named those who consider correlation as evidence and continuity as proof of the validity of causation 'the Hushawiya of the people of analogy.' He said: And these are not counted among the jurists"(6).

Al-Ghazali said: "Correlation must be rejected by every analogist"(7), this is his statement in al-Mustasfa, but in Shifa al-Ghalil his statement differs(8).

On the conditions of the cause:

They agreed that the cause (illa) must be indicated by the Sharia. This is to be understood through one of the paths of reasoning (ta'leel). This matter has been clarified in what has preceded.
2- The reason (illah) must mean a motivating factor and not merely an indicator. Al-Amidi said: "They differed on the permissibility of the reason in the original sense being merely an indicator, and the preferred view is that the reason in the original sense must mean a motivating factor, that is, it must include a valid wisdom intended by the Legislator in enacting the ruling. Otherwise, if it were merely a descriptive characteristic without any wisdom, but merely an indicator, then reasoning based on it in the original sense is impossible"(1). This matter has been clarified previously in the explanation of the meanings of the reason.
3- The reason (illa) must be effective in the ruling. Al-Zarkashi said: "In mentioning the conditions of the reason: the first is that it must be effective in the ruling; if it does not affect it, it cannot be considered a reason... Thus, al-Mawardi and al-Ruyani mentioned it, and what they mean by effectiveness is suitability. Better than their expression is the saying of Professor Abu Mansur: that its description must be one that is valid for linking the ruling to it"(2).
He also said: "Some have permitted reasoning based solely on the indicative evidence (al-amara al-tardiyya). The truth is the opposite, and it must include a ruling that motivates the obligated person to comply and serves as a valid witness for linking the ruling to it."(3)
He said: "The judge (al-Qadi) stated in (al-Taqrib): the meaning of the cause (illa) being effective in the ruling is that it is judged that the jurist's (mujtahid) presumption is that the ruling is present when it is established due to it and not due to anything else"(4). There is an important disagreement regarding the condition of effectiveness and its meaning between the Shafi'is and the Hanafis, which I will mention in its place, if Allah wills.

(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/180.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. 4/119.
(3) The same place.
(4) The same place.


[Page 81]

4- It must be a clear and defined description. Clarity and definition are the opposites of ambiguity and obscurity. The obscure and unstable cannot be used for reasoning. An example of this is the hardship of travel, which is not defined; therefore, it was not considered in the hardship of the porter and the baker in the city, making travel a defined description that includes the unstable wisdom of hardship. Thus, reasoning based on hardship is not valid, but travel is correctly counted as a cause that includes the reason. Al-Amidi said: "Most scholars have held that it is impermissible to reason a ruling based solely on wisdom that lacks a defining characteristic, while a minority have permitted it" (1). He said: "We know that the legislator only permitted ease in long travel to alleviate the defined hardship of long travel to a specific destination and did not link it to the hardship itself because it is something that fluctuates and varies. For this reason, he did not permit the heavily burdened porter in the city, even if it is assumed that his hardship exceeds that of the traveler every day by a mile, even if he is in utmost comfort and ease, because that is something that varies and fluctuates" (2).
5- It must be free from any legal evidence against it. Al-Zarkashi said: "It must be free from its condition, meaning that it should not be contradicted by a text or consensus, because analogy (qiyas) is a branch of it and is only used in its absence; thus, it cannot be a negation of it. If either of the two contradicts it, it is invalid" (3).
6- The reason must be consistent. Al-Zarkashi said: "It must be consistent, meaning that whenever it exists, the ruling exists" (4). If it exists and the ruling does not exist, it means that it is not a reason.
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/180.
(2) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, p. 181.
(3) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/122.
(4) The same source.


[Page 82]

7- The reason (illah) must be transitive. This means that the ruling extends from the original case to the branch. Everyone agrees on the validity of this condition for the soundness of analogy (qiyas). However, they differ on the validity of the reason if it is not transitive. Some of the usul scholars consider the description a reason for the original case even if the ruling cannot be extended to a branch by analogy. Others prohibit considering it a reason on the basis that there is no benefit in reasoning with it. The benefit of the reason is the transference of the ruling from the original case to the branch. Al-Amidi said: "Everyone agrees that the transitivity of the reason is a condition for the validity of analogy, and on the validity of the limited reason(1), whether it is explicitly stated or agreed upon. They only differ on the validity of the limited reason if it is neither explicitly stated nor agreed upon, such as the reasoning of the Shafi'i school regarding the prohibition of usury (riba) in the two currencies based on the essence of their value(2)"(3).
And Shams al-A'imma al-Sarakhsi said: "The disagreement is regarding the condition of transitivity, and our position is that reasoning with a text in a way that does not allow for transference is not permissible at all. According to al-Shafi'i, this reasoning is permissible, but it does not constitute analogy. He permitted reasoning with the text on usury in gold and silver based on their value, even if it does not transfer. We do not permit that, and our position is that the ruling of reasoning is the transference of the ruling of the original case to the branches"(4).
__________
(1) The limited reason refers to the description that has been established as a reason for the ruling of the original case, and cannot be transferred to a branch, such as theft being a reason for cutting off the hand; the text indicates reasoning for the ruling of the original case with it. However, there is no branch to which the ruling can be transferred by analogy based on the commonality of the reason. Applying the ruling of cutting off the hand in another context is based on the indication of the text, that is, by the generality of the text and not by analogy. Among the related disagreements among the analogists here is another disagreement, which is whether the evidence for the reason is the reason itself or the evidence of the address that indicated it and the reason? The Shafi'is and the theologians went with the former, while the Hanafis went with the latter.
(2) See: Footnote number 4, page 61 of this book.
(3) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/192.

[Page 83]

8- That a single ruling should not have two causes simultaneously in one scenario. Al-Amidi said: "There is a disagreement regarding the permissibility of attributing a single ruling in one scenario to two causes simultaneously; some have prohibited this absolutely... while others have permitted it absolutely... and some have differentiated between the stated and inferred causes, permitting it in the stated causes and prohibiting it in the inferred ones... The preferred view is that of the first opinion" (1).
And al-Zarkashi said: "It is permissible to attribute a single ruling to different types based on different causes for one person by consensus, such as attributing the permissibility of killing Zayd for his apostasy, and Amr for retribution, and Khalid for adultery" (2). He also said: "The Prophet explicitly stated different causes, each of which is independent in permitting blood, as he - peace and blessings be upon him - said: 'The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith, or adultery after chastity, or killing a believer unjustly'" (3) (4).
It appears from the texts of the imams that there is a prohibition against attributing a ruling to two causes, and the consensus reported, as mentioned by al-Zarkashi, does not pertain to the cause by which analogy (qiyas) is established. The causes mentioned in the hadith are all limited causes, so a branch cannot be analogized to a root through them, and the application of the ruling in any case is based on the evidence of the text and not on analogy. Or the attribution may be understood in the sense of an indicator rather than a motivator. Al-Zarkashi, when presenting the differing opinions regarding attributing more than one cause, said: "The permissibility is absolute, which is the correct view and the view of the majority, as the judge said in al-Taqrib, and then he said: 'And based on this, we say, considering that the causes are signs and indicators of the rulings, not causes that necessitate them'" (5).

As for the distinction between the specified cause (illa mansusah) and the inferred cause (illa mustanbatah), it is based on the fact that the specified cause, as in the above hadith, is called a cause even if it is a cause for the ruling of the original only, meaning it is a limited cause. The prohibition regarding the inferred cause is because the inferred cause is based on the principle of reasoning, not on the evidence of texts or consensus. Accordingly, the establishment of a second cause is considered a refutation of the first cause.
9- Among the matters they differed on is the permissibility of specifying the cause. Al-Amidi said: "They differed on the permissibility of specifying the inferred cause; most of the followers of Abu Hanifa, Malik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted it, while most of the followers of al-Shafi'i prohibited it. It has been said that this is reported from al-Shafi'i. Then, those who permit its specification agreed on the permissibility of specifying the specified cause, and they differed on the permissibility of specifying the inferred cause if there is no impediment or loss of condition in the place of deviation. Most prohibited it, while a minority permitted it. Those who prohibit the specification of the inferred cause differed on the permissibility of specifying the specified cause."(1)
The most important factor in this difference, in general, is the difference in terminology regarding the meanings of specified and inferred. Those who consider the specified cause to be that which comes through one of the two paths of text or consensus permit the specification of the specified cause and consider it akin to the specification of other texts. These individuals consider the inferred cause to be that which comes through the path of indication and hint, and they differ on the permissibility of specifying it, rejecting all other paths.
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/194.


[Page 85]

As for those who associate the following rationale with the method of indication and hinting at the specified rationales, like those that come through the method of text or consensus, they argue about the difference in the permissibility of specifying the stipulated ones due to the disagreement in specifying those that come through the method of indication and hinting. The derived rationale according to this group is the rationale that comes through all other methods such as analogy (qiyas), opposition (al-‘aks), examination and division (sabr wa taqsim), and similarity (munasaba) and resemblance (shabah), and they do not permit specifying it. They assert that the specification of the derived rationale is not permissible, because the failure to consider the described attribute through these methods is akin to nullifying the attribute or akin to its non-establishment altogether. This is due to the lack of confidence in these methods in the first place. Thus, the branching of disagreement in this issue and the confusion in the transmission from the imams is attributed to the differing intentions behind the terminologies, and this is something that should be noted when studying the books of the imams of usul (usul al-fiqh) concerning analogy and rationale.
Al-Zarkashi said: "Know that the cause (illa) is either rational (aqli) or textual (sam'i). The rational cannot be restricted by the consensus of scholars of reasoning... They only differed regarding the textual, which can either be derived (mustanbata) or explicitly stated (mansusa). If it is derived, then al-Mawardi and al-Ruyani firmly asserted that it cannot be restricted in the sense that the cause does not remain a proof beyond the specific ruling due to the invalidity of relying on it." (1)
10- One of the conditions of the derived reason ('illa) is that it should not invalidate its original source. This condition applies only to derived reasons and not to those explicitly stated. Al-Amidi said: "The derived reason must not be from the ruling that it is based upon in a way that invalidates the ruling from which it was derived. This is like the reasoning for the obligation of a sheep in the case of zakat due to fulfilling the needs of the poor, as this would negate the obligation of the sheep, and the negation of the original ruling from which it was derived necessarily invalidates the derived reason, as its validity depends on its consideration in that context."(2)
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit. 4/122.
(2) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/215.


[Page 86]

And since this condition is a condition for the derived (mustanbata) rulings only, it means that the specified cause (illah) can invalidate the original ruling, and indeed this is the essence of reasoning (ta‘leel) itself. The cause is what the ruling was established for, and its removal means the removal of the ruling, which is the meaning of invalidation here. Therefore, the consensus on this condition in the derived rulings indicates a lack of confidence in reasoning based on it, and this is only because all paths of the derived rulings are based on the principle that reasoning is fundamental in rulings. This, in turn, leads the jurist (faqih) to search for a strong cause in his view, so if he finds that reasoning with this theoretical cause leads to the removal of the ruling with the removal of the cause, he will abandon reasoning based on it. An example from al-Amidi above is clear in this; reasoning for the obligation of zakat based on providing for the poor implies the cancellation of the obligation of zakat if there are no poor people, which negates the original obligation of zakat, thus invalidating reasoning based on this description.
Al-Zarkashi said: "If it is derived, the condition is that it does not invalidate the original or invalidate part of it, so that it does not lead to abandoning the preferred (rajih) for the less preferred (marjuh), as the presumption derived from the text is stronger than that derived from derivation, because it is a branch of this ruling, and the branch does not invalidate its origin; otherwise, it would necessitate returning to itself in invalidation."(1)
11- One of the conditions of the cause ('illa) is that it should not be the same as the subject of the original ruling (hukm al-asl); if it were so, the application of the ruling in other cases would not be by analogy (qiyas) and these cases would not be branches (furu') but rather a direct application of the text, and these cases would be the basis (manat) of the ruling. The cause of the original ruling would then be limited.
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/137. And al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul. p. 208.


[Page 87]

Al-Amidi said: "Most scholars have stated that the condition for the cause of the original ruling is that it should not be the subject of the original ruling nor a part of its subject. Others have permitted it, and the preferred view is to differentiate, which is that it is impermissible in the original but permissible in the part."(1) He also said: "If the cause were specifically the subject of the original ruling, then the cause would be limited... Yes, this is only possible if the cause of the original ruling is not transitive."(2) He added: "As for the part, it is not impermissible to use it as a cause due to the possibility of the generality of the original and the branch."(3)

Al-Zarkashi said: "If it is transitive, meaning it exists outside the original, it is required that the causation in the subject be only a part of it. It cannot be imagined to be transitive, unlike the limited, where this is permissible."(4)

The Third Topic
The Path of Analogy and Appropriateness

Introduction:
Previously, the concept of appropriateness was mentioned as a condition of the cause, which is a pillar in analogy (qiyas). Some of the usul scholars have made it a distinct path of causation with its own conditions. The following discusses the topic of appropriateness, its conditions, and its categories.
The reasoning based on the appropriate description is founded on the principle that the original rulings are based on reasoning. If the Sharia indicates the cause through explicit or implicit text, consensus, or by deduction through hints and indications, then that is sufficient. If it does not indicate, one must search for the most suitable description for reasoning. The most suitable is the one that is most appropriate, provided that the Sharia does not indicate its rejection or abrogation. The appropriate description is one that results in a benefit or harm depending on whether the ruling is a command for action or a prohibition against it.
However, determining the appropriate beneficial description in the ruling is influenced by the jurist's perspective on what constitutes benefit and what constitutes harm, as well as their view on the issue of goodness or badness in actions. A jurist may perceive a benefit that later, upon examination and research, turns out to be a harm, and vice versa, or that the Sharia has abrogated or invalidated it, or that there is something more beneficial and more appropriate for reasoning.
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ahkam. 3/179.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/140.


[Page 88]

This has led to details and restrictions in defining the appropriate (munasib) and its conditions among the usuliyyin (scholars of Islamic jurisprudence), resulting in expressions such as recognized public interest (mashlaha mu'tabara), abrogated public interest (mashlaha mulghah), remote public interest (mashlaha mursala), and legislatively accepted public interest (mashlaha murtada shar'an), as well as the objectives of creation (maqasid al-khalq) and the objectives of the Legislator (maqasid al-shari'). There was also a division of the appropriate into real rational and imaginary persuasive. "The first is that which, the more one investigates and examines it, the more its appropriateness is confirmed, while the second is that which is initially imagined to be appropriate, but when subjected to research and scrutiny, its appropriateness falls away and reveals itself to be without substance" (1). Furthermore, it was divided into necessary (daruri), need-based (hajji), and improvement-based (tahsin). Al-Zarkashi said: "The categories of the appropriate in terms of reality and persuasion are divided into real and persuasive. The real is divided into what occurs in the realm of necessity, the realm of need, and the realm of improvement" (2). He then said: "As for the persuasive, it is that which initially appears to be appropriate, but upon thorough investigation, it turns out otherwise" (3).
Clarifying the meaning of ikhalah and munasibah:
It is noted in the context of the texts of the imams of usul that some of them use the terms ikhalah and munasibah interchangeably, while others differentiate between them. Al-Amidi says: "The fifth approach in establishing the cause is ikhalah and munasibah" (4), and al-Shawkani states: "Munasabah: it is expressed as ikhalah, public interest, inference, and consideration of objectives, and its extraction is called the derivation of the basis (takhrij al-manat), which is the essence of the book of qiyas (analogy) and its area of ambiguity and clarity. The meaning of munasibah is the specification of the cause merely by presenting the appropriateness without any defects, neither by text nor otherwise, and munasibah in language means compatibility, and the appropriate (munasib) is that which is compatible" (5).
__________
(1) See: al-Ghazali, Shifa al-Ghalil, p. 132.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/188.
(3) The same source, 4/192.
(4) Al-Amidi, Al-Ahkam, 3/236.
(5) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 214. And see: Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/186.


[Page 89]

As for Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni, he distinguishes between them. For him, "ikhalah" (الإخالة) is a descriptive term that can be imagined by the observer as a reason for the coming of the ruling. "Munasabah" (المناسبة) is the established fact that the description leads to the benefit or to what the Legislator intends. Thus, "ikhalah" is the claim of the description that leads to the coming of the ruling in accordance with the benefit, while "munasabah" is the emergence and establishment of the causal relationship between the description and the benefit that follows from it, as descriptions are signs and indicators of the ruling, and rulings have come for the sake of benefits. The establishment of the relationship between the description and the ruling makes the description a motivator.
He says: "If a ruling is established in a matter that is agreed upon, and the extractor claims that it is justified by a description he has presented, he is required to substantiate his claim regarding the original matter... If a claimant asserts that the meaning he has presented is a cause for the ruling, this claim is devoid of proof in that the determination of causes is not permissible as previously discussed in the refutation of the rejecters. There must be an appearance of a reason in the mind of the extractor that necessitates the imagination of a specific meaning in its establishment, and he is required to present it" (1). Then he said: "What the scholars have relied upon and what the esteemed Abu Ishaq has accepted is the establishment of the cause of the original matter by considering its 'ikhalah' and its 'munasabah' with the ruling, while being free from impediments and invalidators and conforming to the principles" (2). He said: "If it is said: If the one who establishes a cause presents an acceptable reason in 'ikhalah', it is accepted, and it is said to him: Not every 'mukhil' (مخيل) is a cause, and not every public interest (maslaha) is an acceptable reason in rulings, from where do you claim that what you have presented is of the kind that can be relied upon? For 'ikhalah' is divided, and the reasons for public interest are absent, and the Sharia does not see the ruling as connected to all of them, and the narrators have not documented the paths of conjectures for the Companions and their directions. So if the claim of connection to every benefit is invalidated and it is not clear to us what the predecessors relied upon, how does the very 'ikhalah' indicate anything?" (3). Then he said: "If 'ikhalah' appears and the meaning is free from invalidators and the presumption is strong, then that is certainly of the kind that the predecessors relied upon" (4). Then he said: "If it is said: Then 'ikhalah' with safety is what indicates. We say: No, but if 'ikhalah' is established and the 'munasabah' is apparent and the invalidators are removed, then that aligns with the path of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them" (5).
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni, al-Burhan. 2/524. Paragraph: 756.
(2) Al-Juwayni, al-Burhan, p: 526. Paragraph: 759.
(3) The same source, 2/527. Paragraph: 759.
(4) The same location.
(5) The same source, p: 528. Paragraph: 762.


[Page 90]

The observer of these statements will understand the meaning of "ikhalah" and "munasaba." "Ikhalah" means the claim of a descriptive attribute as a cause. However, this - as he said - is a claim that must be proven, and the way to prove it is through the emergence of the appropriateness of the description and the removal of invalidating factors. His statement: "The ikhalat are divided" means that the attributes that can be claimed are numerous and varied; some are valid while others are nullified, so this alone is not sufficient. Even if it is said that this description contains a public interest (maslaha), this is also not enough. His statement: "The avenues of istislah (public interest) are negated" and his statement: "Not every istislah is an accepted avenue" mean that merely having the description be a public interest or containing a public interest is not sufficient to establish its validity for reasoning. From here, his meaning of "munasaba" is understood, which is that the described attribute - being a public interest - must have a public interest that is accepted by the Sharia. Or that the establishment of the ruling based on that description necessitates the realization of that public interest logically. As for the first, which is that the public interest is accepted by the Sharia, this is what he means by the term "removal of invalidating factors." Therefore, the meaning of "munasaba" can only be the necessity or establishment of the realization of the public interest from the establishment of the ruling based on the description. This establishment occurs through a preponderance of evidence and does not require certainty. This meaning is confirmed by his statement: "If the ikhalah appears and the meaning is free from invalidating factors and there is a preponderance of evidence, then this is among what the early scholars have certainly related."(1)
Al-Razi said: "People have mentioned two things in defining appropriateness: the first is that it leads to what is in accordance with human benefit in terms of acquisition and preservation, and it may be expressed as acquisition by bringing benefit and preservation by repelling harm... The second is that it is compatible with the actions of rational individuals in customs. It is said: this pearl is suitable for this pearl, meaning their combination in a compatible string, and this robe is suitable for this turban, meaning their combination is compatible."(2) Then he said: "The first definition is the statement of one who attributes the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, to the rulings and public interests, and the second definition is the statement of one who rejects it."(3)
__________
(1) The same source, p. 527. Paragraph: 759.
(2) Al-Razi, al-Mahsool. 5/157 - 158.
(3) The same location.


[Page 91]

If we scrutinize the two definitions, we will find them practically intertwined. The second means that the benefit (maslaha) is typically associated with the ruling, so the benefit is contingent upon the relationship between the cause and the effect, and this association serves as a reason for justifying the ruling based on the description(1). This is not a justification for the actions of Allah, while the first definition implies – in his view – a justification for the actions of Allah, which he rejects(2).
Al-Ghazali said: "Establishing the cause by demonstrating its suitability to the ruling and being satisfied with mere suitability in establishing the ruling is a matter of disagreement. It arises from the fact that what is meant by suitability is that which aligns with the objectives of benefits (masalih) such that if it is added, it becomes coherent. An example of this is our statement: 'Wine is prohibited because it removes reason, which is the basis of obligation, and this is suitable.' Not like saying: 'Because it produces foam' or 'Because it is preserved in a container,' for that does not correspond"(3).
He said: "As for the benefit, it originally refers to bringing about a benefit or averting harm, and we do not mean that. For bringing about benefit and averting harm are the objectives of creation and the welfare of creation in achieving their objectives. Rather, we mean by benefit the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia, and the objectives of the Sharia concerning creation are five: to preserve their religion, their lives, their intellect, their lineage, and their wealth. Thus, everything that entails the preservation of these five foundations is a benefit. And everything that undermines these foundations is a harm, and averting it is a benefit. When we use the term 'suitable' and 'appropriate' in the Book of Qiyas (analogy), we mean this category"(4). This clarifies what he means by benefit, which is what has been established as valid in Sharia. This aligns with what is found in al-Juwayni's works. It also agrees with what is found in al-Amidi regarding the definition of suitability, as will be discussed later.
__________
(1) However, it should be noted that al-Razi rejects the notion of cause and effect because, in his view, this is a justification for the actions of Allah. Rather, he states that Allah has made things occur alongside one another. Likewise, he considers benefits to be correlated with actions, not one being the cause of the other. Or that benefits are correlated with rulings. His detailed statement will come in the third section of the second chapter.
(2) Al-Razi, al-Mahsool. 5/157 - 158.
(3) Al-Ghazali, al-Mustasfa. 2/297.
(4) Al-Ghazali, al-Mustasfa, 1/286.


[Page 92]

Al-Amidi says: "Abu Zayd said: 'The appropriate (munasib) is a term for that which, if presented to the intellects, would be accepted by them' (1). However, he saw that this definition, although linguistically accurate, is insufficient in the realm of proving the cause (illah). He said: 'There is no way for the debater to prove it against his opponent in the context of discussion, for the opponent may say: This is something my intellect has not accepted, so it is not appropriate for me, even if the intellect of another has accepted it' (2). This points to the differing concepts among people regarding what is appropriate and what is not. Therefore, Al-Amidi's definition includes what Al-Juwayni elaborated on regarding the necessity of proving the correlation of the benefit (maslaha) with the linking of the ruling to the description, and that the benefit must be legally acceptable or something that is suitable to be intended by the legislator; this condition prevents disagreement in the consideration of what constitutes a benefit and what constitutes a harm (mafsada). He said: 'The truth of the matter is that the appropriate is a clear, defined description from which it follows that the arrangement of the ruling in accordance with it results in what is suitable to be intended by the legislation of that ruling, whether that ruling is negation or affirmation, and whether that intended outcome is the attainment of a benefit or the prevention of a harm' (3).
Al-Zarkashi reported from Ibn al-Hajib al-Maliki: 'The appropriate is a clear, defined description that logically results from the arrangement of the ruling upon it what is suitable to be intended from the attainment of a benefit and the prevention of a harm. If the description is hidden or not defined, its concomitant is considered, which is the presumption, for the unseen does not inform the unseen, like travel due to hardship' (4).
Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi said: 'And its meaning is that the establishment of the ruling is followed by a benefit' (5).
Al-Qarafi said: 'The appropriateness is what entails the attainment of a benefit and the prevention of a harm' (6).
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ahkam. 3/237.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) See: Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit. 4/187.
(5) Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, Rawdat al-Nazir wa Jannat al-Manazir. p. 268, edited by Saif al-Din al-Katib, Dar al-Kitab al-Arabi - Beirut, 1st ed., 1401 AH - 1981 CE.
(6) Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi, Sharh Tanqih al-Fusul fi Ikhtisar al-Mahsol. p. 391. Dar al-Fikr, Cairo.


[Page 93]

The other definitions in various books of usul (principles of jurisprudence) do not deviate from what has been mentioned above.
It is noted about these definitions that their fundamental pillar is that it must logically follow from linking the ruling to the description that a benefit is achieved or a harm is averted. Some have added, particularly the scholars of usul from the Shafi'i school, that the attainment of benefit or the averting of harm must be something that is suitable to be intended by the legislator. This excludes the possibility that the suitable is purely a rational benefit, meaning a benefit that is not supported by a legal ruling, in addition to the requirement that it must be free from invalidators.
As for the definitions that restrict the suitable description to being apparent and precise, this is for the sake of its suitability for reasoning, as one of the conditions of a reason is that it must be an apparent and precise description, regardless of the method by which it is derived.
Categories of suitability:
The suitable description is divided according to the strength and weakness of the suitability and according to its consideration or lack thereof. As for the strength and weakness of the suitability, it is divided into two types: imaginary persuasive and real rational. The first is the description that, the more one examines it, the weaker it becomes, leading to its suitability being dismissed. The second is the description that, the more one researches it, the stronger and clearer it becomes, and it has three levels: necessities, needs, and embellishments. Each of these levels has its complements(1).
From the perspective of consideration and lack thereof, the suitable is divided into considered, unconsidered, and abrogated. Al-Shawkani said: "Know that the suitable is divided according to the testimony of the Sharia to its compatibility and effect, or lack thereof, into three categories: either it is known that the Sharia has considered it, or it is known that it has abrogated it, or neither is known"(2).
1- Considered:
The term "considered" is used in relation to two meanings: the first is the description or meaning that is indicated by a legal evidence; this description or meaning is supported by a text or legal evidence, thus it is considered. This is agreed upon for reasoning by the analogists.
__________
(1) See: Al-Mahsool by al-Razi, 5/159, and thereafter, and Irshad al-Fuhul by al-Shawkani, p. 215, and Shifa al-Ghalil by al-Ghazali, p. 132, and Al-Bahr al-Muhit by al-Zarkashi, 4/192.
(2) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 217.


[Page 94]

The second: What is considered is the description that has been affirmed by a ruling but not by a text or evidence. In other words: what is considered is what has been established in accordance with a ruling or rulings. In a third expression, it is the description that can be imagined in a ruling of the established rulings supported by legal evidence. This meaning is what is intended here.
Al-Amidi said: "The description is either considered in the view of the legislator or it is not considered; if it is considered, its consideration is either by text, consensus, or by arranging the ruling in accordance with it in a case of text or consensus" (1). Al-Shawkani said: "What is meant by consideration is to bring forth the ruling in accordance with it, not to explicitly state it or allude to it; otherwise, the cause would not be derived from the correlation, which is what is meant by their saying that it has been affirmed by a specific origin. Al-Ghazali said in Shifa al-Ghalil: The meaning of the affirmation by a specific origin for the description is that it is inferred from it in that the ruling has been established legally in accordance with it" (2). For example: in the ruling of the non-inheritance of the murderer, the meaning of treating contrary to the intended purpose is observed; based on the fact that the murderer, by killing his ancestor, intends to obtain the inheritance or hasten it, and treating him contrary to his intention is a meaning present in the ruling, this meaning (treating contrary to the intended purpose) is a considered meaning. The legal ruling is the witness to this meaning, or it can be said that this meaning, which has not been indicated by a text or consensus, has come with a ruling in accordance with it. This is the meaning of consideration, which is different from the consideration that is indicated by a text or consensus regarding the description or meaning. The latter has no disagreement, unlike the testimony of the ruling for the description or the coming of a ruling in accordance with the description, regarding the acceptance of this consideration there is significant disagreement.
Types of consideration:
If the consideration is for the very description present in the ruling or its basis, it is a consideration for the very description or its particularity in the ruling. If the consideration is for a description broader than the description present in the ruling or its basis, it is a consideration for the generality of the description or its genus in the ruling.
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, Ahkam. 3/246.
(2) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul. p. 217.


[Page 95]

An example of this is the prohibition of alcohol. The ruling is based on the description of intoxication, and if consideration is directed towards the description of intoxication, it is a consideration of the essence of the description in the prohibition. Therefore, it cannot be compared to the impairment of reason by narcotics because it is not intoxication, but it can be compared to nabidh (fermented drink) because it is intoxication.
And if consideration is directed towards the description or meaning of the impairment of reason, it is broader than intoxication and includes the impairment of reason by alcohol, narcotics, and others. It is a consideration of the generality of the description or its genus, and narcotics can be compared to it. This is the consideration of the genus of the description in the ruling. Al-Amidi said: "This is like the meaning of intoxication, for it is suitable for the prohibition of nabidh, and the essence of intoxication has been established in the prohibition of alcohol, while the effect of its genus has not been demonstrated in its essence." (1)
Another example is the description of hardship in the concession of travel; it is a suitable description supported by the rulings of shortening prayers, combining prayers, and breaking the fast while traveling. If the consideration in these concessions is for the hardship of travel, it is a consideration of the essence of the description or its particularity in the ruling. And if the consideration is for the generality of hardship or exhaustion or difficulty, it is a consideration of the generality of the description or its genus because hardship has types, such as the hardship of travel, the hardship of work, the hardship of jihad, the hardship of menstruation, and others.
However, if the consideration is for a ruling that is broader than the ruling that supports the description, it is a consideration of the description in the generality of the ruling or in its genus. An example of this is the consideration of the description of siblinghood from both parents in precedence in inheritance over siblinghood from the father. The ruling here is the guardianship of inheritance, and the description is the precedence of siblinghood from both parents over siblinghood from the father. Thus, the consideration of this description in the guardianship of inheritance is a consideration of the description in the essence of the ruling. The consideration of the description in the generality of guardianship leads to comparing the guardianship of marriage to the guardianship of inheritance, where siblinghood from both parents is given precedence in the guardianship of marriage. The generality of guardianship encompasses the guardianship of inheritance and the guardianship of marriage. This is a consideration of the description in the generality of the ruling.
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam. 3/246.


[Page 96]

If the consideration is for a description that is broader than the description to which the ruling has testified, and for a ruling that is broader than the ruling that has testified to the description, then it is the consideration of the genus of the description in the genus of the ruling. An example of this type is what al-Amidi mentioned: "The consideration of the genus of the common hardship between the menstruating woman and the traveler in the genus of alleviation, for the specific hardship of the menstruating woman is not the same as the specific hardship of the traveler, but rather of its genus, and the specific alleviation for the traveler by the omission of two units of prayer is not the same as the alleviation for the menstruating woman by the omission of prayer, but rather of its genus" (1).
Accordingly, the consideration in the testimony of the ruling to the description has four types (2):
1- Consideration of the specific description in the specific ruling.
2- Consideration of the genus of the description in the specific ruling.
3- Consideration of the specific description in the genus of the ruling.
4- Consideration of the genus of the description in the genus of the ruling.
Types of what is considered:
__________
(1) The same source, 3/247 - 248.
(2) See: al-Ihkam by al-Amidi, 3/246 - 249. And al-Bahr al-Muhit by al-Zarkashi, 4/193 - 194, and other foundational books of usul.


[Page 97]

If the consideration is for the essence of the description in the essence of the ruling, then it is the influencing factor, and there is a detailed explanation. As for the three categories, which are the consideration of the essence in the genus, the genus in the essence, and the genus in the genus, if there are parallels that testify to the description, meaning other rulings in which the consideration of the description appears, it is called a suitable description. If there are no parallels, meaning the description is only testified to by one ruling, it is called strange. Al-Ghazali said: "The suitable is divided into what aligns with the meanings of the Sharia and corresponds with its actions in considering the meanings, and into what is strange that has no genus" (1). He also said: "As for the suitable, we mean that its genus is influential in that ruling even if its essence is not known in that ruling in another place" (2).
Accordingly, the considered suitable is divided into three categories: influential, suitable, and strange.
A - Influential:
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Shifa al-Ghalil. p. 148.
(2) The same source: p. 149. He said in Al-Mustasfa: "And the presumption has ranks, and the strongest is the influential... followed by the suitable, and then the suitable that does not align. It also has degrees, even if it is weak, but it varies according to the strength of the suitability, and it may lead to the presumption of the jurists in some cases, so it cannot be definitively invalidated, and the degrees of suitability cannot be precisely defined at all. Rather, each issue has its own taste that the jurist should consider." 2/305. The strength or weakness of the suitability has led to the division of the suitable into real and rational, and to placing the description in ranks, the strongest of which is the necessary, followed by the needful, then the embellishing.


[Page 98]

Al-Shawkani says: "The appropriate is either influential or non-influential. The non-influential is either suitable or unsuitable. It can be strange, transmitted, or abrogated." Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 218.
Al-Ghazali said: "The appropriate is divided into influential, suitable, and strange... The meaning of being influential is that its effect is evident in the ruling by consensus or text, so there is no need for the appropriateness" (1). Al-Amidi said: "If it is considered by a text or consensus, then it is the influential one" (2). This means that, according to al-Ghazali, the appropriateness is not a condition for the description that establishes its influence or causation by text or consensus. The reasoning based on the influential is considered one of the strongest types of analogy. Al-Ghazali said: "Analogy is of four types: the influential, then the appropriate, then the similar, then the extension. The lowest of these is the extension, and every proponent of analogy must reject it. The highest is the influential, and every denier of analogy must accept it" (3).
Al-Shawkani said: "The influential is that the text or consensus indicates that it is a cause that shows the effect of the essence of the description in the essence of the ruling or its type in its type" (4).
Thus, the influential is the description that has been established by evidence to have an effect in the ruling; its consideration is not merely a matter of the ruling coming in accordance with it or the ruling testifying to it, but rather its consideration is akin to the testimony of the text or consensus.
__________
(1) Abu Hamid Muhammad al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa fi Ilm Usul al-Fiqh, 2/297, Al-Matba'a al-Amiriya, Bulaq, Egypt, 1322 AH.
(2) Al-Amidi, Al-Ahkam, 3/247.
(3) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa, 2/318.
(4) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 218.


[Page 99]

The influential factor (mu'athir) according to the usuliyyin (jurisprudents) of the Shafi'i school and in the principles of theologians (mutakallimin) in general is a counterpart to the appropriate (mulayim) and the strange (gharib), unlike the usuliyyin of the Hanafi school. The latter have made influence a condition of the cause (illa), and therefore do not accept the path of appropriateness (munasaba) at all; rather, appropriateness for them is a condition for reasoning (ta'leel) based on description (wasf). Thus, they do not accept merely the consideration of the description as a testimony (shahada) for the ruling (hukm) but require the testimony of the text (nass), which they refer to as justice (adala), meaning the justice of the description and its suitability for reasoning. The term appropriate (mulayim) in their texts does not mean what others among the theologians intend; rather, they mean exactly what others refer to with the term appropriate (munasib). Al-Ghazali said: "Know that the influential factor is accepted by consensus among those who advocate analogy (qiyas), and Abu Zayd al-Dabusi restricted analogy to it, saying: only the influential factor is accepted. However, he provided examples of the influential factor, indicating that he accepted the appropriate but also called it an influential factor" (1). The meaning of this text is that the Hanafis accept only the influential factor.
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa. 2/299. This statement by Al-Ghazali, that Al-Dabusi accepts the appropriate and calls it an influential factor, indicates that the Hanafis reason based on the appropriate, which is strongly rejected by the Imams of Hanafi jurisprudence.


[Page 100]

Al-Bazdawi said: "Justice (adl) for us is the effect. And by effect, we mean what has an effect in the Sharia"(1). The commentator on the principles of al-Bazdawi in Kashf al-Asrar said: "The Sheikh explained in some of his writings with this phrase: And by influence, we mean that the nature of that description has an influence in establishing the nature of that ruling in the case of the ruling, either indicated by the Book or by the Sunnah or by consensus. That is, the effect of this description is established by these proofs. Some of the usuli scholars mentioned that the highest types of influential analogy (qiyas) are"(2). He cites the saying that the influential is the highest type of analogy attributed to some usuli scholars and not to himself. He states that the influential has four categories: the specific in the specific, the specific in the general, the general in the specific, and the general in the general(3). Meanwhile, al-Ghazali distinguishes between the influential and the appropriate: "The difference between them is that the influential is that which has shown the effect of its essence in the essence of the disputed ruling by consensus or text in the place of dispute or outside of it... As for the appropriate, we mean that its genus is known to be influential in the genus of that ruling"(4). Thus, the influential according to al-Bazdawi is divided into these four categories, while according to al-Ghazali, the influential is one of the four categories. This disagreement applies to the imams of usul from the Shafi'i and Hanafi schools.
B - The Suitable:
__________
(1) The pride of Islam al-Bazdawi, The Foundations of the Pride of Islam al-Bazdawi. 3/512, edited by Abdullah Mahmoud Muhammad Omar, Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya - Beirut, 1st edition, 1418 AH - 1997 CE, printed with its commentary: The Unveiling of Secrets, by Ala al-Din al-Bukhari.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar 'an Usul Fakhr al-Islam al-Bazdawi, 3/512, see: the previous footnote.
(3) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar 'an Usul Fakhr al-Islam al-Bazdawi, p. 513.
(4) Al-Ghazali, Shifa al-Ghalil, p. 148 - 149.


[Page 101]

It is a suitable description supported by many rulings, or at least two rulings: one ruling that demonstrates the consideration of the specific description in the specific ruling, and another ruling or rulings from which it is inferred that the description has been recognized in the ruling or its genus, or its genus in the genus of the ruling.
However, it should be noted here the difference between the Imams of the Hanafi school and others, all of whom mentioned these types. The Hanafis did not permit the generalization of the description or ruling based solely on the existence of evidence for it in other rulings; rather, they stipulated that the effect of the description or its genus must be established by legal evidence and not merely by the occurrence of the ruling in accordance with it. Just as they required that the essence (ayn) in the essence must be impactful, they also required impact in all types of consideration. And just as they did not see the occurrence of the ruling in accordance with the description as indicative of reasoning, they also did not see any indication of generalization or categorization in the abundance of evidence. Al-Bazdawi said: "Justice for us is the effect" (1), and the commentator in Kashf al-Asrar said: "As for the reference to the principles, it does not lead to modification, and the utmost that can be said is that the texts are in agreement with the description, resulting in an abundance of parallels, but abundance of parallels does not confer strength to the description" (2), and he said: "Because the description is a cause for a legal ruling just as the ruling is, it cannot be established except by legal evidence" (3).
Thus, what is appropriate is what has been established regarding the consideration of the genus of the description in the essence of the ruling or in its genus, or the essence of the description in its genus. The disagreement regarding it is in the establishment of consideration. If the establishment is by evidence, it is agreed upon among the analogists; if it is by the testimony of the ruling to the description and the existence of parallels for it, then there is much disagreement regarding it.
__________
(1) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi. 3/512.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 3/513, and the reference to the principles means presenting the description that has evidence for it in a ruling to other rulings that support it, and it is said based on that that its consideration or the consideration of its genus has been recognized in the Sharia.
(3) The same source. pp. 509 - 510.


[Page 102]

Among its examples is the permissibility of combining the two prescribed prayers (salat) due to hardship. The ruling on the permissibility of combining during travel supports the description of hardship, and the permissibility of combining them in a settled place during rain also supports the description of hardship. The hardship of rain and the hardship of travel are two types of hardship that fall under the category of hardship, and considering hardship here is a consideration of the category of the description without evidence, but only through the extrapolation of rulings. It has been said that this example has its own complexities(1).
It is also exemplified by the exemption from the two rak'ahs (units of prayer) for the traveler due to hardship, and the exemption from making up prayers for the menstruating woman due to hardship. Thus, the consideration of general hardship here is a consideration of the category of the description. This example also has its own complexities(2).
C - The strange (ghareeb):
This is a suitable description, whose consideration has appeared in a single ruling. The scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) from the Shafi'i school have deemed it valid for reasoning, while the Hanafi school has rejected it. Al-Amidi said: "The legislator must have considered the particular description in a particular ruling without showing the consideration of its essence in the generality of that ruling in another agreed-upon origin, nor its genus in that same ruling, nor its genus in its genus, nor has it been indicated that it is a cause by text or consensus, neither explicitly nor implicitly, such as the meaning of intoxication" (3). He then said: "If we were to assume the absence of texts indicating that intoxication is a cause, it would not be considered by text either, and this is the suitable strange which is disputed among the analogists, and some have denied it, though their denial is not well-founded as it leads to suspicion regarding reasoning" (4).
__________
(1) See: al-Ansari, Abdul Ali Muhammad bin Nizam al-Din, Fawatih al-Rahmut Sharh Muslim al-Thabut, 2/265, printed with al-Mustasfa by al-Ghazali, the Amiriya Press in Bulak, Egypt, 1322 AH.
(2) See: al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 217. And see: al-Ghazali, Shifa al-Ghalil, p. 149.
(3) Al-Amidi, al-Ahkam, 3/247.
(4) The same source.


[Page 103]

Al-Ghazali said: "As for the strange (gharib) that has not shown its effect or its suitability to the type of actions of the legislator, an example of this is our saying: 'Wine is prohibited because it intoxicates,' thus in its meaning, every intoxicant is included, although the effect of intoxication has not appeared in another context, yet it is suitable. This is an example of the strange if it were not for the indication provided by His saying: { Indeed, Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants } (1). Another example is our saying that a woman who has been divorced three times during the illness of death inherits because the husband intended to evade her inheritance, which is opposed by the opposite of his intention, analogous to the killer, for he does not inherit because he hastens the inheritance, thus it is opposed by the opposite of his intention. The reasoning for the killer's deprivation is a reasoning based on a suitability that does not align with the type of actions of the Sharia, as we do not see the Sharia in another context addressing its type, so its suitability remains merely strange. If the deprivation were reasoned by his transgression through killing and this were made a punishment for the aggression, it would be a reasoning based on a suitable correlation that is not effective, for the crime itself, although its effect appears in punishments, does not show its effect in deprivation from inheritance" (2).
It is noteworthy here that the reality of the strange suitability and its examples among those who affirm it, such as al-Amidi and al-Ghazali, as has been clarified, is the same reality and examples of the remote suitability among those who affirm it, as will be shown. Al-Amidi mentioned as an example of the strange suitability: "Considering the type of hardship shared between the menstruating woman and the traveler in the type of alleviation, for the specific hardship of the menstruating woman is not the same as the specific hardship of the traveler, but rather of its kind, and the specific alleviation for the traveler by dropping two units of prayer is not the same as the alleviation for the menstruating woman by dropping prayer, but rather of its kind" (3).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 91.
(2) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa. 2/298. This text is useful - if examined closely - for distinguishing between the effective, the suitable, and the strange.
(3) Al-Amidi, Al-Ihkam. 3/247 - 248.


[Page 104]

Al-Shawkani mentioned an example of the strange (ghareeb) by saying: "Considering the type of description in the type of ruling, such as the reasoning for the punishment of drinking being eighty lashes, as it is a presumption of slander due to it being a presumption of accusation, it is necessary to establish it in its place by analogy (qiyas) to seclusion (khalwa), as it is a presumption of illicit sexual intercourse, thus it is established in its place."(1)
The scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) among the Shafi'is have stated that the strange analogy (al-qiyas al-ghareeb) is valid for reasoning. Al-Amidi said: "Some have rejected it, and their rejection is not justified because it provides a presumption for reasoning"(2). Al-Ghazali said: "As for the strange analogy, this is a matter of ijtihad (independent reasoning), and it does not seem unlikely to me that this may prevail in the presumption of some mujtahids (jurists), nor is there a decisive proof indicating the invalidity of their ijtihad"(3).
As for the Hanafis, they rejected it and dismissed every avenue of analogy altogether. This is a type of statement from their imams: "As for imagination... it is a false matter because it is merely a form of conjecture, as imagination and conjecture are one and the same, and conjecture does not avail against the truth at all. It cannot be said that conjecture is considered in the Sharia in terms of the obligation to act upon it like the report of a single narrator or analogy, for we say that what is considered is that which has a definitive proof establishing its obligation to act upon it, not mere conjecture. There is no proof here establishing its consideration in the Sharia, so it must be disregarded."(4)
2- The annulled:

It is a description that has not been established by a ruling of consideration, and the consideration has appeared for its opposite. Al-Asnawi said: "The appropriate description is of three types: the first is that the legislator (shari) disregards it, meaning that he presents the branches in opposition to it, and there is no doubt that it is not permissible to use it for reasoning" (1). He then said: "This is like the obligation of fasting for two months as expiation for sexual intercourse during the day in Ramadan for the owner, even though it is more effective in restraining him than emancipation, but the legislator has disregarded it by making emancipation obligatory from the outset, so it cannot be considered" (2).
Al-Amidi said: "The appropriate description that has not been established by any original consideration in any way, and yet its disregard and the legislator's disinterest in it have appeared in a particular case, is something that has been agreed upon to be invalidated and cannot be relied upon" (3). He then cited the same example mentioned above from Al-Asnawi.
Al-Shatibi said: "What the law has rejected cannot be accepted, for the appropriateness does not necessitate a ruling by itself; rather, this is the view of the proponents of rational improvement" (4). He then cited the same example mentioned above, attributing it to Al-Ghazali, and said: "This is appropriate because the purpose of the expiation in the law is deterrence, and the owner is not deterred by emancipation but is deterred by fasting, and this fatwa is invalid" (5).

[Page 106]

It is a description that is appropriate, the consideration or rejection of which is unknown. It has been referred to as public interest (maslaha) that is not explicitly stated, as well as implicit reasoning and public interest (istislah). Some scholars of usul (usul al-fiqh) have included it among the discussions of reasoning. Al-Zarkashi said: "The discussion on analogy has already been addressed, regarding the appropriate matters that the Lawgiver has either considered or rejected. The discussion here pertains to what is unknown, meaning what the Lawgiver has remained silent about in terms of consideration and disregard, which is referred to as public interests that are not explicitly stated and is called implicit reasoning. For this reason, it is termed 'not explicitly stated,' meaning it has neither been considered nor rejected. Imam al-Haramayn and Ibn al-Sam'ani referred to it as reasoning, while al-Khwarizmi expressed it in al-Kafi as public interest (istislah). He stated that the meaning of public interest is the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia by preventing harm to the creation. Imam al-Ghazali explained it as finding a meaning that suggests a ruling suitable for it rationally, while there is no agreed-upon basis, and the reasoning is applicable here. Ibn Burhan explained it in al-Awsat as not being based on a general or specific principle, and there are differing opinions on it" (1). The meaning of the implicit reasoning has differed among scholars of usul, and opinions have conflicted regarding its acceptance or rejection. The majority hold that it is not suitable for reasoning. Dr. Mustafa al-Bagha stated: "The words of the scholars of usul almost converge on the fact that the claim of public interest is a matter of disagreement, and the prevailing opinion is that it is not suitable for reasoning since there is no evidence for its consideration, and only Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) has adopted this view" (2).

(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/377. See also: Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 241, and al-Mustasfa, 1/284, and al-Ahkam, 4/361.
(2) Mustafa Dhib al-Bagha, The Impact of Disputed Evidence in Islamic Jurisprudence, p. 43, Dar al-Imam al-Bukhari - Damascus.


[Page 107]

The transmission of the scholars' statements on this matter without verifying the intended meaning for each of them has led to conflicting reports. Dr. Muhammad Hasan Hayto said: "Know that the issue of the use of the mursal (transmitted) evidence has encountered much confusion, leading to conflicting reports and divergent opinions"(1). The attribution of this opinion to Imam Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) is well-known, and it has been attributed to him in an unregulated manner. Some have attributed it to the Shafi'is and the Hanafis, while others have attributed it only to the Shafi'is without the Hanafis. Some have claimed its presence in all schools of thought, while others have agreed on its rejection and denied its attribution to Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). Below are some of those reports:
Al-Juwayni said: "Al-Shafi'i and most of the companions of Abu Hanifa went to rely on reasoning even if it does not stem from an agreed-upon ruling in principle"(2), while al-Amidi took the opposite view and said: "The appropriate reasoning is the unqualified... and the jurists from the Shafi'is, Hanafis, and others have agreed on the prohibition of relying on it, which is the truth"(3). Al-Qarafi said: "What is unknown in this matter is the unqualified public interest (maslaha murasala) that we advocate, and upon investigation, it is general in the schools of thought"(4). The transmitted statements from al-Ghazali have posed difficulties, as he said: "Whoever seeks public interest has legislated just as whoever approves has legislated"(5). He also said: "Any public interest that returns to preserving a legal objective known to be intended by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus is not outside these principles, but it is not called analogy (qiyas) rather it is called unqualified public interest (maslaha murasala)... If we interpret public interest as preserving the objectives of the Sharia, then there is no basis for disagreement regarding it, rather it must be definitively established as evidence"(6).

Al-Shatibi said: "He elaborated on it as one who is deeply immersed in understanding the meanings of public interest (maslaha), while considering the intention of the Lawgiver so that he does not deviate from it or contradict any of its principles, to the extent that many scholars found many aspects of his elaboration objectionable, claiming that he had removed the yoke and opened the door to legislation, and how far removed he was from that! May Allah have mercy on him." (1) Al-Juwayni said about him: "It was seen that he established interests far removed from the usual interests and known meanings in the Sharia, and this led him to innovate killing and taking wealth based on interests that he presumed to exist, even if he did not find a basis for those interests in the principles. He said: The Imam of the Two Holy Sanctuaries (Imam al-Haramayn) was bold in what he attributed to Malik regarding excess in this principle, and this does not exist in Malik's books or in any of his companions' books." (4) Al-Amidi said: "The appropriate transmitted report... And if the transmission is correct from him, it is more likely that he did not say this regarding every interest, but rather regarding those interests that are necessary and universally established." [Page 109]

Dr. Hito says: "As for attributing the statement to Malik with this type of indirect reasoning, it is a disputed attribution"(1). Dr. Hito has proven the error of attributing many statements to Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him)(2).
This amount of contradiction is due to the differing meanings of "the transmitted (al-mursal)" among the conflicting parties and the narrators. The term "the transmitted" has been used to mean that which has not been known to be abrogated or disregarded entirely, meaning it has not been witnessed by any ruling. It has also been used to mean something that is appropriate or strange.
As for the first meaning: everyone has agreed to reject it. This is what is meant by denying its attribution to the Shafi'is and the Hanafis and by denying it from Malik.
As for the second meaning: the majority rejected it, and those who accepted it stipulated that it must be appropriate. It was reported that there is consensus on its rejection if it is strange. Some said it could be accepted, and the details are as follows:
As for whether it is sent (marsool) in general, here are some opinions on it:
Al-Amidi said: "The interests (masalih) are divided according to the testimony of the Sharia into those that are recognized and those that are annulled, and those that have neither recognition nor annulment. The latter is referred to as the unqualified suitable (al-munasib al-mursal)... This category is uncertain between the two aforementioned categories, and its classification into one of them is not more valid than the other. Therefore, it is prohibited to use it as evidence without a recognized testimony that indicates it belongs to the category of the recognized rather than the annulled."(3)
Al-Zain al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam said: "Likewise, there is no ruling except for Him (i.e., for Allah), so His rulings are derived from the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), sound analogies (qiyas), and accepted proofs. No one has the right to deem something good (istihsan) or to employ public interest (maslaha mursala), nor to follow someone whom he has not been commanded to follow."(4)

(1) Hayto, his introduction to the selected comments on the principles, margin. p: 354 - 365.
(2) The same place.

(4) Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam, The Principles of Rulings in the Interests of the People, p. 304, Al-Rayan Foundation - Beirut, 1410 AH - 1990 CE, revised new edition.


[Page 110]

Al-Ghazali said: "Istislah (public interest) is not a fifth root in itself, but whoever seeks istislah has legislated just as whoever deems something good has legislated" (1). He also said: "This is one of the illusory roots, for whoever thinks it is a fifth root has erred, as we have referred the public interest to the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and the objectives of the Sharia are known through the Book (Qur'an), the Sunnah (traditions of the Prophet), and consensus (ijma). Thus, any public interest that does not return to the preservation of an objective derived from the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus, and is among the strange interests that do not align with the actions of the Sharia, is invalid and discarded. Whoever resorts to it has legislated just as whoever deems something good has legislated" (2).
Similarly, it is well-known among the Hanafis that they reject and dismiss every method of analogy as a root. They reject the analogy even if it is considered valid, as they require an effect. Ibn Humam al-Din al-Iskandari, the Hanafi, said: "This category known as istislah (public interest) is rejected, as there is no evidence for its consideration, and it is a legal evidence, thus it must be rejected" (3).
It is well-known among their scholars that they say: "No evidence, no consideration." Al-Ansari said: "Istislah (public interest) is a proof according to Malik (may Allah have mercy on him), while the preferred view among the majority of scholars and jurists is its rejection. Our argument is: there is no evidence without consideration from the legislator, even if it follows the dictates of reason, and this cannot be accepted from one who advocates analogy" (4).
Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi said: "This is called istislah (public interest) and we do not call it qiyas (analogy) because qiyas refers to a specific root, and the correct view is that it is not a proof because it is known from the legislator that the preservation of blood is paramount in every way. Therefore, mutilation was not legislated even though it is the most effective deterrent and punishment, nor was killing for theft or drinking alcohol legislated. If a ruling is established for the sake of one of these interests, it is not known that the Sharia preserves that interest by establishing that ruling; it would be an imposition of the Sharia based on opinion and a ruling based on pure reason" (5).

Mujd al-Din ibn Taymiyyah said: "The public interests (masalih mursala) cannot be used as a basis for rulings. This was stated by al-Baqillani and a group of theologians" (1).
Ibn al-Hajib al-Maliki said: "The public interests are interests that do not have a foundational basis in the Sharia, even if they align with the principles of public interests and are accepted by reason" (2). He then said: "We have no evidence, so it must be rejected, as in the case of istihsan (juridical preference)" (3).
Similarly, al-Fakhr al-Razi rejected them if they are understood in this sense, stating that they are rejected by consensus, even though he is among those who accept public interests, which indicates that he does not mean by 'public interests' what is universally accepted. He said: "A suitable reason that does not correspond to or have a specific foundational basis is thus rejected by consensus, and an example of this is the deprivation of the murderer from inheritance, opposing his intended purpose if we assume there is no text regarding it" (4).
We find the same position with al-Shatibi; if it is understood in the broad sense of 'public interests', he clarifies that what is thus understood is invalid and constitutes legislation by reason, and he conveys that this public interest is rejected by consensus. He states: "The suitability does not necessitate a ruling by itself; rather, this is the view of the proponents of rational improvement. However, if the meaning becomes clear and we understand from the Sharia that it should be considered in deriving rulings, then we accept it, for what we mean by public interest is what is understood to be taken into account in relation to people regarding public interests and the prevention of harms in a way that reason cannot independently grasp. If the Sharia does not support that meaning, but rather rejects it, it is thus rejected by the agreement of the Muslims" (5).

[Page 112]

He said: "As for the reasoning behind prohibiting killing for inheritance, the application of the opposite of the intended purpose is to be estimated if there is no text in accordance with it. This reasoning is not established in the actions of the Sharia by obligation nor by its compatible matters in such a way that there exists a recognized type for it; thus, it is not valid to use it as reasoning nor to base a ruling upon it by consensus. Such a thing is legislation from the one who claims it, and it cannot be accepted" (1).
Based on these texts, especially from those who adopt the concept of public interest (maslaha), it becomes clear that inferring from the mursal (unattributed hadith) does not mean inferring from the public interest; this implies making reason a legislator, which is unanimously rejected. Therefore, the meaning of the mursal for those who accept it can only be understood as either compatible or strange.
This matter is confirmed by what we find among some of the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) who divide the mursal itself into nullified, strange, and compatible. This means that the mursal which may be accepted or disputed is that which is strange or compatible. Al-Ansari said: "The mursal is divided into what is known to be nullified by text or consensus... and into what is not known. If no one knows in it one of the considerations of compatibility based on its type or its kind in the type of ruling or its kind in the specific ruling, but it is also not known to be nullified, then it is the strange mursal, which is called the public interests (masalih mursala). If one of the considerations of compatibility is known in it, then it is the compatible mursal" (2).
Al-Ghazali said: "The difference among the jurists regarding the strange compatible: that which does not fit, and the compatible: that which does not have a specific origin is what is referred to - in the language of jurists - as mursal reasoning, meaning relying on the compatible, interest-based meaning that appears in the branch without citing a specific origin" (3). He said: "As for the strange compatible - that which does not fit and does not have a specific origin - this is rejected: there is no known disagreement in it" (4).
