Al-Shawkani said: "Ibn al-Hajib stated in his Mukhtasar al-Muntaha: 'The non-accepted (hadith) is the mursal (unattributed report); if it is strange or its abrogation is established, it is rejected by consensus. If it is appropriate, Imam al-Ghazali explicitly stated its acceptance and mentioned that Malik and al-Shafi'i held this view, while the preferred opinion is its rejection. Al-Ghazali conditioned its acceptance on the necessity of the public interest (maslaha) being certain and comprehensive'" (1). He also said: "The strange (hadith) that is not appropriate is unanimously rejected" (2). The transmission of consensus on the rejection of the strange (hadith) contradicts what was previously reported from al-Ghazali and al-Amidi, where al-Ghazali said: "The appropriate strange (hadith) is a matter of ijtihad (independent reasoning)" (3). Al-Amidi said: "Some have denied it, and their denial is unfounded because it leads to conjecture through reasoning" (4). The conflicting statements regarding the strange (hadith) stem from differing interpretations of its meaning. In fact, al-Ghazali himself, who stated the possibility of its acceptance, is the same one who reported its rejection without disagreement. However, he clarified his intent each time; he rejected it if it meant mursal, and stated its acceptability if it meant that it was supported by a ruling.

(2) The same source.

[Page 114]

Al-Razi said: "A suitable analogy that does not have a specific foundational evidence to support it, meaning that it considers its genus within its genus, but there is no foundational evidence indicating the consideration of its specific instance within its specific instance, and this is what is known as public interest (maslaha) that is not specified."(1) Then he said: "An example of the effect of the genus within the genus is the reasoning for rulings that do not have specific foundational evidence, such as when Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) considered drinking as equivalent to slander, treating the presumption of something as equivalent to its actual instance, analogous to treating seclusion with a woman as equivalent to having sexual intercourse with her in terms of prohibition."(2) This same example was mentioned by al-Shawkani as an example of a strange analogy.(3)
Thus, the mursal (transmitted without a chain of narration) according to those who accept it is either strange or suitable; it does not have a specific origin that testifies to it, nor has it ever had a witness to its origin. As for what is mursal in general, it is rejected without dispute.
The appropriate strange (ghareeb) is rejected by al-Shatibi. He does not suffice with the testimony of one origin or a few origins to affirm the consideration of the type, but rather he requires that many origins testify to it, to the extent that it reaches certainty in his view. He says: "It must be compatible with the actions of the Sharia, which means that there exists for that meaning a type that the legislator has considered in general without specific evidence, which is the general reasoning known as the unqualified public interest (maslaha mursala)"(4). He also says: "Every legal origin that does not have specific textual evidence and is compatible with the actions of the Sharia, and whose meaning is derived from its evidences, is valid and can be relied upon and referred to if that origin has become certain by the totality of its evidences... and this falls under the general reasoning that was adopted by Malik and al-Shafi'i"(5).

(3) See p. 86 of this book. This example also contradicts what has been reported about the consensus on rejecting the strange analogy. Its interpretation is that al-Razi does not consider this example to be of the strange kind; rather, he regards it as appropriate. He has an argument for this that is not the subject of our discussion.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-I'tisam. 2/375.

[Page 115]

As for what was previously quoted from al-Qarafi: "Upon investigation, it is general in the schools of thought." If what he meant by public interest (maslaha) or the appropriate cause (al-munasib) is the meaning we are searching for, then the statements mentioned above decisively refute his claim.
It should be noted here - even though this is not our topic - that the public interest (maslaha) which is general in the schools of thought and accepted by consensus is not that which has no specific ruling, but rather that which has no specific text, while being supported by general or comprehensive evidence that includes it under its categories or parts without being explicitly mentioned. In this sense, it includes, for example, the compilation of the Qur'an that was done by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) and the codex that was compiled by Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), and the documentation of the registers that was done by Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him)(1). These matters and similar ones fall under general or comprehensive evidences such as: "What is necessary for the obligation to be fulfilled is itself obligatory," and "There should be no harm nor reciprocating harm," and "The default ruling of things is permissibility unless there is evidence for prohibition," among others. All these actions are unqualified by specific or particular evidence that states the incident explicitly, but they are included under general or comprehensive evidence. This meaning is what al-Shatibi intended as he clarified in al-I'tisam and al-Muwafaqat(2).
Conditions of the appropriate description:
Those who advocate for the path of appropriateness have set two conditions for reasoning based on the appropriate description:
First: The description must be considered. That is, the ruling that is being reasoned must have that description present in it. In other words, the ruling must be in accordance with it.
__________
(1) See: al-Ansari, Fawatih al-Rahmout. 2/301.
(2) We will dedicate a discussion later - if Allah wills - to al-Shatibi's intended meaning of public interests.


[Page 116]

The second: It must be free from opposition and nullification. This means that the description should not be annulled. Nullification is the text that states the cancellation of the description, as in the fatwa regarding fasting for two consecutive months for the sultan who engaged in sexual relations during the month of Ramadan. As for opposition, it refers to the existence of another ruling or rulings that contradict or oppose the description. This is similar to the concession for breaking the fast and combining the two obligatory prayers while traveling for the indulgent king. These rulings opposed the description of hardship.

Therefore, those who reason based on the appropriate must present the description against the principles, meaning against the rulings, to clarify its lack of opposition. Al-Bazdawi said: "Justice for us is the effect... Some of al-Shafi'i's companions said that his justice is based on being capable, then presenting it against the principles as a precaution for its safety from contradiction and opposition. Some of his companions said rather that his justice is based on presenting it against the principles, and if no principle contradicts or opposes it, it becomes just. It must be presented against two or more principles. According to the first view, it is permissible to act upon it before presentation, and according to the second, it is not permissible because it becomes a proof through it. According to the first opinion, it became a proof by being capable" (1). Then he said: "As for presenting it against the principles, it does not achieve the adjustment" (2) meaning according to him.

The commentator in Kashf al-Asrar said: "The contradiction of the description: nullifying itself by an effect, text, or consensus that contradicts it, or presenting a case where the ruling deviates from the description. The opposition of the description: presenting another description that necessitates a contradiction to what that description required without addressing the description itself. The meaning of presenting the description against the principles is that it is compared with the laws of Sharia; if it matches and is free from nullifications and impediments, then the principles have testified to its validity and it has become a proof" (3).

Chapter Two
The Emergence of the Idea of the Objectives of Sharia

It contains a brief overview of the emergence of the idea, and three sections:

Section One: The arguments that led to the idea of objectives.
Section Two: The emergence of the idea of the objectives of Sharia.
Section Three: The introduction to the idea of objectives according to Imam al-Shatibi.

Chapter Two
__________
(1) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi. 4/513.
(2) The same source, p. 519.
(3) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar. 3/514.


[Page 117]

The Emergence of the Idea of the Objectives of the Sharia

A brief overview of the emergence of the idea:
I will present below a brief overview of the emergence of the idea, followed by a detailed explanation and documentation from the statements of the imams and their arguments, starting from where I left off in the previous chapter, namely the disagreement regarding the concept of suitability, whether it is a method of reasoning or not.
It has been clarified - previously - the meaning of suitability, and that some of the imams adopted it as a method of reasoning - standing on its own - and set conditions for it, thus categorizing suitability into sections. Some others rejected its status as a method and considered it a condition for the validity of reasoning by description through any method used. Some made it a condition in certain methods but not others.
The scholars of the Shafi'i school state that the suitable description in the ruling is one that is related to the presumption of being a reason, and presumption is applicable in legal matters; therefore, the method of suitability must be followed. The imams of the Hanafi school counter this by asserting that not all presumptions are legal, and they require that the description be influential for the reasoning to be accepted.
If we take rulings such as the prohibition of usury or the obligation of zakat on certain wealth but not others, or the prohibition of men wearing gold and silk but not women, or the prohibition of using gold and silver utensils for food, the intellect seeks suitable descriptions in these rulings or the wisdom behind them. Those who advocate the method of suitability argue for reasoning based on these rulings. Those who oppose it consider this reasoning to be arbitrary without evidence, akin to mere opinion. They require that the description be influential, meaning that its effect must be established by evidence.
Those who adopt this method have delved deeply into their research and elaborated on it in defense of it and others as well, such as the method of analogy. The debate intensified, particularly regarding the topic of the unspecific suitability or inference.


[Page 118]

As a result of this debate, al-Juwayni came up with the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), which form the criteria for appropriate description. The assertion of an objective or objectives for the Sharia and the attachment of the appropriate description or meaning to this objective strengthens the reasoning based on description, as this allows for the application of the appropriate description according to the objectives of the Sharia. Or as his student al-Ghazali later expressed it, that the public interest (maslaha) should follow the established interests, which are the five universal principles.
However, this idea did not negatively or positively affect the principles of those who reject this approach, namely the esteemed Hanafis. Therefore, we find them mentioning it by saying: "And they said."
The idea of the objectives of the Sharia and reasoning based on the appropriate description necessitated another discussion. This is that the original principle in legal rulings is reasoning. Therefore, whatever does not have its reason established by the agreed-upon methods among most jurists, such as text, consensus, indication, and hint, must have a reason established for it if possible. If the ruling allows for reasoning, it must be reasoned.
Al-Amidi elaborated on this principle, the disagreement regarding it, and the evidence for each group in his book al-Ihkam, while al-Razi discussed it in al-Mahsool, where al-Amidi affirmed the principle of reasoning, and al-Razi declared it invalid, even though he accepts analogy (qiyas) and reasoning and supports the approach of appropriateness. The reality of the matter— as will become clear— is that what al-Razi definitively deems invalid is reasoning concerning the essence of Allah, and I have referred to the meaning of reasoning according to him in the previous chapter(1).
Then al-Shatibi came with his Muwafaqat, where he referred in the book of objectives— from his book al-Muwafaqat— to al-Razi's position and his rebuttal, affirming reasoning for the actions and rulings of Allah— Exalted is He— and that this is definitive. He said: "We have inferred from the Sharia that it was established for the interests of the servants, an inference that al-Razi and others do not dispute... If the inference indicates this and is beneficial for knowledge in such a matter, then we conclude that the matter is consistent in all details of the Sharia"(2).
__________
(1) See p. 51.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/2 - 3.


[Page 119]

This amount of disagreement, like that between al-Razi and al-Shatibi, is where the former asserts the invalidity of the principle of reasoning, while the latter asserts its validity and its presence in all details of the Sharia. He firmly states that al-Razi is mistaken by saying: "Induction is something that neither al-Razi nor anyone else disputes," emphasizing the importance of the principle of reasoning and its significance for the method of suitability and for the use of general evidence. Therefore, it is necessary to address this principle with sufficient detail.

It should be noted that there is a significant difference between the methodologies of al-Amidi and al-Shatibi regarding reasoning. There is also a distinction between al-Shatibi's concept of public interests (masalih) and harms (mafasid) and the concept of those who preceded him who spoke of reasoning based on public interests and harms. The following will clarify and document what we have presented.

First Topic
The arguments that led to the idea of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia)

The evolution of the debate from the method of suitability to general evidence:
We previously discussed suitability as a method of reasoning. We covered the categories of suitable descriptions and their conditions, as well as the disagreement regarding them. The suitable description, according to those who advocate it, must be considered valid in Sharia, and its validity is established by the coming of a ruling in accordance with it. Thus, the ruling that attests to the description serves as a principle, and the description itself is the reason, making reasoning based on suitability akin to analogy (qiyas).


[Page 120]

And since this appropriate description is a hypothetical description and there is no evidence from the Sharia to indicate that it is a cause, those who do not accept the method of appropriate reasoning rejected the reasoning by the appropriate description altogether. On the other hand, most of those who reason by the appropriate description rejected reasoning by the transmitted (marasil) and the strange (gharib), and they spoke of the suitable (mulayim): which has been supported by many rulings, or at least two rulings. From the existence of evidence for the description and its abundance, they argued that the strength of the appropriate description comes from the fact that the rulings of the Sharia have been in accordance with it, or have testified to it, or that this description or meaning aligns with the principles of legal interests (masalih shar'iyya). Thus, a new issue arose, which is that considering this description in reasoning does not return to a specific origin, and consequently, it is not part of analogy (qiyas) because the existence of an origin is a pillar in analogy, and the origin is absent here. Hence, the expressions of unregulated interest (maslaha mursala) and unregulated reasoning (istidlal mursala) arise, which refers to a meaning that does not have a specific origin but whose meaning aligns with the principles of the Sharia (1).
And what indicates this matter is what al-Juwayni mentioned in the types of analogy, where he said: "Legal consideration, and its categories (2):
__________
(1) For example, al-Shatibi said: "Every legal origin that does not have a specific text supporting it and is suitable for the actions of the Sharia and whose meaning is derived from its evidence is valid and can be relied upon if that origin has become established by its collective evidence." Then he said: "This includes the type of unregulated reasoning that Malik and al-Shafi'i relied upon, for although it does not have a specific origin supporting the branch, it has a general origin supporting it." Al-Muwafaqat 1/16. As for his statement that the witness is a general origin that is established, it indicates that he does not suffice with mere abundance of witnesses but requires a beneficial abundance that leads to certainty.
(2) The numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, from the researcher, indicating that analogy in this classification has four categories.


[Page 121]

1 - The inclusion of the unspoken matter with that which is explicitly stated and the differing with the agreed upon due to its similarity in meaning(1).
2 - Or the suspension of a ruling in a manner that is suggestive of it, appropriate to it in the context of the Sharia, while referring it back to an original where the ruling is established according to consideration.
3 - And linking a ruling as we have mentioned(2), without the observer finding an original with an agreed ruling that testifies to it, and this is what is called: inference (istidlal).
4 - And likening something to specific similarities that it encompasses without the obligation of it being suggestive of appropriateness, which is called analogy of resemblance (qiyas al-shabah)(3). These are the avenues of consideration in the Sharia"(4).
The focus here is on the second and third categories, where the second refers to the path of appropriateness, stating: "while referring it back to an original where the ruling is established according to consideration," while the third states: "without the observer finding an original with an agreed ruling that testifies to it," and it is termed inference. Although inference is not analogy since it does not fulfill all its conditions, there is a closeness between them in that inference is linking a ruling in a manner according to the statement of al-Juwayni above; therefore, it is included in the categories of analogy, just as the first category is counted among the categories of analogy due to the inclusion of the unspoken matter with that which is explicitly stated.
__________
(1) This category does not hold up to being called analogy, as there is no analogy of a branch to an original; rather, the unspoken matter takes the ruling of the stated one by the indication of the word, and it is not analogy. This is akin to the concept: what is understood from the word in a place other than the place of utterance. See: al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/63. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: { So do not say to them [even] "uff" } [al-Isra 23], thus hitting is prohibited because it is more deserving of prohibition than expressing annoyance towards them, this is from the concept because it is understood from the address and is not from the utterance of the address. This is not an analogy of hitting to annoyance, rather it is more deserving of the ruling than annoyance, and it is from the indications of language. See: al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/64.
(2) As we have mentioned: that is, as we mentioned in the previous point, meaning: in a manner suggestive of it appropriate to it in the context of the Sharia, but it lacks the original.
(3) We mentioned this category in the discussion of the paths of reasoning. pp. 65 - 66.
(4) Al-Juwayni, al-Burhan. 2/514. Paragraph: 730.


[Page 122]

The meaning of reasoning (istidlal):(1)
As has been clarified, the intended meaning of reasoning here is not its linguistic connotation, but rather it is a term that contrasts with inference (istinbat) and has emerged as a subject and influence in the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), incorporated into its discussions under the influence of logic and theology. The one who reasons - in this sense - does not derive a ruling based on the indications of texts, but rather imagines certain meanings that he sees as appropriate and proposes them, relying on the possibility of their acceptance by the Sharia in his view and the absence of any evidence that negates them. Therefore, we find al-Juwayni differentiating between the second and third categories mentioned earlier, stating in the first of them: "By referring it to an established origin in which the ruling is in accordance with the view," and in the second: "Without the observer finding an established origin with a consistent ruling that testifies to it, and this is what is called reasoning."
__________
(1) It is mentioned in Lisan al-Arab by Ibn Manzur: "And the proof (dalil): what one uses to reason. The proof is the indicator - and it has guided him to the path, guiding him with indication and evidence, and the opening is the highest." 11/248.


[Page 123]

Al-Shawkani said in his definition of reasoning: "In their terminology, it is that which is neither a text, nor consensus, nor analogy" (1). He then said: "They differed regarding its types; it was said that there are three: the connection between the two rulings without specifying a reason, otherwise it would be analogy. The second: the presumption of continuity (istishab). The third: the legislation from before us. The Hanafis stated this. Among its types, there is a fourth type which is juristic preference (istihsan). The Malikis stated that among its types there is a fifth type which is the public interest (maslaha) that is not specified" (2). He said: "The public interest... was mentioned by a group of scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) in the discussions of reasoning, and for this reason, some called it the unrestricted reasoning, and Imam al-Haramayn and Ibn al-Sam'ani referred to it as reasoning" (3). Al-Amidi said: "As for its meaning in language, it is a verbal noun derived from seeking evidence and the guiding path to the desired, and as for in the terminology of jurists, it is sometimes used to mean mentioning the evidence, whether the evidence is a text, consensus, analogy, or otherwise, and it is sometimes used to refer to a specific type of evidence... which is an evidence that is neither a text, nor consensus, nor analogy... and it has various types" (4). He then mentioned types that are all related to logic and the method of arranging premises and deriving conclusions (5).
Thus, reasoning is a type of evidence that is neither a text, nor consensus, nor analogy. What is meant here is the public interest, which resembles analogy and the method of suitability in that it connects a ruling to a suitable meaning, and it is not analogy and differs from suitability in that there is no original source that supports the meaning, but the meaning exists in many legal branches.
__________
(1) Al-Shawkani, Irshad al-Fuhul, p. 236.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, p. 241.
(4) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, 4/361.
(5) The same source, 4/361 - 366.


[Page 124]

It has been established previously that the appropriate analogy (al-mursala) in the method of analogy is not an absolute analogy; rather, it refers to what is considered valid. So why is there a distinction between them, and why is the reasoning not counted as a form of analogy (qiyas)? In other words, how can it be said that the valid appropriate meaning in reasoning, which links the ruling to it, does not have an original source (asl), while it is said that this meaning is applicable in many rulings? Can one of these rulings not be considered an original source, and the description or appropriate meaning within it be regarded as a cause, thus making the matter a case of analogy?
The answer is: Yes, reasoning is based on the justification by an appropriate description, but it differs from the method of analogy in that this meaning is not derived from a specific ruling. If we were to relate it to a specific ruling, it would be analogy. However, when claiming an appropriate description in a specific ruling, it does not hold, as there may be other descriptions in the ruling that are more appropriate than it. Thus, it is not correct to justify the ruling by this meaning while neglecting what is more appropriate. This applies to other rulings as well. Therefore, it is said: there is no specific original source that supports it. Meanwhile, the valid meaning in reasoning, even if its existence or the strength of its appropriateness is weaker than others in each individual ruling, the abundance of its presence in the rulings leads to a stronger consideration of it, and it may make it an original source or a principle in legislation, rather than merely a cause in the ruling. When examining numerous rulings, it is noted that it is not specifically present in any one of them, but the observer feels that it is an original source or is realized in these meanings through their convergence. For this reason, reasoning does not revert to analogy or to the method of analogy, even though it is based on justification, because it lacks one of the pillars of analogy, which is the original source.


[Page 125]

The appropriate meaning in deriving a specific ruling from a principle may be considered an analogy (qiyas), but the existence of other rulings that support that meaning makes it a foundational principle in legislation. This, according to those who accept it, is stronger than analogy. For this reason, al-Shatibi said: "Every legal principle that does not have a specific text to support it and is compatible with the actions of the Sharia and whose meaning is derived from its evidences is valid and can be relied upon, provided that this principle has become established through its collective evidences. Because the evidences do not necessarily have to indicate certainty about the ruling in isolation without the addition of others to them, as previously mentioned. This is because that is nearly impossible. This includes the unqualified reasoning (istidlal al-mursal) that Malik and al-Shafi'i relied upon, for although it does not have a specific principle to support the branch, it has a general principle that supports it, and a definitive general principle may equal a specific principle and may even surpass it depending on the strength or weakness of the specific principle" (1). Al-Juwayni said: "I take those causes as my refuge and make the arguments close to them, even if they are not their specific instances, so that they are as if they are principles. The reasoning is considered valid. Considering meaning by meaning is preferable to considering form by form in a comprehensive sense" (2).
Therefore, those who accept it responded to those who rejected it and said that it leads to reliance on reason and the wisdom of philosophers, stating: even if it does not have a supporting principle, it leads to reliance on reason and the wisdom of philosophers if we pursue it in an unregulated manner. If it is regulated by Sharia guidelines, then it is legitimate. These beneficial meanings, even if they do not have recognized meanings supporting them, are close to or similar to them. And even if they do not have specific principles supporting them, they are based on established foundational rulings, and even if those meanings are not established, their foundations are.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/16, and al-Shatibi's condition of certainty for considering the meaning is specific to him and his methodology.
(2) Al-Juwayni, al-Burhan, 2/726, paragraph: 1142.


[Page 126]

Al-Juwayni said: "Al-Shafi'i and most of the followers of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) went to rely on reasoning even if it does not stem from an agreed-upon ruling in principle, but he does not permit deviation, distance, or excess; rather, he allows the suspension of rulings based on interests that he sees as similar to the recognized interests in agreement and to the interests based on established, firm rulings in the Sharia" (1).
Al-Ghazali said: "Any interest that relates to the preservation of a legal objective known to be intended by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus is not outside these principles; however, it is not called analogy (qiyas) but rather a remote interest (mursala). For analogy is a specific principle, and the fact that these meanings are intended is known not by a single proof but by many proofs that are countless from the Book and the Sunnah, and indications of circumstances and various signs, which is why it is called a remote interest. If we define interest as the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia, there is no room for disagreement about it; rather, it must be affirmed that it is a proof" (2).
As an example of this, the meaning of preserving wealth, even if there is no specific ruling attesting to it—according to some observers—there are many rulings whose meanings return to the generality of this meaning. The prohibition of theft, the punishment for it, the prohibition of looting, embezzlement, and fraud, the prohibition of betrayal in the work of partners, the prohibition of extravagance and waste, the restriction of the foolish, the prohibition of misappropriation, the prohibition of consuming wealth unlawfully, the encouragement to fulfill trusts and to announce lost property, and others, all can indicate this general meaning and that it is considered in these rulings. This is stronger than relying on the ruling of the prohibition of theft—for example—to argue for the preservation of wealth as a reason of analogy and relevance in the path of relevance. Therefore, they made the preservation of wealth a principle that is observed and relied upon in legislation. Below is a statement of the arguments of both parties regarding the position on relevance and reasoning, and their rebuttals.
Evidence of those who advocate for relevance and reasoning:

(1) The same source, 2/721. Paragraph: 1130.

The heated debate between those who accept and those who reject the approach of suitability and reasoning has led to the emergence of the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) and its clarification. I will summarize below the evidence of those who advocate for it, then I will substantiate it with texts from the imams and subsequently clarify the responses of the refuters to show how the idea of the objectives emerged. Below are their arguments in summary:
1 - They stated that the texts and their meanings are insufficient for issues and events. And that no event is devoid of a ruling from Allah, Exalted is He, attributed to the Sharia of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him). Therefore, it is necessary to provide reasoning for the rulings, and thus the principle in rulings is reasoning. This necessitates reasoning based on what is appropriate, and it requires a disciplined continuation in pursuing meanings. What does not have its reason established through the pathways of text, consensus, indication, and allusion, if an appropriate meaning appears in it, then it must be reasoned with unless it is abrogated or opposed.
2 - They said that the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) would elaborate on understanding the meanings of public interest (maslaha), and those who came after them followed this practice, without establishing criteria for what should be followed and what should not be followed from these meanings. This indicates the validity of this elaboration, provided that these meanings and interests are derived from the sources of the Sharia. The evidence is established in the actions of the Companions.
3 - They said that the appropriate descriptions and meanings, and those similar to them, are matters that relate to conjecture regarding their causes. The legal rulings are derived from conjecture, so the reasoning based on appropriateness is thus legal, as is the evidence. Below are the texts that indicate this:
Al-Juwayni said: "As for al-Shafi'i, he said: 'We know with certainty that no incident is devoid of the ruling of Allah, Exalted is He.'"(1) And he said: "The previous imams did not leave any incident, despite the multitude of issues and the abundance of judgments and fatwas, without the ruling of Allah, Exalted is He... Based on this, we know that they - may Allah be pleased with them - proceeded in establishing rulings with confidence in their applicability to incidents, actively seeking to affirm them in what arises and occurs."(2)
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/723, paragraph: 1133.
(2) Al-Juwayni, al-Burhan. 2/723, paragraph: 1133.


[Page 128]

He said: "If the sources of evidence were limited to the texts and the meanings derived from them, the door of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) would not be wide enough, for the texts and their attributed meanings do not constitute more than a room from the sea of the Sharia. If those who came before had not relied on meanings in situations they had not encountered before, their abstention from issuing rulings would have exceeded their engagement, and this, if it coincided with a confirmation, would leave no room for the deniers of inference to be unsettled" (1). He said: "Then al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) supported this by saying: Whoever examines the conditions of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), who are the role models in reasoning, will not find any one of them in the councils of deliberation establishing a principle or deriving a meaning and then building a case upon it. Rather, they delve into various opinions without regard to whether the principles existed or not. Therefore, if the vastness of ijtihad is established, and it is impossible to limit what is vast to the texts, and in addition to that, the scholars among the Companions did not concern themselves with seeking the principles, all of this leads to the conclusion of inference" (2).
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) The same source, 2/723 - 724. Paragraph: 1134.


[Page 129]

He said: "It has become clear to us that they - may Allah be pleased with them - in the long ages and extended periods did not confine themselves to fixed opinions, but rather they would engage in reasoning as those who do not see a limit to the avenues of opinion, and they viewed the paths of consideration as not restricted. Then the later generations would follow the earlier ones and did not concern themselves with mentioning limited avenues that could not be exceeded. Thus, we know by necessity of reason that they were receiving meanings and benefits from the sources of the Sharia that they relied upon in incidents where there were no texts. If they presumed something and their opinion was not contradicted by a principle from the principles of the Sharia, they would apply it, and it became clear that they were not seeking certain knowledge but were content with presuming something as knowledge"(1). Al-Ghazali said: "There is no way to limit oneself to the influential factor because what is sought is the predominance of presumption. Whoever examines the analogies (qiyas) of the Companions - may Allah be pleased with them - and their juristic efforts knows that they did not condition every analogy on the cause being known through text and consensus"(2). He said: "We have not seen from the consensus of the Companions - may Allah be pleased with them - anything other than following the predominant opinion, and they did not specify the types of predominance of presumption nor did they distinguish one type from another"(3).
Al-Amidi said: "If it is established that the rulings were legislated for the interests of the servants, then if we see a legislated ruling that entails a matter of public interest (maslaha), it must either be that this is the objective of legislating the ruling, or it is something that has not been made apparent to us. It cannot be what has not been made apparent to us, otherwise the legislation of the ruling would be merely an act of devotion, which contradicts the principle(4) as previously established. Therefore, it remains that it is legislated for what has been made apparent. And if this is presumed, then it must be acted upon, because presumption is obligatory to follow in the Sharia."(5)
Al-Razi said: "We say: the relationship (munasaba) provides an indication of causality, and it is obligatory to act upon this indication."(6)

The Hanafi scholars rejected the approach of analogy, in addition to the evidence, and deemed it invalid as it does not yield a legally acceptable presumption. Below are some texts they use to refute the aforementioned proofs:
As for the texts and their meanings not being sufficient for the issues and occurrences, since the texts are finite and the occurrences are infinite, the former cannot draw from the latter like a drop from the ocean. Sheikh Muhibullah ibn Abd al-Shakur said: "This is what is called public interest (maslaha mursala), which is considered a proof by Malik, while the preferred view among the majority is to reject it. Our argument is: there is no proof without consideration, even if it follows the path of reason. They said:
First: If consideration were not taken, many occurrences would be left unaddressed. We say: we deny the necessity of this conclusion because the generalities and analogies are comprehensive. Furthermore, the absence of a specific proof serves as a basis for permissibility (1).
Second: The Companions were content with considering public interests. We say: rather, they only considered what they were aware of regarding the type or nature of it (2).
The commentator on al-Tahrir, Ibn Humam al-Iskandari, a Hanafi, said: "This category known as public interest (maslaha mursala) is preferred to be rejected, as there is no proof for consideration, thus it must be rejected. They said: many occurrences would be left unaddressed. We say: we deny the necessity of this conclusion, meaning we do not concede that the absence of consideration leads to occurrences being devoid of rulings, as the generalities and analogies are comprehensive. Even if it were absent, the negation of every specific proof entails that its ruling is original permissibility, meaning if in a particular incident there is no source from the four evidences, one acts according to a general principle established in the Sharia by consensus, which is original permissibility, as it is the default for things (3).

[Page 131]

As for what they said regarding the principle that the basis of rulings is reasoning, if a reason is not established by text, consensus, or indication and hint, and the suitability is apparent, then reasoning must be applied. The Hanafi scholars have also rejected this. Imam Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari said: "The criterion of distinction is a condition for us just as it is a condition for them. However, for them, the criterion of distinction is the cause, while for us it is the effect... But we need, before that, that is, before clarifying the distinction and beginning the reasoning, to establish evidence that the original matter we want to reason about is a witness, that is, it is reasoned in the present case and is not limited to its instance, but its ruling extends to others, just as the ruling established from the two paths extends to the pierced navel by consensus, so reasoning may be applied to it after the evidence has been established that it is a cause, because the original in the texts, although it is reasoning, is established through the apparent, and we have found from the texts that are not reasoned by consensus, and it is possible that this specific text is among that group, so it is not permissible to rely on that principle and impose it on others with this possibility" (1). Al-Bazdawi said: "We do not accept the argument based on the principle that reasoning is fundamental in the texts, but it is necessary to establish evidence that this specific text is indeed reasoned" (2).
As for their claim that the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) reasoned based on suitable descriptions and beneficial meanings and that they built rulings on meanings close to beneficial meanings, they rejected it. Al-Ansari said: "They also said: The Companions were content with considering benefits, and they were not denied, thus it became consensus. We say: Their being content with it is disputed. Rather, they only considered as causes what they were aware of regarding the consideration of its type or its kind in the type of ruling or its kind. This requires you to conduct an investigation until the reality becomes clear to you" (3).
__________
(1) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar. 3/436.
(2) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazduri. 3/438.
(3) Al-Ansari, Fawatih al-Rahmut, 2/266.


[Page 132]

As for their statement that the appropriate description or inference leads to conjecture, and that conjecture is applicable in legal matters, they also rejected it. Al-Bazdawi said: "As for imagination, it is a false matter because it is mere conjecture without any reality, and it is internal and does not serve as evidence against the opponent nor as a legal proof" (1).

He also said in Kashf al-Asrar: "As for imagination... it is a false matter because it is merely a form of conjecture, as imagination and conjecture are one and the same, and conjecture does not provide anything of truth. It cannot be said that conjecture is considered in the law in terms of the obligation to act upon it like the report of a single narrator or analogy, for we say that what is considered is that which has a definitive proof for its obligation to act upon it, not mere conjecture, and there is no proof here for its consideration in the law, thus it must be disregarded" (2).

Al-Ansari said: "Contrary to the Hanafis, who do not accept imagination at all, because although it may lead to conjecture, it is not binding according to what the legislator has established... And if it does not lead to the conjecture of the legislator's consideration, it is not a legal proof; rather, it is merely a product of the mind and thus not considered. Perhaps this is what al-Nasafi meant, that it is mere conjecture, meaning it is not the conjecture of the legislator's consideration, so it does not provide anything of truth. If you say: 'Imagination certainly leads to conjecture and consensus has been established on the consideration of conjecture,' he said: 'The consensus on acting upon conjecture is only on the condition that it is - that is, conjecture - legal and derived from the law, and a conjecture for the consideration of the legislator'" (3). He also said, quoting Imam al-Nasafi: "The fact that the description is imaginative, meaning it evokes in the heart the imagination of correctness: it does not provide anything of truth, and its utmost is to be like inspiration. It is not a valid proof" (4).

The second section
The emergence of the idea of the objectives of the Sharia

The intensification of the debate:
__________
(1) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi. 3/518.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar 3/518.
(3) Al-Ansari, Fawatih al-Rahmut, 2/301.
(4) The same source.


[Page 133]

This debate between the two parties, one presenting evidence and the other refuting it, weakens the position of those who adopt the approach of analogy (qiyas) and reasoning. Their weak position can be summarized in one point, which is that considering a specific description in a particular ruling and claiming it as a cause is an arbitrary judgment without evidence. Consequently, it relies on mere rational conjecture, which is not a legal conjecture. This leads to the weakness of their position in reasoning, as it is based on considering appropriate descriptions in numerous rulings. The refuters said: "The utmost that can be said in this regard is that the texts may align with the description, resulting in numerous parallels, and with numerous parallels, strength in the description is not achieved." (1)
__________
(1) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar. 3/513.


[Page 134]

This debate led to further research, reflection, and deepening of understanding. Al-Juwayni (may Allah have mercy on him) defended the approach of analogy (qiyas) and the use of reasoning, accusing those who rejected them of a lack of understanding of these principles. He responded to the claim that it rules without evidence and relies on reason, stating that this only applies to those who do not follow al-Shafi'i's (may Allah be pleased with him) method in this regard. He said about Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions: "In general, they have neither a little nor a lot of knowledge of the principles of jurisprudence. If one of them establishes a ruling for a matter, we will refute it in the details of the branches, for their companion did not base his rulings on principles, but rather he issued them based on what came to him. Thus, whoever among his companions wants to organize his rulings according to a principle will find himself contradicting in the details of the branches" (1). He also said: "As for Abu Hanifa, we do not deny his sharp intellect and the quality of his mind in grasping the nature of transactions and the ranks of governance. He is excellent in this field and adept at formulating issues well, but he is not knowledgeable about the principles of the Sharia, which for him are divided into an origin he is ignorant of or has overlooked and forgotten, and another that he adhered to and understood. He approached the categorization of chapters as one who did not draw from the foundations. It is remarkable that he did not take care to gather reports and narrations to base his issues upon, but rather he connects the branches based on what he sees and then seeks support from what he reaches in agreement" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/587. Paragraph: 784.
(2) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/748. Paragraph: 1180. This statement from al-Juwayni (may Allah have mercy on him) can only be seen as an unjust accusation against Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) and his companions. My aim here is not to discuss this accusation, but I will quickly point out its fallacy. It is refuted by the very text that affirms the sharp intellect of the greatest Imam and the quality of his mind. Furthermore, we have not found what al-Juwayni claimed, that Abu Hanifa's companions have neither a little nor a lot of knowledge of the principles, but rather we found them, like others, to be leaders and scholars, and they are the ones who were called jurists (fuqaha) in contrast to the theologians (mutakallimun). As for the claim that Abu Hanifa is not knowledgeable about the principles... etc., it is countered by the stability of the school and the acceptance of the community over hundreds of years. Were it not for the fact that the school is based on principles and foundational rules and systematic reasoning, it would have faded away and would not have lasted even a single generation. The fact that the science of the principles of jurisprudence was not established with its rules, limits, and conditions until the time of Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) and afterward does not harm Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him). If it were harmful to him, it would also be harmful to the Companions, the Followers, and all the Imams before him, which is not the case. We do not think there is any reason for this injustice from al-Juwayni except the intensity of the debate and the strength of the arguments of his opponents, which narrowed his perspective and blocked his avenues of reasoning, prompting him to attack his opponents in opinion. Therefore, we see him saying what he says about Abu Hanifa and his companions (may Allah be pleased with them), and we will see some of that regarding Malik and his companions (may Allah be pleased with them), and we will see him praising al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) greatly.


[Page 135]

The strong arguments of the followers of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) may have led al-Juwayni to further research and delve deeper until he presented the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in the form that we will explain, and thus it is presumed that he was the first to articulate it in this manner.
Al-Juwayni discusses the claim that reasoning is a form of adjudicating opinion in the Sharia, saying: "As for what the judge(1) mentioned regarding the matter being beyond regulation and resorting to the dissolution and returning the matter to the opinions of those with sound minds, this only applies to Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) and his followers if what has been narrated about him is correct"(2).
He said about Malik (may Allah have mercy on him): "His opinion establishes benefits that are distant from the usual benefits and the known meanings in the Sharia, and this led him to innovate killing and taking wealth based on benefits that are likely to be required, even if he did not find a basis for those benefits in the principles, and there is no stopping at that; rather, the opinion is his, whatever he sees fit, and it is detached from the suspicions and interests"(3).
He then said: "We say to Malik (may Allah have mercy on him): Is it permissible to rely on every opinion? If he refuses, we find no reference to settle upon except for the approximation that al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) accepted, and if he did not mention regulation and stated that what has no text or basis is returned to unregulated opinion and the approval of those with intellect, this is indeed a great intrusion and a departure from regulation"(4). Then he said: "This is a difficult position that no believer would dare to take, and its course is to return the matter to the minds of the wise and the judgments of the judges, and we are certain that the matter is contrary to that... If what Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said—if it is correct—were permissible, the wise during the time of Khosrow Anushirvan would have taken justice and governance(5) as their criterion, and this leads to chaos that cannot be independently managed. If Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) and his followers approach the opinion from the established principles in the Sharia, then what they have brought forth is the doctrine of al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him)"(6).
__________
(1) The judge: Abu Bakr al-Baqillani.
(2) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/725, paragraph: 1138.
(3) The same source, p: 721, paragraph: 1128.
(4) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan, 2/725 - 726, paragraphs: 1139 - 1141.
(5) Governance: The king governs his subjects with governance. And to govern the people is to take care of them. And to manage wealth is to rectify and govern it. Al-Fayruzabadi, Al-Qamus Al-Muhit p: 1244.
(6) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan, 2/725 - 726, paragraphs: 1139 - 1141.


[Page 136]

Therefore, al-Juwayni criticizes those who rely on inference, and he emphasizes the need to adhere to established principles in the Sharia. He said: "As for al-Shafi'i, he is the most knowledgeable of Allah's creation regarding the principles of the Sharia and the most precise in them, and the most astute and quick-witted in deriving them and applying them appropriately and arranging them in their ranks... However, his time was short and his opportunity limited... and he passed away at just over fifty, and that period did not allow for more than the mastery of the principles therein, so it was easy for his companions to build upon them"(1). He said: "If it is asked: What is the meaning of the approximation that you attributed to al-Shafi'i? We say: This is the crux of the matter, and we say: There are established principles with known reasons that the jurists have agreed upon, and al-Shafi'i said: I take those reasons as my refuge and I make the inferences close to them even if their specific instances are not present, so that they are as if they are, for example, principles and the inferences are considered based on them, and considering the meaning by meaning in approximation is preferable to considering one form by another in a comprehensive sense"(2). He said: "Al-Shafi'i and most of the companions of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with them both) went to rely on inference even if it did not stem from a unanimously agreed-upon ruling in principle, but he does not permit distance, excess, or extremism; rather, it is permissible to link rulings to interests that he sees as similar to the recognized interests in agreement and to the interests based on rulings that are firmly established in the Sharia"(3).
He also said: "Not every public interest (maslaha) is an accepted face."(4)
__________
(1) The same source, p. 749, paragraph: 1182.
(2) The same source, p. 726, paragraph: 1142.
(3) The same source, 2/721, paragraph: 1130.
(4) The same source, p. 527, paragraph: 760.


[Page 137]

Among this is the statement of his student al-Ghazali: "As for public interest (maslaha), it originally refers to bringing benefit and repelling harm, and we do not mean that. For bringing benefit and repelling harm are the objectives of creation and the welfare of creation in achieving their objectives. Rather, we mean by public interest the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia, and the objectives of the Sharia concerning creation are five: to preserve their religion, their lives, their intellect, their lineage, and their wealth. Everything that involves the preservation of these five foundational principles is considered public interest, and everything that jeopardizes the preservation of these five foundational principles is considered corruption, and repelling it is public interest. When we use the terms 'appropriate' and 'suitable' in the book of analogy, we mean this category" (1). He said: "The fact that these meanings are intended is known not by one proof but by many countless proofs... And if we define public interest as the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia, there is no room for disagreement on it, and it must be established as a proof" (2).
This defense of the approach of appropriateness and the idea of inference led to the emergence of the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in the hands of al-Juwayni. It was later crystallized by his student al-Ghazali, based on texts such as: "Considering the meaning by the meaning in approximation," "interests similar to the recognized interests by consensus," "interests based on established and fixed rulings in the Sharia," and "intended meanings known not by one proof but by many countless proofs from the Book and the Sunnah" (3).
The classification of rulings according to their outcomes or their public interests:
The assertion of these objectives is based on presenting the Sharia, that is, its rulings, in a manner that highlights its care for public interests. In other words, it is based on adapting the Sharia in a way that supports the claim of the validity of considering appropriateness, whether it is a specific analogy in a ruling or a general one.
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, al-Mustasfa. 1/286.
(2) The same source, 1/311.
(3) See the texts mentioned above from al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali.


[Page 138]

It is redundant to mention, after it has become clear, that Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni (may Allah have mercy on him) was the first to attempt to establish the validity of reasoning by appropriate description through the adaptation of the Sharia for the purpose of examining it in light of its objectives of public interest (maqasid al-sharia) - and Allah knows best - where he categorized the rulings according to their purposes or objectives or meanings into five categories. The matter later evolved, at the hands of the supporters of this methodology, into three categories along with their complements, which are the necessities, the needs, and the embellishments, along with the complements of each. He stated under the title: "On the classifications of the causes and principles": "What these individuals have mentioned are the principles of the Sharia(1). We categorize it into five categories:
"One of them is what is rationally understood and is a foundation. The rational meaning of it leads to a necessary matter that must be adhered to, and this is akin to the ruling of the Sharia regarding the obligation of retribution (qisas) at its proper time, as it is justified by the preservation of the sanctity of blood and the deterrence against aggression towards it. When the observer who derives rulings clarifies this in the foundation of retribution, he can apply it and extend it to where the foundation of this meaning is realized, which facilitates the justification of its origin... It has also been established in the Sharia that when the foundations are firmly established, there is no need to seek the realization of its meaning in individual cases."(2)
He said in this section: "And it is that which is based on necessity"(3).
This section is what was later referred to as the necessities, which are the essential universals: the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and property.
__________
(1) The term "principles of Sharia (usul al-sharia)" here refers to the legal rulings, as a legal ruling that is reasoned is a principle upon which analogical reasoning (qiyas) is based, and it is one of the pillars of qiyas. Likewise, if it is a subject of inquiry and examination to understand its objective or reason.
(2) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan. 2/602, paragraph: 901.
(3) The same source, p. 604, paragraph: 906.


[Page 139]

"The second type: that which pertains to public need and does not reach the level of necessity. This is like the validation of rental agreements, which are based on the pressing need for housing while being unable to own it and the reluctance of its owners to provide it as a loan. This is a clear need that does not reach the level of necessity prescribed in sales and others" (1). Al-Juwayni has classified sales under the first type.
This section is what has been termed the rank of needs.
"The third type: that which does not pertain to an urgent necessity or a public need, but it indicates an objective in seeking a virtue or in negating its opposite. It is permissible for this category to include the purification from ritual impurity and the removal of filth" (2). This section is what has been termed the improvements.
"The fourth type: that which is not based on need or necessity, and the attainment of its objective is explicitly recommended from the outset" (3). This section resembles the third in that it does not rely on necessity or public need and is considered recommended. It differs from it in that the third is supported by innate inclinations such as cleanliness, and its attainment does not fall outside the first and second types, such as the writing of a contract by a slave and his meeting with his owner regarding his ownership, which goes against the principle that the slave is owned by the master" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/602, paragraph: 902.
(2) The same source, p. 602, paragraph: 901.
(3) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan, p. 603, paragraph: 904.
(4) The same source, paragraph: 904, and see p. 616, paragraph: 931.


[Page 140]

"The fifth category: that which does not present any meaning at all to the jurist (mustanbit), nor any necessity or need or encouragement towards a virtue. This is very rarely the case. For if it is impossible to derive a specific meaning, it does not prevent one from conceiving a general one. An example of this category is purely physical acts of worship. They do not relate to any defensive or beneficial purposes. However, it may be said that the continuity of these acts maintains the worshippers' flexibility in adhering to the rules of submission, and the renewal of the covenant through the remembrance of Allah, Exalted is He, serves as a deterrent against immorality and wrongdoing. This applies in general, and when the discussion in this category reaches determinations such as the number of units of prayer (rak'ahs) and similar matters, the one making the analogy (qiyas) does not hope to derive a meaning that necessitates the determination in matters whose origins cannot be analogized" (1). Al-Razi referred to this classification in Al-Mahsool, following al-Juwayni in it (2).
After al-Juwayni, scholars began to classify the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) into three categories: necessary, need-based, and complementary. Each category has its own supplements or complements. This does not mean the elimination of some of the five categories mentioned by al-Juwayni, but rather their inclusion within the three.
__________
(1) The same source, p. 604, paragraph: 905.
(2) Al-Razi, Al-Mahsool 5/ 159 - 162.


[Page 141]

Al-Amidi said: "The purpose of the legislation of rulings... cannot be anything other than being among the necessary objectives (maqasid al-daruriyyah) or not among the necessary objectives. If it is among the necessary objectives, then it is either a fundamental principle or not a fundamental principle. If it is a fundamental principle, it pertains to the five objectives that no community or law has ever neglected, which are: the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and wealth. The preservation of these five objectives is among the necessities and represents the highest ranks of appropriateness. The limitation to these five types is based on reality and the knowledge of the absence of any necessary objective outside of them in practice... And if it is not a fundamental principle, it is the supplementary aspect that complements the necessary objective, such as the emphasis on preserving intellect by prohibiting even a small amount of intoxicants that lead to larger quantities... And if the objective is not among the necessary objectives, it is either something that people need or something that people do not need. If it is something that people need, then it is either a fundamental principle or not a fundamental principle. If it is a fundamental principle, it is the second category that pertains to additional needs, such as the authority of a guardian to marry off a minor not due to a necessity that compels it, but out of need... And if it is not a fundamental principle, it is the supplementary aspect that serves as a completion and fulfillment of the second category, such as observing compatibility and the customary dowry in the marriage of a minor, as it leads to the continuity of marriage and the fulfillment of its objectives... And if the objective is not among the additional needs, it is the third category, which pertains to improvement and adornment and the observance of the best practices of customs and transactions, such as depriving slaves of the capacity to bear witness, as a slave is of lower status and rank because he is subjugated to the owner and occupied with serving him, thus it is not befitting for him to hold the position of testimony due to its honor and great significance, following what people are accustomed to and consider among the virtues of customs" (1).
Such a classification of the objectives of rulings is based on two matters:
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ahkam. 3/240 - 241.


[Page 142]

The first: The reality of people as individuals and as a community. A person is in need, and these needs can be divided into these categories. Some of them must be secured or fulfilled and satisfied, and if they are not satisfied, it leads to death or to a significant corruption of life and relationships. Some of them, if not satisfied, cause the person to suffer from hardship, difficulties, and distress. And some, if not satisfied, do not lead to this or that, but they are what the soul inclines towards or what the body requires. Based on this reality, a person is driven to satisfy and fulfill these needs. This drive increases and strengthens according to the intensity of the need. And since a person is a social being, and everyone is driven to achieve satisfaction and is keen on it, they need a system or law that organizes the relationships between people and the ways of satisfaction, clarifying for each of them their rights, powers, restrictions, and obligations.
By nature, a person views what fulfills their needs or satisfies their instincts, or what leads to that, as a benefit or interest, and views what corrupts their fulfillment of needs and satisfaction of instincts or prevents them from that, and what causes them pain or leads to that, as a corruption and harm.
The second: An examination of the rulings of Islam and the conditions of the societies in which Islam was applied shows that Islam came with commands and prohibitions that lead to the satisfaction of these needs in varying degrees, which results in the security of the individual and their tranquility, as well as the security, prosperity, and advancement of society.


[Page 143]

However, this presentation of the Sharia (Islamic law) serves to indicate what the application of the Sharia leads to for the individual and society, and it indicates that bringing about benefits and averting harms are results, or among the results, of applying the Sharia. Therefore, the objection and response to those who adopt the path of suitability and reasoning, and this methodology in considering the description or the beneficial meaning, remains the same; rather, this argument may provide them with further evidence for their rebuttal. It is necessary, according to the Hanafi (school of thought), to establish that these results or benefits are intended by the legislator, and this can only be proven by a legal evidence. Furthermore, the objective of the legislator in the ruling is a result of its application; so is the result of the ruling or its cause a reason for it? Thus, the matter has remained a subject of significant contention and debate. Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi said: "The correct view is that this is not a proof because it is not known from the legislator that he preserves lives by every means; therefore, mutilation was not legislated even though it is the most effective deterrent and warning, nor was killing legislated for theft or drinking alcohol. If a ruling is established for a benefit among these benefits, it is not known that the Sharia preserves that benefit by establishing that ruling, as it would be placing the Sharia based on opinion and ruling by pure reason." (1)
For example, cutting off the hand of the thief leads to the reduction or elimination of theft, and it leads to the preservation of wealth, which is one of the essential objectives. However, this objective, which is the preservation of wealth, does not serve as a reason for cutting off the hand of the thief, because the usurper, the embezzler, and the fraudster are not punished by the Sharia, even though this objective exists in the prohibition of embezzlement, usurpation, and fraud.
__________
(1) Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, Rawdat al-Nazir wa Jannat al-Manazir. p: 150.


[Page 144]

Therefore, this idea - the idea of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) - has not negatively or positively affected the principles of the Hanafi school (madhhab). Al-Ansari said: "The Hanafis do not accept the concept of istihsan (juridical preference) at all, because although it may lead to a presumption, it is not binding on the legislator (Shari) according to what it indicates. It is also not presumed that the legislator has established it for the sake of the many exceptions, as in cases of known cancellation, such as arduous crafts, which are more suitable for alleviation than the hardship of travel. However, the legislator considered the former and disregarded the latter. As for the public interests (masalih mursala), they are also suitable, but they have not been considered in the Sharia. If they do not lead to a presumption of the legislator's consideration, they are not a legal proof but rather a product of the whims of the mind and thus are not considered. Perhaps this is what Nasafi meant, that there is no presumption of the legislator's consideration, which does not contribute anything to the truth. If you say: istihsan certainly leads to presumption and consensus has been established on the consideration of presumption, he said: the consensus on acting upon presumption is only on the condition that it is - that is, the presumption - legally established from the direction of the Sharia and a presumption according to the legislator" (1).
As for what the proponents of the argument have said regarding the idea of maqasid, that the meaning has led to many rulings in accordance with it, it is stronger than analogy (qiyas) and serves as a basis for legislation. They have referred to the testimony of the rulings as being in accordance with the principles or conforming to the principles, but the Hanafis have also rejected this. The commentator on the principles of al-Bazdawi said: "As for the texts being in accordance with the description, it results in a multitude of similarities, and with the multitude of similarities, strength in the description is not achieved" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Ansari, Fawatih al-Rahmut 2/301.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar 3/512, and the intended modification refers to the establishment of the effect of the description.


[Page 145]

Thus, the disagreement remained as it was, returning to the dispute over how to consider wisdom (hikmah), public interest (maslaha), or objectives (maqasid). Those who reject reasoning based on appropriate descriptions see this consideration as a mere imaginary notion or a mental obsession, a conjecture that is not supported by the sacred law, and therefore has no validity. From here, the arguments of those who justify based on objectives emerged, asserting that reasoning is a legal necessity and that it is the foundation of rulings. Accordingly, reasoning based on beneficial meanings is not mere arbitrariness but rather a legal conjecture because it is the foundation; otherwise, the ruling would be merely an act of devotion, which contradicts the principle. This is the subject of the next section.

Section Three
An Introduction to the Idea of Objectives (Maqasid) According to al-Shatibi

A brief overview of this section:
The main topic of this section is the principle of reasoning, that is, the assertion that the foundation of rulings is reasoning. Some jurists have relied on the idea that the Sharia is based on bringing about benefits and preventing harms in order to establish certain pathways in reasoning, particularly the pathway of appropriateness. Establishing this reasoning necessitated proving several issues:
First: ... proving that Allah, Exalted is He, does not act except for a purpose or wisdom, and His legislation is a result of His actions, thus establishing that the legal rulings are reasoned. Since some legal rulings cannot be expected to have known reasons, such as numbers, quantities, and shares, it cannot be said that rulings are reasoned; rather, it should be said that the foundation of rulings is reasoning.
Second: ... that wisdom must be a benefit and not a harm, and the benefit either pertains to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servant. Allah, Exalted is He, is free from benefits and harms, so the benefit must pertain to the servant.


[Page 146]

The third: ... If we find a legal ruling that entails a certain benefit, the assertion that Allah - Exalted is He - legislated this ruling for this benefit is a conjecture, and Allah has commanded us regarding conjecture, so this conjecture is legal, and the reasoning based on this benefit is legal reasoning.
The debates regarding the first and second issues have led to theological discussions related to the creation of actions and attributes. Some, like al-Amidi, for example, argued that the rulings are justified by the benefits of the servants and that this is based on occurrence and consensus. The Mu'tazila also held this view, asserting it as a necessity. Al-Razi firmly rejected the notion of justifying Allah's actions and rulings, and he established the justification of benefits for the rulings without needing a foundational justification. Then came al-Shatibi, who countered al-Razi's position and firmly established the justification of actions and rulings in all details of the Sharia, but in a manner different from that adopted by his predecessors in order to prove this principle.
Thus, we are faced with three different approaches to establishing the justification of rulings by means of wisdoms and benefits: the first is that of al-Amidi, the second is that of al-Razi, and the third is that of al-Shatibi. As for the approach of the Mu'tazila, its subject is not analogy (qiyas) or objectives (maqasid), but rather the necessity of doing what is best in relation to Allah, which is a rejected claim because Allah does what He wills and decrees what He wants, and His actions and decrees are the measure and cannot be compared to anything.
As for the third issue, which is that Allah - Exalted is He - has commanded us regarding conjecture, and whether this ruling is legislated for this benefit is a legal or non-legal conjecture, the opinions on this have been clarified in the previous discussion, and they will be referenced here to the extent that the research necessitates.


[Page 147]

Evidence of those who affirm the principle of reasoning:
A group of the imams of usul (principles of jurisprudence), after dividing the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) into necessities, needs, and enhancements, sought to establish evidence for this reasoning. Al-Amidi said under the title (Establishing evidence that suitability and consideration are proof that the description is a reason): "The rulings were legislated for the interests of the servants. As for the fact that they were legislated for objectives and purposes, this is indicated by consensus and reason. The consensus is that the jurists are unanimous that the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are not devoid of wisdom and purpose, even if they differ on whether this is by way of obligation, as the Mu'tazila said, or by way of agreement and occurrence without obligation, as our companions said. As for reason, it is that Allah, Exalted is He, is wise in His creation. The consideration of purpose in His creation must either be obligatory or not obligatory: if it is obligatory, then it is not devoid of purpose; and if it is not obligatory, then acting for the purpose is closer to being in accordance with reason than acting without purpose. Thus, the purpose is necessarily inferred from His actions, and if the purpose is necessary in His creation, then the rulings are from His creation, and they are for a purpose and objective. The purpose must either return to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servants. There is no way to the former due to His transcendence above harm and benefit, and because it contradicts consensus, so only the latter remains." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam 3/250. It is noteworthy in this text and similar ones that the establishment of the principle of reasoning has shifted the discussion of the reason from the meaning that the legislator has made a reason for the ruling to discussions related to the essence of Allah.


[Page 148]

Then he said: "Moreover, the rulings are what the Messenger brought, and they were a mercy to the worlds due to His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds } (1). If the rulings were devoid of wisdom that returns to the worlds, they would not be a mercy but rather a punishment, as the obligation of adhering to them would be mere toil and hardship. Also, His saying, Exalted is He: { And My mercy encompasses all things } (2). If the legislation of the rulings concerning the servants was not for a wisdom, it would be a punishment, not a mercy for the reasons mentioned. Furthermore, his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "There is no harm and no harming in Islam" (3). If the obligation of the rulings were not for a wisdom that returns to the servants, then their legislation would be pure harm, and that would be contrary to Islam, which is against the text" (4).
Then al-Amidi concluded with the result, saying: "And if it is established that the rulings were legislated for the interests of the servants, then if we see a legislated ruling that entails a beneficial matter, it must either be that this is the objective of legislating the ruling, or that which is not apparent to us. The objective cannot be that which is not apparent to us; otherwise, the legislation of the ruling would be mere obedience, which is contrary to the principle, as previously established. Therefore, it remains that it is legislated for what has become apparent. If this is presumed, then it must be acted upon, because presumption is obligatory to follow in the Sharia, and this is indicated by the consensus of the Companions on acting upon presumption and the obligation to follow it in legal rulings" (5).

It is authentic due to the abundance of its supporting evidence, and the addition in "Islam" is from the narration of al-Tabarani in al-Awsat. See: Nasb al-Rayah by al-Zayla'i, 4/386.
