[Page 149]

After that, al-Amidi began to respond to the objections that arise against this approach in reasoning and to the issues he presented within that context, particularly his statement that Allah does not legislate except for a purpose and an objective. Then, assuming the acceptance that Allah does not legislate except for a purpose and an objective, how can it be established that this presumed wisdom of the jurist is indeed the same as the intended objective of the legislator in the ruling? He said: "If it is said: We do not concede that the legislation of rulings necessitates the wisdom and the objectives, because the legislation of rulings is the work of Allah, Exalted is He, and His work either necessitates wisdom and objectives, or it does not. The first is impossible for seventeen reasons" (1). He then presented the objections to the necessity of rulings for wisdom and objectives and refuted them one by one (2). The debate on these issues is entirely outside the framework of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) and falls within the realm of logic and discourse. Below are examples of these objections and the responses to them:
The first objection as presented by al-Amidi: "There are two positions regarding the actions of servants: one position states that the actions of servants are created by Allah, Exalted is He, and the other position states that they are created by the servants themselves. Whoever claims that they are created by Allah, Exalted is He, must accept that He is the creator of disbelief, sins, and all kinds of evils, while there is no wisdom or purpose in creating these things. And whoever claims that they are created by the servants, then they are created for them through Allah's creation of the ability for them to do so, and His creation of the ability that necessitates these matters is also not for a wisdom" (3).
The second objection: "If His action necessitated wisdom, then why did He cause the deaths of the prophets and grant respite to Iblis, and why did He necessitate the eternal punishment of the people of Hell in the Fire, due to the lack of wisdom in that?" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/251.
(2) The same source, 3/251 - 256.
(3) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, 3/251 - 256.
(4) The same location.


[Page 150]

And al-Amidi's response to these two objections is: "From three aspects: The first: That ability (qudra) only pertains to creation and existence, and nothing else; disbelief (kufr) and types of sins and evils are related to disobeying the prohibition of the Lawgiver, and that is not related to ability in any way. The second: Even if we concede that all of that is created by Allah, we do not claim that wisdom (hikmah) necessarily accompanies His actions absolutely, so that it applies to every created thing; rather, we only claim that in matters where wisdom can be considered, which is possible in everything except for types of evils and sins, and we do not claim that categorically, but rather apparently. The third: Even if we concede that wisdom necessarily accompanies His actions absolutely, we do not concede the impossibility of that in the cases they mentioned, as it is possible that what follows from them has a ruling that only the Lord knows."(1)
Among the examples of these objections is: "The sixteenth: that wisdom is sought only in the case of one whose soul inclines towards bringing benefit or repelling harm, and the Lord, Exalted is He, is free from that."
The seventeenth: Wisdom is sought in the actions of one whose actions, if devoid of wisdom, would incur blame and be considered frivolous. And the Lord is exalted above that, as He is the one who acts in His dominion as He wills and chooses, without being questioned about what He does. As He, Exalted is He, said: { He is not to be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned }(2), and even if His actions do not necessarily entail wisdom, that is what is sought"(3).
Al-Amidi responded to these last two objections: "Regarding the sixteenth objection, it is denied what they mentioned about the consideration of wisdom; rather, wisdom is sought in an action where, if wisdom were found in it, it would not be prohibited, but rather it would generally occur."
And regarding the seventeenth [point], what they mentioned is only necessary in the case of one for whom it is obligatory to consider wisdom in their actions, and the Exalted One is not like that, according to what is indicated in our theological writings."(4)
The evidence of the refuters:

Thus, the establishment of the principle of causation (ta'leel) by this group was only through theological discussions about the essence of God. Therefore, we see another group that decisively rejects this principle, even though it accepts analogy (qiyas), causation, inference, and the method of suitability. Among the most famous of these is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi. He said: "The suitability implies the presumption of causation, and presumption is (3) acted upon"(1). He also said: "It has been established that suitability implies causation while being certain that the actions of Allah, Exalted is He, are not subject to causation"(2).
Al-Razi attempted to prove the reasoning through the method of suitability, mentioning two approaches in this regard. The first is the method or the evidence presented by al-Amidi. He mentioned it and then returned to it to refute it. As for the second, he affirmed it and supported it.
He said: "The relationship (al-munasaba) indicates the presumption of causality, and this presumption must be acted upon. The first premise(3) is established from two angles: the first(4): that Allah - Exalted is He - legislated the rulings for the benefit of the servants, and this is a benefit, thus there arises a presumption that Allah - Exalted is He - legislated it for this benefit. These are three premises that must be proven with evidence. As for the first premise, its evidence is established through various angles"(5). What is meant by his statement: "As for the first premise" is his statement that Allah - Exalted is He - legislated the rulings for the benefit of the servants, which refers to the essence of causation. He then presented six angles to prove this premise, which do not differ from what al-Amidi presented, but in a more detailed manner(6).

(2) The same source, 5/178.
(3) The first: that is, the first introduction, which is that the relationship (munasaba) provides a presumption of causality.
(4) That is: there are two ways to establish that the relationship (munasaba) provides a presumption of causality, and the first way will be mentioned below. It is noteworthy that he mentions this way and then refutes it.

[Page 152]

He said: "These six aspects indicate that the Exalted One has not legislated the rulings except for the benefit of the servants. Then people differed after that: as for the Mu'tazila, they explicitly stated the reality of this position and uncovered its meaning, saying: It is reprehensible for Allah, Exalted is He, to commit what is wrong, and to act in vain; rather, His actions must encompass a purpose of benefit and aim. As for the jurists, they assert that He, Exalted is He, legislated the ruling for this meaning and for this wisdom, and if they heard the term 'aim', they would declare the speaker a disbeliever, even though the only meaning of that 'lam' (ل) is the aim. Moreover, they say: 'Although it is not obligatory for Allah, Exalted is He, to consider the interests, He does not act except in what is beneficial for His servants, as a favor and kindness, not out of obligation.' This is the discussion regarding the establishment of this premise." (1)
As for al-Razi's refutation of the principle of reasoning behind rulings and interests, it comes in a lengthy discourse, of which we will mention some. He said: "His statement: The specification of a particular case with a specific ruling must have a reason, and that reason cannot return to Allah, Exalted is He, so it must return to the servant. We say: Either you claim that specification must have a specific reason or you do not claim that; in either case, you cannot assert that the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are based on interests." (2) He then presented a lengthy argument to refute the claim of reasoning behind the rulings of Allah, and all of this discussion pertains to the essence of Allah, Exalted is He.
__________
(1) Al-Razi, al-Mahsool, 5/176.
(2) The same source, p. 180.


[Page 153]

And he concluded by saying: "It has been established that the reasoning behind God's rulings (Exalted is He) based on public interests (maslaha) is invalid. This statement, while being an objection to what they have said, is also a definitive indication starting from the issue. Through this, the invalidity of all the arguments they relied upon becomes evident, as they are speculative proofs, while what we have mentioned is a conclusive argument. Then we say: If what you have mentioned indicates that the reasoning behind God's actions (Exalted is He) based on public interests is valid, then we have conclusive evidence that prevents it, which comes from the following aspects:" (1) He then mentioned these aspects, all of which pertain to the essence of God and have no connection to the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). Among these aspects he mentioned:
"The first: that He is the Creator of the actions of the servants, and this prevents the claim that He - Exalted is He - takes into account the interests."(2)
"The second proof: that it is not permissible to justify the actions of Allah - Exalted is He - and His rulings by interests (masalih), is that if one is able to disbelieve but not able to believe, it would necessitate compulsion (jabr), and this undermines the consideration of interests."(3)
"The third evidence: that there has been an obligation imposed that is beyond one's capacity, and this prevents the assertion of taking into account public interests (maslaha)."(4)
Thus, all the aspects or proofs that he presented up to the last one, which is the eighth, where he said: "As for God (Exalted is He), since He is entirely free from interests and harms. Then we see that what predominates in His actions is that which does not serve the interests of creation, how can it be presumed that His actions and rulings are motivated by interests?!" (5).

(2) The same place.
(3) Al-Razi, Al-Mahsool, 5/186.
(4) The same place.
(5) The same source 5/193. I intended by presenting the arguments and objections of both al-Amidi and al-Razi to demonstrate that such a discussion is a logical and theological inquiry that falls outside the framework and objectives of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), and that including it within usul al-fiqh is unjustified; rather, it is resorted to by those whose arguments are weak.


[Page 154]

Although al-Razi rejected the very concept of causation, he affirmed the method of analogy in a different way. He said, after mentioning the first argument in explaining that analogy implies a presumption of causation, which he mentioned and then refuted, "The second argument in explaining that analogy implies a presumption of causation is that we concede that the actions and rulings of Allah cannot be attributed to motives and purposes. Nevertheless, we claim that analogy implies a presumption of causation, and the explanation is as follows: The belief of Muslims is that the rotation of celestial bodies, the rising and setting of stars, and their remaining in their forms and lights are not obligatory. However, since Allah - Exalted is He - has established a habit of keeping them in a constant state, it is no wonder that they will remain tomorrow and the day after with these characteristics. Similarly, the falling of rain during humid clouds, the feeling of fullness after eating, the quenching of thirst after drinking, and burning upon contact with fire are not obligatory, but since the habit has been consistent with these occurrences, it is no wonder that a presumption close to certainty arises regarding their continuity in their patterns. The result is that the repetition of something many times leads to the presumption that whenever it occurs, it will occur only in that manner. Once this is established, we say: When we contemplate the laws, we find that rulings and benefits are closely related, and neither can be separated from the other, which is evident after the establishment of the conditions of the laws. If this is the case, then the knowledge of the occurrence of one necessitates the presumption of the occurrence of the other, and vice versa, without one being a cause for the other or a motive for it(1). Thus, it is established that analogy is a proof of causation, while it is certain that the rulings of Allah - Exalted is He - are not attributed to purposes"(2).
Thus, despite the disagreement between these two groups regarding the very concept of causation, they both agree on attributing causation to the appropriate description, in contrast to those who reject the method of analogy.
Does the concept of causation necessitate the method of analogy?

[Page 155]

The group that does not adopt the approach of analogy does not make this approach necessary for the basis of reasoning, and this is evident from the arguments that were previously clarified when discussing their rejection of the analogy approach. Among these is that if it is established that this is a public interest (maslaha), then establishing that the ruling was legislated by Allah for the sake of this public interest requires evidence. Otherwise, the presumed conjecture here is not the legal presumption that is applied in legal matters, which they have described as mere fantasies of the hearts and whims of the minds. Furthermore, even if the basis of reasoning is established, it has also been established that some rulings are not reasoned. The ruling in question may belong to this category, that is, unreasoned, so it cannot be said to be reasoned except with evidence supporting it. Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari said: "Because the original principle in texts is reasoning, although it is established through apparent means, we have found texts that are unanimously agreed upon as being unreasoned, and it is possible that this specific text is among that group, so it is not permissible to rely on that principle and impose it on others with this possibility" (1). Al-Bazdawi said: "Thus, we do not accept the argument based on the principle that reasoning is fundamental in texts; rather, it is necessary to provide evidence that this specific text is indeed reasoned" (2).
__________
(1) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 3/436.
(2) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi 3/438.


[Page 156]

Al-Ghazali mentioned something of these arguments regarding this matter, saying: "As for the strange appropriateness, this is a matter of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), and it does not seem unlikely to me that some mujtahids (jurists) may be inclined to think so, and there is no decisive evidence indicating the invalidity of their ijtihad. If it is said: 'It indicates its invalidity because it is an arbitrary reasoning without evidence that supports attributing the ruling to its cause,' we say: 'Establishing the ruling in accordance with it indicates that the Sharia (Islamic law) has taken it into consideration and is likely to be true.' If it is said: 'Your statement that establishing the ruling in accordance with it is misleading, for it means that the ruling was sought based on an appropriateness and the legislator prompted the ruling, so he responded to its prompt and acted in accordance with it,' this is arbitrary reasoning because it is possible that the ruling of the Sharia regarding the prohibition of wine is either an act of worship or arbitrary reasoning, similar to the prohibition of pork, carrion, blood, domestic donkeys, and all predatory animals with fangs, and all birds of prey, while the hyena and fox are permissible according to some schools of thought, which are arbitrary reasonings. However, the meaning of intoxication in wine is agreed upon, so it is assumed to be for the sake of intoxication, while a similar agreement does not exist regarding carrion and pork, so it is said that this is arbitrary reasoning, and this is on the assumption that there is no indication in the Qur'an mentioning enmity and hatred. It is possible that there is another meaning appropriate that has not been revealed to us, and it is possible that it is for the sake of intoxication. So these are three possibilities; thus, ruling based on one of these three is arbitrary reasoning without evidence, otherwise, what would favor this possibility? This does not change in the effective cause, as it is known to be a cause by attributing the ruling to it textually or by consensus, such as childhood and the precedence of the brother over the father and mother. The response is: 'We favor this possibility over the possibility of arbitrary reasoning with what we have countered the view of those who deny qiyas (analogy).'"(1) He then said: "As for their statement that perhaps there is another appropriate meaning that is the cause and has not been revealed to us, our souls have inclined towards the meaning that has appeared due to the non-appearance of the other, not due to any evidence that indicates it, for it is pure conjecture. We say: The predominance of conjectures in every case relies on such conjecture and depends on the absence of the appearance of another meaning; if it were to appear, the predominance of conjecture would be invalidated. If this door were opened, qiyas would not be established."(2)
Al-Shatibi's position in brief:
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa, 2/300-301.
(2) The same source.


[Page 157]

This elaboration and the interruption from al-Razi regarding the lack of reasoning for actions and rulings was objected to by al-Shatibi, but he did not engage in a verbal dispute with him. Rather, he affirmed the reasoning for rulings and actions through a different approach than that adopted by al-Amidi and rejected by al-Razi. He relied on a new methodology, which is the inductive reasoning (istiqra) that he deemed conclusive. Consequently, he reached a definitive conclusion that the actions of Allah - Exalted is He - and His rulings are reasoned by the interests of the servants. He said: "Al-Razi claimed that the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are not reasoned by any reason whatsoever, just as His actions are not" (1). He then said: "What is relied upon is that we have inductively derived from the Sharia that it was established for the interests of the servants, an induction that al-Razi and others do not dispute" (2).
Then al-Shatibi mentioned many texts from the Qur'an and referred to others from the Sunnah, all of which indicate purposes for actions or rulings. With the abundance of these texts, he establishes that, in his view, the actions of Allah and His rulings are reasoned by their purposes.
Thus, the idea of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) emerged with al-Shatibi, through his new methodology in proving the reasons and foundations, which is the inductive reasoning that is beneficial for certainty.
As for the disagreement regarding the presumption of interest and whether it is a reason for the ruling, whether it is a legal presumption or merely an illusion, al-Shatibi did not adopt either position, nor did he refute either of them. Instead, he sought to reconcile between them, not being satisfied with such a presumption on the grounds that it is not supported by evidence, but rather it is something that the mind may entertain that this ruling was for the sake of this interest. Likewise, he did not reject this presumption on the grounds that the rulings were established for the interests of the servants, and that this interest may have been intended by the legislator with this ruling. However, he stipulated that there should be a multitude of rulings that give rise to the presumption that they were established for that interest, and thus the beneficial inductive reasoning for certainty is achieved, leading to certainty regarding the reasoning of this interest in legislation. This also illustrates how this idea arose with al-Shatibi regarding the consideration of interests and harms.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/2.
(2) The same source.


[Page 158]

It should be noted that taking an appropriate description or public interest (maslaha) as a reason for a ruling is a form of reasoning based on indicators that have not been proven to be a cause. Therefore, reasoning based on them is negated if a more appropriate description is found, or if it does not apply consistently. Al-Shatibi said: "The purpose of establishing laws is for the interests of the servants in both the immediate and the ultimate, and this is a claim that must be substantiated as true or false, and this is not the place for that, and there has been disagreement about it in the science of theology" (1). He then said: "When it became necessary in the science of usul al-fiqh to establish reasons for rulings specifically, they were established as indicators, and there is no need to delve into this matter" (2). Therefore, these interests or reasons are understood as indicators of knowledge, not as causes, and thus they are not suitable for analogy and reasoning based on them. Consequently, those who reasoned with them aimed to establish the principle of reasoning, as it then becomes akin to a cause and is useful in analogy. However, al-Shatibi did not suffice with the establishment of the principle of reasoning, which he affirmed through induction; he also stipulated that induction must apply to the reason itself or the indicator itself, thus making this reason substantiated in its own right, which is a condition of the Hanafis, making it a cause for legislation and a basis for it. This will become clear during the explanation and elaboration of the concept of objectives (maqasid) according to him.
The meaning of objectives (maqasid) according to al-Shatibi:
Objectives linguistically are the plural of maqsad, which is the thing that is intended. He said in Lisan al-Arab: "Ibn Jinni said: The root of (q-s-d) and its usages in the speech of the Arabs are determination and direction, and moving towards something in a straight manner, whether that is just or unjust. This is its essence in reality, even if it may be specified in some contexts to mean the intention of uprightness without deviation. Do you not see that you sometimes intend injustice just as you intend justice at other times? Thus, determination and direction encompass both" (3).
And he said in al-Qamus al-Muhit: "Al-qasd: the straightness of the path, reliance, and intention; he intends it, and to it, he aims" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat 2/2.
(2) The same source.
(3) Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab.
(4) Al-Firuzabadi, al-Qamus al-Muhit, p. 396.


[Page 159]

As for the technical term, there is no agreed-upon or established definition. The accepted definition in terminology is the linguistic amount present in the term. It is not possible to establish a technical definition for the objectives (maqasid) except after understanding what is meant by them, as the judgment on a thing is contingent upon its conception.
Al-Shatibi did not provide a technical definition for the objectives, but what is found in his book (al-Muwafaqat), especially in its second part, serves to define what he meant by the objectives. There is no harm in this; in fact, there is little benefit in presenting a text that does not help the reader understand the defined reality. Such definitions can only be grasped by someone who has previously understood their reality. Therefore, defining by means of a limit does not benefit him at all; rather, it judges the definition according to his understanding of the defined. Some later scholars have attempted to provide a definition for the objectives, limiting them to the objectives of the Sharia, and perhaps some have referred to objectives for the Sharia and objectives for people. However, they did not highlight the distinction between the objectives of the Sharia and the objectives of the legislator. Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour (may Allah have mercy on him) spoke of general objectives and specific objectives, defining each of them. He said: "The general objectives of legislation are the meanings and rulings considered by the legislator in all circumstances of legislation, which include the characteristics of the Sharia and its general purpose, and the meanings that legislation cannot be devoid of considering; this also includes meanings of rulings that are not considered in all types of rulings but are noted in many of them" (1). He said regarding the specific objectives: "The intended modalities for the legislator to achieve the beneficial objectives of people or to preserve their public interests in their private actions so that their efforts in their private interests do not nullify what has been established for them in obtaining their public interests" (2).
__________
(1) Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, Objectives of Islamic Law, p. 50: Tunisian Distribution Company, Tunisia, 3rd ed., December 1988.
(2) Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, Objectives of Islamic Law, p. 146.


[Page 160]

As for Professor Allal al-Fassi, he said: "The intended meaning of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) is the purpose behind it and the secrets that the legislator has placed with each of its rulings" (1).
Dr. Ahmed al-Raisuni referred to these definitions and others, stating: "Based on the various usages and statements found among the scholars who have discussed the topic of objectives, it can be said that the objectives of the Sharia are the goals that the Sharia has set to achieve for the benefit of the servants" (2).
The Saudi writer Khalid bin Saleh al-Saif referred to these definitions in an article he began with the question: What are the objectives? (3).
Dr. Hamadi al-Abidi points to the definition of Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir bin Ashour, saying: "This is not, in fact, a definition of the objectives because definitions do not take this form; rather, it is a clarification and elaboration of the areas where the objectives of the Sharia are sought. It is more appropriate to limit the definition to saying: 'The objectives are the intended rulings of the legislator in all circumstances of legislation'" (4).
In reality, all these definitions fall short of conveying the intended meaning. This is because the meaning of objectives according to al-Shatibi differs from its meaning according to others who preceded him or from contemporary scholars discussing the objectives. All these definitions, if they are correct, are only valid in the sense that exists in the minds of the definers. They are all far from accurately reflecting al-Shatibi's intent.

(3) Al-Hayat Newspaper, Issue: 12615, September 13, 1997, p. 21.
(4) Hamadi al-Abidi, Al-Shatibi and the Objectives of the Sharia, p. 119.


[Page 161]

It must be noted here that the research is not about the word "qasd" or its derivatives, where and when it has been mentioned, as it is an Arabic word commonly used in the speech of Arabs both in the past and present. Rather, the research is about the objectives (maqasid) in a specific sense, which is the meaning or meanings intended by the scholars of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence). The first to speak about the objectives was Imam al-Juwayni - and Allah knows best - and he, along with the scholars who came after him - except for al-Shatibi - refers to a single meaning of the objectives, which is the necessary, need-based, and enhancement objectives of the Sharia. These can be defined by them as the goals or interests for which the Sharia was established.
As for al-Shatibi, the matter encompasses this definition and goes beyond it, as the objectives for him are the objectives of the legislator and the objectives of the obligated person (mukallaf). The objectives of the obligated person can be defined as the goals or interests that the obligated person seeks to achieve, whether they are worldly or otherworldly.
The objectives of the legislator, however, are broader than the objectives of the Sharia, and the objectives of the Sharia are merely objectives that the legislator intended through legislation, but they are not all the objectives of the legislator. Allah, Exalted is He, created things and has an objective in doing so, according to al-Shatibi, and this objective is His purpose in creation, not in legislation, as creation is not legislation. He, Exalted is He, says: { He created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed } (1), and He says: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (2), so the test and worship here are objectives of the legislator and not objectives of the Sharia.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Mulk, 2.
(2) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.


[Page 162]

If these objectives are limited, according to others besides al-Shatibi, to the objectives of the Sharia, then the objectives of the legislator, according to al-Shatibi, are of four types, one of which is the objectives of the Sharia. He says: "The objectives that are considered fall into two categories: one pertains to the intention of the legislator, and the other pertains to the intention of the obligated person. The first is considered from the perspective of the legislator's intention in establishing the Sharia from the outset, from the perspective of his intention in establishing it for understanding, from the perspective of his intention in establishing it for obligation according to it, and from the perspective of his intention in bringing the obligated person under its ruling. These are four types" (1).
The definitions mentioned revolve around the necessary, need-based, and enhancement objectives of the Sharia, which are only the first type, that is, the intention of the legislator in establishing the Sharia from the outset. This is one aspect of the shortcomings in attempts to define the objectives, and there is another matter in these definitions that contradicts al-Shatibi's intent regarding this type of objectives.
That is, all these definitions suggest that the objectives are the interests and rulings, meaning they are the appropriate meanings that the mind accepts. This understanding, once again, if it is correct according to what is held by others besides al-Shatibi, does not hold true according to what is held by al-Shatibi. For example, Sheikh Ibn Ashur defined them as objectives for achieving beneficial objectives for people or for preserving their public interests. Dr. al-Raisuni's definition is that they are the goals for which the Sharia was established to achieve the benefit of the servants. Dr. al-Abidi defined them as the rulings. As for Professor Allal al-Fasi, he limited them to the goals of the rulings.
Whereas the objectives according to al-Shatibi are what is established as intended by the legislator regardless of whether it is an interest in the habitual sense, or whether it is something that minds accept, or whether it is appropriate or inappropriate.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/2.


[Page 163]

The objectives (maqasid), according to him, are not limited to the goals of the rulings, but rather the rulings themselves are among the objectives, as the rulings are intended by the legislator through the texts. All definitions revolve around the objectives of the rulings, which is the first type according to al-Shatibi, while one of the main focuses of al-Shatibi is the objectives of the legislator in understanding the commands and prohibitions in addition to the intention of worship and compliance. What these definitions mention are the goals of legislation, which are results or causes for it, and the Sharia or rulings are means to achieve the goals or reasons for them.
Therefore, these definitions, in addition to their shortcomings, do not accurately define what al-Shatibi intended, nor the first type of the objectives of the legislator according to him. For example, Dr. al-Raisouni's definition: "They are the goals that the Sharia was established to achieve for the benefit of the servants" is not valid due to the restriction to the benefit of the servants. If this restriction is removed, the definition becomes: "They are the goals that the Sharia was established to achieve," which is correct for al-Shatibi's intended meaning of the objectives of the Sharia, not the objectives of the legislator.
Additionally, what some have referred to as the division of objectives into specific, general, and partial does not exist in al-Shatibi's work, nor is there any evidence in his texts to support it. In fact, his texts refute this claim. This will become clear upon further elaboration, which is central to the idea of objectives according to al-Shatibi. The objectives according to al-Shatibi are universal principles, and they are general in all circumstances, at all times, and for all accountable individuals, while the particulars are not objectives because the objectives are universal principles; rather, the particulars may serve as branches that support the objectives or relate back to them.
Moreover, the objectives, according to al-Shatibi, are definitive principles and not presumed rulings. This is one of the most important pillars of the idea of objectives according to al-Shatibi, which none of the mentioned definitions or published research on the objectives according to al-Shatibi have noted.


[Page 164]

These matters will become clear through analysis, investigation, and documentation in the upcoming chapters of this message. However, I will point out here what is necessary in this regard, in order to complete this topic.
Al-Shatibi says: "The obligations of the Sharia (sharia) relate to preserving its objectives in creation, and these objectives fall into three categories: the first is that they are necessary, the second is that they are needed, and the third is that they are embellishing"(1). And any objective in any of these categories is not established except if it is general and definitive, that is, universal, and not partial or speculative. He says: "The principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) in religion are definitive, not speculative, and the evidence for that is that they relate to the universals of the Sharia, and whatever is thus is definitive"(2). And he says in the same context: "By universals here, I mean the necessary, the needed, and the embellishing."
His explanation of his intent regarding the universals, and his stipulation of the necessity of certainty for them, confirms the requirement of certainty regarding the objectives (maqasid) in his view. He dismisses the notion that the foundational principles for which certainty is required are the general evidences: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas). Rather, he asserts that these certain foundational principles are ultimately related to the universal objectives, which are necessities, needs, or enhancements.
Therefore, these definitions of the objectives (maqasid) are limited and incorrect. The more accurate statement - and Allah knows best - is to say: "The objectives are the goals, and the objectives of the Legislator (al-Shari) according to al-Shatibi are the goals indicated by actions, texts, and rulings as being desired to occur." Thus, actions and divine commands have specific goals, and the legal texts or the discourse surrounding them have goals of understanding and obligation. The rulings have goals that are adherence to them and not adhering to others, and some - but not all - of what results from this adherence.
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/3, 4.
(2) The same source, 1/10.


[Page 165]

These actions, texts, and rulings serve as means in relation to the objectives (maqasid) or as causes in relation to the outcomes or effects. It must be noted here that not every effect resulting from a cause is intended by the legislator (shari). The mere fact that something is a result does not indicate that it is an end or an objective. For example, the marriage of a woman who has been divorced three times leads to her being lawful for the first husband if the second husband divorces her, but this legality is not an end or objective of the legislator, according to al-Shatibi, since marriage with this intention is prohibited. The end is a result and an effect, but not every result or effect is an end or an objective. This is central to al-Shatibi's ideas, and it will become clear in its place, if Allah wills.


Chapter Three


The Criteria of the Objectives of the Sharia (Maqasid al-Sharia) According to al-Shatibi


It contains a brief definition of the subject of this chapter and three sections:


The first section: ... in the introductions.
The second section: ... in the documents.
The third section: ... on the results and the concept of public interest (maslaha)
And the harm (mafsada) according to al-Shatibi.


Chapter Three
The Criteria of the Objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) According to al-Shatibi


The topic of this chapter:
Al-Shatibi dedicated the second part of his book, al-Muwafaqat, to the topic of objectives (maqasid), and he divided the objectives into two categories: the objectives of the Legislator (al-Shari) and the objectives of the obligated (al-Mukallaf). As for the first part of al-Muwafaqat, he titled it the Book of Rulings (Kitab al-Ahkam), in which he discussed the legal rulings, the rulings of obligation and the rulings of status.
The topics that he highlighted in the Book of Rulings (al-Ahkam) were discussed by the imams of usul (usul al-fiqh) before him, and among them are some new aspects. The novelty lies in the perspective on these rulings, whether obligatory, recommended, permissible, disliked, or prohibited, as well as the cause, condition, impediment, firm ruling, concession, validity, corruption, and nullity. This perspective serves the idea of the objectives of the Legislator (maqasid al-sharia) and addresses any objections or refutations against them. Thus, he establishes principles for understanding these rulings and their meanings or objectives. In addition to this, before he begins the Book of Rulings, he presents thirteen introductions, which he considers necessary for understanding his book.


[Page 166]

In fact, there is no principle that he discusses in his book al-Muwafaqat except that it has a share of those introductions.

For the sake of these introductions and principles, this chapter was made, and I have divided it into three sections. The first is about the necessary introductions for the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), the second is about the references or principles that he highlighted in his discussion of rulings, and the third concerns the results and meanings that arise from these principles and introductions, which includes a discussion on the meaning of public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada) according to al-Shatibi. This is essential for understanding al-Shatibi's methodology.

The first section
On the introductions

The subject of this section:
Al-Shatibi divided his book (al-Muwafaqat) into five sections. He began by mentioning the introductions that he considers necessary for understanding his book. He said: "Thus, the book is confined to five sections, the first of which is about the scientific introductions needed to lay the groundwork for the intended goal" (1). He then laid out thirteen introductions. In order to highlight what is necessary from these introductions to clarify his methodology or idea, this section was created.
The principles of jurisprudence are definitive:
Al-Shatibi stated in his first introduction: "The principles of jurisprudence in religion are definitive, not speculative, and the evidence for this is that they pertain to the universals of the Sharia, and whatever is thus is definitive" (2). He then established his proof for this introduction, and among the things he said was: "If it were permissible for speculation to be attached to the universals of the Sharia, it would also be permissible for it to be attached to the foundation of the Sharia (3) since it is the first universal. This is not usually permissible, and by universals here, I mean the necessities, needs, and enhancements. Also, if speculation were permissible regarding the foundation of the Sharia, then doubt could be attached to it, which is not the case, and it would be permissible to change and alter it, which contradicts what Allah, Exalted is He, has guaranteed regarding its preservation" (4). He also said: "If it were permissible to make the speculative a foundation in the principles of jurisprudence, it would be permissible to make it a foundation in the principles of religion, and this is not the case by consensus" (5).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/7. From the preface of the book.
(2) The same source, 1/10 from the first introduction.
(3) What he means by the foundation of the Sharia: the Noble Qur'an. And Allah knows best.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/10.
(5) The same location.


[Page 167]

He said: "The principle, in any case, must be certain, because if it is merely probable, the possibility of disagreement arises, and such a thing cannot serve as a principle in religion based on induction" (1).
He concluded this introduction by saying: "Probabilities do not constitute principles, and this is sufficient to dismiss the uncertain from the principles outright; whatever is based on it that is not certain is derived from the certain" (2).
His statement in the text above: "And by the universals here, I mean the necessities, the needs, and the embellishments" indicates that he does not limit the condition of certainty in the principles of jurisprudence to the sources of legislation such as the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas).
He states in the second introduction: "The premises used in this science (3), and the evidence relied upon in it must be certain, because if they were merely probable, they would not yield certainty in the specific matters pertaining to it, and this is clear" (4). This is because the premises are the foundations or criteria through which, by linking them together or building upon them, one reaches the principles. Since the principles must be certain, their premises must also be certain.
Induction alone is the path to certainty:
__________
(1) The same source, 1/12.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/12.
(3) That is: the science of usul al-fiqh.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/12.


[Page 168]

One of the most important introductions to al-Shatibi's methodology is his third introduction, where he says: "The relied-upon intention (qasd al-awwal)(1) is the legal evidence, and the existence of certainty in it regarding the commonly accepted usage is nonexistent or extremely rare, I mean in the singular pieces of evidence. If they are from the reports of the singular (akhbar al-ahad), then their lack of providing certainty is evident. And if they are mutawatir (consecutively transmitted), then their provision of certainty is contingent upon all or most of its premises being speculative. What is contingent upon the speculative must necessarily be speculative. For it depends on the transmission of languages, the opinions of grammar, the absence of ambiguity, the absence of metaphorical usage, the legal or customary transmission, the implicitness and specification of the general, the restriction of the absolute, the absence of abrogation, the precedence and postponement, and the rational opposition. The provision of certainty while considering these matters is impossible."(2) Thus, al-Shatibi denies the existence of definitive evidence in singular texts, even if they are from the texts of the Noble Qur'an or the mutawatir hadiths. And if we understand his requirement for certainty in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), a question arises: how will this certainty be achieved according to him? He says: "The provision of certainty while considering these matters is impossible, and those who claim its existence have held that it is speculative in itself, but if it is accompanied by observable or transmitted indications, it may provide certainty, and all of this is rare or impossible. The considered evidence here is that which is extrapolated from a group of speculative evidences that converge on one meaning until it provides certainty in it, for the gathering has a strength that separation does not have, and for this reason, the mutawatir provides certainty, and this is a type of it. If a collection of evidence on the issue is obtained that provides knowledge(3), then it is the required evidence, and it is similar to the moral mutawatir, rather it is like the knowledge of the bravery of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and the existence of Hatim, derived from the abundance of transmitted incidents about them."(4)
__________
(1) The first intention: that is, when a command or prohibition comes from the legislator. Thus, the performance of the action is the first intention of the command, and refraining from it is the first intention of the prohibition.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/14.
(3) Knowledge is beneficial: that is, it is beneficial knowledge that is certain. Knowledge is opposed to conjecture.
(4) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat 1/14.


[Page 169]

Thus, al-Shatibi does not rely on anything other than induction (istiqra) to establish certainty in legal matters, and this is one of his innovations; he adopted it in his book and considered it the only way to achieve certainty, stating that it is a characteristic of his work. He said, referring to this third introduction of his: "It has also been explained how to seize certainty from the conjectural, and this is a characteristic of this book, and praise be to Allah" (1).
Induction is when there are numerous pieces of evidence indicating a specific meaning, or rulings that are presumed to have a particular wisdom or result. The indication of the evidence is conjectural, and the notion that the legislator intends a specific meaning or a particular wisdom is also conjectural. It is not valid to take conjectural matters as a basis in jurisprudence or legislation, nor to build upon them. When the evidence or rulings on a specific meaning become numerous and corroborative, this leads to beneficial induction that results in certainty, and these meanings become foundational principles. He said: "When the evidence becomes abundant for the observer, supporting one another, it becomes collectively beneficial for certainty; likewise, the matter is in the sources of evidence in this book, which are the sources of the principles" (2). He added: "However, the earlier scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) may have neglected to mention this meaning and to point it out, leading to its oversight by some later scholars" (3). He warned that through this oversight, we do not attain certainty regarding a legal ruling at all, and that the indication of consensus (ijma) on legal rulings is not established (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/194.
(2) The same source, 1/15.
(3) The same place.
(4) The same place.


[Page 170]

Al-Shatibi has provided many examples in his book that illustrate his inductive method in deriving conclusions; here is one of them: He says, "The ummah, indeed all religious communities, have agreed that the Sharia was established to preserve the five necessities: religion, life, lineage, wealth, and intellect. This knowledge is as certain to the ummah as the necessities themselves, and we do not have a specific proof for this, nor is there a particular origin that we can refer to. Rather, we have recognized its compatibility with the Sharia through a collection of evidence that cannot be confined to a single category. If it were to rely on something specific, it would normally require specification, and the people of consensus would have to refer to it, which is not the case. This is because each of these individually is speculative, and it is not necessary in the case of moral or other forms of tawatur (transmission) that a single report be the one that provides knowledge over all other reports; likewise, it is not necessary here, as all the evidence equally contributes to the inference of speculation if considered in isolation."(1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/15.


[Page 171]

The establishment of the preservation of religion, for example, as a necessary principle, requires—according to him—the definitive proof of the five pillars such as prayer and almsgiving, among others, through induction. He says: "From this path, the obligation of the five pillars such as prayer and almsgiving has been definitively established. Otherwise, if someone were to argue for the obligation of prayer based on His saying, { Establish the prayer } (1) or something similar, there would be several points of contention in the argument itself. However, it is supported by external evidence and the rulings that follow, which have made the obligation of prayer a necessity in religion, and only a skeptic regarding the fundamentals of religion would doubt it" (2). He said: "So when we look at prayer, it comes with { Establish the prayer }. In various aspects, there is praise for those who establish it and condemnation for those who abandon it, and there is compulsion for the obligated to perform it, whether standing, sitting, or lying on their sides, and fighting against those who abandon it or resist abandoning it, among other things of this nature. Likewise, the soul is prohibited from being killed, and killing it makes one liable for retribution, and it is threatened as one of the major sins associated with polytheism, just as prayer is associated with faith. The necessity to provide for the needy is established, as is the obligation of almsgiving and supporting those who cannot rectify themselves, and judges and rulers have been appointed for this purpose, and armies have been organized to fight against those who attempt to kill the soul. The one who fears death is obligated to sustain himself by any lawful means, even if it involves consuming carrion, blood, or pork, among other things that relate to this meaning. Thus, we have certainty regarding the obligation of prayer and the prohibition of killing, and similarly for all other evidence in the rules of Sharia. This is how the principles differ from the branches, as the branches are based on individual pieces of evidence and specific sources, remaining reliant on conjecture, unlike the principles, which are derived from the comprehensive induction of the implications of the evidence, not from individual pieces in particular" (3).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 43.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 1/14.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/15 - 16.


[Page 172]

These texts above clarify his intention regarding induction, and that induction is the only way to reach certainty in religious matters, and that induction is not for the evidences which are the texts, but rather for their meanings, and their meanings are their linguistic implications, rulings, and consequences. All of these are speculative if one relies on isolated texts; thus, they should not be relied upon in legislation unless they are transmitted through continuous narration (tawatur). The tawatur intended here is the tawatur of meanings. Therefore, we see him say: "It is similar to the meaningful tawatur" (1), and look at his statement in the previous text: "Unlike the principles, which are derived from the induction of the implications of the evidences in general." He did not say: "from the induction of the evidences." Rather, he said: "from the induction of their implications," and their implications are their implications or meanings. Then his statement: "in general," does not limit the meanings to linguistic implications but also includes their rulings, objectives, or causes.
__________
(1) See: p. 139 of this research.


[Page 173]

And based on this introduction, one of the most important principles according to al-Shatibi is established, a principle that serves as the spirit of his entire methodology. He says: "And based on this introduction, there is another meaning, which is: every legal principle that does not have a specific text supporting it and is suitable for the actions of the Sharia (1), and whose meaning is derived from its evidence is valid and can be relied upon, and it is referred to if that principle has become established through its collective evidence, because the evidence does not necessarily have to indicate certainty in the ruling by itself without the addition of others to it, as previously mentioned, because that is somewhat impossible. This falls under the category of the general reasoning (istidlal al-mursal) that was adopted by Malik and al-Shafi'i (2).
__________
(1) The meaning of suitability for the actions of the Sharia is clarified in the first chapter, which is that more than one ruling must support the appropriate description. As noted in al-Shatibi's texts, he does not merely use the term "more," but rather stipulates that the abundance must result in a beneficial induction leading to certainty, and it is not necessarily the case—according to him—that the suitable is appropriate. This will become clear in its place, if Allah wills.
(2) In the first chapter, the conflicting reports about Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) regarding the mursal principle or reasoning were mentioned, as well as the conflicting opinions of the Shafi'i scholars regarding the mursal or reasoning, and their differences concerning what is attributed to Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him). We then clarified the differing meanings of mursal among the scholars and the differing positions based on that. The text above attributes to the two Imams (may Allah have mercy on them) the saying of general reasoning, but it restricts that to what is established with certainty and what is consistent with his methodology. This suggests that this inductive methodology in establishing certainty and relying on its results is practiced among the scholars, and perhaps this is part of what he meant by saying: "However, the earlier scholars of usul may have neglected to mention this meaning and to point it out, leading to its oversight by some later scholars." 1/15. Likewise, what was stated in the preface of his book in response to the denial of those who may deny what is presented in his methodology: "Indeed, by the grace of Allah, this is a matter confirmed by the verses and reports, strongly established by the righteous predecessors, delineated by the scholars, and its foundations built by the discerning. When the path is clear, denial is not permissible, and acceptance of what it contains is obligatory." Preface of the book. p. 9.


[Page 174]

For although it does not witness a specific origin for the branch, it has witnessed a general origin, and the general origin, if it is definitive, may equal the specific origin or exceed it depending on the strength or weakness of the specific origin... Likewise, the principle of istihsan (preference)(1) according to the opinion of Malik is based on this principle"(2). We observe in this text that the general principle (ma'nawi) is stronger than the text in its indication, because the general principle is definitive in its meaning, whereas the definitiveness of the text in its meaning is difficult or rare if it exists.
The primary and secondary objectives:
Al-Shatibi says in his seventh introduction: "Every religious knowledge is sought by the legislator only as a means to worship Allah, Exalted is He, and not for any other reason. If another consideration appears in it, it is secondary and by way of following, not by way of the primary intention"(3). This is because when a command or prohibition comes from the legislator, the legislator's intention is to establish what is commanded and to avoid what is prohibited, and this is the primary intention. In other words, the primary intention is obedience without regard to the outcomes or benefits, and thus religious knowledge is what aids in knowing Allah's commands and prohibitions, in order to understand how to obey and how to worship, and this is the meaning of his statement: "a means to worship."
__________
(1) It is attributed to Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "Istihsan is nine-tenths of knowledge." Al-Shatibi means by istihsan the preference of a definitive meaning or principle over analogy, or the specification of analogy by a general meaning. We will dedicate a study to it, if Allah wills.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/16.
(3) The same source, 1/30.


[Page 175]

If it becomes evident that there is a worldly benefit for the obligated person (mukallaf) in either performing or refraining from that action, and if this benefit has been established as a definitive, universal meaning that the legislator intended by enacting that ruling, then it becomes a definitive principle. It is akin to a text, and achieving it with the intention of obedience is akin to the primary intention. If that anticipated benefit—whether definitively or presumably—has not been definitively established as an objective of the legislator in enacting that ruling, it is considered the secondary objective or the dependent objective. That is, it is dependent on the primary objective. According to what al-Shatibi states in his introductions, this second meaning is speculative, thus it is not considered a principle, nor does it hold significance in legislation. However, it cannot be entirely dismissed, as it may be subject to an inductive reasoning that renders it definitive. Therefore, it is examined: if it strengthens adherence to the primary intention, it is considered; if it weakens or opposes the primary intention, it is rejected. The primary intention is worship, and the secondary intention is considered if it serves as a means to the primary intention. Hence, it is termed dependent or additional. For example, the primary intention of seeking knowledge and learning is action. He said: "Any knowledge that does not lead to action has no basis in the Sharia that indicates its commendation" (1). He said: "The Sharia has come for the purpose of worship, which is the objective of the mission of the Prophets (peace be upon them)" (2). He said: "Indeed, the proofs of monotheism have come in this manner in the course of the Qur'an: { except as a reminder } (3), except for this, which is clear in that worshiping Allah is the objective of knowledge, and the verses on this meaning are countless" (4). He said: "The essence of knowledge is action; otherwise, knowledge is a loan and of no benefit" (5). He then said: "No one denies the virtue of knowledge in general except an ignorant person, but it has a primary intention and a secondary intention. The primary intention is what has been mentioned earlier, while the secondary intention is what the majority mention regarding its possessor being noble, even if he is not originally so. And the ignorant person is base, even if he is originally noble...
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/30.
(2) The same source, 1/31.
(3) From verse 3 of Surah Taha.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/31.
(5) The same location.


[Page 176]

"And knowledge is beauty, wealth, and a rank that is unmatched by any other rank" (1).
Then he said: "Knowledge may be sought for the sake of enjoyment and the pleasure of conversing about it, especially the sciences that allow for intellectual engagement and where there is ample room for contemplation of its aspects, and where the path to deducing the known from the unknown is broad. However, each of these pursuits is either a servant of the original intention or not. If it serves that intention, then the pursuit of it from the outset is correct... If it does not serve that intention, then the pursuit of it from the outset is incorrect, such as seeking knowledge for ostentation, to argue with the foolish, to boast among the scholars, to win the hearts of people, or to gain from their worldly affairs" (2). He also said: "The legal objectives (maqasid) are of two types: original objectives and subsidiary objectives. As for the original objectives, they have no share for the obligated person" (3). He said: "As for the subsidiary objectives, they take into account the share of the obligated person, and from them, he obtains what is in accordance with his natural inclination towards fulfilling desires, enjoying permissible things, and fulfilling needs" (4).
Al-Shatibi refers to the subsidiary objectives as those that the rulings lead to, which the servant is inclined towards by nature and instinct. The consideration of these objectives, whether accepted or rejected, depends on whether they are a means to the primary objective or not. If they are a means to the primary objective or serve it, then they are a subsidiary legal objective; if they are not, then they are not an objective for the legislator, although they may be an objective for the obligated person. If they oppose the primary objective, then they are forbidden.
Characteristics of the universals:
__________
(1) The same source, 1/35.
(2) The same source, 1/36.
(3) The same source, 2/120.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/124.


[Page 177]

Al-Shatibi says in his ninth introduction that the religious sciences (ulum al-sharia) correspond to the rational sciences (ulum al-aqliya) in terms of the possibility of certainty regarding them or deriving certainty from them. Just as the legal truths are situational, meaning they are established by the legislator, the truths of existence and things are also situational, established by the Creator. He states: "Situational truths may correspond to rational truths in providing certain knowledge. The knowledge of the Sharia is among them, as knowledge of it is derived from the general induction that organizes its disparate individuals until they become in the mind a collection of general, consistent, established universals that are neither transient nor changeable nor subject to judgment. These are the characteristics of rational universals. Furthermore, rational universals are derived from existence, which is a situational matter, not a rational one, thus they are equal to the legal universals in this regard, and the distinction between them is removed" (1). Accordingly, the legal universals have three characteristics: the first is generality and consistency,... the second is permanence without decay,... and the third is that knowledge is a judge, not something judged upon (2).
The meaning of the first characteristic is that legal rulings apply to the actions of the obligated individuals absolutely; there is no action that is not judged by some legal universal, and if an action is assumed not to be judged by any universal, it is judged by some other universal (3).
__________
(1) The same source, p. 44.
(2) The same source, pp. 44 - 45.
(3) See: the ninth introduction. 1/43 - 44.


[Page 178]

The meaning of the second characteristic is that the general principles (kulliyat) are neither abrogated nor specified nor restricted, nor do they change according to time or place. Rather, what we derive from al-Shatibi's comparison of the legal general principles with the rational general principles is that the legal general principles are not merely definitive truths, but rather absolute definitive truths. They are not restricted to a specific time over another time, nor to a specific place over another place, nor to a specific accountable person (mukallaf) over another accountable person. He says: "You will not find in them, after their perfection, any abrogation, nor specification of their generality, nor restriction of their absoluteness, nor the lifting of a ruling from their rulings, neither according to the generality of the accountable nor according to the specificity of some of them, nor according to a time over another time, nor a state over another state. Rather, whatever establishes a cause is a cause forever and does not cease, and whatever is a condition is forever a condition, and whatever is obligatory is always obligatory or recommended is recommended, and thus all rulings have no cessation or alteration. Even if the obligation were to continue indefinitely, its rulings would remain the same" (1). The meaning of the third characteristic is that there is nothing in the religious sciences that is contradicted by truths, whether they are religious or rational, or that opposes them to the extent that one is compelled to interpret it in a way that the text cannot bear, because it then becomes a ruled matter rather than a ruling (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/45.
(2) Accordingly, the general principles, whether rational or religious, are absolute truths, and the religious truths are also rational truths, because they are based on the definitive rational proof of the prophethood of our master Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), and on the certainty of the truth of his message and report. The certainty that the Qur'an is from Allah is fundamentally a rational path. Accordingly, the religious reports and everything that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) brought, which does not allow for rational inquiry, is based on reason in that the truth of the report is rationally certain.


[Page 179]

Al-Shatibi explains that these universals (kulliyat) are the foundation of the sciences of Sharia and are the sources of rulings. The basis of legislation is what is universal or related to the universal; thus, whatever is like this is central to knowledge, and what is not like this has no consideration according to his methodology. He says: "Some knowledge is central to knowledge, and some is peripheral to knowledge but not central, and some is neither central nor peripheral; these are three categories. The first category is the foundation and the basis upon which the pursuit revolves, and to which the objectives of the firmly rooted (rasikhun) ultimately lead, and that is what is definitive or related to a definitive origin" (1). He said: "The second category, which is counted among the peripheral knowledge and not among the central: is what is not definitive nor related to a definitive origin, but rather to something speculative, or it is related to a definitive origin, yet it lacks some of those characteristics, or more than one characteristic, thus it is speculative (mukhayyal) (2), and it is something that provokes the intellect at first glance and initial consideration without compromising its origin or the meaning of another" (3). This category is dismissed by al-Shatibi (4).
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat. 1/43. We will clarify shortly what al-Shatibi means by referring to a definitive origin.
(2) That is: it instills in the heart an illusion of correctness, so it is something that minds receive with acceptance or that souls find pleasing. In this category fall - according to al-Shatibi - the meanings or descriptions that come in the paths of analogy (masalih) and resemblance (shabah), or through the method of inference as long as they are not definitive.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 1/45.
(4) Al-Shatibi's stance on the meanings that fall into this category resembles the stance of the Hanafi scholars regarding the path of analogy, as it is speculative and does not return to a definitive origin, and the speculation here is not of the type that is applicable in legal matters but rather is purely rational speculation. Therefore, this category is not considered, and meanings may have evidence that completes their three characteristics, making them considered, and they may have what qualifies them from the third category due to their harm to the Sharia. See: 1/46 - 50.


[Page 180]

And the third category is that which is neither from the fundamentals (usul) nor from the ancillary matters (milah), which does not return to a definitive (qat'i) or speculative (dhanni) origin. Rather, its nature is to revert to its origin or to another by way of nullification of what is established as being from the recognized sciences and the principles referred to in actions and beliefs, or what is inclined towards nullifying the truth and establishing falsehood. This is not knowledge because it reverts to its origin through nullification; it is neither stable nor authoritative nor consistent, nor is it from the ancillary matters, because the ancillary matters are those that are appreciated by minds and are pleasing to souls(1). And he said about this category: "If it sways a people and they find it pleasing and seek it, it is due to a passing resemblance and confusion between it and what preceded it, so the foolish may consider it to be based on an origin, and they may lean towards it for that reason. The reality of its origin is delusion and imagination, with no reality to it, along with the ulterior motives and desires that accompany it"(2).
These texts about al-Shatibi indicate or establish his position on the approach of analogy (qiyas) and suitability (munasaba), or how to consider public interest (maslaha), and the following research clarifies his stance on how to consider interests or wisdoms in legislation.
The meaning of returning to a definitive origin:
Al-Shatibi said that the foundation and what is relied upon, which the demand revolves around, is what is definitive or refers back to a definitive origin(3). In his first introduction, he stated: "By the universals here, I mean the necessities, the needs, and the enhancements"(4). In his ninth introduction, he said: "The necessities, the needs, and the enhancements, along with what complements them and completes their aspects, are the foundations of the Sharia, and definitive proof has been established for their consideration, with all branches relying upon them"(5).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/51.
(2) The same place.
(3) See the previous page.
(4) See p. 137 of this research.
(5) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/44.


[Page 181]

The requirement for certainty in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) is well-known and established among jurists. Al-Shatibi referred to this in his first introduction. What the jurists mean by the principles that must be certain are the definitive evidences or the general sources of legislation, which are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas). As for other topics in the principles, such as the paths of reasoning and their conditions, and discussions of generality and specificity, absolute and restricted, and the conditions of narration and narrators, these do not require certainty, and it suffices to rely on preponderance of evidence.
Al-Juwayni said: "If it is said: What is jurisprudence (fiqh)? We say: It is, in the terminology of the scholars of Sharia, the knowledge of the rulings of obligations. If it is said: Most of what is contained in the issues of Sharia is based on conjecture. We say: Conjectures are not jurisprudence; rather, jurisprudence is the knowledge (1) of the obligation to act when conjectures arise. Therefore, the scholars have stated: The reports of the singular (akhbar al-ahad) and the analogies of jurisprudence do not necessitate action by themselves; rather, action must be based on what necessitates knowledge of the obligation to act, which are the definitive evidences regarding the obligation to act when reporting singular reports and applying analogies. If it is said: What are the principles of jurisprudence? We say: They are its evidences, and the evidences of jurisprudence are the textual evidences from the Qur'an, the textual evidences from the mutawatir Sunnah, and consensus, all of which are based on the saying of Allah, Exalted is He. From this perspective, the principles of jurisprudence derive from discourse. If it is said: The details of singular reports and analogies can only be found in the principles and are not definitive. We say: The role of the jurist is to clarify the definitive in acting upon them, but it is necessary to mention them so that the meaning is clarified and the evidence is connected to it." (2)
__________
(1) That is, the certain knowledge of the obligation to act based on the conjectural reports regarding their authenticity or implications, or both.
(2) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan fi Usul al-Fiqh. 1/78 - 79. Paragraphs: 4 - 5 - 6.


[Page 182]

Imam Jamal al-Din Abdul Rahim al-Asnawi said: "As for the reports of the single narrators (ahad), they are invalid because the narration of a single narrator, if it provides any benefit, only provides conjecture. The legislator has only permitted conjecture in practical matters, which are the branches, and not in scientific matters such as the principles of the faith and likewise the principles of jurisprudence, as conveyed by al-Anbari, the commentator on al-Burhan, from all the scholars" (1).
Al-Baydawi said: "The principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) are the knowledge of the evidence of jurisprudence in general, how to benefit from them, and the state of the beneficiary" (2).
Al-Asnawi, in his commentary on the above text, said: "What is meant by knowing the evidence is to know that the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas) are evidence that can be relied upon... Know that the expression 'evidence' excludes many principles of jurisprudence such as generalities, reports of single narrators, analogy, presumption of continuity (istishab), and others. For the jurists, even if they accept working with them, they are not considered evidence for jurisprudence but rather indications of it, for the term 'evidence' among them is only applied to what is certain" (3).
__________
(1) Jamal al-Din Abdul Rahim al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul fi Sharh Minhaj al-Usul, 2/270. Thus, conjecture is acted upon if it is based on a firmly established principle that it is one of the sources of legislation. The hadith attributed to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is obligatory to act upon even if it is not of certain authenticity, because it is firmly established that the Sunnah is one of the sources of legislation, meaning it is revelation.
(2) Al-Qadi Nasir al-Din ibn Umar al-Baydawi, Minhaj al-Wusul ila Ilm al-Usul, 1/5. Along with Nihayat al-Sul of al-Asnawi, Dar al-Ilm - Beirut.
(3) Al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul fi Sharh Minhaj al-Usul, 1/9 - 11.


[Page 183]

The intention of the usuliyyin (principlists), before al-Shatibi, regarding the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that must be definitive is the Qur'an and the Sunnah, along with what they indicate from general sources, which are consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas). As for al-Shatibi, he does not limit the requirement of definitiveness to these sources; rather, the universals (kulliyat) for him are necessities (darurat), needs (hajiyat), and enhancements (tahsinat), as well as what complements them. If we understand that the necessities for him are the preservation of religion, intellect, life, lineage, and wealth, this indicates that these objectives must be definitive to be considered; one cannot suffice with mere conjecture or with them being based on definitive sources like the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Likewise, if we understand that the permissibility of marriage, the removal of harm, and the non-obligation of burdensome duties are among the needs for him, this means they must be established definitively to be considered. The same applies to the category of enhancements and complements. Once these meanings are established, they become principles, that is, sources for legislation in his view, and are used as evidence just as the legal texts are used.
If these meanings are not established definitively through induction, they must either return to a definitive origin or not. If they return to a definitive origin, there is no issue in employing them in legislation. If they do not return, there is a detailed discussion that will be mentioned in its place, if Allah wills. He said: "Every legal evidence is either definitive or conjectural. If it is definitive, there is no issue in considering it... If it is conjectural, it either returns to a definitive origin or does not; if it returns to a definitive origin, it is also considered, and if it does not return, one must be cautious regarding it, and it is not correct to simply accept it." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/7.


[Page 184]

As for the meaning of returning to a definitive origin, an example of this is the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm" (1). This is a report of singular transmission (khabar ahad) that is not definitive, and therefore, according to the methodology of al-Shatibi, it is a particularity and not a definitive universal origin. It is not correct to apply it until it is established that it returns to a definitive origin, nor can it be said here that it is from the Sunnah, which is a definitive source or universal origin, as this is not the meaning of returning to a definitive origin according to al-Shatibi. Rather, the meaning is that the meaning of the hadith is in accordance with a definitive legal meaning, that is, a universal meaning that has been established as universal through the induction of many evidences (particularities) that converge on this meaning. Al-Shatibi states: "His saying, peace be upon him: 'There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm' falls under a definitive origin in this meaning, for harm and reciprocating harm are widely prohibited in the Sharia in particular incidents and universal principles, such as His saying, Exalted is He: { And do not hold them to hurt them, so that you may commit an injustice } (2), { And do not harm them, so that you may make it difficult for them } (3), { A mother should not be harmed regarding her child } (4), and the like. This includes the prohibition of transgressing against lives, properties, and honor, as well as against usurpation and injustice, and everything that is in the meaning of causing harm or reciprocating harm. It includes harm to the self, intellect, lineage, or property, and it is a meaning that is extremely general in the Sharia, with no dispute or doubt about it" (5).
The abundance of texts and evidences used for inference is merely to complete the induction and thus reach certainty. In this way, the meaning of lifting harm becomes a universal origin, and the meaning contained in the hadith aligns with the universal origin, which is a particularity, and thus it can be said that it returns to a universal origin, making it valid.
__________
(1) Its transmission has been previously mentioned.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 231.
(3) Surah At-Talaq, 6.
(4) Surah Al-Baqarah, 233.
(5) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 3/8.


[Page 185]

Thus, the intended meaning of al-Shatibi with the term "foundations" is confirmed, along with his method of establishing them, which is induction, and the meaning of returning to a definitive origin, which is part of his new contributions that provide us with some controls or principles of his methodology. He - may Allah have mercy on him - pointed out this difference between him and the earlier usuliyyin (foundational scholars).
