He said: "Know that the purpose of returning to the definitive origin is not to establish proof of the validity of acting upon it, like the proof that acting upon the report of a single narrator or by analogy is obligatory, for example. Rather, what is intended is something more specific than that, as previously mentioned in the hadith 'There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm' and the issues mentioned alongside it, which is a meaning contrary to that intended by the usuliyyin, and Allah knows best" (1).
The particular and the branch and the difference between them:
It has been clarified previously that the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) are general principles derived from particulars. These particulars are the indications and meanings of the legal texts. And these particulars are speculative and are not considered unless they return to the general principles. The meanings of the legal texts are their linguistic indications, and the descriptions that are conceivable or appropriate for the rulings, and the outcomes and results and causes of the rulings. Although these are speculative, they are indicated by the texts, or they do not indicate them but are merely presumed to be intended by the legislator; these are particulars.
So, if one of these meanings - which is particular - returns to a general origin, it is then called a branch. Accordingly, every branch is particular, but not every particular is a branch. The lack of the particular returning to the general is a distinction that differentiates the particular from the branch.
This difference is evident from the analytical tracing of al-Shatibi's texts where he uses these two terms, and the following is documentation of what we have mentioned:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/12.


[Page 186]

Al-Shatibi said in his first introduction: "The preservation guaranteed in His saying, Exalted is He: { Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it } (1) refers to the preservation of its general principles that are explicitly stated, which is also what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: { This day I have perfected for you your religion } (2). It does not refer to specific issues, for if that were the case, no specific aspect of the Sharia would be neglected in preservation, and this is not the case, as we can assert the permissibility, supported by occurrence, due to the variation of conjectures and the possibility of errors in specific texts, and the occurrence of mistakes in them is certain. Mistakes have been found in the reports of the singular narrators and in the meanings of the verses, which indicates that what is meant by the preserved Reminder is that which is general" (3).
He said in his ninth introduction: "What is definitive or related to a definitive origin, and the blessed Sharia of Muhammad was revealed in this manner, and therefore it is preserved in its roots and branches, as He, Exalted is He, said: { Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it }, because it pertains to the preservation of the objectives (maqasid) that ensure the well-being of both abodes, which are the necessities, needs, and enhancements, along with what completes and supplements them, and these are the roots of the Sharia. Definitive evidence has been established regarding their consideration, and all branches are based upon them, so there is no doubt that they constitute knowledge, a foundation, firmly established, and stable in its pillars" (4).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Hijr, 9.
(2) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 3.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/13.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/43 - 44.


[Page 187]

The first text above states that particulars do not fall within the meaning of preservation intended by the noble verse, while the second text states that the branches are preserved based on the verse itself. By understanding that particulars are the basis for universals, and the meaning of returning to the certain (qat'i), the aforementioned distinction is confirmed(1).

Thus, it becomes clear that al-Shatibi does not adopt the approach of analogy (qiyas) and suitability (munasaba) in the manner that the scholars of the Shafi'i school assert; he also does not dismiss it as the scholars of the Hanafi school have done. Rather, he stipulates that the meaning or description proposed for reasoning must be related to the certain (qat'i), and without that, he does not accept it. He also does not reject it, as there may be particulars that combine with it to form a certain meaning. This is something that must be noted to understand al-Shatibi's methodology.

Section Two
On the Sources
Introduction:
__________
(1) Based on this, it can be said that what the scholars of the book al-Muwafaqat, such as Sheikh Muhammad al-Khidr Hussein from Tunisia, Dr. Abdullah Daraz, and Abu Ubaida Mashhoor bin Hassan al-Salman, have posited in their comments on the introductions of the book, especially the first, second, third, and ninth, is far from the true intent of al-Shatibi regarding these introductions. This also applies to other commentators mentioned by the latter. See: al-Muwafaqat, 1/17 - 18, and thereafter. Volume One, edited by Abu Ubaida Mashhoor bin Hassan al-Salman, 1st edition, 1421 AH. Dar Ibn Afan, Arab Republic of Egypt. It is in 6 volumes.


[Page 188]

They attributed contradiction to al-Shatibi when he said that particulars are not included in preservation while branches are preserved. This is another error on their part that indicates their failure to distinguish between the particular (juz'i) and the branch (far') in al-Shatibi's methodology. See: al-Muwafaqat, 1/12 and 1/44 from the edition of Sheikh al-Tunisi. And 1/32 from the edition of Dr. Daraz. And 1/22 and 1/107 from the edition of Abu Ubaida.
Al-Shatibi dedicated the second section of his book al-Muwafaqat to discussing legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyya), which either pertain to the address of obligation (khitab al-taklif) or the address of status (khitab al-wad'). The address of obligation has five types: obligatory (wajib or fard), recommended (mandub), permissible (mubah), disliked (makruh), and forbidden (haram). The address of status has five types: cause (sabab), condition (shart), impediment (mani'), validity and invalidity (sihha wa fasad), and concession and obligation (rukhsah wa azimah).
Al-Shatibi discussed these types in his book on rulings (1), elaborating particularly on the address of obligation in relation to the permissible (mubah), and regarding the address of status in relation to the cause and the concession and obligation.
This is due to the impact these rulings have on his concept of objectives (maqasid). If we understand that his idea is based on the premise that all legal rulings return to general principles of public interest (maslaha), then the permissible, which is a legal ruling of obligation, meaning what the legislator has allowed between action and inaction, contradicts this principle and undermines his idea, which he views as a definitive general principle. For permission to act means that there is a public interest intended by the legislator, and permission to refrain means that the legislator does not intend the existence of that public interest, and this is a contradiction that undermines the idea that all rulings have objectives or maqasid.
Therefore, al-Shatibi directs attention to the permissible in a different way. He states that the choice in the permissible is in terms of its being particular, and this does not undermine the idea because the public interests apply to the general principles and not to particulars, and in general principles, there is no choice. Thus, the permissible is permissible in the particular but is required to be acted upon or required to be refrained from in the general. The same applies to concession and obligation, as the ruling on taking the concession or refraining from it is permissibility; if both taking the concession and adhering to the obligation are permissible, then where is the public interest? Is it in taking the concession or in adhering to the obligation? This is why al-Shatibi's discussion on the permissible and the concession is extensive, in order to maintain the integrity of his idea.
__________
(1) al-Muwafaqat, 1/68 and onwards.


[Page 189]

As for the study of the cause, it is an important foundation for his idea, as it is based on the notion that the legal rulings have objectives, and that the Sharia was established to achieve these objectives. These objectives are causes or results, and their causes are the legal rulings. Thus, the legal ruling is a cause for an effect, and the required action has an end result that arises from it. Just as the legislator intended to bring about the required action, he also intended for the end result to occur. The prohibited action has an end or result that the legislator intended to prevent from occurring, and just as the legislator intended to prevent the action, he also intended to prevent its result. Therefore, the study of causes and effects is the foundation upon which the idea of objectives (maqasid) rests according to al-Shatibi.
The permissible (mubah):
A reader may be surprised by al-Shatibi's lengthy and detailed discussion of the permissible, and the differences in his reports compared to other usul scholars, to the extent that his discussion of the legal obligations seems to focus solely on the permissible, while his discussion of other rulings—namely, the obligatory, recommended, disliked, and forbidden—is limited to a few sentences or paragraphs.
However, studying these discussions, after understanding his idea of objectives, sheds light on this approach, as al-Shatibi considers the foundational principles he has established and the relationship between these principles as the basis for his opinions and reports regarding the permissible. This necessitates presenting some of the foundational principles or rules of his idea of objectives.
Al-Shatibi concludes—through induction—that the Sharia was revealed for the interests of the servants, and these interests are the objectives of legislation, which can be categorized into three sections: necessary, needful, and embellishing, with each of these sections having its complements.


[Page 190]

Every objective must be absolute and definitive, and it should serve and affirm the necessary objectives, which are: the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and wealth. The embellishments serve the necessities, and both serve the essentials.
The legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyya) must refer to one of the enhancing (tahsiniyya), need-based (hajiyya), or necessary (daruriyya) principles, meaning that the objective of each ruling must support or serve a benefit (maslaha) that has been established through comprehensive and definitive induction in one of the three categories. If the ruling's return to any principle does not become apparent, then it is either to be rejected or suspended.
The meaning of the statement that the Sharia (law) came for the interests of the servants is that there is no ruling that does not bring benefit to the servants, even if it does not result in harm. The notion of the existence of such a ruling implies that it is futile, and there is no futility in the Sharia.
The action required by Islamic law, whether obligatory or recommended, serves a universal principle or more than one of the principles that are the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia).
The action that is prohibited by Islamic law, whether it is forbidden (haram) or disliked (makruh), undermines or serves to undermine a fundamental original principle or more than one of the principles that are the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) or interests (masalih).
With these principles or rules regarding the concept of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), al-Shatibi's discussion of what is permissible (mubah) is directed.
If it is said that what is permissible (mubah) is what the legislator has left to choice between action and inaction, or it is what neither the doer is blamed nor praised for, nor is the one who refrains from it blamed or praised, or it is what is equal in both action and inaction according to the legislator, or what the textual evidence indicates regarding the legislator's address to choose between action and inaction, or something similar to these statements, then this is problematic according to those principles. This is because action has a purpose, and refraining from it misses that purpose. If the intended purpose is achieved by refraining from the action, then performing it would miss that purpose. And if the rulings were legislated only for the benefit of the servants, then it is necessary to prefer one side over the other, or to claim the existence of a fourth level beyond the enhancements that is characterized by not serving any of the three levels nor undermining any of them. However, this claim contradicts al-Shatibi's idea that no legal ruling is devoid of an objective, whether it is to bring about a benefit or to avert harm. So how does al-Shatibi resolve this problem?


[Page 191]

The depiction of the particular and the universal in rulings:
Al-Shatibi addresses this issue by stating that rulings have two perspectives, one as they are particular and the other as they are universal.
He responds to those who say that the permissible (mubah) is to be avoided because one who engages in what is permissible may become distracted from what is required to be done, and he counters those who say that it is required to be done because one who engages in what is permissible has abandoned what is prohibited (haram), saying: "The permissible in the view of the Lawgiver is that which one is free to choose between doing and not doing, without praise or blame for either action or inaction" (1). He states: "The permissible, in its nature as permissible, is neither required to be done nor required to be avoided" (2). Here, that is, in its nature as permissible, it is viewed as a particular; however, if it is viewed as something required to be done or required to be avoided, that is from a perspective in which it serves or undermines the universal.
The permissible is viewed in terms of its particularity and its universality; however, in terms of its universality, there is nothing that one is free to choose because it would be mere play. As for its particularity, that is, a specific legal ruling for a specific action, if one is free to choose it, this means it is stripped of wisdom or objective, and this does not negate the idea of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in al-Shatibi's view because he applies them to universals rather than particulars. He says: "The recognized interests are the universals, not the particulars" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/68.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, 1/91.


[Page 192]

As for looking at the permissible (mubah) from the perspective of the whole, it makes the permissible permissible in part and required in total; it may be recommended in total or obligatory in total, or permissible in part and prohibited in total; it may be disliked in total or forbidden in total. He says: "The permissibility according to the partial and the total is subject to the remaining rulings. The permissible is permissible in part and required in total in the sense of recommendation or obligation, and permissible in part and prohibited in total in the sense of dislike or prohibition. These are four categories: The first: like enjoying the good things of food, drink, transportation, and clothing... If some times are left out while being able to do so, it would be permissible just as if it were done. If it were completely abandoned, it would be contrary to what the Sharia has recommended... And likewise, if all people abandoned that, it would be disliked. The second: like eating and drinking, having relations with wives, buying and selling, and the obligation of permissible earnings... All these things are permissible in part, meaning if one chooses any of these things over others, that is permissible. And if a man leaves them at certain times or circumstances, or if some people leave them, that does not detract from it; if we assume that all people left that, it would be abandoning what is necessary and commanded. Thus, entering into it would be obligatory in total. The third: like strolling in gardens, listening to the cooing of doves, permissible singing, and permissible play with doves or others; such things are permissible in part, so if done one day or in a certain situation, there is no harm in it. If done constantly, it would be disliked, and its doer would be attributed to a lack of intellect and to going against the virtues of customs and to extravagance in doing that permissible act. The fourth: like the permissible things that undermine justice when done continuously, even if they are permissible." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/85. I must point out here that I am presenting the ideas and inquiries of al-Shatibi to fill any gaps or to mend any flaws in his thought, and I am not in the position of discussing them... Otherwise, the question remains: Is not the permissible in part a legal ruling, in which one has a choice? Does this not undermine the complete validity of his idea, leaving the issue unresolved?


[Page 193]

Thus, the characteristic of universality has been attributed to the permissible (mubah) in order to preserve the foundation of the idea of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), so that interests are intended in the permissible even if both sides are equal.
After illustrating the universality and particularity in the permissible, al-Shatibi also establishes that what is recommended in the particular is obligatory in the universal, and what is disliked in the particular is prohibited in the universal, and what is obligatory in the particular is obligatory in the universal. The same applies to prohibitions. He then states: "If the illustration of universality and particularity in the five rulings is established, then evidence may be sought for its validity, and the matter is clear upon reflection on what has preceded in the course of the report; rather, it is, in the consideration of the Sharia, at the level of certainty for whoever examines the Sharia in its contexts" (1). He then said: "It is established in these matters that the considered interests are the universals and not the particulars" (2).
However, the observer of this illustration of universality and particularity in rulings may object to what has been mentioned regarding the permissible in the third and fourth sections (3). The permissible in the particular that is required to be abandoned in the universal, as the action that is required to be abandoned in the universal serves to undermine the universals; how can it then be considered optional, or equal on both sides? This is another issue that al-Shatibi investigates; how does he address it?
The permissible is divided into two categories:
__________
(1) The same source, 1/90.
(2) The same source, 1/91.
(3) See the previous page.


[Page 194]

Al-Shatibi divides the permissible (mubah) into two categories: the first meaning is choice (takhyir), and the second meaning is the lifting of hardship (raf' al-haraj). What is meant by choice is that it is permissible in part, while the action is required in total. What is meant by the lifting of hardship is that it is permissible in part, while the abandonment is required in total. Therefore, it is noted in the text mentioned on the previous page that the term "permissible" (jائز) is used in relation to what is recommended (mandub) in total, as well as in relation to what is obligatory (wajib) in total. As for the third category, which is what is permissible in part but disliked (makruh) in total, the term "permissible" is not mentioned; rather, it states: "there is no hardship in it" (1). He says: "The permissible is used in two senses: one is in terms of being given the choice between action and abandonment, and the other is in terms of saying: there is no hardship in it" (2).
__________
(1) See p. 155. And see: al-Muwafaqat. 1/85.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/92.


[Page 195]

He says: "If it is said that there is no harm in what is permissible (mubah), then it is not included under the choice between action and inaction" (1). Then he said: "The category that requires action in its entirety is the one in which choice is given between action and inaction, as in His saying: { Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you will } (2), and His saying: { And eat from both of them abundantly wherever you wish } (3)... This is indeed a true choice... As for the category that requires inaction in its entirety, we do not know of anything in the Sharia that indicates a true choice in it textually; rather, it is either silent about it or refers to some of it with a phrase that removes it from the ruling of explicit choice, such as naming this world as play and amusement in the context of reproach for those who lean towards it, for it implies that amusement is not something one has a choice in" (4). He said: "In general, it (i.e., the permissible) is of four categories: the first is that it serves a matter that requires action, the second is that it serves a matter that requires inaction, the third is that it serves a matter that allows for choice. The fourth is that it does not contain any of that" (5).
__________
(1) The same source, 1/94.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 223.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 35.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 1/93 - 94. We may wonder, regarding this classification of the permissible and this distinction between the two categories, whether there is some confusion in Al-Shatibi's thought. We have cited his text in defining the permissible as it appears in the first part, p. 68: "What is permissible according to the legislator is that which one has a choice in between action and inaction," and here he mentions that some of the permissible is not something one has a choice in!!
(5) The same source, 1/92 - 93.


[Page 196]

The first category has already been discussed, which is the permissible option (mubah al-mukhayyar). The second has also been addressed, which is the permissible in the sense of lifting hardship (mubah bi-ma'na raf' al-haraj). As for the fourth, since it does not serve any purpose, it means that it neither serves nor undermines any essential, necessary, or enhancing principle, as it does not benefit the servants nor avert any harm from them. Thus, it is fundamentally contradictory to the requirement of being for the benefit of the servants. Therefore, al-Shatibi referred it back to what is required to be abandoned, stating: "As for the fourth, since it does not serve any significant purpose, it is considered frivolous or akin to frivolity in the eyes of rational individuals, and thus it is also required to be abandoned, for it serves only to waste time without any benefit for religion or worldly matters; hence it is a servant of what is required to be abandoned, making it, in totality, required to be abandoned" (1).
As for the third category, which is the permissible part that serves a choice. It is essential to note here that this choice is served, and consequently, it is a universal principle. According to al-Shatibi's idea, a universal principle cannot be a matter of choice; otherwise, it undermines it. In essence, the depiction of universality and particularity in the permissible was intended to prevent the existence of the permissible or the choice in universals. Therefore, after al-Shatibi discussed the fourth category, he returned to this third category to say: "The third category is similar as well, for it serves it, and thus it is also required to be abandoned" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/93 - 94.
(2) Al-Muwafaqat, 1/93. It is noted here that he discussed the four categories as follows: first, then second, then fourth, and then third. He made his opinion on the fourth a prelude to his opinion on the third.


[Page 197]

Thus, there are two types of what is permissible (mubah): one that signifies the choice between action and inaction, which is the action that is required in totality, and one that signifies the lifting of hardship, which is the inaction that is required in totality. However, its being permissible continues to oscillate around the fundamental idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) or the purposefulness of rulings with skepticism. Al-Shatibi explores what might cast doubt on his idea, stating that the permissible in the sense of choice is, from one perspective, partial, and its existence is theoretical; whereas practically, it is the action that is required. As for the permissible in the sense of lifting hardship, the interest (maslaha) lies in leaving it, since it is required to be left entirely. So how can it be permitted when acting upon it negates the interest? Here, al-Shatibi asserts the possibility of a sixth rank of rulings, which is the rank of pardon, and this rank seems to resolve the issue of particulars that do not serve the idea of objectives.
Regarding the permissible that signifies choice, al-Shatibi believes that an action, in its essence, has a rationality in the mind, and it has a reality that differs from its rationality. When it occurs, it does not occur in isolation from circumstances or attributes. For example: walking is permissible, looking is permissible, eating is permissible, and lying down is permissible; however, this ruling pertains to the action as an action, that is, as walking, looking, eating, or lying down. In reality, walking may be towards an act of worship or towards a sin, and the same applies to looking; eating may be for what is permissible or for what is forbidden, and it may occur out of necessity or not. The act of lying down varies in its reality based on circumstances. Actions in reality do not occur without attributes, so should one consider the action from the perspective of its rationality or from the perspective of attributes? He chooses the latter and states: "The purpose of establishing the evidence is to apply the actions of the obligated individuals according to their nature, and there is no dispute in this. However, the actions of the obligated individuals have two considerations: one from the perspective of their rationality and the other from the perspective of their occurrence in the external world" (1). He then says: "If that is the case, then the consideration should be based on what has occurred in the external world, which consists only of actions described by necessary attributes and matters contrary to that. Every obligated individual is addressed in relation to their specific self; thus, they are addressed by what is valid for them to achieve in the external world, which cannot happen except through external necessities; thus, they are addressed by them and not by anything else" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/17.
(2) The same source, 3/19.


[Page 198]

The permissible (mubah) that is chosen seems to be akin to the obligatory (wajib) that is chosen, like the attributes of expiation (kafara). He says: "It is summarized that every permissible act is not permissible in an absolute sense, but rather it is permissible in part specifically, and as for the whole, it is either required to be acted upon or required to be refrained from. If it is said, 'Is this explanation not a contradiction to what was previously stated, that the permissible is that which has equal sides?' The answer is no, because what was previously mentioned is in terms of looking at it in itself, without considering any external matter, and this perspective is in terms of considering it with respect to external matters. So, when you look at it in itself, it is what is called here the permissible in part. And when you look at it according to external matters, it is what is called the required in whole. You see that this nice garment, for example, is permissible to wear; it has equal consideration in the view of the Sharia for both acting and refraining, so there is no intention in either matter. This is a rational reality when considered in this limited regard to the essence of the permissible as it is. And from the perspective of being a protection from heat and cold, a cover for the private parts, and beauty in appearance, it is required to be acted upon. This perspective is not limited to this specific garment nor to this specific time; it is a perspective in the whole, not in part."(1)
__________
(1) The same source, 1/93.


[Page 199]

As for what is permissible (mubah) in the sense of lifting hardship, it is required to be abandoned entirely, and granting permission for it undermines or contradicts the universals. Therefore, al-Shatibi says: "As for the category in which there is no hardship, it is almost akin to following the blameworthy whims; do you not see that it is almost contrary to the intent of the Legislator in seeking the general prohibition in principle? However, due to its scarcity, lack of permanence, and its participation with the servant required to act by chance, as mentioned in its place, it has not been given much attention" (1). Then al-Shatibi mentions that although particulars may oppose the universals, they do not affect them because the universals are established with certainty, and the particulars that oppose the objectives of public interest (maslaha) do not reach the level of universals; thus, they do not undermine the fundamental idea of the objectives. He states: "The particular (2) does not undermine a required principle (3), and although it may open the door in general, it is not influential in itself as a particular, until it combines with others of its kind, and the combination is strengthening (4), and from there the universal that is prohibited, which is contrary to the desired action, is formed" (5). Therefore, if these particulars come together in a universal that encompasses them and returns to it, they will no longer be permissible in the sense of mubah, but will instead be required to be abandoned both partially and universally. However, in reality - according to al-Shatibi's view - they are particulars and do not return to a universal, while at the same time serving to undermine the idea of the objectives.

(1) The same source, 1/96.
(2) That is: from the permissible included under the category of lifting hardship.
(3) It will come in our discussion of the objectives that the particular does not undermine the universal even if it opposes it, because if the particular does not return to a universal, it can be interpreted or rejected.
(4) That is, it does not have an effect until it combines with others and provides a significant consensus; then it becomes universal and must be considered in specifying the universals, but prior to that, it is not considered even if it opens the door for consideration.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/96.


[Page 200]

Based on this understanding of al-Shatibi's intent in his discussion of the permissible (mubah) and its details, it can be judged that most of the explanations and commentaries by the commentators on the book al-Muwafaqat regarding this topic are far from the truth, and indeed have no connection to al-Shatibi's intended meaning, let alone that some of them are not free from confusion and meaningless discourse(1).
The rank of exemption:
This is what leads al-Shatibi to assume a sixth type of rulings, which applies to these particular rulings and others that resemble them in being particulars that do not serve the universals. He says: "It is valid for there to be a rank of exemption between the lawful (halal) and the unlawful (haram), so it cannot be judged as one of the five"(2).
Included in this rank are matters that are not burdensome, concessions (rukhas), and actions devoid of intention, among others. He states: "It makes no difference whether we assume those actions are commanded or prohibited or whether there is choice in them, because if they are neither prohibited nor commanded nor subject to choice, they revert to the category of what has no ruling in the Sharia, which is the meaning of exemption. Even if there is a command or prohibition attached to them, the condition for holding someone accountable for it is the mention of the command and prohibition and the ability to comply, and this is impossible in the case of the mistaken, the heedless, and the forgetful, as well as the sleeper and the insane... Among them is the error in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning)... Thus, the essence of this is that there is no burden on him for what he has left and for what he has done, and among them are the concessions of various kinds, as the texts indicate by stating the lifting of burdens and the removal of hardship and the attainment of forgiveness"(3).

(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/107.

However, al-Shatibi does not determine whether the status of pardon is a ruling or not. He says: "However, the consideration remains regarding whether pardon is a ruling or not, and if it is said to be a ruling, does it pertain to the address of obligation (taklif) or to the address of status (wada)? All of this is possible, but since it does not lead to a practical ruling, clarification in this matter is not emphasized, and it is preferable to leave it. And Allah is the Guide to the Truth" (1).
Licenses and Determination:
What applies to licenses, according to al-Shatibi's methodology, also applies to what is permissible (mubah). He says: "The ruling of a license is permissibility absolutely, in terms of it being a license" (2). He also states: "Is the permissibility attributed to the license of the kind that removes hardship or of the kind that allows choice between action and abstention? What appears from the texts of licenses is that it is in the sense of removing hardship, not in the other sense" (3).

(1) The same source, 1/119. Here, one might wonder, if this does not lead to a ruling, does it not undermine the concept of objectives (maqasid)? And if we say it does not undermine, does that not force us to say that this category of permissible acts and licenses is to be avoided and does not fit the definition of what is permissible?
(2) The same source, 1/214.
(3) The same source, 1/221.


[Page 202]

Therefore, the issue present in the permissible (mubah) regarding the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) is the same as that in the concession (rukhsah). Thus, for him, concessions do not return to general principles nor serve the generalities; they are merely specific, in contrast to the original ruling (azimah). He says: "The original ruling is what has been legislated from the general rulings from the outset, and the meaning of it being general is that it does not pertain to some of the obligated individuals as they are obligated, nor to some situations over others, like prayer for example, which is legislated absolutely and universally for every person and in every situation, as are fasting, almsgiving (zakat), pilgrimage (hajj), jihad, and other rituals of Islam" (1). He says: "As for the concession, it is what has been legislated for a difficult excuse, as an exception to a general principle that necessitates prohibition, while being limited to the places of need therein. The fact that it is legislated for an excuse is the particularity mentioned by the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence). And the fact that it is difficult means that the excuse may simply be need without any existing hardship, and that would not be called a concession, like the permissibility of partnership (qarad), for example" (2). He said: "The original ruling returns to a general foundational principle, while the concession returns to a specific exception from that general principle" (3). These definitions and statements indicate the mentioned issue, which appears here once again, as he said that the original ruling is general and does not pertain to some obligated individuals or situations, then he said that the concession is an exception from that generality, which means that the original ruling has become specific.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/209.
(2) The same source, 1/210.
(3) The same source, 1/11.


[Page 203]

It should not be said here that this exception is a case of specifying the general, known in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence), for this specification contradicts the idea of universals and their properties mentioned by al-Shatibi, including his statement: "You will not find in it, after its perfection, any abrogation or specification of its generality, nor any restriction of its absoluteness, nor the lifting of a ruling from its rulings, neither in terms of the generality of the obligated nor in terms of the specificity of some of them, nor in terms of time over time, nor in terms of condition over condition" (1). It will become clear in the discussion of generality and specificity that specification, in the sense of exception or lifting some of what the text encompasses, is rejected by al-Shatibi; rather, specification for him is the clarification of the meaning of the text, that is, what the general term encompasses. Accordingly, the concessions do not belong to universal principles. He said: "The fact that this legislation is for an excuse that is an exception from a universal principle indicates to you that concessions are not legislated from the outset; therefore, they are not universals, even if they are presented with that, it is incidental" (2).
And there may be those who say: Concessions return to the individual with benefit, as they are justified by hardship, and they implement a universal principle, which is the principle of lifting hardship, like the hardship for the traveler, or for the principle of preserving life, like eating carrion for the one in dire need, or for a complementary principle, like the sitting prayer of the followers when the imam prays sitting, or other such universal principles (3).
__________
(1) The same source, 1/46. And see p. 144 of this book.
(2) The same source, 1/211.
(3) Lifting hardship and not obligating with burdensome difficulties are among the universal principles and belong to the rank of needs. Preserving life is a universal principle that belongs to the rank of necessities. The sitting prayer of the followers due to the imam praying sitting refers to a universal principle of the complements of necessities. Al-Muwafaqat, 1/209 - 211.


[Page 204]

The answer is that al-Shatibi avoids this response and rejects it, because if it initially appears that he is patching a gap in the methodology, in reality, he is destroying more than he is building. For if we find a public interest (maslaha) in the concession and claim that it serves a general principle, the law has stipulated that the original ruling is better: { and to fast is better for you } (1). Al-Shatibi believes that adhering to the original rulings (azaim) is preferable to taking concessions (rukhas). He stated in his argument that concessions are akin to permissibility in the sense of lifting hardship, not in the sense of offering choice: "And the evidence that choice is not intended in these matters is that the majority or all say: whoever does not utter a word of disbelief under coercion is rewarded and in the highest ranks" (2).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 184.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 1/222.


[Page 205]

Add to this, for example: Prayer and fasting are rooted in the preservation of religion, which is one of the necessities. How can breaking the fast, combining prayers, and shortening them be permitted in a journey where hardship is hardly mentioned, or for a wealthy king? However, if the journey involves hardship and significant difficulty, then according to the methodology of al-Shatibi, this elevates the concession from being merely a concession to being something that is required, recommended, or obligatory, and it serves overarching principles, such as the principle of alleviating hardship or not being burdened with what causes significant difficulty, or the principle of preserving life. For example, eating carrion in a state of necessity serves the principle of necessities, which is the preservation of life, and this is a requirement, not merely a concession. Similarly, the sitting of the followers behind a sitting imam is not a concession but rather an obligation and a necessity that complements the necessities, unlike the sitting of the imam, which is a concession if he is able to stand with difficulty. On one hand, and on the other hand, if we concede to returning concessions to overarching principles, this undermines the idea that the overarching principles support and reinforce one another, and that all rulings and principles serve and return to the preservation of necessities, which are the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and wealth. In His saying, Exalted is He: { Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except for one who is forced while his heart is secure in faith } (1). And in His saying, Exalted is He: { And when you travel throughout the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer } (2), the concessions do not support the principles; rather, they undermine them. Indeed, the preservation of religion takes precedence over the preservation of life, and yet uttering the word of disbelief in this case is permissible, as is shortening the prayer in a journey where there is no hardship or difficulty, which does not serve the principle of preserving religion, meaning it does not serve its universality. This leads to the conclusion that the principles do not support one another.
__________
(1) Surah an-Nahl, 106.
(2) Surah an-Nisa, 101.


[Page 206]

If al-Shatibi referred the optional permissible (mubah) to a general principle by directing attention to it being sought in its entirety, then the concession (rukhsah) and the permissible in the sense of lifting hardship did not return to general principles according to him. Therefore, he proposed for them, as we explained in the previous discussion, the rank of exemption, and he stated that partial rulings do not violate general principles. He also said this regarding concessions after confirming that they do not belong to general principles. He stated: "The necessities are not called concessions by the scholars" (1). He said: "The legitimacy of concessions is partial, limited to the place of need. If the traveler’s journey is interrupted, he must return to the original ruling of completing the prayer and observing the fast. The sick person, if he is able to stand in prayer, does not pray sitting, and if he is able to use water, he does not perform tayammum. Likewise, other concessions, unlike loans, partnership, and agricultural contracts, which resemble concessions, are not truly concessions in the sense of this terminology" (2).
The conclusion is that concessions are particulars that do not revert to universals, and even though they are such and do not align with his methodology or his idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), the world will not be disrupted. He says: "The firm ruling returns to a general principle in obligation because it is absolute and general in its essence for all obligated individuals, while the concession returns to a particular based on some obligated individuals who have an excuse, and based on certain conditions and times for those with excuses, not in every situation, nor at every time, nor for everyone. It is like an incidental occurrence to the general principle. The established rule in its place is that if a general matter and a particular matter conflict, the general matter takes precedence because the particular entails a partial benefit while the general entails a general benefit, and the order of the world is not disrupted by the disruption of the partial benefit" (3). He then said: "The legitimacy of the concession is that it should be partial" (4).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/21.
(2) The same source, 1/28.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/224.
(4) The same place.


[Page 207]

It is redundant to say, after clarifying his views on concession (rukhsah) and obligation (azimah), that he believes standing with obligation is better in terms of Sharia than taking concession. Likewise, concessions do not have a universal law; thus, their instances are limited to those mentioned in the texts, and they cannot be analogized. As for what falls under general rules, such as not being tasked with what is beyond one's capacity, the hardships that cause distress, and the removal of hardship, these are considered obligations and not concessions (1).
Causes and effects:
The cause is one of the situational rulings. In the terminology of the jurists (usuliyyin), it is a clear, defined description that the textual evidence indicates as a marker for the existence of the ruling (2). For example, the crescent moon of Ramadan is a cause for the ruling of fasting, and a sale is a cause for ownership and the permissibility of benefiting from the property. The relationship between the cause and the ruling in legal rulings is different from that between the cause and effect in rational matters. For instance, drinking alcohol is a cause of intoxication; thus, drinking alcohol results in intoxication. However, in Sharia, the crescent moon of Ramadan does not contain the ruling of fasting; rather, it exists at its occurrence, not due to a material relationship between cause and effect, but rather by a report from the Legislator who made the description a sign or indicator for the existence of the ruling. This is the understanding commonly held by the jurists regarding the relationship between cause and ruling in legal terminology.
__________
(1) The question remains regarding concessions as it does for what is permissible: does their permissibility undermine the concept of objectives (maqasid)? And does the assertion that they are partial and not universal negate the inquiry?
(2) See p. 53 of chapter one.


[Page 208]

But al-Shatibi establishes a new understanding, and he sees that the legal universals (kulliyat al-sharia) are, although they are either legislative or established by the Lawgiver, equivalent to the rational universals (kulliyat al-aqliyya), because these are also established by the Lawgiver. He says: "The legislative matters may parallel the rational matters in providing certain knowledge, and the knowledge of the Sharia is among them" (1). He also states: "Moreover, the rational universals are derived from existence, which is a legislative matter and not a rational one, thus they are equal to the legal universals in this regard, and the distinction between them is lifted" (2).
And since causes have their effects, and whoever intends to bring about a matter aims to establish its causes, the doer of the cause is considered like the doer of the effect. Thus, the legal rulings are considered causes for effects intended by them. Al-Shatibi said: "Establishing the cause is akin to establishing the effect, whether that effect is intended or not. Because when it is made a cause in the course of customs, it is regarded as if he directly caused it. This is supported by the principle of customary practices, as the relationship of effects to their causes is like that of satiety to food, quenching to water, burning to fire, and purging to scammony(3) and all other effects to their causes. Likewise, the actions that result from our earning are attributed to us even if they are not from our earning, and if this is well-known and established, the custom of the Sharia follows this measure in legal causes with their effects" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat 1/44. See p. 144 of this book.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/44.
(3) [Illegible]: A plant from which a sticky moisture is extracted, dried, and is also named after its plant; it is more effective against the stomach and intestines than all laxatives. Al-Firozabadi, al-Qamus al-Muhit. p. 1447.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/148.


[Page 209]

Therefore, the matter that must be considered in al-Shatibi's discussion of causes is that the legal rulings are causes for intended results. These results are the effects of the rulings or the intended benefits, and the rulings are the means leading to them. Just as the Legislator intended through commands and prohibitions to bring about what is commanded and to prevent what is prohibited, He also intended to achieve certain results from the commanded action and to prevent certain results from the prohibited action. This is the foundational principle of the objectives (maqasid) in al-Shatibi's thought. For this reason, al-Shatibi discussed causes and effects in detail and at length before beginning his book on the objectives.

However, the obligation regarding causes, which are the rulings, even though the effects are intended by the Legislator, does not mean that there is an obligation regarding the effects themselves, as they are not within the capacity of the obligated person nor are they dependent on him; rather, what is within his capacity is the cause that the Legislator has commanded him to pursue. The occurrence of the effect happens within that framework. He said: "The evidence for this is what has been established in the discourse that what is required of the obligated person is to engage in the causes, while the effects are the actions of Allah, Exalted is He, and there is no earning involved for the obligated person" (1), and he said: "Thus, the obligation and address only pertain to what is acquired, so the effects are excluded from the address of obligation because they are not within their capacity; if they were to be addressed, it would be an obligation of what is not bearable, which is not the case" (2).

Furthermore, the fact that the effect is intended by the Legislator through the establishment of the cause does not imply the permissibility of intending to bring about the effect through a means other than the legislated cause, as just as the effect is intended, the primary intention is the cause because the address indicates it and the obligation is placed upon it, and the effect is only understood through it. He said: "The fact that the Legislator did not legislate this cause for this specific effect is evidence that there is a corruption in that causation and no benefit" (3). We will clarify this matter in more detail and with more documentation in the third section of the fifth chapter.

Section Three
On the Results and the Concept of Benefit and Harm in al-Shatibi

Definition of the Research Topic:
