(1) The same source, 1/131.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/148.
(3) The same source, p. 173.


[Page 210]

In the sections on introductions and documents, some rules or principles of al-Shatibi's methodology in establishing the objectives (maqasid) are clarified. The objectives or principles reached are a result of applying this methodology. This section aims to build upon those introductions and documents with ideas, definitions, or concepts that must be considered and relied upon when applying the methodology in order to reach the general rules and principles.
Based on this, this section is to introduce some terms or legal terminology used by al-Shatibi, and understanding their meanings is essential for grasping his methodology, particularly the terms public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada), in addition to the terms cause (sabab), effect (musaab), wisdom (hikmah), and reason ('illah) and the meanings of rulings.
Cause:
As for the cause, its meaning has been clarified in the previous section. It is what the legislator has made a cause for an effect, whether in religious matters or in rational matters. The relevant application in the legal objectives is what is a legal cause. He stated when discussing one of the principles: "What has been discussed in this principle pertains to the effects of causes in terms of whether the causes are lawful or unlawful, that is, from the perspective of what falls under the scrutiny of the law, not from the perspective of what are ordinary causes for ordinary effects" (1).
As has been clarified, the causes are the legal rulings that the legislator has specified, whether as commands or prohibitions, and they are the indications of the texts. Since the legislator has objectives in legislation, he has established rulings so that these objectives become the causes for adherence to them, making the legal rulings causes. The intended outcomes are rulings or effects or interests or reasons, but according to a specific methodology that will be clarified below.
Wisdom:
It is presumed that the ruling was legislated for its sake or for the sake of attaining it, thus it is a cause. However, before it is definitively established that it is intended by the legislator, it can be a plausible description or an appropriate description, making it the presumed intention of the legislator rather than a definitive one, and this has no legal consideration. The wisdoms may be known to the observer, may be presumed, or may be potentially imagined.
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat. 1/171.


[Page 211]

In addition to that, some of the wisdoms may not be perceived or anticipated by a person, even though they may be the most important objective for the legislator. Among the outcomes, a person may feel that there is a worldly benefit for him and may naturally incline towards it, and this is what al-Shatibi refers to as the aim or the share. Therefore, the mere assumption of wisdom, in which the mind wanders, is not to be considered until it is established through the Sharia. He says: "If transmission (naql) and reason ('aql) collaborate on legal issues, it is on the condition that transmission precedes and is followed, while reason is subordinate; thus, the mind should only explore within the limits set by transmission" (1).
He also says: "If we understand through necessity or choice an independent wisdom in the legislation of the ruling, it does not follow that there is not another wisdom and a second and third benefit, and more. Our ultimate understanding is that we have grasped a worldly benefit that is suitable to independently justify the legislation of the ruling, so we consider it under the ruling of legal permission, and we do not know that the benefit and wisdom are limited to what has appeared. If we do not attain knowledge or suspicion from that, we cannot decisively claim that there is no benefit except what has appeared to us. For that is a decisive claim about the unseen without evidence" (2).
It is apparent from this text that it is a response to those who assert the establishment of the cause, wisdom, or benefit, based on its being probable, even though there may be others that have not appeared to us which are stronger in assumption. It seems to be a direct rebuttal to al-Amidi, who said: "If it is established that the rulings were legislated for the benefits of the servants, then if we see a ruling that entails a beneficial matter, it must either be that this is the aim of the legislation of the ruling or something that has not been revealed to us. It cannot be what has not been revealed to us; otherwise, the legislation of the ruling would be merely an act of devotion, which contradicts the principle previously established. Thus, it must be legislated for what has appeared, and if that is presumed, it must be acted upon" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat. 1/53.
(2) The same source, 2/216.
(3) Al-Amidi, Al-Ahkam fi Usul Al-Ahkam. 3/250.


[Page 212]

Al-Shatibi's response to this statement means that he does not suffice with the presumed wisdom. Therefore, he said: "This is not permissible, for there remains the possibility of another wisdom for which the ruling was legislated, so we are, from that perspective, standing with the act of worship" (1), and he said: "If a reason appears to us that is suitable for the independence of the ruling's legitimacy and we are not required to deny anything other than it, then the usuliyyin (jurisprudents) allow for the possibility that the reason may differ from what has appeared to them" (2).
What confirms this in his methodology is his consideration that wisdom is a consequence. He said: "As for the cause, it refers to what has been legislated for a ruling due to a wisdom necessitated by that ruling" (3). He also said: "The wisdoms of the causes are the consequences" (4).
The consequence:
It is the wisdom intended by the Legislator through the legislation of the cause. It is the result of the commanded action that the Legislator intends to achieve through the occurrence of the action, and it is the result of the prohibited action that the Legislator intends not to achieve through the non-occurrence of the action that causes it.
However, not everything that can result from an action or from the omission of an action is a consequence of the cause; therefore, the consequence is what is established as being intended by the Legislator through inductive reasoning that leads to certainty. It is not sufficient for it to be something that can result from the action.
The reason:
The reason is the consequence or the result that the Legislator intended by legislating the ruling. Thus, it is the objective and the wisdom.
One might ask how the reason can be the consequence, while it is closer in meaning to be a cause rather than a consequence? The answer is that in the terminology commonly used among the usuliyyin, the reason is neither a cause nor a consequence; rather, the reason is the motivator for legislation. This has been clarified in the previous chapter. However, for al-Shatibi, the matter is different, and the reason is the consequence according to his methodology.
The explanation of this is that the Legislator only legislated the rulings to achieve objectives, and the objectives are the consequences of the rulings. If we want to know the objective of the Legislator, we look into these rulings and their consequences and intended outcomes, and what is established as such is considered a principle of legislation.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/217.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, 1/185.
(4) The same source, 1/175.


[Page 213]

And if these objectives (maqasid) are the reason for the legislation of rulings, then the rulings are indeed legislated based on them, thus serving as the causes for legislation. The jurist (mujtahid) has no way to know the causes of the rulings except through following and deducing their consequences. For this reason, it is said that the objectives of the Sharia are to bring about benefits and to avert harms, and it is also said that the Sharia is characterized by bringing about benefits and averting harms.
Based on this, what applies to the cause applies to the consequence and to the wisdom mentioned earlier. Al-Shatibi said: "As for the cause, it refers to the wisdoms and benefits that are related to the commands or permissions, or the harms that are related to the prohibitions" (1). It follows that the cause must be definitive: it must be the benefit itself or the harm itself, not its mere possibility. He said: "In general, the cause is the benefit itself, or the harm, not its mere possibility, whether it is apparent or not, whether it is defined or not" (2). He said: "The cause may be known or unknown; if it is known, it is followed, and wherever it exists, the requirement of the command or prohibition exists, whether it is intended or not, such as marriage for the benefit of procreation, and sale for the benefit of benefiting from the contracted item, and punishments for the benefit of deterrence. The cause is recognized here through its known pathways in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). When it is determined, it is known that the intent of the Legislator is what those causes necessitate in terms of action or inaction, and in terms of causing or not causing. If it is unknown, one must refrain from asserting that the Legislator intended this or that" (3). Then he said: "And it is judged by knowledge or conjecture that it is not intended by Him (the Legislator). For if it were intended, there would have been a definitive proof for it" (4) (5).
Meanings of rulings:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/185.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source: 2/276-277.
(4) That is: a definitive proof, not a conjectural indication, because the proofs of definitive matters must be certain.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat: 2/276-277.


[Page 214]

The meanings of rulings are the same as the causes or intended wisdoms of the legislator, such as the preservation of religion and the preservation of life; they are meanings derived from the legal rulings that lead to these outcomes. He said: "It is necessary to pay attention to the meanings for which the rulings were legislated, and the meanings are the causes of the rulings" (1). He also said: "Legal actions are not intended for themselves, but rather for other matters that are their meanings, which are the interests for which they were legislated" (2).
Interest and harm:
It becomes clear from the above that the pursuit of interests and the prevention of harms are the goals and outcomes of the rulings. They are their causes, objectives, and meanings.
However, it should be noted that there is a fundamental difference between the meaning of both interest and harm according to al-Shatibi and their meanings according to those who preceded him among the jurists who assert the superiority of pursuing interests and preventing harms.
For the earlier scholars, interests and harms are what is deemed so by rational individuals and wise people, meaning they are what returns to the obligated individuals in accordance with their innate nature and inclinations, and aligns with their desires and objectives; therefore, they are suitable meanings or descriptions. Thus, the recognized interests for them are the suitable descriptions if a ruling or rulings come in accordance with them (3).
As for al-Shatibi, the interest is what is established as being intended by the legislator, regardless of whether it is suitable or unsuitable. This is done by deducing a meaning or description in the rulings, regardless of whether it is an interest or a harm according to the obligated individuals and their customs. If the meaning is deduced in a way that conveys what resembles a moral consensus, it is a general meaning intended by the legislator, and it is considered an interest if it causes what the Sharia requests, and it is considered a harm if it causes what the Sharia prohibits. This concept of interest and harm according to him is considered a reversal of the conventional meaning among the jurists, and failing to recognize this meaning leads to a misunderstanding of his concept of objectives, or to attributing to al-Shatibi opinions and ideas that contradict the reality of his views and thoughts.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/138.
(2) The same source, 2/268.
(3) This has been clarified in the first chapter.


[Page 215]

Since the benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), in terms of bringing about and averting, are the causes (illal), the objectives (maqasid), the effects (musabbabat), and the meanings of the rulings (ahkam), and since they are frequently mentioned and utilized by al-Shatibi, the failure to ascertain the true meaning of what al-Shatibi intended by benefit and harm leads the researcher in the Muwafaqat to contradictions and diverts him from understanding al-Shatibi's methodology. Therefore, it is necessary to explore and establish al-Shatibi's concept of benefits and harms in detail and separately.
The concept of al-Shatibi regarding both public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada):
The concept of al-Shatibi regarding public interests (masalih) and harms (mafasid) appears in many of his texts, and it is also evident from the manner in which he established that the Sharia (Islamic law) is based on public interests and harms.
Indeed, al-Shatibi attempted to prove this matter in the introduction to his book on the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), responding to al-Razi, who denied the reasoning of the Sharia based on benefits and harms and cut off that discussion. He presented texts that show that the commands of Allah, Exalted is He, and His actions are reasoned, as evidenced by the legal texts indicating that Allah has ruled this for such and such a reason, and has acted thus for such and such a reason, such as His saying: { so that you may attain piety }, { to test you }, { to worship Me }... Since al-Shatibi's method of establishing principles and foundations is through beneficial induction (istiqra), he brought forth numerous texts that explicitly state that the ruling or action was for the sake of a purpose. He pointed to the existence of countless texts indicating that rulings and actions have objectives. Based on the occurrence of induction, he establishes a universal principle that does not fail, which is that the actions and rulings of Allah have purposes and objectives. Thus, al-Shatibi sees that he has definitively proven that the Sharia is reasoned by benefits and harms. Upon examining these texts that al-Shatibi cited, we find that the majority of them do not indicate the intention of the legislator towards what is beneficial or the removal of harm in the sense of what aligns with the interests or desires of people or what rational individuals or wise men deem beneficial for people. Rather, most of them lack a rational or suitable meaning that can be said to bring about a benefit or avert a harm.


[Page 216]

Indeed, the utmost that these texts indicate, which al-Shatibi intended by citing them, is that rulings and actions have objectives or purposes. Since these actions and rulings are from the Legislator, their objectives are thus legal (shar'i). And since they are legal objectives, they are termed benefits (masalih) or harms (mafasid) depending on the legality of the actions or their illegality.
To prove that this is al-Shatibi's concept of benefits and harms, we will discuss the evidence he presented to demonstrate that the Sharia is based on benefits, one by one.
Analytical discussion of al-Shatibi's arguments:
Al-Shatibi said: "The purpose of establishing the laws is solely for the benefits of the servants in both this world and the Hereafter."(1) He also said: "Al-Razi claimed that God's rulings are not based on any reason whatsoever, just as His actions are not, and that the Mu'tazila agreed that His rulings are based on the consideration of the benefits of the servants, and that this is the choice of most later jurists. And when he was compelled in the science of Usul al-fiqh to establish reasons for the legal rulings, he did so on the basis that the reasons are merely signs that indicate the rulings."(2)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/2.
(2) The same source, 2/2 - 3.


[Page 217]

This statement indicates that since the view of justifying the Sharia (Islamic law) based on public interest (maslaha) is the opinion of most later jurists, it is necessary to establish proof for that. The proof that is valid for this issue pertains to the justifications if they are understood as signs of knowledge, that is, abstracted from any wisdom that the jurist may find. This is a reference to his intent regarding public interest, and this is entirely contrary to the methodology of justification adopted by the jurists before him, who justified the Sharia based on public interest. He then said: "The relied-upon position is that we have inferred from the Sharia that it was established for the interests of the servants, an inference that neither al-Razi nor anyone else disputes" (1). He then mentioned twelve texts as evidence, by way of example and not limitation. He said: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, says regarding the sending of the messengers, which is the foundation: { Messengers bringing good news and warning, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers } (2), { And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds } (3). And He said regarding the origin of creation: { And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed } (4), { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (5), { Who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed } (6). As for the justifications for the details of the rulings in the Book and the Sunnah, they are more than can be counted, such as His saying after the verse on ablution: { Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you } (7),
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) Surah An-Nisa, 165.
(3) Surah Al-Anbiya, 107.
(4) Surah Hud, 7.
(5) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.
(6) Surah Al-Mulk, 2.
(7) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 6.


[Page 218]

He said regarding fasting: { Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain piety } (1), and regarding prayer: { Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing } (2), and he said regarding the qibla: { So turn your faces toward it, so that there will not be for the people a reason to argue against you } (3), and regarding jihad: { Permission is given to those who are being fought because they were wronged } (4), and regarding retribution: { And there is for you in retribution a saving of life, O you who have understanding } (5), and regarding the affirmation of monotheism: { Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we have testified, lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware" } (6). The aim is to draw attention, and if induction indicates this and is beneficial for knowledge in such a matter, we assert that the matter continues in all details of the Sharia (Islamic law) (7).
In this way, al-Shatibi sees that he has established conclusive evidence that the legal rulings are based on public interest (maslaha), and we will look - in the following - at this text analytically to understand his intention regarding the reasoning based on public interest. Let us take - then - the texts he used as evidence, each of which is beneficial for reasoning based on public interest, and their abundance forms an induction that suggests something akin to moral consensus.
His first evidence: His saying: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, says regarding the sending of the messengers: { Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners, so that there will not be for the people a reason to argue against Allah after the messengers }" (8).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 183.
(2) Surah Al-Ankabut, 45.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 150.
(4) Surah Al-Hajj, 39.
(5) Surah Al-Baqarah, 179.
(6) Surah Al-A'raf, 172.
(7) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 2/3.
(8) Surah An-Nisa, 165.


[Page 219]

This text is prepared by al-Shatibi as a ruling or action of Allah, Exalted is He, justified by public interest (maslaha). Upon careful consideration, we find it indicative of a goal—one of the objectives—of sending the messengers, or of a result intended to be achieved. The action is the sending of the messengers as bearers of good news and warners, and the result is establishing the proof against the people that they have been given glad tidings and warned, so they cannot say on the Day of Resurrection: "No warner came to us," nor can they say: "How can we be held accountable for doing something we were not forbidden from, and for abandoning something we were not commanded to do?" What al-Shatibi intends here is to establish that the actions and rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, have goals or outcomes for which He acted or legislated. Thus, cutting off the proof for the servants on the Day of Resurrection is a goal or result of sending the messengers that the legislator intends to achieve. It is not a cause in the sense of a cause that is a pillar in analogy (qiyas), for the cutting off of the proof for the servants on the Day of Resurrection is not a cause for a legal ruling, and there is no ruling in this text that is subject to analogy. The fact that al-Shatibi refers to the goal or result or outcome or effect as a cause prompts us to clarify the meanings of these terms in his context so that we do not misplace them.
As for the fact that this cause is a public interest, this is a matter of figurative language and not a matter of recognizing that this matter is a public interest and then observing that the Sharia has commanded or established what a person recognizes as a public interest. Yes, it is not from this perspective, and the intended figurative language is that everything Allah commands is called a public interest or truth or justice, and everything He forbids is called corruption or injustice or falsehood. This is what al-Shatibi means, and to understand the matter, let us look at the text above: is there in this goal, which is that people will not possess a proof on the Day of Resurrection by which they can escape accountability and punishment, a public interest or an aspect of public interest? If no bearer of glad tidings or warner had come to them, they would have been among those in a state of ignorance and would have escaped punishment { And We would not punish until We sent a messenger } (1), so where is the public interest here or the appropriate meaning that, if presented to minds, would be accepted? The cutting off of the proof for the servants on the Day of Resurrection does not fall within the public interest of the servants. Based on this, al-Shatibi's use of this text to argue for justification by public interest indicates that what he means by public interest is what has been established as intended by Allah, Exalted is He, regardless of whether it is rationally meaningful or not.
His second evidence: { And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds } (2).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Isra, 15.
(2) Surah Al-Anbiya, 107.


[Page 220]

This text has two aspects of meaning regarding the justification of the Sharia (Islamic law) based on public interest (maslaha). The first aspect is the one adopted by the scholars who argued for the justification of the Sharia, stating that since it is a mercy, it must return to the servants with benefits and avert harm and evils from them. Thus, the pursuit of benefits and the prevention of evils become the justification for the rulings. This is not the aspect of reasoning that al-Shatibi relied upon, as we know that al-Shatibi does not suffice with a single text or isolated texts to establish meaning. Al-Shatibi's intention in citing this text is the second aspect, which is that the actions and rulings of Allah are justified. This text is one of the particulars that support this meaning. In other words, Allah, Exalted is He, performed the act of sending, and the text indicates that His action has a purpose, which is mercy. Thus, this meaning, which is the justification of actions and rulings, is realized in this particular instance. This is the intended meaning in all of his twelve arguments; if his intention with this text were the first aspect, it would not strengthen all the other texts.
Therefore, this text establishes that the sending of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) was for a purpose.
Since al-Shatibi used this text as evidence for reasoning based on public interest (maslaha), this indicates that he uses the term "reason" to refer to the objective. As for the fact that this reason is a public interest, it can be said that mercy is a public interest for the servants, and thus the legislator aimed for it. However, this is not what al-Shatibi intended; rather, his point is that the mercy for the worlds is an objective of the legislator, and therefore it is a public interest. This text does not imply that what a person considers to be a public interest is what the Sharia has come to indicate, because the meaning of the text is that the message is a mercy for the servants, regardless of the commands and prohibitions it contains; it is a public interest for the worlds in whatever commands and prohibitions it includes, however they may be.
His third proof: { And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed }(1).
__________
(1) Surah Hud, 7.


[Page 221]

This text was brought by al-Shatibi here because it states a purpose or result of creation, which is {to test you which of you is best in deed}. This is added to his other proofs for the purpose of establishing induction. The common or shared meaning that these texts converge upon is the indication of a purpose or result of action. The inference from this text regarding causation serves as evidence for al-Shatibi's designation of the intended purpose or result as a cause. If we consider what al-Shatibi calls a cause here, we would recognize the difference between it and the cause of analogy (qiyas). The test (ibtila) is not a cause of analogy. There is no ruling in this text that can be applied to a specific incident by analogy based on the commonality of the test. All that these texts, which al-Shatibi uses as evidence, affirm is the existence of purposes for actions.
As for the fact that this purpose is a public interest (maslaha), there is no dispute that it is inappropriate to say regarding the actions, commands, and prohibitions of Allah, Exalted is He, anything other than that they are public interest, truth, and justice, and not merely what a servant perceives as a public interest or a suitable description or wisdom in the eyes of the wise and discerning. In fact, the matter seems to be quite the opposite, as this text indicates the control of the Creator over His creations. Where is the public interest that a person feels or that the mind perceives in creating a human to be tested, either towards Paradise or towards Hell? Before a person is created, how can they comprehend or understand the assertion that their creation and testing is a public interest for them? This does not reveal any aspect of public interest, and this confirms that al-Shatibi uses the term public interest for what has been established as intended by the legislator, even if it is not rationally comprehensible.


[Page 222]

His fourth proof: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (1). This also applies to what was previously mentioned, as it has been presented to prove the purpose or intended result of the legislator from creation { to worship Me }, and it also confirms the aforementioned concept of al-Shatibi regarding the term public interest (maslaha). If what he meant by this term was the description or appropriate meaning that is understood by rational individuals and wise people, then this text would contradict his aim. This text is cited by those who oppose reasoning based on public interests. And where is the interest of the nonexistent in creating him for obligation? There is no reasonable interest, and this affirms the earlier mention of al-Shatibi's intention with the term public interest.
His fifth proof: { He who created death and life to test you which of you is best in deed } (2), and this is essentially the same as his third proof. It has been presented to increase the evidence. What has been said about what preceded it can be said here.
His sixth proof: { Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you } (3). It is also noted that he cited this because it includes mentioning the result that can arise from this obligation { to make }, { to purify you }, { and to complete His favor }. Even if a person recognizes the benefit in cleanliness or purification, he cannot adopt a form of cleanliness in place of the prescribed form. Considering these objectives as public interests indicates that they are regarded as such because they are intended by the legislator, not that Allah, Exalted is He, legislated what the servants perceive as beneficial.
__________
(1) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.
(2) Surah Al-Mulk, 2.
(3) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 6.


[Page 223]

His seventh proof: { Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain piety }(1). The evidence in this proof is in { that you may attain piety }. Al-Shatibi establishes through this that the obligation is for specific purposes, and their being intended by the Legislator makes them a public interest (maslaha). There is no appropriate meaning in this text to be pointed out. And if it is said that piety is a public interest, this contradicts the essence of the idea and does not support the claim of reasoning based on public interests, because piety is obedience. This text is similar to the text: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } in its indication of this matter.
His eighth proof: { Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing }(2). Here, al-Shatibi also uses the text to establish a result or outcome of the ruling, and that this outcome is intended by the Lawgiver, thus it is a public interest (maslaha). This proof is similar to the previous one.
His ninth proof: { So turn your faces toward it, so that there will be no argument against you from the people } (3). The obligation is for the sake of achieving the result { so that there will be }, thus the result becomes an objective of the obligation. There is no reason to call this objective a public interest (maslaha) except that it is intended by the legislator.
His tenth evidence: { Permission is granted to those who are fought because they have been wronged }(4).
Al-Shatibi uses this text as evidence to establish that the ruling ordained by Allah, which is the permission to fight, is aimed at lifting the oppression that has befallen them. Thus, this objective is intended by the legislator (al-shari) with the ruling, and for this reason, the permission to fight has a purpose. An example of this is his following evidence.
His eleventh proof: { And there is for you in legal retribution (qisas) a life, O you who possess intellect }(5).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 183.
(2) Surah Al-Ankabut, 45.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 150.
(4) Surah Al-Hajj, 39.
(5) Surah Al-Baqarah, 179.


[Page 224]

He establishes through this reasoning that the legislation of retribution (qisas) is for a purpose or outcome, which is to eliminate intentional murder or transgressions or to reduce them. Thus, this outcome is intended by the Legislator, and it is established that the actions or rulings of the Legislator are justified by their purposes. Since the purposes are intended by the Legislator, they are considered public interests (masalih).
This text and the one preceding it can be said to have as their aim a benefit according to common sense and nature or according to rational individuals, and this is correct. However, this is not the basis of al-Shatibi's reasoning, as it does not align with his other proofs. Rather, his intended purpose, which is supported by all his other arguments, is to establish the existence of a purpose for the ruling or action, regardless of whether it is rational or not. His next and final proof clarifies and emphasizes this matter.
His twelfth proof: { Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we bear witness, lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: Indeed, we were of this unaware } (1).
The complete text is: { And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify of themselves: Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes } (2) [the verse]. This is what al-Shatibi presented to prove that actions have purposes. The purpose here is to establish evidence against the Children of Adam and to cut off their excuses on the Day of Resurrection. The existence of a purpose for an action or ruling, and the affirmation of this in many actions and rulings, establishes for al-Shatibi that the actions and rulings of Allah have purposes. If this is established and there is a ruling for which there is no text regarding its purpose or the intention of the Legislator behind it, then one must search for a purpose or aim that the Legislator intends from it.
__________
(1) Surah Al-A'raf, 172.
(2) Surah Al-A'raf, 172.


[Page 225]

This is the essence of al-Shatibi's intention behind these arguments. In this last text, we do not perceive a reasonable benefit, for al-Shatibi used this last text as evidence for the reasoning based on public interest (maslaha). The benefit is so that they do not say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were heedless of this." The action that is reasoned is God's witnessing to people against themselves after taking them from the backs of the children of Adam. A person can do nothing but affirm and believe in this text and what it contains. While he may be able to comprehend the necessity of this affirmation, he cannot understand, with the mental capacity he has been given, how the establishment of this proof is contingent upon this witnessing. And where is the benefit for the servants in the cessation of their proof? Based on their testimony against themselves, a testimony in which they have no power or strength? Accordingly, this verse does not indicate any benefit for the servants, neither closely nor remotely. It contains no evidence in this context except that the actions of God, Exalted is He, have a purpose or intended outcome. The purpose of this action by God is to nullify the servants' proof on the Day of Resurrection.
Since al-Shatibi referred to it as a reason and called it a benefit, this means that he names the objectives of the Lawgiver (maqasid al-sharia) as reasons and benefits. Based on what has been mentioned, those who cite some texts from al-Shatibi and rely on his statements intending something other than what he intended, and establish rulings based on worldly interests, goals, and desires, citing his book or his methodology - according to their claim - have not taken the trouble to reflect and think lightly about his arguments.
If al-Shatibi's intention in reasoning based on benefits were what is considered a benefit according to sense, nature, or intellect and observation, his methodology would have been invalid from the outset, because these arguments he presented do not support this indication; rather, most of them contradict it.


[Page 226]

One of those interested in the topic of the objectives of Islamic law (maqasid al-sharia), and who asserts that the objectives are the public interests (masalih) — in a sense contrary to that of al-Shatibi — is Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, who says: "The examination of many evidences from the Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah necessitates certainty that the rulings of Islamic law are contingent upon purposes and reasons that pertain to the general welfare of society and individuals" (1).
This Sheikh — may Allah have mercy on him — did not grasp al-Shatibi's intended meaning of public interest, but he did recognize the meanings of these evidences. Therefore, he concluded that they are not suitable for this argument. He said: "Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi mentioned in the introduction of the book of objectives from his book the title of the definition (2) the sound evidence following the verse on ablution: { Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you } and His saying: { And there is for you in retaliation the saving of life }" (3).
Thus, he considered only two of al-Shatibi's evidences and rejected ten that he deemed unsuitable for argumentation. If what the Sheikh said were correct, it would invalidate al-Shatibi's claim of having achieved a comprehensive examination in this matter and would undermine his methodology from the outset. The correct approach is not to reject al-Shatibi's arguments from this perspective (4), but rather to understand his intended meaning of public interest in the sense we have mentioned. And Allah knows best.
Below are some explicit texts clarifying his intended meaning of public interest and harm.
Some texts regarding al-Shatibi's intended meaning of public interest and harm:
__________
(1) Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, Objectives of Islamic Law. p. 14, Tunisian Distribution Company, Tunisia, 3rd ed., December 1988.
(2) This is the book al-Muwafaqat, and al-Shatibi referred to its introduction as "The Title of the Definition of the Secrets of Obligation."
(3) Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour, Objectives of Islamic Law. p. 16.
(4) It may be valid to reject his arguments from another angle, which is the claim of having achieved a comprehensive examination that leads to certainty, and the claim that the matter is continuous in all details of the Sharia.


[Page 227]

He says: "If it is accepted that the purpose of the Sharia (law) is for the interests of the servants, then it returns to them according to the command of the Lawgiver and within the limits He has set, not according to their whims and desires. Therefore, the legal obligations are burdensome on the souls, and the senses, customs, and experience bear witness to this. The commands and prohibitions remove him from the inclinations of his nature and the pursuit of his desires until he takes them from beneath the prescribed limit... As for the fact that the interests of the obligations return to the obligated person in both the immediate and the delayed sense, this is correct, and it does not necessitate that attaining them be outside the limits of the Sharia or that he obtains them by himself without the Sharia providing them to him, and this is evident"(1). He says: "The pursuit of interests and desires does not contradict the purpose of the Sharia from this perspective because the Sharia is also established for the interests of the servants. If the interest is made subordinate, there is no harm on the doer, except that there is a significant condition here, which is that the means by which he achieves his interest must be shown to be legislated by the Lawgiver for the attainment of such, otherwise the prior matter is the command of the Lawgiver"(2).
He says: "The actions and abstentions, in terms of being actions or abstentions, are rationally equivalent regarding their intended purpose, as there is no rational basis for commendation or condemnation. When the legislator specifies one of the equivalents for the sake of public interest (maslaha) and designates the other for harm (mafsada), he clarifies the reason through which the public interest is achieved, thus commanding it or permitting it. He also clarifies the reason through which harm is achieved, thus prohibiting it out of mercy for the servants. If the obligated person intends exactly what the legislator intended by permission, he has aimed for the public interest in its most complete form, and he is deserving of it being realized for him. However, if he intends something other than what the legislator intended, this often occurs due to a misconception that the public interest lies in what he intended, as a rational person does not intentionally aim for harm. He has thus rendered what the legislator intended as disregarded, while considering what the legislator neglected as a valid aim, which is a clear contradiction to the Sharia."(3)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/117.
(2) The same source, 2/119.
(3) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/231.


[Page 228]

He says: "The fact that the public interest (maslaha) is an interest intended by the ruling and that the harm (mafsada) is likewise a harm that pertains to the legislator is a matter that does not allow for rational consideration based on the principle of negating the good and the bad. If the legislator has enacted a ruling for a specific interest, then he is the one who establishes it as an interest; otherwise, it could rationally be that it is not so, since all things are equal in relation to their original state, and reason has no jurisdiction over their goodness or badness. Therefore, the existence of the public interest is from the legislator, such that reason affirms it and the soul finds reassurance in it. The interests, in their essence as interests, have been concluded to be matters of worship, and what is built upon acts of worship can only be worshipful" (1).
It may be said that many rulings observe the consideration of the interests of the servants in the sense of what they are inclined to according to their senses, nature, and habit, or that many rulings have objectives that align with the aims and purposes of the servants. Al-Shatibi's response here is that the public interest is what the legislator has sought or what was intended for it; if this coincides with the worldly interests of the servants, it is incidental, not fundamental. This is a grace from Allah, Exalted is He, to encourage obedience and worship. He says: "The rulings of the Sharia do not escape the five categories; as for obligation and prohibition, their opposition to the inclination that falls under choice is evident, as it is said: 'Do such and such, whether you have an interest in it or not.' And 'Do not do such and such, whether you have an interest in it or not.' If the obligated person has an interest that aligns with the desire that motivates the command or prohibition, it is incidental, not fundamental. As for the other categories, although their apparent nature falls under the choice of the obligated person, they have entered under the legislator's choice, and thus they revert to being removed from his choice" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, p. 219.
(2) The same source, 2/216.


[Page 229]

He said: "If Allah had willed, He would have imposed it upon us while we turn away from worldly gains, or He would have imposed it upon us while stripping us of the innate inclinations. However, He has bestowed upon His servants what He made a means to what He intended for the cultivation of this world for the Hereafter, and He made the pursuit of these gains permissible, not prohibited, but according to legal regulations that are more effective in terms of benefit (maslaha) and more enduring than what the servant considers to be beneficial { and Allah knows, while you do not know } (1). If He had willed, He could have prevented us from seeking the gains of the Hereafter, for He is the Owner and has the ultimate argument, but He encouraged us to fulfill the rights that are obligatory upon us with the promise of a share for us, and He hastened for us many shares from that which we enjoy on the path of what we have been commanded" (2).
Based on this, al-Shatibi's concept of benefits and harms is that the legal rulings were established for specific purposes. The action required by the Sharia has a desired purpose or purposes, and the action that is prohibited has results that are desired to be absent. These purposes of the rulings are the objectives of the legislator, and since they are objectives of the legislator, what is sought from them is called benefit (maslaha), and what is intended to be avoided is called harm (mafsada), whether it is appropriate or not.
Moreover, among the terms that one should be attentive to their meanings according to al-Shatibi are the terms particular (جزئي) and branch (فرع), and the meaning of returning to the definitive (قطعي), due to the differences in their meanings according to him compared to what may come to the reader's mind. The meanings of these terms have been clarified by him in the first section of this chapter.

Chapter Four
The Intention of the Legislator in Establishing the Sharia from the Beginning
And in Establishing it for Understanding

Introduction:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 216.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 2/123.


[Page 230]

Based on what was mentioned in the previous chapter regarding the criteria set by al-Shatibi for the causes (illal) or objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), he establishes a new matter and considers it a reconciliation between those who differ on the issue of justifying rulings through appropriate attributes or legal meanings, or other matters that some have considered pathways for justification.
For example: the disagreement regarding the reasoning behind the prohibition of alcohol due to intoxication, where the reasoners stated that intoxication is a reason even if it is not explicitly mentioned or understood from the discourse, based on the principle of reasoning and the appropriateness of the description. On the other hand, those who oppose this reasoning argue that it is not indicated by the Sharia nor understood from the discourse, but rather it is something that the reasoner inclines towards and imagines its correctness in his heart; thus, it is a product of the whims of the mind and not from the indications of the Sharia. Al-Shatibi came with his methodology or criteria for reasoning to say that this reasoning or this description, in itself, is not indicated by the legal discourse. Therefore, reasoning based on it is a matter of beautification and vilification. However, since it has been established that legislation was for the sake of goals, reasons, objectives (maqasid) or rulings, it has been established that it is permissible for the jurist (mujtahid) to search for the wisdom behind the prohibition of alcohol. With Al-Shatibi's condition for certainty regarding the reason or objective or that it returns to something certain, the reason determined by the jurist cannot merely be an appropriate description, nor is that a requirement at all; rather, it must be something established through induction or returning to a principle or meaning that is certainly established through that method. Accordingly, the claim of the reason of intoxication, if this meaning is not certain, has no value in the Sharia. However, since the preservation of the intellect is a meaning that the legislator intended to achieve with certainty and has become a firmly established principle in the religion, and since reasoning based on intoxication returns in its meaning to this certain principle - which is the preservation of the intellect - therefore, reasoning based on intoxication is valid.


[Page 231]

Thus, it becomes clear that he agrees with the Hanafis, for example, in that the mere existence of meaning in a ruling or in some rulings does not benefit in the process of reasoning, and he agrees with the Shafi'is in the validity of reasoning or searching for the meanings intended by the Legislator, while he disagrees with the Hanafis in their rejection of this reasoning, and he disagrees with the Shafi'is in being satisfied with the meaning being a presumption of being intended by the Legislator and being satisfied with a few evidences based on the meaning, as in the appropriate cases, or with a single evidence as in the rare cases, or merely its existence in the ruling as in the mursal (unattributed hadith). We have explained this matter in detail in the first chapter.
With these criteria, al-Shatibi enters into the discussion of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and he explained these criteria in the first part of his book, dividing them into two sections: the first is the introductions that he deemed necessary for understanding his book, and the second is the Book of Rulings. As for the objectives, he made them the third section of his book, which occupied the second part of it. The third and fourth parts, which complete his book al-Muwafaqat, contain the fourth and fifth sections, which are applications of his idea regarding the objectives, or his methodology in establishing the principles based on the sciences of the Qur'an and the Sunnah.
The idea of the objectives of the Sharia and their division into three categories: necessary, need-based, and embellishing, along with the addition of supplements for each category, is not new to al-Shatibi; it first appeared through Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni, and Allah knows best. Many scholars followed this matter after him. However, what is new in al-Shatibi's approach is his stipulation of certainty for the objective to be considered legal, and his requirement of induction as a means to that end, as well as his understanding of benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid). Furthermore, his discussion on the objectives is characterized by detail, arrangement, and classification that is absent in his predecessors.
According to him, the objectives are divided into two categories: the objectives of the Legislator and the objectives of the obligated person (mukallaf). The objectives of the Legislator are of four types: the first is His intention in establishing the Sharia from the outset, which is the type that the legal theorists (usuliyyun) referred to before him, and in it, the division of objectives into necessary, need-based, and embellishing occurs.


[Page 232]

The second: his intention in establishing the Sharia for understanding. The third: his intention in establishing the Sharia for obligations according to it, and the fourth: his intention in the compliance of the obligated person and their submission to its ruling. Al-Shatibi says: "The objectives that are considered are of two types: one refers to the intention of the legislator, and the other refers to the intention of the obligated person. The first is considered in terms of the legislator's intention in establishing the Sharia from the outset. And in terms of his intention in establishing it for understanding. And in terms of his intention in establishing it for obligations according to it. And in terms of his intention in having the obligated person submit to its ruling; these are four types" (1).
The subject of this chapter is the first two types. As for the third and fourth types, they are the subject of the following chapter - if Allah wills.
The first discussion
The intention of the legislator in establishing the Sharia from the outset

The meaning of this type:
Establishing the Sharia from the outset refers to the obligation of it, meaning the commands and prohibitions. This type represents the objectives of the legislator regarding obligations, such that the obligations are the causes for their effects, which are the objectives of the legislator through them; it is correct to refer to this type as the objectives of the Sharia.
The objectives are of three categories:
These objectives are understood from the legal discourse and from the legal obligations. Al-Shatibi says: "The obligations of the Sharia relate to preserving its objectives in creation, and these objectives do not exceed three categories: the first is that they are necessary, the second is that they are needed, and the third is that they are embellishing" (2). He then defines the limits of each of these three categories and clarifies that the legislator's intention to preserve them is evident in all obligations of the Sharia, as the obligations of the Sharia are the rulings of acts of worship, customs, transactions, and crimes. In these four, the legislator's intention to preserve the necessities, needs, and embellishments is evident.
An introduction to these three categories:
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat: 2/2.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat: 2/3 - 4.


[Page 233]

He said: "As for the necessities, their meaning is that they are essential for the establishment of the interests of both religion and the world, such that if they are lost, the interests of the world will not proceed in a proper manner, but rather in corruption, chaos, and the loss of life. In the Hereafter, it results in the loss of salvation and bliss, and returning with manifest loss" (1). With this description, the necessities are defined by their specific entities. He states: "The total number of necessities is five: the preservation of religion, life, lineage, wealth, and intellect, and it has been said that they are to be observed in every community" (2). He also said: "As for the needs, their meaning is that they are required in terms of expansion and alleviating the constraints that generally lead to hardship and difficulty resulting from the loss of what is sought. If they are not observed, hardship and difficulty will generally befall the obligated, but it will not reach the level of the ordinary corruption expected in public interests." The public interests, that is, the necessities, and based on this definition, the principle of not imposing what is beyond one's capacity and the alleviation of hardship are foundational or essential rules.
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) The same source, 2/4.


[Page 234]

He said: "As for the enhancements, their meaning is to adopt what is appropriate from the virtues of customs and to avoid the disgraceful conditions that rational minds abhor, and this encompasses the category of noble character (makarim al-akhlaq)"(1). He also said: "The absence of these does not negate a necessary or a needful matter, but rather it falls under the category of enhancement and adornment"(2). To further clarify the limits of each of these ranks, he states: "The needful matters revolve around the necessary ones, as do the enhancements"(3). He says: "For whoever seeks more, the needful matters revolve around expansion, facilitation, alleviation of hardship, and kindness. In relation to religion, this appears in legal instances of concessions in purification, such as tayammum (dry ablution), the lifting of the ruling of impurity when its removal is difficult, shortening the prayer, lifting the obligation of prayer due to fainting, praying while seated or on one's side, and breaking the fast while traveling or ill"(4). He states: "The category of enhancements also operates similarly to the needful matters, as it pertains to acting upon noble character and what is appropriate in the course of customs, such as purifications in relation to prayers according to the opinion of those who consider it to be in this category(5), taking adornment from clothing, the virtues of appearances, perfumes, and similar matters, selecting the best and highest in zakat (almsgiving) and expenditures, and the etiquette of kindness in fasting, as well as in relation to souls, such as kindness and benevolence, and the etiquette of eating and drinking, and so forth, and in relation to offspring, such as maintaining good conduct and parting with kindness"(6). In his book, there are more examples for those who wish to seek further clarification(7).
The operation of these objectives in all obligations of the Sharia:

(5) Purification oscillates between being an enhancement or a complement to the preservation of religion from necessities, which is preferable according to his methodology. Unless it is understood in the sense of cleanliness and the removal of impurities, which are repugnant to nature, the demand for it by the Sharia would categorize it as an enhancement according to his methodology.
(6) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/17.
