[Page 235]

As for necessities, he says: "The foundations of acts of worship are related to the preservation of religion in terms of existence, such as faith, the utterance of the two testimonies, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage, and similar matters. Customs are related to the preservation of the self and intellect in terms of existence as well, such as consuming food and drink, clothing, and housing, and similar matters. Transactions are related to the preservation of lineage and wealth in terms of existence... and crimes, which are encompassed by the command to enjoin good and forbid evil, relate to the preservation of all in terms of non-existence" (1).
Regarding needs, he says: "They pertain to acts of worship, customs, transactions, and crimes. In acts of worship, they are like the concessions that ease the burden of illness and travel (2). In customs, they include the permissibility of hunting and enjoying permissible delights in food, drink, clothing, housing, transportation, and similar matters. In transactions, they include partnerships, agricultural contracts, and forward sales... In crimes, they include rulings on blood money, compensation, oaths, and the liability of craftsmen, and similar matters" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/4.
(2) It was clarified in the previous chapter that concessions are partial and do not relate to general principles, and here he brings them as an example of needs, which are general objectives. The explanation is that some legal concessions do not consider the existence of hardship or difficulty, such as the travel of one who does not experience hardship. Some concessions, however, do show hardship; those that display undue hardship are classified as needs not because of the existence of legal concessions, but because the absence of obligation to endure undue hardships, whether there is a concession or not, is among the foundational needs according to al-Shatibi. Therefore, he did not say "like the easing concessions," but rather qualified it by saying: "in relation to the occurrence of hardship due to illness or travel."
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/5.


[Page 236]

And regarding improvements, he says: "They are applicable in the same contexts as the two prior categories" (1), meaning the necessities and needs. "In acts of worship, such as the removal of impurities, and in general all forms of purification, covering the private parts, adorning oneself, and drawing closer through voluntary good deeds like charity and acts of devotion, and similar matters; in customary practices, such as the etiquette of eating and drinking, avoiding impure foods and drinks, and avoiding extravagance and stinginess in consumption; in transactions, such as the prohibition of selling impurities, the preference for water and pasture, depriving a slave of the position of testimony and leadership, and depriving a woman of the position of leadership and marrying herself... and in criminal matters, such as the prohibition of killing a free person with a slave or killing women, children, and monks in warfare" (2).
Complements or additions to the objectives:
Each section of these three categories is accompanied by what is like a complement or addition. This means that if it were absent, it would not undermine the objective or the foundation. For example, retribution (qisas) is essential for the preservation of life, while its equivalence is complementary. The prohibition of alcohol is essential for the preservation of the intellect, while the prohibition of a small amount that does not intoxicate is complementary. Selling, for instance, is essential for the preservation of wealth, while witnessing and pledging in it are complementary. Purification, for example, is among the improvements, and the recommended acts of purification are complementary. Shortening prayers during travel, which involves hardship, is among the needs, while combining prayers in it is complementary (3).
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/5. It becomes clear from the examples that al-Shatibi provided for the three categories that some of them may be inclined towards by natural dispositions and sound instincts, or in his words when defining improvements "the sound intellects," which may mislead the reader into thinking that these objectives or interests are also so according to rational individuals and wise people, but this is not the case as clarified by his understanding of interests and harms. However, the occurrence of objectives sometimes according to what human characteristics require and what sound instincts aspire to, or in his words "the sound intellects," occurs incidentally as a favor from Allah to encourage obedience.
(3) See: the same source, 2/5 - 6.


[Page 237]

The complement, in as much as it is a complement to an essential, necessary, or enhancing aspect, must be considered a condition, which is that it does not invalidate the original. The invalidation of the original results in the invalidation of the complement. Al-Shatibi gives examples of this, including jihad, which is essential for the preservation of the religion. He says: "Jihad is necessary, and the ruler in it is necessary, and justice in it is a complement to necessity. If the complement returns to invalidate the original, it is not considered. Therefore, the command for jihad with unjust rulers came from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), as well as the command to pray behind wicked rulers, for in abandoning that, one abandons the Sunnah of the congregation, and the congregation is one of the required symbols of the religion, and justice complements that requirement, and the original is not invalidated by the complement." (1)
With the invalidation of the original, the complement is invalidated, whereas with the invalidation of the complement, the original is not invalidated, even though it may be affected in some way. Al-Shatibi considers enhancements to be like the complement to necessities, and both are like the complement to essentials. Thus, the Sharia is based on the preservation of necessities. He says: "The interests of religion and the world are based on the preservation of five matters... If religion is absent, the expected reward will not be realized; if the obligated person is absent, there will be no one to practice religion; if reason is absent, the practice of religion will cease; if progeny is absent, there will be no continuity in the usual manner; and if wealth is absent, there will be no sustenance." (2) This means that the absence of necessities leads to the absence of needs and enhancements. Necessities, along with others, are like the described with the attribute; they cannot exist without each other, while the latter can exist without the former.
The varying ranks of objectives:
__________
(1) The same source, 2/7.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/7 - 8.


[Page 238]

How can one determine whether the objective (maqsad) is of the rank of necessities, needs, or enhancements? We have previously clarified the limits of each rank and provided examples for them. Nevertheless, the reader may wonder what makes pilgrimage (hajj), prayer (salah), or jihad (struggle) classified as necessities. Are they not things that, if neglected, would disrupt life, lead to chaos, and cause life to be lost? There are large societies in the world that do not observe these matters, and yet the feared consequences have not occurred. There are countries and communities that permit fornication, usury, and drinking alcohol, even though prohibiting these is necessary for the preservation of lineage, wealth, and intellect. What then makes, for example, the prohibition of pork and carrion classified as enhancements, or certain animals impure, or alcohol impure, while avoiding impurities is considered an enhancement? Yet, there are people who consume pork and carrion, live in the same place as dogs, drink alcohol, and use alcohol-based perfumes, without finding this to be something that rational minds would reject or that souls would abhor.
Similarly, how can fasting (sawm) be considered a necessity, while the lifting of obligations due to hardships or what is beyond one's capacity is classified as a need? Why is it not the other way around?
Al-Shatibi's answer to this matter is that it is a legal (shari) determination, not a rational one. Just as an objective cannot be classified as such unless the law indicates it through beneficial induction leading to certainty, the rank of the objective is also determined by the law, and this will be clarified with texts from him. However, there is a flawed perspective in viewing these objectives, which is based on identifying objectives or interests according to the prevailing concepts in society, or based on the concepts held by those with insight, knowledge, and experience, or decisions in society. These concepts may be influenced by legal rulings or may not be, and in this regard, these objectives are considered interests and deemed legal, upon which legislation is built. Those who contribute to or serve these objectives are considered legal, while those who undermine them are deemed corrupt and prohibited or unlawful. Al-Shatibi has repeatedly refuted this understanding in his Muwafaqat, yet there are still those who advocate it and attribute it to the law and to al-Shatibi.


[Page 239]

And this division of the objectives (maqasid) can be understood from two perspectives:
The first: The observable reality in humans is that they have needs, and these needs vary in life and differ in the degree of necessity. Some needs are indispensable for human survival, and their absence leads to death; others are essential for the community, and their absence leads to chaos and conflict; some lead to disturbance and hardship; and some are less critical than that, and so on. It is natural for a human, when legislating or trying to understand the philosophy of any legislation, to take into account what they perceive of these needs and the degree of necessity for them. They would formulate their legislation according to what they see as achieving the best outcomes based on their concepts, and it is natural for them to include in their considerations the trade-offs between interests and harms according to their understandings. Thus, a person may consider some needs as essential and others as luxury, and others as falling in between. All of this is based on what they perceive and find within themselves. People differ in this regard based on their concepts; some may see freedom of belief and freedom of opinion and the right to change one's religion as fundamental human rights and a necessary need, thus considering the right to apostasy as a necessity. Others may view this as one of the greatest evils, believing that the necessity is to kill the apostate after giving them a chance to repent if they do not return, as it is essential for preserving the faith. Some may see adultery as a corruption that undermines the fundamental objective of preserving lineage, while others view it as a personal freedom and an interest. Some see usury as a necessity for society and transactions, ranking it among the essentials, while others regard it as a need, and yet others consider it one of the greatest evils.


[Page 240]

The determination of a person regarding benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid) and the preference between them returns to two matters: the first is his characteristics and nature as a human being, which lead him to seek food, drink, shelter, wealth, pride, praise, security, and prosperity, and to aim at preserving his life and satisfying his desires, as well as protecting his children and family, and so on. He feels that these things are benefits or good, and their loss is a harm or evil. The second matter is what concepts are formed within a person, whether as a result of thought and conviction, such as someone who believes that gambling or cheating is forbidden, thus viewing it as a harm even though ownership is a benefit in itself, or that adultery is forbidden, leading him to judge it as a harm, or someone who does not believe in Islam or in resurrection and accountability, seeing gambling, usury, or adultery as a benefit. Or it may not be due to thought and conviction, but rather as a result of upbringing and environment, such as someone who grows up among Muslims and develops a sense of preserving honor and a revulsion towards adultery, and a disgust for pigs or carrion... or someone who grows up among non-Muslims and develops a veneration for idols and feels that destroying them is a harm, or does not feel disgust at kissing dogs or does not find adultery repugnant...
Based on this, people's perspectives on benefits and harms vary, and they contradict and differ in their preferences.
The second aspect from which the classification of objectives (maqasid) and the determination of their ranks arises is what is understood by one who has embraced Islam and realized that he is a servant of Allah, that Islam is Allah's law for all people, that there is no ruling except for Allah, and that it is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, to have any choice in their affair. And that every legislation from anyone other than Allah is tyranny (taghut). Thus, he begins to understand Allah's objectives in legislation, and he starts to affirm what the Sharia has deemed good, and to condemn what it has deemed bad, to magnify what the Sharia has indicated is great, and to belittle what it has indicated is small, and so on. The judgment of what is a benefit and what is a harm thus becomes dependent on the Sharia, determining what is a benefit and what is a harm, and clarifying what is known (ma'ruf) and what is condemned (munkar), what is good and what is evil.


[Page 241]

Similarly, the matter regarding the ranks of the objectives (maqasid) is as follows: the necessities are what the legislator has requested and repeated his request or emphasized it to a certain degree, while the needs are what the legislator has requested and confirmed to a certain degree without reaching the first level. Likewise, what the legislator has requested in a manner that places it at a lower rank is called enhancements.
From this perspective, the second aspect, al-Shatibi divided the objectives into three categories: necessary, needful, and enhancing. Here are a few clear and decisive texts from him that illustrate his methodology in this matter to clarify the rank of the objective within these categories or its rank within a single category.
He says: "Indeed, before the rise of this light (1), we were groping about like the blind, and our minds were running in pursuit of our interests in a disordered manner, due to their weakness in bearing these burdens, and the participation of hasty desires... So we place poisons in the place of remedies (2)... and we derive barren analogies, and we seek the signs of health from a sick body, and we walk on our faces while we think we are walking on the straight path, until the pure compulsion appeared in the face of destiny and the reality of the hands of necessity was raised to the One, the All-Compelling" (3).
__________
(1) This light refers to Islam.
(2) That is, we consider an interest to be a harm and a harm to be an interest.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/2. That is, Islam came and clarified the interests and harms, and the reality of human incapacity and their need for someone to clarify that for them, and that is only Allah.


[Page 242]

He says: "Indeed, these three ranks serve one another and specify one another. If that is the case, then it is necessary to consider the whole in its contexts and according to its conditions. Moreover, the legislator (al-shari) considers from this what cannot be comprehended by minds except through explicit text, which is most of what the Sharia indicates in particulars. This is because rational individuals during periods of ignorance used to preserve those things according to their rational perspectives, but in a manner that did not lead them to justice among creation and equity among them. Rather, during that time, chaos occurred, and one interest (maslaha) would undermine another, or destroy one principle or another. Thus, the legislator came to consider absolute interest and equity at all times, clarifying the interests that are consistent and those that are opposed by another aspect of interest."(1)
The meaning of this text is that in the time of ignorance, when the rulings of the Sharia are obscured and only the general principles or some of them remain, rational individuals strive to preserve what remains by establishing rulings or particulars of their own that they see—through their rational perspectives—as achieving the preservation of those general principles. However, when they preserved one interest, they would destroy another, meaning that they would see evils as interests until the law came and clarified what is considered an interest and what is not.
__________
(1) The same source, 3/15.


[Page 243]

He said: "The concept derived from the position of the Legislator is that obedience or disobedience is magnified according to the magnitude of the benefit (maslaha) or harm (mafsada) resulting from it. It is known from the Sharia that the five essential needs are recognized in every community, and the greatest harms are those that occur from neglecting them. The evidence for this is found in the threats associated with neglecting them, such as disbelief, murder, and what pertains to it, adultery, theft, and drinking alcohol, along with other matters for which a punishment or threat has been established. In contrast, matters related to needs (hajiyat) or enhancements (tahsinayat) do not have a specific threat or a known punishment associated with them. If that is the case, it pertains to a necessary matter, and induction (istiqra) clarifies this" (1). Thus, the necessities are those that the Sharia has specified with a threat or a known punishment to protect them from non-existence. He said: "Each of these ranks, being different in the degree of consideration, has the necessities as the most emphasized, followed by the needs and then the enhancements" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/9.
(2) The same source, 2/12-13.


[Page 244]

He said: "The commands in the Sharia do not all carry the same level of emphasis, nor do they fall under a single intention. The commands related to necessary matters are not like those related to needs, nor are they like those related to enhancements, nor are the matters that complete necessities like the necessities themselves; rather, there is a known distinction between them. Indeed, the necessary matters are not all demanded in the same manner; for example, the demand related to the foundation of religion is not emphasized like that of the soul, nor is the soul emphasized like that of the intellect, compared to other types of necessities (1) and needs as well... Similarly, enhancements are treated in the same manner, word for word... The criterion in this is to examine each matter to see whether it is sought in the first intention or the second intention. If it is sought in the first intention, it is in the highest ranks of that type (2). If it is among those sought in the second intention (3), one must consider whether the necessary can exist without it to the extent that the action can still be called that necessity or not. If it cannot, then that sought matter takes the place of the pillar and the part that is essential to the necessity. If it can be referred to by that name without it, then that sought matter is not a pillar but rather a complement and an addition, either from the needs or from the enhancements, and one should look at its ranks in the order mentioned or similar to it based on what inductive reasoning leads to in the Sharia regarding each part of it" (4).
__________
(1) This means that the order of necessities is as follows, from highest to lowest: religion, then the soul, then the intellect, then lineage, then wealth.
(2) That is, from the five types of necessities.
(3) The meaning of primary objectives and secondary objectives was previously explained in the last chapter. The second objective is a secondary objective that has been established as serving the primary objective, which is the first.
(4) Al-Muwafaqat: 3/120 - 121.


[Page 245]

What this text means is that the five necessities are the primary objectives (maqasid). Other objectives are considered thereafter. If they are such that the necessity cannot be established without them, then they are among the necessities in that category which cannot be established without them. For instance, jihad preserves the religion, and thus it is a necessity for the preservation of the religion, as are the five pillars, the killing of the apostate, the supreme leadership (imama al-uzma), and the prohibition of killing and retribution, which are essential for the preservation of life; therefore, they are necessities in this category, namely the preservation of life. This applies to other categories as well. However, if that category of necessities is not negated or lost by the absence of a particular objective, then this objective is not considered a necessity but rather one of its complements, which may be classified as needs (hajiyat) or enhancements (tahsinat). For example, cleanliness in acts of worship does not undermine the essence of preserving the religion, nor does shortening prayers or breaking the fast while traveling. Similarly, drinking a drop of alcohol does not invalidate the essence of preserving the intellect, so it is not classified as a necessity. The same principle applies to the complements of necessities to determine their classification as needs, enhancements, or complements of either. All of this is based on the examination of the legal texts (nusus) and their meanings. What can be established through examination is considered an objective, while what cannot be established may either serve an objective, thus being a branch related to it, or negate an objective, in which case it is rejected, or it may neither negate nor serve, in which case it is suspended and not considered a branch but rather a detail. A careful consideration of this previous text summarizes this matter from its methodology.


[Page 246]

He also states, affirming this meaning and that the ranks of the objectives (maqasid) are derived from the Sharia: "An action is considered in the Sharia based on the benefits and harms it entails. The Sharia has clarified this and distinguished between actions whose benefits are significant, making them a pillar, or whose harms are significant, making them a major sin. It has also distinguished what is not so, calling the benefits good and the harms minor sins. In this way, what is part of the fundamentals of religion and its principles is distinguished from what is part of its branches and details, and what is known as major sins is distinguished from minor sins. What the Sharia has elevated in the commandments is part of the fundamentals of religion, while what it has placed below that is part of its branches and complements. What it has deemed significant in the prohibitions is part of the major sins, while what is below that is part of the minor sins, and this is according to the extent of benefit and harm" (1).
From the previous two texts, we conclude that al-Shatibi refers to the necessities, which are five, or what cannot be established without these five, calling them the pillars or principles of religion, while what is below them he calls the complements or branches of religion. Violating the necessities is considered a major sin in terms of harms or sins.
This difference in the ranks of the objectives does not mean neglecting any objective under the pretext of preserving what is more certain, nor does it justify contradicting or changing rulings under the guise of objectives, because these objectives are established based on the extrapolation of rulings and their meanings. The rulings serve as the foundations for the objectives, and the objectives are built upon them. By nullifying the foundation, what is built upon it is also nullified. Thus, the objectives are the objectives of the Sharia, and the Sharia is fixed and does not change or alter. It is not correct to invoke the objectives for that reason. This is what is implied in al-Shatibi's statement that the Sharia is infallible, which is the subject of the next discussion.

Second Discussion
The Infallibility of the Sharia
The meaning of this expression:
__________
(1) al-Muwafaqat: 1/149 - 150.


[Page 247]

This means that the rulings of the Sharia (Islamic law) are preserved from change, alteration, abrogation, or distortion, and Allah has taken upon Himself the task of preserving them, so nothing of that sort will occur within them, unlike the previous laws. The evidence for this is from two aspects: the first is the legal texts, such as His saying, Exalted is He: { Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it } (1), and this preservation includes the Sunnah (traditions of the Prophet), even if the texts do not explicitly mention it (2). The second aspect of the evidence is the reality from the time of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) until now, where Allah, Exalted is He, has appointed individuals to preserve this Sharia through their efforts, defending it and striving for it in every science that understanding the Sharia depends upon. Al-Shatibi said: "This blessed Sharia is infallible just as its Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is infallible, and just as its community is infallible in what they have agreed upon" (3). Among those whom Allah has appointed to preserve His religion are the scholars who understood the objectives of the Sharia from the Book and the Sunnah. He says: "And Allah sent from among them leaders who understood from Allah and from His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), deriving rulings and comprehending their meanings from the purposes of the Sharia in the Book and the Sunnah, sometimes from the very words, sometimes from their meanings, and sometimes from the rationale behind the ruling, until they applied the incidents that were not mentioned to those that were, and made the path easy for those who came after them, and thus the matter has proceeded in every science that understanding the Sharia depends upon, which is the very preservation that the transmitted evidences entail, and with Allah is success" (4).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Hijr, 9.
(2) It is clarified in the third chapter that Al-Shatibi's view is that the preservation guaranteed by the verse is for the general principles and not for the particulars. The particulars follow the general principles, which are the particulars that return to the general principles, and thus he said regarding the Sunnah: "And the Sunnah, even if it is not mentioned (i.e., in the guaranteed preservation), is an explanation of it (i.e., the Book) and revolves around it; it is from it, and to it returns in its meanings, so each of the Book and the Sunnah supports the other" Al-Muwafaqat, 2/38.
(3) Al-Muwafaqat, 2/38.
(4) The same source, 2/40.


[Page 248]

One consequence of this is that the particulars derived from texts of uncertain authenticity or uncertain meanings will remain the sources of the universals, and they are the subject of induction. It is not correct to claim the preservation of the universals by any means, for the universals have no path except through these particulars. Just as it is impermissible to neglect the universals, neglecting the particulars is similar. On the other hand, neglecting the particulars is a neglect of the universals. He says: "If a universal principle is established in these three (1) or in any of them, it must be preserved in relation to what the universal entails, which are the particulars. The particulars are intended and considered in establishing the universal; if the universal is neglected, its intended benefit in legislation will also be neglected" (2). He then presented evidence for this and said: "And since this is the case, it indicates that the particulars are included in the demand and preservation of the universals" (3). He said: "If the particulars were not considered and intended in establishing the universal, the command regarding the universal would not be valid in the first place, because the universal, as such, cannot be the object of obligation" (4).
__________
(1) The three: namely, necessities, needs, and enhancements.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/41.
(3) The same source.
(4) This is because these universals are objectives in the sense of results or causes, and obligation only pertains to the causes, not to the results, as they belong to Allah and not to the servant, and obligation regarding them is beyond the servant's capacity.


[Page 249]

And based on this, it is not permissible to disregard or neglect the particulars (juz'iyyat) under the pretext of the universals (kulliyyat), nor is it correct to object here by stating that the absence of individual particulars does not affect the establishment of the universals. He says: "There is no doubt in the necessity of intention towards the particular" (1) and he says: "The absence of the particular there is only due to the preservation of the particular in its universality from another perspective, just as we say that the preservation of lives is legislated, and this is a universal that is definitively intended by the Legislator, then retribution (qisas) was legislated for the preservation of lives, so killing a soul in retribution is a preservation of it by intention, and it necessitates the absence of a particular from the particulars of the universal being preserved, which is the destruction of this soul due to an incidental occurrence, which is the assault on the soul. Thus, neglecting this particular in its universality from the perspective of preserving a particular in its universality as well, which is the assaulted soul... Therefore, the absence of individual particulars from the requirement of the universal, if it is for no incidental reason, is not valid legally, and if it is for an incidental reason, then it pertains to the preservation of the universal from another perspective or to the preservation of another universal; the first case would render its absence detrimental to the universal, while the second case would not render its absence detrimental" (2).
It is not permissible to oppose the rulings under the pretext of the objectives (maqasid):
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/42.
(2) The same source.


[Page 250]

The assertion of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and the varying ranks of these objectives, does not justify the violation or alteration of certain rulings under the pretext of preserving their objectives, nor does it justify neglecting some objectives in order to attain what is higher in rank. This is because the universals cannot be preserved by every means, but only by what Allah has legislated for them. Thus, violating the rulings undermines the objectives even if this is not apparent. The particulars and complements in the Sharia were legislated to preserve the necessities, and they serve them. Therefore, the preservation of the necessities can only be achieved through them. Accordingly, what some may occasionally present as opinions or fatwas that disregard the textual evidence under the pretext of preserving the objectives and claim the permissibility of developing or changing the legal rulings based on that are statements that contradict the idea of objectives according to al-Shatibi. He previously stated that those who sought to preserve the universals based on their rational perspectives failed to do so and ended up neglecting the interests and undermining their foundations. He also says: "Every necessary and complementary matter is merely a servant of the essential necessity and a comfort and enhancement of its specific form... In every case, it revolves around serving it, so it is more likely that the necessity will be fulfilled in its best state" (1). He states: "Since each of these ranks is different in the degree of consideration, the necessities are the most emphasized, followed by the needs and then the enhancements. And since they are interconnected, the invalidation of the lighter one is a boldness towards what is more emphasized and a means of disrupting it. Thus, the lighter one is as if it is a protection for the more emphasized, and the one grazing around the protection is close to falling into it" (2). He further states: "If the necessity can be disrupted by the disruption of its complements, then preserving them for its sake is required" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/42.
(2) The same source, 2/12 - 13.
(3) The same source, 2/15.


[Page 251]

He says regarding the change of rulings under the pretext of public interest (maslaha) or objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia): "If they (i.e., the interests) were established in such a way that their system could be disrupted or their rulings could be invalidated, then legislation would not be based on them(1). For their being interests at that point is no more valid than their being harms, but the Legislator intends for them to be interests in all cases, so their establishment must be in that manner eternally, universally, and generally in all types of obligations and for all obligated individuals and in all circumstances, and thus we have found the matter in it, and all praise is due to Allah"(2).
Interpretation of Some Texts of al-Shatibi:
Many contemporary scholars have approached the texts of the Muwafaqat without paying attention to the true meanings of their content, attributing to al-Shatibi opinions that he does not hold, but rather refutes and clarifies their invalidity. In reality, many of al-Shatibi's texts, if not viewed based on the premises he established and the principles he articulated, and in such a way that the subsequent texts build upon the preceding ones, will lead to ambiguities and suggest contradictions between some of the texts.
Some of the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) have produced reports that hold no value in Sharia, mistakenly believing that they are relying on the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), like one who claims that wherever there is public interest (maslaha), there is the law of Allah, or that the path to what is permissible (mubah) is permissible, or like one who says that Allah has prohibited what our minds perceive as harmful and permitted what our minds perceive as beneficial, or something similar to that.
And if some do this claiming to rely on al-Shatibi, there are those who have realized that al-Shatibi's ideas do not apply to these meanings. Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour - for example - points out, in the context of his assertion that the Sharia is based on the interests of the servants, that most of al-Shatibi's arguments on this matter are invalid. This is due to the fact that what is being argued for according to al-Shatibi is different from what is held by the Sheikh(3).
Therefore, Dr. Abdullah Daraz saw a contradiction between some texts of al-Shatibi.
__________
(1) That is, for the purpose of achieving them, because they are objectives, and the legal rulings are the means to them, or the rulings are causes and the interests are the effects.
(2) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/25.
(3) See p. 181 of this book.


[Page 252]

Al-Shatibi says in the fifth issue of the first type of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia): "The interests (masalih) spread in this world are considered from two perspectives: from the perspective of their existence and from the perspective of the attachment of the legal ruling to them. As for the first perspective: the worldly interests, in terms of their existence here, cannot be purely considered as interests. By interests, I mean those that pertain to the sustenance of human life, the completeness of his existence, and the fulfillment of his sensual and rational attributes in general, so that he is in a state of abundance in every respect. This, in mere habitual terms, cannot be the case because those interests are mixed with obligations and hardships, whether few or many, and are accompanied by, preceded by, or followed by matters such as eating, drinking, clothing, housing, riding, marriage, and others. These matters can only be attained through effort and toil. Likewise, worldly harms (mafasid) are not purely harms in terms of their existence, as there is no harm that is typically imposed without being accompanied by or preceded by much kindness, gentleness, and enjoyment of pleasures. If that is the case, then the interests and harms related to this world are understood according to what predominates. If the predominant aspect is an interest, then it is the understood interest by common consent; if the other aspect predominates, then it is the understood harm by common consent. Therefore, an action with dual aspects is attributed to the predominant side... according to what is customary in similar cases... As for the second perspective regarding the attachment of the legal ruling to them, if the interest is predominant when compared to the harm in terms of habitual judgment, it is the one intended by the Sharia. For its attainment, the demand upon the servants has arisen... If it is followed by a harm or hardship, it is not intended in the legality of that action and its demand. Similarly, if the harm is predominant in relation to the interest in habitual judgment, then its removal is the intended goal in the Sharia, and for this reason, prohibition has been established... If it is followed by an interest or pleasure, it is not the intended goal of the prohibition of that action, but rather the intended goal is what predominates in the situation."(1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/15 - 16 - 17.


[Page 253]

In the eighth issue of the first type of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), he says: "The benefits that are legislated and the harms that are repelled by law are only considered in terms of how they establish worldly life for the sake of the Hereafter, not in terms of the whims of souls in seeking their ordinary benefits or averting their ordinary harms" (1).
These two texts from al-Shatibi in the fifth and eighth issues were seen by Dr. Darraz as contradictory; therefore, he commented on the first text by saying: "The limitation of this view will come in the eighth issue" (2). He commented on the second text by saying: "It is necessary to limit the fifth issue by this so that it does not contradict the apparent meaning there... He based the benefit and harm on what predominates among them in terms of establishing life and attaining the desires that are necessitated by the sensual qualities of man, making it something that is based on being a sought benefit or a repelled harm. Here he says that mere consideration of it as a benefit in the eyes of a person is not considered; what is considered is that it should be such that worldly life is established for the Hereafter, which can only be the case in accordance with the framework of the law that knows the benefit from this perspective, reconciling it with what he has established in the reality of existence" (3). He also said, commenting on another text from al-Shatibi on the same topic: "This alone does not benefit after having previously considered that what predominates in terms of benefit is the benefit, and what is predominant in terms of harm is the harm... Therefore, we said that it is necessary for the correctness of the statement to limit what has preceded by this" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, p. 25.
(2) The same source, 2/26, Dar al-Ma'rifah edition - Beirut, with commentary by Dr. Abdullah Darraz.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, p. 38.
(4) The same location.


[Page 254]

Thus, the issue in this matter has been presented, and before explaining its solution and removal, I would like to point out that Dr. Daraz did not grasp the true meaning intended by al-Shatibi with the terms "maslaha" (public interest) and "mafsada" (harm), understanding them in the sense of benefit and harm. Therefore, he attributed to al-Shatibi the statement that what predominates in terms of benefit is the maslaha, and what is predominant in terms of harm is the mafsada. This is incorrect, and this was not al-Shatibi's statement; rather, he said that what predominates in terms of maslaha is the maslaha understood by custom, and similarly for mafsada. The two matters are different. The maslaha according to al-Shatibi is what has been definitively established as intended by the Lawgiver, and the mafsada is what has been definitively established as prohibited by the Law. As for benefits and harms, they pertain to the interests of the servant and what he loves and dislikes; thus, some benefits are prohibited and some harms are permissible. Therefore, al-Shatibi objected to al-Razi, stating after establishing that the masalih (benefits) and mafasid (harms) are considered in relation to the sustenance of this life for the afterlife: "It is not valid to maintain that the principle regarding benefits is permissibility and regarding harms is prohibition as established by al-Fakhr al-Razi, for there is hardly any true benefit or true harm; rather, most of them are relative" (1), and he adds: "And the masalih and mafasid, if they are related to the address of the Lawgiver... how can it be permissible to generalize this statement that the principle regarding benefits is permissibility and regarding harms is prohibition" (2). Additionally, there is another error, which is the failure to distinguish between al-Shatibi's intention in the fifth issue and his intention in the eighth issue. Dr. Daraz based his objection on al-Shatibi's statement in the fifth issue: "By masalih, I mean what pertains to the establishment of human life and the completion of his existence and attaining what is necessitated by his carnal and rational attributes in general, so that it is a blessing in general."
__________
(1) The same source, 2/27.
(2) The same location.


[Page 255]

To clarify the difference between the two issues, I say: al-Shatibi did not present the fifth issue to define benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), but rather to indicate that they are not limited to mere existence, and that they are limited to the Sharia. As for the text upon which Dr. Daraz based his objection, which raises a problem, its meaning is that what the Sharia has brought forth in terms of commands and prohibitions, and what is established based on it as beneficial and harmful, is what returns to the human being in a way that preserves his life and the completeness of his existence through food, shelter, and other things that his sensual and rational attributes necessitate, such as security, dignity, ownership, and other pleasures of life. These can only be attained through what leads to them, which are the rulings of the Sharia. Therefore, al-Shatibi's text does not say: "By benefits I mean the sustenance of human life and obtaining what his sensual attributes necessitate," but rather says: "By benefits I mean what pertains to the sustenance of human life..." This meaning is clear in al-Shatibi's book for those who reflect upon it, and it will be elaborated upon when discussing the fourth type of the objectives of the Sharia, which is its establishment for compliance. His texts on this matter are numerous; I will mention here a text that suffices for the purpose. He says: "If it is established that the purpose of the Sharia is for the benefits of the servants, then it returns to them according to the command of the legislator and within the limits he has set, not according to their whims and desires... As for the fact that the benefits of obligation return to the obligated person in this world and the hereafter, this is correct, and it does not necessitate that obtaining them is outside the limits of the Sharia, nor that it is attained by oneself without the Sharia providing it to him, which is evident. Thus, it becomes clear that there is no contradiction between this and what has preceded, because what has preceded is a consideration in terms of establishing the benefit and purpose as affirmed by the legislator, not in terms of what is necessitated by whim and desire." (1)
The meaning of the text upon which Dr. Daraz based his objection is that the benefits indicated by the Sharia through induction are those that lead to a person obtaining his shares and purposes, and not that benefits are understood according to what returns to people based on their inclinations and perspectives.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/172 - 118.


[Page 256]

As for the other texts that Dr. Daraz saw as contradictory, what was mentioned in the fifth issue is not intended to define benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), but rather the purpose of the issue is that benefits and harms are viewed from two perspectives. The first perspective is regarding their existence in reality, which here is not absolute; benefits are mixed with harms, and vice versa. That is, the action commanded for a purpose intended by the Legislator results in a legal benefit arising from the action, but the action may also produce other outcomes that are not intended by that command, which may be harms, and vice versa, because harms and benefits are not absolute in reality. For example, jihad is a benefit, and it results in benefits intended by the Legislator, such as the expansion of the authority of Islam, its honor, and the entry of people into it. It also results in the loss of lives, expenditure of wealth, and hardships; are these latter outcomes the intention of the Legislator in jihad? No. Rather, these are harms in the Sharia. Based on this, the saying of al-Shatibi is understood: "If that is the case, then the benefits and harms related to this world are understood according to what predominates." That is, one looks at the benefits, their extent, and the degree of their expectation. Is victory expected or not, and to what degree is that presumed? One also considers the costs in terms of lives and wealth, and the expected outcomes according to those with insight and experience. Therefore, he said: "If the predominant aspect is that of benefit, then it is the understood benefit in customary terms."


[Page 257]

An example of this is also: "Eating, drinking, housing, riding, and marriage, for these matters can only be attained through effort and toil." And as he said: "Those interests are mixed with obligations and hardships." If these are intended interests, then the hardships are evils that are required to be alleviated, according to al-Shatibi. He said: "If the intention of the obligated person is to cause hardship, then he has contradicted the intention of the Lawgiver, in that the Lawgiver does not intend hardship itself with the obligation, and any intention that contradicts the intention of the Lawgiver is void; thus, the intention towards hardship is void, and it is therefore among the things that are prohibited."(1) He also said: "It has been made clear by the Lawgiver that hardship is to be avoided; thus, if He commands something that necessitates it, He does not intend it."(2)
So if interests can only be attained through effort and toil, and these are evils, this means that worldly interests and evils, in terms of their existence in reality, are not absolute, and the ruling on an action is based on what predominates in the situation. He said: "The truth that the Sharia has brought is the combination of these two matters under the consideration of justice, taking from the interests what does not violate an obligation and leaving the interests that do not lead to a prohibition, while maintaining balance in the recommended and the disliked."(3) This indicates his intent with the statement: "And if the other side predominates, it is the understood evil," and with the statement: "According to what has become customary in its like." An explanation of such texts will become clearer and more evident in the discussion of the third type of the objectives of the Sharia, but I will present here a text that clarifies his intent with phrases like "the understood evil or interest" and "according to what has become customary in its like," and his intent in favoring one side over the other based on custom and habit.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/86.
(2) The same source, 2/58.
(3) The same source, 2/99.


[Page 258]

He says that the purchase of grapes, weapons, or a slave, for example, may be for a legitimate purpose (maqasid al-sharia) or for something forbidden (haram). In the first case, it is a benefit (maslaha), and in the second, it is a harm (mafsada). How can one judge which side should be favored over the other when the intention of the actor is hidden from others? In this sense, al-Shatibi speaks of the authority of custom and habit unless the intention of a specific actor is known to be otherwise. He states: "That some benefits are lawful (halal) and some are forbidden (haram) is where the main consideration of the issue lies... that one side is the primary intended purpose by custom, while the other side is a secondary, unintended purpose by habit, unless it is specifically intended and contrary to the norm. There is no doubt that the ruling is for what is primarily intended by custom, while the other has no ruling because if we were to consider the secondary side, it would not be permissible for us to own any of the items or to contract over them, as they contain forbidden benefits... An example of the primacy of lawful benefits is the purchase of a slave with the intention of converting her to Islam for prostitution, purchasing a boy for immoral acts, and buying grapes to turn into wine or weapons to rob... An example of the primacy of forbidden benefits is the purchase of a dog for hunting... and buying wine for vinegar-making and buying the fat of carrion to coat ships or to light for people... If the secondary purpose becomes predominant in intention and precedes in the custom of certain times until what was originally intended becomes as if it were nonexistent, then the ruling reverses. I do not think this can happen in such a general way, but if its occurrence is assumed, the ruling would reverse" (1). More details on this matter will come when discussing the principle of the original and the predominant within the discussion of the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) in chapter nine.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/107 - 108 - 109.


[Page 259]

This is the first aspect of looking at benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), which is that they do not exist in a pure form. As for the second aspect, which is the relation of the legal ruling to them, here there are either pure benefits or pure harms at all times. If the legal demand is for an action, it is for a benefit intended by the legislator. If this action is preceded by, accompanied by, or followed by harms, meaning what is considered harmful by the law, this relates to the fact that benefits and harms do not exist in a pure form in reality. However, these harms are not intended by the legislator with that demand, and their relation to that demand does not imply that they are acceptable or excusable in the legal sense. The existence of certain outcomes for specific rulings is not sufficient to indicate that they are benefits or harms; it is necessary to consider the benefit or harm through the examination of a large number of rulings. Therefore, the benefit established by law remains a benefit, and the same applies to the harm. The fact that harms are related to a desired action and benefits are related to a prohibited action does not change anything regarding the nature of the benefit as a benefit and the harm as a harm, nor does it indicate that benefits have been prohibited or that harms may become desired. This means that benefits and harms are pure in the law, even if they are not pure in terms of existence in reality. Therefore, al-Shatibi says: "The conclusion from this is that the benefits considered by law or the harms considered by law are pure and not mixed with any harms, neither little nor much. Even if it is imagined that they are mixed, they are not in reality so according to the law" (1). Examples of this include work and seeking sustenance for one's dependents, which is a benefit, despite the toil and effort involved; the legislator intended the benefits therein and did not intend the toil and effort. Going out for prayers or seeking knowledge or similar activities, even though there are abominations that are heard and seen along the way, does not change anything regarding what is a benefit and what is a harm. It does not change anything in the legal rulings, and one must avoid abominations as much as possible.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/17.


[Page 260]

He says: "Essential matters or other needs or complementary issues, if they are surrounded by external matters that do not conform to the Sharia, then the endeavor to bring about benefits is valid on the condition of exercising caution to the best of one's ability without hardship, such as marriage, which requires the sustenance of dependents amidst the narrow paths of what is lawful and the vast avenues of what is unlawful and questionable... If such considerations were taken into account in marriage in our time, it would lead to the invalidation of its essence, which is not correct. Likewise, seeking knowledge if it is accompanied by abominations that one hears and sees, and attending funerals and performing religious duties if one can only perform them by witnessing what is not acceptable, does not remove this incidental factor from these matters because they are the foundations of religion and the principles of benefits" (1).
As for al-Shatibi's use of the term "worldly" when he mentions worldly benefits and harms, this is in contrast to the term benefits and harms of the Hereafter, which are the delights of Paradise and the torments of Hellfire. The worldly benefits and harms, although they may not be purely existent in reality, the benefits of the Hereafter are pure benefits, meaning they are untainted by any harms, such as punishment. The harms, that is, the punishment, is pure and not mixed with any benefit for those who are eternally in Hell, while it is mixed with mercy for the monotheists who will return to Paradise. From this mixture, the Fire does not reach their places of prostration and the seat of faith (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/119.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/20 - 21 - 22.


[Page 261]

Thus, it becomes clear that the subject of the fifth issue is consistent and aligned with what is mentioned in the eighth issue, and it is indeed a prelude to it. This is confirmed by al-Shatibi's explanation of how to prioritize and weigh between the two sides where interests and harms conflict in terms of existence, as he states: "In summary, whenever the evidence contradicts, it must be that the two sides are either equal or one is preferred over the other. If they are equal, then there is no ruling from the perspective of the obligated person regarding one side over the other if the equality is evident according to the evidence. Perhaps this does not occur in the Sharia, and if it is assumed to occur, there is no preference except by desire without evidence, and this in matters of the Sharia is invalid by consensus." (1)
As for the eighth issue, it is in harmony with the fifth issue; however, Dr. Daraz's understanding of interests and harms as benefits and detriments, and that they are such according to custom and tradition and based on the views of rational individuals, led him to see an irreconcilable contradiction. Consequently, he made the following comments: "This alone does not benefit after considering previously that what predominates in the direction of benefit is the interest, and what is preferred in the direction of harm is the detriment." He also said: "If the basis of the argument is that rational individuals agree that what is considered is the greater matter, which is the direction of interest that is the foundation of religion and worldly affairs, regardless of the desires of souls, then this can be valid as evidence, but there is no need to mediate the previous premises before it." This indicates that he did not grasp al-Shatibi's intent regarding the fifth issue.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/20.


[Page 262]

As for the clarification of the integration between the two issues, this text confirms it - for example - taken from the eighth issue, which states: "The benefits that are legislated and the harms that are repelled are only considered in terms of establishing worldly life for the afterlife, not in terms of the desires of souls in seeking their ordinary benefits or averting their ordinary harms. The evidence for this consists of several matters: the first is: { And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted } (1). The second is what has been previously mentioned, that the benefits obtained by the obligated person are usually mixed with harms, just as harms are surrounded by benefits. For instance, we say that souls are respected, preserved, and sought to be revived, such that if the matter is between reviving them and destroying wealth, reviving them is preferable. If reviving them opposes the destruction of religion, then reviving religion is preferable even if it leads to their destruction, as in the case of fighting the disbelievers and killing the apostate, and so on. Similarly, if the revival of one soul opposes the destruction of many souls in a conflict, for example, then reviving the many souls is preferable. Likewise, if we say that eating and drinking revives souls and has apparent benefits, even though it involves many hardships and pains in obtaining it initially, in using it at the moment, and in its requirements and consequences ultimately. Nevertheless, what is considered is the greater matter, which is the aspect of benefit that is the foundation of both religion and worldly life, not in terms of the desires of souls" (2).
Al-Shatibi's discussion of some opinions on benefits and harms:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Mu'minun, 71.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 2/25 - 26.


[Page 263]

Al-Shatibi clearly explained his concept of public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada), stating that it is subordinate to the Sharia and not something that is followed. This is not in line with what the earlier scholars considered regarding interests and harms, although al-Ghazali did point to this meaning when he said: "As for public interest, it originally refers to bringing about benefit and averting harm, and we do not mean by that that bringing about benefit and repelling harm are the objectives of creation and the welfare of creation in achieving their objectives. Rather, we mean by public interest the preservation of the objectives of the Sharia, which are five: to protect their religion, their lives, their intellect, their lineage, and their wealth. Anything that entails the preservation of these five foundations is a public interest, and anything that undermines these foundations is a harm, and repelling it is a public interest" (1). By adopting the path of analogy and the strange and remote analogy, he contradicts what al-Shatibi establishes, and it is considered that he justifies public interest in the sense that he stated in this text that he does not mean. This is after incorporating this meaning into the objectives of the legislator.
What we mentioned about al-Ghazali applies to other jurists who consider public interests, such as al-Juwayni, al-Amidi, al-Razi, al-Qarafi, Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam, and others.
This meaning makes public interest—at least theoretically—something that is followed by the Sharia rather than subordinate to it, which leads to complications in the idea of justifying actions based on public interests. From this perspective, al-Shatibi, in his work on al-Muwafaqat, aimed to refine the science of usul al-fiqh.
Therefore, after establishing that public interests and harms are considered in relation to the sustenance of worldly life for the afterlife, and that they relate to enhancement and deprecation, he proceeded to critique or reject some opinions in this field. He rejected al-Razi's statement that the original ruling regarding benefits is permissibility and regarding harms is prohibition, as clarified in the previous pages.
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, al-Mustasfa. 1/286.


[Page 264]

It is also directed at al-Qarafi, as he presented a problem that is considered a refutation of the idea of reasoning based on public interest (maslaha), and it is necessary for all who consider public interests and harms. Al-Shatibi says: "Indeed, al-Qarafi raised a problem regarding public interests and harms and did not respond to it, and it is, for him, necessary for all scholars who consider public interests and harms"(1). Al-Qarafi established that this problem applies to everyone, including the Mu'tazila and others, saying (and the statement is attributed to al-Qarafi): "Because deviating from the principle of public interest and harm is rejected by the principles of the Mu'tazila, for it is foolishness, and they cannot say that the criterion for this is that every public interest for which Allah has threatened punishment for neglecting it, and every harm for which Allah has threatened punishment for committing it, is the intended goal, and what Allah has neglected is not included in our objective"(2). Al-Qarafi's intention here is that the existence of rulings that do not follow the principle of public interests and harms refutes the idea, and he adds (al-Qarafi): "For we say that the threat in your view and the obligation is contingent upon public interest and harm, and it must be, according to you, rationally that Allah threatens punishment for neglecting public interests and committing harms. If you derived the considered public interests and harms from the threat, it would necessitate circular reasoning, and if the derivation in(3) public interests and harms were valid, it would require you to allow that the obligation could come from neglecting public interests and committing harms, and the realities would then be inverted, for what is considered is the obligation, so whatever Allah has commanded is a public interest, and this invalidates your principle"(4). As for those who are not Mu'tazila, who affirm the causality of bringing about public interests and averting harms, al-Qarafi presents them with the following problem: "As for our companions' share of this problem, it is that it becomes impossible for them to say: 'Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, has taken into account absolute public interest and absolute harm... Rather, their way is only to extrapolate from specific instances, and although this detracts from a certain pattern of insight into some of the secrets of jurisprudence, they say: Allah does what He wills and rules as He desires, and Allah considers what He wills and leaves what He wills, nothing more"(5).

(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, p. 29.

The reality is that these issues arise for those who consider benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid) when they are understood as meaning advantages and disadvantages, or the wisdoms (hikmah) and what human attributes necessitate. Therefore, al-Qarafi raised these issues but did not respond to them.
Al-Shatibi addressed these issues, and his response is valid according to his own methodology in considering benefits and harms; thus, his affirmation of the idea of reasoning based on benefit is a correction of the concept of this idea, for both benefit and harm. He says: "As for the Ash'arites, the induction (istiqra) of the Sharia indicates what is considered and what is not considered" (1). Thus, he directs consideration towards the induction that leads to certainty regarding the specific benefit, and he says: "As for the Mu'tazilites, it is the same, because they only consider benefits and harms based on what reason leads them to believe is the way to achieve the general and detailed welfare of the world in benefits or its disruption in harms. They have made the Sharia a revelation of what reason claims without addition or subtraction, so there is no difference between them and the Ash'arites in the outcome of the issue" (2). This means that they do not rely on reason in determining benefits and harms, but rather they rely on the Sharia. Accordingly, there is no issue according to al-Shatibi's methodology because the determination of benefit or harm is referred back to the Sharia. Al-Shatibi critiques the statement of Imam Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam, where he said: "Most of the benefits and harms of this world are known by reason, and that is the essence of most Sharia" (3), and where he said: "As for the benefits and harms of the Hereafter, they are only known through transmission" (4),
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, p. 29.
(2) Same source.
(3) Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam, Qawa'id al-Ahkam fi Masalih al-Anam, 1/7.
(4) Same source, 1/9.


[Page 266]

He said: "As for the interests of the two abodes (darain) and their causes and harms, they can only be known through the Sharia, and if something is hidden from that, it should be sought from the evidences of the Sharia, which are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), sound analogy (qiyas), and correct reasoning. As for the interests of this world and their causes and harms, they are known through necessities, experiences, customs, and credible conjectures. If something is hidden from that, it should be sought from its evidences. Whoever wishes to know the correspondences, interests, and harms, and which are preferred and which are not, should present that to his intellect, assuming that the Sharia did not address it, and then build upon that the rulings, for hardly any ruling will fall outside of that except what Allah has made obligatory upon His servants without informing them of its benefit or harm."(1)

[Page 267]

Al-Shatibi says, objecting to the statements of Ibn Abd al-Salam: "Some people have said that the interests of the Hereafter can only be known through the Sharia, while those of this world can be known through necessities, experiences, customs, and conjectures" (1). He then states: "As for the claim that what pertains to the Hereafter can only be known through the Sharia, that is as he said. However, what he said regarding worldly matters is not entirely accurate, and if it were as he claimed, there would be no need to refer to the Sharia except for the dissemination of the interests of the Hereafter specifically, which is not the case... Custom prevents the independent intellects in this world from discerning their interests and harms in detail, unless this speaker intends that knowledge of them is obtained through experiences and others after the Sharia has established its principles, and there is no dispute about that" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/30 - 31.
(2) The same source. These statements that al-Shatibi attributed to Ibn Abd al-Salam suggest that the latter is a Mu'tazili, especially since al-Shatibi did not mention the name of the speaker. Dr. Daraz commented on these statements by saying: "It resembles the doctrine of the Mu'tazila." See Dr. Daraz's commentary 2/48 from al-Muwafaqat, Dar al-Ma'rifah edition. However, from the words of Ibn Abd al-Salam: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, is not obligated to bring about the interests of the good nor to avert the harms of the evil, just as He is not obligated to create, provide sustenance, impose duties, reward, or punish. Rather, He brings about the interests of the good and averts the harms of the evil out of grace towards His servants. If the matter were reversed, it would not be wrong, for there is no constraint upon Him" (Qawaid al-Ahkam, 1/10). Among other things, Ibn Abd al-Salam said: "And Allah, Exalted is He, has commanded the establishment of harmonious interests and excluded some from that command. He has prohibited similar harms and excluded some from that prohibition" (Qawaid al-Ahkam, 1/6). This confirms the existence of the issue mentioned by his student al-Qarafi.


[Page 268]

One of the issues discussed by al-Shatibi is the disagreement among jurists regarding rulings. If one of them says that an action is permissible, and another says it is forbidden, then considering the benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), if the action is harmful, how could it be permissible according to the first, and if it is beneficial, how could the second prohibit it? This is a problem for those who consider benefits and harms.
Al-Shatibi states that there is no problem here; if it is permissible according to the first, this means that its benefit is predominant in his view, and if it is forbidden according to the second, this means that it is harmful in his view. Thus, the consideration of benefits and harms differs among jurists, and there is no issue. He said: "Some later scholars - namely al-Qarafi - claimed that the argument for benefits only holds if the correct opinion in matters of ijtihad (juristic reasoning) is singular, because the rational principle is that the predominant cannot be both the thing and its opposite. Rather, whenever one is predominant, the other must be less so, and this necessitates that the correct opinion is one, which is the opinion of the one who rules by the predominant, while the others must be mistaken as they rule by the less predominant. This contradicts the principle of those who claim correctness with those who say that the laws are based on benefits. This is what he said, and he quoted his teacher Ibn Abd al-Salam in response, stating that these individuals must say that this principle only applies to consensus rulings" (1). He then refuted this claim, saying: "The benefits or harms in matters of disagreement are established according to what is in the reality of the matter for the jurist and in his view, and there is no difference here between the mistaken and the correct. If the Maliki is convinced that the excess interest in fresh fruits and vegetables is permissible, then the aspect of benefit for him is the predominant one, and it is also so in reality as he perceives it" (2). This means that the action is permissible according to Sharia and thus is a benefit for him. "And if the Shafi'i is convinced that interest in this case is not permissible, then it falls under the ruling of forbidden interest for him, and the aspect of benefit for him is the less predominant one, not the predominant one, and it is also so in reality as he perceives it" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/36.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, 2/37.


[Page 269]

That is, the action is forbidden (haram) and thus the benefit (maslaha) derived from it is outweighed, as it is considered a harm (mafsada) in his view. He then said: "Contradiction only occurs if the preferred (rajih) is considered less preferred (marjuh) from the perspective of one observer; rather, it is from two observers, each of whom believes that the reason upon which the ruling is based exists in the subject according to what is in the reality as he perceives it and in his assumption." (1)
These texts and opinions in al-Shatibi's view emphasize the difference in his understanding of benefit (maslaha) and harm (mafsada) compared to the prevailing understanding among others. He also affirms that the intended meaning for him is that the benefit is what has been established as intended by the Legislator (Shari) regardless of whether it is suitable or unsuitable.

Section Three
The Intention of the Legislator in Establishing the Sharia for Understanding

The meaning of this type:
Al-Shatibi discusses under this type of the objectives of the Legislator five issues related to the Arabic language, in which he establishes the principles that must be followed in order to understand the Sharia from its sources, that is, from the legal texts. He clarifies how meanings are derived from words and structures, what meanings are considered, and what meanings are not considered.
He also discusses whether the meanings of rulings are among the indications of the texts or not. The meanings of rulings are the derived meanings that are taken from the legal objectives.
The Sharia is in the Arabic tongue and style:
__________
(1) The same location.


[Page 270]

The Sharia (Islamic law) was established to achieve the objectives of the Lawgiver (al-Shari) in creation. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the Sharia and the objectives of the Lawgiver. For this reason, the Lawgiver addressed people in a manner they could comprehend, speaking to them in Arabic, using Arabic words, structures, and styles. He obligated them to understand the reports and rulings according to the implications of the texts as understood by the Arabs. Al-Shatibi says: "This blessed Sharia is Arabic, and there is no place for foreign tongues in it" (1). Al-Shatibi does not mean by this that the Qur'an does not contain foreign words; this has been addressed by the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence). Rather, his point is that "it was revealed in the language of the Arabs, with its specific words and styles of meaning, and that it speaks in accordance with what it is naturally inclined to in its language, addressing the general with the intended meaning of its apparent sense, and the general intended in one aspect and the specific in another, and the general intended as specific, and the apparent intended as non-apparent. All of this is understood from the beginning, middle, or end of the speech, and it speaks in a way that its beginning indicates its end or its end indicates its beginning" (2). He then said: "It is not possible to understand the language of the Arabs from the perspective of understanding the language of the non-Arabs due to the differences in structures and styles" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/42.
(2) See: the same source, 2/43 - 44.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/44. Al-Shafi'i mentioned this matter in several places in his book (al-Risala), perhaps most notably on pages 51 - 52 - 53. Among what he said: "Indeed, Allah addressed the Arabs in His Book in their language according to what they know of its meanings, and among what they know of its meanings is the expansiveness of their language, and that its nature is to address something in a general apparent sense intended as the general apparent, and the beginning of this suffices for its end, and a general apparent intended as general that includes the specific, and this is indicated by some of what they were addressed with therein. And a general apparent intended as specific, and the apparent is known in its context to be intended as non-apparent. All of this is known from the beginning, middle, or end of the speech. And it begins a matter in its speech that clarifies its first word in it from its last, and it begins a matter that clarifies its last word in it from its first... and it speaks of something that it knows by meaning without clarification by word, just as it defines by indication, and this is considered among its highest speech due to the exclusivity of its scholars over those who are ignorant of it" (See: al-Risala, paragraphs 175, 174, 173). Among what al-Shafi'i said: "The language of the Arabs is the most expansive of languages in its methodology and has the most words, and we do not know of anyone other than a prophet who can encompass all its words, but nothing escapes it from its generality, so that there is no one among them who does not know it" (al-Risala, p. 42, paragraph 139). In (al-Risala), there are sections with the following titles: Clarification of what was revealed from the Book as general intended as general that includes the specific, clarification of what was revealed from the Book as general apparent that encompasses both general and specific, clarification of what was revealed from the Book as general apparent intended as entirely specific. See, pp. 53 - 62.


[Page 271]

He pointed out that the one who alerted to this matter was Imam al-Shafi'i in his Risala, but many who came after him did not take it in this manner (1).
Accordingly, it is impossible to translate the Qur'an and convey it into a non-Arabic tongue, because while the words and meanings of phrases can be transferred to another language, the style has an impact on the meanings, which cannot be translated. However, it is permissible to interpret the Qur'an for the general public and for those who are unable to understand its meanings, and it is permissible to translate the words and phrases, but this is merely a transfer of their meanings without preserving the effect of the style, which provides additional meanings that serve the meanings of the words and phrases (2).
The illiteracy of the Sharia:
Al-Shatibi says: "The illiterate (ummi) is one who is attributed to the mother, remaining on the original state of birth from the mother, having not learned a book or anything else, thus he is in the original state in which he was born" (3). He says: "This Sharia is illiterate because its people are likewise; as for the fact that its people are so, it is decisive due to His saying, Exalted is He: { He it is Who has sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among themselves } (4) and His saying: { So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet who believes in Allah and His words } (5), and in the hadith: 'I was sent to an illiterate nation' (6), and also 'We are an illiterate nation; we do not calculate nor write' (7)" (8) and other such evidence.

(1) Same source, 2/42.
(2) Same source, 2/44 - 46.
(3) The same place.
(4) Surah Al-Jumu'ah, 2.
(5) Surah Al-A'raf, 158.
(6) Narrated by Ahmad (22308) with the wording: "I was sent to an illiterate nation."
(7) Narrated by al-Nasa'i (2112) with the same wording. And by al-Bukhari (1780) and Muslim (1806) and al-Nasa'i (2111) and Abu Dawood (1975) and Ahmad (4775) with the wording 'we do not write' preceding 'we do not calculate.'
