[Page 272]

Al-Shatibi's intention in this is that the legal texts must be understood based on their implications, as they were revealed to people for them to comprehend. They addressed them according to their existing knowledge and sciences, and if they had been addressed with something they were unfamiliar with or similar to it, they would not have understood it, and it would not have been a miracle for them. He states: "If it were not in accordance with what they were familiar with, it would not have been a miracle for them, and they would have dismissed it as not being in line with what we are accustomed to, since we have no experience with such speech" (1), just as if the Qur'an had been revealed in a foreign language.
And if the Arabs, to whom the Qur'an was revealed, had some knowledge, it is considered for the purpose of understanding the legal discourse, as they were addressed according to their characteristics, sciences, or knowledge. Therefore, if new sciences or meanings arise that they are unfamiliar with, they are not specifically intended in the address of the legislator, even if they are within the capacity of the words. The same applies if new meanings arise for words they used to employ. Thus, words are interpreted by the meanings that were in use at the time of their revelation. He says: "It is essential in understanding the Sharia to follow the customary understanding of the unlettered ones, namely the Arabs to whom the Qur'an was revealed in their language. If the Arabs have a consistent custom in their language, it is not correct to deviate from it in understanding the Sharia. If there is no custom, it is not correct to interpret it based on what is unfamiliar to them, and this applies to meanings, words, and styles" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/47.
(2) The same source, p. 53.


[Page 273]

And from this, it follows that the meanings understood from the texts are those that are grasped by the general public, not just the elite. It also follows that the accepted meanings of the texts regarding doctrinal and practical obligations are what the general public, for whom the Qur'an was revealed, understands. It is not correct to require philosophical and logical premises or sciences that are only available to the elite in order to understand them. He says: "What is valid in the realm of understandings and comprehension is what is general for all Arabs, so it should not be forced beyond what they can grasp according to the words and meanings, for people in understanding and the obligation therein are not on the same level or close to one another, except that they are similar in public matters."(1)
He says: "The doctrinal and practical obligations must be such that an unlettered person can comprehend them, so that they can enter under their rule"(2). And he says: "If they were only understood by the elite, the Sharia would not be general, nor would it be suitable for the unlettered, and it has been established that it is so. Therefore, the meanings that must be known and believed in must be easy to grasp. Moreover, if they were not so, it would necessitate imposing upon the general public what they cannot bear, which is not the case, as mentioned in the fundamentals"(3).
Al-Shatibi indicates that he does not mean to allow the common people to derive rulings and establish legal truths, but rather that the plausible meanings of the texts, the valid ones, are those that follow that course. The one who engages in deriving and establishing meanings and legal truths is the qualified mujtahid (jurist) for that purpose. This matter will be elaborated upon in the discussion of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/56.
(2) The same source, 2/58.
(3) The same place.


[Page 274]

Therefore, al-Shatibi turns away from delving into the discussions of the attributes of Allah, which are beyond the comprehension of the servant, and directs attention to the texts that are the subject of disagreement and dispute in this matter to what is actionable. He considers deep investigation into them a departure from the requirements of the Sharia. He says: "Thus, you find that the Sharia has only defined divine matters in a way that can be understood, and has deferred other matters, defining them according to the implications of names and attributes, and has encouraged reflection on the created beings as a semblance of that, and has referred what leads to confusion to a general principle, which is His saying, Exalted is He: { There is nothing like Him } (1)" (2). He says: "The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) did not convey to us any engagement in these matters that would serve as a foundation for researchers and those who overreach, nor did it come from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), nor from the followers who are to be emulated" (3). He said: "Thus, deep investigation into them and seeking what the majority does not share in understanding is a departure from the requirements of the original Sharia, for the soul may rush to seek what is not required of it, leading it into a darkness from which it cannot escape" (4).
Based on this - also - he refutes the claim that the Qur'an contains all sciences, including natural sciences and logic, citing His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have sent down to you the Book as a clarification for all things } (5), and His saying: { We have not neglected in the Book anything } (6). Such meanings are not known, and no one among those who preceded has claimed them, so they cannot be established. It is not permissible to attribute to the Qur'an what it does not imply, just as it is not correct to deny from it what it does imply, and one must limit oneself in seeking to understand it to all that is attributed to the Arabs, including the meanings of words and structures, and their styles (7).
The meanings are the primary objective of the texts:

And this is undoubtedly without dispute. The speech and the texts were intended for a specific purpose, which is their meanings. Therefore, attention was given to the meanings of words and their implications, to the implications of structures, and to the meanings of letters. This is why the scholars of jurisprudence (fiqh) and the scholars of principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) paid attention to the sciences of language and their implications. Al-Shatibi says: "The concern for the meanings dispersed in the discourse is the greatest objective based on the fact that the Arabs were concerned with meanings, and they only refined the words for their sake. This principle is well-known among the people of Arabic. The word is merely a means to attain the intended meaning, and the meaning is the objective, and not every meaning; for the individual meaning may not be taken into account if the composite meaning is understood without it" (1). The individual meaning refers to words like hand, eye, their hands, our eyes, and with you, among others, in the verses that raised discussions about attributes, and to the word abba in His saying: { And fruit and abba } (2). He says: "In the collection of al-Isma'ili, which is narrated on the authority of Sahih al-Bukhari from Anas ibn Malik, that Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) recited { And fruit and abba } and said, 'What is abba?' Then he said, 'We were not tasked with this,' or he said, 'We were not commanded with this.' It is also reported from Anas that a man asked Umar ibn al-Khattab about His saying { And fruit and abba }, 'What is abba?' Umar said, 'We were forbidden from delving deeply and being overly concerned.' It is well-known that he admonished Dubay' when he frequently asked about the verses of the sent ones and the violent winds and similar matters. The apparent meaning of all this is that he only forbade it because the composite meaning is generally known, and no legal ruling can be based on performing these actions... If understanding the individual word were a prerequisite for understanding the composite meaning, it would not be considered a burden but rather a necessity, as was narrated from Umar himself regarding His saying: { Or He takes them with fear } (3), for he was asked about it on the pulpit, and a man from Hudhayl said to him: 'Fear among us means belittlement,' then he recited (the long meter):

The traveler feared it, like a monkey... as the ship feared the return of the spring (1).
Omar said: "O people, hold on to the record of your poetry from the time of ignorance, for in it is the interpretation of your Book... If this is the case, then it is necessary to pay attention to understanding the meaning of the address" (2).
This is if the meanings are the meanings of the words and texts; however, if what is meant by meanings are the meanings of rulings, that is, the rulings or presumed interests for them, which, if established through induction, become certain legal interests and objectives (maqasid); and if they are not established as such, they are treated according to their service or destruction of established objectives, and are considered or rejected based on that. In this sense of the term meanings, al-Shatibi discusses whether this is from the indications of language or something for which speech was intended or not, and he concludes that it is not from the indications of language, and this will become clear in what follows.

Al-Shatibi says: "The Arabic language, in terms of its words that indicate meanings, has two perspectives: one from the standpoint of being words and expressions that are absolute indicators of absolute meanings, which is the original indication, and the second from the standpoint of being words and expressions that are restricted indicators of serving meanings, which is the secondary indication" (1). He says: "As for the aspect of the original meaning, there is no doubt about its validity in indicating rulings absolutely, and there can be no disagreement in this regard, such as the forms of commands and prohibitions and generalities and particularities... As for the aspect of the secondary meaning, is it valid to consider it in indicating rulings in terms of understanding additional meanings beyond the original meaning or not?" (2).

To clarify al-Shatibi's (may Allah have mercy on him) intention regarding the secondary meaning, he provided the example he mentioned. He said: "If an action occurs in existence for Zayd, such as standing up, then if every speaker wants to inform about Zayd's standing, he will achieve what he intends without any difficulty" (1). The meaning understood from the report here is the original meaning. He then said: "As for the second aspect, it is that which is specific to the Arabic tongue in that narration and that report, for every report in this aspect necessitates matters that serve that report" (2). He then said: "That is, you say at the beginning of the report, 'Zayd has stood up,' if there is no concern for the one being reported about, but rather for the report itself. If the concern is for the one being reported about, you would say, 'Zayd has stood up.' In response to the question, 'What is the status of that standing?' you would say, 'If Zayd has stood up.' In response to the denial of his standing, you would say, 'By Allah, Zayd has stood up'" (3). He then said: "All of this revolves around reporting Zayd's standing, so such actions, which change the meaning of the same speech according to them, are not the original intention. Rather, they are complements and supplements" (4). Based on this, if this difference in reporting were considered among the original meanings, it would not be possible to translate any speech from Arabic into the speech of the non-Arabs, let alone translate the Qur'an (5).

Based on al-Shatibi's clarifications, the derived meaning (ma'na tab'i) can be defined as a meaning that serves the original meaning but is not one of the indications of speech. The meaning becomes clearer when al-Shatibi responds to those who assert that the derived meaning is one of the indications of speech. He cites their statement, saying: "They argued that the maximum duration of menstruation is fifteen days based on his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), 'One of you remains in her menstruation for half of her lifetime' (1), and the intended meaning is to inform about the deficiency in religion, not to inform about the maximum duration, but exaggeration necessitated mentioning that, and if the increase had been mentioned, it would have been addressed. Al-Shafi'i argued for the impurity of a small amount of water that is not altered based on his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), 'If one of you awakens from his sleep, he should not dip his hand into the vessel until he washes it' (2)"(3). Based on this, what has come in legal texts such as His saying, Exalted is He: { Prohibited to you are dead animals, blood, and the flesh of swine } (1), and His saying, Exalted is He: { Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, stone alters [to other than Allah], and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it } (2), and His saying, Exalted is He: { As for the thief, the male and the female, amputate their hands in recompense for what they earned as a deterrent [punishment] from Allah } (3), and His saying, Exalted is He: { The female and the male adulterer, lash each one of them with a hundred lashes } (4), the prohibition of the aforementioned items such as carrion, blood, swine, and intoxicants... and the prohibition of theft and adultery are among the original meanings and the original implications of the speech. As for what may be argued as the rationale for these rulings or taken as wisdom for them without the existence of a term indicating that or texts from which it can be inferred, such as saying that the rationale or wisdom is the harm caused by carrion, blood, or swine, or the intoxication caused by alcohol, or that the preservation of life, preservation of intellect, preservation of wealth, and preservation of lineage is the meaning of these rulings or the intent of the Legislator behind them, this is not among the implications of the texts. If it were among them, it would be one of the original meanings; rather, the fact that it is intended by the Legislator is a conjecture that is not supported by legal evidence, and it is additional to the original meanings. So, can rulings be derived from it or built upon it?
There is no ruling for the dependent indication:
Al-Shatibi presents a discussion on this issue, providing the evidence of those who affirm it, and he presents the evidence of those who oppose it, concluding with the statement: "The result is that inferring from the second aspect regarding rulings is not established, thus it cannot be applied at all"(5).

(1) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 3.
(2) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 90.

(5) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 2/68.


[Page 282]

Then he says: "It has become clear that there is a conflict of evidence in the issue, and it has appeared that the stronger position from both sides is that of the prohibitors, thus the situation necessitates that the second position, which indicates the derivative meaning, has no indication of an additional legal ruling whatsoever" (1).
The summary of the evidence of the prohibitors is that these derivative meanings are either indicated by the text or they are not. If they are indicated by the text, then they are among the original meanings and are considered valid, and can be used as evidence for rulings because they are among the indications of language. If they are not indicated by the text, then the one who claims them is required to provide legal evidence. If there is no legal text that indicates them in any type of linguistic indication, then they are mere conjectures and assumptions that cannot be attributed to the Sharia. In reality, this disagreement that al-Shatibi raises and clarifies his position on is the disagreement mentioned in the second chapter between those who advocate for reasoning based on presumed wisdom, and building rulings upon it on the grounds that they are conjectures, which are acceptable in legal matters, and those who reject considering these meanings and rulings based on the fact that there is no evidence for them, thus they hold no validity, as they describe them as mere figments of the heart or whims of the mind.
From here, al-Shatibi's approach to this issue is that these meanings hold no validity in legislation as they are presumed rulings, and there is nothing to prevent the intended wisdom from being something else. There is also nothing to prevent it from being the opposite of the intended wisdom of the legislator, but a person may perceive the ugly as beautiful or the beautiful as ugly.
Thus, al-Shatibi's condition for a beneficial induction that leads to certainty in considering these meanings as legal objectives is that it establishes for him the compatibility of this meaning with the actions of the Sharia (2).
However, the reader of al-Shatibi may wonder whether what al-Shatibi asserts, that such an induction is beneficial in considering these meanings with certainty, is correct?

(1) The same location.
(2) Now, the reader can refer to the reading of the third introduction from al-Shatibi's introductions, to gain more confidence in what we have presented to him regarding his methodology, and to increase his understanding of the importance of that introduction and what it contains for his methodology.


[Page 283]

If the secondary meanings in individual texts are not considered, from where will the consideration arise if the texts are numerous? In other words, if the consideration of meaning depends on the convergence of evidence on that meaning, from where will the consideration arise if none of this evidence has any indication of that meaning? This is according to his statement, "The situation necessitates that the second aspect, which indicates the secondary meaning, has no indication of a legal ruling whatsoever."

Among al-Shatibi's statements regarding the exaggeration in rejecting the consideration of meanings that may be claimed to be intended by the Legislator without any evidence indicating them, either through original indication or through established induction, is his saying: "What assures us from Allah's questioning us on the Day of Resurrection: From where did you understand that I intended such and such a genus by what I revealed in my saying: { And they think that they are doing well } (1) or my saying: { He said, 'Indeed, I am of those who dislike your work' } (2)? For claiming such a thing about the Qur'an, that it is intended by the speaker, is dangerous; rather, it returns to the meaning of His saying: { When you receive it with your tongues and say with your mouths that of which you have no knowledge, and you think it is insignificant, while it is, in the sight of Allah, عظیم } (3) and that it is a statement in the Book of Allah based on opinion" (4).

The Third Topic: ... Between the Sharia and its Objectives or Between Worship and Following Meanings.

Chapter Five
The Intention of the Legislator in Establishing the Sharia for Obligations According to It
And in the Inclusion of the Obligor Under Its Rules

Introduction:
This chapter is to discuss the third and fourth types of the objectives of the legislator. What is noteworthy here is al-Shatibi's expression in the third type: "for obligations according to it," especially when we consider the title of the fourth type: "the inclusion of the obligor under the rules of the Sharia." What is the difference between the two types?
The difference between them can be understood if we refer to the fourth type as the intention of the legislator in establishing the Sharia for obligations through it, which means the intention of worship and compliance. As for the third type, it is the obligation according to it, meaning the implication of worship and compliance, which is burden and hardship. It has been understood from the legislator that the intention is for the benefit of the servants and for ease, which is contrary to hardship and pain. The legislator intends through the Sharia to alleviate hardship. Is there a contradiction here? Does obligation cease with hardship? Is there a limit to the hardship that would lift the obligation, and how can we reconcile the original intention of worship and compliance with the original intention of benefit and alleviation of hardship?
This is the subject of the chapter, which I have divided into three sections: the first to clarify al-Shatibi's intent and methodology in explaining the intention of the legislator in establishing the Sharia for obligations according to it, and the second and third to clarify his methodology in explaining the intention of the legislator in including the obligor under the rules of the Sharia.

The First Topic
The Intention of Obligation According to the Sharia

The Meaning of This Type:
The subject of this type is that the legislator does not impose obligations that are beyond the capacity of the obligor, nor those that entail excessive hardship, because one of the objectives of the legislator is, from the outset, to alleviate hardship and remove constraints. However, absolute hardship cannot be entirely avoided, as it is inherent in every obligation. What, then, is the criterion for the hardship that Allah does not impose obligations upon, and the hardship for which Allah, Exalted is He, obligates actions that are accompanied by similar hardship?


[Page 285]

It has been mentioned regarding his third introduction that he said: "Unlike the principles, they are derived from a comprehensive examination of the implications of the evidence, not from individual cases specifically" (1). This is because the implications of the evidence are the meanings of the texts and the meanings of the rulings. That is, they are the linguistic indications and the causes of the rulings. The legal meanings are the meanings that are derived, whether from the texts or from the rulings, and they are the universals or definitive principles of the Sharia. These universals must be applied when considering the texts, meaning that the meanings of the texts should be directed in such a way that the meaning derived from them does not contradict the principles, and any meaning that contradicts a principle is rejected, which is the meaning of applying the universals with the particulars. When the Exalted says: { And do not die except while you are Muslims } (2), the text can imply more than one meaning, and it has been established in the principles that there is no obligation for what is beyond one's capacity, so any meaning that contradicts this principle is rejected; therefore, the meaning shifts from the obligation of not dying to its implications.
The obligation that entails hardship is to be considered, as it has been established that the legislator intends to alleviate hardship and that he intends to impose what is commanded. These are two principles from which a contradiction arises, and they are from the implications of the Sharia, that is, from its universal principles. So what does the Sharia necessitate in this case?
This is the reason al-Shatibi chose this title. As for the term: "obligation" in the title, it carries the meaning of burden and hardship. What is meant by this is that there is no action without some burden, and the commitment of the obligated person to the commands of the Sharia necessarily entails hardship, regardless of its extent. Does the legislator intend to remove all hardship? Al-Shatibi answers in the negative. This opens the door to a complex topic, or one that requires understanding in the law and in the policy of the law, which is the estimation of the hardship that lifts the obligation.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/16.
(2) Surah Al-Imran, 102.


[Page 286]

In Islamic law, there are well-known principles such as: "Necessities permit the prohibited," "Hardship brings about facility," "When the matter becomes narrow, it expands," "Need takes the place of necessity," or others that may or may not be valid. Some contemporary scholars use such principles in their excuses, justifications, or fatwas. Should such principles be taken at face value? Is the prohibited allowed by any necessity or merely by need, and is hardship taken as evidence for leniency? No, and no one has said this. So what are the controls? This is the essence of this type of objectives of the legislator.
The principles and foundations that al-Shatibi diligently sought to verify and establish are primarily aimed at resolving issues of this kind, that is, establishing the foundations and rules that govern particulars and meanings when they are a source of doubt and confusion or of disagreement and divergent views.
It is worth noting that the principles established by al-Shatibi in this type of objectives, such as not being obliged to do what is beyond one's capacity, and not being obliged to endure extraordinary or excessive hardship, and the lifting of hardship, are principles of need (hajiyat), because they revolve around ease, alleviation, and kindness towards the obligated person, which is the definition of needs.
Obligation and ease:
It has been established in the principles that Allah, Exalted is He, does not impose on the servant what is beyond his capacity. Therefore, al-Shatibi addresses this quickly, but he discusses what follows from it. He says: "It has been established in the principles that the condition for obligation or its cause is the ability of the one obligated. What the obligated person cannot do is not validly imposed upon him legally, even if it is rationally permissible (1)... And we say: If it appears from the legislator at first glance the intention to impose what is beyond the capacity of the servant, that is actually related to its precedents or its consequences or its indicators. The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: { And do not die except while you are Muslims } (2), and His saying in the hadith: "Be the servant of Allah who is killed and do not be the servant of Allah who kills" (3), and His saying: "Do not die while you are an oppressor" (4), and what is similar to that is not required from it except what falls under the capacity, which is Islam, refraining from oppression, abstaining from killing, and submitting to the command of Allah, as well as everything else of this nature" (5).
__________
(1) Unlike the Mu'tazila, and unlike what is necessitated by rational good and evil, or by establishing benefits and harms by reason, assuming that reason is capable of that.
(2) Surah Al-Imran, 102.
(3) Narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad (21461).
(4) I could not find it.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/72.


[Page 287]

On this basis, a person is not tasked with what does not fall under their ability, including the traits they are naturally endowed with, such as hunger and thirst and similar matters; they are not required to eliminate these, but they are asked to control themselves from inclining towards what is unlawful. As for traits that are ambiguous in nature, such as love, hatred, anger, and others, they are to be examined; the request may either be directed towards their antecedents or their consequences. He states: "What is inherent in human nature in terms of traits inevitably leads to acquired actions, so the request is directed at those actions, not at what they originated from" (1). This is similar to love, where the request pertains to the causes, as in the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "Exchange gifts, and you will love one another" (2). And regarding the desire for unlawful sexual relations, it is a consequence for which a person is required to eliminate its cause, which is the provocative gaze (3). As for anger, for example, a person is required to manage its consequences, such as refraining from revenge. He says: "Even if the provocation is not within their ability, the request pertains to the consequences, like anger provoking the desire for revenge, just as the gaze provokes the desire for unlawful relations" (4).
He concludes by saying: "If it is arranged in this manner, it is not correct to impose a duty regarding them themselves, even if it appears outwardly that such an imposition is evident; it is directed towards something other than that which precedes it, follows it, or coincides with it, and Allah knows best" (5).
Directing the implications of the request towards the consequences, antecedents, or accompanying factors, in accordance with this principle, necessitates the application of other principles to determine what the request pertains to, and the meaning to which it is directed cannot be considered valid except after establishing its meaning through induction.
Obligation and hardship:
The legal rulings or principles related to hardships differ according to the variations of these hardships, and this difference necessitates clarifying the meanings of hardship. Based on its reality, al-Shatibi identifies four meanings for it:

(5) The same source, 2/75.


[Page 288]

The first: that what is meant by it is general in what is not possible to achieve and in what is possible to achieve if it is unbearable, like a disabled person who attempts to stand, or a person who attempts to fly in terms of it being a hardship that is futile; thus, its ruling is like that of what is not possible to achieve, and this has been clarified.
The second: that what is meant by it is the burdensome hardship, that is, the one that is beyond the usual, which leads to a disturbance in the mind or soul, or forces one to abandon obligations or commit prohibitions. Therefore, this type of hardship does not entail a demand for what necessitates it, and it is the place of concession(1).
The third: that what is meant by hardship is the ordinary hardship, that is, the one that is not burdensome, which accompanies ordinary tasks, and what these tasks require in terms of effort and cost. Such hardships have no effect on obligation.
The fourth: that what is meant by hardship is the opposition to desires, in that the obligation takes the obligated person away from indulging in their desires, and such hardship has no effect on obligation(2). The legislator does not intend to remove it.
The basis of the non-obligation regarding burdensome hardships:
__________
(1) The meaning of the concession intended here will be explained later.
(2) See: al-Muwafaqat. 2/80.


[Page 289]

Al-Shatibi says: "For the legislator did not intend to impose burdens that cause hardship in it" (1) and he presented evidence through useful inductive reasoning, including His saying, Exalted is He: { And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them } (2), and His saying: { Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us } (3), and His saying: { No soul is charged except with that within its capacity } (4), and His saying: { Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship } (5), and His saying: { And He has not made upon you in religion any difficulty } (6), and His saying: { Allah intends to lighten for you, and mankind was created weak } (7), { Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you } (8), and in the hadith: "I was sent with the easy, lenient religion" (9), and "Whenever two options are presented to him, he should choose the easier one as long as it is not sinful" (10), and other evidences (11). He said: "If He had intended hardship, He would not have intended ease or relief, but would have intended difficulty and hardship, which is false" (12),

[Page 290]

He said: "If the purpose of the Sharia (law) were to impose hardship and difficulty, and it has been established that it is intended for ease and facilitation, then combining the two would be a contradiction and a discrepancy, and it is free from that." (1)
Difficulties are evils:
Accordingly, the legislator intends for ease and facilitation for the obligated person, and aims to eliminate difficulties. According to his methodology, difficulties are evils that must be removed, and it is forbidden for the obligated person to intend them for their own sake. He says: "The obligated person should not intend difficulty in the obligation due to the great reward for it; rather, he may intend the action that has a great reward because of its great difficulty." (2) And he said: "Nothing from the objectives of the obligated person is valid except what aligns with the intention of the legislator. If the intention of the obligated person is to impose difficulty, then he has contradicted the intention of the legislator, since the legislator does not intend the difficulty itself in the obligation. Any intention that contradicts the intention of the legislator is void; thus, the intention towards difficulty is void, and it is therefore among the things that are prohibited. What is prohibited has no reward in it; rather, it incurs sin if the prohibition rises to the level of being forbidden. Seeking reward by intending to enter into difficulty is a contradictory intention." (3) And he said: "His prohibition of hardship is well-known in the Sharia to the extent that it has become a definitive principle in it. If the intention of the legislator is not to impose hardship on the self, then the intention of the obligated person towards it is opposed to what the legislator intended by the known and established alleviation. If his intention contradicts the intention of the legislator, it is void and invalid. This is clear, and may Allah grant success." (4) And he said: "It has been made known by the legislator that difficulty is prohibited." (5) However, this raises a question: difficulties are inherent to human actions, and there is no obligation without difficulty. How can it be consistent that the legislator intends to eliminate difficulties while also requiring adherence to obligations? The answer from al-Shatibi, according to his methodology, is that the legislator's intention to eliminate difficulties is a general principle that does not fail.
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) The same source, 2/86.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/89.
(4) The same source.
(5) The same source, 2/85.


[Page 291]

When the obligation is established with what entails hardship, the solution is that not everything termed hardship is considered hardship in Islamic law; that is, these hardships are not the meaning that the principle of alleviating hardships refers to, from one perspective. From another perspective, if the obligation falls on something that entails hardship which the legislator intended to alleviate, then two principles come into conflict: the principle of compliance and the principle of alleviating hardship. Here, one must weigh the interests and harms, and the ruling will be based on what predominates in the situation, meaning that one must weigh the demand for action due to the benefit of compliance against the demand for abstention due to the harm of hardship.
Usual hardship is not termed hardship:
... It has been established through induction that every obligation involving hardship, no matter how slight, indicates a definitive general principle that the legislator imposes obligations that entail hardship. Here, two principles come into conflict: the principle of alleviating hardships and the principle of acting upon what entails hardship. Al-Shatibi saw the solution in that not every hardship is considered hardship in Islamic law. What is the criterion for what is considered and what is not? Al-Shatibi states: "There is no dispute that the legislator intends to impose obligations that entail some cost and hardship, but it is not usually termed hardship, just as the pursuit of livelihood through various trades and crafts is not usually termed hardship because it is a possible and customary practice that does not prevent the costs associated with it from being carried out in the usual manner. Rather, rational people and those accustomed to such practices consider those who refrain from it to be lazy and condemn them for it. Likewise, the usual obligations" (1). He adds in clarifying the required criterion: "To this meaning returns the distinction between hardship that is not usually considered hardship and that which is considered hardship, which is that if the action leads to its discontinuation or to some of it, or to a disruption in the individual, their wealth, or their condition, then the hardship here is outside the usual. If it does not involve any of that in the usual case, it is not usually considered hardship, even if it is termed a cost" (2). He then said: "Based on this, one should understand the obligation and what it entails of hardship" (3). He then went further, rejecting the notion that usual hardships are termed hardship, thus eliminating the conflict between the two principles. He said: "What results from ordinary actions is not usually termed hardship. The conclusion is that obligations involving customary matters and those of their kind do not entail hardship, as previously stated; what results from the obligation is not termed hardship" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/82 - 83.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 2/85.


[Page 292]

He said: "If it is not outside the norm but occurs in a manner similar to the hardship that arises in ordinary tasks, then the legislator, even if he did not intend for it to occur, does not intend to remove it either. The evidence for this is that if he had intended to remove it, the obligation would not remain, since every ordinary or extraordinary task entails effort and obligation to a degree, whether little or much" (1).
... Along with these hardships is the hardship of opposing one's desires, which is not taken into account in obligations because one of the objectives of the legislator is to divert the obligated person from following their desires to compliance. He said: "Opposing what the souls desire is difficult for them, and it is hard to depart from it" (2). He said: "But the legislator intended by establishing the Sharia to divert the obligated person from following their desires so that they become a servant of Allah. Therefore, opposing one's desires is not one of the hardships considered in obligations, even if it is difficult in the course of habits, for if it were considered to the extent that alleviation would be legislated for it, that would contradict the purpose for which the Sharia was established, and that is invalid" (3).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/105.
(2) The same source, 2/103.
(3) The same location.


[Page 293]

... Under the following of desires (hawa) fall many positions, fatwas, or actions for which their proponents invoke the attainment of benefits and the prevention of harms, under the title of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and the identification of benefits and harms based on desires, or the advantages or disadvantages that may befall a person. For this reason, it becomes permissible to commit prohibitions or neglect obligations, under the pretext of preserving a position, job, or wealth, or seeking knowledge, and they refer to the sacrifices, hardships, or harm they may face as harms. Although this way of thinking has no basis in religion, as it renders what the legislator has commanded as harmful and what He has prohibited as beneficial. The falsehood is magnified when the proponents of such claims cling to al-Shatibi and his methodology, as he criticized this approach and referred to these considerations as desires, and he cited in the context of discussing the hardship of opposing desires the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: { Have you seen the one who has taken as his god his own desire, and Allah has led him astray despite his knowledge? } (1) and His saying: { They follow not except assumption and what their souls desire. } (2), and His saying: { Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord like one to whom his evil deed has been made attractive, and they follow their desires? } (3). He then said: "Just as hardship can be worldly, it can also be otherworldly. For if actions lead to neglecting an obligation or committing a prohibition, it is considered a greater hardship in terms of the Sharia than the worldly hardship that does not compromise religion. The consideration of religion takes precedence over the consideration of the self and others in the view of the Sharia." (4)
The recognized hardships or those intended to be alleviated:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Jathiya, 23.
(2) Surah An-Najm, 23.
(3) Surah Muhammad, 14.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 2/104.


[Page 294]

... It clarifies the meaning of the hardships that the legislator intended to alleviate, and thus it is forbidden for the servant to seek them. These are the hardships that are beyond the norm, which lead to a cessation of the required actions or some of them, or that cause a disruption in the individual. Such is the case with hardship. It is intended to be alleviated by law. Among the hardships is that the obligated person imposes upon themselves actions that, due to their nature or their abundance, lead to a shortcoming in their duties. He says: "Know that hardship is lifted from the obligated person for two reasons: the first is the fear of being cut off from the path and the aversion to worship and the dislike of obligation, which encompasses the fear of causing corruption to their body, mind, wealth, or state. The second is the fear of shortcoming when competing obligations related to the servant of different types arise, such as their duty to their family and children alongside other obligations that may come in the way. Perhaps delving into some actions will distract them from others and prevent the obligated person from fulfilling them, and perhaps they intend to burden both sides with excessive scrutiny, thus cutting them off from both" (1). Here, there is a conflict between the principle of compliance and the principle of alleviating hardship, which is a genuine hardship that is legally termed as hardship, meaning that which the legislator intended to alleviate.
... For such hardships, it is legislated to ease the obligation or grant concessions, making these hardships reasons for licenses. However, it should be noted that some ordinary hardships may be burdensome for certain obligated individuals, while some burdensome hardships for the general public may be ordinary for some. Likewise, there are places in the Sharia where licenses exist without any significant or burdensome hardship. So what is the meaning of a license, and how can the obligation be eased or lifted if its cause is found?
Meaning of the license:
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/91.


[Page 295]

... The term "license" (rukhsah) is used in more than one meaning, but the intended and predominant meaning is that which corresponds to the exemption (azimah) in the rulings of legal status (ahkam al-wad‘), which is what the jurists (usuliyyun) derive from. This is the meaning that al-Shatibi employed in his discussion of licenses and exemptions as types of legal rulings, and in this sense, it is: "what has been legislated for a difficult excuse as an exception to a general principle that necessitates prohibition, while being limited to the places of need therein" (1).
It can also be used in other meanings mentioned by al-Shatibi (2), among which we will mention what concerns us here. He says: "The term 'license' may refer to what has been alleviated from this nation in terms of severe obligations and burdensome actions, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: { Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us }" (3) (4). He mentioned some evidence that indicates the principle of lifting hardships. In this sense, the concession (tarakhus) refers back to a definitive general principle from the essential needs (al-usul al-hajiyyah), and not in the sense that the jurists commonly use.
... The first technical definition refers to the licenses explicitly stated by the Sharia, which are permissible to use as soon as their cause exists, even if the hardship is absent, such as the license for shortening (qasr) or combining (jam‘) prayers during travel. These licenses are specific, and thus it was said about them, "as an exception to a general principle," and therefore they cannot be analogized and are limited to their specified instances.
... As for the second definition, it is what al-Shatibi intended by concession (tarakhus) or alleviation in the presence of hardship or burdensome difficulties.
__________
(1) The same source, 1/290.
(2) The same location.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 286.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/212.


[Page 296]

... In both cases, the burdensome hardship (al-mashaqa al-mu'ntah) is the reason established by Islamic law for the concession (rukhsah), but since hardships are relative, meaning they differ among individuals and cannot be standardized, the legislator has set specific reasons (causes) to identify them. Therefore, if the reason exists, it is permissible to act upon the concession even if the burdensome hardship does not exist, because the concession is explicitly stated. If the reason exists along with the burdensome hardship, such as when there is a significant hardship during travel, it becomes obligatory to relieve the hardship, similar to how a person in dire need must eat something unlawful, for example. It is called a concession because it falls under the definition of a concession.
... He says: "The true hardship is the reason established for the concession; if it does not exist, the ruling is not obligatory, unless the presumption arises, which is the reason, taking the place of the wisdom, in which case the reason becomes sufficient for permissibility rather than obligation" (1). He also says: "There is no specific criterion or fixed limit for the considered hardship in alleviations that applies to all people; therefore, the law has established the reason in many cases to take the place of the cause because it is the closest presumption of the existence of hardship, leaving each individual to what they find... and leaving much of it to ijtihad (independent reasoning)" (2). Let us pay attention to his statement: "in many cases," meaning the explicitly stated concessions. This indicates that some of them do not have a reason established by the law that takes the place of the cause, and thus we apply the cause itself for alleviation, which is the true hardship. Here, the concession in the second sense comes into play, which is in the presence of the true hardship, meaning the burdensome one. His statement: "and leaving each individual to what they find..." indicates that some actions may be difficult for some and easy for others; therefore, these concessions are relative just as the hardships are relative. He says: "The concession is relative, not original, meaning that everyone is an expert in taking it for themselves unless a legal limit is set that they must adhere to" (3). He said: "There may be a man who is accustomed to cutting through difficulties until it becomes a habit for him, and he does not feel burdened or distressed by it... and another man is the opposite" (4). He said: "Many people can endure in their illness what others cannot, so the concession is legislated for one of the two men but not the other, and there is no doubt about this" (5).
Reasons for concessions:

[Page 297]

... It has been established that true hardship is the reason for concession. However, since hardship is relative and people differ in their ability to bear it, the Sharia has specified a number of concessions that exist when their causes are present, such as the concessions of shortening prayers, combining prayers, and breaking the fast while traveling. These concessions are deemed permissible in general according to al-Shatibi. However, if there is a significant hardship, taking the concession becomes obligatory, even though it is still referred to as a concession. He said: "There is no doubt that the concession here is akin to decisive commands, and for this reason, the scholars have stated that it is obligatory to eat carrion out of fear of death; if one does not do so and dies, he will enter the Fire" (1). Hardship is divided into two categories: habitual and non-habitual. The former is not intended to be alleviated by the Sharia, while the latter requires a concession to be taken. He said: "When the hardship faced by the obligated person in fulfilling the obligation is beyond the usual hardships encountered in ordinary actions, to the extent that it leads to religious or worldly corruption, the aim of the Legislator in this case is to generally alleviate it" (2). The action that causes this hardship is prohibited, and it must either be completely removed or alleviated.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/223.
(2) The same source, 2/105.


[Page 298]

... The difference in hardships among people makes the allowances vary according to what they can bear, as the allowance is justified by the hardship that is burdensome or unusual: the ruling revolves around the reason for it, whether it exists or not. He says: "The prohibition is for a reason that is rational in meaning and intended by the legislator (1). If this is the case, then the prohibition is contingent upon the existence of the reason. When what the Messenger - (peace and blessings be upon him) - justified is present, the prohibition is directed and applicable; and if it is not present (2), then the prohibition is absent, as people in this regard are of two types" (3). He then mentioned two categories of people: one category experiences work that causes them additional hardship beyond what is usual, affecting them or others, and these are the majority of those obligated. He said regarding them: "Such individuals should not engage in actions that involve this, but rather they should take allowances" (4). He indicated that the allowance should be according to what is legislated, saying: "They take allowances according to what has been legislated for allowances if it is something that cannot be abandoned, or they abandon it if it is something that can be left, which is the implication of the justification" (5).
... The second category consists of ascetics, pious worshippers, or Sufis, or the people of states, as he refers to them in various places in his book. These individuals can endure what others cannot because their love for Allah has led them to renounce their desires, benefits, and pleasures, even if they are permissible. Thus, they are able to fill their time with more religious duties. These individuals are not required to take allowances because the justification is absent in their case (6).
... There is another category of people that al-Shatibi mentions in other parts of his book, which are the people of desires in contrast to the people of states. These individuals may find that abandoning the disliked (makruh) and performing the recommended (mandub) could lead them to a more severe disliked action or to a forbidden (haram) act, or result in abandoning a greater recommended act or an obligation. In this case, it is preferable for them to abandon the recommended act or to perform the disliked act.

... However, the ruling of what is permissible (halal) and forbidden (haram) does not change for them, and these - the possessors of fortunes - must take advantage of the areas of concession. It is said: "These must fulfill their allotted shares that are permitted to them by the Sharia, but in a manner that does not compromise any obligation upon them nor harm their shares. We have found that not taking advantage of the areas of concession in relation to them leads to a situation of harm or harms that are significantly detrimental according to the Sharia" (1).
Conditions of concession:
... The fact that one is not obligated to do what is beyond their capacity, and that one is not tasked with burdensome difficulties, is a legal matter that does not involve reason. Likewise, the areas of concession and the type of concession are legal matters; therefore, there are conditions for the concession. Some of these conditions have been mentioned previously, namely that the difficulty must be burdensome. Below, these conditions are mentioned to complete the discussion.
... It is said: "If the difficulty leads to the disruption of a fundamental principle, then the principle of determination (azima) should not be considered, as completing the act of worship here and performing it as it should leads to its being nullified from its origin. Thus, performing what one is capable of from it, which is the essence of the concession, is what is required" (2). This difficulty is also associated with hardship, as it is said: "Hardship applies to one who is afflicted by hardship to the extent that it prevents them from their necessities and needs" (3). Likewise, there is necessity, as it is said: "The state of necessity has been clarified as that which one fears will lead to the loss of life, and this can only occur after being unable to perform acts of worship and daily activities, and it is, in itself, also an excuse" (4). These definitions clarify a condition of the difficulties, which is the disruption of a fundamental principle. He refers to it as burdensome or real, as has been clarified.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/98 - 99.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/233.
(3) The same source, 1/219.
(4) The same source, 1/218.


[Page 300]

... Among the conditions is that the hardship must be actual or certain to occur; it is not sufficient for it to be based on conjectures and unproven estimates, for this is an illusion that has no validity. He says: "Indeed, conjectures and unproven estimates fall under the category of illusions, which are varied. Likewise, the desires of the souls estimate things that have no reality; thus, it is correct to adhere to the principle of determination (azimah) except in cases of severe and debilitating hardship, for patience is preferable unless it leads to a detriment to the intellect or religion of a person. The reality of this is that one cannot bear patience, for one is only commanded to be patient if one is capable of it. You will find through observation that severe hardship does not have its illusion attached to it; rather, its ruling is weaker based on the fact that illusion is often not truthful in many situations. Therefore, hardship is not real... and it is preferable to remain with the principle" (1). That is, with determination; however, if the occurrence of this hardship is uncertain between being realized and being conjectured, and it is likely to occur according to the course of customs, then this is a domain for the jurists.
... Among the conditions is that the determination of hardship should not align with desires. He says: "The principles of the Sharia are opposed to desires... and often hardships arise and increase due to opposing desires, and following desires is contrary to following the Sharia, and one who follows desires finds everything difficult, whether it is inherently difficult or not" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 1/233.
(2) The same source, 1/230.


[Page 301]

One of its conditions is that the ruling regarding it being burdensome or outside the norm must be based on the Sharia, and it may be said that this relates to the two previous conditions. However, it differs from them in that the hardship may undermine a fundamental principle, and yet there is no concession (1), such as the hardships of jihad. He says: "The fact that it is difficult for some people or in some situations does not remove it from being intended for Him" (2), meaning for Allah, Exalted is He. He says: "The hardship may reach in customary actions to what is thought to be unusual, but in reality, it is customary, and its hardship in such a case is what is customary, as the hardship in a single action has two extremes and a mean, an upper extreme... and a lower extreme... and the mean is what is predominant and most common" (3). Accordingly, hardship may increase, leading one to believe it has become unusual, while for those familiar with the flow of customs, meaning what has been established by the Sharia in obligations, it remains in the middle. It has been understood from the objectives of the legislator in obligations that hardships occur for the servants as a test and trial. If that is the case, then to judge whether the hardship is customary or not must be based on the Sharia; otherwise, the test and trial would be invalidated. He said: "The incidental difficulties that befall the servants are a test and trial for the faith of the believers and the hesitation of the uncertain until it becomes clear who has believed in his Lord with certainty from those who are in doubt. If all obligations were to be invalidated by every hardship that arose, then the fundamental principles would be invalidated as previously mentioned, and nothing would be distinguished from that, nor would the pure be distinguished from the impure" (4).
__________
(1) This is because the degree of hardship considered in Sharia varies according to the actions, and this will become clear shortly when discussing the moderation of the Sharia.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/227.
(3) The same source, 2/106.
(4) The same source, 1/228.


[Page 302]

... One of the conditions for seeking a concession (rukhsah) is that the concession must be in accordance with the Sharia, so one should not escape from the hardship that the Sharia has allowed him to escape from except through the Sharia itself. He should take what the Sharia has granted him in terms of alleviation and not follow his whims. This matter pertains to the concepts of good and evil, and there is no room for reason in it. He said: "Every difficult matter for which the legislator has provided an exit, the legislator intends for the obligated person to seek that exit if he wishes, as is the case with the legal concessions that provide an exit from hardships. If the obligated person seeks to exit in the manner prescribed, he will be complying with the command of the legislator and taking precautions in his matter. If he does not do so, he will fall into two prohibitions: the first is his opposition to the intention of the legislator, whether that opposition is in a mandatory, recommended, or permissible act; and the second is that he will close the doors of ease upon himself and lose the exit from that difficult matter from which he sought to escape in a manner not prescribed for him" (1).
... And he said: "The obligated person in seeking alleviation is commanded to seek it from the prescribed means, because what is sought in terms of alleviation is certainly attainable in both the present and the future in general. If he seeks it from another path, what he seeks in terms of alleviation will not be certain nor even probable, neither in the present nor in the future, neither in general nor in detail" (2). And he said: "Returning to the means established by the legislator is a return to the means of attaining benefit and alleviation in its entirety, unlike returning to what contradicts it" (3).
The moderation of the Sharia:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/240.
(2) The same source, 1/243.
(3) The same location.


[Page 303]

... "The Sharia (law) operates in its obligations according to the middle, most just path, taking from both sides with a share that has no bias in it, falling under the earnings of the servant without hardship upon him or dissolution" (1). With this meaning, al-Shatibi concludes this type of objectives of the legislator, and this meaning has been clarified previously, and there is no need to reiterate it and the intention of al-Shatibi behind it, except for what sometimes circulates from meanings that have no reality concerning the middle and moderation or the moderation of the Sharia. The concept of the middle is the actual matter between two extremes, such that one of them signifies strictness and the other signifies dissolution, or one signifies excess and the other signifies deficiency, or what may be imagined from two sides on either side of the middle. Accordingly, the term middle is used to mean or with the intention of improvement or beautification or acceptance of what occurs between two extremes. The same can be said about justice. Dr. Muhammad Said Ramadan al-Bouti states in his presentation of evidence regarding the consideration of the Sharia for public interests: "His Exalted is He's saying: { Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allah instructs you. Indeed, Allah is ever Hearing and Seeing }" (2). The essence of justice between two things or two persons is the equation and balance between them in a matter, so what is meant by it is then to observe moderation between the extremes of excess and deficiency in everything, and the true organization of people's interests and their harmony with one another is nothing but a straight line that separates the extremes of excess and deficiency in their affairs, and these are two extremes that inevitably lead to corruption" (3).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/110.
(2) Surah an-Nahl, 90.
(3) Muhammad Said Ramadan al-Bouti, The Controls of Public Interest in Islamic Law, p. 71. 5th ed., Al-Risalah Foundation, Al-Dar Al-Muttahida, 141 AH - 1990 CE.


[Page 304]

In reality, the terms justice and moderation have a pleasant impact on the soul, but they, like the terms oppression, excess, and negligence, cannot be understood in isolation unless they are connected to a foundational understanding. The man-made and distorted laws have their own definitions of justice and oppression or what they call good and evil, and if we were to examine the justice within them and compare it to our Sharia, we would find it to be sheer oppression, and we would find the truth within it to be falsehood and goodness to be a vice... These terms can only be understood through what they signify, that is, through what the Sharia has come to teach us is justice, oppression, goodness, or otherwise. In other words, to say that the Sharia is justice or the Sharia is moderation, if what is meant is that we know what justice and moderation are, and the Sharia commands us to adhere to what we know, is incorrect. The correct meaning is that the Sharia has come with commands and prohibitions, and what it has commanded is justice and moderation, and by knowing this, one understands what justice and moderation are, and what is contrary to them. Accordingly, the statement that justice is the straight line between the extremes of excess and negligence is a statement that lacks meaning. For this statement to have a tangible reality, one must know what excess is and what negligence is. Could it not be that what a person sees as excess is actually moderation and justice, or it is negligence? And what they see as negligence is actually justice and moderation, or it is excess? And what they perceive as justice or moderation could be excess or negligence. Is this not also consistent with the assertion that the notions of good and evil are based on Sharia rather than reason? Therefore, it is necessary to point out the frequent misreadings of al-Shatibi regarding this matter. Promoting terms like moderation or centrism or the centrism of the Sharia without specifying a foundation to embody these terms in meanings is superficial in thought and understanding. Al-Shatibi does not define moderation based on the feeling of what is excess or negligence, but rather he defines excess and negligence by deviating from moderation.


[Page 305]

He says: "Moderation is known by the Sharia, and it may also be known by customs and what most rational people witness, as in extravagance and stinginess in expenditures" (1). Thus, when he places the truth with moderation, he defines moderation as that which is indicated by the Sharia, or you could say that which is indicated by the Sharia is moderation or the middle ground. As for his statement: "and what most rational people witness," he has placed this in matters where the Sharia has designated the resolution to custom or to those with knowledge and expertise, such as the dowry of the equivalent (mahr al-mithl), the wage of the equivalent (ajr al-mithl), and the expenses of the equivalent (nafaqa al-mithl). And in defining the rich and the poor, extravagance and stinginess, all these matters are relative.
In this sense, al-Shatibi's statement that the Sharia operates in obligations according to its requirements on the middle and just path comes. He then says that if there comes in the obligations of the Sharia a tendency towards one of the extremes, that is part of the policy of the Sharia in either strictness or leniency, depending on the inclination of the obligated person towards the other side. He says: "If you look at a general Sharia ruling, you will find it advocating moderation; if you see a tendency towards one of the extremes, that is in response to a reality or expectation on the other side... Accordingly, if you see in the transmission from those considered in the religion a deviation from moderation, know that this is in consideration of a reality or expectation on the other side" (2).
The difference in the degree of customary hardship due to the difference in actions:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/114.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/113 - 114.


[Page 306]

This further clarifies what was mentioned above, which is that the hardship that is considered outside the norm in one action may not be regarded as such in another action, even if it is heavier or more severe. Thus, moderation varies according to the different actions. He says: "The fatigue and hardship in customary actions differ according to those actions... but every action in itself has a customary hardship that is comparable to the hardship of similar ordinary actions" (1). He states: "The hardship in a single action has two extremes and a mean" (2). His phrase "in a single action" indicates this meaning, and thus the customary hardship and the non-customary hardship are recognized by the Sharia, and in each action individually. The Sharia may consider the hardship to be non-customary in one action, while it is lighter for the obligated person than what it considers customary in another action. He says: "Much of what appears at first glance as hardships that are outside the norm may not be so for one who is knowledgeable about the flow of customs, and if it does not fall outside the norm, there would be no intention by the legislator to alleviate it like other customary hardships" (3). He said: "When Allah, Exalted is He, said: { march forth, light and heavy } (4), then said: { if you do not march forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment } (5), this is a point of severity because it implies that there is no concession at all for staying behind, except that it is, according to the evidence on alleviating hardship, applicable to the utmost burden in customary actions such that marching forth is feasible and one can proceed" (6). This means that although the hardship here is heavy, the Sharia considers it customary in such an action, and it does not fall under the principle of obligation that is unbearable or what a person cannot perform. He said: "The essence of hardship is constriction, so whatever is among the customary hardships in actions similar to it is not considered hardship either linguistically or in the Sharia, especially since this type of hardship is established for a legal wisdom, which is purification and testing" (7).

The Second Topic
The Intention of the Legislator in the Obligated Person Submitting to the Rules of the Sharia

Introduction to this Type:
... This is the fourth type of the objectives of the legislator (maqasid al-sharia), and it is the most important according to al-Shatibi, while the previous three types serve it. The first type, which is that the obligations relate to the preservation of necessities, needs, and enhancements, clarifies the goals and reasons for the Sharia so that they serve as foundations upon which the particulars and branches are directed and built. The second type, which is the establishment of the Sharia for understanding, clarifies the principles for comprehending the meanings of words, structures, and texts, in order to know the meanings and rulings. The third type, which is the establishment of the Sharia for obligation according to it, clarifies how to implement the texts while preserving the foundations or universals, and it essentially refers to the application of both the universals and particulars without neglecting either, in order to derive the subsidiary rulings. Thus, the three types serve the process of arriving at the legal ruling. The subject of the fourth type, the obligated person submitting to the rules of the Sharia, is obedience; when a command or prohibition comes from the legislator, obedience is required, and it is not permissible to issue a fatwa contrary to that or to deviate from it for any reason. If there is an exception or concession in a particular case, then the legal demand does not originally encompass that case.
... While the second and third types do not raise any significant jurisprudential or foundational disputes that affect methodology in reasoning and derivation, the first and fourth types provoke considerable debate.


[Page 308]

... The scholars who preceded al-Shatibi and spoke of the first type of objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) argued for the reasoning behind rulings based on wisdoms, on the premise that these wisdoms are the beneficial meanings or appropriate descriptions that, if presented to minds, would be accepted. However, al-Shatibi's understanding of the concept of benefit (maslaha) differed from that of his predecessors. The difference between the two is like the difference between their saying: what is presumed to be rationally beneficial or is felt in the heart as a benefit or intended wisdom behind the ruling is a reason, and his saying: what is definitively established through the induction of rulings as a goal or intended by the Legislator is a reason and a benefit. In other words, they say: the benefit is a reason. He says: the reason is a benefit.
... The difference between the two methodologies is one that turns matters upside down. This difference is not limited to what has been clarified regarding their understanding of benefits and harms, but extends to other matters(1).
__________
(1) The idea of reasoning based on benefit or legislation based on it has become widespread in our time, and as a result, clear invalid opinions and fatwas have been issued. Some have resorted to ideas they attribute to the Sharia, such as bringing about benefits, preventing harms, necessity, facilitation, the flexibility of the Sharia, and the permissibility of changing rulings with the change of time. These individuals did not adhere to the conditions set by the imams who advocate for benefits. Among these conditions is that this reasoning should not lead to the invalidation of the ruling being reasoned for, and that the beneficial description used for reasoning should not be contradicted by a text or opposed by a beneficial meaning that is used to reason for another ruling. Some contemporary scholars have argued for the necessity of expanding the scope of what is permissible (halal) through what they call broad juristic preference (istihsan) and broad analogy (qiyas), meaning not being bound by the conditions for the validity of analogy or preference because those conditions entered the science of usul al-fiqh through Greek logic. This was advocated by Dr. Hassan al-Turabi in his book Renewal of the Foundations of Jurisprudence.


[Page 309]

He called in his book for an approach that does not adhere to individual texts, but rather relies on a collection of texts from which the general meaning or the type of public interest (maslaha) is derived, and then legislation is based on that general meaning. In this case, there is no concern for the new legislations contradicting individual texts. Sheikh Rashid al-Ghannouchi followed him in this approach in his book (Public Freedoms in the Islamic State). In a press interview with the Lebanese magazine al-Shiraa, Sheikh al-Ghannouchi responded to the notion that his ideas are strange by Islamic standards, saying: "We are still governed by the complex of the text," and he said: "Al-Turabi is the teacher of a generation, and I am one of them." Legal rulings in our time have been given according to the whims of those in power, to the extent that it has been attributed to some the saying: "You have the opinion, and I have the evidence." And to another, the saying: "Present to me what benefits the people, and I will present to you the evidence." See: an article titled (Response to Fabrications Against al-Shatibi) by Mahmoud Abdul Karim Hassan, 1994 CE. And see: al-Muwafaqat, edited by Abu Ubaida, in his introduction to the book, vol. 1, footnote, p. 42.


[Page 310]

... Therefore, you find him in many instances in al-Muwafaqat addressing fatwas that are issued citing public interest (maslaha) or necessity, and addressing leniency without a license, and addressing the jurists who present such opinions based on the assertion that the Sharia of Islam is lenient and accommodating. He says, for example: "The leniency of the Hanif (haneef) is only present within the bounds of what is consistent with its principles, and it is not the pursuit of concessions or the selection of opinions based on whims that is established from its foundations" (1), and he says: "The pursuit of concessions is a leaning towards the desires of the souls, and the law has come with a prohibition against following desires... Some may permit this in situations where they claim necessity and compelling need based on the principle that necessities permit the prohibited, thus taking what aligns with their objective... This too is of the previously mentioned category, as its essence is taking what aligns with the present desire, and the locations of necessity are well-known in the Sharia" (2). He then says: "Piety and religiousness are scarce among many who position themselves to disseminate knowledge and issue fatwas" (3), and we will discuss this matter in detail - if Allah wills - in the chapter on ijtihad and taqlid.
... For this reason, we find al-Shatibi in this type of objectives (maqasid) to be thorough and meticulous, discussing the issue of legislation for the interests of the servants, and relating it to the principle of obedience and servitude to Allah. He discusses the issue of changes in people's customs with the variation of times and places, clarifying that this has no effect on the legal rulings, and he discusses the issue of adhering to the text or following meanings, indicating that following meanings must not deviate from the text under any circumstances.
... The volume of al-Shatibi's discussions in this type of objectives amounts to the total of his discussions in the three previous types, and it occupies - approximately - half of the second part of the book al-Muwafaqat.
The principle of obedience or servitude:

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 4/81.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 4/81.

[Page 311]

... Al-Shatibi emphasizes that adherence to commands and prohibitions is fundamental in the Sharia, and that servitude to Allah must be present in every action of the accountable person. Any action that does not involve worship of Allah is following one's desires. He stresses that determining benefit (maslaha) and harm (mafsada) is contingent upon the provisions of the legislator, and that following what one perceives as beneficial without considering the ruling of the Sharia regarding that benefit is purely following one's desires, and whatever is thus is entirely invalid.
... He states: "The legal objective of establishing the Sharia is to free the accountable person from the call of their desires so that they may be a servant of Allah by choice, just as they are a servant of Allah by necessity" (1). He then provides evidence that conclusively supports his methodology. He says: "The evidence for this consists of several matters: the first is the explicit text indicating that the servants were created to worship Allah and to submit to His commands and prohibitions, such as His saying: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. (56) I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want them to feed Me. } (2). And His saying: { And command your family to pray and be steadfast therein. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. } (3). And His saying: { O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous. } (4)... and other verses commanding worship in general and its details specifically. All of this refers back to returning to Allah in all circumstances and submitting to His rulings at all times, which is the essence of worshiping Allah... The second is what indicates the blameworthiness of opposing this objective, starting with the prohibition against disobeying Allah's command and the condemnation of those who turn away from Allah... The root of this is following one's desires and yielding to the obedience of immediate interests and fleeting passions... The third is what is known through experiences and customs, that religious and worldly benefits cannot be attained by indulging in following desires and aligning with interests" (5). Based on this, there is no action of the servant that does not involve worshiping Allah; thus, it must be accompanied by the intention of compliance, and this can only be with permission from the legislator. This is because what is good and bad, or beneficial and harmful, is known through the Sharia, and if the Sharia has no role in defining this, then what is followed is desire, as the matter is confined between the Sharia and desire, with no third option.
