He says: "Indeed, Allah has made following desires opposed to the truth and has made it its counterpart... He has confined the matter to two things: revelation, which is the Sharia, and desire; there is no third option. If that is the case, then they are opposites, and when the truth is determined in revelation, it is directed against desire... All of this is clear in that the intent of the Legislator is to move away from following desires and to enter into servitude to the Lord" (1).
... By making revelation and desire counterparts, he negates the existence of a ruling of reason, and what is imagined to be a ruling of reason in opposition to the ruling of the Sharia is merely desire. Accordingly, what is said to be wisdom or public interest (maslaha) according to rational people and wise individuals, if it is not established by revelation, is desire. Based on this, he established principles and said: "If this is established, it follows that principles arise from it, including that any action in which desire is followed absolutely, without regard to command or prohibition or choice, is absolutely invalid, because an action must have a bearer that compels it and a motivator that calls to it. If there is no entrance for the Legislator in that, then it is only the result of desire and lust, and whatever is thus is absolutely invalid because it contradicts the truth absolutely" (2). Among these principles is: "Following desire is a path to what is blameworthy, even if it comes within the praiseworthy" (3), because if it becomes clear that it is opposed by its very nature to the nature of the Sharia, then wherever it competes with its requirements in action, it is to be feared... For it is a cause of neglecting commands and committing prohibitions" (4).

Or one who issues a fatwa and participates in ruling by other than what Allah has revealed, claiming to serve the interests of Muslims, and in all of this there is neglect of commands and committing prohibitions, as Allah says: { And prohibited is interest } Al-Baqarah, 275 and His saying: { And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the wrongdoers } Al-Ma'idah, 45, and others.

... Among them is: "Following one's desires in legal rulings is a pretext for manipulating them to achieve one's aims, making them like a tool prepared to seize one's objectives, like the show-off who uses righteous deeds as a means to what is in the hands of people" (1).
... Al-Shatibi emphasizes the principle of compliance and its existence in every action of the servants, and this principle is not contradicted by the fact that the purpose of the Sharia is to preserve the interests of the servants, nor by the fact that the rulings take into account human nature, desires, and sensual characteristics. This objective is an end and a result, that is, a consequence of the causes, and the causes are compliance. The Sharia is established based on the requirement of worship and compliance, { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (51:56), and not based on the desires and aims of the servants. This is what the types of legal rulings necessitate. He says: "No one has the right to claim that the Sharia was established based on the desires and aims of the servants, as the rulings of the Sharia do not escape the five categories. As for obligation and prohibition, their contradiction to the requirement of indulgence that falls under choice is evident, as it is said to him: Do such and such whether you have an aim in it or not, and do not do such and such whether you have an aim in it or not. If the obligated person happens to have a compatible aim and a desire that motivates him according to the command or prohibition, it is by accident, not by origin. As for the other categories, although their apparent nature falls under the choice of the obligated person, they have entered by the legislator's inclusion of them under his choice, thus they revert to being removed from his choice" (2). Then he says: "Thus, the permissibility of the permissible, for example, does not necessitate its absolute inclusion under the choice of the obligated person as it is a decree from the legislator. At that point, his choice would be dependent on the legislator's stipulation, and his aim would be derived from the legal permission, not from natural indulgence. This is precisely what removes the obligated person from the impulse of his desires so that he becomes a servant of Allah" (3) (4).
__________

(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/116.
(4) In these statements, there is a denial of the Western idea of public freedoms in Islam. This idea stems from the notion of separating religion from life... and that man is free and not bound by any law or system, except what he chooses for himself. Hence, they spoke of the rule of the people, which led to the idea of democracy in Western systems. The concept of public freedoms is different from the meaning of freedom that opposes slavery, and it is a concept of disbelief because it implies that there is no rule of Allah, nor legislation except for the people. Similarly, the concept of permissibility (ibaha) in Islam is not a matter of freedom but is based on the idea of servitude to Allah, who alone has the right to command, prohibit, permit, and prevent. Thus, permissibility is a choice from the legislator, and the servant is bound to accept this choice, and he is not free; he cannot prohibit what is permissible nor obligate it. Therefore, the claim of the idea of public freedoms in Islam is a mistaken claim that contradicts the legal principles, and the greater errors are what come in the details of this idea. For example, Sheikh Rashid Ghannouchi in his book (Public Freedoms in the Islamic State) argued that the purpose of preserving the intellect is one of the necessities in the Sharia, meaning freedom of belief and freedom of opinion, even though these freedoms contradict general and specific principles in Islam that are not limited to the preservation of religion or the obligation to rule by what Allah has revealed and the obligation to kill the apostate, among other things. See: al-Muwafaqat, edited by Abu Ubaida, in his introduction to the book, vol. 1, footnote, pp. 42-53. Also see: articles titled (Integrating Islamic Communities into Western Societies) by Mahmoud Abdul Karim Hassan, 1997 CE.


[Page 314]

The interests and harms are known only through the Sharia:
... This objective of the legislator in establishing the Sharia is the servitude of man to Allah, which is definitive and there is no disagreement about it. If any disagreement arises regarding it, it pertains to differences in the meanings of words and expressions, not to the essence of its meaning. If we consider the interest in the reasoning based on the perspectives of rational individuals and those who reflect, this falls under the category of rational enhancement and deprecation, which contradicts this objective of compliance. This raises issues for those who advocate for interests, some of which have been mentioned by al-Qarafi and Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam. Al-Shatibi has also responded to them, asserting that they do not exist according to his methodology because he has a different understanding of interests and harms. Al-Shatibi emphasizes, after establishing the principle of compliance, that the determination of interests and harms is a Sharia matter that relates to enhancement and deprecation, and therefore it must return to the principle of compliance. If a wisdom appears in reasoning that is suitable for justifying the ruling, it should not be considered before obtaining conclusive induction, as there may be other wisdoms, and it may not be established through induction, making its consideration an arbitrary judgment without evidence and a misinterpretation of the legislator's intent. He states: "The fact that an interest is an interest intended by the ruling and a harm is a harm likewise is something that is specific to the legislator; there is no room for reason in this based on the principle of negating rational enhancement and deprecation. If the legislator has enacted the ruling for a particular interest, he is the one who establishes it as an interest; otherwise, it could logically be that it is not so, as all things are equal in relation to their original state, with no judgment from reason regarding their goodness or badness. Therefore, the existence of an interest as an interest is from the legislator, such that reason affirms it and the soul finds reassurance in it. Interests, as they are interests, have been concluded to be acts of worship, and what is built upon acts of worship can only be worshipful" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/219. And see the nineteenth issue of the fourth type of matters regarding the intent of the legislator.


[Page 315]

If we consider al-Shatibi's opinion regarding the second type of objectives of the Lawgiver (maqasid al-shari'a), which is to establish understanding, where he stated that the texts do not indicate the secondary meanings, in addition to the fact that the public interest (maslaha) is what has been definitively established through induction, it seems that al-Shatibi is rejecting the method of reasoning by appropriate description and is refuting the justification of the Sharia by bringing about benefits and repelling harms in the conventional sense held by its proponents.
... This is what led Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour to see that most of al-Shatibi's arguments for justifying the Sharia are invalid(1). This is also what prompted Dr. Ahmed Rissouni to label this opinion of al-Shatibi as one of the negative effects of theological discourse, asserting that the reason for al-Shatibi's stance is his influence by the Ash'ari perspective. Dr. Rissouni states under the title: "Understanding benefits by reason": "The well-known issue in theological discourse and in the science of Usul al-Fiqh regarding the issue of good and evil... because al-Shatibi himself did not escape some of its negative effects, specifically his influence by the Ash'ari perspective on the subject. In fact, this Ash'ari perspective is still prevalent - if not dominant - today"(2).
__________
(1) See: p. 181 of this book.
(2) Ahmed Rissouni, The Theory of Objectives in Imam al-Shatibi, p. 263.


[Page 316]

... To establish the Ash'ari (Ash'ariyya) position of al-Shatibi, al-Raisuni mentions what he calls the essence of the Ash'ari theory, along with some texts from al-Shatibi. He says: "They do not consider anything good except through the enhancement of the Sharia; without the enhancement or condemnation of the Sharia, there is neither good nor evil, and all matters are equal. This is precisely what al-Shatibi reiterates" (1). He states: "The Ash'ari influence is evident in his words, as it entails the denial of the goodness and badness of actions, meaning that they, in themselves, are either beneficial or harmful, for actions and omissions, in reason, are 'equally similar'; thus, there is no enhancement or condemnation by reason, and this is the essence of the Ash'ari theory" (2). He then defends the idea that goodness and badness in actions are intrinsic and that reason can, and has the right to, enhance and condemn. He observes that some scholars have refrained from this statement to avoid being associated with the Mu'tazila, not because they see it as incorrect, mentioning among them Abu al-Ma'ali al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali, for example. He says: "It seems to me that Abu al-Ma'ali... has deviated from the bounds of the Ash'ari theory" (3). He adds: "And although the Imam of the Two Sanctuaries was compelled to this extent of acknowledgment of enhancement and condemnation." He remarks: "It is strange what disputes and conflicts can do, that you find Imam al-Ghazali—who is a giant of Islamic thought—fearing and warning against being attributed to him what has been attributed to these individuals regarding the influence of the Mu'tazila, as he was inclined to assert the understanding of reason regarding benefits" (4). Dr. al-Raisuni then attempts to prove the validity of the claim regarding the enhancement and condemnation by reason (5).
The intent behind these statements by Dr. al-Raisuni is to highlight the contradiction between al-Shatibi's methodology and others regarding the issue of reasoning based on benefits and harms. In fact, the assertion of the causality of bringing about benefits and repelling harms for legal rulings necessitates the claim of enhancement and condemnation by reason.
__________
(1) Ahmad al-Raisuni, The Theory of Maqasid in Imam al-Shatibi, p. 264.
(2) Ibid, p. 265.
(3) Ibid, p. 267.
(4) Ibid, p. 274.
(5) Ibid, pp. 276 - 293.


[Page 317]

It should be noted here that the issue of whether good and evil are determined by the Sharia (shar'i) rather than by reason (aql) is a definitive matter. As for the disagreement regarding the ability of reason to determine good and evil, for those who affirm its capability, it does not imply that it grants legitimacy to what is deemed good by reason. On one hand, neither al-Juwayni nor al-Ghazali leans towards the correctness of the rational determination of good and evil. Al-Juwayni says: "The ruling attributed to its subject is not an inherent quality within it. Thus, when we say: drinking alcohol is forbidden, the prohibition is not an intrinsic quality of drinking. If we deem drinking permissible in necessity, it is like forbidden drinking in choice. What is meant by it being forbidden is that it is related to the prohibition, and what is meant by it being obligatory is that it is related to the command"(1). He also says: "Among the rulings of the Sharia are the determination of good and evil, which are related to commands and prohibitions. Nothing is deemed evil in the ruling of Allah, Exalted is He, for its own sake, just as nothing is deemed good for its own sake"(2).
Al-Ghazali says: "If this discourse from the Legislator does not exist, then there is no ruling. For this reason, we say that reason does not determine what is good or bad, nor does it necessitate gratitude to the Benefactor, and there is no ruling for actions before the arrival of the Sharia."(3)
Following the words of the two imams, al-Juwayni and al-Ghazali, leaves no room for what Dr. al-Raisuni has imagined.
Those who justify by means of public interest (maslaha) do not see this as legislation by reason; rather, they view it as being in accordance with the legal command, unlike their opponents. If the matter of this justification becomes problematic and necessitates a rational improvement or condemnation, it is rejected without hesitation. If Dr. al-Raisuni believes that the resolution of the issue lies in asserting the legitimacy of rational improvement and condemnation, then he has strayed far.
The conflict between reasoning based on public interest (maslaha) and the authority of the Sharia (hakamiyyat al-sharia):
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan, 1/79, paragraph: 8.
(2) The same place, paragraph: 9.
(3) Al-Ghazali, Al-Mustasfa, 1/55.


[Page 318]

... There is no contradiction between these two principles according to al-Shatibi, as the benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid) are determined by the Sharia, meaning that whether something is a benefit or a harm falls under the category of commendation and condemnation. However, a contradiction arises if the benefit is considered according to the perspective of rational individuals and those who deliberate, and their determination of what is suitable or what constitutes a benefit and what constitutes a harm. Those who hold this view have their evidence for reasoning based on benefits, so do their proofs contradict the principle of worship and compliance?
... The answer according to al-Shatibi is: Yes, they do contradict. Therefore, he attempts to negate this contradiction in a way that turns matters upside down. After he concluded the proof and establishment of the principle of compliance as a definitive objective of the Lawgiver, he turned to what he fundamentally relied upon to justify the Sharia by bringing about benefits and repelling harms, and he reconfigured it in another way. He said: "If it is said: The establishment of the laws is either in vain or for a wisdom, the first is invalid by consensus, and Allah, Exalted is He, said: { Did you think that We created you in vain? } (1), and He said: { And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain } (2), { And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them as play. We did not create them except in truth } (3). If it is for a wisdom and benefit, then the benefit is either directed to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servants. Its return to Allah is impossible because He is Self-Sufficient, and it is impossible for benefits to return to Him as clarified in the science of theology. Thus, it remains that it returns to the servants, which is necessitated by their interests, for every doer seeks the benefit of himself and what aligns with his worldly and otherworldly affairs, and the Sharia has guaranteed this demand within the framework of obligation. So how can it be denied that the Sharia is established according to the interests of the servants and the motives of their desires? Furthermore, it has been previously stated that the Sharia came in accordance with the interests of the servants and confirmed their shares as a favor from Allah according to what the scholars assert, or as an obligation according to what the Mu'tazila claim. If this is established as a true objective of the Lawgiver, then what contradicts it is false" (4). This text presents an objection to al-Shatibi regarding how he establishes benefits, and al-Shatibi responds to this text not by denying or refuting it, but by affirming it while directing its meaning or interpretation in a way that differs from the conventional or immediate understanding.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Mu'minun, 115.
(2) Surah Sad, 27.
(3) Surah Al-Dukhan, 38 - 39.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 2/117.


[Page 319]

He says: "The answer is that the establishment of the Sharia (law) is, if it is accepted that it is for the interests of the servants, returning to them according to the command of the Lawgiver and to the extent that He has defined, not according to their whims and desires. Hence, the legal obligations are burdensome on the souls... The commands and prohibitions remove a person from the inclinations of his nature and the pursuit of his desires until he takes them from beneath the legal limit, and this is precisely the intended meaning, which is the very essence of opposing whims and desires. As for the fact that the interests of the obligation return to the obligated person in this world and the Hereafter, this is correct, and it does not necessitate that attaining them is outside the bounds of the Sharia, nor that he can attain them by himself without the Sharia providing them to him, which is evident. This clarifies that there is no contradiction between this statement and what has preceded, because what has preceded looked at the establishment of interest and desire as affirmed by the Lawgiver, not as dictated by whim and desire." (1)
What is noticeable in this text, and in the entire book of al-Muwafaqat, is that al-Shatibi's intended meaning by the term "considered interest" (mashlaha) in the Sharia is different from the commonly understood meaning among others. The commonly understood meaning uses other terms such as interest, desire, benefit, and whim.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/117 - 118.


[Page 320]

... Al-Shatibi's intention in raising the contradiction is that the interests of the servants, their purposes, and their desires are not realized or attained by following them, but rather they are realized by adhering to the rulings of the Sharia. A servant may perceive the fulfillment of his benefit, purpose, or satisfaction of his need through a certain means, and if he follows it, then that is following one's desires (hawa), even if he believes that this is a benefit and that the Sharia was revealed for the sake of benefits. This belief is not legitimate, and this is not a benefit according to al-Shatibi. If the realization of benefits and purposes and the satisfaction of needs is permissible, not every means to that is permissible; the purpose may be legitimate, such as ownership, but the means to it may be forbidden, such as gambling, deceit, usury, and theft. If ownership is permissible, it can only be attained through permissible means. This is the meaning of his statement: "The commands and prohibitions remove him from the inclinations of his nature and the pursuit of his desires until he takes them from beneath the permissible limit," and his statement: "Nor should he attain them by himself without the Sharia providing them for him."
... Thus, al-Shatibi states that the Sharia was established for the interests of the accountable individuals in both abodes, but interests can only be known through the Sharia. It is not correct for the accountable individual to seek his share except through the means prescribed by the Sharia, and his meaning ultimately leads to the conclusion that there is no difference between saying that the Sharia was established for the servants and saying that the servants were created for the Sharia, which is the implication of His saying, Exalted is He: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (1).
__________
(1) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.


[Page 321]

... So if the purposes of the servants and their benefits and desires are found in fulfilling the needs of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sovereignty, security, women, leadership, and other matters, did the Sharia come with the most upright system to ensure that people satisfy their true needs, and thus the Sharia is for their sake? Or is the Sharia merely commands and prohibitions from Allah that people must comply with, as Allah created in people what He created of needs, desires, and instincts that drive them to obedience? The Sharia commands the worship of Allah and submission and humility before Him, and Allah created in people the innate disposition towards faith and worship as a kindness to them and assistance in obedience, and commanded them to preserve life, to marry, to care for the family, and to provide for them, and created in them desires and emotions that assist them in that? Which of the two is the correct interpretation? Answering this requires evidence, whether rational or textual. If the arguments of those who assert the primacy of interests in the sense of benefits and advantages are based on the first interpretation, al-Shatibi adopts the second interpretation. He says: "The wisdom of the All-Wise and All-Aware has decreed that the establishment of religion and the world is only valid and sustained by motives from humans that drive them to acquire what they need for themselves and others. He created in them the desire for food and drink when they experience hunger and thirst to motivate them to seek to fulfill this need as much as they can. Likewise, He created in them the desire for women to motivate them to acquire the means to reach them. He also created in them the discomfort from heat and cold and unexpected occurrences, which serves as a motivation to acquire clothing and shelter. Then He created Paradise and Hell and sent the messengers, clarifying that stability is not here, but rather this world is a cultivation for another abode, and that eternal happiness and eternal misery are there; however, the means to attain them are acquired here by adhering to what the legislator has defined or by deviating from it...


[Page 322]

And if Allah had willed, He could have imposed it while disregarding the interests, or He could have imposed it while stripping away the innate motivations, but He has made it easier for His servants by making it a means to what He desires of cultivating this world for the Hereafter and has made the acquisition of these interests permissible, not prohibited, but according to legal regulations that are more beneficial and more enduring than what the servant considers to be beneficial { and Allah knows, while you do not know } (1). And if He had willed, He could have prevented us from seeking the interests of the Hereafter, for He is the Owner and has the ultimate argument, but He has encouraged us to fulfill the obligatory rights owed to Him by promising us a share of it and has hastened for us many shares that we enjoy along the way of what we have been commanded to do (2).
... So did al-Shatibi affirm the idea of reasoning by bringing about benefits and repelling harms, or did he diminish it?! This depends on the meaning of benefit and the meaning of harm, that is, on the concept of each. It is clear that he has refuted it if it is understood in the sense recognized by the jurists before him, or in the common sense today.
The objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) are of two types: primary and secondary:
... It follows that the Sharia takes into account the interests of the servants and their purposes and characteristics, but this consideration does not mean following them in legislation; rather, it means following the legal rulings because the interests are achieved through them. The preservation of religion, life, wealth, and other objectives of the Sharia are also interests and objectives for the servants.
The interests of the servants and their benefits are variable and changeable, while the rulings of the Sharia are fixed. Therefore, al-Shatibi refutes al-Razi's statement that the original ruling regarding benefits is permission and regarding harms is prohibition. He also says, "How many a person of desires wishes that a certain permissible thing were prohibited, to the extent that if he were entrusted with legislation, he would prohibit it" (3), and he says, "Even if it were assumed that it were made permissible for him, he would make it obligatory, and then the matter regarding that very permissible thing might turn around, so he may love what he hated today and vice versa, thus a ruling cannot be established in absolute terms" (4).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 216.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/122.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/116.
(4) The same source.


[Page 323]

However, the interests of the servants may align with the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), meaning they may serve it, such as the drive to work for earning a livelihood, marriage, fulfilling desires, and responding to human nature. So, are these objectives considered Sharia objectives? That is, is the pursuit of interests among the objectives of the Sharia? He says: "The Sharia objectives are of two types: original objectives and subsidiary objectives. As for the original ones, they are those in which there is an interest for the obligated person, and they are the necessities recognized in every community" (1). Then he said: "As for the subsidiary objectives, they are those in which the interest of the obligated person is taken into account, through which he attains what he is naturally inclined to, such as fulfilling desires, enjoying permissible things, and fulfilling needs" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/120.
(2) The same source, 2/122.


[Page 324]

As for his statement that there is no benefit for the obligated person (mukallaf) in the necessities, while he affirms in many places that all obligations of the Sharia return to the individual with immediate or delayed benefits, for example, he says: "The necessities are of two types: one is that which has an immediate benefit for the obligated person aimed at enabling the individual to fulfill the interests of himself and his dependents in terms of sustenance, housing, clothing, and other transactions such as sales, rentals, marriages, and other means of earning that sustain human structures. The second is that which does not have an immediate intended benefit, such as the obligatory acts of worship, both physical and financial, like purification, prayer, fasting, almsgiving, pilgrimage, and similar acts, or from the obligations of communal responsibility, such as public offices like caliphate, ministry, representation, judiciary, prayers, jihad, education, and other matters that have been legislated generally for public interests" (1). His statement that "there is no benefit for the obligated person in these matters" is from the perspective that they are commands and prohibitions that must be adhered to based on the principle of compliance, regardless of the outcomes they lead to. Yes, they do lead to the benefit of the servant. However, in terms of being necessities, meaning established interests in the Sharia, they must be adhered to because they are legitimate, not because they lead to benefits, as benefits are not fixed, and the servant's view of his benefits is fluctuating, while these necessities are fixed. He says: "We only say that there is no benefit for the servant in them as necessities because they fulfill absolute general interests that are not limited to one state or form, nor to one time over another" (2). He also says: "This is evidenced by the fact that if the servant were to choose contrary to these matters (3), he would be restricted and prevented from his choice. Hence, he becomes devoid of benefit and is ruled upon in himself. If he were to have a benefit in them, it would be from another perspective that is subordinate to this original objective" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/123.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/120.
(3) These matters are the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and wealth.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/121.


[Page 325]

Al-Shatibi focuses on establishing that the necessary objectives (maqasid) are those that take into account the obligations of the accountable person (mukallaf), thus countering any objections to his previous opinion regarding the intention of compliance and his understanding of public interest (maslaha) and its justification. Therefore, he introduces an important idea within the context of his research, which justifies his statement that he considers the obligations of the accountable person in matters of necessity. This is that the objectives of the Sharia, even though they pertain to the accountable person by affirming their interests, also, in the process, pertain to affirming the interests of others, whether the accountable person has a share in the interests of others, such as a wife or a son, or others whom he desires to fulfill their purposes, or whether he does not have a share in their interests, as in leases and sales and other transactions. He fulfills his share through housing, while others fulfill their share through ownership of the rent, even if he has no desire or inclination whatsoever for the other to fulfill their share.


[Page 326]

He says that the original objectives (maqasid) are divided into essential (ainiya) and sufficient (kafiya). As for the essential, it is upon every accountable person to preserve their religion, self, intellect, lineage, and wealth. As for the sufficient: "It is contingent upon others to fulfill it generally among all accountable individuals so that public affairs, which cannot be established without it, may be rectified" (1). He speaks regarding actions that involve the attainment of benefits through lawful means: "This category is divided into two: one category involves fulfilling interests directly without intermediaries, such as fulfilling one's own interests directly (2), and the other category involves fulfilling interests through the benefits of others, such as fulfilling the duties of spouses and children, and earning through what benefits others, like rents, leasing, trade, and other forms of crafts and earnings. All of these seek the individual's share, and in doing so, they serve the interests of others, creating a cycle among people, just as some parts of the human body serve one another so that the benefit is achieved for all" (3). This means that the benefits that are attained and the advantages that result from the rulings of the Sharia have outcomes that circulate among people; they are related to a general system in society and a network of relationships and public interests. Not all of this is grasped by the observer; if one perceives certain benefits or rulings, there are others that remain unrecognized. He states: "If we understand through necessity or choice an independent wisdom in the ruling of the law, it does not necessitate that there are not other wisdoms and benefits, second, third, and more. Our ultimate understanding is that we have comprehended a worldly benefit that is suitable to independently justify the ruling, and we have considered it under the ruling of legal permission, while we do not know that the benefit and ruling are limited to what has appeared. If we do not attain knowledge or conjecture from this, we cannot decisively claim that there is no benefit in the ruling except what has appeared to us, for that is a decisive claim on the unseen without evidence, which is not permissible. There may be another wisdom for which the ruling was established, and we have become from those wisdoms standing with devotion" (4)
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) Such as acts of worship to preserve religion, and to preserve oneself and one's intellect.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/124.
(4) The same source, 2/219.


[Page 327]

Therefore, viewing necessities as having no share for the accountable person (mukallaf) is to prevent the share that may result from it from becoming the legal objective, as this would waste many other shares. Taking these shares or benefits as objectives under the pretext that the Sharia intended to fulfill them has repercussions on the network of relationships and public interests in society, in addition to what it may lead to in terms of neglecting commands and prohibitions.
... An example of this is the ruling on the killing of an apostate (murtad). The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him" (1), and the companions unanimously agreed on this ruling and acted upon it. It is one of the necessities in the preservation of the religion. Researchers may mention a ruling regarding it, such as their saying that apostasy weakens the strength of Islam, confuses the weak among the Muslims, and affects others as it prevents or delays their entry into it, among other things, and killing the apostate prevents all of that. Therefore, this ruling has benefits for society and individuals. In our time, there are those who say that the apostate should not be killed, claiming that the dangers have been removed, and that Islam and Muslims today are not affected by such an act; the difference is vast between the reality of Muslims in the city and their reality today. By applying the meaning of the original objectives (maqasid) according to al-Shatibi, the ruling on the apostate must be viewed as a necessary principle stripped of share, and it should not be lifted even if circumstances change. The mentioned rulings, which may be cited, are not all the rulings, and moreover, not applying the text nullifies the act of worship, even if some of these rulings are established with certainty and thus become benefits, they do not annul the text, because adherence to it is also a principle as it returns to a definitive meaning, which is the preservation of the religion. On the other hand, any imagined wisdom that leads to abandoning the meaning of the text is rejected, because the meanings of rulings are only established through induction, and the induction here serves to contradict the principles, thus it is certainly rejected, following the methodology of al-Shatibi himself.

(1) Al-Bukhari, Chapter on "No one should be punished with the punishment of Allah" (2794), (6411), Al-Tirmidhi, Chapter on "What has been reported regarding the apostate" (1378) and he said: "Hasan Sahih and this is the practice." Al-Nasa'i (3991) - (3997). Abu Dawood (3787) and Ibn Majah (2526) and Ahmad (1775).


[Page 328]

... As for the consideration of interests, which he called the subsidiary objectives (maqasid tab'iyya), this means that the legal rulings pertain to the obligated person in terms of preservation, security, care, and obtaining what is necessitated by their sensual attributes. Induction has indicated this, so the attainment of these interests has become a legal objective, and it is permissible for the obligated person to intend through their actions the fulfillment of these needs and the attainment of these desires, and for their actions to be aimed at acquiring these interests. However, he still referred to them as subsidiary objectives in contrast to the original objectives, meaning that it is permissible for him to intend them, but only within the limits of what is legally permissible; that is, it is not permissible for him to pursue them except through actions that are legally authorized. In this case, the intention of interests strengthens the idea of worship, and this was previously mentioned in his seventh introduction where he said: "Every legal knowledge is sought by the legislator only as a means to worship Allah, Exalted is He, and not for any other reason. If another consideration appears in it, it is only secondary and by way of the second intention, not the first" (1), and he mentioned in this introduction his proofs, including: "The law was only revealed for the purpose of worship, which is the objective of the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them" (2). He said: "Every subsidiary objective is either a servant of the original intention or not. If it serves it, then the intention towards it from the outset is correct... But if it does not serve it, then the intention towards it from the outset is incorrect" (3).
... Thus, the subsidiary objectives are legal objectives that the obligated person also intends because they align with their nature and attributes, but it is not permissible to intend them if that is through violating the legal rulings or texts. He said regarding those who take their interests without adhering to the commands and prohibitions: "As a precaution against those who take it without considering the command and prohibition, and this is the blameworthy interest, for they do not refrain from what has been prescribed for them but rather act boldly like an animal that knows nothing but walking in its desires" (4).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/30.
(2) The same source, 1/31.
(3) The same source, 1/35 - 36.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/133.


[Page 329]

... And if it is the nature of man to seek his interests, then among these interests are those that are lawful, meaning those that are subordinate objectives, and others that are not. The obligated person (mukallaf) may take a lawful or unlawful path to achieve his objective. Likewise, the mukallaf may act with the intention of seeking his interests, or he may do so with the intention of compliance, or with both intentions together.

All these cases will be discussed in detail - if Allah wills - in the next chapter, the chapter on the objectives of the mukallaf.

The third section
Between the Sharia and its objectives
Or between worship and following meanings

The subject of this section:
It has been clarified in the first type of the objectives of the legislator that the Sharia was established to preserve the interests of the servants. The rulings of the Sharia have goals that result from adhering to its rulings, and the legislator intended them by enacting the rulings. It has also been clarified in the fourth type that one of the objectives of the legislator is adherence to the commands and prohibitions.

Between these two types, questions arise. If the rulings were enacted for the interests of the servants, are the rulings a means to those interests, so can the rulings be changed to preserve their goals? And if certain goals for the rulings have been established that the legislator intended, is the mukallaf obligated to the goals, that is, to the effects of the rulings, just as he is obligated to the rulings? And is it valid for the mukallaf to intend goals other than those intended by the legislator?

And if the intention of the legislator is compliance and worship, is it valid for the mukallaf to comply without regard to the intended goals of the legislator? And is everything that results from the rulings or arises from them considered interests or objectives of the legislator? How can one distinguish what is intended by Him - Exalted is He - from what is not? And do interests and harms change with the change of customs according to the change of times and places? And does this have an effect on the rulings?

For such questions and similar ones, this section was created, and the answers will come within it - if Allah wills - according to the methodology of al-Shatibi.
The universality of the Sharia and its stability:
... Al-Shatibi emphasizes within the objective of worship and compliance the universality and stability of the Sharia. It is general for all obligated persons, and no mukallaf is exempt from it at all, and it is general for all actions; there is no action except that you find the Sharia governing it. No mukallaf is exempt from a general ruling in any action except by a specific legal text that does not extend its ruling to the mukallaf, and this does not undermine the principle, which is the universality of the Sharia.


[Page 330]

... Among what the generality of the Sharia (Islamic law) necessitates is the stability of its rulings in every time and place; otherwise, it would not be general for those obligated by it. The revelation has ceased after the death of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), so there is no abrogation, and what is good does not become bad, nor does what is bad become good.
... If some rulings change, it is due to the change in their underlying reasons (manat), such as when the legislator has linked the ruling to a reason, and the ruling changes according to the presence or absence of that reason. Or it may be that the legislator has arranged the rulings based on certain attributes, so the ruling changes according to the attribute, such as puberty in legal responsibility (taklif), which may differ from place to place or from person to person. Legal responsibility may apply to one person at the age of eleven, for example, and to another at the age of fifteen. This change, in this sense, is not a change in the essence of the address, but rather a stability, as the condition of puberty in legal responsibility is fixed and does not change.
... Likewise, the rulings that are affected by the intention (niyyah) or purpose (maqsad) of the obligated person, such as prostrating to Allah, Exalted is He, or to an idol, or the utterance of the two testimonies (shahadatayn) in faith or hypocrisy, depend on the intention of the doer. Here, the intention or purpose is part of the underlying reason for the ruling, meaning it is part of the act, and the ruling is a ruling on an act that changes with its change according to the address.
... Similarly, the rulings that have words as their causes, such as marriage (nikah), divorce (talaq), and emancipation (itaq), occur with the utterance of the words that indicate them. The meanings of the words may change, as people may become accustomed to certain words for meanings or to meanings for certain words, and the customs of one group may differ from another, leading to a change in the ruling based on those words accordingly. This does not affect the fact that the words are causes, as the words were established for their meanings. If the connotations of the words change, the consideration is given to the connotations or meanings and the words that indicate them.


[Page 331]

... Likewise, the rulings that the legislator has linked to custom (urf), where the intended meaning of custom here refers to the terms or quantities that are commonly recognized, such as saying: this commodity is for a thousand. Is it a thousand lira, dollar, or dinar? Or if it is a dinar, is it an Iraqi, Jordanian, or gold dinar? And similarly, the meanings of the terms used in contracts and transactions. And like the estimation of expenses or the estimation of wages or the dowry or the price. These matters may change according to places, times, people, or conditions, and the rulings are based on these terms and estimations. Thus, although it may be said that there is a change in the rulings, it is not a change based on time or place, but rather a change in reality and conditions. For example, if the law prescribes for a divorced woman a maintenance equivalent, then what changes is the amount of maintenance, which depends on the condition of the divorced woman, and this is not a change in the ruling, as the ruling is that she has maintenance equivalent to her, and this is established.
... For example, the prohibition of carrion in normal circumstances and its permissibility in cases of necessity is not a change in the rulings, as its prohibition is established in that case, and its permissibility is established in the other case. Similarly, it is said about wine: it is forbidden, but if it turns into vinegar, it becomes permissible; this is not a change or reversal in the rulings, but rather the prohibition of wine is established and the permissibility of vinegar is established. Accordingly, the legal rulings are fixed and permanent.
... Therefore, it is not correct to say: the change of rulings is not denied by the change of time and place (1). If the change is restricted to the meanings mentioned above, it then becomes related to the bases of the rulings, that is, to changes in the realities or conditions that are part of the action to which the ruling pertains.
__________
(1) See for example: The Theory of Objectives (Maqasid) by Imam al-Shatibi by Dr. Ahmad Rayesuni, p. 288, where he says: "However, it is also undeniable that there are many interests - and harms - that are affected by the differences in conditions and circumstances, leading to changes in their situations and priorities, and altering their benefits and harms... which necessitates a new consideration and appropriate estimation, and all of this affects the rulings in some way." He also states: "In any case, I do not wish to delve into the topic of the change of interests and the change of rulings with the change of times and conditions, but I only wanted to point out a wide area of fields that require a kind of refinement of the intellect and its corruption through its estimation of the changing and renewed interests and harms and what they require of appropriate rulings," p. 288.


[Page 332]

... Al-Shatibi's focus on the universality of the Sharia and its permanence, and his mention of this matter within the objective of worship and compliance, affirms his concept of benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid) and refutes the claim of the Sharia's evolution and flexibility and the permissibility of changing its rulings. He states: "Among the characteristics of the Sharia is 'universality and consistency; therefore, the legal rulings regarding the actions of the accountable individuals are absolute, even if their specific instances are countless. There is no action imposed, nor movement or stillness claimed, except that the Sharia governs it, both individually and collectively, which is the meaning of its being general" (1). Among its characteristics also is "permanence without abrogation; therefore, you will not find in it, after its completion, any abrogation or specification of its universality, nor restriction of its absoluteness, nor lifting of any of its rulings, neither in terms of the generality of the accountable individuals nor in terms of the specificity of some of them, nor in terms of one condition over another. Rather, whatever establishes a cause is a cause forever and does not cease, and whatever is a condition is always a condition, and whatever is obligatory is always obligatory, or recommended is recommended, and so on for all rulings; they do not cease or change. Even if the obligation were to continue indefinitely, its rulings would remain the same" (2).
... He says: "If it is established that the legislator intended through legislation to establish benefits for the Hereafter and this world in a manner that does not disrupt their order, neither in terms of the whole nor in terms of the part, and whether it is of the nature of necessities, needs, or embellishments, then if it were established in such a way that its order could be disrupted or its rulings could be violated, the legislation would not be intended for it, for its being benefits in that case is no more valid than its being harms. Rather, the legislator intends for it to be benefits absolutely; thus, its establishment must be in that manner eternally, universally, and generally for all types of obligations and the obligated individuals in all circumstances, and thus we have found the matter therein, and all praise is due to Allah" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/44.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/45.
(3) The same source, 2/25.


[Page 333]

... Accordingly, the interests (masalih) and harms (mafasid) according to the methodology of al-Shatibi are fixed and do not change, and they are what the legislator has established as reasons for the Sharia. The concept of interests and harms is not the same as benefits and detriments, as the latter are relative and not fixed. The rulings are not justified by them. He says: "Generally, benefits and detriments are relative and not real, and the meaning of being relative is that they are benefits or detriments in one situation but not in another, and in relation to one person but not another, or at one time but not at another" (1).
... He also says: "It is not correct to continue to assert that the original principle regarding benefits is permission and regarding detriments is prohibition, as stated by al-Fakhr al-Razi, for there is hardly any real benefit or real harm (2), rather, they are mostly relative, and if the interests and harms are related to the address of the legislator, and we know from His address that it is directed according to circumstances, individuals, and times, so that a specific benefit is permitted at one time or situation or for one person, and not permitted if it is otherwise, then how can one justify the statement that the original principle regarding benefits is permission and regarding detriments is prohibition" (3).
... The meaning of his statement that the Sharia is directed according to circumstances, individuals, and times is that the rulings of the Sharia, in general and in totality, encompass all actions for all accountable individuals at all times. For example, the Sharia has clarified the rulings regarding carrion, blood, and pork in ordinary circumstances, and it has also clarified them in cases of necessity. It has clarified, for instance, the ruling of jihad for the accountable individuals in times of ability, and it has also clarified it in times of inability, illness, or disability.
The customary practice (urf) and its consideration according to al-Shatibi:
__________
(1) The same source, 1/26.
(2) That is, what may be a benefit for one person may be a detriment for him in a different situation or at another time or for another person. This is unlike the interest that is established by the Sharia, which is real, thus being an interest for every person in every situation and at every time. Therefore, it is not correct to replace the term real benefit or real harm with mere benefit or mere harm.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/27.


[Page 334]

... Custom ('urf) is not a source or a basis for legislation, but rather the Sharia (Islamic law) governs customs. Since the Sharia is general and comprehensive, it has assigned a ruling to every action. Certain actions may emerge from among the permissible actions that people become accustomed to, or actions that people abandon, or actions that are specific to certain occasions or times. Thus, abandoning a customary action, performing an abandoned action, or engaging in actions specific to certain occasions may become noticeable and call for interpretations. Alternatively, this action may become a term or a euphemism for a specific meaning or intention.
... An example of this is the complete white dress or the complete black dress for women; the former has become, in current custom, indicative of weddings, while the latter indicates mourning. There are also certain garments that have become, in general or specific custom, indicative of the profession of the wearer.
Another example is certain styles of clothing, head coverings, or shoes, which are originally permissible for both men and women. However, in custom, certain styles have become specific to men and others to women. Thus, in people's understanding, women wearing what is specific to men is seen as imitating them or as a lack of modesty and religion. Similarly, men wearing what is specific to women is viewed as imitating them and as a lack of modesty and religion.
Another example is that the 'awra (private parts) of a man is what is between the navel and the knee, and the original ruling is that revealing or covering anything other than that is permissible. If people become accustomed to covering more than the 'awra, then a man going out in public while covering only what is 'awra would be contrary to custom and indicative of a lack of modesty or a deficiency in manliness or something else.
Similarly, it is permissible for a man to uncover his head as well as to cover it, and some people may develop a custom regarding this.


[Page 335]

... These are examples of what is meant by custom (urf). The term custom may be used to refer to what people commonly agree upon in applying certain words to specific meanings, such that the indication of the word towards the meaning becomes a matter of customary truth, and this is akin to terminology. It may also refer to what people commonly agree upon regarding estimations of wages, prices, dowries, and the values of goods...
... The intended meaning of custom here is that which was mentioned in the examples above. This is not a source of rulings; rather, it requires a ruling from the Sharia. The Sharia came to judge the actions of people and their customs and traditions. Therefore, if it becomes customary for a woman to expose her neck, hair, or legs without it being considered reprehensible, this has no legal value, and these things remain private parts (awra) whose exposure is considered ugly.
... Thus, the custom that must be taken into account is what the Sharia has indicated is permissible, and then it becomes a sign or indication of something else as in the examples above. This does not change the rulings. For example, if a particular action becomes indicative of something that is legally reprehensible, this action becomes reprehensible according to the Sharia. For instance, if a man covers only his private parts while exposing everything else, and this becomes considered ugly in the eyes of people, then its prohibition in the Sharia does not mean that the private parts have changed; rather, the prohibition is due to contradicting modesty. The Sharia has commanded modesty. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Modesty is a branch of faith" (1), and there is no doubt that such an action contradicts modesty.
... However, if the action is not permissible, it cannot become an accepted custom, and opposing such a custom is a requirement of the Sharia. This is the concept of custom and its consideration according to al-Shatibi. Below are some of his texts to document what we have mentioned.
__________
(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari in Faith, (8), and Muslim in Faith (50) and (51), and Ibn Majah (56) and (57), and al-Nasa'i (4918), and Abu Dawood (4056), Ahmad (9333).


[Page 336]

... He says: "Continuous customs are of two types: the first type is the legal customs that are affirmed or denied by legal evidence. This means that the Sharia has either commanded them as obligatory or recommended, or prohibited them as disliked or forbidden, or permitted them in action or abstention. The second type consists of the customs that are prevalent among people for which there is no legal evidence for their denial or affirmation. As for the first type, it is always established like other legal matters... either good in the view of the Lawgiver or bad; they are among the matters that fall under the rulings of the Sharia, and they cannot be changed even if the opinions of the obligated individuals differ regarding them. It is not valid for what is considered good in this context to become bad, nor for what is considered bad to become good, until it is said, for example... that uncovering the private parts is neither a fault nor bad, so it is permissible, or something similar. For if such a thing were valid, it would be abrogation of the established and continuous rulings, and abrogation after the death of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is invalid, so the lifting of legal customs is invalid" (1). Al-Shatibi continues: "As for the second type, customs may be established or they may change, and nonetheless, they are causes for rulings that are derived from them. The established ones are like the existence of the desire for food, drink, and sexual intercourse... If they are causes for consequences that the Lawgiver has ruled upon, there is no doubt in considering them and building upon them and ruling according to them at all times. As for the changing ones: some may change in custom from good to bad and vice versa, such as uncovering the head, which varies according to the regions in reality. It is considered bad for those of honor in the Eastern lands but not bad in the Western lands. Thus, the legal ruling differs according to that, so it is a defect in justice among the people of the East and not a defect among the people of the West. Additionally, there are expressions that differ in conveying meanings, so the expression may shift from one meaning to another... like the differences in expressions according to the terminology of craftsmen... or in relation to the predominance of usage in certain meanings, until that term is understood to convey a specific meaning that it previously did not, or it was ambiguous and became specific..."
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/197 - 198 - 199.


[Page 337]

This often occurs in oaths, contracts, and divorce, both implicitly and explicitly... Among them are those that differ based on matters external to the obligated person, such as puberty, which is considered based on the customs of people regarding wet dreams or menstruation, or reaching the age of one who experiences wet dreams or menstruates" (1).
... Then al-Shatibi emphasizes the stability of rulings, saying: "Know that what has been mentioned here regarding the difference in rulings due to differing customs is not, in reality, a difference in the essence of the command, because the Sharia is established as being eternal and everlasting, even if the world were to continue without end, and the obligation likewise does not require further elaboration in the Sharia. Rather, the meaning of the difference is that when customs differ, each custom returns to a legal origin that is judged accordingly, as in the case of puberty, for example, where the obligation is lifted from the child before reaching puberty. Once he reaches puberty, the obligation falls upon him... And similarly for other examples, the rulings are stable and follow their causes wherever they may be, and Allah knows best" (2).
The obligation of rulings is not an obligation of their objectives:
Al-Shatibi states that the legal ruling is related to the action of the servant, and the action is a cause for an effect. Since the effects are not from the actions of the servant and are not within his capacity, the obligation does not fall upon them. Therefore, when a command to act is given, it is not a command regarding its outcome.
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/199 - 200.


[Page 338]

Since the establishment of the cause is akin to the establishment of the effect in both legal and rational matters, the legality of the cause indicates the legality of the effect. The prohibition of the cause indicates the illegality of its effect. Thus, the demand for action indicates that its outcome is beneficial, while the prohibition of action indicates that its outcome is harmful, except that the obligation pertains to the cause and not to the effect. What is required legally is to perform the action or to refrain from it, not to aim for the attainment of benefit or the avoidance of harm, because the attainment or avoidance is an effect, and it is not within the capacity of the obligated person to establish or remove it as an effect; to impose an obligation regarding it is to impose an obligation regarding what is beyond one's ability. In brief: the command regarding the cause indicates the legality of its effect but does not imply a command regarding the effect itself. If it is said that there may be multiple effects of the cause, resulting from the required or permitted action what is intended to be attained legally, and also resulting what is unintended or what is desired to be removed, the Shatibi responds that the legality of the action indicates the legality of its effect, but it does not necessitate the legality of everything that results from or is caused by it. The required action may produce what is desired to be removed, and refraining from what is prohibited may eliminate what is desired or legally permissible to exist. He states: "The legality of causes does not necessitate the legality of effects, even though the correlation between them is usually valid. This means that if a legal ruling of permissibility or prohibition or other rulings of obligation is attached to the causes, it does not necessarily follow that the rulings are attached to their effects. Therefore, if a command is given regarding the cause, it does not necessitate a command regarding the effect, and if it is prohibited, it does not necessitate a prohibition regarding the effect, and if one is given a choice regarding it, it does not necessitate that one is given a choice regarding its effect."(1)
He then said: "The evidence for this is what has been established in discourse, that what is for the obligated person is to engage in the causes, while the effects are the actions of Allah, Exalted is He, and there is no earning in them for the obligated person."(2)
__________
(1) Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/130.
(2) The same source, 1/131.


[Page 339]

Then he said: "The inference of this meaning in the Sharia is conclusive, and if that is the case, the causes that one is obligated to act upon fall under the generality indicated by reason and revelation. Thus, the causes are what the servants' gains are attached to, rather than the effects. Therefore, the obligation and its address only relate to what is acquired, while the effects are excluded from the address of obligation because they are not within their capacity. If they were to be addressed, it would be an obligation to do what is beyond one's ability, which is not the case" (1).
Accordingly, the primary aim of the command and prohibition is to carry out what is commanded and to refrain from what is prohibited, regardless of the effects and outcomes, as they are not in the hands of the obligated but rather in the hands of the Legislator. Thus, when the obligated person performs an action, they should consider its ruling and adhere to that ruling, rather than looking at its cause to determine whether it is beneficial or harmful (2). He says: "It is not necessary for the obligated person, in engaging in the causes, to pay attention to the effects or to intend them; rather, the aim is to operate under the established rulings, whether they are causes or not, whether they are justified or not. The evidence for this is what has been previously mentioned, that the effects return to the one who causes them, and they are not within the capacity of the obligated. If that is the case, then what is necessary is to consider what pertains to their own acquisition, while what is beyond that is not necessary and is what is sought" (3). Furthermore, among the legal obligations, there are those that have a share for the self and to which there is an inclination, which prevents one from entering under the requirement of the demand (4)" (5).

(1) The same location.
(2) Considering the outcomes of actions and their effects is obligatory for the jurist looking to determine the ruling of the action, and not for the one who engages in the ruling. This matter will be detailed when discussing the principle of the outcomes of actions.
(3) That is: and it is what is required to be proven.
(4) That is: the legal demand.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/133.


[Page 340]

Thus, the causes are intended by their effects, and they are intended by the one who established the causes as causes; they are intended by the legislator (al-shari) and not by the obligated person (al-mukallaf), and their attainment is through these causes. Therefore, the obligated person must adhere to the causes, that is, to the legal rulings, and it is not upon him to consider or take into account the effects, which are the interests (masalih) and harms (mafasid).
He said: "The establishment of causes necessitates the intention of the establisher towards the effects, I mean the legislator" (1). Then he said: "It follows from the intention to establish them as causes that there is an intention towards what arises from them, namely the effects" (2). Then he said: "The legal rulings were legislated to bring about interests or to avert harms, and these are certainly their effects" (3). Then he said: "If the effects were not intended by the causes, their establishment as causes would not be valid; however, they were imposed as such. Therefore, they must be established as causes, and they cannot be causes except for effects. Thus, the establisher of the causes intends the occurrence of the effects through them" (4), and if this is established, and the causes are intended by the legislator, it follows that the effects must be so as well" (5).
Thus, the legislator's intention with the Sharia is to bring about interests and avert harms, and this is achieved through what he has legislated. It is not upon the obligated person to consider the intended interests and harms; rather, it is upon him to adhere to what has been legislated for him. However, is it permissible for him to consider the results and strive to attain them? Al-Shatibi says: "There is no explicit evidence in the Sharia that mandates seeking the intention of the effect" (6). He said: "If it is said to you: The legislator commanded and prohibited for the sake of interests. You say: Yes, and that is for Allah, not for me; for what is upon me is to cause the means, and the attainment of the effects is not upon me. So I direct my intention towards what has been made obligatory upon me and entrust what is not upon me to the One who is responsible for it" (7).
