(2) The same source, 1/134.
(3) The same source, 1/135.
(4) Through it, meaning: it is not valid for the obligated person to intend it except through the action that the legislator has made a cause for it.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/135.
(6) The same source, 1/136.
(7) The same source.


[Page 341]

Then he said: "If it is established that there is no obligation to intend the cause, then the accountable person (mukallaf) may abandon the intention to it absolutely, and he may intend it" (1).
As for abandoning the intention to the cause, this has been discussed previously. As for the permissibility of intending it, this does not mean that the act is permitted or prohibited based on the anticipated outcome, whether it is beneficial or harmful, as this would lead to the permissibility of some prohibited acts or the prohibition of some permissible, recommended, or obligatory acts based on the results they produce. Rather, the opposite is intended, which is that it is valid for the mukallaf to consider the effects if this strengthens adherence to the cause and encourages further commitment to it. However, if it weakens adherence to the cause, meaning the legal ruling, then this itself is a harm, and it is not valid. Al-Shatibi provides several examples of this. For instance, someone who earns a living to support himself and his family, as considering the outcomes may motivate him to work harder for greater earnings and better care for his family. Similarly, someone who obeys Allah to please Him and enter His Paradise, as contemplating these goals may drive him to greater sacrifice, generosity, patience, righteousness, striving, and commitment, thus reinforcing the cause. Here, it is valid for the mukallaf to consider the outcomes. He says: "This intention, when accompanied by the causation, is correct because it is an attention to the prevailing customs. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: { Allah is the One who made the sea subservient to you, so that ships may sail upon it by His command and that you may seek of His bounty } (2)" (3). Then he said: "Thus, the essence of this is to seek what Allah prepares for him through this cause, which returns to reliance on Allah and turning to Him" (4). Then he said: "If that is the case, then paying attention to the outcomes and intending them is considered in customary matters, especially for the jurist (mujtahid)" (5)
__________
(1) The same source, 1/135.
(2) Surah Al-Jathiya, 12.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 1/137.
(4) The same source, 1/137 - 138.
(5) The same source, 1/138.


[Page 342]

He said: "The criterion is that if turning to the effect (muscab) strengthens the cause and completes it, and encourages one to strive to fulfill it, then it brings about benefit (maslaha). But if it tends to undermine the cause by nullifying it, weakening it, or being negligent towards it, then it brings about harm (mafsada)" (1).
He concluded that: "The one who refrains from focusing on the effects is of a higher rank and has a purer deed if he is engaged in acts of worship, and he receives greater reward in customary matters" (2).
Based on the fact that benefits and harms do not exist in isolation, the cause leads to its intended effects, accompanied by what is not intended by the Legislator, but rather what is intended to be lifted. He says: "An example of this is the command to enjoin good and forbid evil, for it is legislated because it is a cause for establishing the religion, manifesting the symbols of Islam, and suppressing falsehood in any form. It is not a cause in the legal sense for the destruction of wealth or life, even if it leads to that along the way... The establishment of punishments and retribution is legislated for the benefit of deterring corruption, even if it leads to the destruction of lives and the spilling of blood, which in itself is a harm... As for the prohibited causes, such as invalid marriages, they are forbidden even if they lead to the attachment of offspring and the establishment of inheritance and other rulings, which are benefits" (3).
Then he said: "There is no legislated cause except that it contains a benefit for which it was legislated. If you see it leading to a harm, know that it does not arise from the legislated cause. Likewise, there is no prohibited cause except that it contains a harm for which it was prohibited. If you see it leading to a benefit in appearance, know that it does not arise from the prohibited cause, but rather each of them produces what it was established for in the Sharia" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 1/166.
(2) The same source, 1/159.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/167.
(4) The same source, p. 168.


[Page 343]

Thus, not everything that is based on a cause or observed in its attributes, rulings, or meanings that is acceptable to rational individuals takes the ruling of the caused. This leads to a question about how to distinguish between these results to know what is intended by the Sharia (law) to be a goal and an objective, and what is not, so that it can be disregarded. The answer lies in the method of induction for these attributes or meanings.
If there is a meaning or an imagined result presumed in a few rulings, this meaning or cause is not definitively considered intended by the legislator, and thus it is not taken into account, even if it is caused by these rulings; these rulings do not constitute a legal cause for it. However, if this result is found in numerous rulings that exceed enumeration, then this result or meaning has the continuity (tawatur) that al-Shatibi mentioned resembles the conceptual continuity. At that point, this result becomes a cause, and the rulings that support this meaning become a legal cause. That is, they are legislated for this cause. In this way, a distinction is made between legal and non-legal results or causes, or those that are intended by the legislator through the ruling and those whose intention by the legislator is not established.
If a ruling is legislated for specific interests that have been established through induction, and this ruling results in a harm, it does not mean that the existence of that harm as a cause of the ruling indicates that it is intended by the legislator. Rather, this is because interests and harms are not purely distinct. This result is recognized as a harm from its induction in many other rulings, where the beneficial induction is available to establish that the legislator intended to eliminate it. Thus, the legislator's intention to eliminate it is a definitive principle, and the existence of doubt or presumption in results, outcomes, or causes being intended by the legislator is a possibility or presumption that has no legal value. For the objectives or interests and harms are generalities or fundamental principles that can only be established through definitive evidence derived from induction.


[Page 344]

The legal causes (al-masbabat al-shar'iyya), meaning those intended by the Legislator, are those that have been established definitively, and this matter has been previously explained. He said: "The legal rulings were established to bring about benefits and avert harms, and they are certainly their causes"(1).
Al-Shatibi states that: "The prohibited causes are causes of harm, not of benefit, just as the permissible causes are causes of benefit, not of harm"(2). He then says: "The point is that the permissible causes cannot be causes of harm, and the prohibited causes cannot be causes of benefit, as this is not valid in any case"(3).
What this statement means is that the cause which is established as intended to occur through a permissible reason is a benefit (maslaha) and not a harm (mafsada), regardless of its suitability to human nature, perception, and disposition. And what is established as intended to be removed through a prohibited reason is a harm (mafsada) and not a benefit (maslaha), even if it is something that human nature tends to favor by virtue of instinct or habit, or if it is something that rational individuals and wise people incline towards.
The legal connection between the cause and its effect:
It is not correct for the legal ruling to be intended for anything other than what the legislator intended, nor is it correct to achieve or intend what the legislator intended through a ruling that was not legislated for that purpose. Al-Shatibi says: "The causes, inasmuch as they are legal causes for their effects, were legislated to achieve their effects, which are the benefits sought or the harms repelled"(4). He also says: "The effects, in relation to their causes, are of two types: the first type: those for which the causes were legislated either with the primary intention, which pertains to the original objectives (maqasid al-sharia), or with the secondary intention, which pertains to the subsidiary objectives... The second type: anything other than that which is known or presumed that the causes were not legislated for, or it is not known or presumed that they were legislated for or not legislated, thus the categories come to three:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/135.
(2) The same source, 1/167.
(3) The same source, 1/168.
(4) The same source, 1/171.


[Page 345]

One of them: What is known or presumed to be the reason for which the law was established, thus the causation of the one who causes it is valid because he approached the matter from its proper avenue and sought it through what the legislator permitted to seek in relation to what he also permitted to seek. This is because we have assumed that the legislator intended by marriage, for example, procreation primarily, followed by establishing a home and forming alliances with the family of the woman due to their nobility or religion or something similar, or providing service or attending to his interests, or enjoying what Allah has made lawful from women, or beautifying oneself with the wealth of the woman, or desiring her beauty, or being pleased with her religion, or refraining from what Allah has prohibited, or something similar as indicated by the Sharia. Therefore, what this causative agent intended is, in general, the intention of the legislator. (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/171 - 172.


[Page 346]

"The second: what is known or presumed to be a cause that was not legislated for its sake from the outset. The evidence indicates that this causation is incorrect because the cause was not originally legislated for this presumed effect. If it was not legislated for it, then it does not result in its wisdom of bringing about a benefit or averting a harm concerning what was intended by the cause; thus, it is invalid. This is one aspect, and a second aspect is that this cause, regarding this presumed objective, is not legislated, so it becomes like a cause that was not legislated at all. If an unlegislated causation is invalid, then likewise what was legislated if it is taken for something it was not legislated for. A third aspect is that the fact that the legislator did not legislate this cause for this specific effect is evidence that this causation contains a harm and not a benefit, or that the benefit for which the cause was legislated is negated by that effect, making the cause in relation to it mere frivolity." (1) "The third: it is when the cause is intended for an effect that is neither known nor presumed to be intended by the legislator or not intended at all. This is a point of consideration and a matter of ambiguity and confusion. This is because if we were to cause it, it could be that this cause is not designated for this presumed effect, just as it could be designated for it and for others. In the first case, the causation would be unlegislated. In the second case, it would be legislated. If the action is in a state of uncertainty between being legislated or unlegislated, then proceeding with the causation is unlegislated." (2)
__________
(1) The same source, 1/173.
(2) The same source, 1/181. And see: 1/171 - 182.


[Page 347]

Then he said: "The reason is only prescribed in relation to a specific, imposed, known matter, not absolutely" (1). And he said: "Rather, we know that many of the reasons were legislated for matters that arise from them and were not legislated for matters, even if they arise from them and are contingent upon them... So when we know that it is legislated for specific matters, what is unknown to be legislated for it is unknown in ruling, thus the legitimacy of proceeding is not valid until the ruling is known" (2). Then he said: "If this is established and a causation is clarified that we do not know whether it is what the Legislator intended with the prescribed causation or not, it is necessary to pause until the ruling on it is known. For this, there is a principle by which what is intended by the Legislator from the consequences of causes and what is not prescribed can be clarified, and it is mentioned in the Book of Objectives (maqasid)" (3). Accordingly, al-Shatibi believes that achieving the legal objective is only valid through the legal method that the Legislator has established. And although the method is legal, it is not valid to adopt or utilize it to achieve a legal objective unless the Legislator has established that method for this objective. It is not valid to prevent theft except by cutting off the hand, and the punishment cannot be replaced by another. And cutting off the hand is only valid for what it has been legislated for. Likewise, applying jihad for other than what it has been legislated for is not valid. And it is not valid, for the sake of establishing the ruling by what Allah has revealed, which is a legal objective, to adopt means or methods that have not been legislated for it, such as charitable institutions, for example, even if they are permissible, they are not prescribed for this objective. Or like participating in governance through disbelief, for this was not established for this purpose, let alone that it is prohibited by law.
Customs and acts of worship between following meanings and devotion:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/181 - 182.
(2) The same source, 1/181. And see: 1/171 - 182.
(3) The same source, 1/181 - 182.


[Page 348]

... If it is established that the rulings have their intended purposes as intended by the Legislator, which are the interests (masalih) or the causes (illal), then there are some rulings for which no cause can be found that is suitable for extending the ruling by analogy, even if a cause is known that is characterized by a generality that does not allow for analogy to be applied. This is similar to the reasoning for acts of worship, which is based on devotion and compliance. Therefore, there are some rulings for which one should not seek a cause, and there are rulings for which one must provide a rationale or follow the meanings in order to ascertain their causes.
The meaning of following the meanings:
... The causes or interests are not considered valid unless they are definitively established through induction. The method of induction is to examine the rulings and derive the meanings and judgments that result from them. What the mind typically considers when reflecting is the rational meanings or appropriate descriptions; however, the existence of a specific meaning in a few texts is not sufficient for it to be considered valid. There must be a large number of rulings that contain that meaning for it to be valid, which resembles the concept of moral transmission (tawatur al-ma'nawi) in the terminology of hadith science. Thus, imagining a valid meaning in a few rulings is not enough for it to be considered, and it must be established in numerous rulings that exceed enumeration. This establishment or search for meaning or its pursuit in the rulings is what is meant by following the meanings. Al-Shatibi did not intend by following the meanings to apply a meaning merely due to the existence of an imagined or presumed connection between it and the ruling.
... Following the meanings is not limited to appropriate descriptions or those that the mind perceives the wisdom in. Any meaning that is established through induction is definitively considered valid in Sharia merely due to the existence of a causal relationship between it and the rulings that were induced. However, most of what the Legislator has used to justify the rulings is the appropriate, which, when presented to the minds, is readily accepted. Therefore, the key in following the meanings is to consider the rulings first, and then examine their causes or meanings, regardless of whether they are appropriate or not. In reality, most of the justifications in Sharia have come with appropriate descriptions or rational meanings. Al-Shatibi says: "When transmission and reason support the legal issues, it is on the condition that transmission precedes and is followed by reason, so reason does not roam in the field of reflection except to the extent that transmission allows it" (1). He also said: "The Legislator has elaborated on the causes and rulings in legislating the chapter on customs... Most of what he justified in it was the appropriate, which, when presented to the minds, was readily accepted" (2).
In contrast to following the meanings is devotion (ta'abud), which means not seeking any meaning or intended interest behind the ruling—any cause—other than the interest of obedience and compliance.
Acts of worship are not justified:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/53.
(2) The same source, 2/213.


[Page 349]

... Al-Shatibi says: "The original ruling regarding acts of worship for the accountable person is to worship without considering the meanings" (1). This means that the original principle is that one should not seek a reason for them. His use of the term "original" indicates that there are rare or few cases where it is permissible to pursue a specific meaning to see if it is established or not. Al-Shatibi supports this with several points: "Among them is induction, for we have found that purification extends beyond its required place, and likewise, the prayers are specified with particular actions in specific forms; if they deviate from these, they are not acts of worship... And so it is with other acts of worship such as fasting and pilgrimage, and we understand from the general wisdom of worship the submission to the commands of Allah, Exalted is He, and the individual acts of submission and glorification of His majesty and turning to Him. This extent does not provide a specific reason from which a specific ruling can be understood" (2). There is no need to mention all his other proofs on this matter, and Al-Shatibi's intent is that acts of worship are not to be rationalized, and it is not permissible to seek a reason for them. Even if there are some rulings on acts of worship that can carry certain meanings that may be very appropriate and provoke thought, they should be disregarded and not considered, because the principle that acts of worship are not rationalized is a definitive principle established by induction and other matters. Thus, it is not correct to pursue this meaning in other rulings to prove it through induction. He states: "It is necessary to take in this category worship without considering the meanings as a principle built upon and a pillar to rely on" (3). As for the rare cases where it is permissible—though not obligatory—to follow the meaning, they are when a text or consensus indicates a specific meaning; this meaning is one of the meanings of the proofs and not one of the meanings of the rulings. He says: "Unless it is clarified by a text or consensus a desired meaning in some cases, there is no blame on one who follows it, but that is rare and not a principle; rather, the principle is what is prevalent in the matter and predominates in the context" (4). As for the fact that the intended meaning by a text or consensus differs from others, it is because it is one of the indications of the texts or their meanings, and not one of the indications of the rulings.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/211.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/212.
(3) The same source, 2/213.
(4) The same source, 2/212.


[Page 350]

As for the fact that it is permissible to follow the meaning in this case but not obligatory, this is because this meaning is speculative and cannot be considered unless it is related to a definitive origin, and this can only be established through induction. Following the meaning may affirm it or negate it; if it negates it, then it is confirmed to adhere to the act of worship, and if it affirms it, then the origin of worship is also established by the same method, that is, through induction. Therefore, it has no effect on acts of worship, neither by establishment nor by negation. He says: "What is purely for Allah, like acts of worship, has its origin in the act of worship which is based on the incomprehensibility of the meaning, such that analogy cannot be applied to it. If its meaning is not comprehensible, it indicates that the intention of the Legislator is to adhere to what He has defined and not to exceed it" (1). As for the comprehensible meaning that has been established as intended by the Legislator, it must be applied in matters other than acts of worship. Moreover, although some acts of worship contain indications of reasoning or suggest a connection, the conditions for reasoning are either absent or incomplete in them. Therefore, such descriptions or meanings do not extend the rulings, such as theft being a reason for cutting off the hand and adultery being a reason for stoning; however, analogy does not occur here, nor does the ruling extend beyond its place. This is stronger in acts of worship, as in forgetfulness being a reason for prostration. We say: "He stole, so his hand was cut off; he committed adultery, so he was stoned; he forgot, so he prostrated." These reasons, while they are understood in general terms, are not understood in specific terms. The understanding is of the general crime or sin and the general punishment or excuse. However, specifying this with that is not comprehensible, as it could logically be said: "He stole, so he was imprisoned," or "He forgot, so he repeated," or something else. The same applies to reasoning based on hardship in shortening prayers, breaking the fast, and combining prayers. He says: "Moreover, the appropriateness in them (i.e., acts of worship) is counted among those that have no counterpart, such as hardship in the traveler's shortening of prayers, breaking the fast, and combining between the two prayers, and similar matters. To this, most of the understood reasons in the chapters of acts of worship are not understood in specific terms, like his saying: 'He forgot, so he prostrated'" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/221.
(2) Refer to its source.


[Page 351]

And His saying: "Allah does not accept the prayer of any one of you if he becomes impure until he performs ablution" (1), and His prohibition of prayer at the two ends of the day, and His reasoning for that being that the sun rises and sets between the horns of the devil (2), as well as what the scholars of dissent use in analogizing ablution to the necessity of intention... and similar matters that do not indicate a clear, precise meaning suitable for establishing a ruling upon without dispute, but rather are termed as resembling (shabah), such that those who assert it do not agree upon it, and it is only used for analogy by those who do so when they find nothing else. If we do not have a clear reason supported by evident pathways, then the solid foundation that we should resort to is to adhere to what has been defined without transgressing to anything else, for we have found that the Sharia, when we examined it, revolves around acts of worship in the realm of worship, thus it is a fundamental principle therein (3). Accordingly, acts of worship are not to be reasoned or analogized.
The principle in customary practices is reasoning:

(2) Al-Bukhari (3032) and Muslim (966) and (987) and al-Tirmidhi (148), who said: "Hasan Sahih," and al-Nasa'i (507).

... Al-Shatibi mentioned customs (adat) in the introduction of his book on the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) and categorized them as one of four sections: acts of worship (ibadat), customs, transactions (muamalat), and crimes (jina'at). He exemplified this with the consumption of food, drinks, clothing, and other consumables (1). However, in this research, he refers to them as one of two categories: acts of worship and customs. Therefore, it means here what is aside from acts of worship in terms of rulings. He states: "The essence of customs is the consideration of meanings" (2), and he supports this with several points, the first of which is induction. He says: "We found that the legislator aimed at the interests of the servants, and the ordinary rulings revolve with it wherever it goes. You see a single thing being prohibited in a situation where there is no interest, but if there is an interest, it is permissible, like the dirham for dirham for a deferred period, which is prohibited in sale but permissible in a loan... We did not find this in the realm of acts of worship as we understood it in customs. And Allah, Exalted is He, said: { And there is for you in retaliation the saving of life, O you who possess intellect } (3), and He said: { And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly } (4), and in the hadith: "A judge should not rule while angry" (5), and He said: "There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm" (6), and He said: "The killer does not inherit" (7) (8). Then he said: "And so on, which cannot be enumerated, all of which indicates, and indeed states, the consideration of the interests of the servants, and that permission revolves with them wherever it goes, as clarified by the paths of reasoning. This indicates that customs are among those matters where the legislator relied on the consideration of meanings" (9).

(2) The same source, 2/211.

(6) Previously cited.

[Page 353]

... These meanings, although they are not from the indications of the texts, serve as foundational principles or definitive reasons upon which the rulings are established. This means that these rulings are issued based on the application of those principles. Thus, these rulings are particulars in relation to them, and the meaning of the principles is embodied within them. This is the meaning of the descent of the universals to the particulars, and therefore attention must be paid to the meanings, that is, to a specific meaning or meanings present in the ruling, and then to follow this meaning to achieve its induction, which then becomes a universal principle and a reason for public interest (maslaha). For example, in the hadith "the killer does not inherit," one can imagine the meaning of treating the opposite of the intended purpose as a punishment, or that whoever hastens a matter before its time is punished by being deprived of it. So, are these meanings principles or rules in the Sharia upon which the rulings are based? These meanings are not fixed as principles of the Sharia, even though they can be imagined in the ruling, and therefore it is necessary to trace this meaning and observe its presence or absence in many other rulings, and to note its occurrence or non-occurrence where it can be applied, and thus the induction that confirms or negates the meaning is achieved. This attention to meanings must occur in customary practices based on the principle that the Sharia was revealed for the interests of the servants, and these interests are the principles upon which the Sharia was established, and these interests must be present in the rulings. However, since the rulings can be imagined to contain many meanings or rulings, and it cannot be determined that this meaning is what the Legislator intended or upon which the ruling was established, it is necessary to conduct an induction for this meaning, because with the abundance of rulings, the meaning becomes stronger, and by being beyond limitation, it becomes definitive and intended by the Legislator and serves a public interest. He says: "The Legislator has expanded in explaining the reasons and rulings in legislating the domain of customs, as previously illustrated, and most of the reasons mentioned therein are based on suitability, which, when presented to the intellects, are accepted. Thus, we understand from this that the Legislator intended to follow the meanings rather than to rely solely on the texts, unlike the domain of worship, where the known is the opposite of that" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 2/213.


[Page 354]

... However, al-Shatibi makes exceptions here for some rare cases, as he did regarding acts of worship. This is because acts of worship are not governed by meanings unless there is a text or consensus indicating a specific meaning. Likewise, in customary practices, meanings are followed unless there is an element of worship; in that case, one must adhere to the texts. He says: "If this is established and the predominant aspect of customary practices is to pay attention to meanings, then if there is an element of worship, one must submit and adhere to the texts, such as the request for the dowry in marriage, the slaughtering in the specified manner for permissible animals, the fixed shares in inheritance, the number of months in the waiting periods for divorce and completion, and similar matters where there is no room for intellects to understand their specific benefits, so that others can be analogized to them"(1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/214.


[Page 355]

... These acts of worship and customary practices, although it is not correct to pay attention to their meanings in the sense that analogy (qiyas) cannot be applied to them or based on them, they do have a comprehensible meaning, even if it is not one that is suitable for analogy. This is in addition to the general meaning, which is worship. He says: "If it is said, is there a reason for these acts of worship (ta'abudat)(1) that can be understood as the specific intent of the legislator or not? The answer is that, as for acts of worship, their required action is mere submission without addition or reduction. Therefore, when Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) was asked about the obligation of a menstruating woman to make up fasting but not prayer, she said to the questioner: 'Are you a Haruriyya!' in denial of her asking about such a thing, as the act of worship was not established to understand its specific reason. Then she said: 'We were commanded to make up fasting and we were not commanded to make up prayer'(2). This supports the idea of worship over reasoning based on hardship, and the saying of Ibn al-Musayyib regarding the legislator's equal treatment of the fingers: 'It is the Sunnah, my nephew'(3), which indicates that there is no reason. As for customary practices and some acts of worship, they also have a comprehensible meaning, which is the regulation of the means of public interest (maslaha)... Thus, the legislator has set specific limits that should not be exceeded, such as eighty lashes for slander, one hundred lashes and exile for fornication without marriage, and the cutting of the hand at the wrist, and in the specified amounts"(4).
It is necessary to consider worship in customary practices:
__________
(1) That is, acts of worship, and customary practices that are exempted from the principle of paying attention to meaning.
(2) Narrated by Muslim in the chapter on the obligation of making up fasting for the menstruating woman but not prayer (506), (508), and by al-Tirmidhi (120) who said: it is good and authentic. And by al-Nasa'i (379) and Ahmad (22908).
(3) Al-Muwatta, chapter on what has been narrated regarding the blood money for fingers (1355).

[Page 356]

... This does not mean - in any way - that the recognized meanings in the rulings of customary practices, that is, those established through induction, or in other words: the public interests (masalih), can lead to the annulment of rulings based on them. This is due to the necessity of applying both the general principles and the specific cases together, as these rulings are the ones that the Legislator has made a pathway to the public interests, and thus they cannot be annulled on the pretext that the intent or meaning has been understood, and therefore the rulings can be changed while preserving the objectives (maqasid) and meanings. This is because devotion (ta'abud) exists in all rulings, whether they are related to acts of worship (ibadat) or customary practices (adat). He says: "Everything in which the consideration of devotion is established, there is no branching from it, and everything in which the consideration of meanings is established, devotion must also be considered in it" (1). He presents many proofs for this matter, including that understanding a purpose or interest of the ruling does not mean understanding all the intended interests behind it, and that the optimal way to achieve the intended goal is the legislated way, as well as the purpose of compliance and others. Based on this, he concludes: "Every legal ruling is not devoid of the right of Allah, Exalted is He, which is the aspect of devotion" (2). This will be discussed in greater detail in the next chapter, the chapter on the objectives of the accountable person.

Chapter Six
Objectives of the Accountable Person

... It contains an introduction and three sections:

Section One: Objectives and Intentions.
Section Two: Actions of the Accountable Person and Their Objectives.
Section Three: Legal Stratagems.

Chapter Six
Objectives of the Accountable Person

Introduction:
Al-Shatibi said: "The objectives that are considered are of two types: one that pertains to the intent of the Legislator and the other that pertains to the intent of the accountable person" (3). The first type of objectives, which pertains to the intent of the Legislator, has been clarified in the previous sections. The second type, which is the objectives of the accountable person, will be clarified - if Allah wills - in this chapter.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/214.
(2) The same source, 2/221.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/1.


[Page 357]

It has become clear that the objectives (maqasid) are results or causes. The causes are the actions performed by the accountable person (mukallaf) that lead to those results; they serve as means for the objectives. The actions performed by the mukallaf may be legislatively commanded, prohibited, or permitted.
The objectives of the mukallaf from his actions may be compliance with the command of the legislator, meaning they may be otherworldly objectives without regard to a worldly objective. They may also be worldly, that is, the attainment of desires and interests, according to what Allah has instilled in humans of characteristics and passions(1). They may also combine both intentions: the intention of compliance and the intention of seeking benefit.
What is the effect of the mukallaf's intention on the validity of the action, whether in terms of reward or punishment in the Hereafter, or in terms of its occurrence and the resulting effects in this world? Is it permissible for the mukallaf to intend his interests and benefits while also intending compliance? Is it permissible for him to aim for results that Allah did not legislate those actions for? Is it permissible for him to intend legitimate objectives through illegitimate actions? And what is the ruling on actions performed by the mukallaf devoid of any intention?
__________
(1) Many texts indicate these characteristics, as does the reality of human beings. Allah, Exalted is He, said: { Beautified for people is the love of that which they desire - of women and children, heaped-up sums of gold and silver, fine branded horses, and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of worldly life, but Allah has with Him the best return. } (Al-Imran, 14).


[Page 358]

... And He said: { And you consume inheritance with [greedy] consumption (19) and you love wealth with [intense] love } Al-Fajr, 19-20.
... And He said: { Indeed, mankind was created anxious (19) when evil touches him, impatient (20) and when good touches him, withholding (21) } Al-Ma'arij, 19-21.
Is it permissible for the accountable person (mukallaf) to initiate actions with the intention of making his non-Sharia objectives Sharia-compliant? This is known as legal tricks (hiyal). Like someone who gives charity from some of his wealth or spends it to evade zakat, or like someone who undertakes a journey to permit himself to break his fast, for example, or like someone who marries a woman who has been divorced three times so that he can divorce her with the intention of making her lawful for her first husband.
For such actions, and for such objectives and what arises or branches from them, al-Shatibi discussed the category of the objectives of the accountable person. This chapter was written to clarify al-Shatibi's position on these issues.
Since intention and purpose and their effects on the actions of the accountable person are matters extensively discussed by the scholars, and al-Shatibi's statements are both consistent and inconsistent with each other, the opinions and views of the scholars on this matter will be addressed before presenting al-Shatibi's views on it.

Section One
Objectives and Intentions

Intention and purpose and the difference between them:
Al-Ghazali said: "Know that intention, will, and purpose are terms that convey the same meaning, which is a state and quality of the heart that is encompassed by two matters: knowledge and action. Knowledge precedes it because it is its origin and condition, and action follows it because it is its fruit and branch" (1). He also said that intention "is the will and the impulse of the soul by virtue of desire and inclination towards what is in accordance with the objective, either in the present or in the future. The primary mover is the desired objective, which is the motivator, and the motivating objective is the intended purpose, and the impulse is the purpose and intention, and the activation of the ability to serve the will by moving the limbs is the action" (2).
Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi said: "In language, as in the dictionary, it is to intend something with intention, which can be emphasized or softened: to aim for it. In Sharia, as in al-Talwih, it is the intention of obedience and drawing closer to Allah in performing the action" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Abu Hamid Muhammad ibn Muhammad, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/365, Dar al-Ma'rifah - Beirut.
(2) The same source.
(3) Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi, Zain al-Din ibn Ibrahim, who passed away in 970 AH, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 24, 2nd edition, 1442 AH - 1999 CE, edited by Dr. Muhammad Mut'i al-Hafiz, Dar al-Fikr al-Mu'asir - Beirut, Dar al-Fikr - Damascus.


[Page 359]

He said: "Al-Baydawi defined it as, in Sharia, the intention directed towards an action seeking the Face of Allah, Exalted is He, and in compliance with His command. Linguistically, it is the movement of the heart towards what it sees as aligned with a purpose of bringing benefit or averting harm, whether in the present or in the future" (1).
And al-Suyuti said: "Its place is the heart in every instance because its reality is intention in general, and it is said: the intention concurrent with the action, which is a description of the action of the heart. Al-Baydawi said: Intention is the movement of the heart towards what it sees as bringing benefit or averting harm, whether in the present or in the future. And the Sharia specified it as the intention directed towards an action seeking the pleasure of Allah, Exalted is He, and in compliance with His command" (2).
Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali said: "Know that intention in the language is a type of purpose and will, even though a distinction has been made between these terms" (3). He then mentioned what implies a rejection of this distinction, as will become clear. It is evident from the previous texts of the scholars regarding intention and purpose that they are interchangeable in meaning in the language, considering that the term purpose is broader than the term intention, which is indicated by al-Suyuti's statement: "Its reality is intention in general," and Ibn Rajab's statement: "Intention in the language is a type of purpose and will."

(1) The same source.
(2) Al-Suyuti, Jalal al-Din Abdul Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, who died in 911 AH, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair fi Qawa'id wa Furu' Fiqh al-Shafi'i, p. 76, 2nd ed., 1414 AH - 1993 CE, edited and commented by Dr. Muhammad al-Mu'tasim Billah al-Baghdadi, Dar al-Kitab al-Arabi - Beirut.

[Page 360]

As for the distinction between intention (niyyah) and purpose (qasd), it has become clear that purpose is broader and intention is more specific. This is evident upon careful examination of the texts mentioned earlier, which indicate that intention is invoked in the presence of the action; it is not sufficient for there to be merely a purpose or desire in the heart, but this must be accompanied by the intention to bring about the action. Therefore, al-Baydawi stated in his definition: "It is the will directed towards the action," and al-Suyuti said: "It is said to be concurrent with the action." As for his statement: "And that is a matter of the heart," this emphasizes that it is a type of purpose, with its place being the heart, similar to it. Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali said: "Those who differentiate between intention and will and purpose and the like do so because they believe that intention is specific to the first meaning mentioned by the jurists. Some of them said: Intention is specific to the action of the one intending, while will is not specific to that, as a person may want from Allah to forgive him without intending that" (1).
__________
(1) Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jamia al-Uloom wal-Hikam, pp. 16-17.


[Page 361]

Upon closer examination, we notice a distinction in the linguistic usage in that the term "intention" (niyyah) is more specific than the term "purpose" (qasd). For example, we have observed the scholars saying: "the purpose of the legislator" (maqsad al-shari), "the purposes of the legislator" (maqasid al-shari), and "the purposes of the Sharia" (maqasid al-sharia), but they did not say "the intention of the legislator" or "the legislator's intentions" or "the intentions of the Sharia." Likewise, they did not say "the will of the Sharia" (1).
__________
(1) The term "will" (irada) as it appears in the texts of the scholars means purpose and intention, and it has come in many legal texts. Allah, Exalted is He, said: { Among you are some who want this world, and among you are some who want the Hereafter. } { Al-Imran: 152 }, and He said: { You desire the pleasures of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter. } { Al-Anfal: 67 }, and He said: { Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment. } { Hud: 15 }, and He said: { Whoever desires to harvest the Hereafter. } { Ash-Shura: 20 }, and He said: { And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His face. } { Al-An'am: 52 }, and He said: { And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His face, and let not your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the life of this world. } { Al-Kahf: 28 }, and He said: { And whatever you give in usury to increase within the wealth of the people will not increase with Allah, but whatever you give in zakat, desiring the face of Allah, those are the multipliers. } { Ar-Rum: 39 }. It may also be expressed in the Qur'an with the term "seeking" (ibtigha) as in His saying: { Except seeking the face of his Lord, the Most High. } { Al-Lail: 20 }, and His saying: { And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and assuring themselves. } { Al-Baqarah: 265 }, and His saying: { And you spend nothing except seeking the face of Allah. } { Al-Baqarah: 272 }. See Jam' al-Ulum wal-Hikam by Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, p. 17.


[Page 362]

As for the distinction that Ibn Rajab referred to in the previous text by saying: "due to their assumption that the intention (niyyah) is specific to the first meaning mentioned by the jurists..." it indicates that some scholars have made a distinction between a legal meaning of intention and a linguistic meaning. The linguistic meaning is simply the intention in general, and thus the intention is broader than the specific legal meaning, which is the specification of intention as the intention to comply with the command of the Legislator or the intention of drawing closer to Allah. This is what is indicated by the texts of Ibn Najim and al-Suyuti, which they quoted from al-Baydawi. This is in contrast to al-Ghazali and Ibn Rajab, for example, who only referred to the linguistic meaning.

This specification of the meaning of intention in a legal sense leads to the use of the term intention for acts of worship. However, in the case of customary actions, it is only when the intention of the obligated person is to draw closer to Allah and comply with the command. The term intention can be used here because it is general, whereas when the intention of the obligated person is for their own purposes and desires, such as the intention to acquire ownership or to satisfy desires, the term used is intention. Therefore, it is said that intentions transform customary actions into acts of worship. Ibn Najim al-Hanafi said: "There is no reward except by intention" (1). Al-Ghazali said: "There is nothing from the permissible actions except that it can hold an intention or intentions that can make it one of the merits of drawing closer to Allah and attain high ranks; how great is the loss of one who is heedless of this" (2).

The effect of intention on actions (3):

(1) Ibn Najim al-Hanafi, al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 14.
(2) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/371.
(3) That is, in terms of the validity or invalidity of actions and the resulting reward or punishment in the Hereafter, or in terms of their sufficiency and the consequences of those actions in this world. Ibn Najim al-Hanafi said: "It is of two types: the Hereafter, which is reward and deserving of punishment, and the worldly, which is validity and invalidity." He considered actions based on intention with regard to the Hereafter, and denied considering them with regard to validity and invalidity in this world. He said: "The Hereafter is intended by consensus, as it is agreed that there is no reward or punishment except by intention, so the other is negated as being intended." Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 14.


[Page 363]

Bukhari narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Actions are judged by intentions, and for every person is what he intended. So whoever's migration is for Allah and His Messenger, then his migration is for Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration is for a worldly benefit he may attain or a woman he may marry, then his migration is for that which he migrated towards" (1). And in Muslim, it is narrated in the wording: "Indeed, actions are judged by intentions, and indeed, for every person is what he intended..." (2).
Al-Suyuti transmitted the consensus (tawatur) from the scholars regarding the significance of this hadith (3). Likewise, Al-Hafiz al-Asqalani said: "It has been transmitted in consensus from the scholars regarding the significance of this hadith. Abu Abdullah said: There is nothing in the reports of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) that is more comprehensive, richer, and more beneficial than this hadith" (4). It has been reported from many scholars, including al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah be pleased with them), that it constitutes one-third of Islam. And from al-Shafi'i, that it encompasses seventy chapters of jurisprudence (5).

[Page 364]

Regarding the meaning of the hadith, actions are of two types: acts of worship (ibadat) and customary practices (adat). Those who said that intention (niyyah) means purpose and did not specify intention in a legal sense, which is the intention to seek Allah's pleasure and comply with His command, have interpreted the meaning as applying to the validity of actions whether they are acts of worship or customary practices based on the validity of the intention, which is the seeking of Allah's pleasure. If actions lack this intention, then the intention is invalid, and thus the actions are invalid because actions are judged by intentions. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani said: "The intention in the hadith is understood in its linguistic meaning" (1), and he said: "The implication is: there is no action except by intention, so the intent is not to negate the existence of the action, as it can exist without intention, but rather to negate its rulings such as validity and completeness; however, the interpretation as negating validity is more appropriate" (2). Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, in his explanation of the hadith, said: "With this, al-Bukhari began his book (al-Sahih) in the position of its introduction, indicating that every action not intended for the sake of Allah is void and has no fruit in this world or the Hereafter" (3). His statement: every action, means whether it is from acts of worship or customary practices, which is what al-Ghazali also held, as will be clarified.
__________
(1) Al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari bi Sharh Sahih al-Bukhari, 1/13.
(2) The same source.
(3) Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jamia al-Uloom wal-Hikam, p. 13.


[Page 365]

As for those who specified the intention (niyyah) with the particular legal meaning, they differentiated between acts of worship (ibadat) and customary actions (adat). The acts of customary actions are valid, even if they are not intended to comply with the Sharia, but they do not yield any reward. As for acts of worship, intention is a condition for their validity. Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali said: "There has been a disagreement regarding the interpretation of the saying: 'Actions are judged by intentions.' Many of the later scholars claim that its interpretation is: actions are valid or recognized or accepted based on intentions, and based on this, the actions refer specifically to the legal actions that require intention. However, actions that do not require intention, such as customary actions like eating, drinking, dressing, and others, or like returning trusts and guaranteed items, such as deposits and usurpations, do not require any intention, so all of this is excluded from the generality of the actions mentioned here. Others said: No, the actions here are in their generality, and nothing is excluded from them" (1).
The essence of this disagreement returns to consensus regarding acts of worship, as there is no disagreement that the validity of acts of worship depends on intention. As for customary actions, they are the subject of disagreement and detail, and those who limit the meaning of the hadith "Actions are judged by intentions" to acts of worship emphasize that the intentions of the doer affect customary actions. Therefore, they established a "legal" principle broader than the hadith on intention, based on the hadith and other legal texts, which is the principle: "Matters are judged by their intentions."
__________
(1) The same source, p. 15, and the first opinion is what al-Shatibi states, as will become clear.


[Page 366]

The principle of matters is based on their objectives (1):
__________
(1) Some books on analogies and similarities mention that some jurists trace certain legal schools back to a few dozen principles. Refer to the book of analogies and similarities by al-Suyuti, pages 35 - 38, and the book of analogies and similarities by Imam Taj al-Din al-Subki, pages 10 - 12. Al-Suyuti mentioned that the entire Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) school can be reduced to four principles: the first: certainty is not overruled by doubt, the second: hardship brings about ease, the third: harm must be eliminated, and the fourth: custom is authoritative. Among what he said is: "Some later scholars have remarked that the status of these four as the foundations of jurisprudence is debatable, as most of it does not return to them except through intermediaries and effort." Some jurists added a fifth principle to these, which is: "matters are based on their objectives," based on the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "Actions are judged by intentions." He also said: "Islam is built upon five [pillars]." [This hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Faith, number (7), (4153), and by Muslim in the chapter on the pillars of Islam and its great foundations, number (16), (20), (21), and by Ahmad, number (4567), and by al-Tirmidhi, number (2534), who said it is good and authentic, and by al-Nasa'i, number (4915)]. Jurisprudence is based on five, and al-'Ala'i said: this is very good, for Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "This hadith encompasses a third of knowledge." page 37.


[Page 367]

... ... Imam al-Suyuti said: "Know that Qadi Husayn mentioned that the foundation of jurisprudence (fiqh) is based on four principles," then he mentioned the four mentioned above. He said: "And those who claim to be precise assert that a fifth has been neglected, which is that matters are judged by their intentions (maqasid). He said: Islam is built upon five, and jurisprudence is based on five." Al-Suyuti added: "In my view, if one intends to refer jurisprudence to the five in a forced and contrived manner, then the fifth is included in the first and also in the second. Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam referred all of jurisprudence to the consideration of public interests (masalih) and the prevention of harm (dar' al-mafasid), and if he were pressed, he would say: I refer everything to the consideration of public interests, for the prevention of harm is among them. He would say regarding this: one of these five is sufficient, and it is more likely that it is the second. And if one intends a clear reference, it exceeds fifty, even over two hundred." p. 12. As for the scholar Ibn Najim al-Hanafi, he counted them as six, arranging them as follows: there is no reward except by intention, matters are judged by their intentions, certainty is not overruled by doubt, hardship brings about ease, harm must be eliminated, and custom is authoritative. See: al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, pp. 1-3.


[Page 368]

Al-Suyuti said: "The basis of this principle is his saying - peace and blessings be upon him -: 'Actions are judged by intentions.' This is a well-known authentic hadith narrated by the six imams and others from Umar ibn al-Khattab"(1).
It is thus comprehensive in this text for both acts of worship and customary practices. Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi said under the title: "Matters are judged by their intentions": "Selling juice from someone who makes it into wine is not prohibited if the intention is for trade, but it is prohibited if the intention is for fermentation; the same applies to planting a vineyard. Similarly, grape juice intended for vinegar or wine, and the act of boycotting for more than three days depends on the intention; if the intention is to boycott a Muslim, it is prohibited, otherwise it is not"(2), and the examples mentioned in the above text are not acts of worship.
Therefore, they said that intention was legislated to distinguish acts of worship from customary practices and to differentiate the ranks of acts of worship from one another; as for customary practices, intention is not a condition for them, but rather the condition is that the intention must be lawful. This is in addition to the condition that the act itself must be lawful.
Ibn al-Sabki said: "It also includes(3) the principle: intention to distinguish acts of worship from customary practices and to differentiate the ranks of acts of worship from one another. The first is like sitting in the mosque, wavering between sitting for i'tikaf and sitting for rest, and like ablution and ghusl, wavering between cooling off and cleaning, and seeking closeness; without intention, the act of worship would not be distinguished from others, nor would it be valid"(4). He said: "As for the second, which is their saying: to distinguish the ranks of acts of worship from one another, it is like distinguishing voluntary prayer from obligatory prayer"(5).
__________
(1) Al-Suyuti, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 38.
(2) Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 22.
(3) In it: i.e., in the principle of matters being judged by their intentions.

[Page 369]

Al-Suyuti said similarly: "The purpose for which the intention (niyyah) was legislated is primarily to distinguish acts of worship from customary practices and to differentiate the ranks of acts of worship from one another... Abstaining from things that break the fast may be for health reasons or treatment, or due to a lack of need for it... Giving money to others may be a gift or a connection for a worldly purpose, or it may be an act of devotion such as zakat, charity, or expiation... Each of ablution (wudu), full-body washing (ghusl), prayer (salah), and fasting (sawm) may be obligatory (fard), a vow (nadr), or supererogatory (nafl), and dry ablution (tayammum) may be for ritual impurity or major impurity, while its form is the same."(1)
Ibn Najim al-Hanafi said: "They said: The objective in it is to distinguish between acts of worship and customary practices, and to distinguish some acts of worship from others"(2).
Sincerity and Associating Partners in Objectives:
Al-Ghazali said: "Know that everything can be imagined to be mixed with something else, and when it is purified from its mixture and freed from it, it is called pure, and the action that is purified and sincere is called sincerity (ikhlas)."(3) He also said: "So, whenever the motive is singular in its intention, the action that results from it is called sincerity in relation to the intended purpose. Whoever gives charity with the sole intention of showing off is sincere, and whoever's intention is solely to draw closer to Allah Exalted is He is sincere. However, it is customary to reserve the name of sincerity for the intention of drawing closer to Allah Exalted is He, free from all impurities."(4)
As for associating partners (tashrik), it is the opposite of sincerity (ikhlas). Al-Ghazali said: "Sincerity is opposed by associating partners, so whoever is not sincere is a polytheist. However, polytheism has degrees; sincerity in monotheism is opposed by associating partners in divinity"(5). He also said: "Sincerity and its opposite both enter the heart; their place is the heart, and this occurs in intentions and purposes"(6).
__________
(1) Al-Suyuti, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, pp. 46 - 47.
(2) Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi, Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 24.
(3) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din. 4/379.
(4) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din. 4/379.
(5) The same place.
(6) The same place.


[Page 370]

And the sharing in the objectives (maqasid) is the sharing between the intention of complying with the command of the Legislator or drawing closer to Him and the intention of fulfilling one's own desires. Among the desires of the self, some are for show (riya) and some are not for show; show is when one acts to be seen by people, such as someone who acts to be seen by the prince or others to gain esteem in their eyes because these people can see. As for one who acts with the intention of profit or gain or enjoying good things, this is an intention for the desires of the self and not show. Al-Qarafi said: "To perform the commanded action and draw closer to Allah, Exalted is He, with the intention of seeking His face and for people to esteem him or for him to be esteemed in their hearts, so that their benefit reaches him or harm is repelled from him, this is the basis of one category of show, and the other category is to perform an action without intending the face of Allah at all, but only for people. This category is called: show of sincerity, while the first is the show of polytheism, because this does not involve sharing but is purely for creation, and the first is for creation and for Allah, Exalted is He"(1). He also said: "As for absolute sharing, like one who strives to attain the obedience of Allah through jihad and to obtain wealth from the spoils, this does not harm him, nor is it prohibited by consensus, because Allah, Exalted is He, has made this for him in this act of worship. He distinguishes between striving to have people say that he is brave or for the imam to esteem him so that his gifts from the public treasury increase; this and similar actions are forbidden show, and between striving to obtain captives, horses, and weapons from the enemy's wealth; this does not harm him even though he has shared, and this is not called show because show is to act so that he is seen by others among His creation, and sight is only valid from creation. Therefore, for one who does not see or perceive, it cannot be said that the action is show in relation to him, and the wealth obtained from the spoils and similar matters cannot be said to be seen or perceived, so the term show does not apply to these intentions due to the lack of sight in them"(2).(3)
Based on what has been mentioned, one can detail the ruling on sharing between the intention of compliance and the intention of desire.
__________
(1) Al-Qarafi, Shihab al-Din, al-Furuq: 3/22, difference: 122.
(2) Thus is the text. Perhaps its origin is: to act to be seen by...
(3) Al-Qarafi, Shihab al-Din, al-Furuq: difference 122, 3/22 - 23.


[Page 371]

As for the intention of compliance and drawing closer to Allah devoid of any other intention, this is the highest rank of deeds and the purest. As for the intention of seeking personal gain, if it stems from ostentation (riya), it is blameworthy (1), whether in acts of worship or in customary practices, and whether it is the ostentation of associating partners with Allah or mere ostentation. Al-Qarafi said: "Know that ostentation in acts of worship is associating partners with Allah, and it leads to sin, wrongdoing, and invalidation" (2). He also said: "The purposes of ostentation are three: seeking honor, gaining worldly benefits, and averting worldly harms. The latter two stem from the first, for when one seeks honor, worldly benefits are drawn to him and harms are repelled from him; this is the ultimate purpose in reality. Thus, this is the principle of ostentation that invalidates deeds, as agreed upon by consensus" (3). Al-Ghazali said: "Whoever is motivated solely by ostentation is at risk of destruction" (4).
As for seeking personal gain without ostentation, if it is devoid of the intention of compliance, it is invalid in acts of worship because acts of worship— as previously clarified— require intention. Al-Ghazali said: "Acts of obedience are linked to intentions in their validity and in the multiplication of their merit" (5).
__________
(1) Scholars have elaborated on this matter, as a person may initially perform an action with the intention of obedience or otherwise, and then a form of ostentation may overwhelm him, making it difficult to escape from it. We will mention this when detailing al-Shatibi's view on the association of intentions.
(2) Al-Qarafi, Shihab al-Din, Al-Furuq, 4/22-23. Distinction: 122.
