(4) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/379.
(5) The same source, 4/370.


[Page 372]

And if it pertains to customs, it is according to intention. If the intention is lawful, then the action is valid; if the intention is unlawful, then it is invalid (1). Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi said: "Selling juice to someone who makes it into wine is not prohibited if the intention is for trade, but if the intention is for fermentation, it is prohibited, and the same applies to planting a vineyard. Likewise, grape juice intended for fermentation or for wine. The prohibition of severing ties is threefold depending on the intention; if the intention is to sever ties with a Muslim, it is prohibited, otherwise it is not. The mourning of a woman for a deceased other than her husband is also threefold depending on the intention; if she intends to refrain from adornment and perfume for the sake of the deceased, it is prohibited for her, otherwise it is not" (2). However, even if the intention for benefit is lawful, being devoid of the intention of compliance and drawing closer to Allah renders the action devoid of reward, for there is no reward without intention.
__________
(1) Our discussion is confined to validity and invalidity in terms of the consequences of sin or reward, and is not a ruling in this world.
(2) Ibn Nujaym al-Hanafi, al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, p. 22.


[Page 373]

As for when the intention of self-interest is mixed with the intention of obedience and drawing closer to Allah, this is where the disagreement and elaboration arise. Al-Qarafi - as has been clarified - distinguished between showing off (riya) and other forms of self-interest, deeming the former as forbidden and nullifying to actions. As for al-Ghazali, although he distinguished between them in terms of prohibition and permissibility, he did not differentiate between them regarding their effect on the action that is mixed with intentions. He said: "Enjoyment and pleasure are not sins, but one will be questioned about them, and whoever is held to account will be punished, while one who engages in something permissible in this world will not be punished in the Hereafter, but their enjoyment in the Hereafter will be diminished in proportion to it, and it is a great loss to hasten towards what perishes and lose out on an everlasting increase in enjoyment" (1). He said: "Now we will discuss one who is motivated by the intention of drawing closer to Allah, but this motivation is mixed with another motive, either from showing off or from other forms of self-interest. An example of this is one who fasts to benefit from the health gained through fasting while intending to draw closer to Allah, or one who frees a slave to rid himself of their burden and bad character, or one who performs Hajj to improve their health through the movement of travel, or to escape from harm that may befall them in their homeland" (2). He then said: "These self-interests, if they are the sole motivators, the severity of the matter is clear for their owner, but we are considering the case where the original intention is to draw closer to Allah and these matters are added to it" (3). He said: "The psychological motive may be equal to the religious motive, stronger than it, or weaker" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/371 - 372.
(2) The same source, 4/379.
(3) The same source, 4/380.
(4) The same source.


[Page 374]

Then he said: "Know that if an action is not purely for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He, but is accompanied by a trace of showing off (riya) or personal desires, then people have differed on whether this entails reward, punishment, or nothing at all, so that it has neither merit nor demerit. As for that which is intended solely for showing off, it is certainly upon him and is a cause of condemnation and punishment. As for that which is purely for Allah, it is a cause of reward. The consideration lies in the mixed intention. The apparent reports indicate that there is no reward for it, and the reports are not free from contradiction on this matter. What seems to be the case - and knowledge is with Allah - is that one should look at the strength of the motive. If the religious motive is equal to the personal motive, they will counterbalance and cancel each other out, and the action will be neither for him nor against him. If the motive of showing off is predominant and stronger, then it is not beneficial and is, moreover, harmful and leads to punishment. Indeed, the punishment in this case is lighter than the punishment for an action that is purely for showing off and does not contain any trace of seeking closeness. However, if the intention of seeking closeness is predominant in relation to the other motive, then he will have a reward commensurate with the strength of the religious motive" (1). He also stated that seeking worldly gain is not forbidden, but seeking it through acts of religion is forbidden due to the presence of showing off and the alteration of worship from its proper place (2).
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/384.
(2) The same source, 4/385.


[Page 375]

Al-Qarafi and al-Shatibi opposed him in this matter. As for al-Qarafi, he said: "Similarly, one who performs Hajj and associates with it the intention of trade, such that most or all of his intention is to travel for trade specifically, and Hajj is either intended alongside that or not intended at all, and it occurs as a secondary matter by agreement, this does not invalidate the Hajj nor does it incur sin or disobedience. Likewise, one who fasts to improve his health or to achieve the removal of an illness that fasting contradicts, and healing is his primary intention or part of his intention, and he undertakes fasting alongside these intentions, these intentions do not invalidate his fast. Rather, the Lawgiver commanded it in his saying - peace and blessings be upon him -: 'O young people, whoever among you is able to marry, let him do so, and whoever is not able, then let him fast, for it is a shield' (1), meaning it cuts off desires. Thus, he commanded fasting for this purpose, and if it were invalidating, he would not have commanded it in acts of worship and their like, including renewing one's ablution and intending to cool off or cleanse oneself. All these purposes do not involve glorifying the creation" (2). He then said: "Indeed, it does not prevent that these purposes mixed with worship may diminish the reward, and that if the worship is free from them, the reward increases and the reward becomes greater. As for sin and invalidation, there is no way to it" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Bukhari (4637), 5/1950. And Muslim (2485), (2486), and Ibn Majah (1835). In it: for it is more lowering of the gaze and more protective of the private parts. There are narrations without: O young people.
(2) Al-Qarafi, Shihab al-Din, Al-Furuq, difference 122, 3/23.
(3) The same source.


[Page 376]

As for al-Shatibi, his opinion will be clarified in detail below; however, two matters should be noted: First, actions that are devoid of intention altogether, whether the intention is to comply or otherwise, such as the actions of the coerced, the forgetful, the sleeping, the insane, the child, and similar cases, are outside the scope of this discussion. Second, the actions that are dependent on intention for their validity and for the hope of reward in the Hereafter, or for their validity and acceptance in this world, are only the actions that are originally lawful. If the action is unlawful, then the validity of intention or the goodness of purpose does not rectify it. Al-Ghazali said: "Sins do not change their nature by intention, so the ignorant should not misunderstand this from the general statement of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), 'Actions are judged by intentions,' thinking that a sin can turn into an act of obedience by intention, like one who backbites another person to please someone else's heart, or feeds a poor person with someone else's money, or builds a school or a mosque or a ribat with unlawful money while intending good. All of this is ignorance, and intention does not affect its being oppression, aggression, and sin; rather, intending good through evil, contrary to the requirements of the Sharia, is another form of evil. If one knows this, he is opposing the Sharia. If he is ignorant of it, he is sinful due to his ignorance, as seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim. Good deeds are only recognized as good by the Sharia, so how can evil be good? Never!"(1)
__________
(1) Al-Ghazali, Ihya Ulum al-Din, 4/368 - 369.


[Page 377]

Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali said: "Indeed, the entire religion revolves around performing the commanded acts, avoiding the prohibited ones, and refraining from doubtful matters" (1). He then said: "This is accomplished through two matters: the first is that the outward action conforms to the Sunnah, and this is what is encompassed in the hadith of Aisha: 'Whoever introduces something into this matter of ours that is not part of it, it is rejected' " (2). The second is that the inward intention of the action is directed towards the Face of Allah, as indicated in the hadith of Umar: "Actions are judged by intentions." Al-Fudayl said regarding the saying of Allah, { He will test you to see which of you is best in deed } (3): "It means the most sincere and the most correct." He said: "If an action is sincere but not correct, it will not be accepted; and if it is correct but not sincere, it will not be accepted until it is both sincere and correct. The sincere action is that which is for Allah, Exalted is He, and the correct action is that which is in accordance with the Sunnah" (4).

Section Two
The Actions of the Responsible and Their Objectives

The Impact of the Objectives of the Responsible on Actions According to al-Shatibi:
Actions are of two types: lawful actions and unlawful actions, and the focus of this research now is on lawful actions. As for unlawful actions, they will be the subject of the subsequent research.
__________
(1) Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jamia al-Uloom wal-Hikam, p. 20.
(2) Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on reconciliation (2499), and al-Bukhari also narrated in the Book of Knowledge in the chapter on when a worker or ruler makes a mistake contrary to the Messenger without knowledge, his ruling is rejected: "Whoever performs an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected," and Muslim in the chapter on judgments regarding invalid rulings and the rejection of innovations (1718), and Abu Dawood (1406), and Ibn Majah (14). And Ahmad (24840) and (24995), and in some narrations, there is a substitution for it.
(3) Surah Al-Mulk, 2. And Hud, 7.
(4) Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, Jamia al-Uloom wal-Hikam, p. 20.


[Page 378]

And the principle: "Actions are judged by their intentions" is acknowledged by al-Shatibi in the same sense mentioned by the jurists in the previous discussion, even though he does not state it explicitly. He said: "Indeed, actions are based on intentions, and the objectives are considered in transactions of both acts of worship and customary practices, and the evidence for this meaning is not limited; it suffices for you that the objectives differentiate between what is customary and what is an act of worship, and in acts of worship, between what is obligatory and what is non-obligatory, and in customary practices, between the obligatory, the recommended, the permissible, the disliked, the prohibited, the valid, the invalid, and other rulings. A single action may be intended for one purpose and thus be an act of worship, while if intended for another purpose, it would not be so; rather, it may be intended for one thing and thus be an act of faith, and intended for another thing and thus be disbelief, such as prostrating to Allah or to an idol. Furthermore, when an action is associated with intention, it is connected to the legal rulings, and if it is devoid of intention, none of those rulings apply to it, such as the actions of a sleeping person, an inattentive person, or a madman"(1). He also said: "Indeed, all actions that fall under choice do not become acts of worship except with the intention for that. As for what is established as an act of worship, such as prayer and pilgrimage, there is no doubt about it, while customary practices do not become acts of worship except through intentions"(2).
The lawful actions are either intended by the obligated person solely for compliance, which are the primary objectives, or they are intended solely for their own interests, which are the secondary objectives. Alternatively, they may intend both purposes together.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/225.
(2) The same source, 2/228.


[Page 379]

If one intends to comply without considering what worldly benefits may come from it, then that is the purest and highest of deeds. Nevertheless, his benefits will still be attained within that. If he considers his benefits and intends them in his action, but he aims for compliance and does not seek his benefits except through the lawful means, then his action is legitimate, and there is no doubt about its validity. He says: "An action that aligns with the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) is either in accordance with the original objectives or the secondary objectives" (1). He also said: "If it aligns with the requirements of the original objectives in such a way that they are taken into account in the action, there is no doubt about its validity and soundness, whether it is free from personal gain or whether personal gain is considered, because it corresponds to the intention of the Legislator in the original legislation" (2).
He said: "The primary objective, when sought by the obligated person, includes the intention of everything the Legislator intended in the action, whether it is to achieve a benefit or to avert harm. The one acting upon it intends to fulfill the command of the Legislator, either after understanding what was intended or merely out of obedience to the command. In any case, he is intending what the Legislator intended. If it is established that the intention of the Legislator is the most comprehensive and foremost of objectives, and that it is pure light untainted by ulterior motives or personal gain, then the one receiving it in this manner is taking it in a pure, complete, and untainted manner, not falling short of the Legislator's intent... As for the secondary intention, it does not entail all of that, because the one who takes the command and prohibition with the intention of personal gain has limited his intention to that gain, thus restricting its generality and failing to rise to the level of the first" (3). Therefore, he says: "When actions are based on the original objectives, obedience becomes greater, and if they are opposed, disobedience becomes greater" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/134.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, 2/225.
(4) The same source, 1/141.


[Page 380]

This is due to his methodology regarding causes and effects. As for when the action aligns with the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), but this alignment is incidental or due to necessity, meaning it was not intended to align, then the action is valid in one sense and invalid in another. It is valid in the sense that its effects will be realized in this world; it absolves one of liability, acquires property, permits sexual relations, and nullifies any judicial claims where there is a claim. It is invalid in the sense that no reward will be assigned to it. The doer may incur blame and sin, depending on the intention and purpose, as he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Actions are judged by intentions." The rulings regarding acts of worship differ in this matter from those regarding customary practices. Al-Shatibi has a thorough discussion on this, which I will summarize briefly. He states: "What the servants are commanded to do falls into two categories: the first is acts of worship... and the second is customary practices. As for the first, it cannot be devoid of a worldly or otherworldly benefit; if it is otherworldly, this is a benefit established by the Sharia (1)... If it is established by the Sharia, then seeking it is valid... If the benefit sought through acts of worship is in this world, it is of two types: one type relates to the improvement of one’s reputation and the good opinion of people, and the belief in the virtue of the doer due to his action, and the other type relates to attaining one’s benefit in this world. This can be divided into two: one pertains to what concerns the individual himself, while being heedless of seeking the admiration of people through the action, and the other pertains to seeking admiration in order to gain wealth, status, or other benefits. Thus, there are three categories: the first relates to improving the opinion of people and believing in virtue; if this intention is pursued, there is no doubt that it is showing off (riya) because it is driven by the desire for praise and to be thought well of, while he still performs his obligatory or voluntary prayers, which is clear. If it is secondary, it is a matter of consideration and scholarly interpretation, and the scholars have differed on this principle" (2). Al-Shatibi tends to validate the act of worship in this case, which is when the pursuit of a good opinion of him is secondary and not primary.
__________
(1) This refers to the gardens of paradise and what is therein.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/147 - 150.


[Page 381]

He says: "Regarding the man who prays to Allah and then finds within himself that he loves to be seen and loves to be noticed on the way to the mosque and dislikes to be noticed on the way of others... that is, the devil comes to a person when he is pleased by the sight of people seeing him doing good and says to him: 'You are showing off,' whereas this is merely something that occurs in his heart that he cannot control" (1). Then he brings his arguments for this, and continues to mention the three categories, saying: "The second is what pertains to the individual himself while being heedless of showing off to others. Among its examples is: praying in the mosque for the sake of enjoying the company of neighbors, or praying at night for the sake of monitoring or observing conditions, the second: fasting to save money or to take a break from cooking or to protect oneself from pain or an illness that is anticipated or from a previous bout of indigestion, the third: giving charity for the pleasure of generosity and favoring others... the seventh: performing ablution for the sake of cooling down, the eighth: seclusion (i'tikaf) to escape from paying rent... the eleventh: performing pilgrimage (hajj) on foot to save on transportation costs. This point is also a matter of disagreement if the mentioned intention is subordinate to the intention of worship" (2). Al-Shatibi went on to validate the worship here, although it is preferable to separate the intention of worship from the intention of worldly matters. As for the third category, he states: "The third pertains to showing off... it is the blameworthy showing off in the Sharia, and the worst of it is the actions of the hypocrites who enter Islam outwardly with the intention of securing their blood and wealth" (3).
This is regarding the first category related to acts of worship, as for the second category related to customary practices, he states: "As for the second, which is that the action is a reform of the customary practices among the people, such as marriage, sale, and leasing... this is also a share that has been established by the legislator and taken into account in commands and prohibitions, and this is known from his intention through the laws set for it. If this is understood in general, then seeking it from that angle does not contradict the intention of the legislator, thus it is rightful and valid..." (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 1/150.
(2) The same source, 1/151 - 153.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/153.
(4) The same location.


[Page 382]

He says: "The seeker of his share, if he does not intend compliance in any way but seeks his share in a manner that if he could achieve it in a non-permissible way, he would take it, but he is only able to do so through the permissible way—does the initial intention exist in his case...? The answer is that it exists... because if he has no way to reach his share through the non-permissible, then his return to the permissible way is an intention towards it, and the intention towards the permissible way includes compliance with the command or acting according to the permission, which is the original first intention even if he is not consciously aware of it in detail" (1).
He says: "To act with the awareness of compliance out of necessity, like one who intends to gain pleasure from a certain woman, and when he cannot do so through fornication due to her refusal or the prohibition by her family, he contracts a marriage to reach his goal—this is also invalid in the second sense because he only returns to the ruling of compliance out of necessity and insofar as it leads to his objective, not because of the permissibility of the Sharia, even though it is not invalid in the first sense. An example of this is the zakat taken under duress, which is valid in the first sense if it absolves the obligation and clears the debt, but invalid in this second sense" (2). The meaning of the two texts above is that the act itself in marriage or zakat, there is no sin in the first and it absolves the debt in the second; the act itself is valid, while the invalidity, and perhaps the sin attached to it, is due to another act, which is his intention and purpose of disobedience, and this is from the actions of the heart.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/155 - 156.
(2) The same source, 1/207.


[Page 383]

To clarify al-Shatibi's position here accurately, it is necessary to point out his distinction between performing an action that aligns with the intention of the Lawgiver with the intention of compliance out of necessity, as in the marriage mentioned above, and performing the same action without regard for compliance or non-compliance, where the compliance occurred by coincidence, that is, without intention on the part of the obligated person, and performing the same action but with the intention of non-compliance, where the compliance occurred by mistake. As for the first, it has been clarified. As for the second, its ruling is invalidity in acts of worship, and in customary matters, it is valid(1). As for the third, its ruling is like the second... In all cases, sin attaches to one who intends to oppose the intention of the Lawgiver or to one who does not regard it. He says: "If one intends to oppose the command of the Lawgiver, then whether in acts of worship he complies or opposes, what he opposes is not considered because it is contrary to the intention in general. In customary matters, the original ruling is to consider what complies and not what opposes, because what does not require intention for its validity in actions does not regard compliance with the legal intention or its opposition, like one who contracts a contract intending it to be invalid but it turns out to be valid, or one who drinks a syrup thinking it is wine, except that he bears the sin for intending to oppose. As for one who does not intend compliance or non-compliance, he is acting merely out of chance or negligence, and its ruling in acts of worship is invalidity due to lack of intention to comply, and in customary matters, it is valid if it complies with the intention of the Lawgiver"(2).
That is, the intention of compliance is a condition for the validity of acts of worship, whereas for customary actions it is not. The actions of customary practices are not invalidated or rendered corrupt by the absence of the intention of compliance, nor if the intention of compliance did not cross one's mind.
He said: "When an action occurs in accordance with the subordinate objectives (maqasid al-tabi'a), it can either be accompanied by the primary objectives (maqasid al-asliya) or not. As for the first, it is an action of compliance without doubt, even if it is a pursuit for personal gain; and as for the second, it is an action driven solely by desire and inclination."(3)
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/156 - 157.
(2) The same place.
(3) The same source, 2/142.


[Page 384]

Then al-Shatibi explained his meaning of companionship and inclination, saying: "Companionship is either through action, an example of which is to say, for instance: this food or this clothing, or this tangible object has been permitted for me by the Sharia to enjoy, so I enjoy what is permitted and work to obtain it because it is allowed. Or it is through potential, an example of which is entering into the causation of that permitted thing from the allowed avenue, but the very permission did not cross his mind; rather, it occurred to him that this is reached through such and such a path. If he reaches it through that, then in ruling it is like the first, provided that the path leading to the permitted is permissible from his side, except that companionship through action is superior" (1). Thus, al-Shatibi contradicts, indeed opposes, al-Ghazali significantly on this issue, especially regarding the topic of sincerity and sharing in objectives. He says: "If it is said: how can the intention of the legislator for sincerity in ordinary actions and the prohibition of sharing in them be achieved? It is said: this means that they should be performed according to what is legislated. They should not be intended for a pre-Islamic act, nor a satanic innovation, nor resemble those outside the faith, such as drinking water or honey in the manner of drinking wine, or eating what is made to glorify the festivals of the Jews or Christians even if made by a Muslim, or what is slaughtered in imitation of pre-Islamic practices, and similar acts that are a form of glorifying polytheism" (2). This is the elaboration of what he stated in the Book of Rulings, where he said: "Ordinary matters are only considered valid if they do not contradict the intention of the legislator, and the appearance of agreement is not a condition" (3).
Agreement and disagreement with the intention of the legislator:
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/143.
(3) The same source, 1/181.


[Page 385]

It has been previously clarified that the objectives of the Legislator (maqasid al-sharia) are of two types: original and subsidiary. The original objectives are those for which there is no consideration for the obligated person (mukallaf). They mean performing an action or refraining from it based on a command or prohibition without regard to interests or outcomes, and interests only arise within the framework of obligation. As for the subsidiary objectives, they are legal objectives that take into account the interests of the obligated person, such as ownership and enjoyment, and so forth. These are objectives that the obligated person may intend through their actions, and Allah - Exalted is He - has legislated rulings for their sake. Thus, the rulings are causes for them, and these interests are legal objectives, so it is permissible for the obligated person to intend them through these causes, just as it is permissible for them not to intend them, but rather to intend compliance only through those causes.
According to rational division, the actions of the accountable person (mukallaf) may conform to the command and prohibition, making the form of the action legitimate. However, the intention of the doer behind their action may be lawful or unlawful, meaning it may be in accordance with the law or contrary to it.
Similarly, an action can be contrary to a command or prohibition, so the form of the act may be unlawful, but the intention of the doer may be lawful or unlawful.
These are four categories that al-Shatibi elaborated on. Although there was a previous mention of some of this in the earlier discussion, it was in terms of conformity or non-conformity to the intent of the legislator, and not in terms of opposition to the intent of the legislator.
There is a fifth category that will be referred to after explaining these four categories, which is when the action is legal (shar'i) and the intention is legal (shar'i), but the action was not legislated for this intention, rather for another. Similarly, the benefit or intention in general was not intended by the legislator (shari') with this action, but rather with another. This is like the act of cutting off a hand; it is a legal action, and the intention of deterrence is a legal intention. However, cutting off the hand of an apostate or a fornicator is not legal. This is because cutting off the hand, which is legal, was not established for deterring the apostate or the fornicator, even though deterring them is legal.


[Page 386]

As for the four categories, al-Shatibi says: "The doer of the action or the one who leaves it may either have his action or his abandonment in accordance with or in opposition to the law, and in both cases, his intention may be to comply with or to oppose the law, thus all are four categories. The first is that he acts in accordance with the law and intends to comply, such as prayer, fasting, charity, pilgrimage, and others, which are intended to fulfill Allah's command and perform what is obligatory or recommended. Likewise, abandoning adultery, alcohol, and other immoralities is intended for compliance, so there is no doubt about the validity of this action. The second is that he acts in opposition and intends to oppose, such as abandoning obligatory acts and committing prohibitions intentionally; this is also evident in its ruling. The third is that the action or abandonment is in accordance with the law while the intention is to oppose, which has two types: one is that he does not know that the action or abandonment is in accordance, and the other is that he knows it. The first is like a man who has intercourse with his wife thinking she is a foreign woman, or a drinker of jallab thinking it is alcohol, and one who abandons prayer believing it is still due upon him while he has actually performed it and is free from it in reality. This type has the intention of disobedience through opposition" (1). He said: "When we look at his intention, we find him violating the sanctity of the command and prohibition, so he is disobedient merely by intention, but not disobedient merely by action. The reality is that he is sinful in relation to the right of Allah, but not sinful in relation to the right of the servant, like the usurper who thinks he is taking the property of the one from whom it is usurped, while it is actually the property of the usurper himself. Thus, there is no claim against him from the one he intended to usurp from, but there is a claim against him in relation to the sanctity of the command and prohibition. The principle is that every obligation includes the right of Allah and the right of the servant" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/234.
(2) The same source, 2/235, and we will discuss in a separate study in this chapter about the right of Allah and the right of the servant.


[Page 387]

As for the second type, he said: "The second is that the action or abstention is in accordance, but he is aware of the conformity, and yet he intends to oppose it. An example of this is praying for show to gain worldly benefits, or to gain respect among people, or to avert death from himself, and the like. This category is more severe than the previous one, and its essence is that this worker has made the legal subjects that were intended as means for other matters, which the Legislator did not intend them for, thus it includes hypocrisy, ostentation, and tricks against the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, and all of this is invalid because the intention opposes the intention of the Legislator in essence, so it is not valid at all" (1).
As for the fourth category, which is that the action or abstention is contrary while the intention is in accordance, al-Shatibi elaborates and expands on it. He says: "The fourth category is that the action or abstention is contrary while the intention is in accordance; it is also of two types. One is that it is done with knowledge of the opposition, and the other is that it is done in ignorance of it. If it is done with knowledge of the opposition, this is innovation, such as establishing new acts of worship and additions to what has been legislated. However, it is common that one does not dare to do this except with a type of interpretation, and yet it is condemned as stated in the Qur'an and the Sunnah" (2).
As for if the action is contrary to the command or prohibition while being ignorant of the opposition, but the intention is in accordance with the intention of the Legislator and the worker intends to conform, this is a matter of consideration, ijtihad, and disagreement, and there is no single rule regarding its judgment. Al-Shatibi indicated that it is a thorny issue. This is because it cannot be judged as invalid since the correctness of the intention in the action affects the ruling on it, nor can it be judged as valid since the opposition to the command and prohibition also affects it.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/236.
(2) The same source.


[Page 388]

He said: "If the action is contrary while being ignorant of the contradiction, there are two perspectives. The first is that the intention is in accordance, so it is not contrary from this angle. Although the action is contrary, actions are judged by intentions, and the intention of this worker is one of compliance; however, ignorance has led him to the contradiction. One who does not intend to oppose the Lawgiver outright does not fall under the category of intentional contradiction in both intention and action. Thus, his action, from this perspective, is generally considered, and there is no absolute rejection of it. The second perspective is that the action is indeed contrary, for the intention of the Lawgiver in commanding and prohibiting is compliance. If he does not comply, then he has opposed that intention, and the contradiction of intention does not negate the compliance that motivates the action because the intention of the Lawgiver was not achieved in that action in any way, nor did the intention align with the action, resulting in the whole being contrary, just as if both were contradicted together, thus compliance is not achieved" (1). He then said: "Both perspectives oppose each other in themselves and also oppose each other in terms of preference, for if you prefer one, the other presents a reason for preference, leading to mutual opposition. Therefore, this matter has become obscure in the Sharia" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/238.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/238.


[Page 389]

The lack of compliance leads to a ruling of invalidity, except that the validity of intention with ignorance of the violation necessitates the correction that ignorance may occur in the Sharia in the same way as forgetfulness or error for which there is no accountability (1). Therefore, some of these actions may be rectified. However, he did not clarify a principle regarding this. He said: "If it is said: His (peace and blessings be upon him) statement: 'Actions are judged by intentions' indicates that these actions, even if they are in violation, may be considered, for the intentions are the souls of actions, thus the action has become a body with a soul in general. If that is the case, it is considered, unlike when the intention is in conflict with the action or when both are in conflict, for then it is a body without a soul, and it does not fulfill the implication of his statement: 'Actions are judged by intentions' due to the lack of intention in the action. It is said that if this is conceded, it is opposed by his (peace and blessings be upon him) statement: 'Every action not in accordance with our command is rejected' (2), and this action is not in accordance with his command (peace and blessings be upon him), thus it is not considered but rather rejected. Also, just as a body without a soul is of no benefit, so too is a soul without a body" (3). Then he said: "Thus, the issue was very problematic" (4).
Thus, should the aspect of the compliant intention be considered to validate the action, or should the aspect of the conflicting action be considered to invalidate the action, or should both aspects be considered? (5).
__________
(1) This is unlike what we mentioned from al-Ghazali in the previous discussion of this chapter.
(2) This was previously cited in relation to the hadith: "Whoever introduces something into this matter of ours that is not part of it, it is rejected."
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/239.
(4) The same location.
(5) We note here that the violation is with ignorance of the violation, meaning with the assumption that it is not a violation.


[Page 390]

Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) holds that it is necessary to apply both sides; what can be corrected should be corrected, such as forgetfulness (sahw) in prayer. What can be avoided should be avoided, as in the case of the missing person (mufqood) if his wife marries another man and he returns. The error can be rectified by prioritizing the first husband, or the first husband is prioritized if he returns before her marriage. What cannot be rectified is disregarded. Al-Shatibi's statement on this is: "And disregard what must be disregarded that cannot be rectified" (1). An example of this is eating forgetfully during Ramadan, and in the case of the missing person, if his wife marries and he returns after her marriage, she belongs to the second husband (2).
Among Al-Shatibi's statements regarding the application of both sides is his saying: "So apply the implications of agreement in lifting the punishment and penalty, and apply the implications of disagreement in not relying on that action and not building upon it, until what must be corrected is corrected, leaning towards the intention as well, and disregard what must be disregarded that cannot be rectified" (3). He said: "Count those who err in actions and statements as ignorant of the ruling of the forgetful" (4). He stated: "This is evident in purification (taharah), prayer (salah), fasting (sawm), pilgrimage (hajj), and other acts of worship, as well as in many customary matters such as marriage (nikah), divorce (talaq), foods, and drinks, and it is supported by evidence indicating the lifting of accountability for error and forgetfulness.
As for errors in financial matters, the aspect of intention is considered regarding the Hereafter, while the aspect of action is considered concerning the rights of others in this world. Therefore, it is liable for compensation, and ignorance in this regard is treated like knowledge or intent. He said: "In financial matters, it is liable for compensation in ignorance and intent because we say: the ruling on liability for property is different, as the error in it is equivalent to intent in the resulting liability for its destruction" (5).

[Page 391]

It is agreed upon that an error in action, if it is not intended to contravene, or if it is intended to comply with the intention of the Lawgiver, then the accountability in the Hereafter for it is lifted. It is also agreed upon that this accountability is not lifted absolutely, whether in this world or the Hereafter. Al-Shatibi said: "And in the hadith: 'Mistakes, forgetfulness, and what one is compelled to do are lifted from my community' (1), and this is a generally agreed-upon meaning with no opposition, although they differ regarding the lifting of accountability: whether it is specific to the accountability in the Hereafter or not. They also did not disagree that the lifting of accountability in general is not valid" (2)(3).
As for the fifth category, which is that the action is lawful and the intention is lawful, but the action was not legislated for this intention, or was not established in the law as a cause for this effect, it has been clarified within the fourth type of the objectives of the Lawgiver under the title of the legal connection between the cause and the effect. The following is its explanation as mentioned by al-Shatibi in the section on the objectives of the obligated person.
__________
(1) Narrated by Ibn Majah in the chapter on the divorce of the compelled and the forgetful (2033) and (2034) with the wording: "Indeed, Allah has overlooked" instead of "lifted." And (2035) with the wording "placed."
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/241.
(3) Al-Suyuti said: "Know that the legal maxim is: 'Forgetfulness and ignorance absolve one from sin absolutely.' As for the ruling, if they occur in neglecting a commanded act, it does not absolve, rather it must be rectified, and the reward associated with it is not attained due to the lack of compliance, or in performing a prohibited act that is not in the category of damage, then there is nothing in it, or if it involves damage, the liability is not lifted. If it incurs punishment, it is a doubt regarding its abrogation." Al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair, pp. 239 - 240. And see the discussion on the ignorant, the forgetful, and the compelled, pp. 337 - 374 of the same book.


[Page 392]

He said: "The intention of the legislator (shari') for the accountable person (mukallaf) is that their intention in action should align with the intention in legislation" (1), meaning that the accountable person, even if they act with the intention of compliance in accordance with the command and prohibition, that is, according to the original objectives (maqasid), must also ensure that the intended outcomes, if they exist for the accountable person (2), align with the subsidiary objectives. If the accountable person intends from the action a benefit, a gain, or an outcome, then this outcome must be one that the legislator intended to achieve through this action. Otherwise, intending it through this action or this means signifies a contradiction to the intention of the legislator. The objectives of the legislation have been established by the legislator through specific actions, so if the accountable person intends through these actions objectives other than those, this constitutes a violation in that the accountable person has made these objectives means to others, which they are not in the law, and it is also a violation in that the legal objectives intended by the accountable person have specific actions designated by the legislator, thus adopting actions other than what the legislator has established is neglecting what Allah has legislated. Al-Shatibi said: "Whoever seeks in the obligations of the Sharia something other than what it was legislated for has contradicted the Sharia, and whoever contradicts it, their action in contradiction is void. So whoever seeks in the obligations of the Sharia what was not legislated for them, their action is void" (3). He also said: "If the accountable person intends exactly what the legislator intended by permission, they have sought the path of benefit in its most complete form, and they are worthy of attaining it. But if they intend something other than what the legislator intended, this is usually due to the misconception that the benefit lies in what they intended, for the rational person does not directly intend the path of harm. They have made what the legislator intended neglected in consideration, and what the legislator neglected as an intended consideration, which is a clear opposition to the Sharia" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/230.
(2) We have previously mentioned that the accountable person can intend their gains through legal actions alongside their intention of compliance, and they may also not intend them; hence we said: if they exist for the accountable person. If they do not intend them and only intend compliance, they will attain them as part of their compliance, and this action is purer and of a higher rank.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/231.
(4) The same source.


[Page 393]

He said: "The accountable person (mukallaf) is only obligated to perform actions based on the intention of the legislator (shari') behind the command and prohibition. If the intention is something other than that, then it becomes, by the intention of the one intending (qasid), a means to what he intended, not the objectives, since he did not intend the intention of the legislator, so it becomes intended for another purpose, making the action or abstention a means to it. Thus, what is considered by the legislator as intended becomes a means for him, and what has this characteristic nullifies the legislator's decree and undermines what he has established" (1).

He said: "The one who takes what is legislated (mashru') without the intention of the legislator towards that objective is indeed taking something that is not truly legislated, because the legislator only legislated it for a known purpose by obligation. Therefore, if he takes it with the intention of something other than that known purpose, he has not brought forth that legislated matter at all. If he has not brought it forth, he contradicts the legislator in that taking, as he becomes like one who acts contrary to what he was commanded and neglects what he was commanded" (2).

Section Three
Legal Devices (Hiyal)

Definition:
Al-Shatibi said in defining legal devices: "Its essence is presenting an action that appears permissible to invalidate a legal ruling and to transform it in appearance into another ruling" (3). He said: "Like the one who gifts his wealth at the end of the year to evade zakat. For the essence of the gift is permissible, and if zakat were to be prevented without a gift, it would be prohibited" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/232.
(2) Same source.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/114. Ibn Najim al-Hanafi said in his book al-Ashbah wa al-Nazair: "The art of legal devices is the collection of hila, which is the skill in managing affairs. It is the turning of thought until one finds a solution." He said: "Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, differed in expressing this, with many choosing to express it as the Book of Legal Devices, while many chose the Book of Legal Loopholes," p. 477.
(4) Same source.


[Page 394]

The rulings that can be reversed are those that exist or are lifted based on causes, conditions, or impediments, such that the accountable person (mukallaf) has a hand in creating or removing these causes, conditions, or impediments. If he does not have a hand in them because they are beyond his capacity, then legal stratagems (hiyal) do not apply, because a stratagem is an action of the accountable person. Al-Shatibi said: "The actions that occur in existence which necessitate matters for which they are legislated or established fall into two categories. One is beyond the capacity of the accountable person, and the other can be included within his capacity. The former can be a cause, a condition, or an impediment" (1). A cause is like the necessity that permits the consumption of carrion, the fear of hardship that permits the marriage of female slaves, the incontinence that exempts one from the obligation of ablution for each prayer in the presence of an external factor, and the setting or rising of the sun or the dawn that necessitates those prayers and similar matters. Conditions are like the passing of a year being a condition for the obligation of zakat, and reaching puberty being a condition for accountability in general, and the ability to deliver being a condition for the validity of a sale, and maturity being a condition for managing an orphan's wealth, and sending messengers being a condition for reward and punishment, and matters of that nature. An impediment is like menstruation being an impediment to sexual intercourse, divorce, circumambulation of the House, the obligation of prayers, and fasting, and insanity being an impediment to performing acts of worship and exercising control over affairs, and similar matters.
__________
(1) The same source, 1/128 - 129.


[Page 395]

The second type is that which is within the capacity of the accountable person (mukallaf). They are able to create the cause, condition, or impediment, or they can remove it, thereby causing a change in the legal ruling. Examples of this include: "As for the cause, it is like the marriage being a cause for inheritance between the spouses, the prohibition of marriage relations by marriage (mahram) and the permissibility of enjoyment, and slaughter being a cause for the permissibility of eating, and travel being a cause for the permissibility of shortening prayers and breaking the fast, and killing and wounding being causes for retribution (qisas), and adultery, drinking alcohol, theft, and slander being causes for the imposition of those punishments, and similar matters" (1). Examples of the condition include the marriage being a condition for the occurrence of divorce or for the permissibility of reconciling with a divorced woman after three divorces, and the ability to defend oneself being a condition for stoning the adulterer, and purity being a condition for the validity of prayer, and intention being a condition for acts of worship" (2). Examples of the impediment include "the marriage to a sister being an impediment to marrying another sister, and the marriage to a woman being an impediment to marrying her aunt or maternal aunt, and faith being an impediment to retribution for the disbeliever, and disbelief being an impediment to the acceptance of good deeds" (3).
Thus, in this second type, the accountable person can perform these actions which are causes, conditions, or impediments for others, thereby causing a change in the legal ruling. They may perform these actions with the intention of complying with the command of the legislator in them or achieving their legal objectives, or with the intention of changing the rulings. If it is with the intention of changing the rulings, it is termed legal stratagems (hiyal). Therefore, al-Shatibi frequently mentioned legal stratagems when discussing these three aspects of legal rulings: cause, condition, and impediment (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/129.
(2) The same source, 1/130.
(3) The same source, 1/130.
(4) The same source, 1/ Book of Rulings.


[Page 396]

Al-Shatibi said in an additional explanation regarding legal stratagems for the purpose of examining the ruling of Sharia on them: "Before considering their validity or lack thereof, it is necessary to explain this stratagem. Allah, Exalted is He, has mandated certain things and prohibited others, either absolutely without any condition or arrangement based on a cause, such as the obligation of prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, and similar acts, and as He has prohibited adultery, usury, murder, and the like. He has also mandated certain things contingent upon causes. Likewise, He has prohibited others, such as the obligation of zakat, expiations, fulfilling vows, and the right of preemption for a partner, as well as the prohibition of the divorced woman and the benefit from what is usurped or stolen, and similar matters. If a person responsible for fulfilling these obligations causes the removal of that obligation from himself or makes that which is prohibited permissible through some means of causation, so that the obligation appears not to be obligatory or the prohibition appears to be lawful, this causation is called a stratagem (hila) or legal stratagem (tahhil). For instance, if the time for prayer arrives while he is present, and it becomes obligatory for him to pray four units, he may seek to cause the removal of all of them by drinking alcohol or taking a mind-altering medicine until the time passes and he is devoid of his senses, like one who has fainted. Or he may shorten the prayer by initiating a journey to shorten it. Similarly, if someone is overshadowed by the month of Ramadan, he may travel to eat, or if he has wealth sufficient for pilgrimage, he may gift it away or destroy it in some manner to avoid the obligation of pilgrimage. Likewise, if he desires to have intercourse with another's slave girl, he may seize her and claim she has died, then be compensated for her value and have intercourse with her that way, or he may present false witnesses for the marriage of a virgin with her consent, and the judge rules accordingly. Or if he wishes to sell ten dirhams for twenty on credit, he may set the ten dirhams as the price for a garment and then sell the garment back to the original seller for twenty on credit. Or if he intends to kill someone, he may set a prepared trap for him, such as setting a spear or digging a well, and similarly, he may evade the obligation of zakat by gifting away the wealth or destroying it, or by gathering what is scattered or dispersing what is gathered, and so on with other examples of making the unlawful permissible and removing the obligatory."(1)
The ruling of Sharia on stratagems according to al-Shatibi:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/265 - 266.


[Page 397]

Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) held that legal stratagems (hiyal) in religion are generally not permissible, and this means that there are very few cases in which legal stratagems are allowed. Therefore, it is necessary to have a criterion to determine the cases in which legal stratagems are permissible. Legal stratagems are actions undertaken by a legally responsible person with the intention of changing a legal ruling, which contradicts the intention of the Lawgiver. So, what are the cases in which this contradiction is valid? Al-Shatibi's answer is that if this contradiction is intended to oppose the objectives of the Lawgiver, then it is prohibited. However, if this contradiction is intended to preserve the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), then it is permissible.
He said: "The legal ruses (hiyal) in religion in the mentioned sense are not generally permissible"(1). It has been previously stated that legal ruses can occur in causes, conditions, and impediments. An example of this in causes is as he said: "In the school, if someone swears by divorce that so-and-so will pay his due by a certain time, then fears breaking his oath due to non-payment, he may divorce his wife until the time elapses and the oath is broken, and he is not considered to have a wife, as the breaking of the oath does not apply to him, even though his intention is blameworthy and his action is blameworthy because he has resorted to a ruse that invalidated a right. Thus, the violation is prohibited even if it resulted in the avoidance of breaking the oath"(2). Another example is: "The ruses of the people of 'aina in making the commodity an intermediary in selling one dinar for two dinars for a deferred payment"(3).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/266.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/170.
(3) The same location.


[Page 398]

Among the examples regarding conditions, he said: "If his action or inaction is intended as a condition to negate the effect of the cause so that no consequence follows from it, then this is an invalid action and a futile endeavor"(1). And he said: "This action renders what has established a cause for a legal ruling, whether for the sake of bringing about a benefit or preventing a harm, as mere play with no ruling or benefit in it. This contradicts what has been established in the principle of interests (masalih) that they are taken into account in rulings, and it is also contrary to the intention of the Legislator (Shari') in that when the cause has been established and exists, it becomes a legal requirement for its effect, but it is contingent upon the fulfillment of a condition that completes the cause. Thus, this actor or one who refrains, intending to negate the ruling of the cause, is aiming to oppose the Legislator in establishing a cause. It has become clear that opposing the intention of the Legislator is invalid, so this action is void"(2).
Accordingly, if the accountable person (mukallaf) performs an action with the intention of nullifying a ruling, then their action is blameworthy because it opposes the intent of the Lawgiver. However, if they perform it for a reason related to lawful benefit (manfa'a mashru'a), then it is permissible even if it results in nullifying a cause or changing a ruling, and this does not fall under legal tricks (hiyal) at all.
He said in response to those who claim that it is permissible to use legal tricks, such as spending all or part of one's wealth before the due date to avoid the obligation of zakat: "This reasoning only applies if one does not intend to negate the ruling of the cause; however, if the intention is to do so, it is an invalid reasoning because the Sharia has definitively annulled it"(3). He then said: "This is only because he has introduced a condition or removed a condition that negates what the first cause necessitated; likewise, the one who spends his due amount with the intention of negating what is required of him in terms of obligatory payment"(4). He then said: "Thus, bringing about conditions or removing them with that intention is what is prohibited, and if it is prohibited, it contradicts the intention of the Lawgiver, and therefore it is invalid"(5).
