(1) The same source, 2/192.
(2) The same source, 2/193, and see: al-Muwafaqat, vol. 1, issues 11, 12, 13, 14 from the discussion on causes in the second section of the book of rulings.
(3) The same source, 1/193.
(4) The same source, 1/194.
(5) The same place.


[Page 399]

One of the examples of a barrier is a man who has the minimum threshold for zakat but is in debt; the debt prevents him from fulfilling his zakat obligation. If he incurred the debt out of necessity, there is no issue with that. However, if he took on debt to avoid the obligation of zakat, this is an incorrect action. He said: "And if it is the second case, which is that he does it, for example, as a means of preventing the effect of the cause that necessitates that what is required does not occur, then this is an incorrect action." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/201.


[Page 400]

This is al-Shatibi's position on legal tricks (hiyal), which is that they are not permissible based on the fact that they contradict the intent of the Legislator. As for his statement: "not permissible in general," it means that there are cases in which legal tricks are permissible. The decisive factor in this is the intention of the obligated person; if their intention in lifting or changing the ruling contradicts the intent of the Legislator, then it is a blameworthy trick, but if their intention in the trick, that is, in changing the ruling, preserves the intent of the Legislator, then it is a permissible trick. An example of a permissible trick according to him is a believer uttering a word of disbelief under compulsion with the intention of preserving their life. He says: "If this is established, then the tricks that have been previously invalidated, condemned, and prohibited are those that undermine a legal foundation and contradict a legal interest. If we assume that the trick does not undermine a legal foundation nor contradict a legal interest recognized by the Sharia, then it is not included in the prohibition and is not invalid" (1). This is the criterion or principle for him regarding the permissibility or invalidity of tricks. Based on this, tricks in terms of their ruling are divided into three categories. He said: "The matter regarding them is that they are of three categories: the first is unanimously agreed upon as invalid, such as the tricks of hypocrites and show-offs; the second is unanimously agreed upon as permissible, such as uttering a word of disbelief under compulsion, for the ratio of trickery in preserving blood with the first intention without believing in its implications is like the ratio of trickery with the word of Islam in preserving blood with the first intention as well. However, the latter is permitted due to being a worldly interest with no inherent corruption either in this world or the Hereafter, unlike the former, which is not permitted due to being an inherent corruption in the Hereafter. Worldly interests and corruptions in the Hereafter are prioritized in consideration over worldly interests and corruptions by consensus, as it is not valid to consider a worldly interest that undermines the interests of the Hereafter. It is known that what undermines the interests of the Hereafter is not in accordance with the intent of the Legislator, thus it is invalid. This is why there has come condemnation of hypocrisy and its people as it has. And likewise, all that follows this reasoning. Both categories reach the level of certainty.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/270.


[Page 401]

As for the third, it is the place of ambiguity and confusion, and the views of the scholars have diverged regarding it, as there has not been a clear, definitive evidence to establish its connection to either the first or second category. Nor has a purpose been clarified by the legislator that is agreed upon as intended, nor has it been shown that it contradicts the public interest (maslaha) for which the Sharia was established concerning the specific issue at hand. Thus, this category has become a subject of dispute among the disputants, with some testifying that it does not contradict the public interest, making the trickery permissible, while others argue that it contradicts the public interest, rendering the trickery impermissible. It cannot be said that one who permits trickery in some issues acknowledges that it contradicts the intention of the legislator; rather, they permit it based on their understanding of his intention, and that their issue falls under the category of permissible trickery that the legislator intended" (1).
It is well known that the opinion of permitting trickery is attributed to the Hanafis. Therefore, al-Shatibi's division of trickery into three categories serves as a basis for reconciling the disagreement regarding the ruling on trickery to an agreement, which is the agreement on considering the principle or rule that the ruling on trickery depends on whether it undermines a legal principle or contradicts a legal interest or not. The issues of trickery that have caused disagreement revert to this principle. He mentioned two examples of these issues. The first is the marriage in which trickery is employed to make permissible the divorced woman for her husband after three divorces. The second is the sales of deferred payments where trickery is used to sell one dirham for two dirhams on credit. He mentioned the arguments of those who permit these tricks and the arguments of those who prohibit them. He clarified while explaining the two opinions that they revert to the pursuit of aligning with the intention of the legislator and not contradicting it, as well as aligning with the legal interests that the Sharia has recognized and not contradicting them. He then said: "Let us suffice with these two examples, for they are among the most famous issues in the realm of trickery, and the reasoning applied to them can be applied to other matters" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/270 - 271.
(2) The same source, 2/273. See also 2/270 - 273.


[Page 402]

It is worth mentioning here that the issues of legal tricks (hiyal) intertwine with the issues of legal means (dhara'i) since the trick itself is a means. Just as al-Shatibi categorized legal tricks into three types, the means are also categorized into three types. He said while discussing the tricks whose rulings are disputed: "The statement of the one who says that this is based on the principle of the means is not beneficial here, for the means are of three types: some of which are agreed upon to be prohibited ... some of which are not agreed upon to be prohibited ... and some of which are disputed" (1).
Furthermore, the principle regarding the ruling on tricks is based on the original outcomes of actions. He said: "Among them (2) is the principle of tricks, for its well-known reality is the presentation of an action that appears permissible to nullify a legal ruling and to superficially transform it into another ruling, so the outcome of the action here is a breach of the principles of the Sharia in reality" (3). He then said: "But this is on the condition of intending to nullify the legal rulings, and those who permit tricks, like Abu Hanifa, also consider the outcome" (4).
He then said: "But this is on the condition that one does not intend to nullify the ruling, for this specific intention is prohibited as it is defiance against the legislator, just as if one refrains from paying zakat. Abu Hanifa does not disagree that the intention to explicitly nullify the rulings is clearly prohibited. As for nullifying them implicitly, that is not the case; otherwise, gifting would be prohibited at the end of the year altogether, and no one among them would say this. Therefore, they agreed on the prohibition of intending through faith, prayer, and others merely to secure oneself and wealth, like the hypocrites and the show-offs, and the like. Thus, it becomes clear that trickery regarding legal rulings is generally invalid when considering the outcome" (5).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/273.
(2) That is: and among the principles based on the original outcomes of actions.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/114.
(4) The same location.
(5) The same location.


[Page 403]

He said: "Similarly, the same applies to legal tricks (hiyal) according to those who permit them unconditionally, for they base their allowance on the belief that the legislator (al-shari) has an intention in bringing about benefits (masalih) and preventing harms (mafasid). Indeed, the Sharia was established for this purpose. For example, if the marriage of the one who makes permissible (muhallil) is validated, it is validated on the assumption that it is likely that the intention of the legislator is to permit the attainment of the benefit of the two spouses in it, and likewise for other issues, as evidenced by the validity of pronouncing the word of disbelief (kufr) out of fear of killing or torture and in other general and specific benefits. It is not possible to establish a proof in the Sharia that invalidates every legal trick, just as there is no proof that validates every legal trick. Rather, only those that oppose the intention of the legislator are invalidated, and this is agreed upon by all the people of Islam, while there is disagreement in the issues where the evidences conflict."(1)
The ruling on what is based on legal tricks:
If what we have explained is the ruling on legal tricks, what is the ruling on what results from legal tricks in this world? Al-Shatibi mentions that the practice of legal tricks is of two types: either it is considered existent and results follow from it, or it is considered non-existent. If its existence is acknowledged, there is a disagreement on the matter. However, if it is deemed non-existent, nothing that the obligated person intends will result from it. He says: "The ruling that the cause necessitated remains as it was before this action, and the action is null and void, of no benefit and has no ruling, such as when one gifts property before a year to someone who has persuaded him to return it to him after the year as a gift or otherwise. And like the one who gathers the separated (things) until the messenger comes, then it is returned to separation, or the one who separates the gathered (things) likewise, then it is returned to what it was."(2) Thus, the action that is a legal trick in this case is considered as non-existent or not realized. However, if the action is deemed existent, there are three opinions on the matter:
__________
(1) The same source, 2/234.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/194.


[Page 404]

The first: It is that the action is invalid because it contradicts the intention of the legislator, so its effects do not follow from it, and it is akin to what is considered non-existent in terms of its effects. The difference between them is that there was no agreement on the return of the gift, or it did not revert to the gathering after separation or to the separation after gathering. He said: "The intention in it has become non-legitimate, so the action in it is contrary to the intention of the legislator, and it is in the ruling of what has not been acted upon, and it is united with the first category(1) in ruling, so no ruling follows from this action. An example of this is if one spends the nisab before the year in its benefits or gifts it in a gift that he does not return, or gathers the separated or separates the gathered, all with the intention of evading zakat, but he did not return to what he was before the year."(2) Then he said: "So it is like the nonexistent, invalid, and it is joined with the first category."(3)
The second: It is that this action with this intention is non-legitimate and involves disobedience, yet its effects do follow. So the one intending to travel for the purpose of breaking the fast and shortening the prayer achieves that, and the marriage of the divorced woman three times with the intention of making her lawful for her ex-husband is valid by her divorce. He said: "And upon this principle is based the validity of what al-Lakhmi says regarding the one who donates part of his wealth to exempt himself from zakat, or travels in Ramadan with the intention of breaking the fast, or delays a prayer that is due from its preferred time to pray it in travel as two rak'ahs. Or a woman delays a prayer after its time has entered in the hope that she will menstruate so that it is lifted from her. He said: All of this is disliked, and it is not obligatory upon this in travel to fast nor to pray four rak'ahs, nor for the menstruating woman to make up her prayer."(4)
__________
(1) The first category is the one mentioned above where the action is considered as if it does not exist.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/195.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 1/196.


[Page 405]

The third: differentiating between the rights of Allah and the rights of human beings. The rights of human beings refer to the rights of the servant himself who performs the action that is a means. The effects of the action are based on whether it is a right of the servant. Its effects are nullified if it is a right of Allah. An example of the right of the servant is traveling to shorten prayers or to break the fast. An example of the right of Allah is the distinction between the community and the gathering of those who are separated in zakat. He said: "And the third is to differentiate between the rights of Allah, Exalted is He, and the rights of human beings"(1). However, if both rights are combined in one action, the right of Allah, Exalted is He, and the right of the servant, then the matter becomes one of consideration and ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) to favor one of the two sides, and the ruling will be for the dominant side according to the jurist. He said: "And what remains is that if both rights are combined, it is a matter of consideration and ijtihad to favor one of the two sides according to what appears to the jurist, and Allah knows best"(2).
The right of Allah and the right of the servant:
These two expressions are used to refer to what the obligated person has no choice in, which is the right of Allah, and to what they have a choice in, which is the right of the servant.
The meaning of the right of the servant is that he is legally free to either claim his right or to waive it. As for the right of Allah, the servant does not have the authority to waive it. The right of Allah also includes the rights of others among the servants, so the servant cannot waive the rights of others. Al-Shatibi said: "Everything that pertains to the rights of Allah does not allow for any choice on the part of the obligated person in any case, whereas what pertains to the right of the servant in himself allows him the choice. As for the rights of Allah, the evidence that they are not waived and do not revert to the choice of the obligated person is abundant, and the most prominent of it is the complete induction in the provisions of the Sharia and its sources, such as purification in its various forms, prayer, zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, enjoining good, and forbidding evil, the highest of which is jihad, as well as the related expiations, transactions, eating, drinking, clothing, and other acts of worship and customs that establish the right of Allah or the right of others among the servants. Likewise, all offenses are on this scale; it is not permissible to waive the right of Allah in them at all."(3)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/196.
(2) The same source, 1/196.
(3) The same source, 2/262.


[Page 406]

The right of the servant is not an inherent right, but rather it is by the decree of Allah - Exalted is He - that this right exists. Likewise, the right of the servant contains a right of Allah. Al-Shatibi said: "From here, the scholars say that some obligations are rights of Allah alone, which pertain to worship, and some are rights of the servant. They say regarding the latter that it also contains a right of Allah, as in the case of a murderer who is pardoned; he is to be struck one hundred times and imprisoned for a year"(1). He then said: "Thus, every obligation has become a right of Allah; what is for Allah is for Him, and what is for the servant returns to Allah in terms of Allah's right in it and in terms of the servant's right being one of Allah's rights, since it is within Allah's authority not to grant the servant any right at all"(2).
Accordingly, the right of the servant is not absolute, for every obligation therein is a right of Allah.
The rights of Allah are of two types. The first: what is a right of Allah that is purely His, which cannot be waived, such as acts of worship. The second: the rights of others, which the servant cannot waive on behalf of others; however, that other person has the right to waive their own right. Unlike the acts of worship from the first category, which cannot be waived. The rights of others include sales, exchanges, and expenditures, so the servant must fulfill the right that is owed to the one who has it. If that latter person waives their right, then that is their choice.
The right of others over the servant is one of the rights of other servants, therefore it is not absolute, and it includes a right of Allah. If the other party waives their right, it is nullified, and the right of Allah remains. This is "as in the case of a murderer who commits intentional killing; if he is pardoned, he is struck with a hundred lashes and imprisoned for a year, and in the case of a murderer by treachery, there is no pardon for him. And in the punishments (hudud), if they reach the ruler regarding matters other than retribution, such as slander and theft, there is no pardon in them even if the one entitled to the right forgives"(3).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/219.
(2) The same source, 2/219.
(3) The same place.


[Page 407]

The right of the servant manifests in two aspects. The first: it includes the right of Allah and the right of the servant, but the right of the servant is predominant. This is what Allah has granted the servant in terms of the right of choice, as in his choice of types of consumables, such as food, drinks, clothing, and other things that are lawful for him, as well as in types of sales, transactions, and claims to rights. He has the right to waive them, to exchange them, and to dispose of what is in his possession without restriction, provided that his actions align with the good customs he is accustomed to (1). However, it is not permissible to forfeit the right of Allah; thus, it is not valid for the accountable person to consume what Allah has prohibited of foods, drinks, or clothing, nor to engage in what Allah, Exalted is He, has forbidden in transactions or in what he possesses.
The second: it includes the right of Allah and the right of the servant, but the right of Allah is predominant, yet the right of Allah has been waived, leaving only the right that Allah has granted to the servant. An example of this is the preservation of life and intellect, among other rights, which are rights of Allah over the servants and not rights of the servants over one another. The evidence for this is that Allah has not left this to their choice. If Allah, Exalted is He, completes a servant's life, body, and intellect, it is not valid for the servant to forfeit them. Unless the accountable person is afflicted with something of that nature without any fault or cause of his own, and as a result, he loses his life, intellect, or a member of his body, then the right of the servant is established, since the right of Allah has lapsed, as what has occurred cannot be reversed. What remains of the right of the servant is a right against others, like a debt among debts, which he may choose to collect or to forgo (2). An example of this is retribution (qisas) and blood money (diya), which serve as compensation for what the victim has lost in terms of his own interests or body. The right of Allah has lapsed, and there is no compensation for it, just as what has occurred that can be remedied, such as illnesses, if seeking medical treatment is not obligatory.
Here, the right of Allah, Exalted is He, has lapsed because it cannot be fulfilled, and the right of the servant remains, which the Sharia has granted him the right to collect or to waive.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/264.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/263.


[Page 408]

Based on the methodology of al-Shatibi, which holds that all obligations are for the benefit of the servants in this world or the Hereafter, every obligation contains a right for the servants either immediately or eventually. He said: "Just as every legal ruling contains a right for the servants either immediately or eventually, based on the premise that the Sharia was established for the interests of the servants" (1). As for what pertains to the servant from worldly benefits, it falls under the servant's right. And what pertains to him in the Hereafter is the right of Allah. He said: "The right of the servant is what pertains to his interests in this world; if it is from the interests of the Hereafter, it is included among what is referred to as the right of Allah" (2). The right of the servant or his shares that return to him due to the right of Allah are what are called the subsidiary objectives (maqasid al-tabi'a), and it is permissible for the servant to waive his right, such as waiving his right to inheritance or to the spoils of jihad or to blood money (diya) or retribution (qisas), or for a woman to waive her right to maintenance and similar matters.
Based on the above, actions concerning the right of Allah and the right of the servant fall into three categories. Al-Shatibi says: "Actions concerning the right of Allah and the right of the human being are three categories: the first is what is purely the right of Allah, such as acts of worship, and its essence is devotion as previously mentioned; if the action conforms to the command, it is valid, otherwise it is not" (3). He then says: "The second is what includes both the right of Allah and the right of the servant, with the right of Allah being predominant, and its ruling reverts to the first" (4), because if the right of the servant is rendered legally insignificant, it is like that which is not considered; for if it were considered, it would be the one that is considered, and the assumption is the opposite, such as in the case of killing oneself, as the servant has no choice in surrendering himself to be killed without necessity, such as during trials and the like" (5). He then says: "The third is what both rights share, with the right of the servant being predominant" (6).
The effect of intention in what is the right of Allah or the right of the servant:
__________
(1) The same source, 2/221.
(2) The same location.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/221.
(4) That is, it is considered a right of Allah; if the action conforms to the command, it is valid, otherwise it is not.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/222.
(6) The same source, 2/223.


[Page 409]

This has been detailed in the preceding part of this chapter, but I mention it here in terms of the division of actions into rights of Allah and rights of the servant.

What pertains to the obligations that are a right of Allah or where Allah's right is predominant must be performed with intention, that is, with the aim of obedience and compliance. What pertains to the rights of the servant, where the servant's right is predominant, can be valid without intention; however, if it is done without intention, there is no reward for it, and if done with intention, there is a reward. Thus, the obligated person has performed the action for the sake of Allah's right therein. Al-Shatibi said: "It has been established that every obligation is not devoid of worship, and if it is not devoid, it requires intention, like purifications and other acts of worship. However, the obligations that involve the right of the servant include some that are valid without intention, which we understand from the legislator as prioritizing the servant's side, such as returning deposits, wrongful gains, and obligatory expenditures. Among them are those that are not valid except with intention, which we understand to prioritize Allah's right, such as zakat, sacrifices, and hunting. Those that are valid without intention, if done without intention, will not be rewarded; if done with the intention of compliance, they will be rewarded. Likewise, abstentions, if left with intention. This is agreed upon."(1) He said: "What predominates in the direction of the servant, the servant's right is obtained without intention, so the action here is valid without intention and is not worship of Allah. If the direction of the command is observed, then from that direction it is worship, so intention is necessary, meaning it does not become worship except by intention; it is not that intention is obligatory or required, but rather that the intention in compliance makes it worship, as if one lends in compliance with the command to facilitate for the Muslim or if one lends for a worldly purpose, as well as in buying, selling, eating, drinking, marriage, divorce, and others."(2)

Chapter Seven
The Methodology of Al-Shatibi in Understanding the Sharia
It contains an introduction and three sections:

Section One: The Methodology of Al-Shatibi in Understanding the Sharia.
Section Two: The Methodology of Al-Shatibi in Understanding the Quran.
Section Three: The Methodology of Al-Shatibi in Understanding the Sunnah.

Chapter Seven
The Methodology of Al-Shatibi in Understanding the Sharia

Introduction:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 2/220.
(2) The same source.


[Page 410]

The discussion of al-Shatibi's methodology in understanding the Sharia is a discussion about his innovations in this regard, and what he has raised and highlighted that distinguishes him from his predecessors among the imams of usul (principles) in the rules and foundations of understanding and deduction.
The sources of legislation are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas), and the methodology of understanding the Sharia is how to comprehend what these sources have brought. The rules that are relied upon for this purpose include those that relate to all these sources collectively, as well as those that pertain to each of them individually.
In this chapter, al-Shatibi's methodology in this matter will be clarified in three sections. The first addresses the general rules in this regard, that is, those that pertain to all sources. The second discusses the rules for understanding the Qur'an, while the third addresses the rules for understanding the Sunnah.
As for consensus and analogy, they refer back to the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and therefore al-Shatibi did not examine them separately, but rather alluded to them in scattered references throughout his book. He said: "The book of legal proofs: and the consideration of them in general, and concerning each one of them in detail, which are the Book and the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy" (1). He also said: "The second part: concerning the proofs in detail, which are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and opinion. And since the Book and the Sunnah are the foundation for everything else, we have limited our consideration to them" (2).
The rules that al-Shatibi discusses regarding the sources of legislation in general are rules that pertain to the four sources, and those that relate to the Qur'an and the Sunnah are built upon and detailed from them. Therefore, I have titled the first section "al-Shatibi's Methodology in Understanding the Sharia," which is the title of the chapter itself. The second section is titled "al-Shatibi's Methodology in Understanding the Qur'an," and the third section is titled "al-Shatibi's Methodology in Understanding the Sunnah."

The first section
Al-Shatibi's Methodology in Understanding the Sharia

The subject of this section:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/2.
(2) The same source, 3/200.


[Page 411]

It has been mentioned in the introduction to this chapter that this discussion addresses the rules related to sources of legislation in general. That is, it pertains to all of them, and these rules are divided into two categories: the first relates to how to implement the legal texts from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, meaning how to apply the meanings of the texts to events and actions, and the same applies to how to implement the implications of analogy (qiyas) and what has been agreed upon. The second relates to the subsequent attributes of the texts in terms of definiteness and similarity, abrogation (naskh), generality and specification, commands and prohibitions, general and specific, and unrestricted and restricted. The first pertains to how to derive meanings, which are both general and specific meanings. The second pertains to how to determine these meanings, as it is influenced by similarity, ambiguity, abrogation, specification, or restriction.
It should be noted that the discussion of these two categories here is only in relation to al-Shatibi's methodology specifically, that is, in terms of its novelty as a methodological approach.
Al-Shatibi's perspective on the implications of legal texts:
Al-Shatibi believes that the implication of individual texts on meanings is a probabilistic implication. He denies the existence of a definitive implication of the text on the meaning. As for the implication of rulings on their objectives or purposes, al-Shatibi completely denies considering them if reliance is placed on individual rulings.
His denial of definitive implication is indicated by his statement: "The relied-upon in the primary intention is the legal evidence, and the existence of definiteness in it based on the commonly known usage is nonexistent, or extremely rare, I mean in individual evidences. If they are from the reports of individuals, then their failure to provide definiteness is evident. And if they are mutawatir (consecutively reported), then their provision of definiteness is contingent upon premises, all or most of which are probabilistic. What is contingent upon the probabilistic must be probabilistic, as it depends on the transmission of languages, grammatical opinions, the absence of ambiguity, the absence of metaphor, legal or customary transmission, implicitness, specification of the general, restriction of the unrestricted, the absence of abrogation, precedence and postponement, and rational opposition. The provision of definiteness while considering these matters is impossible." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/13. He has another similar text. See: 2/32.


[Page 412]

And what is not a definitive meaning cannot be applied. Al-Shatibi stipulates that for a proof to be applied, it must be definitive or refer to a definitive meaning (1). He says: "Every legal proof is either definitive or speculative. If it is definitive, there is no doubt in considering it, such as the proofs for the obligation of purification from ritual impurity, prayer, almsgiving, fasting, pilgrimage, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, unity of the community, justice, and similar matters. If it is speculative, it is either based on a definitive origin or not. If it is based on a definitive origin, it is also considered valid; if it is not, one must be cautious with it, and it is not correct to categorically accept it. However, it is of two types: one that opposes an origin, and one that neither opposes nor agrees with it. Thus, all of them fall into four categories. As for the first, it does not require explanation, while the second, which refers to a definitive origin, is also clearly applicable, and this applies to most reports of the individual narrators, as they clarify the Book" (2). He then says: "As for the third, which opposes a definitive origin and is not supported by a definitive origin, it is rejected without doubt. Two points serve as evidence for this: the first is that it contradicts the principles of the Sharia, and what contradicts the principles of the Sharia cannot be valid because it does not belong to it, and what does not belong to it cannot be considered part of it. The second is that it has no evidence supporting its validity, and what is like that is disregarded" (3). Let us pay attention here to the second point in the evidence for rejection. It is that it has no evidence supporting its validity. This indicates something new according to Al-Shatibi, which is that the legal meaning or legal proof requires a meaning that supports it in order to be accepted. It becomes clear in the context of the entire text that the supporting evidence must be a definitive meaning. He then says: "As for the fourth, which is speculative and neither supported by a definitive origin nor opposes a definitive origin, it is subject to consideration. Its category is that of the strange analogy. It may be said that it is not accepted because it establishes a law that is not consistent with what has been established in its like."
__________
(1) This has been clarified earlier. See: the first section of the third chapter.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/7.
(3) The same source, 3/8.


[Page 413]

And induction indicates that it is nonexistent, and these two points weaken the reliance on it absolutely, as it is in a state of doubt, thus there remains no presumption of its establishment. This is because it does not have a decisive original that opposes the principles of the Sharia, as the lack of agreement constitutes a violation, and everything that contradicts a decisive principle is rejected; thus, this is rejected (1). Let us examine this text. The legal evidence is considered contradictory, and one cannot categorically state its acceptance even if it does not oppose a decisive principle, and the reason for this is that it is not supported by a decisive original, even though this evidence is a legal text from the Qur'an or the Sunnah. Nevertheless, he stated that it is in a state of consideration.
He continues: "One may argue that the application of conjecture in general is established in the details of the Sharia, and this is one of its instances, and although it does not conform to a principle, there is no contradiction in it either, for if the lack of agreement supports rejection, the lack of contradiction supports acceptance, and they oppose each other. The principle of working with conjecture is acknowledged. An example of this is found in the hadith where he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'The killer does not inherit' (2). Scholars have applied the appropriate and unusual in the chapters of analogy. Even if it is rare in its category, that does not harm if the evidence indicates its validity" (3).
This text is significant in illustrating al-Shatibi's perspective on legal texts and how to derive meanings from them. He does not accept the meaning unless it is supported by a decisive meaning or falls under it. As for his statement: "One may argue that the application of conjecture is generally established," this is not his opinion, and thus he concluded the sentence with: "And although this is rare in its category, that does not harm if the evidence indicates its validity." In addition to his previous statement: "And induction indicates that it is nonexistent."
__________
(1) The same source, 3/12.
(2) Previously cited.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/12.


[Page 414]

It should be noted that he cites the hadith: "The killer does not inherit." The disagreement among the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) is regarding the consideration of the meaning of acting contrary to the intended purpose that the hadith supports. This meaning is not among the implications of the text of the hadith, while al-Shatibi discusses the application of the hadith itself, and his intent is that the idea of acting contrary to the intended purpose, if established definitively, would then allow for the application of the hadith because it would then refer back to a definitive meaning. We also observe that he considers this hadith to be an appropriate oddity, and we have previously explained that the scholars of usul who reason based on oddities regard the oddity as a description that is observed in a single ruling and does not have a witness, or has only one witness, and the term witness means a ruling that aligns with the meaning(1). Here, he has made the hadith odd, and it requires a definitive witness, meaning that the meaning of acting contrary to the intended purpose must be established definitively. Therefore, we found him in another place mentioning the principle of acting contrary to the intended purpose as a question with a tendency to accept it, as it has partial witnesses available to it, but it does not have the inductive reasoning that leads to certainty. He says: "But the question remains whether the causation should be considered as being contrary to the intention of the legislator in such a way that it does not result in what the cause intended, thus establishing the principle of acting contrary to the intended purpose, and the ruling is applied based on it if that intended purpose is determined, which is the implication of the hadith regarding the disinheritance of the killer, and the implication of the jurisprudence in the hadith prohibiting the gathering of the dispersed and the dispersing of the gathered out of fear of charity. Likewise, the inheritance of the divorced woman during illness, or the perpetuation of prohibition on one who marries during the waiting period, and many similar cases"(2). If acting contrary to the intended purpose were a universal principle that supports the meaning of the hadith "The killer does not inherit," then al-Shatibi's citation of the hadith as an example of the fourth category that does not have a universal principle supporting it would not be valid.
__________
(1) See: Chapter One, p. 85.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/184.


[Page 415]

What confirms what we have mentioned is his saying: "The report of an individual (khabar al-wahid) is acceptable in practice if it is based on an established principle; otherwise, one should refrain from acting upon it. Its being based on an established principle refers to it being a particular under a general Qur'anic meaning" (1). His statement about refraining means not applying the hadith and not rejecting it, as there may be an inductive reasoning that makes its meaning refer back to a definitive meaning. His saying: "refers to it being a particular under a general Qur'anic meaning" means the Sunnah clarifying the Book, and any meaning that has no basis in the Book is not taken (2). However, al-Shatibi's intent goes further than that, as he requires that any meaning of any text must refer back to a definitive meaning, even if it is a Qur'anic text.
Therefore, one should note his statement above: "under a general Qur'anic meaning." Not: "under a Qur'anic meaning." If we combine the issues that al-Shatibi asserts, which are that the meaning must be general, that individual pieces of evidence do not provide certainty, including the texts of the Qur'an, while knowing that all Qur'anic texts must be acted upon, a question arises: how is certainty established regarding the meanings of the Qur'an? This issue will be addressed in the next section - if Allah wills - which is al-Shatibi's methodology in understanding the Qur'an. The aim here is to establish al-Shatibi's position on the implications of texts regarding their meanings, which is that they are not taken or considered unless they refer back to a definitive meaning. These meanings are particulars, as are the meanings of rulings, which are the wisdoms. They are particulars, but not considering them does not mean rejecting them unless they oppose a definitive or general principle. If they do not oppose a general principle, there may be many particulars that agree with them and support them in meaning, thus making the meaning a definitive principle, and these particulars become branches referring back to it.
Previously, he mentioned that the characteristic of his book (al-Muwafaqat) is how to capture the universals from the particulars (3).
Both particulars and universals must be acted upon:
__________
(1) The same source, 4/5.
(2) Al-Shatibi's view that the Sunnah does not independently legislate will be clarified later.
(3) See: the first section of the third chapter. And see: al-Muwafaqat, 4/194.


[Page 416]

The derivation of legal rulings requires the application of both particulars and universals together, and although the universals are established through the induction of particulars, it is not correct to apply the universal while neglecting the particular. For example: "If it is known that the preservation of necessities is considered, but knowledge of the specific means of preservation has not been attained, then there are various ways of preservation that the intellect may grasp or may not grasp, and if it does grasp them, it may do so in relation to one condition rather than another or one time rather than another" (1). An example of this is that knowledge of the principle of preserving wealth, for instance, is not sufficient to clarify the ruling on whether the thief should be imprisoned, executed, have a hand cut off, or something else, all of which are consistent with the principle, and it is not sufficient to distinguish between the deceiver, the usurper, and the thief in terms of ruling. Knowledge of particulars requires knowledge of universals for the validity of derivation, as particulars can have multiple meanings, and the correct meaning is the one that refers back to a universal, and if it contradicts a universal, it has contradicted a definitive one, which is not valid, and the negation of universals is also a negation of particulars.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/5.


[Page 417]

Al-Shatibi says: "If that is the case, and the particulars (1) are the foundations of the Sharia, then what is beneath them is derived from those general foundations, just as particulars relate to their generals in every type of existing thing. Therefore, it is necessary to consider those particulars in light of these generals when applying the specific evidences from the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy, for it is impossible for those particulars to be independent of their generals. Thus, one who takes a text, for example, in a particular while disregarding its general has erred, and just as one who takes it for a particular while disregarding its general is mistaken, so too is one who takes the general while disregarding its particulars. The explanation of this is that acquiring knowledge of the general is only through the presentation of particulars and their examination. The general, in its essence, is not known to us before knowledge of the particulars, and it does not exist in the external world; rather, it is contained within the particulars as established in the rational sciences. Therefore, to stand with the general while disregarding the particular is to stand with something that has not yet been known without knowledge of the particular. The particular is the manifestation of knowledge of it. Furthermore, the particular is not designated as a particular except because the general is fully realized in it and is its basis. Thus, disregarding the particular as such is, in reality, disregarding the general itself, and that is a contradiction" (2). For the sake of preserving life, for example, which is a general principle, it is necessary to apply the particulars that indicate the permissibility of consuming pork or carrion in cases of necessity, or uttering disbelief under coercive duress, and the permissibility of redeeming one's life with wealth, and the prohibition of redeeming it with the life of another Muslim or by revealing secrets and plans that expose Muslims to defeat and extermination.
__________
(1) The designation of particulars as foundations applies to what is particular in relation, but it is a general principle, such as the obligation of prayer, zakat, and the other five foundational rules in religion. All of these, according to al-Shatibi, are definitive foundations, but they are particular in relation to the principle of preserving religion, and what is beneath them are the particulars that are the sources of these rules.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/3.


[Page 418]

Thus, the universals cannot do without the particulars, and likewise, the particulars cannot do without the universals. For example, His saying, Exalted is He: {Say, "Be stones or iron"} (1), the verse. The text allows for meanings, including obligation and despair, but the prohibition of imposing obligations that cannot be borne or are impossible is a universal principle. To interpret the text as an obligation would contradict the universal, so it is necessary to apply the universal and interpret the text in another way, which is despair. Similarly, in His saying, Exalted is He: {Then bring a surah like it} (2), the verse. The universal principle, which is the prohibition of imposing what cannot be borne, must be preserved, so the meaning shifts from obligation to the challenge intended to induce incapacity. The same can be said for His saying, Exalted is He: {Taste, indeed you are the honored, the noble} (3), where the meaning shifts from obligation or otherwise to humiliation. In His saying, Exalted is He: {And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers} (4), the text allows for the meaning of reporting and the meaning of obligation, but the universal principle, which is the necessity of the truth of the reporter, shifts the meaning from reporting to obligation, which is prohibition. This is the meaning of al-Shatibi's statement: "It is necessary to consider those particulars in light of these universals when applying the specific evidences from the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy."
The universal is not violated by the opposition of individual particulars to it:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Isra, 50.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 23.
(3) Surah Ad-Dukhan, 49.
(4) Surah An-Nisa, 141.


[Page 419]

This is an important issue in al-Shatibi's methodology, which is that if a meaning is established as a universal principle and then there are particular instances that contradict it, does this invalidate the entire induction, thereby nullifying the universal principle? This is similar to cases of retribution (qisas) or in jihad, and the expenditure of funds in that context, as well as the rulings on spoils and gains, while it is known that among the necessities are the preservation of life and the preservation of wealth. Al-Shatibi states that this does not undermine the principle because it has been established universally and definitively. He says: "These three universals, if they have been legislated for their specific interests, are not negated by the failure of individual particulars. There are examples of this: as for necessities, punishments are legislated for deterrence, even though we find some who are punished but do not desist from what they were punished for" (1). "As for needs, shortening the prayer during travel is legislated for alleviation and to avoid hardship, and the wealthy do not experience hardship, thus shortening is legislated for them. Loans are permitted for the sake of aiding the needy, even though they are also permissible without need. As for enhancements, purification is legislated for cleanliness in general, even though some forms contradict cleanliness, such as tayammum. All of this does not detract from the original permissibility because if the universal principle is established universally, the failure of some particulars to meet the requirements of the universal does not remove it from being universal. Furthermore, the predominant majority is considered in Sharia as a definitive generality because the individual exceptions do not form a universal that opposes this established universal" (2). He then said: "The individual exceptions may be absent due to a ruling outside the requirements of the universal, thus they are not included under it at all, or they may be included but their inclusion is not apparent to us, or they may be included in our view but are opposed by something that is more deserving of consideration. The wealthy may be said to experience hardship, but we do not rule that way due to its obscurity, or we may say regarding punishments that did not deter their subject that the interest is not solely for deterrence" (3). He then said: "In any case, the opposition of particulars does not negate the validity of the establishment of universals for interests" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/35.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/35.


[Page 420]

And if the universal (kulli) is neither annulled nor compromised, is the particular (juz'i) annulled? There is a detailed discussion on this, but in general, it is not annulled because it pertains to another universal principle. Annulment of it would disrupt the universal. He says: "Standing in prayer, for example, and all other concessions that undermine the firm commands and prohibitions are in accordance with the principle of necessities in urgent needs. Similarly, there are exceptions to the prohibitive rules such as 'araya (gifts of fruits), qard (loan), musaqa (sharecropping), salam (forward sale), and the like. If we were to consider all necessities, that would undermine the urgent needs or the necessities as well. However, if we consider the particulars at each level, that would preserve that level and others from the universals, for those three ranks support one another and specify one another" (1).
Thus, al-Shatibi does not see the annulment of either the universal or the particular when a conflict arises, because it is a conflict from one side without the other, or in one situation without another, or in one place without another; it is an apparent conflict. He said: "The universal is considered in its specification of the general particular or its restriction of the absolute and similar cases, such that it does not disrupt the particular at all" (2).
However, if the conflict between the particular and the universal is from every side and there is no way out, the particular must be annulled. He said: "It cannot be said that this is a contradiction because it leads to the particular being disregarded and considered together, for we say that this is from two sides, and because not every particular is considered in every situation" (3).
The definitive and the similar:

(3) The same source, 3/6, and the reader can notice that the contradiction that al-Shatibi attempted to resolve is inevitable, for he had to say that it is possible to disregard the particular. These two principles - for him - cannot coexist or continue together, which are the application of the universals and particulars together and the non-compromise of the universal by the opposition of individual particulars. In cases where the conflict between the universal and the particular does not cease, one of these two principles must be invalidated, and we will discuss this issue in chapter ten.

The purpose of including this research here is to clarify al-Shatibi's methodology in determining the meaning of a legal text when it is ambiguous. Therefore, we will first explain what al-Shatibi means by the definitive (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih).
He says: "The definitive is used in two senses, general and specific. As for the specific, it refers to that which is intended to mean the opposite of the abrogated (mansukh)"(1). He then said: "As for the general, it refers to the clear and evident that does not depend on anything else to clarify its meaning. The ambiguous in the first sense is the abrogated, and in the second sense, it is that which cannot be understood from its wording, whether it can be comprehended through research and contemplation or not"(2).
The intended meaning here is the second, meaning that the definitive is the clear and evident, and the ambiguous is that which cannot be understood from its wording. He said: "When one reflects on this usage, it becomes evident that the abrogated, the ambiguous, the apparent, the general, and the unrestricted are all included under the meaning of the ambiguous, just as the abrogating, what has a fixed ruling, the clarifying, the interpreted, the specified, and the restricted fall under the meaning of the definitive"(3).
Al-Shatibi clarifies that most rulings of the Sharia are definitive. He states that ambiguity is rare, saying: "It is known that ambiguity does occur in legal matters, but the consideration of how much of it exists is whether it is little or much, and what is established is the little, not the much"(4). He also said: "If it were not for the evidence proving that there is ambiguity in it, the statement would not be valid"(5).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/50.
(2) The same source, 3/51.

(5) The same source, 3/52.

Al-Shatibi argues that the ambiguous (mutashabih) in the Sharia is abundant, based on the presence of abrogated (mansukh), ambiguous (mujmal), general (aam), and unrestricted (mutlaq) texts, which frequently occur in the Sharia. He counters this by stating that the abrogating (nasikh) is paired with the abrogated, the clarifying (bayyan) with the ambiguous, the specific (mukhassas) with the general, and the restricted (muqayyad) with the unrestricted; all of this is clarification. He says: "This is indicated by the statement of Ibn Abbas: 'There is no general except that it is specified.' So where is the ambiguity in it when clarification has been achieved? The same applies to other types. It is only considered ambiguous in the absence of clarification" (1). He further states: "If this is established, then clarification is coupled with the clarifier. If the clarifier is taken without clarification, it becomes ambiguous, but it is not inherently ambiguous in the Sharia" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/54.
(2) The same location.


[Page 423]

Al-Shatibi divides the similarity in texts into two categories: real and additional. There is also a third category that does not pertain to the texts but rather to the legal basis (manat). He says: "The similarity that occurs in the Sharia is of two types: one is real and the other is additional, and this pertains to the Sharia itself. There is another type that relates to the legal basis upon which the rulings are applied; the first is what is meant by the verse (1), and its meaning refers to the fact that no way has been made for us to understand its meaning, nor has any evidence been established for what is meant by it" (2). He then said regarding the second type, which is additional: "Its explanation has been established in reality, but the observer has fallen short in their ijtihad (independent reasoning) or has deviated from the path of clarification following their desires, so it is incorrect to attribute the confusion to the evidences; rather, it should be attributed to the observers' shortcomings or ignorance" (3). As for the third category, he said: "The third type of similarity does not return to the evidences but rather to the legal basis of the evidences. The prohibition of eating carrion is clear, and the permission to eat the slaughtered animal is likewise clear. If carrion mixes with the slaughtered animal, confusion arises regarding what is eaten, not regarding the evidence for its permissibility or prohibition" (4).
Similarity does not occur in the general principles (kulliyat) because these are definitive meanings (qat'iyyat) (5).
Examples of real similarity include: "such as the issues of the Ascension (istawa), descent (nuzul), laughter (dhahik), hand (yad), foot (qadam), and similar matters" (6).
Interpretation of the ambiguous:

(1) The verse: { He it is Who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear, they are the foundation of the Book, and others ambiguous. } Surah Al-Imran, 7.

[Page 424]

If the resemblance is real, then it is not correct to interpret it. Seeking its interpretation is the work of those who deviate. However, if it is additional, then it should be interpreted. He says: "Applying interpretation to the ambiguous requires detail; it must either be from the truly ambiguous or from the additional. If it is from the additional, then it is necessary if it is determined by evidence, just as the general is clarified by the specific, the absolute by the restricted, and the necessary by the contingent, and similar cases, because their totality is the definitive, which has been previously explained. As for if it is from the truly ambiguous, then its interpretation is not necessary" (1).
He said: "Moreover, the righteous predecessors among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), the Followers, and those who came after them who followed their example did not address these matters nor spoke about them in a way that necessitates determining an interpretation without evidence, and they are the model and example. To this, the verse indicates this by His saying, Exalted is He: { As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it } (2) the verse" (3). If the ambiguous is something that should be interpreted, meaning its meaning should be specified, then the interpreted meaning has three conditions. He says: "When interpretation is applied to the ambiguous, three characteristics must be considered in the interpreted meaning: it must refer to a correct meaning in consideration, generally agreed upon among the differing parties, and the interpreted term must be capable of it" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/59.
(2) Surah Al-Imran, 7.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 3/59.
(4) The same source, 3/60.


[Page 425]

The first condition relates to what has been previously mentioned, that the legal evidence must be definitive (qat'i) or refer back to something definitive in order for it to be validly applied. Here, it is not required to refer back to something definitive, but rather to a meaning that is valid in consideration. If it refers back to a definitive meaning, there is no doubt that it is valid in consideration. For the interpreted meaning may be potentially acceptable, meaning it does not contradict a principle; if it cannot be validly applied, it cannot be rejected either. Rather, it is subject to induction (istiqra) or the observation of this meaning in other contexts. It is not necessary for it to reach definitiveness in order to be accepted; rather, it must be considered before reaching definitiveness, and this applies to others that share the same meaning, so that the possibility of useful induction for definitiveness is available. As for the third condition, that the interpreted term must be capable of the meaning, this is clear. As for the second condition, that the interpreted meaning must be generally agreed upon among the differing parties, it does not state that there is consensus (ijma), as consensus on one meaning among multiple possible meanings is difficult or rare. Therefore, this condition aims to ensure that the interpreted meaning is not generally dismissed, as this indicates its weakness and that there is a stronger opposing argument(1).
Abrogation (naskh):
It has been mentioned in the definition of the definitive (muhkam) and ambiguous (mutashabih) that the definitive has two meanings: general and specific. It opposes the ambiguous in the general sense and opposes abrogation in the specific sense. Al-Shatibi said in defining abrogation: "They said in the definition of abrogation: It is the lifting of the legal ruling by a later legal evidence"(2).
And just as ambiguity does not occur in general principles, abrogation does not occur in them either. He said: "The general principles of necessities, needs, and enhancements have not been abrogated; rather, abrogation has occurred in specific matters based on the evidence of induction"(3).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/61.
(2) The same source, 3/64.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/70.


[Page 426]

Abrogation (naskh) can only occur in particulars that relate to universals, that is, in branches of law, because if they are not related to universals, then their application has not been established, and what has not been established cannot be subject to abrogation. Likewise, the abrogated (mansukh) in relation to the definitive (muhkam) in Islamic law is few. He said: "For the induction shows that the particular branches in which abrogation and abrogated occurred in relation to what remains definitive are few" (1). It is noted in this text his use of the expression "particular branches."
Just as the abrogated must have been established in the law, so too must the abrogating, and its establishment must relate to a definitive meaning. He said: "If the rulings have been established upon the obligated person, then the claim of abrogation in them can only be made with a verified matter, because their establishment upon the obligated person is first verified, thus lifting them after knowledge of their establishment can only be with a verified knowledge" (2).
Since what was revealed in the law in Mecca consists of universals, and what pertains to branches is few, therefore, in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and istinbat (deduction), there should be a tendency to exclude abrogation regarding what was revealed in Mecca. He then generalized this statement to all rulings, whether they are Meccan or Medinan. He said: "This necessitates that what was among the Meccan rulings claimed to be abrogated should not have that claim accepted except with a decisive proof of abrogation such that it is impossible to reconcile between the two evidences nor to claim definitiveness in both" (3). He then said: "And thus it is said regarding all rulings, whether Meccan or Medinan" (4).
Commands and prohibitions:
__________
(1) The same source, 3/63.
(2) The same source, 3/64.
(3) The same place.
(4) The same place.


[Page 427]

The commands and prohibitions are among the discussions of the Qur'an and the Sunnah. What is meant by discussing them here is to refer to al-Shatibi's methodology in determining the meanings of texts or formulations. A formulation may appear to imply a duty, while its intended meaning is different. It may indicate a command or prohibition, but it is necessary to specify the intended meaning of the command, whether it is obligation, recommendation, or permissibility, and the intended meaning of the prohibition, whether it is prohibition or dislike. Likewise, a term may arise that requires the observer to determine its meaning, whether it is literal or metaphorical, or if it contains an implied meaning or something else. Furthermore, the rulings have objectives, so are these objectives considered in the command and prohibition? Among these indications is what was previously mentioned, especially in the discussion of the intention of the legislator in establishing the Sharia for understanding (1). And there is what will come in the discussion of the principle of blocking the means (2). What we will discuss here is al-Shatibi's general methodology in determining the meanings of the formulations of command and prohibition.
The command necessitates the performance of an action, and the prohibition necessitates refraining from an action, regardless of the intended purpose of the action or the abstention. The action or refraining from it is the primary objective of the legislator in the command and prohibition (3). He said: "The meaning of command and prohibition is the necessity of action and the necessity of abstention. The meaning of necessity is demand, and demand entails a desired outcome, with the intention of achieving that desired outcome, and there is no meaning to demand except this" (4). Until he said: "The command in this is clearer than to require evidence for it" (5).
__________
(1) See: the third discussion of the fourth chapter.
(2) The third discussion of the ninth chapter.
(3) This meaning has been clarified in the first discussion of the fifth chapter. It is the intention of worship and compliance.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/73.
(5) The same location.


[Page 428]

When commands and prohibitions come in a manner that is beyond one's ability, such as His saying, { and do not die except as Muslims } (1), or { say, "Be stones or iron" } (2), or in a way that we know cannot be required in our Sharia, such as His saying, { and whoever wills, let him disbelieve } (3), or { say, "Believe in it or do not believe" } (4), this does not mean the cancellation of obligation or the non-application of texts, or the neglect of forms. Rather, the matter was not an obligation in the first place, and the forms and texts did not imply obligation; rather, they were threats, despair, or impossibility, and this is one of the meanings of the forms themselves. It is a matter of applying both particulars and universals together to determine the intended meaning (5). He said: "As for the matter of impossibility and threat, it is not, in reality, a command, even if it is said to be a command metaphorically; for as previously mentioned, a command, even if metaphorical, necessitates intention, and thus it becomes a command in which the aspect of metaphor can be conceived; otherwise, it is not a command without the intention to bring about what is commanded in any way" (6).
Commands and prohibitions convey their implications, which are the rulings, and the rulings have their objectives, which are the interests (masalih). However, the latter can only occur within the execution of what is requested to be executed and the abstention from what is requested to be abstained from. Indeed, the legal ruling concerning its intended purpose is like the original concerning the branch. It is not correct for the branch to invalidate the original.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Imran, 102.
(2) Surah Al-Isra, 50.
(3) Surah Al-Kahf, 29.
(4) Surah Al-Isra, 107.
(5) We discussed this matter in the first section of chapter five.
(6) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat. 3/74.


[Page 429]

If it is assumed regarding commands and prohibitions that the intention of the legislator is to preserve wisdom or public interest (maslaha), even if this leads to neglecting the form of the command or prohibition, this is not the case. Rather, it returns to the fact that some forms have meanings that are limited to the literal sense, while others are metaphorical. Employing the metaphor instead of the literal meaning is not neglecting the text or the form; rather, it is the very essence of employing them. However, what should be focused on is how to determine the intended meaning: the literal or the metaphorical. This is done by applying both particulars and universals, along with current and contextual indicators.
He says: "Commands and prohibitions are of two types: explicit and implicit. As for the explicit, it has two perspectives: one is from the standpoint of its essence, where no consideration is given to a beneficial reason. This is the perspective of one who treats the mere form as a matter of pure devotion without any reasoning, so there is no difference in this view between one command and another, nor between one prohibition and another" (1).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/85.


[Page 430]

He said: "There is no escape from considering whether we take into account the interests (masalih) in commands and prohibitions or not. If we do not consider them, then it is more likely that we will remain with them in their mere form, and if we do consider them, we will not obtain from their rational basis anything that we can grasp without considering the commands and prohibitions. For although we know the interest in general, we are ignorant of it in detail. We know that the punishment for adultery, for example, is stoning for the married person due to the deterrent effect, rather than beheading, or flogging to death, or a specified number of lashes, or imprisonment, or fasting, or paying a financial penalty like expiations. In the case of the unmarried person, it is one hundred lashes and exile for a year, rather than stoning or killing or increasing the number of lashes beyond one hundred or decreasing it, among other possible forms of deterrence that reason can conceive. All of this indicates that we have not reached a definitive understanding of the interest in what has been specifically defined, as opposed to others. And if we cannot comprehend that, and it is not possible for minds to do so, it indicates that there is an interest in what has been defined that we do not know. The same ruling applies to everything else that we can understand its meaning. As for acts of worship, they are even more so in this regard. Thus, we have no choice but to adhere to the mere commands and prohibitions. Often, an apparent interest may seem to arise from a command or prohibition, while in reality it is contrary to that, as clarified by another text that contradicts it; thus, we must refer back to that text without considering that meaning. Furthermore, it has been mentioned in the book of objectives (maqasid) that every command and prohibition must have a ritual meaning. If this is established, then there is no way to neglect it, as any meaning that leads to disregarding the mere command and prohibition cannot be referred back to. Therefore, if the understood meaning of the command and prohibition is neglected, there is no way to it; otherwise, the result is to revert to the command and prohibition without it. Thus, the matter in the discussion of considering interests is that there is no way to consider them alongside the command and prohibition, which is the point at hand."(1)
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/86 - 87.


[Page 431]

Al-Shatibi mentions cases that may be raised against his previous statement, where it is thought that the interests (masalih) or the intended meanings of the rulings are more deserving than the apparent text or wording. He says: "It cannot be said that neglecting the meanings is a disregard for the known objectives of the Legislator, as in the saying that it is not permissible to perform ablution with water that a person has urinated in; if he urinated in a vessel and then poured it into the water, it is permissible to perform ablution with it" (1), because the prohibition here regarding the second matter does not arise from following the meanings, that is, the meanings of the rulings, but rather from the indication of the wording itself; this is a type of linguistic indication (2). He said: "Following the very texts of the rulings, which are the original, is obligatory because they, along with the meanings, are like the original with the branch. It is not correct to follow the branch while disregarding the original" (3). However, it is the meaning of the wording that must be considered; its indication is not definitive, thus it must be understood in light of other matters that assist in this understanding. He said: "The second of the two considerations is from the perspective of what is understood from the commands and prohibitions as a legal intent based on induction and the accompanying contextual or verbal evidence that indicates the specific interests in the commanded actions and the harms in the prohibited actions" (4). He said: "Just as it may be understood from the essence of the command and prohibition that permissibility exists, even if the wording does not originally imply that. Like His saying, Exalted is He: { And when you have completed your rites, then hunt } (5),
__________
(1) The same source, 3/87.
(2) This is like His saying, Exalted is He: { And do not say to them [so much as], "uff," } (Al-Isra, 23), for it includes a prohibition against striking, and this is a hint from the lesser to the greater, thus it is one of the indications of language. Similarly, as in His saying, Exalted is He: { And if you give one of them a qintar, } (An-Nisa, 20), it is a hint from the greater to the lesser, and likewise His saying, Exalted is He: { So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it } (Al-Zalzalah, 7), the indication of what is not mentioned is one of the indications of the wording.
