(2) It: meaning the Noble Qur'an.


[Page 473]

The third: Knowing the outcome of the servant so that he fears Allah through it and hopes for Him. These three categories fall under one category, which is the intended purpose expressed in His saying, { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me }(1). Thus, worship is the primary intended purpose"(2).


The Third Topic
The Methodology of al-Shatibi in Understanding the Sunnah


The subject of this research:
The Sunnah is the second source of legislation after the Book, and it is an explanation of the Book. Al-Shatibi's opinion, as previously mentioned, is that there is no legislation in the Sunnah that is additional to the Book, meaning no legislation that does not have a basis in the Book. The purpose of this discussion is to clarify how the Sunnah explains the Book according to al-Shatibi, and how the established legal rulings in the Sunnah are traced back to their origins in the Book, especially those that may be used to object to his view that the Sunnah is independent in its legislation and has no basis in the Book.
And what is also meant is to clarify his position that what reaches us from the Sunnah (tradition) that cannot be traced back to a source in the Book (Qur'an) must be paused upon, and it is not correct to act upon it. Likewise, this discussion aims to clarify al-Shatibi's view on the indication of actions regarding legal rulings, as the actions of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) are part of the Sunnah, and the indication of actions is not like the indication of words.
Definition of the Sunnah according to al-Shatibi:
Al-Shatibi uses the term "sunnah" as a source of legislation to refer to what has been transmitted from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) in terms of speech, action, or approval, as well as what has been reported from the Companions or the Rightly Guided Caliphs.
__________
(1) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.
(2) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/225.


[Page 474]

As for what has come from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), it is clear and agreed upon that it is the Sunnah. As for what has come from the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), it refers to their consensus as a source of legislation based on legal evidence that they recognized but has not been transmitted to us. The actions of the rightly guided caliphs also refer back to the reality of consensus. He said, after mentioning meanings that are referred to as Sunnah: "When the preceding is gathered, it results in four aspects in the general sense: his (peace and blessings be upon him) saying, his action, and his approval, all of which are either received by revelation or by ijtihad (independent reasoning) based on the validity of ijtihad in his case; these are three, and the fourth is what has come from the Companions or the caliphs" (1). He said: "The term Sunnah is also used for what the Companions acted upon, whether it is found in the Book or the Sunnah or not, as it is following a Sunnah that was established among them but has not been transmitted to us, or a consensus reached among them or their caliphs. For their consensus is consensus, and the actions of their caliphs also refer back to the reality of consensus as required by their considerations of public interest (maslaha), which includes under this term the public interests (masalih mursala) and preference (istihsan), as they did in the case of the punishment for wine, the liability of craftsmen, the compilation of the Qur'an, and compelling people to read from one of the seven readings, and the recording of records, and similar matters" (2). He means by consensus the consensus of the Companions, not those after them. He said: "The Sunnah of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) is a Sunnah that is acted upon and referred to, and evidence for this includes several matters, one of which is Allah's praise of them without exception and His commendation of their justice and what pertains to it" (3). He said: "It cannot be said that this is general for the Ummah and does not specifically pertain to the Companions over those after them, for we say: First, this is not the case based on the fact that they are the ones specifically addressed, and those after them do not enter with them except by analogy and another proof" (4). His intention is that they are the ones specifically addressed, meaning in praise and in commendation and what pertains to that.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/3.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/2.
(3) The same source, 4/40.
(4) The same location.


[Page 475]

He said: "The statement of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) is a correct statement, with no doubt about its authenticity, for he was sent for that purpose. Allah, Exalted is He, says { And We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them } (1), and there is no disagreement about it. As for the statements of the Companions, if they all agree on what they have clarified, there is also no doubt about its authenticity" (2).
As for the actions of the caliphs within the Sunnah, they are the actions of the rightly guided caliphs, as they pertain to consensus (ijma), and consensus is the consensus of the Companions. Thus, the actions of the caliphs can only be included in the consensus of the Companions if they are the rightly guided caliphs. This is because the caliph has the right to obedience from the Ummah. He compels the people to a legal matter, thereby achieving consensus. Al-Shatibi cites the actions of the rightly guided caliphs and the consensus of the Companions in more than one place in his book with the hadith: "Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me; cling to it with your molar teeth" (3)" (4).
Accordingly, the Sunnah is: the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), his actions, his approvals, and what has come from the Companions by consensus and from the rightly guided caliphs. The latter does not refer to their consensus but rather to what has come from the rightly guided caliph in terms of saying, action, or approval, which has been accepted by the Companions by consensus, thus it returns to the consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.
The Sunnah is an explanation of the Book:

(3) Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2600) who said: It is حسن صحيح (hasan sahih). And Abu Dawood (3991), Ibn Majah (42, 43), Ahmad (16521), and al-Darimi (95).
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 3/196-197 and 4/3.


[Page 476]

Al-Shatibi says: "The Sunnah (tradition) refers back in its meaning to the Book (Qur'an); it is a detailed explanation of what is general, a clarification of what is ambiguous, and an elaboration of what is concise. This is because it is an explanation of it, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them } (1). You will not find in the Sunnah any matter except that the Qur'an has indicated its meaning either in a general or detailed way. Furthermore, everything that indicates that the Qur'an is the totality of the Sharia (Islamic law) and its source is evidence for that" (2).
The Sunnah comes second in its indication of rulings after the Book, as it is an explanation and elaboration of it, so it cannot precede it. Also, the reports of the Sunnah are of uncertain authenticity, while the Qur'an is entirely definitive. The certainty in the Sunnah is in its authenticity as a source of legislation, that is, as a general proof. In fact, al-Shatibi, just as he denied the existence of definitive indications of the texts on meanings, he also denied—or nearly denied—the existence of mutawatir (consecutively reported) reports other than the Qur'an. Thus, the indication of the Sunnah is uncertain from two aspects: from the aspect of authenticity and from the aspect of indication.
He said: "The rank of the Sunnah is to be lower than the Book in consideration, and the evidence for this is as follows: one of them is that the Book is definitive, while the Sunnah is presumed; and the certainty in it is valid in general, not in detail, unlike the Book, which is definitive in both general and detailed terms, and the definitive is prioritized over the presumed, so it follows that the Book is prioritized over the Sunnah" (3). He mentioned other matters. Regarding the existence of mutawatir reports transmitted from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), he said: "What has been mentioned about the mutawatir reports is mostly a hypothetical matter, and you may not find in the prophetic reports anything that can be adjudged as mutawatir up to the time of the incident. Thus, the discussion mentioned in the issue is a discussion about something that is not real or is rarely occurring, and there is little benefit in it, and Allah knows best" (4).
__________
(1) Surah An-Nahl, 44.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/6.
(3) The same source, 4/3.
(4) The same source, 4/5 - 6.


[Page 477]

Returning to what was previously mentioned, that the legal evidence (dalil shar'i) is only accepted if it is definitive (qat'i) or refers to something definitive, it becomes evident to conclude that the prophetic hadith, even if its chain of transmission (sanad) is authentic, cannot be applied unless its meaning refers to a definitive universal meaning (kulli qat'i). Since all universals are found in the Qur'an, as demonstrated in the previous section, the hadith cannot be applied unless it has a basis in the Qur'an. Furthermore, one of the implications of this methodology is that the Sunnah does not contain additional legislation unless the addition is in the sense of detailing a general statement (mujmal) or interpreting an ambiguous one (mutashabih). Since the Qur'an is a clarification of everything { this is a clarification for the people } (1), { and We have sent down to you the Book as a clarification for everything } (2), what the Sunnah brings forth in terms of legislation is an additional clarification and explanation, and not something without a basis in the Qur'an. If something is presented in it that is thought to have no basis in the Qur'an, al-Shatibi refers it back to a Qur'anic origin; otherwise, he refrains from accepting it.
This matter, according to al-Shatibi, contradicts what the imams and jurists (mujtahidun) hold, as it is customary that a hadith necessitates action even if its authenticity is presumed (dhanni), and it is not suspended or rejected unless it contradicts something that is stronger in authenticity to the extent that the contradiction cannot be resolved by specification (takhssis) or restriction (taqyeed). Thus, al-Shatibi differs from the established methodology in that he does not suffice with the condition that the application of a text of uncertain authenticity should not contradict or oppose something stronger in authenticity; rather, he requires, in addition to that, the existence of a definitive meaning from the Qur'an upon which the uncertain (dhanni) can rely.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Imran, 138.
(2) Surah An-Nahl, 89.


[Page 478]

He says: "It has been mentioned at the beginning of the Book of Evidence that the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is acceptable in practice if it is based on an established principle; otherwise, one should refrain from acting upon it, and the fact that it is based on an established principle refers to it being a particular case under a general Qur'anic meaning" (1). He also said: "Because Allah has made the Qur'an a clarification of all things, it follows that the Sunnah (tradition) must be included in it in general" (2). Then he said: "Thus, the Sunnah is, in essence, an explanation of what is contained therein, and this is the meaning of it being referred back to it; furthermore, complete induction (istiqra) indicates this" (3). He then stated: "It has been previously mentioned at the beginning of the Book of Evidence that the Sunnah refers back to the Book, and otherwise, one must refrain from accepting it, which is a sufficient principle in this regard" (4).
Al-Shatibi responds to objections against him by asserting that although the Sunnah is an explanation, it contains additions because it includes what is not found in the Qur'an. He says: "And his statement in the question: 'It must be an addition' is accepted, but is this addition an increase in explanation of what is explained, since the explanation clarifies something not found in the explained text, or is it an addition of another meaning that does not exist in the Book? This is the point of contention" (5). He then clarifies that this addition is an increase in explanation, and since it is an explanation, there is something being explained; thus, there is a basis in the Book. He states: "All of this has its origin in the Qur'an, which the Book clarifies either in summary or in detail or in both ways, and the Sunnah has come to confirm all of that with what is clearer in understanding and more comprehensive in explanation" (6).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/5.
(2) Ibid, 4/6.
(3) The same source.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/6.
(5) Ibid, 4/10.
(6) Ibid, 4/18.


[Page 479]

Based on this, every legislation or obligation brought by the Sunnah must be presented to the Book (Qur'an); if it aligns with the Book, it is valid, and if it does not align, its validity is not established. He said: "Yes, it is permissible for the Sunnah to come with something that does not contradict or agree, but rather with what is silent about in the Qur'an, unless there is evidence to the contrary, which is what has been translated in this matter; at that point, it is necessary for every hadith to agree with the Book of Allah" (1).
However, it is worth noting that the requirement for the Sunnah to agree with the Book, and that the Sunnah does not introduce an addition that is not an explanation or detail of what is in the Book, pertains only to the rulings of obligation, that is, commands, prohibitions, and permissions. Just as there is no ambiguous or unclear verse in the Qur'an that does not lead to an obligation, it is permissible for the Sunnah to come with something that has no basis in the Book, provided it does not lead to an obligation. He said: "Where we said that the Book indicates the Sunnah and that the Sunnah has come only to clarify it, this is in relation to commands, prohibitions, and permissions, or what necessitates that, and in general, what relates to the actions of the obligated in terms of obligation. As for what falls outside of that from the reports of what has happened or what will happen that does not relate to a command, prohibition, or permission, it is of two types: one is that it occurs in the Sunnah as an interpretation of the Qur'an; this is undoubtedly a clarification of it" (2). Then he said: "The second is that it does not occur as an interpretation nor does it contain a meaning of an obligatory belief or action, so it is not necessary for it to have a basis in the Qur'an because it is an additional matter beyond the sites of obligation, and the Qur'an was revealed for that. Therefore, if the Sunnah goes beyond that, there is no harm" (3).
The Sunnah contains the clarification of everything from the legal rulings:

(1) The same source, 4/11.
(2) The same source, 4/30.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 4/31.


[Page 480]

Just as it was previously mentioned that the Qur'an contains the clarification of all matters of legal rulings, so too does the Sunnah, as it includes what is in the Qur'an along with additional clarification and explanation. It should be noted that the difference is that the Qur'an is definitively established in its entirety and in detail, while the Sunnah, in terms of detail, is presumed. The Qur'an presents the general principles, and the Sunnah elaborates on them. Al-Shatibi states in the context of explaining how the Sunnah clarifies the Qur'an: "One should look at what the Book indicates in general, and that it is present in the Sunnah in full, in addition to what it contains of clarification and explanation. This is because the Noble Qur'an came with the definition of the interests of both abodes, bringing them forth, and the definition of their harms, repelling them" (1). He then said: "The Book presented these as foundational principles to which one can refer, while the Sunnah elaborated on the Book and clarified what is contained within it. Thus, you will find in the Sunnah only what pertains to those categories (2); the five necessities, as they are established in the Book, are detailed in the Sunnah" (3). After indicating that the same applies to the needs, enhancements, and complements, he said: "The principles of the Sharia have been completed in the Qur'an and in the Sunnah, and nothing has been omitted from them, and induction clarifies this" (4).
How the Sunnah clarifies the Qur'an:

(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/15.

[Page 481]

The fact that the Sunnah (tradition) is an explanation of the Qur'an is indisputable, but the details of the meaning of explanation or how the Sunnah clarifies the Qur'an, although largely agreed upon, do contain some variation or disagreement in meaning among the scholars. For example, it is well-known that the Sunnah specifies the Qur'an, which is what is meant by it being an explanation. Al-Shatibi rejects specification as previously indicated, and among the scholars, there are those who do not see the specification of the definitive (qat'i) by the speculative (dhanni) (1). Likewise, the Sunnah may introduce independent legislation that has no basis in the Qur'an, and this does not exclude it from being an explanation, as it has a basis, which is the evidence indicating the obligation to adhere to the Sunnah. This meaning is not accepted by al-Shatibi, as for him, the Sunnah being an explanation means that there must be a basis in the Qur'an for what the Sunnah brings, and the obligation to adhere to the Sunnah is the obligation to follow the explanation and details that it provides.
The scholars of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) have various opinions and details regarding the explanation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah, and the first of these, at the forefront, is Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), who made the first chapter in his book (al-Risala) titled "The Chapter on How Explanation Occurs." Under this title, he mentioned five types (2), and among what he mentioned that al-Shatibi does not agree with is the fourth type of explanation, which includes everything that the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) legislated that is not in the Book (3). He stated in his explanation of the types of explanation: "Among them is what he clarified from the Sunnah of his Prophet without a text from the Book" (4). Al-Shatibi mentioned meanings regarding what is meant by the Sunnah being an explanation of the Qur'an, accepting most of them as they are included in the meaning he advocates. He said: "The consideration remains in the aspect by which the Book indicated the Sunnah until it became inclusive of it in general, even though it is an explanation of it in detail" (5). He then remarked: "Indeed, people have various interpretations regarding this meaning" (6). He mentioned six interpretations or aspects:

(2) See: Imam al-Shafi'i, al-Risala, pp. 26-40, paragraph 53-125.
(3) See: the same source, p. 32, paragraph 96.
(4) The same source, p. 33, paragraph 100.

The first: His saying: "Some of it is very general, as if it were akin to taking evidence from the Book regarding the validity of acting upon the Sunnah and the necessity of adhering to it" (1). This meaning is based on the evidences that command taking the Sunnah, including His saying, Exalted is He: { And whatever the Messenger has given you, take it; and what he has forbidden you, refrain from it; and fear Allah } (2). This is an accepted meaning according to al-Shatibi, as taking the Sunnah is a definitive principle, but al-Shatibi requires more than that, which is that the specific meaning from the Sunnah returns to a Qur'anic meaning. Therefore, he provides an example here, saying: "And among those who adhered to it (3) is Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, for it was narrated that a woman from Banu Asad came to him and said: 'I have heard that you cursed so-and-so and so-and-so, the tattooer and the one who has tattoos, and I have read what is between the two boards and did not find what you say.' Abdullah said to her: 'Did you not read: { And whatever the Messenger has given you, take it; and what he has forbidden you, refrain from it; and fear Allah }?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is it' " (4). This is one of the meanings of clarification, which differs from what al-Shatibi intends, as previously explained. He indicates this here by saying: "The apparent statement to her is in the Book of Allah, then he explained that by saying: { And whatever the Messenger has given you, take it } , without mentioning the saying: { And I will surely order them to change the creation of Allah } (5), for that verse encompasses all that is in the prophetic hadith" (6). It appears in this statement that al-Shatibi relates the meaning of the prohibition of tattoos to the Qur'anic meaning { And I will surely order them to change the creation of Allah }.

The second: He said: "Among them is the well-known aspect among scholars, as in the following hadiths, regarding what has been briefly mentioned of the rulings, whether according to the ways of action, its causes, its conditions, its impediments, or its attachments, or similar matters, such as the clarification of the prayers with their various timings, bowing, prostration, and all their rulings, and the clarification of zakat in its amounts, timings, the designated zakatable assets, and specifying what is zakatable and what is not" (1) etc. This meaning falls under the meaning intended by al-Shatibi, as it is an explanation and elaboration of the general.
The third: This is the meaning intended by al-Shatibi, which is the return of the Sunnah to comprehensive Qur'anic meanings that all fall under necessities, needs, improvements, or complements of any of them (2).
__________
(1) The same source, and this third type of the types mentioned by al-Shafi'i for clarification, see: al-Risala, p. 31, paragraph: 95.
(2) The same source, 4/15 - 18.


[Page 484]

The fourth: what pertains to ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), including qiyas (analogy), where qiyas is the linking of a branch to a root. Ijtihad leads to giving a ruling on a matter after the mujtahid (jurist) sees that the legal meaning related to the ruling is such-and-such. Some matters are clear, and the jurist gives them a ruling based on the clear related meaning, or he refers it back to its clear root. In some matters, the jurist may be confused about which Qur'anic root to refer to, whether it is this root or that one. Here, the Sunnah (tradition) comes to clarify the confusion; otherwise, the matter remains a matter of ijtihad. This meaning falls under the category of clarification without dispute (1). Al-Shatibi said: "Among them is the consideration of the field of ijtihad that occurs between the two clear sides" (2). He then said: "And the field (3) of qiyas revolves between the roots and the branches" (4). He explained this meaning by saying: "This is because there is a text in the Book that addresses two sides clearly in it or in the Sunnah, as previously mentioned in the second source, and the intermediary remains subject to ijtihad. The difference arises from the interaction of the two sides, and perhaps the aspect of consideration in it is close to the source, so it is left to the views of the mujtahids as it becomes clear in the Book of Ijtihad. Perhaps it is far from the observer or is a matter of worship that does not follow the path of suitability, and the clarification comes from the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding it, indicating that it is linked to one of the two sides or takes from each one of them in a precautionary manner or otherwise. This is the intended point here" (5).
__________
(1) This meaning was indicated by al-Shafi'i in the Risala and is included in the fifth type of clarification according to him. See: Risala, pp. 34 - 40, paragraph: 104 - 125.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/18.
(3) That is: among them is the consideration of the field of qiyas... etc.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/18.
(5) The same source.


[Page 485]

This meaning of clarification is included in the meaning that al-Shatibi speaks of, because what the Sunnah brings clarifies the origin to which the issue returns; thus, the ruling of the Sunnah refers back to an origin. Within this meaning, al-Shatibi explains how to refer some meanings, which some claim the Sunnah has independently legislated, back to origins found in the Qur'an, which will be elaborated upon in the next discussion.
Fifth: He said: "Among them is the consideration of what is composed of the scattered evidences of the Qur'an from combined meanings, for the evidences may come in different meanings, but they are encompassed by one meaning similar to the command in public interest (maslaha) and preference (istihsan). The Sunnah comes in accordance with that one meaning, and it is known or presumed that this meaning is derived from the totality of those individuals based on the validity of the evidence indicating that the Sunnah has come to clarify the Book" (1). The meaning contained in this text is generally accepted by the imams of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), but there is nothing in it that necessitates mention among them; however, it is important to al-Shatibi. If we examine it, we find it composed of two premises and a conclusion. The first premise is that a new meaning is derived from the totality of evidences that is not indicated by any one of the evidences alone, which is called the indication of the sign from the concept. An example of this is His saying, Exalted is He: { And his gestation and weaning [period] is thirty months } (2), and His saying: { And weaning is in two years } (3). From these two texts, it is understood that the minimum duration of gestation is six months. The second premise is that the Sunnah comes in accordance with this derived meaning, meaning that its meaning refers back to the derived meaning. As for the conclusion, it is that the meaning brought by the Sunnah is a clarification that has an origin in the Qur'an. This is what al-Shatibi seeks, and this meaning mentioned here for clarification is not customary among the imams, as they do not need to prove that the meaning returns to a Qur'anic meaning for it to be considered a clarification. However, al-Shatibi uses this type of indication to establish Qur'anic meanings. Thus, he can refer what is thought to be independently legislated by the Sunnah back to Qur'anic origins. The intention here is not to belittle what al-Shatibi does, for the indication of the sign is one of the accepted indications, but rather to clarify the intent of al-Shatibi. Therefore, attention should be paid to what he said in the above text; he did not say: "the consideration of what is composed of scattered evidences," but rather said: "from the scattered evidences of the Qur'an."
__________
(1) The same source, 4/26.
(2) Surah Al-Ahqaf, 15.
(3) Surah Luqman, 14.


[Page 486]

Therefore, al-Shatibi's example of this type of clarification has a specificity that aligns with his methodology. He said: "An example of this aspect is what was mentioned at the beginning of the book of legal proofs regarding the meaning of his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): 'There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm' (1) from the book" (2). The meaning is that the hadith must refer back to a definitive source in the Qur'an, otherwise it is not accepted. By referring to the verses of the Qur'an that prohibit harm, a general principle emerges that elevates harm, and thus the hadith can be applied without deviating from being a clarification; this meaning falls under the intention he seeks, and it is indeed the secret of his methodology (3).
The sixth point is that the Sunnah clarifies what is in the Qur'an without adding further explanation or detail to it. The Qur'an contains the explanation of everything, including the number of units of prayer and the times of prayers, the details of zakat, and similar matters. All of this is present in the Qur'an, but knowledge of it requires scholars who understand and delve into the secrets of the meanings of the Qur'an. Al-Shatibi's apparent statement refutes this meaning. He said: "Among them is the consideration of the details of the hadiths in the details of the Qur'an, and although the Sunnah provides additional clarification, the holder of this view seeks to find every meaning in the Sunnah indicated linguistically, not from another perspective or explicitly stated in the Qur'an" (4). He then said: "However, the Qur'an does not fulfill this purpose based on the Arabic text and indications that the Arabs use or similar" (5). He said: "Thus, the one who adheres to this does not fulfill what he claims unless he makes efforts in sources that the speech of the Arabs does not accept, nor does it align with what the righteous predecessors or the scholars firmly grounded in knowledge would agree upon" (6).

The position of al-Shatibi is that the Sunnah does not bring about legislation that has no basis in the Qur'an. He faces objections that there are many things in the Sunnah that have no basis in the Book, so he mentions these objections to refute them and to affirm his position. He said, providing examples of what is objected to: "Induction has shown that there are countless things in the Sunnah that are not mentioned in the Noble Qur'an, such as the prohibition of marrying a woman’s aunt or maternal aunt, the prohibition of domestic donkeys, and every carnivorous animal with fangs, the ransom of a captive, and that a Muslim should not be killed for a disbeliever"(1).
He responded to the issue of the prohibition of marrying a woman’s aunt or maternal aunt by saying: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, has prohibited the combining of a mother and her daughter in marriage and between two sisters, and it has come in the Qur'an: { And lawful for you is what is beyond that } (2). Thus, the prohibition by the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) of combining a woman with her aunt or maternal aunt is based on analogy (qiyas), because the reason for which the combination of those mentioned is condemned is present here. It may be narrated in this hadith: 'For indeed, if you do that, you will sever your ties of kinship'(3). The reasoning indicates the basis of the analogy"(4).

As for the soul, which has a blood money (diya), al-Shatibi addressed it and mentioned in addition to it the blood money for limbs, saying: "The blood money for the soul was mentioned by Allah, Exalted is He, in the Qur'an (1), but the blood money for limbs was not mentioned, and it is something that is difficult to analogize to the intellects. The hadith (2) clarifies the blood money for them in a way that seems to follow the analogy that is difficult to determine, so it is necessary to refer to it and to follow its example" (3). The blood money for the fetus is also included with the soul. He said: "Indeed, Allah, Exalted is He, made the soul equal to the soul and distinguished between the limbs in His saying: { And We ordained for them therein a life for a life }" (4)

To the end of the verse, this pertains to intentional acts, whereas for mistakes, the blood money (diya) is due, as He says: { The freeing of a believing slave and a compensation paid to his family } (1). Then he said: "Two parties came into conflict regarding the fetus if the mother aborts it due to a blow or something similar, for it resembles a part of a human being like other limbs and resembles a complete human in its creation. The Sunnah has clarified that its blood money is a quarter of a slave (3) and that it has the same ruling as a person due to the lack of a clear determination of one party over it" (4). Thus, the basis of blood money and the basis of retribution (qisas) are mentioned in the Qur'an; what applies to other limbs has a basis in the Book, and it should be understood through analogy, but its analogy is complex, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) clarified it. After it has been established that the ruling of limbs returns to the Book, the ruling regarding the fetus remains: does it revert to the ruling of a person since it is a complete soul, or does it revert to the limbs since it is a part of its mother? This is something that poses a challenge for the jurist, and the Sunnah has clarified it and provided it with a specific ruling between the two (5).

As for the issue of freeing the captive and that a Muslim should not be killed for a disbeliever, he said: "As for freeing the captive, it is derived from His saying, Exalted is He: { And if they seek your help in religion, it is your duty to help them } (1), and this applies to those who have not emigrated if they cannot emigrate except by seeking assistance from others; thus, it is upon others to assist. The captive in this regard is more deserving of assistance, and this falls under the reasoning based on analogy (qiyas). As for the prohibition of killing a Muslim for a disbeliever, the scholars have derived it from the Book, such as His saying: { And Allah will never give the disbelievers a way over the believers } (2), and His saying: { The companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise are not equal } (3), and this verse is more distant" (4).
The clarification through speech, action, and approval:
This is because the Sunnah clarifies the Qur'an, and the Sunnah consists of the sayings, actions, and approvals of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). The clarification occurs through these three together and separately. Al-Shatibi said: "The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was a clarifier through his saying, action, and approval" (5). Each of these three has a specific characteristic in indication or clarification that the others do not possess, and the most eloquent clarification is when the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) aligns with his action, and likewise, when the action of the Messenger aligns with his approval; this indicates the highest level of emulation.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Anfal, 72.
(2) Surah An-Nisa, 141.
(3) Surah Al-Hashr, 20.
(4) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 4/29.
(5) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 4/175.


[Page 492]

He said: "If the clarification is achieved through speech and action that corresponds to the speech, then it is the ultimate in clarification" (1). In purification (taharah), for example, and in prayer (salah), fasting (sawm), pilgrimage (hajj), and other acts of worship and customs, speech does not convey the manner as action does, just as action does not convey what speech conveys in terms of generality or specificity, or in terms of recommendation, obligation, or permissibility (2). He said: "Speech clarifies generality and specificity in circumstances, times, and persons, for speech has forms that necessitate these matters and similar ones, while action is confined to its doer and his state and does not extend beyond its place at all" (3).
Action, unlike speech, indicates absolute permission of obligation, recommendation, or permissibility, and does not include dislike, because dislike falls under prohibition, and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) does not do what is prohibited. Action is distinguished from speech in that it is more eloquent in demonstrating emulation and compliance (4). He said: "Absolute permission includes the obligatory, the recommended, and the permissible; thus, his actions (peace be upon him) do not fall outside of that; they are either obligatory, recommended, or permissible" (5).
__________
(1) The same source, 3/177.
(2) The same source, 3/177 - 178.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 4/32.
(5) The same location.


[Page 493]

As for the approval of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding an action, it can be understood that the action may be obligatory, recommended, or permissible. The permissible (mubah) may be permissible in part while being required in total, or it may be permissible in part while being prohibited in total. In this case, if it is prohibited in total, it is permissible in the sense that there is no harm in it. This meaning has been clarified in the third chapter of this book. Therefore, approval does not indicate absolute permissibility but rather indicates that there is no harm in the action. He said: "In summary, the approval itself does not indicate absolute permissibility without consideration" (1). He also said: "As for approval, it is understood to mean that there is no harm in the action that he (peace and blessings be upon him) saw and approved of, or heard about and approved of" (2). He said: "What is not harmful is a category that includes types: the obligatory, the recommended, and the permissible in the sense of being allowed and in the sense of there being no harm in it. As for the disliked (makruh), it is not included in this context, because his silence about it indicates its permissibility, equating the action with abstention, and the disliked action cannot be treated that way because the disliked action is prohibited" (3).
Accordingly, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) does not do what is disliked nor does he approve of what is disliked. He may approve of an action and do it, which represents the highest level of emulation. He said: "His approval (peace and blessings be upon him) when it coincides with the action is valid in emulation, without any blemish or degradation from the highest levels of emulation" (4). He may approve of an action without doing it; his approval indicates that the action falls within the four types mentioned above, and his not doing it negates its being obligatory, recommended, or permissible in the sense of being allowed. It remains that it is permissible with no harm in it, and he does not do it because he (peace and blessings be upon him) is at the highest levels of following and emulation. Al-Shatibi said: "An example of this is his turning away from listening to entertainment, even though it is permissible, and his distance from indulging in it, even if he does not feel any harm in using it" (5).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/39.
(2) The same source, 4/36.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 4/39.
(5) The same source, 4/39.


[Page 494]

The conflict between statement and action has a detailed discussion that is not our focus here; what is intended here is to clarify the significance of statement, action, and acknowledgment according to al-Shatibi.
Consensus (ijma):
It has been clarified previously that consensus according to al-Shatibi is from the Sunnah. The consensus referred to is the consensus of the Companions, and it is considered an explanation of the Qur'an and the Sunnah as it reveals a proof that has not been transmitted. He said: "The Sunnah of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) is a Sunnah that is acted upon and referred to" (1). He also said: "For they were the first to receive that from the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and they were the direct recipients of the revelation" (2). Therefore, for the validity of considering consensus in explanation, it must be the consensus of the Companions and must refer back to a general Qur'anic principle. It cannot be said that consensus is an absolute source, as the subject here is not consensus itself, but rather the issue that has been reported to have consensus upon it. This is similar to the Sunnah, which is an absolute source, but in detail, it consists of reports from individuals, and likewise, the transmitted consensus of the Companions is reports from individuals.
Analogy (qiyas):
__________
(1) The same source, 4/40.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/40.


[Page 495]

It relies on the cause (illah), so if it comes through the pathways of text or indication and hint, it returns to the meanings of words and structures, and what was previously stated applies regarding the necessity of referring its meaning to a general principle established through induction. If it comes through the pathway of consensus (ijma), then what was mentioned a moment ago applies regarding the necessity of referring the transmitted matter to a definitive origin. However, if the cause comes through any of the other pathways that rely on the principle of reasoning, it has become clear from his methodology that this is a conjecture that is not supported by any legal evidence, and thus it is among the illusory interests (masalih mawhuma). Therefore, he does not accept any of these causes unless they are established with absolute certainty through the induction of the meaning being reasoned in many particulars, an induction that provides certainty, as mere conjecture is not sufficient for this purpose. He said: "It cannot be said that conjecture is also considered legally in legal rulings, as inferred from the reports of the singular narrators (akhbar al-ahad), analogy (qiyas), and others. What we are discussing, if it is conceded that it does not provide knowledge with consistency and conformity, then it provides conjecture and is thus considered. We say: What is considered among conjectures legally must be based on a legal origin as previously mentioned in its place in this book (1), and what we are discussing has not been based on a definitive or conjectural origin" (2).

Chapter Eight
Ijtihad and Taqlid

It contains an introduction and three sections:

Section One: Criteria of Ijtihad.
Section Two: Criteria of Taqlid and Fatwa.
Section Three: The Principle of the Consequences of Actions.

Chapter Eight
Ijtihad and Taqlid

Introduction:
__________
(1) The same source, 3/7 - 12.
(2) The same source, 4/46, and this text conveys exactly what the texts mentioned earlier from some of the Imams of the Hanafis convey in response to reasoning based on imaginary attributes and suitability and others based on the principle of reasoning. See: Chapters Two and Three of this book.


[Page 496]

One of the aspects that enhances the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in al-Shatibi's work is his clarification of his views on ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), its types, and its conditions, as well as on the mujtahid (jurist) or scholar and their ranks, and on taqlid (following a legal authority) and how to take opinions or fatwas (legal rulings). Likewise, he addresses the fatwa or legal ruling provided by the scholar, distinguishing what can be accepted legally from what must be rejected. This includes his stance on fatwas that adopt ease, permissibility, necessities, needs, leniency, and the choice between opinions as a methodology to be generalized and applied where it is valid and where it is not.
Among the most important aspects that clarify al-Shatibi's methodology and affirm what has been mentioned is the condition he deems essential for the mujtahid, which is that it is not valid for him to issue a ruling without considering the consequences of actions. This is because the Sharia was revealed to bring about benefits and avert harms, and these are its consequences and the consequences of its rulings. Therefore, it is not valid for the mujtahid to give a ruling on an action without considering its outcome.
For this reason, I have structured this chapter into three sections: the first on the criteria for ijtihad, the second on the criteria for fatwa, and the third on explaining and elucidating the principle of the consequences of actions.
Due to the importance of the principle of the consequences of actions in al-Shatibi's thought and its role as the foundation upon which he builds his argument for the rationale of the Sharia, I have followed this chapter with a section that explains three rules that are among the most important he has established based on the principle of the consequences of actions. These are applications of his idea in the objectives of the Sharia: the rule of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i), the rule of public interest (maslaha mursala), and the rule of juristic preference (istihsan). These three rules will, God willing, be the subject of the eighth chapter.


[Page 497]

It is worth noting that what is being discussed here pertains only to the methodology of al-Shatibi or what he distinguished or focused on, and it is not intended to present or refute the opinions of the imams on this matter, as al-Shatibi himself refers to them and their books in matters where he agrees with them.

The First Topic
The Conditions of Ijtihad

Definition according to al-Shatibi:
Al-Shatibi defines ijtihad by saying: "Ijtihad is the exertion of effort in acquiring knowledge or conjecture about a ruling" (1). There is no doubt that he refers to the exertion of effort by the mujtahid (jurist) who has reached a level where his statements can be trusted. Al-Shatibi does not disagree that there is no ijtihad in definitive matters, as will be clarified, but his statement "in acquiring knowledge" relates to the conditions of the mujtahid, including the acquisition of knowledge of the general principles, and in this regard, he exerts effort. However, this effort does not grant him the authority to engage in ijtihad on detailed contentious issues nor to have a respected opinion in them to issue fatwas (legal opinions) for the people, as he is still progressing in knowledge and completing his understanding of the objectives (maqasid) of the Sharia. He said: "The ijtihad that occurs in the Sharia is of two types: one is the ijtihad that is legally recognized, which is issued by those qualified who have undertaken to understand what is required for ijtihad" (2). He then said: "The second is the unrecognized type, which is issued by someone who is not knowledgeable about what is required for ijtihad" (3).
Conditions of ijtihad:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 4/59.
(2) The same source, 4/93.
(3) The same location.


[Page 498]

As for what is necessary for ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), it is essentially - according to al-Shatibi - a single comprehensive matter that encompasses various aspects, which is the complete understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (Islamic law), namely the general principles and the objectives of the rulings pertaining to them. The other matters mentioned as conditions for ijtihad are included in this matter: he said, "The degree of ijtihad is attained by one who possesses two characteristics: the first is a complete understanding of the objectives of the Sharia, and the second is the ability to derive rulings based on that understanding" (1). As for the first characteristic, it means the general principles of the Sharia that fall into three categories and their complements, and it also refers to the detailed rulings and their objectives, which are the branches that relate to those general principles; thus, he said: "on its completeness." All of these relate to achieving benefits and preventing harms. Among what is necessitated by a complete understanding of the objectives is understanding what al-Shatibi meant by benefits and harms, which is that they are based on the designation of the Lawgiver and not according to personal interests, desires, and whims. This has been clarified previously, and al-Shatibi reiterated it here, thus bringing together the reasoning based on benefits and the intention of worship and compliance. He said, "It has been established in the book of the legal objectives that the Sharia is based on considering benefits, and that benefits are only considered based on how the Lawgiver has designated them, not based on the perception of the obligated person" (2). He said, "It has been established through thorough observation that benefits fall into three categories, and when a person reaches a level where he understands the Lawgiver's intention in every issue of the Sharia and in every chapter of its rulings, he has attained a characteristic that qualifies him to take the place of the Prophet's successor - peace and blessings be upon him - in teaching, issuing fatwas, and judging by what Allah has shown him" (3). As for the second characteristic, it cannot be attained except after the first characteristic is achieved, but he made it a second condition because it is a fruit of the first, and the realization of the first cannot occur without the existence of the second. He said, "As for the second, it is like a servant to the first" (4).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/56.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/56.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.


[Page 499]

Then he said: "However, the fruit of understanding only appears in inference, and for this reason it is made a second condition; the first condition is the cause for reaching this rank because it is the intended goal, while the second is a means" (1).
Among the conditions for a mujtahid (jurist) is to attain the level of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) in the sciences of the Arabic language, which is included in the condition of understanding the objectives (maqasid) since it is necessary for the inference from texts and for understanding the objectives. Whoever does not reach this level is merely a follower (muqallid) in language, and his statements regarding the meanings of texts will not be authoritative; he will rely on others whose statements are authoritative, thus lowering his status in understanding the objectives. He says: "If we assume a beginner in understanding Arabic, he is a beginner in understanding the Sharia (Islamic law), or if he is intermediate, he is intermediate in understanding the Sharia, and the intermediate has not reached the level of completion. If he reaches the ultimate level in Arabic, he will likewise in the Sharia, and his understanding therein will be authoritative" (2). He said: "Whoever's understanding is limited is not considered authoritative, nor is his statement accepted; thus, he must reach in Arabic the level of the imams (leaders) in it, such as al-Khalil, Sibawayh, al-Akhfash, al-Jurjani, al-Mazani, and others" (3). Al-Shatibi clarifies that he does not mean that one must be like these imams in all the sciences of language or to delve as deeply as they did in grammar, the subtleties of syntax, and the complexities of language, and so on. Rather, he should be capable of understanding the texts and what they may imply in terms of meanings, what they do not imply, and their generality or specificity, precedence or postponement, metaphor or ambiguity, and so forth, and to reach their level in this so that he may be authoritative in it. He said: "It cannot be said that the usuliyyin (scholars of Islamic legal theory) have denied this exaggeration in understanding Arabic" (4). Then he said: "The aim is to refine understanding so that it parallels that of the Arab to that extent, and it is not a condition for the Arab to know all of the language" (5).

(1) The same source.

(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/60.

[Page 500]

Then he clarified his intention with a text from al-Shafi'i, saying: "Al-Shafi'i indicated in his Risala (Message) this meaning, that Allah addressed the Arabs in His Book in their own language according to what they know of its meanings. He then mentioned what is known of its meanings, the vastness of their language, and that they are addressed in the general with the intention of the general, which includes the specific, and he proves this with some of what is included in the speech. And the general is intended to mean the specific and is known by the context, and the speech informs its beginning about its end and its end about its beginning. And that one speaks of something known by its meaning without the wording, just as one knows by indication, and one may call a single thing by many names and many meanings by a single name. He then said: Whoever is ignorant of this from their language, and in their language the Book was revealed and the Sunnah came, then to attempt to speak in its knowledge is to attempt what some of it is unknown to him. And whoever attempts what he does not know, and what his knowledge does not confirm, then his agreement with the truth, if it agrees with him from where he does not know, is not commendable, and he is not excused for his error if he speaks in matters of which he does not have knowledge of the distinction between error and truth in it. This is his statement, and it is the truth from which there is no escape" (1). Understanding the objectives (maqasid) includes understanding the reasons for revelation, as they are a condition for understanding the meanings of the texts, and this was clarified in the first discussion of the previous chapter.

(1) The same source, 4/61 - 62.


[Page 501]

It is not a condition for ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) that the mujtahid (jurist) be proficient in every science that is necessary for it. Some of what is required for ijtihad can be acquired by the mujtahid from others and accepted from them. He said: "We take the four imams as examples; al-Shafi'i is considered a follower in hadith, having not reached the level of ijtihad in critiquing and understanding it, and Abu Hanifa is the same. Only Malik is counted among them, and you see him in rulings referring to others, such as those knowledgeable in experience, medicine, menstruation, and so on, and he builds upon that" (1). He said: "Most of what has been written in the principles of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence) consists of Arabic topics that the mujtahid is responsible for answering, while other preliminaries may suffice with following, such as discussions on rulings in terms of conception and affirmation, like the rulings of abrogation and the rulings of hadith and similar matters" (2).
Types and levels of ijtihad:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/75. Note that he said: "We take the four imams as examples," but he did not mention Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) and did not count him among those capable of ijtihad in hadith.
(2) The same source, 4/62. See also: p. 58.


[Page 502]

These were the conditions for ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) for those who wished to derive rulings from the texts based on their understanding of them. There is a lower rank for the mujtahid (jurist) in which knowledge of Arabic is not a requirement; he may even be a non-Arabic speaker. However, what is required in this case is knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in general and in detail. There is also a type of ijtihad, as al-Shatibi calls it, which does not require knowledge of Arabic or knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia; this is the ijtihad in determining the context of the ruling. He says: "If ijtihad pertains to deriving rulings from the texts, then knowledge of Arabic must be a condition. However, if it pertains to the meanings of benefits and harms, abstracted from the texts or accepted from the one who has derived rulings from the texts, then knowledge of Arabic is not required; rather, knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail is necessary" (1). He also said: "Thus, whoever understands the objectives of the Sharia in establishing rulings and reaches a level of knowledge of them, even if his understanding comes through translation in a non-Arabic tongue, there is no difference between him and one who understands them through the Arabic language" (2). This rank is lower than the first rank, and its holder does not engage in ijtihad to reach the objectives, nor does he derive rulings based on his understanding of them; rather, he receives the general principles and foundations and learns them from those who have derived them, so he is constrained by his understanding and his school of thought. Likewise, he cannot apply both the general principles and the specific cases together; rather, he only applies the general principles.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/90.
(2) The same source, 4/91.


[Page 503]

And this can only occur in the application of ready-made rulings to their occurrences and in analogy (qiyas). He says: "Thus, the jurists apply the legal rulings to verbal occurrences that are not in Arabic, and they consider the terms in many of the new issues. Furthermore, the analogical reasoning does not require the implications of the terms except in relation to the basis of comparison, which is the original case, and it may be accepted as a given or based on the stated reason or one that is alluded to. This is accepted as a given, while everything else refers back to rational consideration, and to this type belongs the ijtihad (juristic reasoning) attributed to the followers of the imams of ijtihad" (1). Ijtihad, according to him, is divided into ijtihad for deriving the reasons and general principles, ijtihad for branching them out and applying them to their occurrences, and a third ijtihad for determining their occurrences. The latter does not require knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) or knowledge of Arabic. He says: "Ijtihad may relate to the determination of the subject matter, and it does not depend on knowledge of the objectives of the legislator, just as it does not depend on knowledge of the science of Arabic" (2). This is like investigating whether this is wine, which is prohibited, or a beverage, which is permissible, or whether this witness is just, so his testimony is accepted, or a transgressor, so it is not accepted, or whether this person is poor, deserving of charity, or not, so he is not given from it. This does not require knowledge of the Sharia or Arabic, but rather requires knowledge of the subject of the research. Therefore, the person must be knowledgeable in identifying wine, in understanding justice, and in recognizing poverty. If he needs legal information, he can accept it as a given.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/91. The followers of the imams of ijtihad are the jurists of the school, and they follow the methodology of the imam of the school in adhering to its principles, rules, and ijtihadat (juristic opinions). This does not prevent them from differing with him in some opinions. The imam of the school who derives the principles, rules, and rulings is the absolute mujtahid (jurist).
(2) The same source, 4/92.


[Page 504]

He said: "The scholars have always relied on those who are not jurists in these matters, but they considered the people of knowledge regarding what they followed specifically, which is the imitation (taqlid) in determining the applicable rule" (1).
The process of independent reasoning (ijtihad) that leads to knowing the ruling involves the three types of ijtihad, and it is not necessary for a single jurist to perform all of them or to be capable of doing so.
What becomes clear, whether in terms of the types of ijtihad or the conditions of each type, does not imply that it is permissible for the jurist to give an opinion or to issue a fatwa, nor is it permissible to take his statement or fatwa, as these conditions indicate his competence in understanding and giving an opinion. He may not issue a fatwa unless he is formally appointed for fatwa through his words and actions; otherwise, the ability to engage in ijtihad may be possessed by a disbeliever. He said: "The scholars have permitted that ijtihad in the Sharia can occur from a disbeliever who denies the existence of the Creator, the message, and the Sharia, if the ijtihad is based on premises whose correctness is assumed, whether they are so in reality or not" (2). And he said: "The mufti stands in the community in the place of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him)" (3). And he said: "The fatwa from the mufti is obtained through speech, action, and acknowledgment" (4). Based on this, he stated: "The fatwa is not valid from one who contradicts the requirements of knowledge" (5). And he said: "As for his actions, if they are contrary to the actions of the people of religion and knowledge, it is not valid to follow them or to make them a model among the actions of the righteous predecessors, just as his acknowledgment is part of his actions" (6). Then he said: "For the one who contradicts with his limbs indicates his contradiction with his words, and the one who contradicts with his words indicates his contradiction with his limbs, for all derive from one heart matter; this is a clarification of the invalidity of his fatwa in general" (7).
Legitimate ijtihad in Sharia:

(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/58.

[Page 505]

If these are the types of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), then the ijtihad that is relied upon and has the desired goal is the ijtihad that clarifies the ruling when it is ambiguous for the obligated individuals. This is a matter of differing opinions and does not occur in definitive matters where there is no room for disagreement. It is the ijtihad that requires an understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) and the ability to derive rulings from the texts based on this understanding. Thus, the ijtihad that is considered valid in Islamic law is that which is issued by its qualified scholars who possess its conditions first and foremost. It is the ijtihad that aims to clarify the legal ruling in matters that are not definitive, especially those issues that lie in between two differing principles, making it difficult to categorize them under one or the other. This is in contrast to matters that are speculative, where there is no definitive ruling, but one side is evidently favored, while the weaker side is a slight possibility. In any case, one who approaches definitive matters without ijtihad is like one who is circling around a protected area and is close to falling into it. He said: "The ijtihad that occurs in the Sharia is of two types: one is the ijtihad that is considered valid in Islamic law, which is issued by its scholars who are knowledgeable about what is required for ijtihad, and this is what has been previously discussed. The second is the invalid ijtihad, which is issued by someone who is not knowledgeable about what is required for ijtihad, for its essence is merely an opinion based on desire and personal interests, a stumbling in blindness and following whims. Thus, any opinion issued in this manner is undoubtedly not considered valid because it is contrary to the truth that Allah has revealed" (1). As for what is required for this ijtihad, it has been previously clarified as: "Understanding the objectives of the Sharia in their entirety and the ability to derive rulings based on that understanding."
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/93.


[Page 506]

As for what one exerts effort in (ijtihad), he said: "The places of valid ijtihad are those that oscillate between two extremes, where the intention of the Legislator is clear in affirming one and negating the other, so it does not definitively lean towards the side of negation or the side of affirmation" (1). He also said regarding the actions of the accountable person (mukallaf): "If there is a command regarding them, it may either show the intention of the Legislator in negation or in affirmation, or it may not show any intention at all. If no intention is shown at all, it falls under the category of ambiguous matters (mutashabihat), and if it does show intention, it may sometimes be definitive (qat'i) and sometimes non-definitive (ghayr qat'i). As for the definitive, there is no room for consideration after the truth is clear in negation or affirmation, and it is not a place for ijtihad; it is a category of clear matters (wadhihat) because the ruling is truly clear, and anyone who deviates from it is certainly mistaken" (2).
It has been mentioned in the previous chapter when discussing the various opinions on how the Sunnah clarifies the Qur'an that one of them is clarifying what is ambiguous and oscillates between two origins, where the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) clarified the origin that should be adhered to. For example, Allah, Exalted is He, has permitted good things (tayyibat) and prohibited harmful things (khaba'ith), so the status of some items, such as those with fangs among beasts and those with claws among birds, became ambiguous: should they be classified with the good or with the harmful? The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) clarified this in hadiths that prohibit those with fangs among beasts and those with claws among birds, as well as the flesh of domesticated donkeys (3). Thus, the valid ijtihad is that which clarifies what is ambiguous to people regarding its ruling and oscillates between two origins that appear to be equal in terms of classification.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/86.
(2) The same source, 4/87.
(3) Bukhari (5101), (5104), and Muslim (3570), (3575), and Tirmidhi (1374), (1397) who said it is good and authentic, and Nasai (4251), (4273), and Nasai (4267).


[Page 507]

One example of this is the sale of uncertainty (gharar), which the Sharia has prohibited. Among transactions, some are clearly uncertain, while others are clearly not, and there are those that are ambiguous as to whether they are uncertain or not. The determination of this is for the qualified jurist (mujtahid). He said: "Among these is the prohibition of selling uncertainty, and we see that the scholars unanimously agree on the prohibition of selling unborn offspring, birds in the air, and fish in the water. And it is permissible to sell a garment that is filled with something concealed from sight, even though if the filling were sold separately, it would be prohibited. It is also permissible to rent a house for a month with the possibility that the month may be thirty or twenty-nine days, and to enter the bathhouse with the differing customs of people regarding the use of water and the duration of stay" (1). He then said: "Every issue in which there is disagreement in the matter of uncertainty is intermediate between the two extremes, taking on a resemblance from each of them" (2).
Another example is the zakat on jewelry, the testimony of an unknown person, and the ownership of a slave, among others. He said: "They all agreed on the absence of zakat on goods and on the presence of zakat on the two currencies, so the permissible jewelry is situated between the two extremes, which is why there is disagreement regarding it. They agreed on accepting the narration and testimony of the just person and on not accepting that from the corrupt person, so the unknown person is situated between them, leading to disagreement about him. They agreed that a free person owns property while an animal does not own property, and when the slave takes on characteristics from both sides, they disagreed on whether he owns property or not, based on the predominance of the ruling of one side" (3). He then said: "You may not find a significant disagreement among rational people regarding intellectual matters or transmitted matters that is not based on conjecture or certainty, except that it revolves between two extremes in which the disputants do not differ" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/88.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source, 4/88.
(4) The same source, 4/89.


[Page 508]

This does not mean that there is no ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) in other areas. Rather, this is the recognized ijtihad, which leads to clarifying Allah's ruling regarding an action. As for ijtihad in other matters, it occurs during the pursuit of knowledge and advancement in it and understanding the objectives (maqasid) of the Sharia. The student of knowledge learns, studies, and strives to understand the objectives and the reasons behind the Sharia, which includes the necessity of acquiring knowledge of language, hadith, understanding the reasons for revelation, and all other necessary sciences. During this process, he strives to attain knowledge of the objectives in their completeness, but before achieving complete knowledge of the objectives, if he engages in ijtihad in the aforementioned areas, his ijtihad is not considered valid. Therefore, we find him stating in previous texts that ijtihad is the exertion of effort in seeking certainty or conjecture regarding the ruling. We also find him denying ijtihad in definitive matters.
The difference among the mujtahids (those who engage in ijtihad):
The mujtahid exerts his effort to know Allah's ruling regarding an action. What he arrives at is a conjectural ruling, for if it were definitive, it would not require ijtihad, nor would there be room for differing opinions and views. Al-Shatibi said: "As for the definitive, there is no room for discussion about it" (1). He also said: "Whoever goes beyond it is certainly mistaken" (2). Hence, it is said: there is no ijtihad alongside the text, meaning one that is definitive in both its authenticity and its indication.
If the ruling is conjectural, then this is a matter in which the mujtahids differ, and their opinions vary. The ruling regarding an action is the intention of the legislator concerning the related discourse, and it is one and not multiple, which is a definitive matter. Thus, it cannot be that all mujtahids, despite their differences, are correct; rather, only one is correct. This is the case for every ruling in the Sharia. The multiplicity of the legislator's intention regarding a single issue is impossible. Allah, Exalted is He, said: { And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction } (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/187.
(2) Same source.
(3) Surah An-Nisa, 82.


[Page 509]

The jurists (mujtahidun) are rewarded, both the one who errs and the one who is correct. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "If a ruler exercises ijtihad and errs, he will have one reward, and if he is correct, he will have two rewards" (1).
What the jurist arrives at through his ijtihad is what he is most certain is the ruling of Allah, and it becomes the ruling of Allah in his case. It is not permissible for him to abandon it for the opinion of another jurist nor to issue a fatwa except based on it (2). Al-Shatibi said: "The entire Sharia returns to one opinion in its branches, even if there is much disagreement, just as it does in its foundations, and nothing else is valid in it" (3). He also said: "Correctness is in accordance with the intention of the legislator, and error is in opposition to it" (4). He stated: "If it is said that all are correct, it is not absolute but rather relative to each jurist or to those who follow him, as they all agree that no jurist is permitted to retract what his ijtihad has led him to nor to issue a fatwa except based on it" (5). He remarked: "To allow for the existence of two contradictory proofs, if those who advocate this mean contradiction in appearance and in the views of the jurists, not in reality, then what they say is permissible; however, this does not imply the permissibility of contradiction in the proofs of the Sharia. If they intend to allow this in reality, then this is not something that anyone who understands the Sharia would adopt, given the evidence that has been presented against it, and I do not think any of them would say it" (6). It was narrated from Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "This cannot be two differing correct opinions" (7).
Error in Ijtihad:

It has been established that the mistaken mujtahid (jurist) is rewarded. However, this applies to the mujtahid who has reached the level that enables him to engage in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning). Thus, following him is permissible even if the possibility of his error exists, as the correct answer is not definitively established nor is it determined with a specific individual. However, this does not mean that it is permissible to accept the opinion of the mujtahid unconditionally. Some opinions are definitively wrong, even if they are issued by a recognized mujtahid, and this is what al-Shatibi refers to as the scholar's slip. There are also opinions that are judged to be erroneous, even if they may have a chance of being correct or aligned with the intent of the Lawgiver. These are the opinions issued by those whose ijtihad is not valid, meaning those who have not fulfilled the requirements necessary for ijtihad.
As for the first case, his ijtihad is originally valid, but he may misinterpret the text, mistakenly assuming something that the Lawgiver did not intend, or he may not be aware of the text at all. He may even retract his statement, but the statement is known while the retraction is not, so it is not permissible to follow a scholar in their slip or to imitate him in it.
As for ijtihad that comes from those who are not qualified, it is the source of deviation, innovation, disagreement, and division in religion. Those who do not fully understand the objectives (maqasid) tend to cling to aspects of particulars while undermining the universals. Al-Shatibi has warned against such opinions and statements with great caution, repeatedly refuting them and warning against them in al-Muwafaqat, and he elaborated on this extensively in al-I'tisam.


[Page 511]

As for the error that arises from a valid ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), he said: "The error in ijtihad may occur either due to the obscurity of some evidence, leading to misconceptions about what was not intended, or due to a complete lack of awareness of it" (1). He warned against it, citing the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "I fear for my nation after me from three actions." They asked, "What are they, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "I fear for them from the slip of a scholar, from an unjust ruler, and from a following of desires" (2). He also said: "And from Ibn Abbas: Woe to the followers from the missteps of the scholar. It was said: How is that? He said: A scholar may say something based on his opinion, then finds someone who is more knowledgeable about the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) than he is, and he abandons his statement, and then the followers proceed" (3). After clarifying the necessity of being cautious about this, he said: "This is most prevalent when there is negligence regarding the consideration of the objectives of the Lawgiver (Shari) in that matter in which he has exerted effort, and stopping short of the utmost diligence in researching the texts concerning it. Although it may not be intentional and the one who commits it is excused and rewarded, it nonetheless carries a great danger in terms of following his statement" (4). Based on this, he said: "The slip of a scholar cannot be relied upon from any angle, nor can it be taken as a tradition from him, because it is based on a contradiction to the Sharia" (5).

As for the ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) issued by someone who is not qualified for it, where he believes himself or others believe him to be qualified, he said: "It is likely that he believes about himself or he believes others believe about him that he is among the people of ijtihad and that his opinion is valid, and his opposition may sometimes be in a particular matter, which is lighter, and sometimes in a general principle of the Sharia and its overarching foundations, whether they are from the fundamentals of beliefs or actions. You see him taking some particulars that undermine its universals until he reaches what appears to him from his initial opinion without comprehending its meanings nor referring back to the necessity of relying on them" (1). He then said: "What drives this is some hidden desires in the souls" (2). He said: "And this ignorance is aided by a lack of understanding of the objectives of the Sharia" (3). He said: "The root of this category is mentioned in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: { He it is Who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are ambiguous } (4), and in the authentic narration: 'The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) recited this verse and then said: When you see those who follow what is ambiguous therein, they are the ones whom Allah has named, so beware of them' " (5) "(6).
Al-Shatibi clarified that such ijtihad is the source of innovations (bid'ah) and sects. It is the cause of differences in religion and division within it. From it emerged the Khawarij (secessionists), and its signs include division, which is the separation from the community, and then the fragmentation among them, and deviation, which is the following of desires and the following of ambiguous matters (7).
