[Page 514]

This is unlike the permissible and praiseworthy differences. He said: "We found the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) after him differing in the rulings of the religion, yet they did not separate nor become factions because they did not deviate from the religion. Rather, they differed in what they were permitted to do in exercising independent judgment (ijtihad) and deriving rulings from the Book and the Sunnah in matters for which they did not find a text. Their opinions differed on this, and they became praiseworthy because they exerted effort in what they were commanded."(1)
The sign of valid ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning):
It has become clear that the one who possesses valid ijtihad (ijtihad mu'tabar) is the one who understands the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in their entirety and is capable of deriving rulings from the texts based on his understanding of them. The question that arises is how it can be known that he has attained this rank. Al-Shatibi says: "The consideration remains regarding the extent to which, if he reaches it, the address of ijtihad will be directed to him as Allah has shown him"(2). What appears from the examination of al-Shatibi's methodology is that the sign of valid ijtihad consists of three matters:
The first: the application of both universals and particulars together.
The second: considering the consequences of actions.
The third: examining the conditions of the legally responsible individuals in particular.
These three matters arise from the understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and they must manifest during the derivation of rulings, which is the fruit of that understanding.
As for the first, it has been clarified previously, and understanding the objectives (maqasid) is essential; for one who does not understand them cannot apply them, and one who understands the general principles cannot do without the specific details. Thus, understanding the objectives includes understanding the objectives of the detailed rulings. For example, applying the principle of preserving wealth, which is a general principle, in the act of theft, usurpation, or fraud without considering the specific texts regarding these actions is a mistake, as the punishments of amputation, execution, imprisonment, or others all revert to the general principle. This is a clear error; it is not sufficient to apply the general principle alone. Likewise, it is not sufficient to apply the specific details without considering the general principles; this, as has been shown a moment ago, is an entry point for destruction in the Sharia. The concept of objectives refutes it.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/105.
(2) The same source, 4/127.


[Page 515]

As for the second point, which is the consideration of the consequences of actions, it also relates to the alignment with the intention of the Legislator (Shari') from the Sharia. The Legislator has enacted the ruling for a purpose. There may be situations where the ruling itself undermines the purpose for which it was originally established, as in the case of legal tricks (hiyal) and means (dhara'i). Therefore, it is incumbent upon the jurist (mujtahid) during the process of deriving legal rulings to consider the action itself and its consequences. Otherwise, he would undermine the intention of the Legislator in his legislation. He said: "The consideration of the consequences of actions is a legally intended objective, whether the actions are in agreement or in opposition. This is because the jurist does not rule on an action performed by the accountable person (mukallaf) with either approval or disapproval except after considering what that action will lead to. It may be permissible due to a benefit it brings or a harm it prevents, but it has consequences contrary to what was intended. Conversely, it may be impermissible due to a harm that arises from it or a benefit that is repelled by it, but it has consequences contrary to that." (1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/110.


[Page 516]

The third is the consideration of the conditions of the accountable individuals in particular. This relates to understanding the objectives (maqasid) but with a finer focus. The jurist (mujtahid) issues rulings on the accountable individuals based on their specific circumstances, relying on what Allah has granted him of wisdom and the light He has bestowed upon him. This is related to the realization of the legal ruling (tahqiq al-manat) - according to al-Shatibi - but it is a specific type of it. He said: "The realization of the legal ruling is of two types: a general realization, which has been mentioned(1), and a specific realization from that general one"(2). As for the first, which is general, it has been clarified previously. As for the second, he said: "The second, which is the specific consideration, is higher and more precise than this and is, in fact, derived from the result of piety mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: { If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion }(3). It may also be referred to as wisdom, as indicated in His saying, Exalted is He: { He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good }(4)"(5). He said: "The possessor of this specific realization is the one who has been granted light by which he understands the souls and their intentions, the differences in their perceptions, their capacity to bear obligations, and their patience in enduring their burdens or their weakness. He knows their inclination towards immediate gains or their lack of inclination, so he applies to each soul from the rulings of the texts what is appropriate for it, based on the understanding that this is the legal objective in receiving obligations. It is as if he specifies the generality of the accountable individuals and the obligations with this realization"(6). He then said: "This is the meaning of the realization of the legal ruling here"(7). Al-Shatibi supported this type with examples from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him).

He said: "Among these is that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked at different times about the best deeds and the best actions, and he made this known at certain times without being asked. He responded with different answers, each of which, if taken in its absolute or general sense, would imply contradiction with others in detail. In the authentic narrations, it is reported that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked, 'Which deeds are best?' He said, 'Faith in Allah.' He was asked, 'Then what?' He said, 'Jihad in the way of Allah.' He was asked, 'Then what?' He said, 'A righteous pilgrimage' (1). He was also asked, 'Which deeds are best?' He said, 'Prayer at its proper time.' He was asked, 'Then what?' He said, 'Kindness to parents.' He was asked, 'Then what?' He said, 'Jihad in the way of Allah' (2). In al-Nasa'i, it is narrated from Abu Umamah that he said: I came to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and said, 'Command me with something that I may take from you.' He said, 'You should fast, for there is nothing like it' (3). In al-Tirmidhi: 'Which deeds are of the highest rank with Allah on the Day of Resurrection?' He said, 'Those who remember Allah much, and the women who remember' (4) (5). This shows that the answers varied according to the circumstances of the accountable individuals, and this is what al-Shatibi intended by the verification of the specific context.
These three signs must all be present in the mujtahid (jurist); having only two, for example, is not sufficient, even if their presence is significantly established. If all are present, then the degree of the mujtahid's mastery of them will elevate his rank, allowing him to reach the pinnacle of excellence in ijtihad (independent reasoning).

To verify that the mujtahid (jurist) has reached the degree of consideration, it is said that the student of knowledge has three states: a state in which it is clear that he is not among those qualified for valid ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), and thus he must follow (taqlid) without disagreement. A second state in which it is clear that he is among those qualified for valid ijtihad without disagreement, and between these two states lies a third state that is ambiguous and whose matter is unclear, leading to disagreement regarding it.
As for the one in the first state, he is someone who is still examining the particulars and is beginning to grasp the general meanings, but they are not yet complete. He continues to reflect and deduce to understand the objectives (maqasid), allowing his mind to roam within them. Some of these objectives are consistent and established, while others are contradicted by texts, thus failing to establish a universal principle. Therefore, he cannot engage in ijtihad. It was said: "He must alert his mind to reflect on what he has memorized and to investigate its causes, and this arises from a feeling of understanding something that has been acquired, but it remains vague."(1) It was also said: "This student, while remaining in this state, wrestles with the legal sources and is wrestled by them, opposing them and being opposed by them, in the hope of grasping their foundations and connecting with their rulings and objectives, which have not yet been clarified for him. He cannot engage in ijtihad regarding what he is examining because he has not yet established the basis for ijtihad, nor is he in a position where his heart is at ease with what he is trying to ijtihad in; thus, he must refrain and follow (taqlid)."(2)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/127.
(2) The same source.


[Page 519]

As for the one who has a clear state on the other side, he is the one who exhibits the three signs. It is said about him: "He achieves through the legal meanings a status concerning the particular subsidiary issues such that the depth of insight into one side does not prevent him from the depth of insight into the other side; he does not adhere to the generality of one of them without comparing it to the other, and he then reflects on the application of what he has summarized to what is appropriate in the actions of the obligated" (1). And it is said: "There is no disagreement regarding the validity of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) from one who possesses this rank" (2). It is said about him: "And among his characteristics are two matters: the first is that he answers the questioner according to what is appropriate for him in his particular state" (3). "The second is that he considers the outcomes before answering the questions" (4).
As for the one whose state is unclear, he is situated between the two clear sides. He has completed the understanding of the legal universals and the extrapolation of the particulars, and he has not fallen short in this regard at all. However, when he examines the issues, he applies the universals without paying attention to the particulars. It is said about him: "He should conclude by examining what has been established according to what the legal proof has led him to, such that he attains certainty without being opposed by doubt; rather, doubts that arise against him become like the proofs indicating the correctness of what he holds" (5). Then it was said: "But he remains in this state until his memorization slips from his retention of a ruling, even if it is present with him, so he does not care about definitively ruling on the issues, whether he has stated them or opposed them" (6). And it was remarked: "So if the student reaches this rank, is it valid for him to exercise ijtihad in the legal rulings or not? This is a matter of consideration and ambiguity, and it is one in which disagreement arises" (7).

[Page 520]

Al-Shatibi presents arguments from those who claim that one in this condition is very capable of deriving legal rulings, and all of these arguments return to the fact that there is no necessity to apply the particulars since they are encompassed within the universals. If we assume that the universals are complete in his understanding, then applying the universals is equivalent to applying the particulars (1).
As for the arguments of those who prohibit ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) for one in this condition, they all return to the notion that he is not capable of applying the particulars or that he does not apply them. Thus, he does not consider the specifics of circumstances, actions, and the obligated individuals, making it inconsistent for him to be among the people of ijtihad (2).
Al-Shatibi provides two examples of individuals at this level, stating: "Among the examples of this level is the position of those who entirely reject qiyas (analogy) and rely on the texts absolutely, and the position of those who apply qiyas absolutely without considering what contradicts it from the reports in general" (3). He then said: "The people of opinion stripped the meanings and looked at the Sharia through them, discarding the specifics of the words, while the literalists stripped the implications of the words and looked at the Sharia through them, discarding the specifics of the meanings of analogy" (4).
The discontinuation of ijtihad cannot be total:
It has been clarified that ijtihad is of three types, one of which is ijtihad for the purpose of determining the applicable rule (tahqiq al-manat), and this has two types: general meaning and specific meaning. Al-Shatibi argued that all types of ijtihad can cease except for ijtihad in determining the applicable rule in the general sense. If this ceases, it leads to the complete cessation of obligation, unlike the other types. The explanation for this is that determining the applicable rule must occur in every incident; if it is absent, it becomes impossible to apply the rulings. However, if the other types of ijtihad cease, the breadth of the ijtihads of the early scholars suffices for the actions of the obligated individuals, and the new issues that may require rulings are few in comparison to them, which, according to him, does not cause any harm.
__________
(1) The same source. ...
(2) The same source, 4/128 - 129.
(3) The same source, 4/129.
(4) The same source, 4/130.


[Page 521]

He said: "Ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) is of two types: one that cannot cease until the foundation of obligation ceases, which is at the Day of Judgment, and the second that can cease before the end of the world. As for the first, it is the ijtihad related to the determination of the legal rule" (1).
As for the fact that the determination of the legal rule requires ijtihad, it has been previously established. Among what he said in this context is: "When the legislator said: { And bring to witness two just men from among you } (2) and it is established for us that the meaning of justice is a legal one, we need to specify who possesses this attribute. People are not equal in the description of justice; rather, it varies significantly. For when we contemplate the just, we find that their characterization has extremes and a mean: an upper extreme in justice that is undoubtedly clear, like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and a lower extreme which is the first degree of deviating from the requirements of the description" (3). Then he said: "Between them are ranks that cannot be enumerated, and this middle ground is ambiguous; it is necessary to reach the limit of capacity, which is ijtihad. This is what the judge requires in every witness" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/47.
(2) Surah al-Talaq, 2.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/47.
(4) The same source.


[Page 522]

As for the necessity of achieving the relevant criteria (tahqiq al-manat) in every incident, even if its ruling is known, he said: "Actions do not occur in existence in an absolute manner, but rather they occur in a specific and defined manner, so the ruling does not apply to them except after knowing that this specific case falls under that absolute or that general ruling" (1). When this reasoning ceases, knowledge of the rulings is impossible, and thus the obligation is lifted. He said: "The obligation to act is lifted from the one seeking a ruling when the mufti is absent if he has no knowledge of it either through valid reasoning or through imitation" (2). This reasoning does not practically cease because it is attainable and only requires rational consideration and the necessary information that can be derived from the reasoning of the predecessors. He said: "This reasoning is necessary in every time, as the obligation cannot be established without it. If the obligation were to be assumed while the possibility of this reasoning ceasing exists, it would be an obligation to do the impossible, which is not permissible in Sharia just as it is not permissible rationally" (3).
As for the reasoning that can cease, it is of three types. He said: "The reasoning that can cease is of three types: the first is what is called the refinement of the relevant criteria (tanqih al-manat)" (4). Then he said: "The second is what is called the derivation of the relevant criteria (takhrij al-manat)" (5). These two types are useful in claiming the causes and in their examination and validation or rejection. Then he said: "The third is a type of achieving the relevant criteria" (6), and what he means is the specific achievement of the relevant criteria, which has been previously explained.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/49.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/172.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 4/49; the refinement of the relevant criteria, the derivation of the relevant criteria, and the achievement of the relevant criteria have been explained in Chapter One.
(5) The same source, 4/50.
(6) The same location.


[Page 523]

These three types can be interrupted by the cessation of the mujtahids (scholars capable of independent reasoning), but the obligation does not cease with their interruption. He said: "The new occurrences that have no precedent in earlier times are few compared to what has preceded due to the broad scope of understanding and ijtihad (independent reasoning) among the earlier scholars, so it is permissible to follow them in this matter because it is the essence of the Sharia (Islamic law). The Sharia does not become inactive due to the cessation of some particulars, just as if one were to assume the inability to establish the criteria in some particulars while others remain, there is no harm to the Sharia in that."(1)

The Second Topic
Conditions of Ijtihad(2) and Fatwa

The subject of this topic:
The intention of the legislator in enacting laws is to free the obligated person from the call of their desires so that they may be a servant of Allah by choice. Therefore, they must seek the ruling of Allah in their actions. If they are capable of deriving the rulings themselves, they are a mujtahid; if not, they are a muqallid (follower) and must strive to know the ruling of Allah through someone capable of doing so, which is the mujtahid. The mujtahids are not infallible from error, and they differ in knowledge, jurisprudence, and piety, as well as in what makes them mujtahids whose opinions can be followed. They also differ in their ijtihadat (independent reasoning) and fatwas (legal opinions). Just as the mujtahid must strive to understand the intention of the legislator through the understanding of the legal evidences, so too must the muqallid strive to align with the intention of the legislator by following the one whom they believe will achieve that for them. Therefore, it is necessary to know the characteristics and signs that the muqallid must verify or seek assistance with in order to identify the mujtahid they will follow or the fatwa they will adhere to.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/55.
(2) Al-Zarkashi said: "They differed on its reality: is it the acceptance of the statement of the speaker while knowing from where they said it, i.e., from a book, or a Sunnah, or analogy, or is it the acceptance of the statement without evidence appearing for it?" Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/554.


[Page 524]

Likewise, some muftis rely in their fatwas on principles or foundations that they pursue for their own purposes, or they mistakenly believe them to be correct or legitimate when they are not. Therefore, it is necessary to warn these muftis about their methodologies or what they do in issuing fatwas, as well as to caution against such fatwas, and to inform the inquirer or the follower of this so that it becomes a sign of distinction between the mujtahids (scholars capable of independent reasoning).
In order to clarify how to ascertain the condition of the mufti or mujtahid, as well as to indicate the places or some places of deviation in fatwas, this section was written.
The mujtahids and the evidence for the followers:
Since people are obligated to follow the rulings, and the sources of rulings are the legal texts, the followers do not have the capacity to derive rulings from the texts; thus, the texts are nonexistent for them, and they must understand the rulings through someone who comprehends them from the texts. The loss of the mujtahid for the follower is like the loss of evidence for the mujtahid. Al-Shatibi said: "The fatwas of the mujtahids for the common people are like the legal evidences for the mujtahids, and the evidence for this is that the existence of evidences for the followers and their absence is the same since they do not benefit from them at all; thus, examining the evidences and deriving rulings is not within their capacity, nor is it permissible for them at all" (1). He also said: "They are, therefore, the ones who stand in the place of the Legislator, and their statements stand in the place of the Legislator" (2). He further stated: "There is no obligation except with evidence; if there is no evidence for an action, the obligation is lifted. Likewise, if there is no mufti for the action, he is not obligated to it. Thus, it is established that the statement of the mujtahid is evidence for the common person, and Allah knows best" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/173.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.


[Page 525]

And based on that, if a follower (muqallid) is faced with an issue, he should not proceed until he knows Allah's ruling on it, and this is the requirement of obligation and piety (taqwa) (1). Therefore, he must ask those who are knowledgeable about it, who are the people of insight and deduction. He said: "When a religious issue arises for the follower, it is not permissible for him in religion except to ask about it" (2). And he said: "The questioner should not ask someone whose answer is not considered valid in the Sharia" (3). And he said: "If it becomes necessary for him to ask, it is his right to ask only from someone who is among the people of that particular matter he is inquiring about" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi argued that Allah's statement: { And fear Allah, and Allah will teach you } (Surah Al-Baqarah, 282) is not as many people understand, but rather as the scholars in the field of grammar establish, meaning that Allah teaches you in every case, so fear Him. Thus, the second, which is knowledge, is the cause of the first, which is piety. The command to be pious is therefore contingent upon the attainment of knowledge, indicating that knowledge precedes action in a meaningful way. See: Al-Muwafaqat, 4/151-152.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 4/151.
(3) The same source, 4/152.
(4) The same location.


[Page 526]

The follower (muqallid) may find someone to clarify the ruling for him, or he may not find anyone. If he does not find anyone, he is relieved of the obligation according to al-Shatibi. If he does find someone, the opinions regarding his issue may either be unified or varied. If they are unified, there is no problem; but if they are varied, he must prefer one over the others, and he must have a legal basis for his preference; it is not permissible for him to choose arbitrarily. Al-Shatibi said: "There is no difference between the case of the mujtahid encountering evidence and the case of the layman encountering a mufti. The conflict between the two fatwas is upon him just as the conflict between two pieces of evidence is upon the mujtahid. Just as it is not permissible for the mujtahid to follow both pieces of evidence together or to follow one of them without exerting effort (ijtihad) or preference, it is likewise not permissible for the layman to follow both muftis together or to follow one of them without exerting effort or preference. The statement of those who said that if they conflict he may choose (1) is incorrect." (2)
Preference among the mujtahids:
__________
(1) Al-Shawkani said that this is the view of most of al-Shafi'i's followers, Irshad al-Fuhul: 271. There are many opinions on this issue; see: al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/592.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/71.


[Page 527]

The preference of the follower (muqallid) among the jurists (mujtahidin) occurs when their opinions conflict on a particular issue. It is a preference among jurists and not among opinions or fatwas, and this preference among the jurists must be based on characteristics within them that can be discerned and judged. Therefore, the preference of the follower for a jurist depends on their actions. This relates to piety, scrupulousness, and understanding. There is no doubt that knowledge or being more knowledgeable is one of the means of preference, but this matter may be obscure to the follower, or the opinions may conflict, and two scholars may be equal or close in knowledge. Thus, preference can only be based on actions, which indicate the scrupulousness and understanding of the jurist regarding the importance of their actions in front of the public or those who follow them. They realize that they must stand as a jurist through their words, actions, and approvals, not just through their words. This is because "the mufti stands in the community in the place of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him)"(1), for he has inherited knowledge from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and conveys it. For the followers, he is like the legislator through his ijtihad(2). Therefore, it is said: "The fatwa from the mufti is derived from the aspects of speech, action, and approval"(3). Accordingly, the preference of the follower depends on characteristics in the jurist that are:
1. Their actions do not contradict the legal rulings, which is a requirement of justice.
2. Their actions do not contradict their statements, even if the contradiction is within what is permissible, which is a requirement for standing as a mufti.
3. They guide people with their fatwa towards the middle ground, which is the norm of the Sharia and the intent of the legislator.
4. They fear the consequences of issuing a fatwa, which is a requirement of piety, scrupulousness, and fear of contradicting the intent of the legislator.
__________
(1) The same source, 4/140.
(2) The same source, 4/140 - 141.
(3) The same source, 4/141.


[Page 528]

The first description, which is justice, is recognized by the follower (muqallid) through the behavior of the mufti in his words and actions. If he contradicts what is upheld by the people of religion and knowledge, he should not be followed, and his statements should not be taken. This disqualifies him from being preferred over others, as he lacks justice. He said: "As for his fatwas in speech, if his statements are contrary to what is lawful, and this is among his statements, it is possible for them to be contrary to what is lawful, so they should not be trusted" (1). The meaning of the text is that if his statements, which are outside the scope of fatwas, contradict the Sharia, then the same applies to his statements in fatwas, and they may also contradict the Sharia, thus they should not be considered valid. He said: "As for his actions, if they are contrary to the actions of the people of religion and knowledge, it is not permissible to follow them or to take them as a model among the actions of the righteous predecessors, and likewise his approval, as it is among his actions" (2). He said: "For the one who contradicts with his limbs indicates his contradiction in speech, and the one who contradicts in speech indicates his contradiction with his limbs, for all derive from one heart matter. This is a clarification of the invalidity of his fatwa in general" (3). Therefore, the principle he establishes is: "That a fatwa is not valid from one who contradicts the requirements of knowledge" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/145.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 4/144.


[Page 529]

As for the second description, if the actions of the mufti (Islamic legal scholar) align with his statements perfectly, he is in the highest ranks in this description. If there is a contradiction, this is a descent from that rank, and it is necessary to weigh the extent of this contradiction or its locations among the jurists. However, it should be noted here that this opposition does not undermine justice (adala), because if it did, the fatwa (legal opinion) would not be trustworthy at all. He said: "Whoever meets the conditions for being appointed to issue fatwas falls into two categories: one of them is the one whose actions, statements, and conditions are in accordance with his fatwa; he is characterized by the attributes of knowledge and stands in the position of complete compliance, so that if you wish to follow him without asking, you are often free from the need to ask in many actions, just as the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was followed in knowledge through his words, actions, and approvals. This category, when found, is more deserving than one who is not like that" (1). He also said: "Whoever has renounced the superfluous matters that do not undermine justice and is ascetic in them, his renunciation is more beneficial than the renunciation of one who has renounced them but is not abandoning them, for that is a contradiction, even if it is permissible. In opposing the statement with the action here, it prevents reaching the rank of one whose statement matches his action" (2).
As for when the jurists descend from this rank, the one who is preferred among them is the one whose statements align with his actions most frequently. He said: "If the ranks of the muftis differ in this alignment, it is preferable for the follower (muqallid) to follow the one whose statement predominates in alignment with his action" (3). Among the factors for preference is that the follower looks at the locations of alignment and contradiction, for alignment in prohibitions is more preferable than alignment in commands. He said: "The alignment or lack thereof is considered in relation to commands and prohibitions. If he aligns in both, that is perfection; if there is a difference in this regard, meaning aside from the conditions of justice, the alignment in prohibitions is more preferable" (4). This is because avoiding prohibitions is more emphatic and significant in the legal intent (5).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/158.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/159.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.
(5) The same location.


[Page 530]

The third description, which is to guide people towards the middle ground, is that people differ in the extent of their ability to bear obligations and hardships, in their inclination towards acts of obedience and their detachment from worldly matters, and in their relinquishment of interests and rights, or in their pursuit of worldly gains and their insistence on their rights and efforts towards their interests. However, the legislator has set limits for everyone regarding the obligations they must fulfill and the prohibitions they must avoid. Therefore, one who renounces worldly matters and his interests and rights is not permitted to neglect the preservation of his own self and body, nor to obtain what is necessary for his sustenance and that of his family and those whom the legislator has entrusted him to care for and provide for, and so on; he cannot abandon these responsibilities in favor of worship, for example. Likewise, one who is inclined towards the world and its adornments, and what Allah has permitted him from it, has obligations that he must fulfill and rights that he must uphold. Between these two extremes, people vary in their inclination towards permissible and recommended actions and their distance from disliked actions, or their abstention from them, and the state of people in this regard is not uniform. They also differ in their physical and mental capabilities, just as they differ in their spiritual and material motivations. Based on this, it is not permissible for the mufti to exceed the limits of obligations or prohibitions in his fatwa, and what lies between these limits constitutes the middle ground, where what is suitable for one obligated person may not be suitable for another. The assessment of the state of the obligated person returns to the specific determination of the relevant criteria, which has been clarified in the previous discussion. Some obligated individuals may take themselves to task with strict resolutions, distancing themselves from concessions, and they may treat recommended actions as if they were obligatory and abandon disliked actions as if they were prohibited, while such resolutions and recommendations may be burdensome for others, and neglecting disliked actions may be detrimental to them and could lead to sins. The knowledgeable and grounded mufti issues a fatwa that is appropriate for the state of the obligated person in what the law has allowed for flexibility, and when he issues a fatwa concerning a public interest or a matter affecting the community or the public, he guides them towards the middle ground, that is, not according to the state of the least capable among them nor according to the state of the most capable.


[Page 531]

One does not issue a fatwa (legal opinion) based on the weakest among them in body, spirit, or pursuit of the Hereafter, nor based on the strongest among them in that regard, but rather adopts the well-known middle path among them. The term "well-known" refers to what is established in the Sharia regarding guiding people towards this middle ground from what is permitted by law. The follower (muqallid) weighs the opinions of the jurists based on what he observes in their general fatwas, not those specific to individual obligations, as he is not among those qualified to deliberate on that. What is permitted is what the legislator intended to allow, and the middle ground in this context is the most precise intention of the legislator. Al-Shatibi said: "The mufti who reaches the pinnacle of the rank is the one who guides people towards the well-known middle path that is suitable for the public; he does not lead them towards extremism nor incline them towards the side of laxity" (1). He also said: "If he deviates from that with the questioners, he has strayed from the intention of the legislator, and thus what deviates from the middle path is condemned among the knowledgeable scholars" (2). He stated: "If the questioner is led towards hardship and difficulty, it will cause him to resent the religion and lead to a cessation from following the path of the Hereafter, which is evident" (3).
As for the mufti whose rank leads him to adopt a position above the middle ground, people may mistakenly think they should emulate him, causing them to take on burdens that are unsuitable for them. Therefore, he should conceal from the people what he imposes on himself that is above the middle ground, or he should alert them to it. He said: "It may be permissible for the jurist to impose upon himself obligations that are above the middle ground" (4). He then said: "Since he is a mufti by his words and actions, he has the right to conceal what may be emulated from him, for perhaps someone who cannot bear that action will follow him, leading to their downfall. If it happens to be known to the people, he should alert them to it, as the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) used to do, for he surpassed the people in worship and character" (5).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/149.
(2) Same source.
(3) Same source.
(4) Same source, 4/150.
(5) Same source.


[Page 532]

After clarifying that urging people towards moderation is the highest degree in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), he said: "If it is established that urging towards moderation aligns with the intent of the Lawgiver and is what the righteous predecessors adhered to, then the follower should consider which school of thought is most consistent with this path; it is more deserving of adherence and consideration. Although all schools of thought are paths to Allah, preference among them is necessary because it is further from following whims, as previously mentioned, and closer to discerning the intent of the Lawgiver in matters of ijtihad" (1).
As for the fourth description, which is the fear of issuing fatwas (legal opinions), some renowned scholars have mentioned this, specifically Imam Malik ibn Anas (may Allah have mercy on him). They noted their fear of fatwas or of making mistakes in them. Among these characteristics is their frequent saying: "I do not know," and the change in the mujtahid's (jurist's) color when a question is posed to him, and that before answering, he seems as if he is standing between Paradise and Hell. Additionally, he may defer the questioner and postpone the answer until he reflects on it, gather knowledgeable individuals for consultation, and be cautious of his opinion if it appears erroneous or contradicts a legal text. He may also regret if he issues many fatwas, among other things. Regarding this matter, it was reported from Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) that he said: "I have pondered a matter for over a decade, and I have yet to reach a conclusion on it." He also said: "Sometimes a question comes to me, and I think about it for nights." When he was asked about a matter, he would tell the questioner: "Go away until I reflect on it," and the questioner would leave and ponder it. When this was mentioned to him, he wept and said: "I fear that I will have questions on the Day of Judgment, and what a day that will be." When he would sit, he would lower his head and move his lips in remembrance of Allah, not turning right or left. If he was asked about a matter, his color would change; he would turn red, then pale, lower his head, and move his lips, then say: "What Allah wills; there is no power and no strength except with Allah." He might be asked about fifty matters and not answer a single one. He would say: "Whoever wishes to answer a question should consider his own fate before answering, in terms of Paradise and Hell, and how he will be saved in the Hereafter, then he should answer" (2).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/155.
(2) The same source, 4/169.


[Page 533]

And after mentioning a number of these attributes, he said: "These are a set of characteristics that indicate to a person who among the scholars is more worthy of issuing fatwas and being followed, and the differences in these attributes clarify the preferred from the less preferred." (1)
Rejected principles in fatwa:
__________
(1) The same source, 4/172. Many scholars have expressed various opinions regarding the importance and virtue of fatwa, as well as its dangers and the necessity of being cautious about it. Among these is the saying of al-Nawawi: "Know that issuing fatwas is of great danger, significant status, and much virtue, for the mufti is the inheritor of the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them) and is fulfilling a communal obligation, yet he is susceptible to error. For this reason, they said: the mufti speaks on behalf of Allah." He also said: "From Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them), whoever issues a fatwa on everything he is asked about is a fool." He mentioned: "From Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ajlan, if a scholar neglects to say 'I do not know,' he has struck his own neck." He also said: "And al-Shafi'i, when asked about a matter, did not respond, and when asked why, he said: Until I know whether the virtue lies in silence or in answering." And from al-Athram: I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal frequently say: 'I do not know,' and that was regarding matters he was familiar with the opinions on. And from al-Haytham ibn Jamil: I witnessed Malik being asked about forty-eight matters, and he said 'I do not know' in thirty-two of them." He said: "And Abu Hanifa said: Were it not for the distinction from Allah, the Exalted, that knowledge would be lost, I would not issue fatwas; they would have the reward and I would bear the burden." See: The Etiquettes of Fatwa, the Mufti, and the Inquirer by Abu Zakariya Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi al-Dimashqi (631 - 676 AH/1233 - 1277 CE), edited by Bassam Abdul Wahab al-Jabi. Dar al-Bashair al-Islamiyya, 2nd edition, 1411 AH - 1990 CE, which is concise and beneficial on its subject.


[Page 534]

It has become clear that the Sharia (Islamic law) returns to a single intention in its foundations and branches, meaning that the purpose of the legislator in every incident is one, and it is upon the jurist (mujtahid) to exert their utmost effort to align with it in their reasoning (ijtihad). Likewise, it is upon the obligated person (mukallaf) to seek the intention of the legislator by weighing the opinions of the jurists. Accordingly, al-Shatibi rejects fatwas (legal opinions) that do not rely on weighing the evidence. He also rejects the principles that some scholars rely on in issuing fatwas that do not rest on the basis of exerting effort to align with the intention of the legislator. This includes, for example, the follower (muqallid) choosing between the opinions of the jurists when they differ, or the scholar choosing between the opinions of the Companions or the recognized imams, or the mufti selecting for the questioner the easier and lighter option based on the notion that religion is ease and there is no hardship in it, and that the Sharia is lenient and the differences among the imams are a mercy, as well as the generalization of the principle that necessities permit the prohibited and applying it in inappropriate contexts. This also includes pursuing the concessions of the schools of thought (madhahib) and making the differences in a matter a proof for permissibility. Al-Shatibi has followed such opinions and elaborated on them in detail and in refutation.
It should be noted that such fatwas are clearly present in our time, but what is striking is that some of their proponents claim to base them on al-Shatibi and his methodology. They issue fatwas that align with personal desires or the interests of the ruler, sometimes justifying it with renewal and at other times with necessities and needs, citing public interests (masalih) at one time and objectives (maqasid) and the chief of objectives (Sheikh al-Maqasid) at other times, undermining the rulings of the Sharia under the pretext of its objectives, oblivious to the fact that the primary objective of the Sharia is the application of the Sharia itself, and that one of the most important points emphasized by al-Shatibi is that there is no path to the objectives of the Sharia except through the Sharia. Furthermore, they are either neglectful or ignorant of al-Shatibi's concept of public interests and harms and his methodology in reasoning and establishing the objectives based on inductive reasoning that leads to certainty, as well as the fact that the objectives are those of the legislator and not the objectives of those with personal interests and agendas.


[Page 535]

Therefore, this research, in addition to clarifying some of al-Shatibi's views, warns those who mistakenly claim to rely on al-Shatibi and his methodology that al-Shatibi was in opposition to these views and claims.
As for the prohibition of choosing between opinions when they conflict, whether for the mujtahid (independent jurist) or the muqallid (follower), he states: "The benefit of establishing the Sharia is to remove the obligated person from the call of his desires, and allowing him to choose between two opinions contradicts that principle, which is not permissible. The Sharia has been established to encompass a specific benefit in every issue and a general benefit in general. As for the specific, it is expressed by the evidence of each ruling and its wisdom, and as for the general, it is that the obligated person should be under a specific law of the Sharia in all his actions, beliefs, and statements, so that he is not following his desires like a free-roaming animal until he is trained by the reins of the Sharia. If we allow the muqallid to choose from the schools of the imams to select what is most pleasing to them, they will have no reference except to follow their desires in their choices, and this contradicts the objective of establishing the Sharia, so the claim of permissibility in choosing is not valid" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/71.


[Page 536]

As for what some rely on, such as the saying that "differing is a mercy," and what is narrated about the caliph Umar ibn Abdul Aziz that he said: "I would not have liked that the companions of the Messenger of Allah did not differ," and the interpretation of this as indicating the permissibility of choosing between the sayings of the companions and the sayings of the imams, al-Shatibi refutes this meaning and clarifies that the meaning is that if the companions (may Allah be pleased with them) had not differed and their opinion had been one on every issue, it would indicate the prohibition of differing and consequently the prohibition of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning). Thus, the door to ijtihad was opened after them; the breadth and mercy in the differing of the companions lies in the opening of the door to ijtihad and in the fact that the mujtahid (jurist) acts according to what he believes is correct, and among his actions is his fatwa (legal opinion). After mentioning the opinions of some scholars that support his view, he said: "If it were assumed that the companions did not consider these ambiguous subsidiary issues and did not speak about them, while they are the role models in understanding the Sharia and acting according to its objectives, then those who came after them would not have the right to open that door" (1). He then said: "The field would have narrowed for those after the companions, but when they exercised ijtihad and the differing that arose from their striving for correctness made it easier for those who came after them to follow the path. Therefore, Umar ibn Abdul Aziz - and Allah knows best - said: 'I would not be pleased to have the differing of them equivalent to the red camels,' and he said: 'I would not have liked that the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) did not differ'" (2). It is narrated from Imam Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) that he said: "There is no breadth in the differing of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), rather the truth is in one" (3).
__________
(1) The same source.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/71.
(3) The same source, 4/69.


[Page 537]

He says based on the principle of the prohibition of preference: "The neglect of this principle has led many followers of the jurists to give fatwas to their relatives or friends that they do not give to others, following their own desires and whims or the desires of that relative or friend. This has been observed in past times, let alone in our own time, as has the pursuit of the concessions of the schools of thought in accordance with desire and whim" (1). After mentioning examples of these fatwas and condemning them strongly, he said: "This is something upon which there is no disagreement among Muslims who are considered credible in consensus, that it is not permissible, nor is it lawful for anyone to give a fatwa in the religion of Allah except with the truth that he believes to be true, which is accepted by those who accept it and rejected by those who reject it. The mufti is merely a reporter about Allah, Exalted is He, in His rulings, so how can he report except what he believes to be the ruling He has decreed and made obligatory" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/73.
(2) The same source, 4/77.


[Page 538]

As for the claim that disagreement on a matter is evidence of its permissibility, this exceeds the limit, and it is something that al-Shatibi finds objectionable. He says: "This matter has exceeded the limit of sufficiency to the point that disagreement on issues has been counted among the evidences of permissibility, and reliance on the permissibility of an action based on it being disputed among the scholars has occurred both in the past and in the future" (1). He also said: "Sometimes a fatwa is issued prohibiting a matter, and it is said: Why do you prohibit it when the matter is disputed? Thus, disagreement is made a proof of permissibility merely because it is disputed, not due to any evidence" (2). An example of this is the statement of those who said that since people have disagreed about drinks and have unanimously agreed on the prohibition of grape wine while differing on other drinks, we have prohibited what they have agreed upon and permitted what is otherwise (3). After he quoted such statements as being a gross error, and that if they were correct, similar reasoning would apply to usury (riba), currency exchange (sarf), and temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah) because the community has disagreed on them, and that disagreement is not a proof (4), he said: "The one who says this is returning to following his desires and making the opinion that aligns with him a proof for himself, using it to shield himself; he has taken the opinion as a means to follow his whims, not as a means to attain piety, and this is further from being one who is obeying the command of the Lord and closer to being one who has taken his desires as his god" (5). What is surprising is that the proponents of these opinions criticize those who adhere to what they see as correct or preferable. He said: "Sometimes the proponent of this opinion explicitly criticizes those who adhere to the well-known opinion or the one that aligns with the evidence or is preferred among the scholars and that which the majority of Muslims follow, saying to them: You have restricted what is vast and led the people to hardship, and there is no hardship in religion, and similar statements" (6). He then commented: "All of this opinion is erroneous and ignorant of what the Sharia was established for" (7).

Al-Shatibi addresses the fatwas of those who are lenient and follow the concessions of the schools of thought, arguing that the Sharia is accommodating. He cites their statement, among which is: "His saying (peace and blessings be upon him): 'I was sent with the lenient Hanifiyyah'" (1) implies the permissibility of that because it is a type of kindness towards the servant, and the Sharia was not intended to cause hardship to the servants but to achieve benefits" (2). He responds by saying: "And you know from what has preceded in this discussion that the leniency of the Hanifiyyah is only found within the bounds of its principles, and that following concessions or choosing opinions based on desire is not established from its foundations; what has been said is merely a claim. Then we say: Following concessions is a deviation aligned with the whims of the souls, and the Sharia has come with a prohibition against following desires" (3).
As for leniency under the pretext of necessity or need where there is no necessity, he responds by reiterating the hadith regarding the lack of religion and piety among some who assume the role of issuing fatwas. He says: "Perhaps some of them permit this in situations where they claim necessity and urgent need based on the principle that necessities permit the prohibited, so they take what aligns with their interests until the issue arises in a situation where there is no necessity or need to adopt the weaker opinion or one that is outside the school of thought, and then they take the opinion that is established in the school or the stronger opinion in the school. This is also from that earlier category, as its essence is taking what aligns with the present desire, and the conditions of necessity are well known in the Sharia" (4). He then said: "The lack of piety and religion is evident in many who assume the role of disseminating knowledge and issuing fatwas, as previously exemplified. If this door were opened for them, the ties of the school would unravel, indeed all schools of thought, because what is obligatory for one thing is obligatory for its like, and it has become clear that the necessity claimed in the question is not a necessity" (5).

[Page 540]

Among the invalid fatwas that al-Shatibi clarifies and warns against are those fatwas that deviate from the preferred opinion under the pretext of ease and alleviating hardship, which are based on legal principles. This leads to a question: should one adopt the lighter of the two opinions or the heavier? Thus, the choice is not based on what is preferred in accordance with the intent of the Lawgiver, but rather on the lighter or heavier opinion. Those who advocate for the lighter opinion cite the evidence of ease, alleviation of hardship, removal of harm, and the leniency of the Sharia (1). In response to this, he states: "The answer to this has been previously mentioned, and it also leads to the necessity of completely lifting the obligation" (2). He further states: "If hardship arises in the obligation, it necessitates alleviation based on these proofs, then this should apply to purifications, prayers, zakat, pilgrimage, jihad, and others, and it does not stop at a limit except when there remains no obligation on the servant, and this is impossible; thus, what it leads to is similar" (3).

Al-Shatibi summarized some of the harms that arise from leniency in fatwa and the selection among opinions and the pursuit of concessions, mentioning among them:
1 - "Detachment from religion by abandoning adherence to evidence in favor of following dissent."
2 - "Disregard for religion, as it becomes, in this regard, fluid and unregulated."
3 - "Abandoning what is known for what is not known."
4 - "Disruption of the law of public interest (maslaha) by abandoning adherence to what is known."
5 - "Leading to the claim of mixing the schools of thought in a manner that violates their consensus. And other harms that can be enumerated" (4).

Section Three
The Origin of the Consequences of Actions

Its Importance in Al-Shatibi's Methodology:
Al-Shatibi made consideration of the consequences of actions one of the signs of a credible mujtahid (jurist), and he made it obligatory for the mujtahid when considering and deriving rulings, as it is one of the objectives of the Lawgiver. He said: "Considering the consequences of actions is a legally recognized objective" (5).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/83.
(2) The same location.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 4/82.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/110.


[Page 541]

The idea of the consequences of actions (ma'alat al-af'al) is one of the most important concepts in al-Shatibi's methodology, and many rules are built upon it. In fact, considering the consequences is the primary foundation of his approach. The essence of his idea is that the Sharia (Islamic law) was revealed for the benefit of the servants, thus the Sharia has consequences, and the rulings have consequences. For the sake of these consequences, the Sharia was established, making the Sharia and its rulings causes for certain effects. Furthermore, al-Shatibi's assertion that the actions of Allah (Exalted is He) and His rulings are based on reasoning was derived from a survey of the texts whose explicit meanings indicate the purpose behind the action or ruling. The permissible action is permitted for the sake of a goal intended by the legislator, which is the intended benefit from the ruling. The prohibited action has a consequence or result that the legislator intended to eliminate, which is the harm intended to be removed by the prohibition.
These benefits and harms are the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), meaning they are the objectives of the Legislator in establishing the Sharia from the outset.
This is a foundation or principle in legislation according to al-Shatibi's methodology. Actions are sought to be performed or abandoned for the sake of their outcomes. Permissible actions may lead to results that are not intended by the Legislator, and likewise, actions that are prohibited may lead to the removal of results that the Legislator did not intend to remove. Therefore, not everything that results from an action is intended by the Legislator. The intended outcome, whether it is to be established or removed, is understood through induction. This has been explained in detail previously. The outcome that is established through beneficial induction to the point of certainty is what the Legislator intends, whether in existence or removal. This is a basis for legislation or a reason for legislation, or a benefit intended by the Legislator through a command, or a harm intended to be removed by prohibition. In summary, these are the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) or the rulings or outcomes of the Sharia or the rulings.


[Page 542]

However, these permitted or prohibited actions may have situations or circumstances, whether related to the individual obligated (mukallaf) or the circumstances of reality, that do not lead to their intended outcomes in Sharia, or they may lead to outcomes but with results that the legislator did not intend. Here, it is noted that the ruling on the action was for a specific outcome, but the action has resulted in one or more outcomes that may contradict what the legislator intended through legislation. It is also noted that the original principle in legislation is that rulings were established for the sake of their benefits or objectives (maqasid). Thus, the rulings and their outcomes are linked as cause and effect. If this is a fundamental principle in legislation, then when the legislator commanded or prohibited, he did so intending the outcome. Therefore, one who studies the Sharia to understand it must do so on this very basis, because the ruling on the action that the legislator clarified is intended to be adhered to, and likewise, the outcome of the action is intended by the legislator. The action and its outcome are connected as cause and effect, and the legislator intends the cause and its effect. If a disconnection occurs between the action and its outcome in certain situations, or if a connection occurs between the action and an unintended outcome in certain situations, then the jurist (mujtahid) must consider this matter and take it into account when deliberating and exercising ijtihad, because it is significant in the eyes of the legislator, and when the jurist clarifies the rulings for the followers (muqallidin), he is as if he is the legislator.


[Page 543]

This principle, the principle of considering the outcomes of actions, is not a principle like other principles or rules in al-Shatibi's methodology; rather, it is the foundation of his approach and the essence of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia). Most of the other principles and rules that he considers in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and legislation are built upon it. The rules of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i), preference (istihsan), public interest (maslaha), removing harm (raf' al-darar), alleviating hardship (raf' al-haraj), and not imposing what is beyond one's capacity or burdensome difficulties, as well as the rule of legal tricks (hiyal) and others, are all based on this principle, since the objectives of the Sharia are its outcomes, and this principle pertains to the outcomes of actions, and the rulings are indeed rulings on actions.
His proofs:
Thus, we see that al-Shatibi, when he obligated the mujtahid (jurist) to consider the outcomes of actions and provided evidence for this, used the same proofs he employed to establish that the Sharia was enacted for the benefit of the servants. He cited three matters. He said: "The evidence for its validity consists of three matters. The first is that the obligations, as previously mentioned, are legislated for the interests of the servants, and the interests of the servants are either worldly or otherworldly. As for the otherworldly, it pertains to the outcome of the obligated person in the Hereafter" (1), and he said: "As for the worldly, if you contemplate actions, they are precedents for the results of interests, for they are causes for effects that are intended by the legislator, and the effects are the outcomes of the causes, so considering them in the flow of causes is necessary, which is the meaning of considering the outcomes" (2). As for his second proof, he stated that not considering the outcomes of actions contradicts the fact that obligations were legislated for the interests of the servants (3). He added: "Moreover, this leads to not seeking benefit through a permissible action nor expecting harm from a prohibited action, which is contrary to the purpose of the Sharia" (4). It is clear that these two proofs return to the core of his idea that the Sharia was enacted for the interests of the servants.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/111.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source.


[Page 544]

His third evidence is the induction that the Sharia (Islamic law) was established for the sake of goals or outcomes intended by the Legislator. If we refer back to his concept of benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), which is what the Legislator intended through legislation, and to his discussions on causes that were clarified previously, it becomes evident that this evidence here is his proof that the rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, are justified by their objectives. This is what he mentioned at the beginning of the book on the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and it is not something close to it or based upon it, but rather it is the same. He said: "The third is the legal evidences and complete induction that the outcomes are considered in the essence of legality, as His saying, { O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous } (1). And His saying, { Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous } (2). And His saying, { And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers } (3). And His saying, { And do not insult those whom they invoke besides Allah } (4). And His saying, { Messengers as bringers of good tidings and warners } (5).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 21. The intended meaning is that the command to worship is for the sake of its outcome, which is righteousness.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 183. The intended inference is that Allah commanded fasting for its outcome, which is righteousness.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 188. The complete verse is { so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of the people }. The intended meaning is the prohibition of the act to prevent its outcome, which is the oppression of people and the consumption of their rights.
(4) Surah Al-An'am, 108. The complete verse is { and they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge }. The intended meaning is to prevent the outcome by removing its cause, and the outcome is that they insult Allah, Exalted is He.
(5) Surah An-Nisa, 165. The complete verse is { so that there will be for the people no argument against Allah after the messengers }. The intended meaning is that the sending of messengers has an outcome, which is that there will be no argument for the people against Allah.


[Page 545]

And His saying: { Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is a great hardship for you } (1) the verse. And His saying: { And there is for you in retaliation (qisas) life } (2). This is something that considers the outcome in general (3). These texts are indeed used to establish induction, and the evidence in them is that the ruling has appeared and the intended outcome has been made clear. This evidence is itself the proof that the Sharia was legislated for the sake of the interests of the servants (4). In fact, some of these texts used as evidence here are also used as evidence there.
One can critique al-Shatibi's arguments here, as his first and second proofs refer back to the third; they are essentially one proof in reality. This evidence is itself the proof for the reasoning of the Sharia in bringing about benefits and averting harms, so he has not introduced anything new in establishing the consideration of the outcomes of actions, and he did not need to provide evidence. Anyone who adopts his methodology from its origin is obligated to adhere to the principle of the outcomes of actions, and whoever rejects the principle of the outcomes of actions must also reject the methodology from its origin.
Its meaning and application:

(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 179. The intended meaning is that retaliation has an outcome, which is life.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 4/112.
