[Page 546]

It is important to remind ourselves of certain matters at this point, namely that the outcomes of actions are their causes, benefits, rulings, or meanings, and al-Shatibi does not accept them as either beneficial or harmful unless they are established with certainty through induction. The outcomes are definitive universal principles, and without this, they are not considered. The outcome that must be taken into account when examining an action and its result is that which is established with certainty. Since actions are particulars and their results are particulars, considering the outcome is akin to considering the universal principle to which these particular results refer. This is part of the details of his methodology, as previously explained. Below are some of his texts to remind us of this matter, as it is essential for understanding the essence of the outcomes of actions. It is also crucial to remain constantly aware when reading al-Shatibi of what he means by benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid), which are what the legislator intended, regardless of human attributes. They are so in terms of what the legislator has established, not in terms of the whims of souls. He said: "The legitimate causes were established for the benefits of the servants, and they are the wisdom of legislation" (1). He said: "What is prohibited is prohibited due to a harm that results from its action. If it is acted upon, it is under the condition that it leads to the benefits or harms under the cause; ignorance of the benefit or harm or their quantities does not exempt one from this. The matter entails that there is a harm in committing the prohibited act that Allah knows, and for that reason, He prohibited it. The doer is obligated to all that results from that cause of benefits or harms, even if he is unaware of the details of that" (2). He said: "It is necessary to pay attention to the meanings for which the rulings were established. The meanings are the causes of the rulings" (3). He said: "The legal rulings were established to bring about benefits or to avert harms, and they are their causes definitively" (4). He said: "It is established in these matters that the considered benefits are the universals, not the particulars" (5).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/178.
(2) The same source, 1/149.
(3) The same source, 1/138.
(4) The same source, 1/135.
(5) The same source, 1/91.


[Page 547]

Based on this, the obligation to consider the outcomes (mālat) arises because there may be situations where an action deemed permissible is intended for a benefit that is not achieved and may lead to harm, or it may lead to both benefit and harm. Conversely, an action that is prohibited due to harm may lead to a benefit, or its abandonment may result in a greater harm than the harm it causes. Therefore, the jurist (mujtahid) must examine these occurrences and situations, and all of this relates to the realization of the relevant criteria (taḥqīq al-manāṭ), either in a general sense or in a specific sense. In the general sense, it means that the reality has circumstances and conditions that allow for different outcomes of the action, such as going to markets, schools, and attending funerals, and similar activities. These are permissible or legally desired, but these actions may lead to immoralities, such as witnessing nakedness or unlawful mixing, which transforms this reality into a new situation that requires consideration. Similarly, visiting beaches and swimming pools is originally permissible; however, if these places are frequented by naked men and women, then the outcome of this action is witnessing nakedness. Therefore, the jurist must consider the outcome of the action along with the action itself, as this required or permitted action may lead to harm. This does not mean that the action has become forbidden because it has a forbidden outcome; rather, it means that it is necessary to consider the outcome, as considering the outcome is legally required and intended just as considering the action is required and intended. The degree of this harm varies; it is different in visiting beaches frequented by naked individuals compared to public markets where some immoralities may occur or some nakedness may be exposed. Likewise, the benefits that are compared to these harms differ in degree; they are different in leisure and visiting public places and beaches compared to seeking knowledge or attending funerals, and they are different in attending Friday prayers and congregational prayers.


[Page 548]

Similarly, in the case of prohibited actions, their outcome may, in some instances, lead to a benefit (maslaha), or the avoidance of such actions may result in a greater harm than the harm they cause. There are many examples of this, including the avoidance of consuming what is unlawful in a situation where one is on the brink of destruction, or the amputation of a limb that poses a threat to the entire body. Additionally, killing a Muslim without justification is a major sin, but if the disbelievers use him as a shield in war and begin killing Muslims in such a way that he can only be stopped by his death, the matter requires careful consideration, which may lead to the obligation of killing him, or its permissibility, or its prohibition (1).
As for what pertains to the realization of the specific context, it relates to understanding the condition and intention of the obligated person. An action may be recommended (mandub) but could lead the obligated person to cease worship, or it may be obligatory (wajib) but result in harm to his body or impairment of his mind. There are many examples of this. Al-Shatibi said: "In the hadith of the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded that he be left until he finishes urinating, and said: 'Do not interrupt him' (2)" (3).
And there is the hadith that prohibits being overly strict with oneself in worship for fear of ceasing it. All that has been mentioned regarding the realization of the specific context carries this meaning, where an action is originally permissible but is prohibited due to the harm it may lead to, or it is forbidden but the prohibition is overlooked due to the benefit it entails. Likewise, all the evidence indicating the closure of avenues (sadd al-dhara'i) generally involves a permissible act leading to an impermissible one. The original ruling is permissibility, but its outcome is impermissible. The evidence indicating expansion and the lifting of hardship generally allows for actions that are originally impermissible due to the benefit they lead to that is permissible (4).
__________
(1) See: Izz al-Din ibn Abd al-Salam, Qawaid al-Ahkam fi Masalih al-Anam. 1/1009.
(2) Ibn Majah (528) and al-Nasa'i in the Book of Purification.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/112.
(4) The same source.


[Page 549]

Considering this principle does not mean permitting the unlawful (haram) because its outcome is permissible, nor does it mean prohibiting the lawful (halal) because its outcome is forbidden. Rather, it means examining to understand the ruling of the Lawgiver in cases of differing circumstances. Therefore, this is part of the work of the mujtahid (jurist) in his capacity as a mujtahid, who examines the action and its outcome, free from personal desires. Requiring the mujtahid to consider the outcomes is akin to exerting utmost effort and thorough examination. Al-Shatibi said: "The consideration of the outcomes of actions is a legally intended objective, whether the actions are in agreement or in opposition. This is because the mujtahid does not rule on an action performed by the obligated individuals, whether to engage in it or refrain from it, except after considering what that action will lead to. It may be permissible due to a benefit that it brings or a harm that it averts, but it has an outcome contrary to what was intended. It may also be impermissible due to a harm that arises from it or a harm that it prevents, but it has an outcome contrary to that. If one were to declare the first as permissible, it might lead to a benefit that equals or exceeds the harm, thus preventing the declaration of permissibility. Similarly, if one were to declare the second as impermissible, it might lead to averting a harm that equals or exceeds the benefit, so it would not be correct to declare it impermissible. This is a domain for the mujtahid, difficult in its source, yet sweet in taste, praiseworthy in its outcome, in accordance with the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia)"(1). This is the text of al-Shatibi regarding the principle of the outcomes of actions. It is directed to the mujtahid and not to others. He says: "This is because the mujtahid does not rule" and he says: "This is a domain for the mujtahid, difficult in its source." It is also clear that he does not say that the outcome of the action determines its ruling. Rather, he states that it is necessary to consider the outcome when examining, so one should not declare based solely on the examination of the action, nor should one declare based solely on the examination of the outcome. Rather, it is necessary to consider both aspects, based on the legal principles of necessities, needs, and enhancements. And based on the consideration of both general and specific outcomes.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/110 - 111.


[Page 550]

Here, one can refer to some of his statements in the Book of Rulings regarding causes and effects, which may seem contradictory to his text above, where he said: "It is not necessary for the one responsible (mukallaf) to pay attention to the effects or to intend them when engaging in the causes." (1) He also said: "If it is established that there is no obligation to intend the effect, then the one responsible may abandon the intention to it in general, and he may also intend it." (2) From these texts and others, it is understood that although the effect results from the cause, the one responsible is not concerned with the effects or the outcomes; rather, he is concerned with knowing the ruling and adhering to it, regardless of its outcomes. Al-Shatibi responds by saying: "It cannot be said that it has been mentioned in the Book of Rulings that the effects do not need to be considered when entering into the causes, for we say, and it has also been established that it is necessary to consider the effects in the causes, and the discussion has been made regarding that and reconciling the two matters. Our issue is of the second type, not the first, as it pertains to the jurist (mujtahid) who is looking into the ruling of others with regard to being free from personal interests. The jurist is a representative of the legislator in ruling on the actions of the responsible individuals, and it has been established that the legislator intends the effects in the causes." (3)
__________
(1) The same source, 1/133.
(2) The same source, 1/135.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/111.


[Page 551]

The meaning of this text is that the legal ruling (hukm) regarding the actions of a responsible person (mukallaf) when it comes from the legislator (al-shari) is such that the mukallaf should not consider the outcomes (ma'alat) or the benefits or harms that may result from it. This is because the legislator has already taken these into account in the ruling and has judged the mukallaf considering his condition and outcome, along with everything that must be considered. As for the jurist (mujtahid), when he exerts effort to understand the ruling, he must take into account the action and the outcome of the action because, in this regard, he is in the position of the legislator. He, the mujtahid, is responsible when he is making his ijtihad; he is responsible in considering the action and its outcome. Therefore, it is not his place to assume the role of the legislator and change the ruling based on the outcome of the action. Rather, his duty or obligation is to know the ruling of the legislator according to both the action and the outcome together. An example of this is the ruling on carrion (mayta), which is prohibited, but in some cases, such as extreme hunger (khumsa), abstaining from it may lead to the loss of life or to neglecting a necessity (darura). In this case, the ruling changes based on the change in the outcome. The mujtahid did not change the ruling based on benefit or outcome; rather, he derived and understood the ruling of the Sharia. The change in the ruling here is due to a change in the cause (sabab), just as it changes with the change in the action or the basis (manat). Similarly, fasting in Ramadan is obligatory, but in some cases, such as during jihad or for someone afflicted with a certain illness, fasting may lead to neglecting a more important obligation or to compromising a necessity, thus changing the ruling based on what it leads to. The application of this principle, the principle of the outcomes of actions, does not grant the mukallaf or the mujtahid the right to change rulings based on whims. Rather, the ruling changes only where the Sharia indicates that it should. If there is no evidence for changing the ruling, even if it leads to harm, then the ruling does not change. Likewise, the harm does not become permissible or excusable; rather, one should strive to avoid the harm as much as possible. If the Sharia does not indicate a change in the ruling, it does not change, even if it has an outcome contrary to what was intended. Just as the outcome is intended, the ruling itself is intended. He says: "From this principle (the principle of the outcomes of actions) another rule is derived, which is that necessary matters or other needs (hajiyat) or complementary matters (takamuliyat) if they are surrounded by external matters that do not...


[Page 552]

It is legally permissible, as taking on beneficial actions is correct on the condition of exercising caution to the best of one's ability without hardship (1). This means that the required or permitted actions that fall within these categories, even if they lead to harmful outcomes, do not change their rulings, and it is permissible to undertake them despite the harms involved; neither do their rulings change, nor do the harms become benefits. In other words, prohibitions do not become permissible, but one should engage in what is lawful while avoiding what is forbidden as much as possible. If the avoidance reaches a point of hardship or harm or exceeds one's capacity, then the ruling may change based on legal principles, such as the principle that necessity permits the prohibited, or that one is not obliged to do what is beyond their ability, or due to the lifting of harm, or similar considerations. Al-Shatibi provides an example, stating: "Like marriage, which necessitates seeking sustenance for dependents amidst the narrow paths of what is lawful and the vast avenues of what is unlawful and questionable. Often, this compels one to engage in earning for them through means that are not permissible, yet this does not prevent the avoidance of the harm that arises from the expectation of facing the harm of exposure. If such considerations were applied to marriage in our time, it would lead to the invalidation of its essence, which is incorrect. Similarly, seeking knowledge if it involves witnessing immoral acts that one hears and sees, and attending funerals and performing religious duties if one can only do so by witnessing what is not acceptable, does not remove these occurrences from their foundational principles because they are the foundations of religion and the principles of benefits" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/118.
(2) The same source, 4/119.


[Page 553]

The importance of clarifying al-Shatibi's (may Allah have mercy on him) intent regarding the principle of the outcomes of actions in our research lies in the grave errors that are attributed to the Sharia or are adopted as a methodology in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), upon which rulings are based that directly conflict with the texts. This is attributed to al-Shatibi and his methodology, such that un-Islamic ideas become legitimate juristic opinions under the pretext of objectives (maqasid) and beneficial outcomes (mamalat). The examples of the excesses of some contemporary scholars are numerous, and below is one of them, where reliance was placed on al-Shatibi and his ideas regarding benefits (masalih) and harms (mafasid) in terms of bringing about and repelling, especially concerning the principle of the outcomes of actions, where his statements were cited in contradiction to their intended meaning.
Discussion of a Misunderstanding of the Principle of Considering Outcomes:
The magazine "Al-Sirat Al-Mustaqim," published in America, in its issue "59" in the year 1417 AH, published an article titled: "Political Action in American Society" by Dr. Salah Al-Saawi, the director of the Open Islamic University in Virginia. The magazine described the published article as: a foundational jurisprudential perspective being published for the first time. The magazine stated that this study was a response to a question sent by Mr. Nihad Awad, the executive director of the American Islamic Relations Council. What is important here is not the question or the answers but rather the methodology of understanding and deduction. In this foundational perspective, there were many strange statements such as: "Since means take the ruling of objectives, and means take the ruling of ends," etc. He also stated: "Thus, considering means is one of the established principles in determining rulings, and means are those that lead to something permissible or prohibited, so the path to the forbidden is forbidden, and the path to the permissible is permissible," etc.
Among what the author claimed was the permissibility of committing a wrongdoing under the pretext of intending a benefit, and that this wrongdoing is excusable in light of the intended benefit. He attributed this understanding to al-Shatibi and cited his statements mentioned on the previous page. Therefore, I will proceed to explain this text in detail, as it further clarifies al-Shatibi's intent in the text.


[Page 554]

Explanation of the text:
His saying: "The necessary matters or others that are of a needful or complementary nature, if they are surrounded by external matters that do not please the Sharia, then the act of bringing about benefits is valid on the condition of taking precautions according to one's ability without hardship." This means that the actions which the evidence indicates are permissible, whether by obligation, recommendation, or permissibility, do not fall outside the categories of necessity, need, or complementarity; they are benefits that fall under these three categories. These actions, if they have an outcome that is prohibited, then performing them is valid with the possibility of that outcome, meaning that the original consideration of outcomes does not affect the ruling on these actions. And since these actions may lead to something forbidden, one must take precautions against falling into these outcomes or prohibitions to the best of their ability, meaning one must avoid these prohibitions just as one must avoid any forbidden act. And Allah, Exalted is He, does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, so this text does not permit the commission of wrongdoing. His saying: "Like marriage, which necessitates seeking sustenance for dependents amidst the narrow paths of what is lawful, and the vast avenues of what is unlawful and questionable, often forcing one to earn for them through what is not permissible, but this does not prevent it." Marriage, for example, is permissible, and according to al-Shatibi, it is a legal ruling concerning the individual in its particularity, and it is a general, definitive principle concerning the public in its service to necessity. If it is established that it may lead in some cases to something prohibited, such as seeking sustenance for dependents through unlawful means, and it may lead to earning through what is forbidden, then the particularity conflicts with the principle, which is the permissibility of this marriage with regard to outcomes. In these cases, the outcomes of marriage do not invalidate the legal ruling on marriage; this act remains as it is, and its ruling is not changed by its outcomes. The obligated person strives to avoid falling into these outcomes according to their ability, and this does not mean that engaging with these outcomes becomes permissible. And his saying: "For what it leads to, taking precautions against the harm that is greater than the harm of exposure; if such a thing were considered in our time, it would lead to the invalidation of its principle, which is not correct."


[Page 555]

Indeed, these outcomes do not prevent marriage, and if we were to consider the ruling based on this outcome in our time, it would lead to the prohibition of marriage, which is incorrect because it contradicts the established ruling supported by evidence. His statement: "and that is not correct" means that it is not permissible to invalidate or change a legal ruling under the pretext of outcomes. Furthermore, if we were to prohibit marriage, which is a legal ruling, we would fall into greater evils than those of these outcomes. The outcomes are considered in light of the Sharia, and we do not change rulings based on them; rather, we discover the Sharia's consideration of them. Since marriage is permissible, and every permissible matter is a benefit, its invalidation is a harm, whether we realize it or not. According to al-Shatibi, it is a fundamental principle, whether necessary, urgent, or complementary. Thus, if the consideration of these outcomes implies changing the ruling, it leads to the invalidation of a principle, which is incorrect. His statement: "Similarly, seeking knowledge, if it involves hearing disapproved matters, attending funerals, and performing religious duties if they can only be fulfilled by witnessing what is not acceptable, does not remove these matters from their principles" means that what has been said regarding marriage applies to seeking knowledge and the other mentioned matters. All of these are particulars that have been established as permissible by evidence. The fact that they may lead to something prohibited, such as viewing nakedness or hearing what is not permissible to listen to, does not invalidate the legality of these actions, because what invalidates or does not invalidate is the Sharia, and the Sharia has not invalidated them despite the existence of these outcomes. The Sharia has considered the outcomes, and with its consideration of the outcomes, thus were its rulings; they should not be tampered with under the pretext of outcomes, and it is permissible to engage in them with the possibility of their outcomes. This principle, that is, the consideration of outcomes, does not change a legal ruling; it neither makes the unlawful lawful nor prohibits the lawful. If a servant engages in these actions, they must avoid the prohibitions that may result from these actions to the best of their ability. His statement: "Because they are the foundations of religion and the principles of benefits, which is understood from the objectives of the Legislator" means that the foundations are not invalidated by particulars, because the foundations are general.


[Page 556]

The principles of religion, like the beliefs, are definitive and cannot be contradicted by anything. Likewise, the three categories—necessities (darurat), needs (hajiyat), and enhancements (tahsinat)—are understood from the Sharia. The general principle is not invalidated by the opposition of some particulars to it. His statement: "It is necessary to understand them correctly, for they are the basis of disagreement and contention," means that these established principles, which are derived through induction, are contested by some who reject them based on particular cases that contradict them. Therefore, it is essential to understand correctly that particulars do not invalidate the principles. What he means is that there are those who dispute and oppose the validity of the principle of considering the consequences of actions (mala'at al-af'al), based on what has been mentioned in the texts regarding these rejected consequences, which have not affected rulings such as marriage and the pursuit of knowledge, nor have they changed the ruling. Thus, they claim that this principle has fallen. This claim is invalid because the principle is a definitive generality, while what they assert are particular cases and specific issues that do not reach the level of being definitive. His statement: "What is transmitted from the righteous predecessors that contradicts this are specific cases that have no evidence in themselves until their meaning is understood, and they align with what has been established, if Allah wills," means that what the disputants raise in refuting these principles, including the principle of considering consequences, has no evidence, as it is based on particulars. If these particulars converge on a specific meaning and this meaning is subjected to an induction that yields certainty, then it will become clear that this certain meaning and these particulars related to it will align with the principle of considering consequences. This is because the principles are definitive generalities and do not contradict each other, and since they are particulars that have not yet reached this level, they remain speculative in their opposition to the definitive principle and are subject to interpretation.


[Page 557]

And this interpretation of this text is one that observes and considers its methodology and principles that have been established. As for the claim that it is permissible to commit wrong based on the principle of outcomes, this is rejected, and one can refer to al-Shatibi's texts in the discussion of the objectives of the legally responsible (maqasid al-mukallaf), where his views on this matter are clarified in the sixth chapter of this book, where his opinion is that these statements can only arise from ignorance, and if that is not the case, then it is an innovation.

Chapter Nine
On the Application of the Idea:
Three General Principles
This chapter contains a brief definition of the subject of this chapter and three discussions:

Discussion One: The Considered Interests (masalih mursala).
Discussion Two: Preference (istihsan).
Discussion Three: Blocking the Means (sadd al-dhara'i).
The third discussion includes a study of the principle of removing harm.

Chapter Nine
On the Application of the Idea:
Three General Principles

The subject of this chapter:
After clarifying al-Shatibi's methodology in understanding the Sharia and his approach in establishing the general principles and rules, which is the beneficial induction leading to certainty, this chapter comes to explain three general principles that are among the most important rules in al-Shatibi's methodology, which are the considered interests, preference, and blocking the means. This is done in three discussions, and the principle of removing harm is examined within the discussion on blocking the means. The aim of discussing these principles is:
1 - To further clarify al-Shatibi's methodology in understanding the Sharia and deriving rulings, as these principles are universals that he established through applying his idea of inductively extracting meanings and capturing universals, as he expressed it. Since these principles are objectives or reasons, and based on them rulings branch out, they are therefore considered principles for the jurist when deriving rulings.


[Page 558]

2 - Clarifying how al-Shatibi's consideration of these principles differs from that of other imams who acknowledge them, through their specification, and if one may say, the narrowing of their applicability so that he can claim certainty regarding them. After that, he claimed that they are acknowledged and practiced by all, even if they explicitly state their rejection. Among this is his assertion multiple times that the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) is practiced by Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with them), while their failure to apply it in many instances does not detract from its validity, as it is not due to their disregard for the principle but rather for other reasons.

3 - Clarifying the reality of these principles in al-Shatibi's methodology, as these terms: public interest (maslaha mursala), juristic preference (istihsan), and blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) are names for the principles and not their texts. The name does not reveal the true meaning, the context of its application, or its conditions. Therefore, it is incorrect to invoke al-Shatibi or his methodology or the titles of his principles or rules without understanding the reality of all of it, and then issuing opinions or fatwas that permit the unlawful or prohibit the lawful merely by using the name of the principle; this is ignorance, not knowledge, and does not yield true knowledge.

The first section
Public interest (maslaha mursala)

The meaning of public interest (maslaha mursala):
The principle of public interest (maslaha mursala) is based on the unrestricted reasoning (istidlal mursel), which in turn is based on the unrestricted suitability (munasib mursel). The unrestricted suitability is one of the categories of suitability, and suitability is the description that can be claimed as a cause by those who adhere to the path of suitability in analogy (qiyas). It leads to analogy after its conditions are met. However, reasoning is not from analogy because the description that is suitable for reasoning, even if it exists in a branch, does not exist in a specific origin to be compared to. Rather, it is a meaning that is observed to correspond with many rulings or the application of many rulings that correspond to it, thus establishing the description and considering it a valid principle in legislation, supported by many rulings that cannot be traced back to any one of them, as in each of the rulings that testify to its validity, it cannot be a cause since the ruling may be one that is not subject to reasoning or one that has another cause or there may be a description that is more suitable than it. (1)
Public interest (maslaha mursala) according to the imams:
__________
(1) See: the second and third chapters of this book.


[Page 559]

The disagreement regarding public interest (maslaha) in the context of the unregulated interests (masalih mursala) partly stems from the differences in the validity of reasoning based on the sent analogy (al-munasib al-mursil) or the analogy itself. This matter has been discussed in detail. On the other hand, it also relates to differences in terminologies. If we establish that unregulated interests do not revert to analogy, which is the correct view, but rather to reasoning, then the differing opinions on this matter are almost merely disagreements in terms and terminologies. This is without taking into account the position of those who reject analogy, and the application of the meaning of unregulated interests — in that case — is almost unanimously agreed upon(1). The meaning that was rejected by those who opposed unregulated interests is not the same as that intended by those who advocate for it in the context of reasoning. The meaning intended by its proponents was also acknowledged by its opponents under different names. For example, al-Amidi rejected unregulated interests, stating: "The interests, as we have explained, are divided into those that the legislator has recognized and those that he has annulled. This category (i.e., unregulated interests)(2) is ambiguous between the two categories, and it is not more appropriate to associate it with one than the other, thus it is not permissible to use it as evidence without a witness of recognition that indicates it belongs to the recognized rather than the annulled"(3). It has been previously established that al-Amidi and the Imams of the Shafi'i school were among the most ardent defenders of the principle of analogy and its consideration in reasoning, as well as the consideration of the nature of the description in relation to the nature of the ruling, which is what unregulated interests signify for those who advocate for them in reasoning and analogy.

(2) What is in parentheses is an addition by the researcher.
(3) Al-Amidi, al-Ihkam fi Usul al-Ahkam, 4/395.


[Page 560]

What al-Amidi intended by the response in this text is to consider public interest (maslaha) when there is no evidence to indicate it, and this is unanimously rejected. However, what is meant by those who advocate for the unqualified public interest is accepted by all, including those who have rejected it. Al-Qarafi confirms this by stating: "As for the unqualified public interest, it is reported that it is specific to us, and when the schools of thought are lacking, they find that when they compare and differentiate between the two issues, they do not seek evidence by consideration for that meaning by which they compared and differentiated, but rather they suffice with mere suitability. This is the unqualified public interest, and thus it exists in all schools of thought" (1). He also said: "It has been established that the unqualified public interest exists in all schools of thought upon investigation, for they compare and differentiate based on suitability and do not seek evidence by consideration, and we mean by the unqualified public interest only that. What further confirms the practice of the unqualified public interest is that the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) undertook matters for the sake of pure public interest, not due to the presence of evidence by consideration, such as the compilation of the Qur'an, for there was no prior command or analogy regarding it. Likewise, the matter of leaving the caliphate to consultation, the recording of the registers, the minting of currency for Muslims, and the establishment of prisons were actions taken by Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), as well as the demolition of the endowments adjacent to the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) and the expansion of the mosque when it became cramped, which was done by Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), and the renewal of the call to prayer on Friday in the market, which is the first call to prayer" (2). He then said: "And this is very common for pure public interest, and the Imam of the Two Holy Sanctuaries has addressed in his book titled Al-Ghayathi matters that he permitted and ruled upon, while the Malikis are distant from them and have crossed over them for the sake of pure public interest, as well as Al-Ghazali in Shifa al-Ghalil, even though both of them strongly deny our stance on the unqualified public interest" (3).

(1) Al-Qarafi, Sharh Tanqih al-Fusul, p. 394.

(3) The same source, p. 447.


[Page 561]

This text indicates that those who reject public interest (maslaha) are rejecting something other than what its proponents intend. If the examples mentioned by al-Qarafi above refer to the topics of public interest, then these examples are matters of consensus, even if there is disagreement regarding detailed legal reasoning. Those who do not accept public interest refer it to other principles, such as the preservation of necessities or the principle that whatever is necessary for fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory, or the principle of alleviating hardship or harm, or similar concepts. Therefore, there is no real disagreement regarding the principle of public interest; the source of the disagreement lies in the differing understandings of the principle among those who disagree.
The significant disagreement, however, is as previously mentioned, regarding the justification of legal rulings by their purposes or by their benefits. This may lead some followers of the imams and those studying the books of usul to misunderstand and impose their understanding on the school of thought or its imam, or to exploit the idea and use it without its constraints and inappropriately, perhaps even in a way that misrepresents its meaning. For instance, to understand public interest as merely the fact that something is beneficial or leads to a benefit is evidence of its permissibility, or to understand that there is a vacuum in the Sharia, and that there are occurrences without rulings, and that this is left to us to determine its ruling based on benefit or harm—such statements have no basis among any of the recognized imams. It is reported that there is consensus on rejecting this, and this matter will become clear upon the completion of this discussion, if Allah wills.


[Page 562]

The concept of public interest (maslaha) according to al-Shatibi:
The public interest (maslaha) according to al-Shatibi relates to the meaning of unrestricted reasoning, and it contains new elements as does his methodology. For a public interest to be considered, it must be established as valid by the Sharia with absolute certainty through induction, or it must pertain to a general, definitive meaning that has been established in that manner. He stated in his third introduction, after clarifying that the principles must be certain and that mere conjecture is insufficient, and that the path to certainty is through induction: "Based on this premise, there is another meaning, which is that every legal principle that does not have a specific text to support it and is consistent with the actions of the Sharia, and whose meaning is derived from its evidences, is valid and can be relied upon if that principle has become certain through its collective evidences. This is because the evidences do not necessarily have to indicate certainty about the ruling in isolation without the addition of others to them, as previously mentioned, since that is nearly impossible. This includes a type of unrestricted reasoning that was adopted by Malik and al-Shafi'i, for although the branch does not have a specific principle to support it, it has been supported by a general principle. A general principle, if it is definitive, may equal a specific principle or may surpass it depending on the strength or weakness of the specific principle" (1). Accordingly, an action that is not explicitly mentioned in the Sharia as either permitted or prohibited will have its ruling based on the principle that has been established with certainty and has become a foundation to rely upon if this action falls under this meaning or serves it or leads to it.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/16.


[Page 563]

He said: "The legal proofs (adillah shar'iyyah) are of two types: the first is what pertains to pure transmission, and the second is what pertains to pure opinion" (1). Then he said: "As for the first type, it is the Book and the Sunnah, and as for the second, it is analogy (qiyas) and reasoning (istidlal). Each of these can be associated with various aspects, either by consensus (ijma) or by disagreement. The consensus, regardless of how it is articulated, is included in the first type, as is the opinion of a Companion (sahabi) and the legislation of those before us, because all of this and similar matters relate to worship based on a transmitted command, with no personal interpretation involved. The second type includes juristic preference (istihsan) and public interest (maslaha mursala) if we say that they pertain to a rational matter, and they may revert to the first type if we witness that they relate to general meanings" (2). The point here is that public interest (maslaha mursala) relates to pure transmission and also to reasoning; the first is to establish that this interest is a definitive legal interest, and this is derived from the examination of legal texts. Thus, it is related to the first type. The second is to establish that this action falls under this interest and leads to it, meaning that its relationship to the meaning or interest, which is a general principle, is like the relationship of a cause to its effect or outcome.
Accordingly, public interest (maslaha mursala) is one of the types of reasoning (istidlal) according to al-Shatibi, and it is termed "mursala" because it does not have a specific evidence that indicates it or to which it returns, but the interest is definitively established by numerous evidences that exceed enumeration. Thus, public interest (maslaha mursala) becomes a principle upon which the rulings of actions that are causes or means for the interest are built, according to legal controls and limits that will be clarified, God willing.
Places of applying the principle:

[Page 564]

The principle of public interest (maslaha mursala) is based on the combination of two foundations: the foundation of worship and compliance, and the foundation of alleviating hardship. When a mandatory command comes from the legislator, compliance is required; if it is possible, there is no issue. If it is not possible, it may be either because it is not feasible to carry it out and persist in it, which constitutes hardship, or because it can only be performed after fulfilling another obligation. These two scenarios, if they arise in relation to the obligation, necessitate other rulings. If the matter pertains to hardship, then hardship must be alleviated through facilitation. If it pertains to the fact that the action cannot be performed except after fulfilling another, then this other action becomes obligatory just like the first action. The second scenario falls under the first, because if performing an action is only possible through first performing another, then the obligation to do it without fulfilling what is necessary for it is an obligation to do what is impossible or what involves hardship. Therefore, both scenarios relate to alleviating hardship. This is the foundation of the principle of public interest as articulated by al-Shatibi.
It is applied in necessities and needs, but not in enhancements. It is applied in necessities to actions that cannot preserve the necessity except through them, thus the action takes the ruling of preserving the necessity, which is obligation. In needs, it pertains to alleviating hardship and similar matters, leading to facilitation based on the evidence's indications. The rulings of acts of worship are excluded from its application in these contexts; thus, there is no place for public interest in acts of worship. As for what has been mentioned above regarding the foundation of the principle of public interest, al-Shatibi mentioned in his thirteenth introduction a matter, which is that the foundations and principles do not fail or break. If it becomes necessary for them to break or fail, then they are not valid. This is evident in certain instances, including what he termed "entering into actions." By "entering into actions," he means that the actions required of the obligated person must be within the capacity of the obligated person from beginning to end. If they are not, then the command to perform them is not an obligation. He states: "As for entering into actions, it is the crux of the matter and the foundation of preference (istihsan) and public interest, because if the principle leads to a conclusion that entails hardship or something that is not possible legally or rationally, it does not proceed in a straight or consistent manner."(1)
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/64.


[Page 565]

One example of the principle in necessities is the compilation of the Qur'an. He said: "The compilation of the Qur'an was something that was not addressed during his time (peace and blessings be upon him), but when disagreements about the Qur'an arose and became widespread to the extent that one would say to another: 'I disbelieve in what you read,' the compilation of the Qur'an became obligatory; otherwise, it would follow that examining every incident that did not occur in the earlier times would be considered an innovation (bid'a), which is unanimously false. However, such examination falls under the category of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) that aligns with the principles of the Sharia, even if there is no specific text supporting it, and this is what is referred to as public interest (maslaha). Everything that the righteous predecessors introduced in this regard does not differ from it in any way" (1). The evidence here is in his statement: "The compilation of the Qur'an became obligatory," as it was previously permissible, but a situation arose that put the preservation of the religion at risk unless the Qur'an was compiled. He said: "There is no text from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding what they did in this matter, but they saw it as a public interest that aligns with the actions of the Sharia, undoubtedly, as it pertains to the preservation of the Sharia, and the command to preserve it is well known, and to prevent the means to disagreement regarding its foundation, which is the Qur'an, and it is known that there is a prohibition against disagreement in that, with no further elaboration" (2).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/237.
(2) al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 2/377.


[Page 566]

Among the examples of necessities (hajiyat) is the liability of craftsmen. He said: "The rightly guided caliphs ruled that craftsmen should be held liable. Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'People cannot be right without that.' The rationale behind this necessity is that people have a need for craftsmen, and they are often absent from the goods, and they are mostly negligent and fail to safeguard them. If their liability were not established, despite the pressing need to employ them, it would lead to one of two outcomes: either a complete abandonment of contracting craftsmen, which would be burdensome for the people, or they would work without being held liable, claiming loss and destruction, leading to the loss of property, reduced caution, and the possibility of betrayal. Thus, the interest lies in establishing liability" (1). This example regarding the public interests (masalih mursala) is a subject of debate and has led to criticism of the principle, as it resulted in a false condition, which is the liability of the craftsman (2). The truth is that this does not pertain to the principle but rather to the disagreement over the detailed evidence. His statement here about the liability of craftsmen does not indicate that this matter is forbidden and permitted by the principle; rather, it is originally permissible, and due to the need to alleviate hardship, it became obligatory. Note his statement at the beginning of the example that the rightly guided caliphs did this; if this is authentic, it serves as a legal proof, as none of the Companions denied it. However, this is not authentic, and what he attributed to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) is not established (3).

And it was reported from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: 'There is no liability on a shepherd or on a trustee.' 11/109. Based on this, the principle of public interest (maslaha mursala) is a foundational principle of Islamic law according to al-Shatibi and is not a fifth source in itself; it is not a source of rulings but rather a legal methodology applied or utilized during deduction, similar to the principle of presumption of continuity (istishab), the principle of permissibility of things (asl fi al-ashya), or the principle of removing harm. However, if it is taken as a source of rulings such that the requirement of legislation becomes merely looking at whether an action is beneficial or harmful, or whether it is so with the slightest difficulty or cost, then this is a method of innovation (bid'ah) and not legislation.
Categories of interests:
Al-Shatibi discussed in his book (al-I'tisam) those who invoked public interest (maslaha mursala) for their violations and innovations, clarifying the matter further. He said: "Since the place is a slippery slope for the people of innovation to argue for their innovation from this angle, the right approach is to examine the basis of the error that occurs for these people until it becomes clear that public interest is not part of innovation in its origin or conclusion, by the will of Allah" (1). He then said: "The appropriate meaning that connects the ruling does not escape three categories:
The first is that the Sharia witnesses to its acceptance; there is no doubt about its validity nor disagreement in its application, otherwise it would contradict the Sharia, such as the law of retribution (qisas) for the preservation of lives and limbs, among others" (2). This is not part of public interest but rather what is considered either by the testimony of evidence or by the testimony of the ruling. For al-Shatibi, consideration is by the testimony of evidence, or by numerous rulings that collectively form evidence in his view, and consideration is not accepted by the testimony of few rulings.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 2/374.
(2) The same source.


[Page 569]

Then he said: "The second is what the Sharia has witnessed to reject; there is no way to accept it since the analogy does not necessitate the ruling for itself, but rather this is the view of the proponents of rational improvement. Rather, if the meaning becomes apparent and we understand from the Sharia that it is to be considered in necessitating rulings, then we accept it. For what we mean by public interest (maslaha) is what is understood to be taken into account in relation to people by bringing about benefits and repelling harms in a manner that reason cannot independently grasp. Therefore, if the Sharia does not witness the consideration of that meaning, but rather rejects it, it is rejected by the consensus of Muslims" (1). This text indicates that analogy is neither a proof of consideration nor a condition for it; rather, the proof of that is the Sharia's consideration of the meaning, which is understood through induction. This category here is the canceled analogy, so it has no consideration. Among the aberrations of this time, and among the tyranny of ignorance, are the statements and opinions that some consider fatwas, which permit prohibitions under the pretext that they are interests or aimed at interests, attributing this to the unregulated interests (masalih mursala) and to the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) and sometimes to al-Shatibi. How astonishing!
Then he said: "The third: what the specific evidences have remained silent about, neither witnessing its consideration nor its cancellation; this has two aspects: one of them is that a text is reported in accordance with that meaning, such as the reasoning for prohibiting killing for inheritance. The application of the opposite of the intended purpose is to assume that if a text is not reported in accordance with it, then this reasoning has no precedent in the actions of the Sharia by assumption nor in its compatible matters, such that there exists a recognized type for it; thus, it is not valid to reason with it, nor to base a ruling upon it by consensus. Such a thing is legislation by the one who claims it, so it cannot be accepted" (2).
__________
(1) The same source, and his statement: "the analogy does not necessitate the ruling for itself, but rather this is the view of the proponents of rational improvement" means that it is not permissible to argue based on public interest, but rather to argue based on the evidence that established this interest, whether the evidence is specific or not.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 2/375.


[Page 570]

The mentioned point in this regard often leads to error, as it is considered among the public interest (maslaha) based on its definition, which states that it is something that the Sharia has remained silent about, neither affirming nor negating it. Here, it is rejected, and consensus on this is conveyed. Then it clarifies what the public interests (masalih mursala) are that the specific evidences have remained silent about, neither affirming nor negating them, saying: "Secondly, it must align with the actions of the Sharia, which means that there exists a type of this meaning that the legislator has considered in general without specific evidence, which is the general reasoning known as public interests (masalih mursala)" (1).
Thus, it is incorrect to define public interests as those that the legislator has left unclarified and has not mentioned either affirmatively or negatively. With this definition, it is rejected without disagreement, and therefore, it is not correct to make a public interest a proof merely because it is a public interest. Rather, this is the view of the proponents of rational good and evil, and this issue is fundamentally resolved. Among the evidences in this topic is al-Shatibi's statement: "The correspondence does not necessitate a ruling for itself; rather, this is the view of the proponents of rational good." He also conveyed the consensus on the prohibition of reasoning solely based on public interest, even if it were not negated, as stated earlier regarding what the specific evidences have not affirmed or negated: "Thus, it is not correct to justify it or base a ruling upon it by consensus, and such a thing is legislation from the one who claims it, so it cannot be accepted." Al-Razi conveyed the consensus on this matter when he said: "It is appropriate, but does not align, nor does it have a specific foundational evidence; thus, this is rejected by consensus. An example of this is the disinheritance of the killer, opposing him with the contradiction of his intention, if we assume that there is no text regarding it" (2).
Conditions of the rule:
__________
(1) The same location.
(2) Al-Razi, al-Mahsool, 5/167.


[Page 571]

As for the conditions for applying the principle of public interest (maslaha mursala) and the contexts in which it is applied, he said there are three matters: "The first is that it must be compatible with the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in such a way that it does not contradict any of its fundamental principles or any of its evidences. The second is that the general consideration of it is based on what is rational and aligns with reasonable circumstances that, when presented to the intellects, are accepted. Thus, it has no place in acts of worship or matters that are similar to them in the realm of religious rulings" (1). "The third is that the essence of public interests returns to preserving a necessary matter and alleviating a necessary hardship in religion, and it also refers to preserving a necessary matter in the context of 'what is necessary for the fulfillment of an obligation.' Thus, it is a means and not an end, and its relation to alleviating hardship pertains to the realm of facilitation and not to that of strictness" (2). In matters of necessity, the ruling on an action based on public interest means that the action is a means to a known obligatory cause, and a condition for this is that the action itself is not obligatory in essence; otherwise, there would be no place for public interests. He states: "As for it being in the realm of necessity as a means, and what is necessary for the fulfillment of an obligation, if it is stipulated, then it is a legal condition, and thus it has no place in this regard because the text of the legislator has relieved us from further consideration. If it is not stipulated, then it is either rational or customary, and it does not necessarily have to be legal, just as it does not have to be in a known manner. For instance, if we assume the preservation of the Qur'an and knowledge without books is valid, that would be acceptable. Likewise, other necessary interests can be preserved, just as if we assume the attainment of the interest of the greater leadership without an imam, on the condition that there is no text regarding it, that would also be valid" (3). He then said: "If this is established, it is not valid to derive from its domain any of the religious objectives that are not means" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, Al-I'tisam, 2/386.
(2) The same source, 2/389.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.


[Page 572]

As for its application in necessities, he said: "And as for it being in the realm of necessity as a form of alleviation, this is also evident and is a stronger proof for lifting hardship, for there is nothing in it that indicates strictness or an increase in obligation" (1).
Based on this, the principle of public interest (maslaha) is not a justification for claiming that there is a zone of ambiguity in the Sharia or that there are matters about which the Sharia has remained silent without clarifying their ruling, and that rulings are applied based on public interests. Such a claim is rejected by al-Shatibi because the interests themselves can only be known through the Sharia. This is one aspect. On the other hand, there is nothing that the Sharia has remained silent about in the sense of not clarifying its ruling; rather, there are matters for which no specific evidence has been provided, but they are indicated by general principles and analogies. They fall under general or comprehensive rules, and there is no silence from the Sharia in the sense of lack of clarification. It has been previously established that the Sharia contains clarification of everything. Al-Shatibi said: "The silence of the legislator regarding a ruling is of two types: one is that he remains silent about it because there is no compelling reason for it or necessity for it, such as the events that occurred after the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), for these did not exist and then were silent about with their existence; rather, they occurred later, and the people of the Sharia needed to consider them and apply them based on what has been established in its general principles. What the righteous predecessors initiated falls under this category, such as compiling the Qur'an, recording knowledge, and the inclusion of craftsmen, and similar matters that were not mentioned during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and they were not among the events of his time nor was there a necessity for them to be acted upon. This category has its branches that follow its established principles in the Sharia without any doubt" (2).
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/288.


[Page 573]

This silence is not silence in the sense of not clarifying; rather, it is like the silence regarding the ruling on computers, the use of weapons of mass destruction, cars, or cloning. The clarification of these matters is not like the clarification of the ruling on carrion, jihad, marriage, or adultery, as they did not exist during the time of the Prophethood. However, their clarification exists in the Sharia, through the general texts and descriptions and reasons it has brought. This is the meaning of the silence mentioned here. As for the second category of what is left unaddressed, it states: "The second is that it is left unaddressed while the reason for it is present, and no ruling has been established regarding it at the time of the incident, beyond what was in that era. This type of silence is like a text indicating that the intention of the Legislator is not to add to it or reduce from it, because when this reason necessitating the establishment of a practical ruling is present and yet the ruling is not legislated in reference to it, it is explicit that any addition to what was there is an innovation (bid'a) and contrary to what the Legislator intended, as it is understood from His intention to remain at what was defined there, neither adding to it nor diminishing from it" (1). Therefore, al-Shatibi completely refutes the claim that public interest (maslaha) is a proof for the ruling of an action. He also counters what might be expected to be said, that public interest is the arbitration of interests in the areas where the Legislator has remained silent about clarifying them. He presents the rejected statement: "What is left unaddressed by the Legislator does not imply a contradiction nor does it indicate a specific intention from the Legislator without its opposite and contrary. If that is the case, we return to examining the aspects of interests; whatever we find to be beneficial, we accept it in the application of public interests, and whatever we find to be harmful, we abandon it in the application of public interests. What we do not find in this regard, either way, is like all other permissible matters in the application of public interests as well" (2).
__________
(1) The same location.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/289.


[Page 574]

Al-Shatibi's response to this is: "The explanation of the answer is what Malik mentioned, that silence regarding the ruling of an action or abstention here, when the meaning necessitating the action or abstention is present, is an agreement from all who are silent that there is nothing additional to what existed, which is the ultimate in this meaning" (1). He said: "The existence of the necessitating meaning along with the absence of legislation is evidence of the intent of the Legislator to not add to what was already present. If there is an addition, it becomes evident that it contradicts the intent of the Legislator, and thus it is invalid" (2). The implication of this statement and what preceded it is that if there is to be an addition or change, it must be according to the evidence of the Sharia and its principles.

In summary, the principle of public interest (maslaha) according to al-Shatibi is applied to jurisprudence that is based on the principle "what is necessary for the fulfillment of an obligation is itself an obligation" in matters of necessity, and on the principle of alleviating hardship in matters of need, and it does not apply in acts of worship.

Section Two
Istihsan

Istihsan and the positions of the imams regarding it:
Istihsan, according to al-Shatibi, is a foundational principle (usuli) like public interest (maslaha), and it is a method in applying evidence and in legal reasoning. Its definitions are varied and differ. Before delving into it in detail, it is worth noting that its essence does not stray from acting upon the stronger of two evidences when they conflict. This was affirmed by Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) and his followers. It is well-known that it was rejected by al-Shafi'i and the Shafi'is, who strongly criticized it, considering it mere preference based on opinion, or abandoning evidence for opinion. However, in its essence as understood by the Hanafis, they accept it and consider it an act based on evidence. The practice of istihsan has also been attributed to the two imams, Malik and Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them).
__________
(1) The same source, 2/289 - 290.
(2) The same source, 2/291.


[Page 575]

As for Imam Malik, al-Shatibi attributed to him in several places in the Muwafaqat that "istihsan (juridical preference) is nine-tenths of knowledge" (1). Al-Zarkashi said: "And from Ibn al-Qasim: Malik said: 'Nine-tenths of knowledge is istihsan.' Asbagh ibn al-Faraj said: 'Istihsan in knowledge can be more effective than qiyas (analogy)' "(2). Among what al-Zarkashi reported is: "The istihsan that Malik referred to is the opinion based on the stronger of the two evidences" (3). He also said: "Al-Abyari stated: What appears from Malik's school is the opinion of istihsan not as previously mentioned, but its essence is the use of a partial benefit (maslaha) in contrast to a general qiyas, thus preferring the unqualified evidence over the qiyas" (4).
As for Imam Ahmad, Dr. Abdullah bin Abdul Mohsen al-Turki clarified his position in his book (The Foundations of Imam Ahmad's School), where he cited the opinions of prominent Hanbalis and their imams regarding the principles, then concluded that the majority of them chose from the definitions of istihsan that it is abandoning qiyas for a stronger evidence than it, and some say it is the stronger of the two qiyas. They all, based on this definition, affirm istihsan and consider it, stating that it is the position of Ahmad and that it is not an independent evidence, but rather a matter of weighing the evidences against one another. However, if it is based on mere desire, they reject it and consider it as legislating what Allah has not permitted (5).

(1) Al-Shatibi, Muwafaqat, 4/118.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/387.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 4/388.
(5) Abdullah bin Abdul Mohsen al-Turki, The Foundations of Imam Ahmad's School, p. 570, a comparative foundational study, 4th ed., 1416 AH - 1996 CE, Al-Risalah Foundation, Beirut.


[Page 576]

As for al-Shafi'i, he rejected it as previously mentioned, saying: "And he does not say what is preferred, for saying what is preferred is something that is newly introduced without a previous example" (1). He also said: "Indeed, preference (istihsan) is mere indulgence" (2). His companions followed him in this. It has been said that the majority rejected it; al-Zarkashi said: "The majority rejected it to the extent that al-Shafi'i said: Whoever prefers has legislated" (3). He then said: "Our companions said: And whoever legislates has disbelieved, and al-Shafi'i remained silent about the second premise due to its clarity" (4). The correct view is that if it were mere indulgence and a statement in religion without evidence, the majority would not have rejected it alone; rather, Abu Hanifa and his companions would have rejected it as well. The rejection of preference became severe, even affecting Imam Abu Hanifa and his companions. Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari said: "Know that some of those who criticize Muslims have attacked Abu Hanifa and his companions - may Allah have mercy on them - for abandoning analogy (qiyas) in favor of preference, saying that the evidences of the Sharia are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy, and that preference is a fifth category that no one among the scholars of the Sharia, except for Abu Hanifa and his companions, has recognized as a proof of the Sharia, and no evidence has been established for it; rather, it is a statement based on desire. Thus, abandoning analogy for it is abandoning a proof to follow whims or the desires of the soul, which is invalid. He then said: If the analogy they abandoned for preference is a legal proof, then the legal proof is true, and what is after the truth except misguidance" (5). He said: "It has also been reported from al-Shafi'i that he was extreme in rejecting preference, saying: Whoever prefers has legislated, and all of this is an attack without reflection, and a criticism without understanding the intended meaning, for Abu Hanifa - may Allah have mercy on him - is of greater stature and more pious than to speak in religion based on desire" (6).
