(1) Al-Shafi'i, al-Risala, p. 25, paragraph 70.
(2) The same source, p. 507, paragraph 1464.
(3) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/386.
(4) The same location.
(5) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/4; see also: al-Sarakhsi, Usul al-Sarakhsi, 2/200.
(6) The same location.


[Page 577]

Zarkashi said: "Know that when the intended meaning of istihsan (juridical preference) is clarified, the criticism disappears, and Abu Hanifa is innocent before Allah of establishing a ruling without evidence" (1).
Al-Bazdawi said under the title: (The Chapter on Qiyas and Istihsan): "Both are of two types. As for one type of qiyas (analogy), it is that which has a weak effect, and the second type is that which has appeared to be corrupt while its validity and effect are concealed. One type of istihsan is that which has a strong effect, even if it is hidden. The second is that which has an apparent effect while its corruption is concealed. Istihsan, according to us, is one of the types of qiyas" (2).
From here, we understand that the istihsan criticized by al-Shafi'i and others is different from the istihsan advocated by Abu Hanifa. It should not be assumed that Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) or any respected imam would abandon the evidence of the Sharia for his opinion, nor would he speak about the Sharia based solely on his opinion without legal evidence. So what is the istihsan intended by the Hanafis?
What is istihsan:
There have been multiple definitions of istihsan among them, all of which revolve around the idea that istihsan is a process of specification, and it is applied when there is a conflict of evidence. It has been said regarding its essence that it is acting upon the stronger of the two qiyas, that it is the specification of the cause, and that it is the specification of qiyas by the Sunnah (3).
It has also been said that it is the separation of a matter from its counterparts due to a specific evidence that necessitates departing from the first ruling to the second, whether it is based on qiyas or text, as stated by Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi, and it has been said that this is the best explanation of istihsan (4).
It has been said that it is abandoning qiyas and adopting what is more convenient for the people (5).
__________
(1) Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/387.
(2) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi, 4/4.
(3) Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/390.
(4) Same source.
(5) Al-Jurjani, Al-Ta'rifat, p. 22, authored by the noble Sharif Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Ali al-Husayni al-Jurjani al-Hanafi, 816 AH. Edited by Muhammad Basel Ayyoun al-Sud. 1st ed. 1421 AH - 2000 CE, Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya, Beirut.


[Page 578]

The definition of al-Karakhi appears to be the most precise, as it encompasses all examples of istihsan (juridical preference). What reinforces this matter is that they say istihsan is one of the types of qiyas (analogy) or the strongest type of qiyas, but when they provide examples, we see them referring to the application of the general rule to its specific instances, or the general rule applying to its instances as qiyas, even though there is no qiyas or cause in the legal sense, which will become clear through the examples.
Categories of Istihsan:
They also categorize istihsan into sections, including istihsan based on the Sunnah, istihsan based on consensus (ijma), and istihsan based on necessity (darura). These examples do not involve qiyas, nor is it necessary for them to have any qiyas at all. Al-Bazdawi said: "Istihsan has categories, one of which is what is established by evidence, such as salam (forward sale) and ijara (lease), and the continuation of fasting with the action of the forgetful. Among them is what is established by consensus, which is istisna (manufacturing contract), and among them is what is established by necessity, which is the purification of water troughs, wells, and utensils" (1). The commentator in Kashf al-Asrar regarding istihsan based on evidence said: "For qiyas rejects the permissibility of salam because the subject of the contract, which is the object of the contract, is truly nonexistent at the time of the contract, and the contract does not take place outside its subject unless we abandon it based on the evidence that necessitates concession, which is the saying of the narrator: 'And he permitted salam' (2). And his saying, peace be upon him: 'Whoever among you sells, let him sell in a known measure' (3)." (4). His statement in the text: "For qiyas rejects salam" does not refer to legal qiyas, but rather to the generality of the text: "Do not sell what you do not possess" (5), which contradicts the sale of salam. Here, he refers to the application of the text to its instances as qiyas, where each instance is affirmed what is affirmed for others, which is the ruling. This is due to the generality of the text in its instances, so each instance takes the ruling of the other instance itself, as if the application of the ruling to all instances is qiyas. While the matter is, in reality, a general text that applies to its instances and is not qiyas.
__________
(1) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi, 4/6 - 7.
(2) See: the following hadith, footnote number (3).
(3) Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Salam, Chapter on Salam in a Known Measure (2086), and Muslim in the Chapter on Salam (3011), and al-Tirmidhi in the Sales (1232) and said: it is good and authentic, and Ahmad (1836), all with the wording of 'salam' instead of 'salam'. They are of the same meaning.
(4) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/7.
(5) Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Sales (1153), Abu Dawood in the Lease (3040), Ibn Majah in the Trades, Chapter on the Prohibition of Selling What You Do Not Possess and Earning What You Have Not Guaranteed (2178), and Imam Ahmad in the Musnad (4772).


[Page 579]

The specification in the sale of salam means that the text did not apply to the sale of salam, which is one of the forms of sale, so it was a specification of a general text and not a specification of analogy (qiyas). It is a separation of the sale of salam from its counterparts and granting it a ruling different from that of its counterparts. Therefore, it is said that the definition of Abu al-Hasan al-Karakhī is the most precise of definitions. The same applies to leasing (ijara) and the continuation of fasting (sawm); the lease contract is a contract for a benefit that does not exist at the time of the contract and is only fulfilled later. He believes that analogy necessitates the prohibition of the lease contract. The implication is that leasing is a type of sale, and applying the rules of sale to it contradicts the lease contract. This is what he calls analogy, and since the texts have permitted leasing, it takes precedence over analogy. This is, in fact, a specification, and specification always involves a conflict between the general and the specific. Here, there is a conflict between the general text that he called analogy and the specific text, which can also be referred to as its application in its instances as analogy. Therefore, this process of specification, in which the specific is given precedence over the general, is called acting according to the stronger of the two analogies, and he refers to it as istihsan (juridical preference). Some have called it acting according to the stronger of the two evidences. Hence, it was also said that the strongest opinion is the opinion of al-Karakhī: it is the separation of the issue from its counterparts, etc.
This is more clearly illustrated in his example regarding the continuation of fasting with the act of one who forgets. He said in Kashf al-Asrar: "Similarly, eating forgetfully invalidates the fast according to analogy because something cannot remain in existence with the presence of what contradicts it, like purity with ritual impurity and seclusion (i'tikaf) with exiting without necessity. However, it is set aside by the evidence, which is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): 'Continue your fast, for indeed Allah has fed you and given you drink' "(1), and this indicates the implication of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him): 'Were it not for the saying of the people, I would have said: he must make up the fast,' referring to the narration of the evidence "(2). Here, too, there is, in fact, no analogy that necessitates the invalidation of the fast, which means that what is meant by analogy is not the legal analogy in the technical sense, but rather the application of the ruling in all its instances. The ruling is that eating invalidates fasting, and eating forgetfully is still eating, so it should invalidate the fast. What is meant by analogy is the general text, and then it was specified by the evidence, so he did not rule on this eating as he would on its counterparts because it was forgetful eating, and the evidence exempted the forgetful person. Thus, istihsan was a specification and a separation of the issue from its counterparts.
__________
(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari (1797) with the wording: "Let him complete his fast, for indeed Allah has fed him and given him drink," and Muslim (1952), with the same wording, and Abu Dawood (2046).
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/7.


[Page 580]

As for istihsan (juridical preference) by consensus, it is exemplified by istisna (manufacturing contract). The point intended here is that the analogy (qiyas) in question implies the prohibition of istisna, but consensus (ijma) has indicated its permissibility, thus this is a specification by consensus. It is also said here that there is no analogy stronger than analogy itself; rather, there is a consensus that specifies the ruling. It is stated in Kashf al-Asrar: "Among the istihsan is what has been established by consensus, such as istisna, meaning in matters where people engage in transactions, like when a person orders someone to make him a shoe, for example, for a certain price, specifying its characteristics and size, without mentioning a deadline, and whether he hands over the money or not, it is permissible. The analogy implies its prohibition because it is a sale of something non-existent in the present, and it is non-existent in description in the liability. It is not permissible to sell something except after it has been specified in reality, that is, its establishment in liability like salam (forward sale). As for the absence from every aspect, a contract cannot be conceived, but they preferred to leave it by consensus established through the transactions of the community without objection."(1) This is also a specification, and it is not a specification of an analogy but rather of a generality. What is confirmed from this is that istihsan is a specification, and since specification is nothing but a conflict between generality and specificity, the action is taken according to the stronger of the conflicting parties. Therefore, istihsan is acting according to the stronger evidence, which is the specific one. Since it is an action based on the specific and a disregard for the general, it separates the issue from its counterparts and judges it with the specific ruling. The precedence of the specific effect over the general is istihsan. From this, it may be said: the abandonment of the evidence, meaning the general evidence, in favor of istihsan, which may lead one who does not scrutinize to think that it is an abandonment of the legal evidence in favor of personal opinion, but this is not the case at all. It was said: "If it is said: the consensus has opposed the text, which is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): 'Do not sell what you do not have.'"(2) We say: the text has become specific in regard to this ruling by consensus, so the analogy negating permissibility remains in opposition to the consensus, thus its consideration is nullified by the opposition of the consensus."(3)
__________
(1) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/7.
(2) Previously cited.
(3) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/8.


[Page 581]

As for the necessity of preference (istihsan) due to necessity, it is stated: "Among them is what is established by necessity, which is the purification of ponds, wells, and vessels. For analogy (qiyas) negates the purity of these things after they have become impure because it is not possible to pour water on the pond or well to purify it. Likewise, the water entering the pond or springing from the well becomes impure upon contact with the impure, and the bucket also becomes impure upon contact with the water, thus returning to a state of impurity. Similarly, the vessel, if it does not have a hole at its bottom to let the water out when poured from above, will have the impure water collect at its bottom, so its purity cannot be established. However, they preferred to abandon the application of the analogy due to the necessity that requires it for the general public. And necessity has an effect in the abrogation of the ruling" (1).
Here, too, there is no analogy in the legal sense, but rather it is a discussion of reality or the basis, which is that the water has become impure and will not be purified. However, this ruling of the impurity of ponds, vessels, and wells is difficult for the people, so it is ruled to be pure due to necessity. Thus, the ruling of their impurity is specified by necessity, and necessity has its ruling and effect in Sharia. This is a type of preference, and it is evident that it is a specification. It is also evident that it is not a specification of analogy nor an application of the stronger of the two analogies. Although they have referred to the abandoned ruling as analogy and the applied ruling as preference, it is a naming they have given while knowing that there is no analogy or cause. However, there may be a resemblance between the application of the ruling in its various instances by general evidence and the extension of the ruling to different places through the cause. Likewise, the importance of the cause lies in its effect on the ruling; if the effect of a thing appears, it resembles the cause in that regard. Al-Bazdawi said: "Our aim here is to categorize the aspects of causes in relation to rulings. When the cause becomes a cause by its effect, we call that which weakens its effect analogy and that which strengthens its effect preference, meaning a preferred analogy. We give precedence to the latter even if it is hidden over the former even if it is apparent, for the consideration is for the strength of the effect rather than its appearance and clarity" (2).
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 4/8.


[Page 582]

And if this is the concept of istihsan (juridical preference) according to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), then there is no disagreement between him and those who criticize istihsan. However, the question is: why this terminology? Is there a relationship between this term and the act of leaving the general for the specific or taking the stronger of the two evidences? Al-Zarkashi mentioned statements that indicate this inquiry, including: "The disagreement between us and them is merely verbal, for the interpretation of istihsan in a way that they criticize is not something they accept. What they do accept is the deviation in ruling from one evidence to another that is stronger than it. This is something that has not been denied. However, we do not recognize this name as a term for what is said based on such evidence" (1).
What I see regarding this matter is that this terminology may relate to a particularity within the school, as it is reported from Abu Hanifa and the majority of the school that they do not consider the specification of the general by the specific unless the specific is later than the general. If the general is the later one, it abrogates the specific. However, it may be unknown which is later, or it may be presumed that the general is later, but the specific is accompanied by indications that make it more impactful and necessitate its application in consideration and ijtihad (independent reasoning), such as when it is reported that the Companions practiced it. In this case, the principles of the school dictate adherence to the general and neglect of the specific, but the indications accompanying the specific strengthen it, and ijtihad leads to its application and the specification of the general by it. From here - and Allah knows best - expressions like: "what has a strong effect even if it is hidden" and "what has a visible effect and hidden corruption" emerge, and perhaps this is a valid justification for the use of the term istihsan.
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/388.


[Page 583]

As for what has been mentioned above regarding the principles of the school in general and specific matters, al-Bazdawi said: "Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The specific does not abrogate the general, but it is permissible for the specific to be abrogated by it" (1), and Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari said: "The response to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him) is that the general in establishing a ruling is like the specific, then if both are presented in a case and their dates are known, the latter is abrogating if it is the general and is a specification if it is the specific" (2).
If istihsan (juridical preference) is nothing but acting according to the Sharia and acting upon the stronger of the two evidences in cases of conflict, which is the specification, then there is no room for disparaging istihsan or those who advocate for it. However, it may be said that the examples presented for istihsan contain instances that appear to show a deviation from the evidence to something without evidence or a preference for the weaker over the stronger. The response is that this does not pertain to istihsan or its meaning, but rather it relates to the differences in jurisprudential opinions regarding the details of the evidence. A jurist may abandon what is considered evidence from the perspective of another, while it is not considered evidence from his own perspective, and he may advocate for an opinion that his opponent believes has no supporting evidence, leading to the misconception that it is mere caprice and following desires. Additionally, it may be that some followers of the school do not grasp the true statement of their Imam or his evidence, building upon that which is not valid, and this may serve as a pretext for disparaging the school.
Istihsan according to al-Shatibi:
__________
(1) Al-Bazdawi, Usul al-Bazdawi, 1/426.
(2) Alaa al-Din al-Bukhari, Kashf al-Asrar, 1/452.


[Page 584]

Al-Istihsan (juridical preference) according to al-Shatibi does not differ from what has been mentioned above except in that it is a general principle, and general principles are definitive. For him, istihsan is a departure from applying the general principle in one or some of its particulars. Accordingly, the ruling in this particular that deviates from the general must refer back to another general meaning; otherwise, this deviation is not valid. It is the removal of the particular from its dependence on one general to another general, and this is akin to a conflict between general principles or the specification of some general principles by others. General principles are definitive and do not conflict, nor can they be specified, as has been previously explained. Therefore, this conflict is not real but rather exists from one perspective or in one state rather than another. Similarly, specification, in his view, means clarification; thus, the specification of some general principles by others is the clarification of the limits and conditions of the application of each one.
As for the fact that istihsan is a definitive general principle and that which is preferred (mustahsan) refers to a meaning that is definitively established through induction, the evidence for it is akin to the evidence of the unqualified (mursal) evidence, as indicated by his statement: "For although it does not have a specific origin that testifies for the branch, it has a general origin that testifies for it. And the general origin, if it is definitive, may equal the specific origin or exceed it depending on the strength or weakness of the specific origin, just as it may be the case that in some issues, the ruling of all the specific origins that conflict in the matter of preference may exist. Likewise, the principle of istihsan according to Malik is based on this principle because its meaning refers to giving precedence to unqualified evidence over analogy" (1). He also said: "And what is based on this principle (i.e., the principle of the outcomes of actions) (2) is the principle of istihsan, which in Malik's school is taking a partial interest in opposition to a general evidence, and its implication is to return to giving precedence to unqualified evidence over analogy. For the one who prefers does not revert to mere taste or desire but rather to what is known of the intent of the Legislator in general in similar hypothetical matters, such as issues that analogy would require a matter unless that matter leads to the loss of an interest from another perspective or brings about a harm as well" (3). Thus, giving precedence to the partial interest over the general evidence is not istihsan based merely on opinion or desire but rather through the precedence of unqualified evidence; the partial interest refers back to a general meaning that is established by Sharia.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/16.
(2) The text in parentheses is an addition by the researcher.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/116.


[Page 585]

What has been reported from the Hanafis is that it is a preference for the narration (athar), consensus (ijma), or necessity (darura), and here it states the preference for the unqualified reasoning (istidlal al-mursal), which includes these things and others, as it encompasses every interest (maslaha) or meaning that returns to a general meaning through induction (istiqra). The general meanings in the outcomes of actions do not fall outside of necessities (darurat), needs (hajiyat), enhancements (tahsinat), and the complements of each. However, in istihsan (juridical preference) as in the unqualified interests, there is no effect of the interests or particulars that return to enhancements or their complements. It states: "This (i.e., istihsan or the preference for unqualified reasoning over analogy) often coincides with the necessary in relation to the needy, and the needy with the complementary, so that applying analogy absolutely in the necessary leads to hardship and difficulty in some of its instances, thus the place of hardship is exempted, as well as in the needy with the complementary, or the necessary with the complementary, which is evident" (1). Al-Shatibi has provided numerous examples of istihsan in his two books, al-Muwafaqat and al-I'tisam (2). He said: "There are many examples in the Sharia, such as the loan (qard), for it is usury (riba) in its essence because it is a dirham for a dirham for a term, but it has been permitted due to the convenience and expansion it provides to the needy, such that if it remained on the original prohibition, it would cause hardship for the obligated" (3). Thus, a dirham for a dirham for a term is forbidden in sale because it is one of the six usurious categories, and the generality of this ruling necessitates the prohibition of lending a dirham. The prohibition of usury relates to the preservation of wealth from necessities, while the permissibility of the loan relates to needs because needs revolve around expansion and facilitation. Therefore, this particularity, which is lending a dirham, did not follow the prohibition of usury in the necessary but followed the permissibility in the needy, and this is istihsan. If we understand that establishing whether it is from the necessities or from the needs returns to the induction of the texts of the Sharia and their outcomes, we realize that the process of specification or clarification here does not return to mere desire but to the Sharia, and likewise in other examples.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/116.
(2) The same source, 4/117 - 118, and al-I'tisam, 2/393 - 400.
(3) The same source, 4/117.


[Page 586]

He says, for example: "And similar to this is the combining of Maghrib and Isha prayers due to rain, the combining of prayers for a traveler, shortening the prayer, and breaking the fast during a long journey, as well as the prayer of fear and all other concessions that follow this path, for their essence returns to considering the outcome in achieving benefits or preventing harms in particular, where the general evidence would necessitate prohibiting that, for if we were to remain with the original general evidence, it would lead to the negation of what that evidence necessitated in terms of benefit" (1). And he said: "And similar to this is the exposure of private parts in medical treatment, partnership, and cultivation, even if the general evidence necessitates prohibition, and there are many things of this kind" (2). All these examples, even if they are said to be based on preference (istihsan), are ultimately referred back to the evidences of the Sharia. Therefore, after al-Shatibi presented examples of preference, he mentioned Ibn al-Arabi's interpretation of it, saying: "Ibn al-Arabi said in his interpretation of preference that it is the preference for abandoning the implications of the evidence through exception and concession due to opposition to what is opposed in some of its implications" (3).
Accordingly, it can be said about preference what was said about public interest (maslaha), which is that it is not a means to speak about the religion of Allah without evidence from the Sharia. Al-Shatibi said: "For preference can only be by one who prefers, which is either reason or the Sharia. As for the Sharia, its preference and disapproval have been settled because the evidences necessitated that, so there is no benefit in calling it preference, nor in establishing a definition for it that is additional to the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus, and what arises from them in terms of analogy and reasoning. Thus, only reason remains as the one who prefers; if it is based on evidence, then there is no benefit in this naming as it returns to the evidences and not to anything else, and if it is without evidence, then that is the innovation that is preferred" (4). His intention is that there is no benefit in speaking about the Sharia without evidence, even if one claims that it is preference, and whoever thinks that he is preferring in that way is indeed innovating.
The difference between public interest (maslaha) and preference (istihsan):
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) The same place.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/116.
(4) Al-Shatibi, al-I'tisam, 2/390.


[Page 587]

The difference between public interest (maslaha mursala) and juristic preference (istihsan) is that public interest is based on the principle that what is necessary for fulfilling an obligation is itself an obligation for achieving something in necessities, and on the principle of alleviating hardship in needs. As for juristic preference, it involves the specification of the necessary by the need or by the complementary, or the specification of the need by the complementary. Accordingly, they may converge in some cases. The issue may become ambiguous as to whether it is from public interest or from juristic preference, or it may be validly associated with both principles, in the case where the alleviation of hardship in needs from public interest coincides with the specification of needs from juristic preference.
An example of this is what al-Shatibi mentioned among his examples of istihsan (juridical preference), which is the liability of the common worker. He said: "The abandonment of evidence for a benefit, as in the liability of the common worker, even if he is not a craftsman, for the position of Malik in this matter is based on two opinions, like the liability of the bathhouse owner for the garments"(1). Then he said: "If it is said: This is from the category of maslaha mursal (unrestricted public interest) and not from the category of istihsan, we say: Yes, except that they framed istihsan as an exception to the rules, unlike masalih mursal. Such a situation can be envisioned in the matter of liability, as the workers are entrusted by evidence and not by original innocence, so their liability falls within the scope of the exception from that evidence, thus it is included under the meaning of istihsan in that regard"(2).


The Third Section
Blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i)


Definition:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, Al-I'tisam, 2/394.
(2) The same place, 2/394.


[Page 588]

The blocking of means (sadd al-dhara'i) is the prohibition of what is permissible in order to prevent reaching what is prohibited. Al-Shatibi said: "It pertains to the request to abandon what has been established as a request to perform due to a hindrance that arises, and this is a principle generally agreed upon" (1). Al-Zarkashi quoted: "It is the issue that appears to be permissible but leads to the commission of the prohibited, such as selling an item for one hundred on credit and buying it back for fifty in cash; thus, he has reached fifty by mentioning the item" (2). Al-Qarafi said: "Blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) means cutting off the sources of corrupt means to prevent them. Whenever an action that is free from corruption serves as a means to corruption, the owner is prohibited from that action in many cases" (3). The means (dhara'i) are actions that are causes for others, thus they are means. Al-Qarafi said: "And sometimes the means are referred to as dhara'i, which is a terminology of our scholars" (4).
The position of the schools of thought on blocking the means:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/126.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 4/382.
(3) Al-Qarafi, al-Furuq, 2/32. Difference 58.
(4) The same source.


[Page 589]

Al-Qarafi said: "The blocking of means (sadd al-dhara'i) is not a distinctive feature of the Maliki school as many Malikis mistakenly believe. Rather, the means are divided into three categories: the first category is one that the ummah has unanimously agreed to block and prohibit, such as digging wells in the paths of Muslims, as it is a means to their destruction, and likewise, poisoning their food and insulting idols when it is known that such insults are directed at Allah, Exalted is He. The second category is one that the ummah has unanimously agreed not to prohibit, as it is a means that should not be blocked, such as preventing the cultivation of grapes for fear of wine, as no one has ever said this. Similarly, preventing cohabitation in houses for fear of adultery. The third category is one in which scholars have differed on whether it should be blocked or not, such as deferred sales in our view, like someone who sells a commodity for ten dirhams to be paid in a month, having bought it for five before the month. Malik says that he has given away five now and will take ten at the end of the month, so this is a means of lending five for ten with a deferred payment by means of showing the form of sale for that. Al-Shafi'i says that one should look at the form of the sale and take the matter at face value, so it is permissible. These sales are said to reach a thousand issues that are specific to Malik, in which he disagreed with Al-Shafi'i."(1)
Similarly, Abu Hanifa disagrees with the Malikis in this regard, as his opinion on the permissibility of legal tricks (hiyal) means he does not adhere to blocking means. Although those who advocate for it are the Malikis, others disagree with them, Al-Shatibi, Al-Qarafi, and others say that it is applied by all, and the intention is: in some cases. These are the cases that fall under the first category of the three categories of means mentioned by Al-Qarafi.
__________
(1) Al-Qarafi, Al-Furuq, 2/32. Difference 58.


[Page 590]

The principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) is based, according to al-Shatibi, on the foundation of the outcomes of actions (mālat al-afʿāl). This means that if an action leads to something forbidden or prohibited, then it may be deemed necessary to prohibit that action. The means that are blocked are actions that, upon consideration, necessitate their prohibition based on the outcome. However, this generalization does not apply uniformly in Islamic law, and the majority of legal theorists (usuliyyin) argue against it. Nevertheless, al-Shatibi states that both al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa have applied this principle, even though it is explicitly stated by them that it is rejected. He mentions that the scholars have agreed on its application in general, and it is consistent among them. The disagreement lies only in certain cases. He responded to al-Qarafi regarding the contention among scholars about considering the blocking of means: "There are many arguments they use, but they do not benefit, as they indicate the consideration of the law in blocking the means in general, which is a consensus. The dispute is only about specific means, such as deferred sales and the like" (1). He said: "As for al-Shafi'i, it is presumed that he has conducted a general induction regarding the means" (2). He stated: "As for Abu Hanifa, if it is established that he permitted the use of legal tricks (hiyal), then his original stance on deferred sales is only permissibility, and this does not necessitate abandoning the principle of blocking the means, and this is clear" (3). He also said: "The scholars have relied on this meaning and made it a principle that is consistent, which returns to the blocking of means that the scholars have agreed to apply in general, even if they differ in details" (4). Since the induction of legal rulings prevents the unrestricted assertion of prohibiting the permissible to avoid leading to the prohibited, al-Shatibi concluded that the means are divided into three categories, which are the same categories mentioned earlier regarding al-Qarafi: some means are blocked by consensus, some are not blocked by consensus, and some are disputed.
Evidence for the principle:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 3/173.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source, 3/188.


[Page 591]

Al-Shatibi holds that the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) is definitive through induction and is applied. It is indicated by the meanings of the rulings derived from the texts, such as His saying, Exalted is He: {And do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge.} (1). And His saying, Exalted is He: {O you who have believed, do not say [to the Messenger], "Consider us," but say, "Look at us," and listen.} (2). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in the authentic narration: "Indeed, among the greatest sins is cursing a man's parents." They said, "O Messenger of Allah, can a man curse his parents?" He said, "Yes, he insults the father of a man, and thus he insults his father, and he insults his mother, and thus he insults his mother." (3). And he (peace be upon him) refrained from killing the hypocrites because it would lead to the hypocrites saying, "Muhammad is killing his companions." (4) (5).
__________
(1) Surah Al-An'am, 108.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 104.
(3) Bukhari (5516) with the wording "curses" instead of "curses," and Muslim (130) with the same wording, and Tirmidhi (1824), who said: Hasan Sahih, and Ahmad (6243).
(4) Bukhari (3527) and (4525), and Muslim (4682) and (1761), which mention the hypocrites and the Khawarij, and Tirmidhi (3237) who said: Hasan Sahih, and Ahmad (14292).
(5) For a review of the evidence for the principle according to Al-Shatibi, see Al-Muwafaqat: 1/72, 2/250, 3/126, 127.


[Page 592]

The principle is also based on what is called the principle of cooperation, and one of its evidences is His saying, Exalted is He: { And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression } (1). Thus, an action that is permissible, if it leads to something forbidden, is a means to it and is considered as assisting in the forbidden objective; therefore, the means takes the ruling of the objective. If it leads to something that is commanded, it is a means to righteousness and assists in the legally required objective, and it also takes the ruling of the objective. If the action is not a means to anything, it is the absolute permissible (mubah). He said: "The permissible, as it is permissible, is equal on both sides" (2). Then he said: "If it is a means to something prohibited, it becomes prohibited in terms of blocking the means, not in terms of being permissible" (3). Then he said that the permissible: "is of three categories: one category is a means to something forbidden, and thus from that perspective, it is required to be abandoned. A second category is a means to something commanded, like what is assisted in an otherworldly matter" (4). Then he said: "A third category is not a means to anything, and it is the absolute permissible. In general, if it is assumed to be a means to something else, its ruling is the ruling of that other thing" (5). It must be noted that the action he is discussing is the action that is originally permissible. And his saying: "in general" means that it is not absolute. For often an action does not take the ruling of the objective. And when the outcome or objective is prohibited and the action takes the ruling of the objective based on the principle of cooperation, this is also an application of the principle of blocking the means. He said: "The principle of blocking the means applies based on the principle of cooperation in obedience or disobedience, for this principle is agreed upon in consideration, and there are matters in which there is disagreement, such as the means in sales and similar matters, although the principle of blocking the means is also agreed upon, and it also includes the principle of conflicting original and predominant" (6).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 2.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/71.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/71.
(4) The same source, 1/72.
(5) The same location.
(6) The same source, 3/126, 127.


[Page 593]

And the discussion on the conflict between the original ruling and the predominant ruling will come within the discussion of the controls of the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i).
Controls for applying the principle of blocking the means:
The place for applying the principle is in the permissible (mubah), as has been clarified. It is in the permissible that leads to something forbidden (haram). However, this is not applicable to any permissible act, nor to any manner of reaching the forbidden, nor to any forbidden act. Therefore, it is necessary to specify the controls and restrictions for applying this principle.
The first control:
That the permissible act is not permissible due to necessity or need. For what is such, opposing it with the forbidden outcome or with any objections it may encounter from evils is not valid. This is because the assumption is that the obligated person is compelled to it, and necessities are generally excused in the Sharia. In fact, this permissible act may have become obligatory, such as consuming carrion in a state of starvation, or it is needed to the extent that if it is abandoned, hardship will ensue. The Sharia has indicated the removal of hardship, and prohibiting an action due to its outcome leads to hardship for the obligated person. This indicates that the permissible action taken out of necessity or need is not a place for applying the principle of blocking the means.


[Page 594]

This does not only pertain to cases of necessity or hardship but also to what serves a necessary or need-based purpose, such as marriage, which necessitates the sustenance of dependents and may lead to obtaining sustenance through what Allah has forbidden, as well as walking to mosques and in public places where the walker may encounter hearing forbidden things and seeing nakedness. Preventing marriage and walking in the markets places the obligated person in a hardship that the legislator has alleviated and leads to the prohibition of what is originally permissible. He said: "What is originally permissible due to necessity or need is subject to opposing circumstances that may affect the original permissibility, either in reality or in expectation, whether it reverts to the original permissibility through negation or not? This is a matter of consideration and difficulty. The ruling on it is that it is either that one is compelled to that permissible act or not, and if one is not compelled, then either one experiences hardship from leaving it or not. These are three categories. The first is that one is compelled to perform that permissible act, so it is necessary to revert to that original and not consider the opposing circumstance" (1). "The second category is that one is not compelled to it but experiences hardship from leaving it, so the consideration necessitates reverting to the original permissibility and disregarding the emergencies, as the prohibited things have been permitted to alleviate hardship" (2). As for the third category, "it is that one is not compelled to the original permissibility and does not experience hardship from leaving it; this is a matter of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), and the principle of means (dhara'i) applies based on the original cooperation on obedience or disobedience" (3).
However, al-Shatibi elaborates on the second category, which is when leaving the permissible act places the obligated person in hardship, as the hardship in undertaking actions or refraining from them is not of a single degree, and the Sharia has not come to remove all hardship; the harm of the hardship resulting from prohibiting the permissible may be less than the harm of engaging in the prohibited outcome. Al-Shatibi questions: "Does the hardship that follows from leaving the original act equate to the hardship that follows from engaging with the opposing circumstances or not?" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/124.
(2) The same source, 1/125.
(3) The same source, 1/126.
(4) The same source, 1/125.


[Page 595]

The answer - according to his methodology - is that what is originally permissible serves a necessary, need-based, or enhancement principle, and the prohibited outcome is also a servant to a necessary, need-based, or enhancement principle, and its occurrence is contrary to the occurrence of the original permissible. If the permissible action - which is a cause - and the prohibited outcome are both referring to or serving the same original principle, then this is not a place for applying the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i), because the prohibition pertains to the complements of the original and not to the original itself, while the permissible refers to the original. Therefore, it is preferable not to consider what pertains to the complement, and it has been established in the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) that the collapse of the complement does not destroy the original, whereas the collapse of the original does destroy its complements. Thus, here too, the permissible remains permissible and is not affected by incidental matters. However, if the permissible and the prohibited outcome refer to two different originals, then this is something where the outcome may be considered, but it is not in the context of blocking the means; rather, it is in the context of conflict and preference.
Al-Shatibi, responding to the aforementioned question, says: "The absence of incidental matters concerning this original must either be a complement to it in its category or from another category that is an original in itself. If it is the latter, then it is either actual or anticipated. If it is anticipated, it has no effect in the presence of hardship, because hardship from abandonment is actual and is a corruption, while the corruption of the incidental matter is anticipated and imagined, thus it does not oppose the actual at all. As for if it is actual, it is truly a matter of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), and the corruption of the incidental matters therein may be greater than the corruption of abandoning the permissible, and the matter may be the opposite, and the consideration here pertains to conflict and preference. If it is the first case, then there is no valid conflict nor equivalence of the two corruptions, rather the corruption of losing the original is greater, and the evidence for this is as follows: one, that the complement with its complement is like the attribute with the attributed" (1). He then said: "And if the loss of the attribute does not return with the loss of the attributed in general, unlike the opposite, the side of the attributed is stronger in existence and non-existence" (2). "And the second is that the original with its complements is like the universal with the particular, and it is known that when the universal is opposed by the particular, the particular has no effect; likewise here, the corruption of losing the complement has no effect in the presence of the benefit of the complemented" (3).
Thus, the first criterion for applying the principle is established, which is "that one should not be compelled to the original permissible nor should hardship be attached to abandoning it; this is a place for ijtihad and the principle of blocking the means applies here" (4).
As for his statement: "this is a place for ijtihad," it indicates that in this case there are two opinions: one considers the original permissibility and does not consider the opposing incidental matter, while the other considers the opposing incidental matter and negates the permissibility to block the means.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/126.
(2) The same source.
(3) The same source.
(4) The same source.


[Page 596]

He says: "For one who argues based on the principle of permissibility that the original permission relates to a necessary meaning, it has been established that the essence of permissibility, which is choice, is a reality that pertains to necessities, and it is the foundation of interests (masalih); it is, in effect, a servant to them, if it is not, in reality, the same as them. Thus, considering the opposition in the permissible is akin to considering the opposition of the necessary in general, even if it does not appear in detail to be necessary. If this is the case, then the side of the permissible becomes more preferable than its opposition" (1).
As for the second opinion, it states: "For the one who favors the side of the opposition, he may argue that the interest of the permissible, inasmuch as it is permissible, is optional in its attainment or non-attainment, which is evidence that it does not reach the level of necessities. It is always so, because once it reaches that level, it would no longer be optional" (2). What al-Shatibi intends to indicate by presenting these two opinions is to point out that the one who does not apply the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) here does not do so because he does not accept the principle, but rather because blocking the means was deemed less preferable.
For further detail on this principle, one can refer to what al-Shatibi has elaborated regarding the ruling of permissibility, which is that the permissible may be permissible in part, recommended in total, or permissible in part, obligatory in total, or permissible in part, disliked in total, or permissible in part, prohibited in total. What is permissible in part and recommended or obligatory in total is the permissible for necessity or need, and in this case, the principle of blocking the means does not apply. It remains that if the principle of blocking the means is to be applied, it is applied to what is permissible in part, disliked or prohibited in total.
The second principle:
That the means to the prohibited is intended by the obligated in the permissible action. If this is the case, the permissible action becomes non-permissible.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/127.
(2) The same source.


[Page 597]

If an action is permissible in its essence, this means that it has a desired outcome which is intended by the legislator in enacting the action. If another intention is concomitant with this intended outcome, then this other outcome is either permitted or prohibited. If it is permitted, there is no issue; but if it is prohibited, this means that both a command and a prohibition converge on two concomitant outcomes, which is the subject here.
Al-Shatibi states that one of the intentions is subordinate while the other is the principal one, and the ruling is that of the principal one, with its subordinate being attached to it in ruling. This is similar to contracts concerning properties and their benefits; for instance, a contract for ownership of the land entails that the benefits of the land are subordinate to the ownership. Conversely, a contract for the benefits of the land means that the ownership is subordinate to the benefits in some manner, but not entirely. He said: "If the benefits are what is intended, then the ownership is subordinate as it is a means to the intended goal. If he meant that it is entirely subordinate to them, then that is prohibited" (1). He then said: "And if he meant some form of subordination, that is accepted and does not entail any prohibition, for general matters are related to their particulars in some way, and this does not necessitate their complete subordination to them" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/101.
(2) The same source, 3/102.


[Page 598]

This example is to demonstrate al-Shatibi's intended meaning regarding the ruling of the principal (matbu) and its application to the subordinate (tabi). The mentioned issue is based on the assumption of the permissibility of the contract on the person (raqabah) and its permissibility on the benefit, such that if a contract is established on one of them, the other is considered subordinate to the contracted matter, meaning that the subordinate and the principal, which are interrelated, are both permissible. Our issue is whether one of the interrelated matters is permissible and the other is prohibited. In this case, al-Shatibi also states that the ruling applies to the principal, and the subordinate is given the same ruling. He says: "When a command and a prohibition pertain to interrelated matters, and one of them is commanded and the other is prohibited in the case of separation, and one of them is in the status of a subordinate to the other in existence and non-existence, then what is considered from the two implications is what pertains to the principal, while what pertains to the subordinate is nullified and has no legal consideration" (1).
For example, the purchase of grapes may be intended for a permissible purpose, such as eating, or it may be intended for something prohibited, such as making intoxicants. The purchase of a female slave may be intended for concubinage or for service, or it may be intended for prostitution. So, which of the intended purposes is the one that is considered, and which is the principal and which is the subordinate? The intention of the obligated person is not something that can be discerned; it is a purpose that varies from person to person, and this is something that the jurist does not know. Rather, the obligated person is the jurist of himself and knows the prohibition of his action from his intended unlawful purpose. Therefore, the jurist in such cases looks at what is primarily intended according to common understanding and custom, and that is the principal, while he nullifies the consideration of the subordinate and gives the ruling based on the principal. For instance, the original intention behind the purchase of grapes, according to common understanding and custom, is not for wine; the purchase of weapons is not for highway robbery; and the purchase of a female slave is not for prostitution, thus this purchase remains permissible.
__________
(1) The same source, 3/96.


[Page 599]

The original ruling regarding the purchase of wine is, by custom and habit, that it is for drinking, and thus it remains prohibited even if the intention is to ferment it. The same applies to the purchase of the fat of carrion, even if the intention is to use it for painting ships or for lighting. Accordingly, al-Shatibi does not see in the meaning of the principle the prohibition of what is permissible merely because the obligated person may intend to use it to reach something prohibited, even if the intended purpose is religiously forbidden. He says: "In the matter of dependency, what is related to it in terms of demand is disregarded; likewise here, unless the contracting party has a specific intention towards the prohibited, for this has two possibilities: the first is to consider the original intention and disregard the dependent one even if it is intended, and the second is to consider the incidental intention if it becomes prior or as if it were prior, and anything else is like the dependent, so the ruling applies to it. An example of the original permissibility of benefits is the purchase of a female slave with the intention of converting her to prostitution for profit, and the purchase of a boy for immoral acts, and the purchase of grapes to press into wine, and weapons to rob, and some items for deception. In terms of the original prohibition of benefits, the purchase of a dog for hunting and for grazing and farming according to the opinion of those who prohibit that. The purchase of carrion to destroy farms, and the purchase of wine for fermentation, and the purchase of carrion to paint ships or for people to use for light, and similar matters. The regulated principle is the first, and the evidence for it is more, because considering what is intended in terms of originality and habit is what has been established in the Sharia regarding what is intended for permissibility and prohibition, for the purchase of a female slave for benefit in concubinage if she is from the noble class of slaves, or for service if she is from the low class, and the purchase of wine for drinking, and carrion, blood, and pork for eating is the common and usual practice among the Arabs to whom the Qur'an was revealed. Therefore, the related matters of prohibition and permissibility are omitted in the verse: { Prohibited to you are your mothers } (1), until the verse: { And lawful for you is what is beyond that } (2)."(3).
__________
(1) Surah An-Nisa, 23.
(2) Surah An-Nisa, 24.
(3) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 3/108.


[Page 600]

And his statement above: "And the regulated is the first" means that if some of those obligated (mukallaf) show an intention towards the prohibited, they are not judged by that, but rather by what is original or the original intention, which is predominant by custom and habit in society.
Then he said: "If the follower becomes predominant in intention and precedes in the custom of some times until what was originally the case becomes like the nonexistent, then the ruling changes. I do not think this can happen universally, but if it is assumed to happen, the ruling changes. The principle remains established as it was set in the Sharia, and if it does not happen but the intention towards the follower is prevalent, then the original consideration is what is intended like it by custom. The matter is generally disputed regarding the two possibilities, and the principle of means (dhara'i) is also based on the precedence of intention towards the prohibited" (1).
These texts clarify al-Shatibi's intent regarding the intended follower; it is not specifically the intention of the obligated person but rather the intention of the general public regarding the action. If the custom in society changes such that the original intention of someone buying grapes is that they buy them for wine, and for someone buying weapons that they buy them to commit robbery, then the ruling changes accordingly to the change in intention, and the follower becomes the followed. The considered intention is the original intention, and the ruling follows it. Al-Shatibi's statement: "And the principle of means is also based on the precedence of intention towards the followed" means that this reversal in ruling is supported by the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i). This is the meaning of the second criterion for applying the principle, which is the emergence of intention towards that in society such that it becomes the original and everything else is the exception. What strengthens the consideration of this criterion for him is his statement: "For the principle of means is strengthened here since the intention towards the prohibited has been established" (2).
The third criterion:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/109 - 110.
(2) The same source, 3/110.


[Page 601]

The third criterion for applying the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) according to al-Shatibi is that the action permitted by Sharia must lead to harm frequently, not rarely. If its leading to harm is rare, then this does not render it prohibited; that is, the jurist does not issue a fatwa declaring it unlawful. Even if this harm is intended for a specific accountable person, this is something the jurist cannot ascertain and thus cannot rule upon. The condition that the leading to harm must be frequent, not rare, is based on the principle that rulings are made based on the majority, not the rare occurrences, just as the intention is considered based on what is commonly prevalent in society.
If the action leads to the unlawful frequently, it may be predominant, or it may be frequent but not predominant or rare; this is treated as predominant in his view and is prohibited under the principle of blocking the means if the first two criteria are met (1).
This condition has appeared in several places in al-Shatibi's book, most clearly in his elaboration on the principle of removing harm. Below is an explanation of how al-Shatibi applies the principle of removing harm and the overlap between it and the principle of blocking the means.
The principle of removing harm:
Due to the detailed nature of this principle, a structured format with numbers will be used to indicate the various cases of its application and to clarify the instances of blocking the means within it.
Al-Shatibi states in his discussion of the fifth issue regarding the objectives of the accountable person in obligation (2):
"Bringing about benefit or repelling harm, if permitted, is of two types:
1. One type is that it does not result in harming others.
The second type is that it does result in harming others, and this second type is of two categories:
2. One category is when the one bringing about the benefit or repelling the harm intends that harm, such as the one permitted in his commodity with the intention of seeking his livelihood, and his intention includes harming others.
The second category is when he does not intend to harm anyone, which is of two types:
3. One type is when the harm is general, such as receiving goods and selling to those present for those absent, and refraining from selling his house or land when people are in need of it for a mosque or otherwise.
The second type is when the harm is specific, which is of two kinds:
__________
(1) This criterion will be clarified by explaining the principle of removing harm.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/241.


[Page 602]

4. One of them is that the buyer or the defender incurs harm from being prevented from that action, so he is in need of performing it, like the one defending himself against an injustice that he knows will befall another, or rushing to purchase food or something he needs, or to hunt, or to gather firewood, or water, or anything else, knowing that if he obtains it, another will be harmed by its absence; and if it is taken from his hand, he will be harmed.
The second: that he does not incur harm from it, and this is of three types:
5. One of them is what leads to a certain harm, meaning a normal certainty, such as digging a well behind the door of the house in the dark, so that anyone entering will inevitably fall into it, and similar situations.
6. The second: that which its performance leads to harm rarely, such as digging a well in a manner that does not usually result in someone falling into it, and consuming foods that are mostly not harmful to anyone, and similar matters.
The third: what is performed that leads to harm frequently rather than rarely, and it has two aspects:
7. One of them is that it should be predominant, like the sale of weapons from the people of war, and grapes from the wine seller, and what is mixed with it by those whose nature is to deceive, and similar matters.
8. The second condition is that it should be abundant but not predominant, like the issue of deferred sales.
These are eight categories"(1).
Then al-Shatibi clarifies the ruling in each of these eight sections and establishes that the last two sections, the seventh and eighth, are where the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) is applied. The following is a statement of his opinion on each of these sections, assisted by the numbers placed next to each section and the diagram drawn after three pages:
1 - The first section: Al-Shatibi says, "As for the first, it remains on its original basis of permission, and there is no doubt about it"(2).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/241 - 242.
(2) The same source, 2/242.


[Page 603]

2 - The second section: He says: "As for the second, there is no doubt about the prohibition of intending harm in itself, as there is evidence that there is no harm and no reciprocating harm in Islam. However, the consideration remains regarding this action that combines the intention of benefiting oneself and the intention of harming others. Should it be prohibited, thus becoming impermissible, or does it remain under its original ruling of permissibility while the one who intends it bears the sin of their intention? Al-Shatibi believes that this is a matter where disagreement can be imagined and where detailed ijtihad (jurisprudential reasoning) is possible. If preventing the obligated person from acting does not prevent them from achieving their goal through another action, then there is no doubt about their prohibition, as there is no meaning in insisting on the first action except to harm others. However, if they have no alternative to the first action, their right to act takes precedence over the right of others to eliminate the harm, but they remain prohibited from the intention" (1).
3 - The third section: He states: "If the harm is general and unintended, in this case, it is considered. If preventing the action leads to harm that cannot be compensated, then their right takes precedence absolutely, and the action remains permissible. If it can be compensated, then considering the general harm is preferable, and they are prohibited from the action. He said: 'They have increased in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) from other than what its people approved and what they did not. This necessitates prioritizing the public interest over the private interest, but in a way that does not cause harm to the private interest'" (2).
4 - The fourth section: He says: "The right of the one who brings or repels is prioritized even if it causes harm to others, because bringing benefit or repelling harm is desired and intended by the legislator" (3). He said: "Thus, it has become clear that prioritizing the right of the one who is late over the one who is early is not intended by the Sharia except with the waiver of the right of the one who is early, and that is not obligatory for them" (4).
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) The same source, 2/243.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/243.
(4) The same place.


[Page 604]

5 – The fifth category: It is that the action permitted by Sharia leads to a certain harm and that this harm is not intended. It is said that the one who brings about the benefit or averts the harm, if he acts without paying attention to the consequences and without intending to cause harm, and only focused on the fact that the action is permitted, then it is permissible and there is no prohibition in it. However, if he is aware that his action will cause harm to others while he does not suffer harm from refraining from it, then he is prohibited from acting. If he proceeds with the action, he is considered to have transgressed and is liable for the damages of the transgressor in general. Al-Shatibi does not conceive of such an action except in two cases: the first is that the one bringing about the benefit or averting the harm has failed to consider the required perspective, and the second is that he intends to cause harm himself, and both are prohibited by Sharia (1).
6 – The sixth category: He says, "As for the sixth, it is that its outcome leads to harm rarely; it is, in its essence, permitted because if the benefit is predominant, then the rarity of its breach is not considered" (2). He then said, "Thus, the action remains based on the principle of permissibility" (3).
7 – The seventh category: It is when the action leads to harm frequently and predominantly, he says: "It is what leads to harm in a way that is probable, and it allows for disagreement; either the original ruling is permissibility and allowance as previously mentioned in the sixth, or the harm and corruption are likely to occur" (4). Al-Shatibi sees here the application of probability and the lifting of the principle of permission and permissibility. He says: "However, considering probability is more preferable for several reasons: one of them is that probability in matters of actions is treated like knowledge, and it seems to apply here. The second is that what is explicitly stated regarding the prohibition of means is included in this category, such as His saying, Exalted is He: { And do not insult those they invoke besides Allah, lest they insult Allah in enmity without knowledge }" (5) etc., and he mentioned some evidences for the principle of prohibiting means.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/249.
(2) The same source, 2/250.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.
(5) Surah Al-An'am, 108.


[Page 605]

Al-Shatibi mentions in this section that the prevailing principle here is the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) more than the principle of removing harm (raf' al-darar), based on the fact that the obligated person does not intend harm but rather seeks permissible benefits. Therefore, the principle of blocking the means operates on the basis that the intention of harm, which is prohibited, has become the norm, and it has become predominant in this action that it cooperates in sin and transgression or is a ruse (1).
8 - The eighth section: He says, "As for the eighth, which is that its performance leads to corruption frequently, not predominantly or rarely, this is a matter of consideration and ambiguity, and the original ruling is to carry it on the basis of the validity of permission, as per the school of al-Shafi'i and others. This is because knowledge and suspicion of the occurrence of corruption are absent, as there is only a mere possibility between occurrence and non-occurrence, and there is no evidence to favor one side over the other. The possibility of intending corruption and harm does not equate to the actual intention nor necessitate it" (2). He said, "Moreover, it is not correct to consider the one who brings or pushes it here as negligent or intentional, as in knowledge and suspicion, because carrying it on the intention towards them is no more valid than carrying it on the lack of intention towards either of them. If that is the case, then the permitted causation is very strong" (3). What he has stated indicates the continuation of the action on its original permissibility, although he leans towards applying the principle of blocking the means based on the fact that Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) applied it here. He then mentioned examples that justify or permit the application of blocking the means, but not necessitating it. He said, "If that is the case, then the permitted causation is very strong, except that Malik considered it in blocking the means based on the frequency of intention in occurrence" (4). He then said, "The Sharia is based on precaution, taking measures, and guarding against what may lead to corruption. If this is known in general and in detail, then acting upon it is not an innovation in the Sharia, but rather it is a principle of its principles that relates to what is complementary, whether it is necessary, need-based, or improvement-oriented" (5).

(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/250 - 251.
(2) The same source, 2/251.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.
(5) The same source, 2/253.


[Page 606]

Issues or Branches of the Principle of Removing Harm

When the principle of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) and its regulations are clarified, as well as its area of application, which is the permissible (mubah), it follows that what is in the category of permissibles includes that which is at the level of concession (afw). It does not apply to the recommended (mandubat), and not every change that affects rulings falls under the category of blocking the means. However, it is worth mentioning the actions that al-Shatibi has associated with blocking the means, which include the necessity of abandoning the recommended or supererogatory acts and the necessity of performing the disliked (makruh) in certain cases, and this is in the case of the jurist (faqih) who is to be followed, so that the follower does not mistakenly understand that the continuous practice of the recommended or supererogatory acts without interruption is an obligation, nor that the continuous abandonment of the disliked is forbidden. This is to block the means, and he has established principles regarding this. He said: "The essence of the recommended is that it should not be equated with the obligatory" (1). He said: "The permissibles, in terms of their essence, should not be equated with the recommended or the disliked" (2). He said: "The disliked, in terms of their essence, should not be equated with the forbidden or with the permissibles" (3). It should not be said here that the principle has been applied to the recommended or the disliked; rather, the application of the principle here is focused on the continuity that may unintentionally suggest otherwise to the legislator.
