The Concept of Objectives (Maqasid) According to al-Shatibi
Presentation and Discussion

This chapter contains a brief definition of the subject of this chapter and three sections:

Section One: A brief presentation of the concept of objectives according to al-Shatibi.
Section Two: Discussion of al-Shatibi's idea: the universals and induction.
Section Three: Discussion of al-Shatibi's idea: objectives and causes.

Chapter Ten
The Concept of Objectives (Maqasid) According to al-Shatibi
Presentation and Discussion

Subject of this chapter:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/183.
(2) The same source, 3/189.
(3) The same source, 3/190.


[Page 607]

After clarifying the meaning of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi, their categories and types, and how to attain them, as well as how to understand the Sharia and derive rulings based on it, and after establishing al-Shatibi's comprehensive methodology in this regard, which attempts to integrate previous methodologies or principles and foundations of various kinds through the new principles he established for understanding, it remains to examine this idea and these principles and discuss them.
Although he diverged in his innovations from all his predecessors among the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) and presented an unprecedented methodology, he sought to relate the various principles back to his own, even though he sometimes explicitly stated his disagreement with them and insisted that it was a disagreement in substance and not merely in wording.
During this process, al-Shatibi emerged as a profound scholar and jurist, deeply versed in the sciences of the Sharia, knowledgeable about human nature and the conditions of communities, insightful in discerning implications, diving deep into the pearls of meanings, submissive to the evidence and committed to it, eager to understand both the general and specific objectives, warning against extremism just as he warned against laxity.
In light of all this, a question arises that was raised by Dr. Abdullah Darraz in his introduction to his commentary on the book al-Muwafaqat: "If the status of the book is as you mentioned, and its virtue in the Sharia is as you described, then why has it been obscured from view for all these years and not received its due attention, let alone the dedication to its exposition?"(1). The question may go further: why did al-Shatibi's ideas not appear among other scholars, whether his students or others? Why did no one follow him in this regard? Did his ideas die immediately after their birth? Or are his ideas so profound and his methodology so complex that there were no followers for his ideas or practitioners of his methodology?
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat, 1/11, edited by Dr. Abdullah Darraz.


[Page 608]

Dr. Darraz answered the question by stating that this is due to two matters: the first is that al-Shatibi's discussions are innovative and unprecedented, while the known sciences of usul (principles of jurisprudence) were well-established and their path was paved, so those engaged in the sciences of Sharia relied on the well-known explanations and did not feel any deficiency, nor did their ambition extend to addressing the book and exercising thought upon it. The second matter is the difficulty of the book, as if there is a meaning under every word in it(1).
However, the matter—as I see it—does not return to either of the mentioned reasons. For al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) authored the Risala, which was like a spark that ignited a revolution in the science of usul, and had the idea of al-Shatibi succeeded, it might have been a spark of a similar revolution. It is inevitable that there exist many students of knowledge and scholars who would be interested in it. Al-Shatibi must have had students and scholars who revered him and learned from him. If his methodology had the potential for dissemination, it would have spread; as for the difficulty of the book, this would not prevent its understanding, explanation, and development upon it, so the reason must be something else.
The reason relates to the methodology itself, that is, to al-Shatibi's ideas. Although what is in his book is of high value, quality, and level, and most of it adheres to the established norms of the science of usul, it contains what is new, and this newness is foundational, indeed the foundations of the foundations upon which the rules and principles are built. The first of these is the method of induction, the rejection of certainty in Sharia without it, and the rejection of specification in Sharia in the conventional sense. It also introduces new meanings in returning to the certain, and although his new ideas are few in number, they are principles that dominate and govern many branches, and thus the few new principles are significant enough to form an independent methodology that stands on its own and is fundamentally different from all other known methodologies.
__________
(1) Al-Muwafaqat, 1/11, edited by Dr. Abdullah Darraz.


[Page 609]

The awareness of al-Shatibi regarding this led him to attempt to trace the roots of the various schools of thought back to their origins, meaning that his methodology should serve as a foundation for all. This is where the name of his book, al-Muwafaqat, comes from, which will be clarified in the next section.
The innovation and depth in al-Shatibi's research, along with his seriousness and discipline, have motivated many in our time to highlight al-Muwafaqat and its author. Perhaps some have even attempted to draw from it and rely on it. However, the reality is that no one has built upon his methodology or adopted it; on the contrary, what has been attributed to him is what he consistently warned against.
Indeed, what he feared has occurred, as he said: "And thus, it is not permissible for the one who examines this book to look at it with a beneficial or advantageous perspective until he is well-versed in the knowledge of Sharia, its principles and branches, both transmitted and rational, not clinging to imitation and partisanship to a school of thought. For if it is like this, there is a fear that what has been deposited in it may turn into a trial by mere appearance, and if it is wisdom in itself" (1).
The reason for the lack of dissemination of the methodology and its development is, and Allah knows best, due to the methodology itself, specifically the novelty of the methodology that may make the student of knowledge feel a thirst to understand it; once he understands it, he turns away from it. He stated in the conclusion of his book: "The intended purpose has been achieved, and thanks to Allah, the promised accomplishment has been realized, although there remain things that could not be included, as it has not been easy for many of the seekers to grasp them, and few are those who, despite their great thirst for them, have sought them. I feared that they would not reach their source and that they would not be organized in the path of verification of its stray points" (2). If the matter is as al-Shatibi said in this text: "Few are those who, despite their great thirst for them, have sought them," it seems to indicate that the methodology was born dead. This will be clarified through discussion in this chapter. It may also be beneficial before that to briefly present al-Shatibi's idea and highlight its novelty in a comprehensive manner in an independent section, which will be the first section of this chapter, followed by a discussion in the next two sections, and upon Allah we rely.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/53.
(2) The same source, 4/202.


[Page 610]

The First Topic
A brief overview of the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi.


The meaning of the Muwafaqat:
The choice of the name "al-Muwafaqat" (The Concurrences) refers to a meaning intended by al-Shatibi, which is the reconciliation between the schools of thought by clarifying that although they differ in branches, they all revert to recognized principles and foundations among all. The reason for the disagreement is the differing opinions of the imams in tracing issues back to their origins; one favors tracing it back to one origin while another favors tracing it back to a different origin. As for the principles, all of them are recognized and relied upon by the imams. Despite the novelty and provocative nature of his methodology, he states that it is acknowledged by the recognized imams even if they do not mention it or draw attention to it, so it should not be dismissed by those who are unaware of it on the grounds that they have not heard of its like.
As for the meaning of reconciling between the schools of thought, he referred to this by mentioning a striking story. He said: "Due to the secrets of obligation related to this noble Sharia that I have embedded in it, I named it 'The Title of Introduction to the Secrets of Obligation.' Then I transitioned from this theme to a strange chain of narration that astonishes the perceptive and astute. The essence of it is that one day I met some of the scholars whom I had allowed to take a place of benefit from me, and I made my scientific gatherings with them a destination for travel and a place for receiving knowledge. I had begun to arrange and classify the book, casting aside distractions without refining or composing it. He said to me, 'I saw you last night in a dream with a book you authored. I asked you about it, and you told me it was "The Book of Al-Muwafaqat." He said, 'I was going to ask you about the meaning of this elegant title, and you informed me that you reconciled between the opinions of Ibn al-Qasim and Abu Hanifa.' I said to him, 'You have hit the mark with a share of the righteous vision, and you have taken from the prophetic glad tidings a good portion and share, for I have begun to compose these meanings, intending to establish those foundations, for they are the recognized principles among the scholars and the rules upon which the ancients built.' The sheikh was astonished by the strangeness of this agreement, just as I was astonished by traversing this wilderness and accompanying these companions."(1)
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/7 - 8.


[Page 611]

As for his methodology, despite its novelty, it is considered and relied upon by scholars. In addition to his statement in the text above: "For these are the accepted principles among scholars, and the rules established by the ancients," his assertion that "if someone opposes you with anything other than this book, it is an opposition of denial, and they are blind to the aspect of innovation and creativity in it, and they are deceived by the thought that it is something unheard of, nor has anything in the original or subsidiary Islamic sciences been composed in its manner or shaped like it, and you have enough of the evil of hearing it, and of every innovation in the Sharia that it has introduced, so do not pay attention to the objection without testing it, nor throw the possibility of benefit onto something unconsidered, for it is, by the grace of Allah, a matter established by the verses and reports, and its foundations have been built by the insights of the observers. When the path is clear, denial is not required, and acceptance of what it contains and consideration of the validity of what it has presented and acknowledgment of it is necessary, except for what may occur to humans of error and misstep" (1), etc.
His attempts at reconciliation appear in many places, including those related to the reasoning of rulings by the purposes and beneficial meanings. He spoke of reasoning after establishing that the described attribute used for reasoning returns to a meaning that is accepted in Sharia, and he conditioned the acceptance of the meaning on certainty regarding it. Thus, he did not disregard reasoning by the purposes, nor did he leave the matter to mere opinion. He thus approached the Shafi'is by accepting reasoning by the purpose, and he approached the Hanafis by rejecting the notion that the purpose is speculative. However, in reality, he did not agree with either of them; he was distant from the Shafi'is by his condition of certainty regarding the meaning and his rejection of the speculative meaning in several rulings, and he remained distant from the Hanafis as well, for they do not say this type of certainty, as the abundance of analogies does not yield strength in the description according to them (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/9.
(2) This matter has been previously explained and detailed in chapters two and three.


[Page 612]

Among his attempts at reconciliation is his statement regarding generality and specificity. It is known that the Hanafis do not restrict the definitive (qat'i) by the speculative (dhanni); they do not restrict the Qur'an or the mutawatir (consecutively transmitted) Sunnah by a single report (khabar ahad) or analogy (qiyas). This is based on their belief that the indication of the general (al-'amm) towards its specific instances (afrad) is definitive, so nothing from these instances can be excluded by speculative evidence. This is in contrast to the majority of usul scholars, who do restrict the definitive general by the speculative. What al-Shatibi brings forth here is the denial of restriction in its entirety; wherever he speaks of it, it is in the sense of clarification (bayān) (1). Thus, if some instances are specified from the general, this does not mean they are excluded from the generality of the text; rather, it clarifies that they were not included in it from the outset. Here, he approaches the Shafi'is in that the indication of the general towards all its instances is speculative. He has reiterated the texts of al-Shafi'i, stating that the general is used and intended to mean the specific. This is speculative in his view, as he denies definitive indication in the texts, and thus, he does not affirm definitiveness in meaning except through induction (istiqra). He also aligns with the Hanafis in stating that if the meaning is definitively established, it is not restricted. Thus, it becomes a universal principle, and universals cannot be restricted; therefore, the definitive universal cannot be restricted by a particular or by the speculative.
While he approaches both groups, he differs from them; he differs from the Shafi'is by rejecting restriction altogether and by not restricting universals by particulars, that is, the definitive by the speculative. He also differs from the Hanafis by rejecting restriction altogether, which means not restricting the universal by the universal, that is, the definitive by the definitive. Wherever he speaks of restricting some universals by others, he does not intend exclusion but rather clarification, as previously mentioned.
One can observe the approximation and reconciliation in the two mentioned examples, but the reality is that he was different—in both cases—with both groups; therefore, his statement will not be accepted by either of them. This may be one of the factors for the lack of spread of this methodology and its development. In both cases, the method of definitiveness, whether through wisdom or through the indication of the general towards its instances, can only be through induction, which is not customary among either of the groups.
Definitiveness in principles according to al-Shatibi:
__________
(1) See: the first section of chapter seven.


[Page 613]

One of the most important principles according to al-Shatibi is that the foundations must be definitive. He said: "The principles of jurisprudence in religion are definitive, not speculative, and the evidence for this is that they pertain to the universals of the Sharia, and whatever is thus is definitive. The proof of the first is evident through the inductive reasoning that leads to certainty, and the proof of the second is from several aspects: one of them is that they return either to rational foundations, which are definitive, or to the general inductive reasoning from the evidences of the Sharia, which is also definitive, and there is no third option other than the combination of the two, and the composite of definitives is definitive" (1).
The requirement for definitiveness in the foundations is well-known and agreed upon among the imams, but there is a significant difference between what al-Shatibi intended and what they intended, a difference that gives his methodology a direction distinct from theirs. The definitiveness in the foundations that the imams referred to is not about general or universal rules but rather about the sources of legislation, namely the general evidences which are four: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy. These are general evidences from which detailed evidences are derived and from which rules and foundations are understood. For example, the obligation to adhere to the Sunnah is established with definitive certainty, as it is a source of legislation. However, the reports or narrations that come in the Sunnah, or the reports of individual narrators, do not require definitive certainty regarding their authenticity in relation to the Prophet, but rather are taken based on a preponderance of evidence. The same applies to the meanings or implications of the texts, whether from the Qur'an or the Sunnah; it is not required for the implication of a text to be definitive for it to be acted upon, but rather it must be preferred over others.
As for what al-Shatibi intended, it encompasses what they intended and more. Every jurisprudential or foundational rule must be definitive according to him, and every meaning or principle relied upon in the Sharia must be definitive, and the meanings of the texts are the objectives of the Legislator, so they must be definitive or refer back to a definitive meaning that serves it, or be included within the definitive meaning.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/10.


[Page 614]

Therefore, the five necessities are definitive principles of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), and likewise, the rules for removing harm, hardship, and difficulty, and similar matters are definitive rules in the needs (hajiyat). Additionally, the principle of the outcomes of actions (mala'at al-af'al) and the rules of public interest (maslaha mursala), preference (istihsan), and blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i) are all definitive, both in their reality and in their conditions. This is not what the imams of usul intended when they stipulated definitiveness for the principles of jurisprudence; rather, they limited that to what is considered a source for legislation. Al-Shatibi indicates that his intention differs from others in this regard; at times, he directs his words to indicate that his meaning is what is relied upon by the earlier usulists, but they neglected to point it out. At other times, he explicitly states that his intention differs from theirs. He said: "However, the earlier usulists may have neglected this meaning and the indication of it, leading to its being overlooked by some later scholars, which caused confusion in deriving evidence from the verses in their singularity and from the hadiths in their isolation, as they did not take them in a collective manner, thus they were subjected to objections text by text. They weakened the evidence from them regarding the principles of usul intended for definitiveness" (1). He said in another place: "Every legal evidence is either definitive or speculative; if it is definitive, there is no doubt in considering it" (2). Then he said: "And if it is speculative, it is either related to a definitive principle or not. If it is related to a definitive principle, it is also considered; and if it is not related, one must be cautious about it, and it is not correct to broadly state its acceptance" (3). He said: "Know that the purpose of referring to the definitive principle is not to establish definitive evidence for the validity of acting upon it, like the evidence that acting upon the report of a single narrator or by analogy is obligatory, for example, but rather what is more specific than that, as previously mentioned in the hadith: 'There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm' (4), and the issues mentioned with it, which is a meaning contrary to that intended by the usulists, and Allah knows best" (5).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat. 1/15.
(2) The same source, 3/7.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/7.
(4) Previously referenced.
(5) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/12.


[Page 615]

This meaning is spread throughout various places in his book, including what was mentioned above, and one of the most important is the ninth issue of the first type of the objectives of the legislator (maqasid al-shari). He said: "The legislator's intention to preserve the three essential, necessary, and embellishing principles must be based on evidence, and the evidence for that can either be definitive or speculative. The speculative nature of it is invalid, as it is a fundamental principle of the Sharia, and indeed it is the foundation of its foundations. The foundations of the Sharia are definitive, as clarified in its place, so the foundations of its foundations are more deserving of being definitive. If it were permissible to establish them based on speculation, the Sharia would be speculative in both its roots and branches, and this is invalid."(1)
Characteristics of the foundations:
__________
(1) The same source, 2/32.


[Page 616]

The principles (usul) according to al-Shatibi are definitive matters intended by the Legislator. They are established through the induction of particulars, and the particulars are meanings that the texts can bear, or wisdoms and interests that may be intended by the Legislator through the rulings. If many particulars are surveyed and a definitive meaning is established based on the induction, then this meaning is a universal principle. The particulars whose meanings relate to this principle, that is, those that are included in it or serve it, are branches of the principle. However, before the definitive meaning is derived, the particular remains a particular and cannot be considered a branch nor can it be deemed as legislation. Accordingly, the principles are definitive universals. He said: "Some knowledge is from the essence of knowledge, and some is from the embellishments of knowledge, not from its essence, and some is neither from its essence nor from its embellishments. These are three categories: the first category is the principle and the relied-upon, which is the basis of inquiry and to which the objectives of the firmly rooted (rasikhun) ultimately lead, and that is what is definitive or related to a definitive principle. The blessed Muhammadan Sharia is revealed in this manner. Therefore, it is preserved in its principles and branches" (1). He then said: "They are the necessities, the needs, and the enhancements, and what completes them and supplements their aspects, and these are the principles of the Sharia, and definitive evidence has been established for their consideration, and all branches are based upon them, so there is no doubt that it is a foundational science with a solid basis and stable pillars" (2). He then said: "Because knowledge of them is derived from the general induction that organizes the scattered individuals until they become in the mind a collection of consistent, general, stable universals, not vanishing or changing, and ruling rather than being ruled upon, and these are the characteristics of rational universals. Furthermore, the universals are derived from existence, which is a conventional matter, not a rational one, thus they are equal to the legal universals in this regard, and the distinction between them is removed" (3). He said: "Because the guaranteed preservation in the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: { Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it } (4),
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/43, 44.
(2) The same source, 1/44.
(3) The same location.
(4) Surah al-Hijr, 9.


[Page 617]

The intended meaning here is the preservation of its general principles as stated, which is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: { This day I have perfected for you your religion } (1) as well; it is not intended to refer to specific issues. If that were the case, no specific detail of the Sharia would be exempt from preservation, and this is not the case, as we assert the permissibility and support it with occurrences due to the differences in conjectures and the possibilities that arise in specific texts, and the occurrence of errors in them is certain. Errors have been found in the reports of the singular narrators and in the meanings of the verses, which indicates that what is meant by the preserved mention is that which is general in nature (2). The comparison between the texts mentioned above indicates the stated difference between the specific and the branch.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 3.
(2) Al-Shatibi, Al-Muwafaqat, 1/12.


[Page 618]

Thus, what is relied upon in Sharia is the roots and their branches, and the particular is not relied upon unless it refers back to a root to be a branch. The root has characteristics that must be noted, which are mentioned above: "general, consistent, established, unchanging, and governing rather than governed." He explained what he meant by these characteristics, saying: "The generality and consistency; thus, the legal rulings regarding the actions of the obligated individuals are absolute, even if their specific instances are countless. There is no action that is mandated nor any stillness that is claimed except that the Sharia governs it individually and collectively, which is the meaning of its generality. And if there is a specific case in its texts or its rationales, it refers back to the general" (1). That is, if a particular exists that can be considered and specifies this general, it must refer back to another general, and the specification of some generals by others is a form of clarification, which is confirmed by the second characteristic of the generals. He said: "The second is permanence without change; therefore, you will not find in them, after their completeness, any abrogation or specification of their generality, nor restriction of their absoluteness, nor lifting of any of their rulings" (2). He said: "Rather, what has been established as a cause is always a cause that does not cease, and what was a condition is always a condition, and what is obligatory is always obligatory, or recommended is recommended, and so on for all rulings; there is no cessation or change for them, and if the obligation were to remain indefinitely, its rulings would be the same" (3). As for the third characteristic, which is that the generals are governing and not governed, its meaning is that there is nothing in the texts of Sharia that necessitates diverting its meaning to a meaning that the texts do not support. He said: "You will never find in practice anything that governs over the Sharia; otherwise, its being governing would turn into being governed" (4).
These are the three characteristics that distinguish the roots, and any meaning stated in the sciences of Sharia that loses one of these characteristics is not a root and cannot be referred to.
The generals are not contradicted by particulars:
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/44.
(2) The same source, 1/45.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same location.


[Page 619]

This is a necessary conclusion after clarifying the characteristics of universals; the universal is established through the induction of particulars that converge on a meaning, thus becoming a universal principle. If thereafter a particular is found that contradicts or opposes this universal, this does not invalidate the universal, because the universal has been established definitively, and there is no dispute regarding its establishment. As for the particular, it is either related to something definitive or it is not. If it is related to something definitive, this is a case of conflicting definitives, which cannot occur; rather, each has a context in which it is applicable. If the particular is not related to something definitive, it can be interpreted to relate back to something definitive in order to resolve the conflict, or one may refrain from judgment on it, or it may be rejected. Therefore, the universal is not affected by the opposition of particulars and continues to apply as it is. He said: "These three universals, if they have been legislated for specific interests, are not negated by the absence of individual particulars" (1). He said: "If the universal matter is established universally, then the absence of some particulars from the implications of the universal does not remove it from being universal. Furthermore, the predominant majority is considered in Sharia just as the definitive general is, because the absent particulars do not form a universal that opposes this established universal; this is the nature of inductive universals" (2). He said: "The issues of specific entities are particulars, while the consistent rules are universals, and particulars cannot invalidate universals. Therefore, the rulings of universals remain applicable to particulars even if the meaning of the universals does not specifically appear in them" (3).
Induction is the only way to certainty:
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/34.
(2) The same source, 2/35.
(3) The same source, 3/149 - 150.


[Page 620]

It is clear that al-Shatibi does not accept evidence unless it is definitive or refers back to something definitive, and the detailed evidences do not indicate the intended purpose of the legislator with definitive indication. So how can certainty be achieved knowing that the detailed evidences are the evidences of rulings? He said: "The relied upon in the first intention is the legal evidences, and the existence of certainty in them based on the commonly used is nonexistent or extremely rare, I mean in the individual evidences. If they are from the reports of the individual narrators, then their failure to provide certainty is evident. And if they are mutawatir (consecutively reported), then their provision of certainty is contingent upon all or most of its premises being speculative, and what is contingent upon the speculative must necessarily be speculative" (1). He then said: "The only considered evidences here are those that have been extrapolated from a group of speculative evidences that converge on one meaning until they provide certainty in it, for the gathering has a strength that separation does not have, and for this reason, the mutawatir provides certainty. This is a type of it. So if a compilation of the evidences of the issue is obtained that provides knowledge, it is the required evidence, and it is similar to the moral mutawatir, like the knowledge of the bravery of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and the existence of Hatim, which is derived from the multitude of incidents reported about them" (2). He held that this is the only way to establish certainties in the Sharia. He said: "From this path, the obligation of the five foundations such as prayer and zakat and others has been established with certainty. If someone were to argue for the obligation of prayer by citing His saying, the Exalted, { Establish the prayer } (3) or something similar, it would be a matter of consideration in the argument by itself from several angles" (4). This certainty, and consequently this extrapolation, is required to establish anything from the necessities, needs, or enhancements (5), and these and what falls under them are the objectives of the Sharia or its foundations. They do not deviate or falter as previously mentioned.

It has become clear that the indication of the singular texts (akhbar al-ahad) is speculative, and this alone does not warrant their consideration according to al-Shatibi. The texts of the Noble Qur'an are speculative in their indication, and the same applies to the mutawatir (consecutively transmitted) Sunnah, while the reports of singular narrations are even more so. Thus, a singular report, even if its authenticity is established, must be approached with caution unless its meaning returns to a definitive meaning. He does not say: "unless it contradicts something stronger than it," but rather: "unless it is definitive or returns to a definitive meaning."
Similarly, the texts of the Qur'an can bear multiple meanings, and one cannot definitively assert one of them merely by considering the text. The way to understand the text and apply it is by understanding it in light of what preceded it in revelation, as the revelation of the Qur'an was such that the later verses come as clarification and explanation of the earlier ones. The general principles were revealed first in Mecca. Therefore, the Medinan texts are understood in light of the Meccan ones, and the later Meccan texts are understood in light of the earlier ones, and the same applies to the Medinan texts (1). It is necessary to gather the meanings through the abundance of texts that indicate them.
__________
(1) See: the second section of chapter seven.


[Page 622]

And the Sunnah does not contain new legislation; it does not independently legislate but rather clarifies the Qur'an. Therefore, it corrects the meaning of the hadith: "Whatever comes to you from me, compare it to the Book of Allah. If it agrees with the Book of Allah, then I said it; and if it contradicts the Book of Allah, then I did not say it. How could I contradict the Book of Allah, by which Allah guided me?" (1), and it is relied upon. If it is not authentically narrated, its meaning is still established and definitive for him. He said: "Its meaning is correct whether its chain of narration is sound or not" (2). Among his examples regarding the consideration of the implications of texts through induction is what he mentioned about the establishment of necessities, including his statement about prayer: "When we look at prayer, we find the command to establish prayer in various forms, and we find praise for those who establish it and condemnation for those who abandon it, and the obligation for the accountable to perform it, establishing it while standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and fighting against those who abandon it or oppose its abandonment, and other matters of this nature" (3). He then said that through this: "We have certainly learned the obligation of prayer" (4). He said: "And likewise for all other evidences in the principles of Sharia, and this is how the principles differ from the branches, as the branches are based on individual evidences and specific sources, remaining on their original basis of reliance on conjecture, unlike the principles which are derived from the induction of the implications of the evidences in general, not from their individual cases specifically" (5). This is an example of reasoning with the texts of the Qur'an. As for the Sunnah, one of its examples is his saying: "His saying, peace be upon him: 'There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm'" (6), for it falls under a definitive principle in this regard, as harm and reciprocating harm are prohibited throughout the Sharia in specific incidents and general rules, such as His saying, Exalted is He: { And do not hold them to hurt them, so that you may transgress } (7), and { And do not harm them, so that you may make it difficult for them } (8),

And { a mother should not be harmed by her child } (1) is the verse, and from it comes the prohibition against transgressing upon souls, properties, and honor, as well as against usurpation and injustice, and everything that is in the meaning of causing harm or injury. This includes offenses against the soul, intellect, lineage, or wealth, which is a meaning that is extremely general in the Sharia, with no dispute or doubt about it. And when you consider the reports of the singular narrations (akhbar al-ahad), you will find them to be so (2). Thus, the intention of the Legislator to eliminate harm is definitive in the Sharia, and this hadith relates its meaning to this definitive meaning; therefore, it is accepted. This is also the case for all reports of singular narrations according to his statement above.
Indications of rulings:
