[Page 624]

Among the meanings that can be definitively established are the meanings of rulings, not just the meanings of texts. The meanings of rulings are what one can imagine as intended by the ruling, such as wisdom, benefit, cause, or outcome. All of these, if they are what the text can accommodate, must be established through induction, as has been clarified. However, if there is no indication from the text, neither in its explicit wording nor in its implied meaning, then this is something that can be imagined as intended by the legislator in the ruling and can be used to justify the ruling, even if it does not fall under one of the established paths of reasoning, which are the text, consensus, or hints and implications. Yet, it is only acceptable if it is established with certainty, which is done by examining many rulings or particulars that can accommodate this meaning or this reason. Without useful induction for certainty, these meanings are mere illusions and fantasies, and they are not considered because they do not return to a definitive origin; they may even contradict a foundational principle. Among his statements regarding such meanings or justifications is: "What is counted among the salt of knowledge is not part of its essence unless it is definitive and does not return to a definitive origin, but rather to something speculative, or it returns to something definitive but lacks a specific characteristic of those characteristics (1) or more than one characteristic; it is an illusion and something that provokes the intellect at first glance and initial consideration without compromising its essence or the meaning of another" (2). He also said: "Because if it is valid in minds, it does not yield any present benefit other than mere comfort for the souls" (3). The imagined meaning may also contradict a definitive principle; he said: "What is not part of the essence nor the salt: what does not return to a definitive or speculative origin, but rather its nature is to contradict its origin or another by nullification" (4).
__________
(1) That is, the three characteristics of the principles.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/45.
(3) The same source, 1/46.
(4) The same source, 1/50.


[Page 625]

He said: "This, if it inclines towards a people and they find it pleasing and seek it, is due to a superficial resemblance and confusion between it and what preceded it, so the foolish may consider it based on an original principle and thus lean towards it for that reason. The reality of its origin is delusion and imagination, with no truth to it, along with the additional interests and desires that accompany it" (1).
Accordingly, the indications of rulings are the objectives or interests (masalih) that the observer imagines are intended by them; these must be established through induction. This is what is meant by his statement: "similar to moral transmission (tawatur ma'nawi)." However, it should be noted that there is a difference between this transmission and moral transmission in the terminology of hadith science. In hadith science, moral transmission refers to the abundance of texts indicating a specific meaning with variations in wording and narrations; it is an indication of texts, while the transmission that al-Shatibi refers to is an indication of rulings. Therefore, he did not describe his intent as moral transmission; rather, he said: "similar to moral transmission."
This meaning that al-Shatibi seeks to establish through the abundance of rulings that align with it has no indication in the text whatsoever. Searching for it and proving that it is intended by the Legislator requires evidence. It has been previously mentioned that there are those who reject the claim of these reasons and attribute them to mere opinion and the imaginations of hearts. So what is the evidence for the legitimacy of reasoning with them and the permissibility of seeking their induction in rulings? The answer lies in the reasoning behind the actions and rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, and that He does not legislate except for the interests of the servants.
The reasoning of the Sharia with its objectives:
__________
(1) The same source, 1/51.


[Page 626]

The issue of justifying rulings through wisdom, interests, and appropriate descriptions has been the subject of considerable debate among theologians. This issue was introduced into the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) due to its impact on the discussions regarding the pathways of causation, which are the non-prescriptive pathways (1). Al-Shatibi came into this fray to establish a definitive principle, which is that the actions and rulings of Allah, Exalted is He, have purposes, and that He does not act except for a purpose He intends. He aimed to respond to those who rejected this justification, particularly Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, who himself firmly denied the notion that the actions of Allah are justified, while maintaining the claim of justifying rulings and through analogy. Al-Shatibi said: "The establishment of the laws is for the interests of the servants in both the immediate and the ultimate. This is a claim that must be substantiated as true or false, and this is not the place for that. Disagreement has arisen regarding it in the science of theology. Al-Razi claimed that the rulings of Allah are not justified by any cause whatsoever, just as His actions are not. And the Mu'tazila agreed that His rulings are justified by considering the interests of the servants, and this is the choice of most later jurists" (2). He then said: "What is relied upon is that we have inferred from the Sharia that it was established for the interests of the servants through an inference that al-Razi and others do not dispute" (3).
Thus, the justification of the Sharia by the interests of the servants, according to him, can only be achieved through inference, which differs from the reasoning of the earlier scholars who advocated for this justification (4).
__________
(1) See: the first chapter of this book.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/2.
(3) The same source, 2/3.
(4) See: the third discussion of the third chapter of this book.


[Page 627]

The objectives of the Legislator (al-Shari) are broader than the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), as the reasoning behind God's actions means that the Legislator has an objective in every action He performs. He has objectives in the creation of the heavens and the earth and in the creation of man, and these are objectives of the Legislator, not objectives of the Sharia. Among the objectives of the Legislator are also His objectives regarding how to understand the discourse, meaning the principles of understanding the meanings of words and structures, and these are not objectives of the Sharia. Therefore, the objectives in His view are of different types, and all of them are only considered valid if established through induction.
Objectives:
The objectives (maqasid) are of two types: the objective of the legislator (al-shari) and the objective of the obligated person (al-mukallaf). The objective of the legislator has four types. He said: "The objectives that are considered are of two types: one relates to the objective of the legislator and the other relates to the objective of the obligated person. The first is considered from the perspective of the legislator's intention in establishing the Sharia (law) from the outset, and from the perspective of his intention in establishing it for understanding, and from the perspective of his intention in establishing it for obligation according to it, and from the perspective of his intention in bringing the obligated person under its ruling. These are four types."(1)
The first type is the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), which are the necessary, need-based, and enhancement-related interests, along with what is supplementary and complementary to them(2). The second type pertains to the foundational and linguistic rules relied upon to understand the implications of the legal text. The third type is to clarify that the legislator did not intend hardship with the obligation, even though it may be a consequence of the obligation, and to distinguish between the hardships that the legislator intended to alleviate and those that the legislator did not intend to alleviate. The fourth type is that one of the objectives of the legislator is the servitude of the servants and their submission to the command of the legislator, and to divert them from the inclinations of their desires, even if this contradicts what they perceive to be in their interest.
However, two new matters stand out and should be noted regarding al-Shatibi that differ from other scholars of usul (usul al-fiqh) who argue for the justification of rulings based on public interest (maslaha) or the pursuit of benefits and the prevention of harms. These are his understanding of public interest and harm, as well as the meaning of justifying the Sharia (Sharia) based on public interest.
The concept of al-Shatibi regarding public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada):
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/2.
(2) The same source, 2/3 - 4 - 5.


[Page 628]

The public interest (maslaha) according to al-Shatibi is what has been established as being intended by the legislator through the ruling. The harm (mafsada) is what has been established as being intended by the legislator through the ruling when it does not occur. This is known through the examination of texts and rulings. If it is established that an action is commanded, then the action is a public interest; if it is established that it is prohibited, then it is a harm. The same applies to the results, outcomes, or causes of the action. What is established through examination to be the reason for the ruling of the laws is a public interest, as actions are causes for outcomes, as are the rulings of actions. What is established through examination to be the reason for the prohibition of the laws is a harm. This is confirmed by looking at the causal relationship between the ruling and its results and implications. The public interest, according to him, is not merely what brings benefit or what makes the obligated person feel aligned with human inclinations and needs, nor is it a condition for the public interest to be a suitable description. The same applies to the harm; rather, there must be a causal relationship between the ruling and what it is connected to. This meaning is extensively discussed in many places in his book, particularly in his discussions on causes and effects in the Book of Rulings, as well as in his discussions on the fourth type of objectives of the legislator. He said: "Prohibited causes are causes of harms, not of public interests, just as permissible causes are causes of public interests, not of harms" (1). He also said: "If that is the case, it is not correct for anyone to claim that the Sharia was established according to the desires and objectives of the people" (2). He stated: "The fact that the public interest is a public interest intended by the ruling and the harm is a harm likewise is something specific to the legislator, and there is no room for reason in this based on the principle of negation of good and evil. If the legislator has established a ruling for a certain public interest, then he is the one who has established it as a public interest; otherwise, it could logically be that it is not so, as all things are equal in relation to their original status, and reason has no jurisdiction over them in terms of goodness or badness."
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/167.
(2) The same source, 2/116.


[Page 629]

Thus, the fact that the public interest (maslaha) is a public interest is from the perspective of the legislator, such that reason affirms it and the soul finds reassurance in it. The interests, as they are interests, have been viewed as acts of worship (ta'abudiyyat), and what is based on the act of worship can only be an act of worship (1). Accordingly, al-Shatibi's reasoning for the Sharia based on interests means that it must be established for him that the intention of the legislator is present; if it is established, then it is a public interest regardless of human sentiment. This is a new perspective that contradicts the conventional understanding of the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) regarding public interest, and the same can be said for harm (mafsada).
The meaning of reasoning for the Sharia based on interests:
The rulings are causes for effects that are the intended goals of the legislator, and the rulings are established based on this intended goal. From here, this intended goal becomes a reason for legislation, and the jurists discover these reasons through examining the outcomes and effects of the rulings. The intended goal of the legislator exists prior to the rulings, and based on it, the rulings were revealed. For the jurist, the intended goal can only be known through the rulings. Hence, al-Shatibi considers the intended goal to be a reason, even though in meaning, the reason for an action precedes it, while the intended goal comes after it.
This meaning of reasoning, along with the previously mentioned meaning of public interest, leads to the conclusion that the appropriateness of the described attributes is not a condition. If the reason or intended goal is a suitable description that makes the obligated person feel that it aligns with their human nature and purposes, then this is an incidental matter and not the original basis according to the principle of negating beautification and vilification. This differs from the intention of the scholars of usul who spoke of reasoning for the Sharia based on interests; indeed, even if it resembles their expressions, it undermines their idea.
__________
(1) The same source, 2/219.


[Page 630]

Therefore, al-Shatibi refutes all the statements of his predecessors on this matter, saying that if one observes the consideration of the Sharia for the purposes of the servants and their inclinations, and what aligns with what they strive for, this is incidental and not the essence. The essence is that Allah - Exalted is He - created man for His worship, but He favored them by assisting them in their worship by creating in them desires and inclinations that drive them towards obedience. He said: "If it is said: The establishment of laws is either in vain or for wisdom, the first is invalid by consensus" (1), and he continued in his statement: "Because every rational person seeks the benefit of himself and what aligns with his desires in this world and the Hereafter, and the Sharia has guaranteed them this demand within the framework of obligation. So how can it be denied that the Sharia is established in accordance with the purposes of the servants and the motivations of their desires? Moreover, it has already been clarified that the Sharia came in accordance with the purposes of the servants and confirmed their shares" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/117.
(2) The same source.


[Page 631]

Then he responds to this objection by saying: "The answer is that if we concede that the purpose of the Sharia (law) is for the interests of the servants, then it returns to them according to the command of the Lawgiver and within the limits He has set, not according to their whims and desires. Therefore, the legal obligations are heavy on the souls" (1). He said: "The wisdom of the All-Wise, All-Aware has decreed that the establishment of religion and the world can only be rectified and sustained by motivations from the human side that drive him to acquire what he needs for himself and others. Thus, He created for him the desire for food and drink when he is afflicted by hunger and thirst to motivate him to seek to fulfill this need as much as he can. Similarly, He created for him the desire for women to motivate him to acquire the means that lead to them" (2), and so on. He then said: "If Allah had willed, He could have imposed this with disregard for desires, or He could have imposed it while removing the innate motivations. However, He has favored His servants by making it a means to cultivate the world for the Hereafter and has made the acquisition of these desires permissible, not prohibited, but according to legal rules that are more effective in achieving benefits and more enduring than what the servant considers to be beneficial" (3).
These two ideas in al-Shatibi's thought, namely his concept of benefit (maslaha) and harm (mafsada), and his intention in saying that the Sharia was established for the interests of the servants, represent a reversal of what is commonly understood by the scholars of Usul (principles of jurisprudence) who assert that the Sharia is justified by bringing about benefits and preventing harms.
Ijtihad and Taqlid:
Allah created people for His worship, and there is no action except that there is a ruling from Allah regarding it. Therefore, it is upon the obligated person, whether he is an independent jurist (mujtahid) or a follower (muqallid), to seek the ruling of Allah. The ruling of Allah is His intention, which is understood according to what has been previously explained. The ruling of Allah, Exalted is He, is understood by the recognized jurist who comprehends the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail, and who works with both the general principles and the specific cases when exercising ijtihad. He is the one whose conduct aligns with his fatwa, being pious and committed in his statements and actions according to what he issues in fatwas and according to what is known of the characteristics of the righteous predecessors and others among the pious and righteous in religion.
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 2/117.
(2) The same source, 2/122.
(3) The same source, 2/123.


[Page 632]

As for the follower (muqallid), he has no consideration of the legal evidence (adillah shar'iyyah), and his pursuit of the intention of the Legislator (al-shari') is through weighing the opinions of the jurists (mujtahidin), as they serve as legal evidence for him. It is not permissible for him to choose between the opinions, as this would be following his desires.
As for the condition of understanding the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) in general and in detail, when the mujtahid (jurist) reaches this understanding, he can issue a fatwa (legal opinion), and his statement will be considered valid if he is pious, even if he does not know the Arabic language, as he can understand the objectives through reception and translation. He said: "If ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) is related to deriving rulings from texts, then knowledge of Arabic is a must. However, if it is related to the meanings of benefits and harms, abstracted from the texts or accepted from the one who exercises ijtihad in the texts, then knowledge of Arabic is not required; rather, knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail is necessary"(1). He said: "Therefore, whoever understands the objectives of the Sharia from the establishment of rulings and reaches the rank of knowledge of them, even if his understanding comes through translation in a non-Arabic tongue, there is no difference between him and one who understands them through the Arabic language"(2).


The Second Topic
Discussion of al-Shatibi's Idea
Universals and Induction


The topic of this section:
After presenting the idea of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) according to al-Shatibi in detail, and then presenting and highlighting its foundation and pillars briefly in the previous section, we will discuss this foundation and these pillars in this section and the next. The ideas that will be discussed in this section are:
1 - Al-Shatibi's condition that the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) must be definitive.
2 - Induction and its being the only path to certainty.
3 - His statement that the universals (kulliyat) are not violated by the particulars (juz'iyat).
4 - The conceptual transmission (al-tawatur al-ma'nawi).
__________
(1) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/90.
(2) The same source, 4/91.


[Page 633]

These ideas are the pillars of al-Shatibi's (may Allah be pleased with him) concept. Through discussing them, the correctness or incorrectness of some of his ideas becomes evident, such as the meaning of returning to the definitive (qat'i) in his view, and that the legal evidence is only accepted if it is definitive or refers back to something definitive. As for the next section, it will be - if Allah wills - a discussion of the foundation of the idea, which is the principle of reasoning behind the actions of Allah (Exalted is He), and to discuss a necessary consequence of his methodology, which is the possibility for the jurist (mujtahid) who is well-versed in the general principles of the Sharia to dispense with examining its particulars. This includes the non-requirement of knowledge of Arabic for the jurist who is knowledgeable about the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail.
The requirement of certainty in the principles of jurisprudence:
Al-Shatibi held that the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) must be definitive (qat'i) and that they are associated in this regard with beliefs (aqa'id). He clarified that his understanding of the principles differs from that of other scholars of usul. His understanding of the principles refers to the definitive meanings that jurisprudence relies upon or derives from.
Yes, he differs in this from the imams of usul (principles) and the jurists, and this is one of his novelties. This is something I see as a mistake. The seriousness of this mistake is magnified because it is in the principles, and it is not merely a principle among the principles, but rather a principle that governs the principles, indeed it governs the entire methodology.
The error in it is not in its being new, nor in its contradicting the methodology established by the imams, but rather in its subject matter, that is, in the meaning of this principle.


[Page 634]

Indeed, al-Shatibi did not provide evidence for this statement; rather, he presented it as a report, linking the principles to the beliefs in a formulation that could be accepted at first glance. When reading his statements on this matter, the mind shifts to the commonly understood meaning in the words of the imams regarding the necessity of certainty in the principles, which are the sources of legislation, namely the general evidences of jurisprudence, which are the four evidences: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas). However, al-Shatibi went further, intending the principles and rules of jurisprudence in the sense of the discussions of the principles of jurisprudence, such as the indication of a command for obligation or otherwise, or the rule that what is necessary for the obligation to be fulfilled is itself obligatory, or the rule that the default state of things is permissibility unless there is evidence for prohibition, or the rule of public interest (maslaha), or preference (istihsan), or presumption of continuity (istishab). These rules could indeed be subjected to the condition of certainty if they were meant as sources of legislation, that is, evidences standing on their own; however, this is not what al-Shatibi intended. The linking of the principles in the sense of sources of legislation to beliefs and the condition of certainty in them is based on Allah's condemnation of following conjecture and the reproach of those who follow conjecture, and this pertains to beliefs. Allah, Exalted is He, said: { They are nothing but names you have named them, you and your forefathers; Allah has not sent down any authority for them. They follow nothing but conjecture and what their souls desire, and guidance has certainly come to them from their Lord } (1). And He, Exalted is He, said: { Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter will name the angels with female names (27) and they have no knowledge of it; they follow nothing but conjecture, and indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all } (2). And He, Exalted is He, said: { And most of them follow nothing but conjecture; indeed, conjecture does not avail against the truth at all } (3).
__________
(1) Surah An-Najm, 23.
(2) Surah An-Najm, 27 - 28.
(3) Surah Yunus, 36.


[Page 635]

And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {Indeed, those who have differed concerning it are in doubt about it; they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption.} (1). And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {And if you obey most of those upon the earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah. They follow not except assumption, and they are not but falsifying.} (2). And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {Say, "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow not except assumption, and you are not but falsifying."} (3). And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {Are you disputing with me concerning names you have named, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has not sent down any authority?} (4). And Allah, Exalted is He, said: {Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be among the truthful."} (5). These verses and others are explicit in condemning assumption and in condemning the belief and faith in things without authority or proof, and the authority and proof is the decisive evidence, for if it is based on assumption, it is condemned. However, this applies to beliefs and not to legal rulings, as it has been established in the latter— as will be clarified— that it is permissible to follow assumption based on certainty.
The principles that are related to beliefs are the general sources of jurisprudence, for if someone claims that legal obligations are derived from such-and-such person or from such-and-such book or from any source without a decisive proof for that, this is following assumption, which is condemned. This leads to the permissibility of deriving legislations from visions and dreams if there is an assumption that they are good visions for the righteous, and it may lead to the permissibility of deriving legislations from the Torah and the Gospel if there is an assumption regarding some of their texts that they are not altered. All of these are general sources, but these are assumptions, and no decisive proof has been provided to validate these assumptions, and therefore they are rejected.
__________
(1) Surah An-Nisa, 157.
(2) Surah Al-An'am, 116.
(3) Surah Al-An'am, 148.
(4) Surah Al-A'raf, 71.
(5) Surah Al-Baqarah, 111, and Surah An-Naml, 64.


[Page 636]

The principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that are related to beliefs (aqa'id) are those that resemble beliefs in that they are foundational for other matters, while they themselves are not built upon anything else. If they are built upon something else, then they are considered branches, and their validity or invalidity depends on that other matter. Accordingly, the scholars of usul have classified the principles of jurisprudence as the four general proofs. Additionally, there are other rules and principles that are relied upon in ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and istinbat (deduction), for which certainty is not a prerequisite, as they are based on other matters that have been established with certainty. Some have even excluded qiyas (analogy) from the requirement of certainty, considering that qiyas relies on the cause (illah) and its extension, and the source of the cause is the three proofs: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and consensus (ijma). Thus, reliance on the cause and its extension goes back to these three, and qiyas thereafter is merely the action of the one making the analogy, which is speculative. This is similar to reasoning based on reports of the individual narrators (akhbar al-ahad), which is also speculative, but its foundation, which is the Sunnah, is certain, and the obligation to act upon reports of the individual narrators is certain.


[Page 637]

Therefore, the scholars of usul (usul al-fiqh) did not refer to the speculative evidences as proofs, but rather considered them to be indicators; they are signs that point to their meanings. However, the obligation to act upon them or to follow them does not depend on them, but rather on something else, which is the conclusive evidence for acting upon them. The conclusive evidences are the definitive proofs for the obligation to adhere to the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), and analogy (qiyas). The conclusive evidence is not the detailed proof itself, which is different from the jurists, as these indicators are considered proofs by the scholars of usul and the theologians. Al-Asnawi said: "Know that the expression of proofs excludes many principles of jurisprudence such as generalities, reports of the singular (akhbar al-ahad), analogy, presumption of continuity (istihsan), and others. For the scholars of usul, even if they acknowledge them, they are not considered proofs for jurisprudence but rather indicators of it, as the term proof is only applied to that which is certain" (1). He also said: "I say: The proofs of jurisprudence are divided into those agreed upon by the imams and those disputed. The agreed upon are four: the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy, while everything else such as presumption of continuity, public interests (masalih mursala), preference (istihsan), reverse analogy (qiyas al-aks), and taking the lesser of what has been said, and others that will come are disputed among them" (2). He further stated: "As for the auditory evidences, if they are disputed, they only provide conjecture according to those who advocate them, while the agreed upon among the imams are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus, and analogy. As for analogy, it is clear that it only provides conjecture, and as for consensus, if it reaches us through singular reports, it is likewise, and its transmission through mass reporting is very rare. Even if it is assumed, Imam in al-Mahsool and al-Amidi in al-Ihkam and al-Muntaha al-Sul have affirmed that it is speculative. As for the Sunnah, singular reports from it only provide conjecture, while the mass-reported ones are like the Qur'an, their text is definitive but their indication is speculative due to the need to negate the ten possibilities" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul, 1/10.
(2) The same source, 1/44 - 45.
(3) The same source, 1/41.


[Page 638]

And based on that, the definitive evidence (qat'i) that they require for the proof is in the sense of the evidence that is a comprehensive source for legislation. As for other rules, principles, and rulings, they are speculative (dhanni) and are relied upon and followed in the Sharia, and no definitive evidence is required for their establishment or meaning. Rather, the condition is that they must be based on definitive evidence, that is, on the evidence that serves as their source, which are the four agreed-upon evidences. If there is disagreement regarding them, then the evidence (which is the source) must be definitive according to those who affirm it among the jurists.
Al-Zarkashi said: "Then the intended evidences are the Book, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma), analogy (qiyas), and reasoning (istidlal). Imam al-Haramayn and al-Ghazali said: They are three: the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus, and they denied that speculative universal laws are part of the principles of jurisprudence. He said in the summary: What the scholars have accepted is that what cannot be known, such as reports and analogies, is not considered part of the principles of jurisprudence." (1) He then said: "If it is said: The reports of the singular narrators (akhbar al-ahad) and analogies do not lead to knowledge and they are among the evidences of the rulings of the Sharia, it is said to him: The principles are concerned with establishing evidences on the obligation of implementation, and that is what is understood through definitive evidences. As for the practice, it is derived from them, thus it pertains to jurisprudence rather than its principles. He said in al-Burhan: If it is said: Most of the legal issues are speculative, we say: Speculation is not jurisprudence; rather, jurisprudence is the knowledge of the obligation of action when speculation arises. Therefore, the scholars said: The reports of the singular narrators and analogies do not necessitate action by themselves; rather, action must be based on what necessitates knowledge of action, which are the definitive evidences regarding the obligation of action when the reports of singular narrators are narrated and analogies are established. He said: Although they are found only in the principles of jurisprudence, the role of the jurist is to clarify the definitive in acting upon them." (2)
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 1/18 - 19.
(2) The same source, and see: Al-Juwaini, al-Burhan, 1/78 - 79, paragraphs: 4 - 5 - 6.


[Page 639]

In these previous texts, there are two matters: the first is that detailed evidences provide a presumption, and there is conclusive evidence that it is obligatory to act upon this presumption; the second is that presumption is acted upon in legal matters because it is based on conclusive evidence that has established, with certainty, the obligation to rely on it as a source or reference, and not every presumption is legal, but only that which is based on conclusive legal evidences. These two matters, along with the texts of the aforementioned imams, indicate al-Shatibi's deviation from the established methodology, and the error in what al-Shatibi has claimed, as these texts contain evidence for the obligation to act upon the presumptive without requiring that the presumptive meaning returns to a conclusive meaning; rather, the condition is to return to a conclusive source. If we add to this that al-Shatibi did not provide evidence for what he stated, nor did he clarify any errors in the statements of the imams, then this condition he imposed is invalid, especially since he claims that this is what the verses and reports have established and what the righteous predecessors acted upon. The inclusion of principles in beliefs is valid if the principles are those that do not depend on anything else; if they are dependent on something else, then they are branches of others, even if they are principles from which others branch out. In this case, if they are presumptive, there is no harm in that if there is conclusive evidence for the obligation to act upon them.
The obligation to act upon the presumptive:
What further confirms the error in al-Shatibi's view regarding the principles for which he required conclusive evidence, and the mistake he built upon that, is that the legal evidence must either be conclusive or refer back to something conclusive. The conclusive evidences for the obligation to act upon the presumptive, if its source is conclusive, do not require that its meaning returns to a conclusive meaning.


[Page 640]

The statements of the imams have multiplied regarding this matter, and reports have been transmitted in this sense, in response to those who deny the validity of acting upon the report of the individual (khabar al-wahid). This is despite the fact that the report of the individual is subject to doubt from two aspects: from the aspect of its authenticity and from the aspect of its indication. In contrast, the texts of the Qur'an are only subject to doubt from the aspect of their indication. As for consensus (ijma), in terms of its transmission, it is similar to the report of the individual, and in terms of its indication, it may be similar or stronger. Analogy (qiyas) relates to the three, and there are decisive and numerous proofs that establish the obligation to act upon the report of the individual that is deemed to be attributed to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) without any condition other than that it does not contradict a stronger evidence, and this is not the subject of discussion.
Al-Zarkashi said: "Indeed, al-Shafi'i authored a book on the validation of the report of the individual (khabar al-wahid), and at the beginning he mentioned the well-known hadith: 'May Allah have mercy on the one who hears my words'(1). Abu Dawood objected and said: He established the report of the individual by the report of the individual, and a thing cannot be established by itself, like someone who claims something and is asked: Who witnesses for you? He replies: I witness for myself. The companions said: What he mentioned is invalid, for al-Shafi'i did not rely on a single hadith; rather, he mentioned around three hundred hadiths and indicated the ways of deriving evidence from them, and the totality is what supports it"(2).
__________
(1) Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Knowledge from the Messenger of Allah, under the chapter on the encouragement to convey what one hears with the wording: "May Allah brighten the face of a servant..." with the number (2582), and Ahmad (16153), and al-Darimi (230), and it is found with the same wording in the Great Dictionary of al-Tabarani, under the chapter on the letter zay.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 3/321.


[Page 641]

Al-Juwayni summarized the many proofs by saying: "The usuliyyin (scholars of Islamic jurisprudence) have elaborated extensively on the ways to respond to the deniers, and our preferred approach consists of two paths: the first is based on a widely accepted matter that only a denier would dispute and only a stubborn person would reject. This is that we know with certainty from our minds that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) used to send messengers and entrust them with conveying the rulings and details of the lawful and unlawful. He would sometimes accompany them with written texts, and their transmission of the commands of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) was on the basis of individual reports (ahad), and they were not necessarily infallible. Thus, their reports were subject to doubt, and this was established as a certainty, widely accepted without any refutation, as it is supported by the concept of tawatur (transmission of reports by a large number of people). Only something that is astonishing can refute the widely accepted. This is one of the paths. The second path is based on the consensus of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), and their consensus on acting upon the reports of individuals is transmitted widely. We do not doubt that in matters of events, they sought rulings from the Book of Allah, and if they did not find a mention for the matter at hand, they would turn to seek the reports of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and they would hasten to rely on the transmission of the trustworthy and reliable without disagreement."(1) Al-Zarkashi also mentioned a similar statement.(2)
The independence of the Sunnah in legislation:
Al-Shatibi argued that the Sunnah (tradition) does not independently legislate based on the premise that the Qur'an contains clarification of everything, and that the Sunnah serves as an explanation of it. Accordingly, the Sunnah does not introduce anything that lacks a basis in the Qur'an, neither in terms of subject matter, meaning, or type.
The commentary on this statement is that the fact that the Qur'an contains the explanation of everything, and that the Sunnah (traditions of the Prophet) explains the Qur'an, does not mean that the Sunnah cannot independently legislate, nor that the Sunnah cannot introduce obligations that have no basis in the Qur'an. The indication of the Qur'an regarding the Sunnah and the obligation to derive rulings from it is part of the explanation and completes the explanation. The indication of the Sunnah regarding matters not found in the Qur'an does not contradict the fact that the Qur'an is an explanation.
__________
(1) Al-Juwayni, Al-Burhan, 1/388, paragraph: 539 - 540.
(2) See: al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 3/320.


[Page 642]

It cannot be said that the Qur'an contains an explanation of everything in this sense, which is that every meaning indicated by the Sunnah (tradition) is present in the Qur'an. Rather, it can be said that there is nothing brought by the Sunnah except that it has a basis in the Qur'an, and this is a point of contention. As for the assumption that the Sunnah does not bring anything that is not in the Qur'an, how can this be the case?! Does the Qur'an command prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and other matters that have been mentioned in a general way and clarified by the Sunnah? Is this clarified in the Qur'an? What the Sunnah has brought, is it not an independent legislation even if it has a basis in the Qur'an?
The issue of the independence of the Sunnah in legislation or lack thereof is intended to address whether the Sunnah brings something that has no basis in the Qur'an or not, and not whether it contains additional clarification or not. The Sunnah certainly contains additional clarification; otherwise, how would we be guided in our prayer if it were not for the Sunnah?! All that the Sunnah has brought in terms of specification, restriction, and clarification of what is general in the Qur'an that is not explained therein is additional legislation that the Sunnah has independently established.


[Page 643]

As for what al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) cited from His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have sent down to you the Book as a clarification for all things } (1). And His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them } (2). This does not support his view. As for the first verse, the Book clarifies everything, and one of the means of its clarification is the Sunnah, for the Book indicates the Sunnah, and the indication of the Book towards the Sunnah makes the clarification of the Sunnah regarding things part of the clarification of the Book regarding them. If one person says to another: "Do such and such, and everything that so-and-so tells you," or "And everything I command you in an independent book," does his statement, "and everything that so-and-so tells you" or "and everything I command you in an independent book," constitute a deficiency in clarifying what he has commanded him, or do the commands that come from so-and-so or those that appear in an independent book count as part of the clarification of what the first person wants? Therefore, the fact that the Book is a clarification for everything does not contradict the Sunnah bringing forth what is not in the Qur'an or has no basis in the Qur'an. The Qur'an has linked the command to obey Allah, Exalted is He, and to obey His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). He, Exalted is He, said: { O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger } (3). And He, Exalted is He, said: { Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah } (4). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I was given the Qur'an and something like it with it" (5).
__________
(1) Surah an-Nahl, 89.
(2) Surah an-Nahl, 44.
(3) Surah an-Nisa, 59, and Surah Muhammad, 33.
(4) Surah an-Nisa, 80.
(5) Al-Shawkani, Nail al-Awtar min Ahadith Sayyid al-Akhiyar, Sharh Muntaka al-Akhbar, Book of Foods and Hunting, Chapter on the principle that the default ruling for substances and things is permissibility until prohibition is established. He mentioned the hadith in the wording: "I was given the Qur'an and something like it with it" and said: it is an authentic hadith, 8/111. Dar al-Ilm - Beirut, and it was narrated by Ahmad (16546), and it has variants in the wording: "I was given the Book...".


[Page 644]

And as for His saying, Exalted is He: { And We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them }, it does not indicate that the Sunnah is not independent in legislation. Rather, it indicates that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) conveys, clarifies, details, and explains what has come in the Qur'an. There is nothing in the wording of the text or its implication that indicates that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) does not clarify anything other than what has come in the Qur'an. Allah, Exalted is He, revealed to His Prophet the Sharia of Islam, and this was through what He revealed to him from the Qur'an and from the Sunnah. Thus, he (peace and blessings be upon him) clarifies the Qur'an and clarifies the Sunnah, and both are revelation. Allah, Exalted is He, said: { And he does not speak from [his own] inclination (3) It is not but a revelation revealed } (1). This is confirmed by the texts that require obedience to the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and clarify that Allah, Exalted is He, has given him the Qur'an and something like it with him(2).
Therefore, the inquiry of whether the Sunnah is independent in legislation or not is essentially about whether the Sunnah brings forth a command that has no basis in the Qur'an or not, meaning whether it has no kind or type to refer to in its subject matter, that is, in meaning. The claim that the Sunnah does not come with that requires evidence, and there is no evidence; rather, the evidences allow for that.
Thus, the evidences that rely on this matter are the extrapolation of the obligations of the Qur'an and the obligations of the Sunnah, that is, their occurrence or non-occurrence, and it has been established that they do occur. This is like the prohibition of the flesh of domesticated donkeys and every predator with fangs and every bird with talons(3). So, if the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) permitted these things, would the permissibility contradict a principle in the Qur'an? Is it not that if the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) had not prohibited them, their ruling would be permissibility based on the principle: the default ruling of things is permissibility unless there is evidence of prohibition?
__________
(1) Surah Al-Najm, 3 - 4.
(2) See: Imam al-Shafi'i, Al-Risala, pp. 79 - 104, paragraph: 258 - 308.
(3) The hadiths mentioned earlier.


[Page 645]

As for al-Shatibi's (may Allah have mercy on him) statement that Allah, Exalted is He, has permitted the good things (tayyibat) and prohibited the evil things (khaba'ith), and that there remain things whose ruling is unclear to the jurist and it is difficult for him to determine whether they belong to the good things or the evil things, this is an attempt to adapt the issue to align with his methodology and has no basis in truth. For if it were not for the prohibition of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), no one would doubt that they are permissible based on the principle of permissibility, and thus they would be considered among the good things. The prohibition of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is what rendered them among the evil things in the sense of being prohibited, and Allah knows best. Moreover, al-Shatibi did not inform us of the basis of the evil things and the basis of the good things.
Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "The Messenger of Allah established with the Book of Allah and legislated in matters for which there is no specific text in the Book" (1).
Al-Zarkashi (may Allah have mercy on him) stated under the title (The Sunnah Independent in Legislation): "For this reason, the Imam of the Two Holy Sanctuaries did not separate the Sunnah from the Book, and he said: Everything the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) says is from the statement of Allah, Exalted is He, so there is no point in mentioning a distinction between the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Shafi'i explicitly stated in the Risala that the Sunnah is regarded as revealed like the Qur'an" (2). Among what he cited regarding the independence of the Sunnah in legislation is: "Such as the prohibition of the meat of the domesticated donkey and every carnivorous animal with fangs, which are not explicitly mentioned in the Book" (3).
As for the hadith that instructs to present the hadiths to the Book, which al-Shatibi validated its meaning even if its chain of narration is not authentic, al-Shafi'i said about it: "No one has narrated this who has established his hadith in anything, whether small or large" (4).

[Page 646]

And it was brought to Professor Ahmad Muhammad Shakir, the verifier of the book Al-Risala, a commentary on the hadith "What comes to you from me, compare it with the Book of Allah; whatever agrees with it, I have said it, and whatever contradicts it, I have not said it." He stated: "This meaning has not been reported in any authentic or good hadith; rather, many phrases have been reported, all of which are fabricated or extremely weak to the extent that none of them is suitable for proof or citation" (1). He then mentioned that among those who reported it are those who are known for fabricating hadith, and he cited the statements of the hadith scholars that it is a false hadith with no basis and that it was fabricated by the heretics and is indeed fabricated (2).

" (3). He also said: "Some opposed it and said: We compare it with the Book of Allah and found it contradicting the Book, for we did not find in it that only what agrees with the Book is accepted, but rather we found the command to obey him and the prohibition of opposing his command is a ruling in all cases" (4).

"

(4) The same location.
This is the meaning that al-Shatibi affirmed, disregarding its chain of transmission, considering it a definitive meaning in his view, and made it one of the pillars of his methodology. This is a meaning that the Imams of hadith and the Imams of fiqh reject. How can al-Shatibi claim that this methodology has been firmly established by the righteous predecessors and endorsed by the scholarly elite?
This idea regarding the certainty of the principles and the return to the definitive, and the hesitation in considering the reports of the singular narrators (akhbar al-ahad) until a return to a definitive meaning is established, is one of the most important pillars of al-Shatibi's methodology. It is therefore fitting that this methodology should be buried in its cradle.
Induction:
Induction is the most important pillar in al-Shatibi's methodology; it is the only way to ascertain meanings and to understand the principles of the Sharia in his view. The certainty of the meanings of texts relies on the negation of ten premises, which is impossible. The meanings of rulings are speculative interests (masalih) that have no indication in the texts, so many rulings must converge upon them to achieve a useful induction that then acquires legal value and is considered as reasons (illa) for the Sharia.
As for the claim that the texts do not indicate their meanings with certainty, this claim relies on unrealistic perceptions or logical assumptions. The texts indicate meanings that may be definitive, or they may be overwhelmingly apparent in a certain meaning, or they may allow for multiple meanings equally. Even if they are not definitively indicative in themselves, certainty may be derived from contextual clues or statements. Certainty is not conditioned in anything other than beliefs or the principles attached to them, which are sources of legislation.


[Page 648]

The ten possibilities that have been mentioned are not present in every example, and the absence of those that do exist is not impossible. For instance, His Exalted saying: { Establish the prayer } (1) does not necessitate induction to ascertain the certainty of the obligation of prayer. Understanding the transition of the meaning of prayer from its linguistic reality to its legal reality, and other objections that may arise, is not impossible. Likewise, the definitive rulings such as the obligation of faith, fasting, almsgiving, pilgrimage, truthfulness, justice, benevolence, and fulfilling trusts, as well as the prohibition of theft, adultery, usury, the killing of the soul which Allah has forbidden, and the prohibition of carrion, blood, and pork, are definitive and were not established through induction. Rather, they were derived from the texts, supported by the clarification of the Sunnah, the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), consensus, and the transmission of the texts and actions in a mutawatir manner. A single text can be definitively indicative, such as His saying: { Prohibited to you is carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine } (2), and His saying: { And Allah has permitted trade and prohibited usury } (3). If certainty necessitates certainty in the meanings of words or the benefit from certain indications, then this is possible and actual, and not impossible.
It is not correct that texts cannot indicate meanings with certainty, nor is it correct that certainty can only be achieved through induction.
As for the induction of the meanings of rulings, its discussion will come separately under the title: the meaningful transmission (al-tawatur al-ma'nawi).
The application of induction (istiqra) with the aim of reaching legal truths requires defining its meaning and how to apply it through agreed-upon examples or known rulings so that it can be utilized in the search for understanding what is unknown in terms of rulings. This is something that al-Shatibi did not do; rather, he imposed the method of induction without proving its validity and without providing a definition of it.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 11, 43, 83, and others from the surahs.
(2) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 3.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 275.


[Page 649]

And when the meaning of induction (istiqra) is understood, it becomes clear that it has no place where al-Shatibi placed it. The imams relied on deduction (istinbat) as a rational method for understanding and arriving at rulings, not induction. So, what is induction?
Al-Asnawi said: "Induction is the inference of a ruling in particulars based on its establishment for the general rule" (1). He said: "It is divided into complete and incomplete; the complete is the establishment of a general ruling in a category for its establishment in all its particulars" (2). As for the incomplete: "It is the establishment of a general ruling in a category for its establishment in some of its individuals, and this does not provide certainty, as it is possible that the ruling of what has not been induced from the particulars is contrary to what has been induced from them" (3).
An example of this is to say: in this box, there is a collection of pieces; if one examines them one by one and finds that they are all iron pieces, one can say: all the pieces in the box are iron. This is complete induction, and this ruling is general. If one takes a piece from the box randomly, it is certainly iron based on the general ruling. However, if one examines most of the pieces or all but one and finds iron, this is incomplete induction, and if one takes a piece randomly, one cannot rule that it belongs to the same category as the induced ones, and it is not correct to issue the general ruling at all.
Thus, induction is the establishment of a ruling for the whole or the totality through its establishment for the parts one by one. If the subject to be induced is known and limited, complete induction can be achieved by examining all one by one. If it is not limited, then complete induction is not possible. Induction is different from deduction; induction leads to the general ruling based on the ruling on the particulars, while deduction leads to the ruling on the part based on the general or overall ruling. The general ruling resulting from complete induction is also considered deduction, because the general ruling is derived from the ruling on the whole.
__________
(1) Al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul, 1/361.
(2) The same source, 4/377.
(3) Al-Asnawi, Nihayat al-Sul, 4/377.


[Page 650]

Both induction and deduction are rational methodologies of knowledge, meaning they are ways of thinking aimed at reaching conclusions. Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr said: "The reasoning that human thought typically engages in is divided into two main categories: one is deduction, and the other is induction. Each of the deductive and inductive proofs has its own methodology and distinctive path. By deduction, we mean any reasoning whose conclusion is not greater than the premises from which that reasoning is derived" (1). He also said: "By induction, we mean any reasoning in which the conclusion is greater than the premises that contributed to that reasoning. For example, it is said: this piece of iron expands with heat, and that one expands with heat, and this third piece also expands with heat; therefore, all iron expands with heat" (2). He stated: "In cases of induction, the inductive proof jumps from the specific to the general" (3).
What all Muslims unanimously agree upon is that Islam has come with legal texts from which legal meanings are derived through deduction, including rulings. The rulings are general concerning the obligated individuals and actions, and they are universal through the causes that transfer them from one type of action to another. These causes are deduced from the legal proofs. When a text is presented, the meaning is taken from it, and the text or its indication is not considered a part of the meaning, nor is it a phenomenon that must be repeated in many texts and indications to establish the general meaning. This repetition is the consistency that benefits from induction, as al-Shatibi mentioned, and rulings are not derived in this manner; rather, they are derived from the indications of the texts, that is, from the detailed proofs. Therefore, jurisprudence (fiqh) is defined as the knowledge of practical legal rulings derived from their detailed proofs.
__________
(1) Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, The Logical Foundations of Induction, p. 5, Dar al-Taaruf for Publications, Beirut, 5th ed., 1406 AH - 1986 CE.
(2) The same source, p. 6.
(3) Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, The Logical Foundations of Induction, p. 7.


[Page 651]

There is no process of induction that follows in order to arrive at universals from which the rulings of particulars can be derived, because the texts are present and ready to derive rulings from them, and the rules themselves are derived from the texts and may be speculative or definitive, and the rulings branch out based on them because they are originally legal rules derived from the legal texts.
This induction, although it is a correct rational method, has no place in the indications of the texts. Al-Shatibi, by relying on induction, treated the legal texts as one would treat natural and material phenomena, as if the texts are phenomena that have attributes and characteristics that are their meanings, and these characteristics have causes or results that are the rulings and interests. Just as a researcher looks for the characteristics of things to discover them and for the causes and effects of phenomena to understand them and benefit from that and build upon it, through observation, testing, following, and induction, al-Shatibi did the same to understand the meanings of the texts and the causes of the Sharia and its principles. Al-Shatibi himself affirms this matter; therefore, after explaining the characteristics of the universals in his methodology, he said: "These are the characteristics of the rational universals, and also the rational universals are derived from existence, which is a conventional matter, not a rational one, thus they are equivalent to the legal universals in this regard, and the difference between them is lifted" (1). Likewise, when he spoke about causes and effects in the Sharia, he supported his view with the causes and effects in rational matters or in material occurrences, saying: "The establishment of the cause is like the establishment of the effect, whether that effect is intended or not. Because when it is made a cause in the course of customs, it is considered as if it directly causes it, and this is supported by the principle of customary practices, as the relationship of effects to their causes is like the relationship of satiety to food, and quenching to water, and burning to fire, and diarrhea to senna, and all other effects to their causes. Similarly, the actions that result from our earning are attributed to us even if they are not from our earning. And if this is customary and known, the custom of the Sharia follows the same measure in legal causes with their effects" (2).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/44.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/148.


[Page 652]

Based on this, the method of induction (istiqra) is not appropriate here, in addition to the fact that the legal texts are not material phenomena that can be induced; the legal texts have implications that must be acted upon, whether they are speculative or definitive. This method contradicts what the recognized imams have established, thus it is erroneous and cannot be acted upon.
Moreover, this induction is incomplete and cannot be thorough; it does not allow for certainty at all according to the reality of induction. It is not an induction of most particulars, but rather, as al-Shatibi says, it is an induction of many particulars, and this many is not the majority. Therefore, it is not correct according to the method of induction to establish the universal through this incomplete induction and to give a ruling based on what has been induced for what has not been induced. Yes, the many texts that converge on a single meaning may emphasize the importance of this meaning or increase the degree of conjecture about it, and certainty may be attained regarding it. This is not induction but rather deduction (istinbat); meanings are deduced from the texts and may imply others. If there is a shared meaning in many texts, the abundance of texts leads to a presumption that it is the intended meaning, thus the meaning is established, but this is not induction. If induction were required, the meaning would not be established. It is not necessarily the case that this meaning is universal; this depends on the meaning itself. If there are many texts indicating the prohibition of adultery or the obligation of prayer, these rulings do not become universal because they are particular in their subject, even if they are definitive. If a single text indicates a general or universal principle, it should not be dismissed on the grounds that the indicator is a single or speculative text, such as his saying - peace and blessings be upon him -: "There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm" (1). It is a report of singular transmission (khabar ahad) and it is also a universal principle; it does not need to be definitive to be so, nor does it require what al-Shatibi has gathered of evidence on the meaning, even though the abundance of evidence may affirm the meaning and potentially make it definitive.
__________
(1) Its transmission has been previously mentioned.


[Page 653]

And indeed, there is a speaker who says that incomplete induction (istiqra' naqis) leads to certainty in the universal ruling and results in its application to what has not been induced, and in a decisive manner. For we find that iron expands with heat, and the observation is repeated without exception, thus the same ruling is applied to all iron. Wood floats on water, and this is ruled for all wood, and people die, leading to a ruling on the living and those who will be born. The sun rises every day and sets, leading to the conclusion that this will happen tomorrow and the day after, and that it was happening before our existence. We have a strong feeling that these rulings are definitive, even though what has been induced is much less than what has not been induced. Therefore, it is not correct to object to the validity of incomplete induction and its ability to yield certainty.
The response is that induction in such cases can only be incomplete, and even if it may be extensive, it will not be majority-based. Nevertheless, it does provide a ruling on what has not been induced. Yes, but this is not due to the induction itself, rather it is due to something else in addition to this induction, and this thing is akin to the cause that leads to the extension of the ruling from what has been induced to what has not been induced, and to everything that contains this rational or logical cause (and not a legal one). This cause, along with induction, leads to the generalization of the ruling, and a ruling is made on what has not been induced by analogy. In the example of iron that expands with heat, the cause is the similarity or the absence of difference between what has been induced and what has not been induced. This leads to the establishment of the universal and its application, even if those who apply this cause here do not realize it. People carry the concept that what is established for one thing is established for its like, and this operates within them even without their intention, just as blood circulation occurs in the body; it exists within a person as their mind forms and grows. The failure to recognize the effect of this similarity or other potential hidden causes for the ruling is what leads to error, causing one to mistakenly believe that incomplete induction is beneficial, and the same can be said for all the other mentioned examples.


[Page 654]

The rising and setting of the sun and the moon, and their repeated occurrence in a regular manner, leads to the feeling that there is a system governing this movement, which is what causes it to recur regularly and without fail. This system serves as the cause for the occurrence of this regular movement. This cause or system is what prompts the ruling tomorrow or the day after, based on the perceived system. Since the cause present today will also be present tomorrow, the matter will repeat. If it were known that the one who established this system would change it tomorrow, and that the sun would not rise or would rise from the west, the ruling would change, which confirms that the generalization and its application to what has not been examined is not due to induction but rather to the cause. Two points affirm this interpretation:
First: The examined particulars are very few and hardly worth mentioning compared to what has not been examined; it suffices for the examined to be a single individual or one particular so that the desired description or ruling can be understood from it, and then the cause (the logical analogy) thereafter becomes the reason for the general ruling to be applied to the rest. Therefore, the cause is the reason for the generality, not induction.


[Page 655]

The second: The general ruling that extends from what has been inferred to what has not been inferred does not extend to that which does not contain the cause. Thus, the ruling on iron does not extend to anything that is not like it. Likewise with wood, and with humans, as well as with the sun and the moon and the celestial bodies; one cannot rule on the moon tomorrow in the same way as one rules on the sun tomorrow, nor vice versa, because the cause in both cases, although it is the system, is different: the system of the sun is not the same as the system of the moon. The reason for the generality is the cause, not the inference. This is the incomplete inference in material phenomena, which is only beneficial if one knows that a cause exists. So how can it be applied to the texts of the legislator, which have multiple meanings? If inference requires a cause to be beneficial, and al-Shatibi uses inference to understand the causes, then each of the two requires the other and does not exist without it. Therefore, the method of incomplete inference is invalid and rejected, and it has no existence at all in the legal texts. These causes will not be found through this method, and if they are found, they will be found through deduction as legal causes, not as material or logical causes.
The opposition of the particular (al-juz'i) to the universal (al-kulli):
Al-Shatibi argued that the universal (kulli) is not contradicted by the opposition of the particulars (juz'i) to it, based on the fact that the universal has been established universally through induction, thus it is definitive, while the particular is speculative. Therefore, either the particular should be interpreted to agree with the universal, or it should be rejected.
He also went on to state that it is necessary to apply both the general principles (kulliyat) and the specific cases (juz'iyat) together; one cannot do without the general principles in place of the specific cases, nor without the specific cases in place of the general principles.
These two matters are correct in terms of their outcomes, but they do not hold up based on their methodology, meaning they do not hold up based on the fact that the universals are inductive universals derived from particulars. There is a contradiction in the matter that al-Shatibi tried to resolve.


[Page 656]

He said regarding the application of universals and particulars together: "It is impossible for particulars to be independent of their universals. Thus, whoever takes a text, for example, in a particular while disregarding its universal is mistaken; likewise, whoever takes the universal while disregarding its particulars. The explanation of this is that acquiring knowledge of the universal is only through the examination and observation of particulars. The universal, in its essence, is not known to us before knowledge of the particulars, and it does not exist in the external world; rather, it is contained within the particulars, as established in the intelligibles. Therefore, to focus on the universal while disregarding the particular is to stand with something that has not been established in knowledge without knowledge of the particular, and the particular is the manifestation of knowledge of it. Moreover, the particular is only designated as such because the universal is fully present within it and is what sustains it. Thus, disregarding the particular as such is, in reality, a disregard for the universal itself, and that is a contradiction. Furthermore, disregarding the particular altogether leads to doubt regarding the universal, since such disregard occurs only when there is a contradiction with the universal or a presumed contradiction with it. If the universal contradicts the particular, while we only derive it from the particular, this indicates that knowledge of that universal has not been established, as it is possible that the particular contains a part of the universal that the considered part does not include. If this is possible, there is no alternative but to return to the particular in understanding the universal, and this indicates that the universal cannot be considered in isolation without considering the particular" (1). He then said: "If a universal principle is established through induction, and then a text comes regarding a particular that contradicts the principle in one of the ways of contradiction, it is necessary to reconcile the two in consideration" (2). He then said: "In this case, it is not possible for the principles to be violated, and if this is established, the universal cannot be considered while the particular is disregarded" (3).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/3.
(2) The same source, 3/4.
(3) The same location.


[Page 657]

This text is important in the methodology of al-Shatibi. It contains several points, including that particulars (juz'iyyat) are the source of universals (kulliyyat), and without particulars, universals would not be known. There is no meaning in the universals that is not present in the particulars, and if a universal conflicts with a particular, this means that the universal has not yet been realized as a universal. Therefore, it is necessary to return to the particular to verify the true meaning of the universal and to regulate it in order to resolve the conflict. If the universal is firmly established as a universal and it contradicts the particular, then the contradiction must be resolved, and neither can be disregarded. The universal is firmly established and definitive, so its contradiction is not valid, and the particular cannot be disregarded for the sake of considering the universal. The universal, as he said, is sourced from the particulars, and doubt in the particular is doubt in the universal.
But this differs in another context. He said: "The established principles are generalities, and the particulars cannot invalidate the generalities; therefore, the rulings of the generalities remain applicable to the particulars even if the meaning of the generalities does not specifically manifest in them."(1)
And this is a contradiction with what has preceded, for how can the meaning of the universals (kulliyat) be applied to the particulars (juz'iyat) without that being evident, when the universals are known only through the particulars, and the particular is the manifestation of knowledge of the universal?! And he said: "If they oppose each other, then either both are to be applied together, or both are to be neglected, or one is to be applied without the other, meaning in the case of opposition. Applying both together is invalid, and likewise neglecting them both, because that is applying the opposition between the speculative (dhanni) and the definitive (qat'i), and applying the particular without the universal gives preference to the particular over the universal, which is contrary to the principle. Thus, the only remaining option is to apply the universal without the particular, which is what is required"(2). And this is a clearer contradiction with what has preceded, for here he says: "Applying both together is invalid," whereas there he said: "It is not possible to apply one and disregard the other." Here he says: "Applying the universal without the particular is what is required," while there he stated that doubt in the particular is doubt in the universal, and that one must consider how to reconcile between them. This contradiction is due to the methodology, which is induction (istiqra).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 3/149.
(2) The same source, 3/150.


[Page 658]

It may be said: However, what al-Shatibi has proposed is the relied-upon and established position among the imams, which is the application of the legal rules and principles when applying the detailed texts, as well as in cases of conflict between the definitive (qat'i) and the speculative (dhanni), where the speculative is rejected if reconciliation between them is not possible.
The response is that this is correct, but there is no contradiction in the methodology of derivation (istinbat) because the doubt regarding the speculative and its rejection does not imply skepticism about the definitive, as the definitive is not derived from the induction of the speculative or the particulars. Furthermore, if the universal (kulli) conflicts with the particular (juz'i) or the general (aam) with the specific (khass), one can specify one by the other, and this is not considered a contradiction or a negation of anything, because the universal is not derived from the induction of the particulars. Therefore, it was said at the beginning of the discussion of this issue that these two matters according to al-Shatibi are correct in terms of their outcomes, but they do not align based on his methodology. In addition to this contradiction in methodology, the negation also arises from two aspects:
First: The particular that he suggested neglecting, if it conflicts with the universal and reconciliation is not possible, may be a text of a sound hadith or the meaning of a Qur'anic text. The universal he speaks of is neither truly universal nor definitive, as has been clarified, since the induction he refers to is incomplete and not comprehensive. Therefore, interpreting the meaning of the text or rejecting the hadith due to its opposition to this universal is not valid in an absolute sense.
Second: This methodology necessitates reliance on the universals at the expense of the particulars, which is what al-Shatibi attempted to evade. This matter will be discussed, God willing, in the third section of this chapter.
The moral transmission (tawatur al-ma'nawi):
Al-Shatibi held that induction provides a transmission similar to moral transmission, and he likened the certainty derived from induction to the certainty of the bravery of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and the existence of Hatim, which is a certainty caused by transmission due to the abundance of reports that support it.


[Page 659]

The evidence provided by continuous transmission (tawatur) does not rely on induction but rather on abundance with conditions (1). Al-Zarkashi said: "Continuous transmission, linguistically: is the succession of things one after another with a pause, and terminologically: it is the report of a group whose collusion on a lie is impossible due to their number, about something perceived" (2). He also said: "Tawatur can be verbal or it can be conceptual, which means that those previously mentioned come together on reports that refer back to a single report, such as the bravery of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and the generosity of Hatim" (3). He then mentioned that some have disputed Ali's bravery because his bravery is continuously transmitted both verbally and conceptually (4).
Thus, abundance in tawatur refers to a multitude united on a report. If the report is a narration from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), it is a hadith of definitive authenticity, and it may be definitively indicative or it may not be so. If the multitude is united on several reports, some narrating one report and others narrating another, and so on, and each of these reports does not reach the level of tawatur, they all share a certain meaning. This meaning would then be considered continuous, and this is the conceptual tawatur, and the meaning is definitive.
The particulars inferred by al-Shatibi are of two types: legal texts and legal rulings. If the induction is for legal texts, there is no issue regarding the result, and it may be the conceptual tawatur itself and not similar to it, as if it were an induction of the implications of singular reports, except that this is not induction but rather deduction from the texts. The discussion about the induction of particulars when they are legal texts has previously been addressed under the title: "Induction" in this section. The current discussion is about the induction of legal rulings and their meanings.
__________
(1) See: Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 3/296 - 301.
(2) The same source, 3/296.
(3) The same source, 3/311.
(4) The same location.


[Page 660]

The legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyya) are among the meanings of the legal texts (nusus shar'iyya) and their implications, as well as the legal principles (qawa'id shar'iyya). The words and texts are those for which a meaning is sought; once the meaning is known, the intention of the Legislator (al-Shari') behind it is understood. The legal meanings are those intended by the Legislator, and the servant has no knowledge of them except through revelation from Him, Exalted is He. The sources of Allah's revelations - Glory be to Him - are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, consensus (ijma'), and analogy (qiyas), and considering the differences, they are the Qur'an and the Sunnah and what they guide towards. These are the sources of the legal texts, and there can be no legal meaning unless it originates from the legal texts.
