Accordingly, if the meanings of the rulings that al-Shatibi refers to are the implications of the legal texts, then they are legal; if they are not, then they are not legal. If they are among the implications of the texts, then they are meanings of the texts, and thus they are considered valid.
What al-Shatibi means by the meanings of the rulings are their purposes (hikm), or their causes (musaabibat), or their benefits (masalih), or their objectives (maqasid), or their reasons (illal), and he does not mean that they are meanings of the texts.


[Page 661]

The meanings of rulings do not exist; rather, there are meanings for the words and sentences that these words and sentences indicate in any type of indication(1). If the meanings are known, there is no point in searching for meanings for them, nor is it correct to say that these meanings are intended by the legislator, for if they were intended by him, he would have established a proof for them or set a sign for them. At that point, they would be among the indications of the texts, and there is no harm in allowing thought or imagination to roam regarding the reasons for the rulings, their causes, their objectives, and their wisdom, especially since there is something in the soul that drives one to this, leading to the assumption of meanings or rulings that one may find reassurance in or take delight in. However, it is not permissible in any case to attribute any legal value to these assumptions, nor to ascribe them to Allah - Exalted is He - by saying they are intended by Him, or that they are a cause for His ruling, for such assumptions are mere fantasies and are not based on any legal source, and since there is no evidence for them, they hold no significance.
Al-Shatibi does not disagree with this; rather, he affirms it. He does not accept legal conjecture (dhann shar'i) at all unless it is based on a definitive meaning (ma'na qat'i). Such justifications for rulings are mere conjectures that hold no weight. However, if the rulings converge on a meaning and there is a comprehensive examination (istiqra'), then the meaning becomes definitive, and it serves as a benefit (maslaha), a cause ('illa), a principle (asl), and an objective (maqsad), all in a definitive manner.
The objection is how this moral transmission, or the corroboration from individual rulings on this meaning, will occur, as there is no legal value for this meaning in any ruling, since rulings do not indicate meanings, and these meanings are not among the implications of the texts.
__________
(1) The linguistic indication is confined to three: correspondence, implication, and entailment. The first: the indication of the word on the entirety of what it was designated for. The second: its indication of a part of the named thing. The third: its indication of what is outside the named thing but necessary for it. See: al-Zarkashi, al-Bahr al-Muhit, 1/417 and 1/420.


[Page 662]

If there is no legal value to this meaning in each of the rulings that are being extrapolated, how will the meaning acquire legal value through their aggregation? If a person is tested, for example, with twenty questions and receives a zero on each question, how can their total be one hundred out of one hundred? How can one reach certainty about the meaning from the extrapolation of the particulars in which this meaning is imagined if it holds no legal significance in any of those particulars? This brings to mind the saying of the Hanafis mentioned earlier: "By the abundance of analogies, strength in description is not attained."
As for al-Shatibi's example of the bravery of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and the generosity of Hatim, it does not belong to the category of extrapolating the meanings of rulings. The bravery of Ali and the generosity of Hatim are indications from the texts reported about them, not indications of the meanings of the texts. They are truly from the mutawatir (consecutively reported) in meaning if the texts are authentic; however, some have contested that the bravery of Ali is from the mutawatir in wording.
Al-Shatibi's error here arises from two aspects:
First: An error in methodology, which is the claim of specific objectives of the Lawgiver without any evidence. Moreover, he asserted certainty about them, not to mention the incomplete extrapolation and what it entails.


[Page 663]

Secondly: Al-Shatibi himself has established that these meanings do not have any legal indication; rather, they serve the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), which are derived from the texts (1). If they had a legal indication from the texts, they would be among its original objectives. Nevertheless, he has categorized them, based on his observations, as definitive general objectives, which is not sound. Consider his statement, for example: "What assures us from Allah's questioning us on the Day of Resurrection about how you understood from me that I intended such and such classification based on my statement: { And they think that they are doing well } (2), or my statement: { He said, 'Indeed, I am of those who are the warners' } (3), for to claim such a thing about the Qur'an and that it is intended by the speaker is dangerous; rather, it refers back to His statement: { When you receive it with your tongues and say with your mouths that of which you have no knowledge, and you think it is insignificant, while it is, in the sight of Allah, great } (4), and to the fact that it is an opinion in the Book of Allah" (5).

Perhaps someone might say: The assertion of these objectives or causes—according to his view—is based on the premise that the original principle is the justification of rulings; therefore, he traces the rulings to verify their legal causes.

The response is: This principle, even if accepted, permits justification, but the causes are numerous and the imaginations are more so. Identifying this cause or that without any guidance, indication, or sign from the Sharia that points to the type or nature of the cause is a claim without evidence. Therefore, alongside this principle, there must be a method for the cause or evidence for it. Thus, you find that the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) who affirm the principle of justification also establish methods for the cause, such as analogy (qiyas), suitability (munasaba), similarity (shabah), examination and division (sabr wa taqsim), and extension and reversal (tard wa 'aks), among others.

Section Three
Discussion of Al-Shatibi's Idea
Objectives and Causes
__________
(1) See: al-Muwafaqat, 2/63 - 68, the fifth issue, and see: Section Three of Chapter Four of this book.
(2) Surah Al-Kahf, 104.
(3) Surah Ash-Shu'ara, 168.
(4) Surah An-Nur, 15.
(5) al-Muwafaqat, 3/248.


[Page 664]

The topic of this discussion:
Here, we continue what we began in the previous section, which is the discussion of the concept of objectives (maqasid) according to al-Shatibi. What we will discuss in this section is the foundation of the idea, which is that His actions - Exalted is He - are purposeful, and that they are purposeful for their ends or objectives. This section will also address one of the important outcomes of this methodology, which is the independence of the jurist (mujtahid) from the particulars in jurisprudence (ijtihad) if they have comprehended the objectives in general and in detail.
Al-Shatibi - may Allah have mercy on him - was not the only one who spoke about the principle of purposefulness or the objective behind actions, so we will briefly discuss those statements. It is worth mentioning here that this topic was presented in some detail in the first chapter.
The principle of purposefulness:
There are two directions in this research that may be confused by some, so it is necessary to distinguish between them. The first is that the actions of Allah - Exalted is He - are purposeful, for He does not act except for a purpose, and this is what wisdom necessitates. The opposite of this is frivolity, and Allah is far above that. If it is established that He does not act except for a wisdom or purpose, this applies to His rulings, so there must be an intention behind every ruling, which is the reason for the ruling, thus necessitating the purposefulness of rulings.
The second is that the legal rulings (ahkam) are purposeful, based on the evidence indicating that the Sharia is a mercy for people and a healing. Also, based on observation, one finds that the rulings of the Sharia are aligned with interests or reasons for them, and one also finds rulings that are justified by reasons that indicate consideration of interests, which shows that the principle is the purposefulness of rulings based on interests.
As for the first direction, it is a theological discussion that has no relation to the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), even if it is included in its studies, nor is it related to analogy (qiyas), although some have linked it to that. It has been clarified previously that al-Razi rejected the purposefulness of Allah's actions and the term "purpose" in relation to Allah's actions categorically, even though he supports analogy and the principle of purposefulness for rulings.


[Page 665]

The second direction is a methodological inquiry, provided that it is separated from the reasoning behind God's actions, regardless of the outcome, meaning whether the principle is reasoning or non-reasoning.
Al-Zarkashi said: "Ibn al-Hajib transmitted in his discussion on classification and division the consensus of the jurists that a ruling must have a cause, and this was questioned based on the well-known principle that the actions of Allah are not attributed to a purpose"(1). He also said: "Know that the position of the Ahl al-Sunnah (People of the Sunnah) is that His rulings are not attributed to a cause in the sense that He does not do anything for a purpose, nor is He compelled by anything to do something; rather, He is Allah, Exalted is He, capable of bringing about benefits without their causes and eliminating harms without any motivators. The jurists said: The rulings are attributed to a cause, and they did not oppose the Ahl al-Sunnah, but what they meant by causation was wisdom. The Mu'tazila and those who agreed with them among the jurists restricted His actions with wisdom and narrowed them to the aspect of benefit"(2). Thus, it is common among Muslims to distinguish between the two matters, and that Allah, Exalted is He, does not act for a purpose. In the discussions of the theologians among the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence), there are arguments that support the position of those who oppose attributing causes to the actions of Allah, and indeed their evidence is conclusive, as al-Razi said.
The response to the reasoning behind the actions of Allah, Exalted is He:
The proponents of this idea differ regarding the methods of proof. The foundation of the concept for some of them is that Allah - Exalted is He - is wise in His creation. The consideration of purpose in His creation must either be obligatory or not obligatory. If it is obligatory, then it does not lack the intended purpose; and if it is not obligatory, then acting with a purpose is closer to being in accordance with reason than acting without a purpose(3).
__________
(1) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/111.
(2) The same source, 4/112.
(3) See: al-Amidi, al-Ihkam, 3/250, and see: the third section of the second chapter of this book.


[Page 666]

One of the responses to this reasoning is that Allah is Wise in His actions and in His refraining from actions; He is Wise absolutely. However, what necessitates that Allah's actions be closer to what is rational must be based on knowledge and reason that only He possesses, which elevates His wisdom to that of Allah's, to the limitless. As for one whose wisdom is nothing compared to Allah's wisdom, what rationality is he speaking of?! Such statements reflect a negligence in comparing Allah to humans, which can be said about the actions of rational beings and wise individuals. Allah - Exalted is He - is Wise, and humans do not comprehend His wisdom because they only grasp some of the wisdom and rationalities that pertain to their tangible experiences, while the unseen world is concealed from people. What necessitates that the effects or manifestations of Allah's wisdom be related to human perceptions and tangible experiences, when Allah - Exalted is He - says: { And Allah knows, while you do not know } (1).
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 216.


[Page 667]

The limitations and shortcomings of human intellect, along with its inability to comprehend the essence of Allah and to investigate the unseen, prevent it from grasping Allah's wisdom in His creation and rulings without revelation from Him, Exalted is He. A person may perceive what is beneficial as harmful and what is harmful as beneficial, and may see what contradicts wisdom. If one were to compare the unseen to the tangible, they might arrive at conclusions that contradict established truths. This is similar to those who claim that Allah only acts for a purpose; they have likened Allah to a human being, arriving at a conclusion that implies Allah, Exalted is He, is in need of a purpose. Such statements apply to humans, not to Allah. If the logic of these individuals were applied to itself, it could lead to conclusions that contradict their own results and are flawed. For example, one of Allah's actions is creation, and it could be said: Allah existed alone before creating anything. He either created for a purpose or without a purpose. If He created for a purpose, that purpose must have existed eternally, yet He did not create them from eternity, leaving only the possibility that He created without a purpose, which is flawed. The source of this flaw lies in the application of reason to matters beyond its knowledge, similar to those who assert a purpose. Furthermore, the error itself permeates the conclusions they have built upon. They have stated: Allah does not act except for a benefit, and the benefit must either pertain to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servant. Allah is free from harm and benefit, so it must pertain to the servant. This also delves into the unknown. By employing their own logic, one could argue: Allah does not act except for a benefit, and the benefit must either pertain to Allah or to the servant. Since His action, Exalted is He, is the creation of the servant, the benefit of this creation must either pertain to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servant. It cannot pertain to the servant because prior to creation, he is nonexistent, and no benefit can be conceived for the nonexistent.


[Page 668]

It remains only that the public interest (maslaha) should return to Allah, Exalted is He, and this is invalid, as it involves employing reason in matters where it should not be applied, and taking ignorance as evidence for knowledge. If there must be a statement regarding the public interest and its return to some source, the most correct assertion is that the public interest either returns to Allah, Exalted is He, or to the servant, or to what we do not know, and thus this argument is invalidated.
Some have argued that His actions - Exalted is He - are not subject to reasoning, yet the principle regarding actions is that they are justified by public interest (1), based on the observation of the correlation between rulings and interests. This reasoning is based on incomplete induction, and therefore it is not valid, as it has been established previously that incomplete induction cannot serve as evidence; rather, the evidence is the accompanying cause.
Among the proofs that His actions - Exalted is He - are justified, and that He does not act except for a purpose or intention, is what al-Shatibi has posited, which is based on induction, but it differs from the induction mentioned above - that of al-Razi. Al-Razi conducted an induction of rulings to establish the principle of justification by interests, while denying the justification of actions. As for al-Shatibi, he conducted an induction of texts, by extensively citing the texts that mention intention, as in His saying: { so that He may test you }, { and that He may complete His favour }, { to worship Me }, { so that you may attain piety }, { so that there will be no argument for the people against Allah after the messengers }. And so on (2).
__________
(1) See al-Razi's statements in the third section of the second chapter.
(2) See al-Muwafaqat, 3/2, and see the details of this proof in the third section of the third chapter.


[Page 669]

This argument is invalid even if there are many such texts, because it is an incomplete induction that does not encompass every action or ruling. Just as there are many texts that indicate intention, there are also many texts in which intention is not apparent. Furthermore, the texts that al-Shatibi presented do not indicate causes, and it is not rational to link them to the reasoning of rulings based on their objectives. Additionally, much of what al-Shatibi used as evidence can be argued in the opposite direction of what he intended.
Thus, al-Shatibi's proof regarding the principle of reasoning is refuted from several angles:
First: This induction is incomplete, so it does not provide any benefit, nor does it achieve the desired outcome unless supported by a textual evidence. If such evidence exists, there is no need for the incomplete induction.
Second: The existence of many texts in which the legislator did not mention an intention contradicts the claim of induction, such as His saying, Exalted is He: { And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam" } (1), and His saying, Exalted is He: { And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow" } (2). And His saying, Exalted is He: { For those who swear to abstain from their wives, there is a waiting period of four months } (3), and His saying, Exalted is He: { And the divorced women wait for three menstrual periods } (4), and His saying, Exalted is He: { And Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden interest } (5). It is no more valid to interpret these texts as supporting an objective than it is to interpret those as negating it.
Third: Many of al-Shatibi's arguments regarding intention and purpose are based on conjecture and are not suitable for establishing reasoning for actions and rulings. These arguments fall into two categories:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 34.
(2) Surah Al-Baqarah, 67.
(3) Surah Al-Baqarah, 226.
(4) Surah Al-Baqarah, 228.
(5) Surah Al-Baqarah, 275.


[Page 670]

One of them is like His saying, Exalted is He: {Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may attain piety} (1). This text indicates the intention of achieving piety, and piety itself is the fear of Allah, obedience to Him, and not opposing His command while seeking His pleasure. This intention does not return except to control, and there is nothing in it that indicates that the rulings are justified; it is not something upon which that can be built. Among this is also His saying, Exalted is He: {And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me} (2). Such a statement also does not return to establishing an intention or purpose upon which the justification of rulings can be built, neither in a way that, if presented to minds, would be accepted, nor through causes or outcomes.
The second is like His saying, Exalted is He: {To test you}, {So that there will not be}, {So that it will not be for the people}. These indications do not contain anything suitable to be built upon as a fundamental justification for rulings. They are news from the Legislator that conveys the obligation of worship and piety and that they should strive in that, warning them that they will have no excuse on the Day of Judgment regarding what has reached them from the message. So how can one connect and derive the justification of rulings from such texts?!
Sheikh Muhammad al-Tahir ibn Ashour has deemed all of al-Shatibi's arguments on this matter as invalid except for two. So what kind of induction remains after that?
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 183.
(2) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.


[Page 671]

The fourth: What al-Shatibi used as evidence for the objective can be turned around to argue against it. In His saying, { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me }. If someone asks: Why did Allah create people, and the answer is: So that they may worship Him. This does not satisfy what is in the heart if the goal is to know a reason or objective, and the question transforms into another question: Why does Allah want people to worship Him? What is the purpose of that? The text does not mention the purpose; rather, it commands worship without stating an intention or objective. Thus, in every proof presented by al-Shatibi, one could argue the opposite of what he intended, asking what the purpose is of testing people to see who is best in deeds, and likewise, what is the purpose of cutting off people's arguments on the Day of Judgment. Therefore, every text that al-Shatibi brought, which mentions intention or goal, also contains a lack of mention of that, indicating the invalidity of such reasoning.
In truth, there is no answer to such questions except to say: { He will not be asked about what He does, but they will be asked } (1), { He does what He wills } (2), { He is the doer of what He intends } (3), { Indeed, Allah judges what He wills } (4).
Therefore, those who argued about the prohibition of usury (riba), claiming it is like sales, were not given an answer that clarifies the differences between sales and usury, or explains the wisdom behind the prohibition of usury. Rather, the answer came as a decree, as He said: { Those who consume usury will not rise except as one rises whom Satan has struck with madness by his touch. That is because they say, "Trade is just like usury," but Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden usury } (5). Thus, what al-Shatibi used as evidence is not suitable for proving his claim.
Objectives and reasons:
__________
(1) Surah Al-Anbiya, 23.
(2) Surah Al-Imran, 40, and Al-Hajj, 18.
(3) Surah Al-Burooj, 16, and Hud, 107.
(4) Surah Al-Ma'idah, 1.
(5) Surah Al-Baqarah, 275.


[Page 672]

Al-Shatibi aimed to establish the principle of reasoning by affirming objectives (maqasid) for the legislator from the rulings, which are the causes and outcomes of adherence to the legal rulings. He considered these objectives as reasons without addressing or proving that the intended purpose of the ruling is its reason.
According to what Al-Shatibi presented, the objective is a reason, and the objective itself is a cause, result, and outcome. The ruling is the cause that leads to the objective, and based on this logic, the legal ruling is the cause of its reason. An example of this is the ruling of cutting off the hand for theft. The legislator's intent behind the ruling is deterrence, so deterrence is the reason for the ruling, and the ruling is the cutting off of the hand, making deterrence the reason for the cutting. Deterrence is a result of the cutting, which is the ruling, thus the ruling is a cause for it, and the ruling is the cause of its reason. Is this correct? And is the reason for the ruling a result of it? Therefore, does the reason for the ruling exist after it? In other words, is the objective a reason?
Another example from his evidence in proving the reasoning of the Sharia is His saying, Exalted is He: { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (1). Worship is an objective for the legislator, and it occurs after creation. Is it a reason for creation, making the reason exist after its effect? Is the depiction of the matter in this way in these two examples, the example of theft and the example of creation for worship, correct, or is there confusion and ambiguity in the matter?
No, the matter is not as such, even if it appears straightforward at first glance. The objective is not a reason, and the reason is not an objective, and the ruling is not a cause for its reason, and the reason for the ruling does not exist after it; how could it, when it only exists with it and through it and ceases to exist with its absence! It is the motivator for it or against it.
__________
(1) Surah Adh-Dhariyat, 56.


[Page 673]

Yes, indeed, there is a mixture and confusion in the matter, and the fact that the cause does not precede the ruling is an agreed-upon matter. It either precedes it or occurs simultaneously in time, without disagreement, neither in legal causes nor in rational causes. Al-Zarkashi said: "Know that there is no disagreement that the cause precedes the effect in rank, and they differed on whether it precedes it in time or occurs simultaneously, with the majority of the Mu'tazila and jurists holding that it occurs simultaneously, and they supported this with His saying, Exalted is He: { Allah takes the souls at the time of their death } (1)." Then he said: "The second view is that it is with it"(2). That is, it occurs simultaneously in time. He then said: "The rational causes occur simultaneously with their effects because they are inherently influential, while the situational causes precede the effect, and the legal causes are from the situational ones"(3).(4)
Based on the consensus reported by al-Zarkashi, the methodology that is fundamentally based on this confusion between the cause of the ruling and its objective is rejected from its origin. To eliminate this confusion and disorder, it is necessary to clarify the point of error and its cause.
As for the point of error, in the example of theft, the cause of the punishment is theft itself, not deterrence, as deterrence is a result or objective. Theft, which is the cause, occurs before the ruling or simultaneously with it, which is the obligation of cutting off the hand. The relationship between the cause and the effect does not fail; wherever theft is found, the ruling, that is, the obligation to cut off the hand, is found. As for deterrence, it is a result that may or may not exist, and this is the case with all punishments.
In the example of creation for the purpose of worship, worship is an objective or result that may or may not exist, as in the case of the disbeliever or the sinner. There is no cause here, because creation is one of the acts of Allah, Exalted is He. It is worth mentioning that the cause is the cause of the ruling, not the cause of the action. Theft is the cause of the obligation to cut off the hand, not the cause of the cutting itself, because the action itself may or may not occur, as it depends on the choice of the accountable person, who may obey or disobey, as is the case with any ruling.
__________
(1) Surah Al-Zumar, 42.
(2) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/110.
(3) The same source, 4/111.
(4) Al-Zarkashi, Al-Bahr Al-Muhit, 4/111.


[Page 674]

The reason for this error is that those who confuse the cause (illah) and the objective (maqasid) divert their minds from considering the ruling and its cause to examining the method of the Legislator in legislation. They imagine that the Legislator has laws or a method for legislation upon which the rulings are based, and they attempt to discover these laws. Whether this is correct or not, the diversion of the mind to this direction and the attempt to uncover the principles upon which the Legislator legislates is an overstepping of human boundaries that involves a hidden analogy of the Creator to the created. Such a matter may be valid for humans and in rational matters, but it is not valid concerning Allah, Exalted is He. As a practical example for further clarification and distinction:
If the person responsible for organizing traffic sees the need to place signs on the roads to organize the flow and eliminate its problems, and then does so and the flow becomes organized, he may ask: What is the reason for placing the signs? The answer is: organizing the flow. He may then ask: What is the reason for the organized flow? The answer is: the signs. Thus, these two answers present a confusion; one makes organizing the flow the reason for the signs, while the other makes the signs the reason for organizing the flow. The correct understanding is that if we are considering the ruling and its reason, this corresponds here to considering the organized flow and the signs. The signs are what led to the order, and if they are removed, problems arise. They precede the organization in existence; thus, they are the cause, and it cannot be that the order is the cause.


[Page 675]

As for the one who answers that the organization of movement is the cause of the signs, this is a mistake. The organization of movement is indeed the intended purpose of establishing the signs and a result of them. It is only thought to be a cause if one looks at what is in the mind or reasoning of the one who decided to establish them. This person observed the movement and found it needed organization, so he decided to set rules for that purpose and established signs that lead to the desired objective. Thus, if the purpose of organizing movement is considered a cause, it is not a cause for the signs or for establishing the signs; rather, it is a cause for the decision to establish them by the one responsible for that. The organization of movement, in reality, is a result and not a cause. If this result is considered a cause, it is a cause for what is in the mind of the decision-maker. When the answers differ, as mentioned above, the reason for that is that each answer pertains to something different from the others. If distinction is not made, confusion occurs.
Therefore, the objective is not a cause, and the cause is not an objective, and the objectives of the Legislator (Shari) are not causes for the rulings. If we move from this example, that is, from the motivations of people and their objectives in their rulings and actions to the causes of the legal rulings and their objectives, two matters should be considered:
First: The objective intended to be achieved by this decision may be attainable through means other than this decision, and this does not apply to legal rulings. If we know the intention of the Legislator behind the ruling, the ruling cannot be changed under the pretext of achieving the objective. For example, if we know that cutting off the hand for theft does not deter, this does not justify changing the ruling. This is not contradicted by al-Shatibi but rather affirmed by him(1).
__________
(1) See: The second section of the third chapter, the study of causes and effects.


[Page 676]

The second: The intention of the decision-maker can be understood by following his statements and actions and through understanding his mentality and analyzing his psychology, as this falls within the limits of human perception. This cannot be applied to the Creator, so it cannot be said that He has an intention or a cause without revelation from Him. Attempting to comprehend a method for Him in legislation or laws involves an error in comparing the Creator to the created. This is what al-Shatibi did through what he called the universal laws, the fundamental principles, and the true interests (masalih). He built all of this on the objectives of the Legislator (maqasid al-sharia), which he sought to understand through induction and established as definitive causes.
This methodology also responds from this perspective, which is considering the objective (maqasid) as a cause and what is built upon that from the analogy (qiyas) of the Creator to the created.
This methodology has led to a dangerous outcome, and indeed it is a sign of the error in the methodology that necessitates a reconsideration of it, which is the reliance on the general principles (kulliyat) over the specific details (juz'iyat), which is the next topic.
Reliance on the universals over the particulars:
It is evident from al-Shatibi's methodology that legislation has objectives (maqasid) which are its reasons or general principles upon which the particulars are derived or for which they exist, and these particulars are the texts and rulings. The rulings are among the objectives of the texts, and both of them share those general principles as their objectives.
The universals (kulliyat) can only be understood through the induction of particulars (juz'iyat), for they are their source and evidence. Were it not for the particulars, the universals would not be known. It is also clarified that it is necessary to apply both particulars and universals together, for applying the universal without the particular is an error, just as applying the particular without the universal is(1).
It may be objected against al-Shatibi that what is the need to apply the particular (juz'i) if the general (kulli) has been understood from it, for the meaning of the particular is present within it, and examining the particular thereafter is a burden. If a contradiction is assumed between the particular and the general, or if there is a specificity of the particular that is not considered in the general, this means that the general is not truly general after all, which contradicts the assumption; thus, there is no need to apply the particular(2).
__________
(1) See: the first section of this chapter.
(2) See: al-Muwafaqat, 3/2 - 7.


[Page 677]

However, al-Shatibi explicitly responds to this objection and asserts the necessity of considering both the particular and the general together, saying: "The result is that it is essential to take into account the particulars while considering their universals, and vice versa, and this is the ultimate perspective of the jurists in general, and to this their opinions in the aims of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) ultimately lead" (1).
Yet, the objection raised against al-Shatibi here is valid; the disregard for particulars is necessary for the methodology, even though al-Shatibi stated his rejection of it. In fact, some of what he said indicates this disregard, and it appears that al-Shatibi recognized this matter as a logical consequence of his methodology, leading him to become confused and to struggle with the issue, hesitating to dismiss opinions by neglecting particulars, which will become clear. Among the indications of this matter is his statement regarding the validity of ijtihad by someone who understands the objectives (maqasid) both generally and in detail, even if he does not have knowledge of Arabic. He said: "Thus, whoever understands the objectives of the Sharia from the establishment of rulings and reaches a level of knowledge of them, even if his understanding comes through translation in a non-Arabic tongue, there is no difference between him and one who understands them through the Arabic tongue" (2). He also said: "If ijtihad is related to deriving rulings from texts, then knowledge of Arabic is a necessary condition; however, if it pertains to the meanings of benefits and harms that are independent of the requirements of the texts or are accepted by the one exercising ijtihad in the texts, then knowledge of Arabic is not required in that case. Rather, knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail is what is necessary" (3). Thus, this jurist does not know Arabic, so he cannot consider the particulars; he does not examine the texts nor derive from them, but he only applies the general principles on the condition that he has knowledge of them in general and in detail. Knowledge of Arabic is a condition for the jurist who derives from the particulars in order to reach an understanding of the general principles, and unless he attains knowledge of the general principles in general and in detail, he cannot engage in ijtihad, whether he is knowledgeable in Arabic or not.
__________
(1) The same source, 3/6; see: the first section of this chapter.
(2) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/91.
(3) The same source, 4/90.


[Page 678]

Knowledge of Arabic is for the purpose of reaching the universals from the particulars; once this is achieved, there is no need for Arabic, and there is no difference thereafter between one who receives it through translation while not knowing Arabic and one who understands it in Arabic. This statement indicates the possibility of dispensing with examining the texts for the sake of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning).
What also points to this is his statement regarding the conditions of a valid mujtahid (one who exercises ijtihad): "The degree of ijtihad is attained only by one who possesses two qualities, the first being a complete understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia), and the second being the ability to derive rulings based on that understanding" (1). One might think that the second quality includes the condition of applying the particulars, but this is not the case, because the second—according to al-Shatibi—is a means to the first. It is the one that demonstrates the attainment of understanding the objectives, and it is what shows the possibility of deriving rulings based on this understanding. He said: "The fruit of understanding only appears in derivation; therefore, it was made a second condition. The first is the reason for reaching this rank because it is the objective, while the second is a means" (2).
These texts prompt a careful examination of the true intent of al-Shatibi regarding this matter, which leans towards the idea of dispensing with the particulars, especially since he emphasizes the complete understanding of the objectives: "Knowledge of the objectives of the Sharia in general and in detail," "Understanding the objectives of the Sharia in its completeness," as well as his statement: "When a person reaches a level where he understands the intent of the Legislator in every issue of the Sharia and in every chapter of its chapters, he has attained a quality that is the reason for his being placed in the position of the successor to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) in teaching, issuing fatwas, and judging by what Allah has shown him" (3).
__________
(1) The same source, 4/56.
(2) The same location.
(3) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/56.


[Page 679]

What also indicates this is what he said when discussing the ranks of scholars (1), where he categorized them into three ranks: the first is one whose understanding of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) has not yet been established, so his ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) is not valid, and he must refrain and follow (taqlid). The third is the rank of those firmly grounded in knowledge, and there is no disagreement regarding the validity of ijtihad from such a person. The second rank is the one in question here, and it indicates the sufficiency of ignoring the particulars.
He described the characteristics of the person in this second rank of knowledge, summarizing that he has a complete and thorough understanding of the general principles of the Sharia, but when he engages in ijtihad, he applies the general principles and does not engage with the particulars. Al-Shatibi then questioned whether a person in this rank is capable of valid ijtihad or not, stating that this is a matter of consideration and ambiguity, and it is a point of contention. He then mentioned the arguments of those who permit his ijtihad and the arguments of those who prohibit it, concluding that the issue remains problematic.
The evidence that this methodology necessitates the validity of neglecting the particulars consists of two points:
First: His statement that the issue remains problematic, and based on his assertions regarding the obligation to apply both particulars and general principles together, he should have sided with the prohibitors without hesitation. However, he did not do so, which suggests that the methodology aligns with neglecting the particulars for one who has completed the general principles. Likewise, he did not side with the permitters, as this would contradict his statements about the necessity of applying both particulars and general principles together, which led to claims of his inconsistency on this matter.
Second: All the arguments of the prohibitors are refuted according to his methodology and his texts, as he asserts that the general principles are definitive and inductive, thus they cannot be opposed, violated, or specified. Nevertheless, he did not refute the arguments of the prohibitors here; if he had, it would contradict what he previously established about the necessity of applying the particulars, as they all revert to the neglect of the particulars by the person in this rank. The following provides evidence for the aforementioned:
__________
(1) See: the same source, 4/127 - 132.


[Page 680]

As for the description of the one who possesses this rank, he said: "He should conclude by reflecting on the realization of the meaning of what he has attained according to what the legal proof has led him to, such that he achieves certainty and is not opposed by doubt; rather, doubts that arise for him become like the proofs indicating the correctness of what he holds" (1). Then he said: "However, his condition continued until his memorization slipped from his retention in a ruling, even if it was present with him, so he does not care about making definitive rulings on the issues whether he has stated them or opposed them" (2). Then he questioned: "If the student reaches this rank, is it permissible for him to exercise independent juristic reasoning (ijtihad) in legal rulings or not? This is a matter of consideration and ambiguity and one in which disagreement arises" (3). He then clarified what he sees as arguments for those who permit it, saying: "The one arguing for permissibility may say: If the legal objective has become clearer to this student than the sun, and the meanings of the legal texts have become evident to him until they cohere and some support others, and there remains no need for him in understanding their realities, then what he has attained is the entirety of the Sharia and the foundation of the doctrine and the source of obligation. Therefore, it does not matter whether he looks into its specific provisions or its particular issues or not. For his examination of that does not increase him in knowledge; if it were so, he would not have reached this rank, and we have assumed him to have reached it, which is contradictory.
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/127.
(2) The same source, 4/128.
(3) The same location.


[Page 681]

And a second point is that the examination of particulars and texts is intended to reach that general legal objective so that one can base their fatwas upon it and refer to it in their judgments of ijtihad. If this objective is already achieved, then descending to particulars is a pursuit of obtaining what is already obtained, which is impossible. And a third point is that the general legal objective is only realized through understanding the particulars and specifics, and by their meanings one ascends to what they aspire to. If the situation does not govern him due to the predominance of the general meaning, it is, in reality, governing because the general meaning is derived from it. For this reason, you will not find someone at this level issuing a ruling on a matter unless there are supporting and affirming evidences for him; otherwise, it would not support or affirm him. Thus, it is established that someone at this level is very capable of deriving rulings and exercising ijtihad, which is the objective(1).
All the arguments of those who permit this revolve around the lack of necessity to consider the particulars, because the benefit of examining them is achieved through the examination of the universals.
As for his clarification of what the opponents of the ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) of the one in this rank can use as evidence, he said: "The opponent can argue against the permissibility from several angles"(2). He mentioned three angles:
The first: This involves neglecting the particular, which is an error, and one who does not consider the particular cannot rise to the level of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning), "for it has been established in the Book of Evidence that considering the universal while disregarding the particular is an error, just as in the opposite case."(3)
__________
(1) The same place, and the reader can observe the strength and mastery of this mujtahid.
(2) al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/128.
(3) The same source, 4/129.


[Page 682]

The second: "That particularities have characteristics suitable for each of their respective contexts that are not suitable for other contexts, as in marriage, for example, it is not permissible for it to be treated like exchanges in every respect, just as it is not permissible for it to be treated like gifts and donations in every respect" (1). He said: "And for every particular there is a characteristic that is suitable for it and not suitable for others, as in the concessions in acts of worship, customs, and other rulings. If that is the case, and we know that all of them refer, for example, to the preservation of necessities, needs, and embellishments, then applying the preservation of these in every context in a uniform manner is not possible; rather, it is necessary to consider the particularities of circumstances, categories, and other specific particulars" (2).
The third: "That this rank necessitates that if particularities are not considered, then their contexts, which are the actions of the accountable individuals, should not be considered either. Just as universals apply to every particular absolutely, it would necessitate that they apply to every accountable individual absolutely without considering their particularities, and this is not correct" (3).
Then he said on behalf of the opponents: "The holder of this rank cannot descend to what is required by the rank of the mujtahid (scholar), so it is not consistent with this for him to be among the people of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning)" (4).
Upon examining the arguments of the opponents, it becomes clear that they all return to the failure to apply particulars, and that particulars have their own specific characteristics, whether in actions or in the accountable individuals.
__________
(1) The same place.
(2) The same place.
(3) The same place.
(4) The same place.


[Page 683]

After presenting the arguments of both sides, he said: "And if it is established that each possibility has its basis, then the issue, according to true consideration, remains problematic" (1). This position is strange and confused, for based on what has been established regarding the necessity of applying both universals and particulars together, he should have rejected the arguments of those who permit without hesitation, rather than finding the matter problematic. Furthermore, based on what has been established regarding the method of obtaining universals, he should have refuted the evidence of the forbidders that discusses the specificity of particulars and the specificity of the obligated individuals, for this evidence does not only prevent the ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) of one at this rank, but it also undermines the methodology itself as it prevents the acquisition of universals from particulars. He had previously rejected it when the matter pertained to the correctness or error of his methodology. He said: "If it is said: extracting the universal meanings from particular occurrences is not clear from several aspects: one of them is that this is only possible in rational matters, not in religious matters" (2). "And the second: that the specificities entail, in terms of specificity, a meaning additional to that general meaning or many meanings, and this is clear in rational matters because what is shared is not the same as what distinguishes" (3). "And the third: that the specifications in the Sharia are many, so a place is specified by one ruling and a similar one by another ruling, and likewise, different matters are combined under one ruling" (4).
The second and third aspects here are the second and third arguments in the evidence of the forbidders against the ijtihad of one who does not apply particulars. He responded to these three aspects by saying: "The response to the first is that it is possible in religious matters as it is in rational matters" (5). "And to the second, they did not organize the general meaning from the specific cases until they knew that the specificities and what distinguishes them are not considered" (6). "And to the third, it is the problem raised against the opinion of analogy, and what the usuliyyin (jurisprudential scholars) have said is the answer here" (7).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 4/129.
(2) The same source, 3/170.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 4/171.
(5) The same location.
(6) The same source, 4/172.
(7) The same source.


[Page 684]

So why did he not use these answers or refer to them to refute the arguments of the prohibitors? Especially since they undermine his methodology, not just the validity of the ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) of the one in this rank. And why did he not refute the arguments of the permissors, especially since they assert the validity, indeed the necessity, of relying on the general principles over the particulars? Instead, he became confused and perplexed by the matter and refrained from accepting or rejecting either of the two opinions, preferring to leave the issue ambiguous and under consideration. He stated that the matter, according to true consideration, remains problematic. The least that can be affirmed is that considering the matter as open to discussion and problematic is a doubt regarding what has been established for him, which is the necessity of applying both particulars and general principles together, indicating his acceptance of the validity of applying general principles while neglecting the particulars. This is a dreadful outcome for the methodology and leads to its invalidation.
Other observations:
There are other observations and objections to al-Shatibi's methodology, such as his rejection of the specification of general principles and their restriction, and his rejection of exceptions to them, as well as his statements regarding what is permissible (mubah) and the concession (rukhsah).
For instance, what is permissible is what the legislator has allowed between action and inaction, which contradicts the principle that the Sharia was established for the interests of the servants. This principle, according to his methodology, is a general and definitive one that does not change or falter; otherwise, it would not be general nor would it be a principle. Permissibility represents an equality between the desire for action and the desire for inaction, and according to the principle, the desire for action implies that there is an objective for the legislator in the action, while the desire for inaction implies that there is a harm resulting from the action, which the legislator intends to remove. Thus, the concept of permissibility contradicts this principle, which undermines the entire methodology. Therefore, al-Shatibi concluded that permissibility in this sense is permissibility in the particular. Permissibility in the particular must either be required in the whole or prohibited in the whole. Thus, he denies the existence of permissibility in the whole. This is merely an attempt to correct his idea or patch its shortcomings. In any case, this problem remains since permissibility in the particular is an existing legal ruling, which contradicts the idea of it being a general principle that does not change and is not subject to exceptions.


[Page 685]

The concession (rukhsah) also contradicts the foundational purpose of the Sharia in serving interests (masalih) if it does not pertain to a hardship that is truly significant, such as the travel of a wealthy king. This is because there is a conflict between it and the firm command (azimah); if the intent of the legislator is present in the firm command, then the concession undermines the original principle if it is permissible without necessity or need. Therefore, it has been argued that concessions should be classified under the category of what is permissible (mubah) as part of what is required to be abandoned entirely. However, the concession is a legal ruling that exists, and this does not align with the overarching principle according to his understanding of universality. Thus, al-Shatibi was compelled to oppose his own principles, stating: "What has been legislated from concessions is that the legality of concessions is partial, limited to the place of need; for when the traveler’s journey is interrupted, he must return to the original principle of completing the prayer and observing the fast" (1). He also said: "The conclusion is that the firm command returns to an initial universal principle, while the concession returns to a particular exception from that universal principle" (2). The evidence is that al-Shatibi was forced to accept exceptions from the universals, which contradicts the characteristics of universals in his view, and consequently, it contradicts the methodology.

Conclusion
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/211.
(2) The same source.


[Page 686]

The stance towards al-Shatibi's methodology is not the same as the stance towards al-Shatibi himself, nor should it be. Rather, the researcher feels, while presenting the concept of the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) as understood by him to researchers and those interested in it and in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) in general, that the most significant person who critiques it is al-Shatibi himself. This is due to the affection that has developed within the researcher towards a man who combined genius and faith, knowledge and morality, ambition and piety. His intellect elevated him, and his soul, filled with fear and hope, urged him to rise, aspiring like the devoted and active worshippers. His psyche was exalted, and his intellect, filled with thought and wisdom, urged him to ascend, leading him to the asceticism of the grateful worshippers. The elevated intellect was coupled with the noble psyche in a believing person, which gave rise to a love for Allah, and the sweetness of faith bore fruit, guiding the seeker on his path. When the researcher saw the seeker stumbling and the paths becoming difficult, compassion and empathy were added to love and affection, as he witnessed the esteemed and enlightened scholar being obstructed by the ultimate goal from the path and being blinded to the subtleties of the truths. He wished he could be a student of his, a companion who would guide him with two eyes, sparing him from distractions that would divert him from perception or hinder his understanding. For great and pious individuals are rare and pass by infrequently, and there is no infallibility after the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) for anyone. Therefore, to assist them in obeying Allah and to serve in the service of Allah's commands is indeed an act of righteousness and obedience. To strive to correct them with etiquette, to enlighten them with wisdom, and to obey them and draw near to them sincerely for Allah and out of piety is a great endeavor, as great as their deeds, and beneficial as the fruits of their production, and it is a rarer opportunity than they are. The mistakes and missteps from them are a loss for those with them and for those around them, even if they are rewarded.


[Page 687]

The affection, esteem, and respect that the researcher holds for al-Shatibi makes him the first to critique his ideas. It also makes those who carry the concerns of al-Shatibi the first to present this research along with what they have concluded from the critique.
What al-Shatibi undertook was an attempt to reform the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) to correct what he sees as widespread errors, to emphasize what he considers neglected principles, to discard what does not belong to it, and to alert to areas where there is presumed disagreement but no actual disagreement. This was aimed at correcting and regulating discussions in usul al-fiqh that have grown, developed, branched out, and become detached from their foundations and controls.
For example, his rejection of the prevailing concept of public interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada) is notable; although he spoke of reasoning based on bringing about benefits and averting harms, and it initially appeared, as many uncritical observers thought, that he made public interest the foundation of legislation, he actually dismantled this understanding and shifted this reasoning from one path to another and opposing one. This is something he is attested to. It is one of the most important objectives in his book. Therefore, he referred to it at the beginning of the preface of his book, saying: "Indeed, before the rise of this light, we were groping about like the blind, and our minds were running in pursuit of our interests in a disordered manner, due to their weakness in bearing these burdens and participating in the immediate whims, on the battlefield of the self, which is caught between the two extremes of the worst. We would place poisons in the places of remedies, seeking healing like one grasping at water, and we continued to swim between them in the sea of illusion, drifting, and wandering in our ignorance of the evidence in a dark night, and we would deduce the barren analogy, and seek the traces of health from the sick body, and we would walk face down, thinking we were walking on the straight path, until the pure compulsion appeared in the face of fate, and the reality of the hands of necessity was raised to the One, the All-Prevailing" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/2.


[Page 688]

He, by saying that the objectives of the Sharia (maqasid al-sharia) came to correct a misunderstanding, saw the objectives of the Sharia as if they were merely the objectives or interests of the people as perceived by them. He came to distinguish between the two types and to say that the objectives of the Sharia are objectives of the legislator, derived from the Sharia itself, and anything else is mere delusion and imagination. The first objective of the Sharia, when a command or prohibition is issued, is submission and adherence. Thus, the primary objective of His saying, "Do" is to perform the action, and the primary objective of His saying, "Do not" is to refrain from the action. In this way, the servant, who is a servant by necessity, becomes a servant by choice. This is something that is evidenced by him.
He, by saying that the Sharia was established for the interests of the servants in both abodes, and although this statement aligns with the views of many others, he, with his new understanding of interest (maslaha) and harm (mafsada), and with his methodology in how to determine what constitutes an interest and what constitutes a harm, has transformed the meaning of this statement to become consistent with the assertion that the servants were created for the sake of the Sharia. { And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me } (1), and thus he aimed to prevent the transgression of the limits of the Sharia under the pretext of interests and objectives, and this is something that is evidenced by him.
He, by saying that the legal rulings established by the legislator as a means to legal objectives should not be taken as a means to other objectives than those which the legislator has designated as their goals, and that the legal objective should not be approached by any means other than what the legislator has made a path to it, has attempted to prevent manipulation of the religion under the pretext of its objectives, and has safeguarded his idea from being used for purposes other than what he intended. This is something that is evidenced by him.
__________
(1) Adh-Dhariyat, 56.


[Page 689]

And despite the errors in his methodology, in its foundations and pillars, he did not build upon it any deviant branches. Whenever his principles led to results that were not acceptable, he would pause and not proceed, unconcerned, as his piety prevented him from continuing. Thus, when his methodology led him to rely on generalities over specifics, he halted and did not allow the fact that he had exerted his utmost effort in formulating his idea, which was the fruit of his lifetime, to push him toward a disgraceful statement; rather, he paused in contemplation, as if he anticipated that someone would follow his methodology and provide a solution to this dilemma.
Similarly, when he determined that a report from a single source (khabar ahad) should be paused upon if it did not refer to a definitive meaning, it seemed that deep down he could not accept pausing on the application of a hadith that had no legal opposition, merely because it did not refer to a definitive meaning. Therefore, he stated that in this case, there is no harm in applying such a hadith, arguing that the scholars have applied the unusual analogy and associated this with it. Thus, despite the apparent corruption of the methodology, no deviant branches emerged in al-Shatibi's work. It was as if, despite his belief in his methodology and principles, he felt that safety lay in conforming to the predecessors among the righteous predecessors and the good scholars regarding what they issued in jurisprudence; he strived to avoid contradicting them, despite the accusations of inconsistency that this might bring upon him.


[Page 690]

Despite the critique of al-Shatibi's idea and methodology, the book al-Muwafaqat is almost a comprehensive work in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh). Although it does not elaborate on the research and issues of consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas), what is presented therein serves as foundational principles for them, and a thorough examination of his book indicates his views on these matters. It is filled with foundational and jurisprudential benefits, well-structured in its expression, formulation, and arrangement. The author embarked on it earnestly and with determination, carrying a scientific and objective intent. His ideas are interconnected, with the latter built upon the former, and the depth of thought is profound to the utmost degree, featuring an exploration that only the diligent, patient, and broad-minded can achieve. This does not contradict the assertion of the methodological errors and contradictions. These errors and contradictions stem from incomplete induction and the illusion that it is complete, as well as from the piety that sometimes leads him to refrain from a ruling based on the methodology, either out of doubt or relying on the notion that the rare has no ruling. The errors of ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) and inference do not diminish his scholarly status and intellectual capacity. Few are those who do not err, but the danger of his error lies in the principles rather than in the branches.
Studying al-Muwafaqat is an analytical endeavor, following his ideas in various contexts while considering that his words, sentences, issues, and their arrangement are all intentionally chosen. This confirms that al-Shatibi carries a concern and aims for a significant matter—in his view—and that he spent many years contemplating ideas, during which he took the Qur'an as a companion, friend, and confidant, reflecting and pondering, yet he found no foundational principle upon which his ideas could stand nor any connection that could form them into a coherent entity or methodology, wandering in thought in search of evidence to support his ideas and breathe life into them. When he found none, he settled his thoughts on induction.


[Page 691]

It was indeed deserving of compassion, for the feeling of the greatness of invention, in isolation, due to the absence of supporters and followers, along with the lack of evidence and the passing of years, and the scarcity of those who discuss and advise, leads one to believe in fantasy and to free the mind from its constraints, like a thirsty person who sacrifices his life for a mirage. Perhaps al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him and reward him for his efforts) came upon induction (istiqra) or induction came upon him, thus he leaped over the reality that if this is valid in rational matters, it is not valid in religious matters, so he was like one who jumped into the sea fleeing from death by burning to death by drowning, then began to weave from his imagination ropes to cling to. Al-Shatibi's discovery of induction was like breathing life into the body of his ideas. Therefore, he referred to induction as a spirit in more than one place in his book, and what indicates this is his description of the hardships he faced in writing his book: "Indeed, I have traversed in pursuit of this objective paths that are both pleasant and unpleasant, and I have endured the trials of my journey, both good and bad, and I have encountered from its opposing faces both frowning and smiling, and I have suffered from its differing riders, both prohibitive and permissive. If you wish, you can find it to be a toil of travel, or a result of the hardships that have laid me low, or from battling the hindrances that have left me wounded; there is neither a pleasant life nor a comforting death. In summary, the most difficult thing that the traveler on the path encounters is the loss of guidance, with a mind that is dim due to the lack of the light of discernment, and a heart afflicted by the shocks of illusions, so he walks without a path and belongs to no tribe, until from the Generous Lord, the Kind Benefactor, the Guide of whom He wills to the Straight Path, the spirits of those bodies were revived for him, and the realities of those forms appeared, and the meanings of those labels became evident" (1).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/6.


[Page 692]

Al-Shatibi believed that there were others who were confused like him, and he expected them to embrace what he had brought forth and to follow him in it. He took great pride in this, which matched his struggles and efforts in that regard, so he refined his idea and called for its completion, not realizing that he was stifling it at its birth. He said: "As for what follows, O seeker of the truths of the highest sciences, aspiring for the most splendid results of dreams, thirsting for the sweetest sources of understanding, hovering around the sanctuary of the apparent decree, hoping to grasp its hidden meaning, meanings intertwined in the unraveling of those decrees, it is time for you to listen to one whose desires align with yours, and to engage with the sorrow of one who shares your grief, and to return, as you share with him the essence of his whispers, until he conveys to you his complaint, so that you may walk with him on this path as he has walked, and traverse in its murkiness, where its light mingles with darkness as it flows, and in the morning, if Allah wills, you will praise the outcome of the journey" (1). He also said, describing his book to those who would approach it: "Let this book be, O pure friend and loyal companion, a support for you in traversing the path, and an explanation of the meanings of harmony and success" (2). He said: "Indeed, it has brought you closer in your journey, and informed you how to ascend in the sciences of the Sharia (Islamic law) and where to proceed, and it has guided you from the paths of the travelers on the back, and has sought for you the brides of wisdom and then granted you the dowry, so take a step of determination, and by the grace of Allah, you will arrive" (3). Then he said: "At that point, it is the right of the contemplative observer, if he finds a deficiency in it, to complete it, and to have good thoughts about one who has endured the nights and days, exchanging toil for comfort and wakefulness for sleep, until he has gifted him the result of his life and bestowed upon him the orphan of his era" (4).
__________
(1) Al-Shatibi, al-Muwafaqat, 1/5.
(2) The same source, 1/8.
(3) The same location.
(4) The same source, 1/9.


[Page 693]

Regardless of al-Shatibi's methodology or his idea, what he intended is indeed worthy of pursuit, which is returning to the roots, refining them, and reconciling them by removing the disagreements based on differing terminologies and misunderstandings, and by eliminating foreign ideas that bear no fruit or that have no relevance to the foundations of jurisprudence but were inserted into its discussions due to speculative theology (kalam).
This reform can only be carried out by true scholars who return to the roots, to the Qur'an and the Sunnah and what they guide towards, learning from them and acting upon them, liberating themselves from the constraints of Western thought and its conformity, giving no weight or consideration to customs that are not endorsed by Islam, even if widespread, nor to thoughts or rulings that do not stem from its creed, even if dominant. They are neither ashamed nor disturbed by the contradiction of Islamic rulings that have become alien to the ideas and concepts of the backward and degraded Western civilization, whether they are prevalent or new; they strive for the supremacy of Islam as a creed and system, not to reconcile it with others under the pretexts of false flexibility and spurious development.
This reform is carried out by true scholars who liberate themselves from the alien understandings of terms such as moderation (wasatiyya), objectives (maqasid), renewal (tajdid), moderation (i'tidal), dialogue (hiwar), freedom (hurriyya), and similar concepts, which are taken and called for with truncated meanings that deviate from what Islam has brought and from the understanding of the noble companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and the righteous scholars.
This reform is carried out by true scholars who realize that they ought to be the heirs of the prophets, so they rise with zeal and determination, moving forward confidently and speaking truthfully, to bear witness to humanity, { And thus We have made you a just nation that you will be witnesses over the people and the Messenger will be a witness over you } (1).
Yes, the Sharia has objectives, but they are the objectives of the Sharia and the objectives of the Legislator, not the whims of souls. The meaning of the objectives of the Sharia is not the flexibility of Islam or its rulings that can be folded, twisted, expanded, or contracted to conform to any reality or to be shaped in a way that pleases this party or that, and then it is said: this cannot be denied, for Islam is evolving!
__________
(1) Surah Al-Baqarah, 143.


[Page 694]

The Sharia came with analogical reasoning (qiyas) and reasoning (ta'leel), and the basis in transactions or customs is reasoning, while in acts of worship it is devotion and lack of reasoning. However, the reason is what has been established in a legal context or indicated by legal evidence, and it must meet the conditions of reasoning; it is not the figments of the imagination or the proposals of minds, let alone the claims of the distorters.
In conclusion, I ask Allah, the Exalted, for mercy and abundant reward for al-Shatibi, and I ask Him to make this work of mine sincere for His noble face and to benefit others through it. I also ask Him for forgiveness and pardon for anything my pen may have strayed into, or my tongue may have slipped on, or my thoughts and imagination may have exceeded. Furthermore, I ask Him for abundant reward and recompense for everyone who taught me, advised me, and benefited me in this knowledge and in this book, and to forgive me, my parents, and the believers.
